āyapotthakaṃ.meaning_2: revenue register; treasury account book; book of income
āyapotthakaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text. An account ledger listing the family's income and holdings.
āyapotthakaṃ.example_1: Athassa rāsivaḍḍhako amacco āyapotthakaṃ āharitvā suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimuttādibharite gabbhe vivaritvā ‘‘ ettakaṃ te, kumāra, mātu santakaṃ, ettakaṃ pitu santakaṃ, ettakaṃ ayyakapayyakānan ’’ ti yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā dhanaṃ ācikkhitvā ‘‘ etaṃ paṭipajjāhī ’’ ti āha.
āyapotthakaṃ.translation_1: Then, his family steward brought the treasury book, opened the rooms filled with gold, silver, jewels, pearls, and so on, and said, “My young master, this much belongs to your mother, this much to your father, this much to your grandparents,” and after explaining the wealth down to the seventh generation, he said, “This all belongs to you; manage it.”

bherisaṅkharathāni.meaning_2: drums, conches and chariots; sound of drums, conches and chariots
bherisaṅkharathāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of bheri, saṅkha and rathāni (nominative plural of ratha). Probably construed with saddaṃ as an item in the list of sounds, though the verb is not in this verse line.
bherisaṅkharathāni.translation_1: “The sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of drums, the sound of conches, and the sound of chariots,

yaṃnūnimaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] yaṃ nūna imaṃ, an idiom expressing a suggestion; accusative singular of ayaṃ modifying pūtikāyaṃ.
yaṃnūnimaṃ.translation_1: “Why don’t I cast away this foul body, filled with various corpses, without attachment and without need,

pariruddho.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Past participle used as an adjective. Nominative singular masculine modifying a person or city; here in a simile of one surrounded by enemies.
pariruddho.translation_1: “Just as a sick person, when a doctor exists who can treat the disease, does not get that disease treated—that is not the doctor's fault,”

kilesapariruddho.meaning_2: obstructed by defilements; blocked by mental impurities
kilesapariruddho.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominal adjective in the nominative singular modifying the person in the simile. Past participle pariruddha is from pari + √rudh 1; kilesa is a noun in the compound.
kilesapariruddho.translation_1: He contemplated further: Just as a person fond of adornment might discard a corpse hung around their neck and go on happily, so too, I must discard this foul body, without attachment, and enter the city of Nibbāna. Just as men and women might defecate in a waste area and then go away without looking back, without any desire to take it with them, discarding it with disgust, so too, I must discard this foul body and enter the Deathless city of Nibbāna. Just as a ship's captain might discard a dilapidated, leaking boat without any desire and go, so too, I must discard this body, which leaks from nine wounds, and enter the Nibbāna city. Just as a person carrying valuables amidst thieves, seeing the danger of them being stolen, might discard the thieves and take the safe path, so too, this body is like a great thief; if I were to have attachment to it, my 'jewel' of noble path-wholesome qualities would be destroyed. Therefore, I must discard this thief-like body and enter the Nibbāna city.

uṭṭhāpaniyabhāvo.meaning_2: state of being woken up; the fact of having to be roused
uṭṭhāpaniyabhāvo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Third of the eight dangers (ādīnava) of using a leaf hut; nominative singular in the text, naming that danger. uṭṭhāpaniya is a gerundive from uṭṭhāpeti (caus of uṭṭhahati).
uṭṭhāpaniyabhāvo.example_1: Paṇṇasālāparibhogasmiñhi aṭṭha ādīnavā – mahāsamārambhena dabbasambhāre samodhānetvā karaṇapariyesanabhāvo eko ādīnavo, tiṇapaṇṇamattikāsu patitāsu tāsaṃ punappunaṃ ṭhapetabbatāya nibandhajagganabhāvo dutiyo, senāsanaṃ nāma mahallakassa pāpuṇāti, avelāya vuṭṭhāpiyamānassa cittekaggatā na hotīti uṭṭhāpaniyabhāvo tatiyo, sītuṇhapaṭighātena kāyassa sukhumālakaraṇabhāvo catuttho, gehaṃ paviṭṭhena yaṃkiñci pāpaṃ sakkā kātunti garahāpaṭicchādanabhāvo pañcamo,‘‘ mayhan ’’ ti pariggahakaraṇabhāvo chaṭṭho, gehassa atthibhāvo nāma sadutiyakavāsoti sattamo, ūkāmaṅgulagharagoḷikādīnaṃ sādhāraṇatāya bahusādhāraṇabhāvo aṭṭhamo.
uṭṭhāpaniyabhāvo.translation_1: For in the use of the hut, there are eight dangers: the necessity of gathering building materials with great effort is one danger; the constant need for maintenance because grass, leaves, and mud keep falling is the second; a lodging naturally goes to the senior monk, and if one is woken up at the wrong time, the mind does not become unified; thus, being woken up is the third; the body becomes delicate due to the avoidance of cold and heat is the fourth; it is possible for one who has entered a house to commit some evil; thus, concealing faults is the fifth; the act of grasping with the notion of “mine” is the sixth; the existence of a house implies living with a second person; thus, living with others is the seventh; being common to lice, bedbugs, house-geckos, etc., is the eighth.

pajati.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Not pajati; the text has a spelling with h dropped. Third person singular present of pajahati. The reading is uncertain; context requires 'abandoned'.
pajati.example_1: Iti ime aṭṭha ādīnave disvā mahāsatto paṇṇasālaṃ pajati.
pajati.translation_1: Having thus seen these eight dangers, the Great Being abandoned the hut.

lājāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The greeting in the text is neuter plural. PEU: lājīyante ye teti lājā; Thī lājā, pu lāja.
lājāni.example_1: Te punadivase mahādānaṃ sajjetvā nagaraṃ alaṅkaritvā dasabalassa āgamanamaggaṃ alaṅkarontā udakabhinnaṭṭhānesu paṃsuṃ pakkhipitvā samaṃ bhūmitalaṃ katvā rajatapaṭṭavaṇṇaṃ vālukaṃ ākiranti, lājāni ceva pupphāni ca vikiranti, nānāvirāgehi vatthehi dhajapaṭāke ussāpenti, kadaliyo ceva puṇṇaghaṭapantiyo ca patiṭṭhāpenti.
lājāni.translation_1: The next day, they prepared a great donation, decorated the city, and decorating the road for the arrival of the Ten-Powered One, they filled in water-damaged spots with soil, leveled the ground, scattered sand the color of silver strips, scattered parched rice and flowers, raised flags and banners of various colors, and placed rows of banana plants and full water-pots.

alaṅkarituṃ.meaning_2: to adorn; to decorate; to make ready; to clear (a path); to prepare
alaṅkarituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -tuṃ of alaṅkaroti (alaṃ + √kar). In both sentences used of preparing or clearing the Buddha's path; the commentary glosses it in the sense of making ready rather than merely decorating.
alaṅkarituṃ.example_1: ‘‘ buddhoti kho ghosamattakampi loke dullabhaṃ, pageva buddhuppādo, mayāpi imehi manussehi saddhiṃ dasabalassa maggaṃ alaṅkarituṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti.
alaṅkarituṃ.translation_1: “Even the mere sound of the word ‘Buddha’ is rare in the world, let alone the arising of a Buddha. It is fitting that I, too, should join these people in clearing the path for the Ten-Powered One.”
alaṅkarituṃ.example_2: Sumedho buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ gahetvā cintesi ‘‘ ahaṃ imaṃ okāsaṃ iddhiyā alaṅkarituṃ sakkomi, evaṃ alaṅkato pana mama manaṃ na paritosessati, ajja mayā kāyaveyyāvaccaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti paṃsuṃ āharitvā tasmiṃ padese pakkhipi.
alaṅkarituṃ.translation_2: Sumedha, filled with joy having the Buddha as his object, thought, “I could clear this section with my psychic power, but doing so would not bring satisfaction to my heart. Today, it is fitting for me to perform a physical service.” He carried soil and dumped it into that spot.

maṇiphalakasetu.meaning_2: bridge of jewelled planks; jewelled bridge
maṇiphalakasetu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Simile in the Jātaka prose for the ascetic's body lying across the mud. Nominative/accusative singular in the text; the compound is maṇi + phalaka + setu, where setu is a u-stem.
maṇiphalakasetu.example_1: Sumedhatāpaso akkhīni ummīletvā alaṅkatamaggena āgacchantassa dasabalassa dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ asītiyā anubyañjanehi anurañjitaṃ byāmappabhāya samparivāritaṃ maṇivaṇṇagaganatale nānappakārā vijjulatā viya āveḷāveḷabhūtā ceva yugalayugalabhūtā ca chabbaṇṇaghanabuddharasmiyo vissajjentaṃ rūpaggappattaṃ attabhāvaṃ oloketvā ‘‘ ajja mayā dasabalassa jīvitapariccāgaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, mā bhagavā kalalaṃ akkami, maṇiphalakasetuṃ pana akkamanto viya saddhiṃ catūhi khīṇāsavasatasahassehi mama piṭṭhiṃ maddamāno gacchatu, taṃ me bhavissati dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā ’’ ti kese mocetvā ajinacammajaṭāmaṇḍalavākacīrāni kāḷavaṇṇe kalale pattharitvā maṇiphalakasetu viya kalalapiṭṭhe nipajji.
maṇiphalakasetu.translation_1: Sumedha the ascetic opened his eyes and saw the Ten-Powered One approaching along the decorated path, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, embellished with the eighty subsidiary characteristics, surrounded by a fathom-wide aura, and releasing six-colored rays of Buddha-light—like lightning flashes across a jewel-colored sky, appearing in pairs, and swirling. Seeing that supreme form, he thought, “Today, it is fitting for me to sacrifice my life for the Ten-Powered One. May the Blessed One not step into the mud; rather, may he and his four hundred thousand Arahants tread upon my back as if walking on a bridge of jewels. That will be for my welfare and happiness for a long time.” He loosened his hair, spread his deerskin, matted-hair bundle, and bark-robe upon the black mud, and lay down on the mud like a bridge of jewels.

ugghāṭento.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle, masculine nominative singular, in a simile (ugghāṭento viya). Nasal assimilation ghaṭ + ṇa, hence ghāṭ; doubled initial g of the root after the prefix u.
ugghāṭento.example_1: Dīpaṅkaropi bhagavā āgantvā sumedhatāpasassa sīsabhāge ṭhatvā maṇisīhapañjaraṃ ugghāṭento viya pañcavaṇṇappasādasampannāni akkhīni ummīletvā kalalapiṭṭhe nipannaṃ sumedhatāpasaṃ disvā ‘‘ ayaṃ tāpaso buddhattāya abhinīhāraṃ katvā nipanno, ijjhissati nu kho imassa patthanā, udāhu no ’’ ti anāgataṃsañāṇaṃ pesetvā upadhārento ‘‘ ito kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni atikkamitvā gotamo nāma buddho bhavissatī ’’ ti ñatvā ṭhitakova parisamajjhe byākāsi –
ugghāṭento.translation_1: The Blessed One Dīpaṅkara also arrived and stood at the head of Sumedha the ascetic. Opening his eyes, which were perfect with the clarity of five colors, as if opening a jeweled lion-window, and seeing Sumedha the ascetic lying on the surface of the mud, he thought: “This ascetic has made his resolve for Buddhahood and has lain down; will his aspiration be accomplished or not?” Applying his reasoning with his knowledge of the future, and knowing that “After four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand aeons from now, he will become a Buddha called Gotama,” while still standing in the middle of the assembly, he answered:

virajjhiya.meaning_2: having missed; having failed to reach; having lost
virajjhiya.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -iya of virajjhati (vi + √rādh), here with paṭibhitthaṃ, 'having missed the opposite landing'. The PEU splits it as vi + radha + ya + tvā, indicating the same absolutive sense (virajjhitvā).
virajjhiya.example_1: ‘ Yathā manussā nadiṃ tarantā, paṭibhitthaṃ virajjhiya;
virajjhiya.translation_1: “‘Just as humans crossing a river, if they miss the opposite landing,’”

dakajā.meaning_2: born in water; living in water; water-born (of flowers)
dakajā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it qualifies pupphā (flowers), agreeing with thalajā in the compound pair thalajā dakajā. The PEU suggests dakaja + jana + kvi, but it is better analysed as daka + ja (√jan).
dakajā.example_1: ‘ Thalajā dakajā pupphā, sabbe pupphanti tāvade;
dakajā.translation_1: ‘Flowers of the land and flowers of the water, all bloom at that time;

tepajjubho.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text tepajjubho is a word-boundary sandhi: te (nominative plural of ta) plus pajjubho, a proper name (perhaps a mountain). Treated here as sandhi; printed as one word in the edition.
tepajjubho.translation_1: Both of these resound today; you will certainly become a Buddha.

tampajjubbhijjate.meaning_2: that indeed has burst forth; that truly has welled up
tampajjubbhijjate.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Textual word of doubtful analysis; probably taṃ + pa + ud + bhijjate (√bhid, passive). Meaning taken from the sentence, where it refers to water rising from the earth.
tampajjubbhijjate.translation_1: That water, too, rises today from the earth; surely, you will become a Buddha.

sopajja.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Lexicalised compound of 'so' (this) and 'pajja' (today); used adverbially in the text. Alternative: a-stem neuter with adverbial sense.
sopajja.example_1: Sopajja vāyati gandho, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.
sopajja.translation_1: that scent, too, wafts today; surely, you will become a Buddha.
sopajja.example_2: Sopajja saṃsayaṃ patto, atthaṃ gaṇhāhi mā mukhan ’’ ti.
sopajja.translation_2: Today I too have reached uncertainty about life. So accept what is beneficial, do not open your mouth (to blame women).”

paṭilaggitaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it modifies vālaṃ (the tail) and is nominative singular neuter. The form paṭilaggitaṃ shows the past participle of paṭilaggati.
paṭilaggitaṃ.translation_1: “Just as a camarī deer, whose tail has caught on something,

hetvā.meaning_2: having taken; having removed; having carried away
hetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of harati (√har, take, seize); root_sign left empty as -tvā is not in the sign list. In the text it occurs in the idiom ubhato koṭīsu hetvā majjhe osāpeti, 'taking both ends ... bringing them to the middle', i.e. removing them from the two extremes.
hetvā.example_1: Evaṃ tāsaṃ hadaye patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ disvā sabbāpi tā daḷhaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhāya punappunaṃ sammasanto anulomapaṭilomaṃ sammasati, pariyante gahetvā ādiṃ pāpeti, ādimhi gahetvā pariyante ṭhapeti, majjhe gahetvā ubhato osāpeti, ubhato koṭīsu hetvā majjhe osāpeti.
hetvā.translation_1: Having thus seen that they were established in his heart, he made them firm with a vow and, repeatedly contemplating them, he contemplated them in forward and reverse order; taking the end, he led it to the beginning; taking the beginning, he placed it at the end; taking the middle, he brought it to both sides; taking both ends, he brought them to the middle.

āluḷento.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle masculine nominative singular of the causative āluḷeti; used both literally (stirring water, churning the ocean) and figuratively (harassing an opponent). PEU analyses it as ā + luḷa + ṇe + anta and gives meanings similar to the above.
āluḷento.example_1: Bāhirakabhaṇḍapariccāgo dānapāramī nāma, aṅgapariccāgo dānaupapāramī nāma, jīvitapariccāgo dānaparamatthapāramī nāmāti dasa pāramiyo dasa upapāramiyo dasa paramatthapāramiyo yantatelaṃ vinivaṭṭento viya mahāmeruṃ matthaṃ katvā cakkavāḷamahāsamuddaṃ āluḷento viya ca sammasi.
āluḷento.translation_1: The relinquishing of external goods is called the perfection of giving; the relinquishing of limbs is the perfection of giving in a higher degree; the relinquishing of life is the perfection of giving in the ultimate degree. Thus, he contemplated the ten perfections, the ten higher perfections, and the ten ultimate perfections, churning them like one churning oil, and contemplating them as if he were churning the great ocean of the world-system by using the great Mount Sineru as a pestle.
āluḷento.example_2: Mitacintī pacchato āgacchanto jālagandhaṃ sallakkhetvā tesañca jālakucchiṃ paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ ñatvā ‘‘ imesaṃ kusītānaṃ andhabālānaṃ jīvitadānaṃ dassāmī ’’ ti cintetvā bahipassena jālakucchiṭṭhānaṃ gantvā jālakucchiṃ phāletvā nikkhantasadiso hutvā udakaṃ āluḷento jālassa purato patitvā puna jālakucchiṃ pavisitvā pacchimabhāgena phāletvā nikkhantasadiso udakaṃ āluḷento pacchimabhāge pati.
āluḷento.translation_2: Thoughtful, coming behind, noticed the scent of the net and, knowing they had entered the belly of the net, thought, 'I will give the gift of life to these lazy fools,' and after contemplating, went to the side of the net, tore the belly of the net, appeared as if he had broken through and emerged, splashed the water, dropped in front of the net, then entered the belly of the net again, tore it from the back part, appeared as if he had emerged, splashed the water, and fell behind the net.

sañcuṇṇamathitā.meaning_2: crushed and churned; pulverized and ground; smashed and pounded
sañcuṇṇamathitā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of sañcuṇṇa (crushed) and mathita (churned). Nominative plural in the verse, referring to beings struck against each other.
sañcuṇṇamathitā.translation_1: Crashed into each other there and were pulverized.

byadhitamānasā.meaning_2: with a troubled mind; mentally afflicted; distressed in mind
byadhitamānasā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative plural in the verse, agreeing with the distressed beings. byadhita is a past participle of byadhati (√vyadh).
byadhitamānasā.translation_1: “Distressed, terrified, afraid, dazed, and troubled in mind,

koṭisatamabodhayi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular of bodheti, here with the augment a- and the ending -yi; the form is preceded by koṭisataṃ in the preceding compound; metrical variant of abodhesi.
koṭisatamabodhayi.translation_1: ‘‘At the first realization, the Buddha awakened a hundred billion;

virocituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive used with na sakkoti (nāsakkhiṃsu) meaning 'was unable to shine' and with na deti 'does not allow to shine'. From vi + √ruc (shine).
virocituṃ.example_1: Ettakaṃ kālaṃ candimasūriyādayo attano pabhāya virocituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, rattindivaparicchedo na paññāyittha.
virocituṃ.translation_1: During that time, the moon, sun, and other celestial bodies were unable to shine with their own radiance; the distinction between night and day was not known.
virocituṃ.example_2: Antevāsika ayaṃ rāhu nāma candasseko upakkileso, virocituṃ na deti, ahampi rāhugahitaṃ candamaṇḍalaṃ disvā ‘‘ idaṃ parisuddhassa candamaṇḍalassa āgantukena upakkilesena nippabhaṃ jātaṃ, mayhampi idaṃ rajjaṃ upakkileso, yāva candamaṇḍalaṃ rāhu viya idaṃ nippabhaṃ na karoti, tāva pabbajissāmī ’’ ti cintetvā tadeva rāhugahitaṃ candamaṇḍalaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā mahārajjaṃ chaḍḍetvā pabbajitoti.
virocituṃ.translation_2: “Student, this Rāhu, by name, is one corruption of the moon; he prevents it from shining. I too, seeing the moon’s disk seized by Rāhu, thought, ‘This pure moon’s disk has become lusterless due to an incoming corruption. This kingdom is also a corruption for me. I will go forth before this (kingdom) makes me lusterless like Rāhu does the moon’s disk.’ Having thought thus, taking that very moon’s disk seized by Rāhu as my object, I abandoned the great kingdom and went forth into renunciation.”

ravanakasakuṇādīnañca.meaning_2: and of sounding birds and other creatures
ravanakasakuṇādīnañca.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of ravanakasakuṇādīnaṃ (genitive plural) and ca. The compound ravanakasakuṇādīnaṃ is ravanaka + sakuṇa + ādīnaṃ.
ravanakasakuṇādīnañca.example_1: Divā sūriyālokena viya sattā niccaṃ buddhālokeneva vicariṃsu, sāyaṃ pupphitakusumānaṃ, pāto ravanakasakuṇādīnañca vasena loko rattindivaparicchedaṃ sallakkhesi.
ravanakasakuṇādīnañca.translation_1: Beings always lived by the Buddha-light alone, as if by sunlight during the day. The world perceived the distinction between night and day by the flowers blooming in the evening and the birds chirping in the morning.

veṭhāpetvā.meaning_2: causes to be wrapped; has (someone) wrapped; has (something) wound
veṭhāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā of the causative veṭhāpeti; here 'having had his whole body wrapped'. Some editions read veṭhāpetvā as a simplex absolutive of veṭheti.
veṭhāpetvā.example_1: So kira bodhisattakāle ekassa buddhassa cetiyaṃ disvā ‘‘ imassa buddhassa mayā jīvitaṃ pariccajituṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti daṇḍadīpikāveṭhananiyāmena sakalasarīraṃ veṭhāpetvā ratanamattamakuḷaṃ satasahassagghanikaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ sappissa pūrāpetvā tattha sahassavaṭṭiyo jālāpetvā taṃ sīsenādāya sakalasarīraṃ jālāpetvā cetiyaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karonto sakalarattiṃ vītināmesi.
veṭhāpetvā.translation_1: It is said that in his time as a Bodhisatta, on seeing the relic mound of a certain Buddha, he thought, “I ought to sacrifice my life for this Buddha.” He had his whole body wrapped like a torch-pole; he filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, with a rim a cubit wide, with ghee and lit a thousand wicks in it. Taking it on his head and setting fire to his entire body, he spent the whole night circumambulating the relic mound.

samatalo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes the ground being level like a kasiṇa circle. Nominative singular in the text.
samatalo.example_1: ‘‘ Sādhu karissāmī ’’ ti gantvā ekaṃ padesaṃ olokesi, dvādasaterasayojanappamāṇo padeso kasiṇamaṇḍalaṃ viya samatalo ahosi.
samatalo.translation_1: “Very well, I shall do it,” he said, and having gone, he looked at a certain area; an area measuring twelve or thirteen leagues became as level as a circle of clay.

upasoṇā.meaning_2: name of a female disciple; Upasoṇā
upasoṇā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of one of the two chief female disciples of Buddha Koṇḍañña. Nominative singular in the text.
upasoṇā.example_1: Tassa bhagavato nagaraṃ khemaṃ nāma ahosi, sudatto nāma rājā pitā, sirimā nāma mātā, saraṇo ca bhāvitatto ca dve aggasāvakā, udeno nāmupaṭṭhāko, soṇā ca upasoṇā ca dve aggasāvikā, nāgarukkho bodhi, navutihatthubbedhaṃ sarīraṃ, navutiyeva vassasahassāni āyuppamāṇaṃ ahosi.
upasoṇā.translation_1: The city of that Blessed One was named Khema, the father was a king named Sudatta, the mother was a queen named Sirimā, the two chief disciples were the elders Saraṇa and Bhāvitatta, the attendant was an elder named Udena, the two chief female disciples were the elder nuns Soṇā and Upasoṇā, the Bodhi tree was a Nāga tree, the body was ninety cubits high, and the lifespan was ninety thousand years.

upasālo.meaning_2: name of a chief disciple of the Buddha Paduma
upasālo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name. Nominative singular in the text, paired with sālo.
upasālo.example_1: Padumassa pana bhagavato campakaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, asamo nāma rājā pitā, asamā nāma devī mātā, sālo ca upasālo ca dve aggasāvakā, varuṇo nāmupaṭṭhāko, rāmā ca surāmā ca dve aggasāvikā, soṇarukkho nāma bodhi, aṭṭhapaṇṇāsahatthubbedhaṃ sarīraṃ ahosi, āyu vassasatasahassanti.
upasālo.translation_1: The city of the Blessed One Paduma was named Campaka, the father was a king named Asama, the mother was a queen named Asamā, the two chief disciples were the elders Sāla and Upasāla, the attendant was an elder named Varuna, the two chief female disciples were the elder nuns Rāmā and Surāmā, the Bodhi tree was a Soṇa tree, the body was fifty-eight cubits high, and the lifespan was a hundred thousand years.

phaggunī.meaning_2: name of a chief female disciple of the Buddha Sikhī; the Phaggunī constellation
phaggunī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A proper name of a nun, nominative singular in the text; also the name of a lunar mansion.
phaggunī.example_1: Tassa bhagavato dhaññavatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, sudevo nāma khattiyo pitā, anomā nāma mātā, saddasālo ca jitamitto ca dve aggasāvakā, vāseṭṭho nāmupaṭṭhāko, uttarā ca phaggunī ca dve aggasāvikā, mahāsoṇarukkho nāma bodhi, sarīraṃ aṭṭhāsītihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, navutivassasahassāni āyūti.
phaggunī.translation_1: The city of that Blessed One was named Dhaññavatī, the father was a king named Sudeva, the mother was a queen named Anomā, the two chief disciples were the elders Bhaddasāla and Jitamitta, the attendant was an elder named Vāseṭṭha, the two chief female disciples were the elder nuns Uttarā and Phaggunī, the Bodhi tree was a great Soṇa tree, the body was eighty-eight cubits high, and the lifespan was ninety thousand years.

salalarukkho.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Here the Bodhi tree of the Buddha named in the Jātaka prose. Nominative singular in the text.
salalarukkho.example_1: Tassa nagaraṃ haṃsavatī nāma ahosi, pitā ānando nāma khattiyo, mātā sujātā nāma devī, devalo ca sujāto ca dve aggasāvakā, sumano nāmupaṭṭhāko, amitā ca asamā ca dve aggasāvikā, salalarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ aṭṭhapaṇṇāsahatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, sarīrappabhā samantato dvādasa yojanāni gaṇhi, vassasatasahassaṃ āyūti.
salalarukkho.translation_1: The city of that Blessed One was named Haṃsavatī, the father was a king named Ānanda, the mother was a queen named Sujātā, the two chief disciples were the elders Maṅgala and Sujāta, the attendant was an elder named Sumana, the two chief female disciples were the elder nuns Asbā and Amitā, the Bodhi tree was a Sāla tree, the body was fifty-eight cubits high, the radiance from his body reached twelve leagues all around, and the lifespan was a hundred thousand years.

katiṃsakappe.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] katiṃsa is an indeclinable numeral meaning 'thirty-one'. Locative singular in the text: 'ito katiṃsakappe' = 'in thirty-one aeons from now'; sometimes explained as 'in the thirty-first aeon'.
katiṃsakappe.example_1: Sopi naṃ ‘‘ ito katiṃsakappe buddho bhavissasī ’’ ti byākāsi.
katiṃsakappe.translation_1: He too declared of him, “In thirty-one aeons, you will be a Buddha.”

nūpapajjare.meaning_2: certainly they are not born (in); surely they do not arise (in)
nūpapajjare.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of na + upapajjare (u- initial after na → nū; the emphatic nu reading is also possible). The verb is 3rd person plural present of upapajjati with the augmentless-preterite sense; the negative na is common in verse.
nūpapajjare.translation_1: Even when dwelling in heavenly realms, they are not born in the non-percipient state.

koṭṭiyantopi.meaning_2: being prodded; being beaten; being struck
koṭṭiyantopi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle masculine nominative singular of a passive/causative verb meaning 'to prod, beat' (denominative from koṭṭa, 'a stick'). Written with -yy-. The final -pi is an enclitic (even); the form in the text is koṭṭiyanto.
koṭṭiyantopi.translation_1: “Even when being pierced by stakes, even when being prodded with lances,

sañchannatalo.meaning_2: whose surface is covered (with); having a surface spread over (with)
sañchannatalo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi describing the earth covered with lotuses; nominative singular in the text (sañchannatalo ahosi).
sañchannatalo.example_1: Tassa taṃ siriṃ daṭṭhukāmā viya andhā cakkhūni paṭilabhiṃsu, badhirā saddaṃ suṇiṃsu, mūgā samālapiṃsu, khujjā ujugattā ahesuṃ, paṅgulā padasā gamanaṃ paṭilabhiṃsu, bandhanagatā sabbasattā andubandhanādīhi mucciṃsu, sabbanarakesu aggi nibbāyi, pettivisaye khuppipāsā vūpasami, tiracchānānaṃ bhayaṃ nāhosi, sabbasattānaṃ rogo vūpasami, sabbasattā piyaṃvadā ahesuṃ, madhurenākārena assā hasiṃsu, vāraṇā gajjiṃsu, sabbatūriyāni sakasakaninnādaṃ muñciṃsu, aghaṭṭitāniyeva manussānaṃ hatthūpagādīni ābharaṇāni viraviṃsu, sabbadisā vippasannā ahesuṃ, sattānaṃ sukhaṃ uppādayamāno mudusītalavāto vāyi, akālamegho vassi, pathavitopi udakaṃ ubbhijjitvā vissandi, pakkhino ākāsagamanaṃ vijahiṃsu, nadiyo asandamānā aṭṭhaṃsu, mahāsamudde madhuraṃ udakaṃ ahosi, sabbatthakameva pañcavaṇṇehi padumehi sañchannatalo ahosi, thalajajalajādīni sabbapupphāni pupphiṃsu, rukkhānaṃ khandhesu khandhapadumāni, sākhāsu sākhāpadumāni, latāsu latāpadumāni pupphiṃsu, thale silātalāni bhinditvā uparūpari satta satta hutvā daṇḍapadumāni nāma nikkhamiṃsu, ākāse olambakapadumāni nāma nibbattiṃsu, samantato pupphavassā vassiṃsu, ākāse dibbatūriyāni vajjiṃsu, sakaladasasahassilokadhātu vaṭṭetvā vissaṭṭhamālāguḷo viya, uppīḷetvā baddhamālākalāpo viya, alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ mālāsanaṃ viya ca ekamālāmālinī vipphurantavāḷabījanī pupphadhūmagandhaparivāsitā paramasobhaggappattā ahosi.
sañchannatalo.translation_1: As if desiring to see that splendor of the Bodhisatta, the blind regained their sight, the deaf heard sounds, the mute spoke, the hunchbacked became straight, the lame walked, all beings in bondage were released from their fetters, fires went out in all the hells, hunger and thirst ceased in the ghost realm, animals were freed from fear, all beings were cured of illness, all beings spoke lovingly, horses neighed sweetly, elephants roared, all musical instruments played of their own accord, ornaments worn by humans rattled without being touched, all directions became serene, a soft cool wind blew for the comfort of all beings, unseasonable rain ceased, water welled up from the earth, birds ceased to fly in the air, rivers stopped flowing, the ocean water became sweet, the entire earth was covered with five-colored lotuses, all flowers blossomed everywhere—both those on land and in water. Flowers blossomed on trunks, branches, and vines. Lotuses on stalks emerged from the earth, and lotuses emerged in the air. Flowers rained down from the sky, divine music played in the air, and the ten-thousand-fold world-system became like a garland whirled around, like a tight bouquet, like a beautifully arranged flower seat, like a single garland, like a waving fan of flowers, and it became perfectly radiant, scented with incense and flowers.

kāḷadevīlo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of the ascetic devoted to King Suddhodana's family in the Jātaka commentary; nominative singular in the text. The PEU entry gives the spelling kāḷadevala, and a variant devila is also recorded.
kāḷadevīlo.example_1: Tasmiṃ samaye suddhodanamahārājassa kulūpako aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī kāḷadevīlo nāma tāpaso bhattakiccaṃ katvā divāvihāratthāya tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ gantvā tattha divāvihāraṃ nisinno tā devatā kīḷamānā disvā ‘‘ kiṃkāraṇā tumhe evaṃ tuṭṭhamānasā kīḷatha, mayhampetaṃ kāraṇaṃ kathethā ’’ ti pucchi.
kāḷadevīlo.translation_1: At that time, a hermit named Kāḷadevala, who was devoted to King Suddhodana’s family and a master of the eight attainments, having finished his meal, went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven for his day’s abiding; seeing the devas playing joyfully there, he asked, “Why are you playing so joyfully? Tell me the reason for this.”

kusumbakapupphappamāṇāni.meaning_2: of the size of a kusumbha flower; as big as a safflower flower
kusumbakapupphappamāṇāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative plural agreeing with avasesāni. Kusumbaka is the safflower (Carthamus tinctorius) or a similar flower; compound of three members.
kusumbakapupphappamāṇāni.example_1: Tesu hi sabbamahantaṃ āmalakapupphappamāṇaṃ, avasesāni kusumbakapupphappamāṇāni ahesuṃ.
kusumbakapupphappamāṇāni.translation_1: Of them, the largest was the size of an emblica flower, and the rest were the size of kusumbha flowers.

samparivārayitvā.meaning_2: having surrounded; having attended on; having accompanied
samparivārayitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of samparivārayati. In the first sentence the women surround and entertain him; in the second, the adorned noblewomen are described as surrounding (him).
samparivārayitvā.example_1: Tāvadeva ca naṃ sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā naccagītādīsu susikkhitā devakaññā viya rūpasobhaggappattā itthiyo nānātūriyāni gahetvā samparivārayitvā abhiramāpentiyo naccagītavāditāni payojayiṃsu.
samparivārayitvā.translation_1: At that very moment, women, adorned with all ornaments, well-trained in dance and song, and beautiful as celestial maidens, surrounded him with various instruments, entertaining him with dance, song, and music.
samparivārayitvā.translation_2: 480. “Those noblewomen, slender-waisted like golden vines, adorned and surrounding you;

nirumbhitvā.meaning_2: having suppressed; having blocked; having stopped
nirumbhitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it refers to the devas blocking the sound so that no one heard it. Absolutive of nirumbhati (ni + √rudh, obstruct).
nirumbhitvā.example_1: So saddo sakalanagaraṃ pattharitvā gaccheyya, devatā pana taṃ saddaṃ nirumbhitvā na kassaci sotuṃ adaṃsu.
nirumbhitvā.translation_1: That sound would have spread throughout the entire city, but the devas suppressed it so that no one heard.

cuḷaṃ.meaning_2: top-knot; crest; diadem ornament (worn on the head)
cuḷaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the sentence cuḷaṃ is accusative singular, coordinated with moḷiyā and taken up by the Bodhisatta before throwing it into the sky. Spelling varies between cuḷa, cūḷa and culla; the meaning here is a head ornament rather than the adjective 'small'. The root link is uncertain.
cuḷaṃ.example_1: Bodhisatto saha moḷiyā cuḷaṃ gahetvā ‘‘ sacāhaṃ buddho bhavissāmi, ākāse tiṭṭhatu, no ce, bhūmiyaṃ patatū ’’ ti antalikkhe khipi.
cuḷaṃ.translation_1: Grasping the top-knot and diadem, the Bodhisatta prayed, “If I am to be a Buddha, let this stay in the sky; if not, let it fall to the ground,” and tossed it into the firmament.

padahitukāmo.meaning_2: wishing to exert; wanting to strive; desirous of making an effort
padahitukāmo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A compound of the infinitive padahituṃ and kāma; nominative singular used adverbially with mahāpadhānaṃ. Describes the Bodhisatta's resolve before the great striving.
padahitukāmo.example_1: Bodhisattopi rañño paṭiññaṃ datvā anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno āḷārañca kālāmaṃ udakañca rāmaputtaṃ upasaṅkamitvā samāpattiyo nibbattetvā ‘‘ nāyaṃ maggo bodhāyā ’’ ti tampi samāpattibhāvanaṃ analaṅkaritvā sadevakassa lokassa attano thāmavīriyasandassanatthaṃ mahāpadhānaṃ padahitukāmo uruvelaṃ gantvā ‘‘ ramaṇīyo vatāyaṃ bhūmibhāgo ’’ ti tattheva vāsaṃ upagantvā mahāpadhānaṃ padahi.
padahitukāmo.translation_1: After giving the promise to the king, the Bodhisatta wandered by stages until he approached Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputta, attained their meditative absorptions, but not being satisfied with their attainment as it was not the path to awakening, and wishing to show his physical and mental strength to the world with its devas, he went to the Uruvelā region, found a delightful spot, and began his great striving.

kili.meaning_2: kili! (an onomatopoeic sound; a ringing, tinkling noise, as of metal vessels striking together)
kili.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] An imitative sound word; in the text it occurs twice (kili kili) and describes the ringing of the three almsbowls when struck. Recorded in PEU as 'the voice of kiliki' and 'a sound made when gold cups touch each other'. Sometimes treated as a noun meaning such a sound.
kili.example_1: Sā sotaṃ chindamānā nadīmajjhaṃ gantvā majjhamajjhaṭṭhāneneva javasampanno asso viya asītihatthamattaṭṭhānaṃ paṭisotaṃ gantvā ekasmiṃ āvaṭṭe nimujjitvā kāḷanāgarājabhavanaṃ gantvā tiṇṇaṃ buddhānaṃ paribhogapātiyo ‘‘ kili kilī ’’ ti ravaṃ kārayamānā paharitvāva tāsaṃ sabbaheṭṭhimā hutvā aṭṭhāsi.
kili.translation_1: The bowl cut through the current, went to the middle of the river, and then, like a horse consummate in speed, went upstream against the current for about eighty cubits, sank into a whirlpool, went to the abode of the King of the Kāla Nāgas, struck the bowls used by the three previous Buddhas—making a ‘kili kili’ sound—and settled beneath those three bowls.

kilīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Possibly a contracted or variant form of kīḷati (√kīḷ, ā-contraction). The related entries kilama/kilami instead suggest √kilam (be weary), which does not fit a present ending in -ti; no sentences were supplied to confirm the reading.

ālikhitumpi.meaning_2: to scratch; to draw; to paint; to depict
ālikhitumpi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text as ālikhitumpi, with the emphatic particle -pi; the infinitive depends on samattho. Appears in a simile about a painter (cittakāra) or sculptor who cannot even draw such a shape.
ālikhitumpi.example_1: Tānipi kho tiṇāni tathārūpena saṇṭhānena saṇṭhahiṃsu, yathārūpaṃ sukusalopi cittakāro vā potthakāro vā ālikhitumpi samattho natthi.
ālikhitumpi.translation_1: Those blades of grass settled in a configuration that even the most skilled painter or sculptor could never replicate.

ummūletvā.meaning_2: having uprooted; having torn out by the roots
ummūletvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā from the denominative/causative ummūleti (u + mūla); used in the text with pātesi and kātuṃ, of trees being uprooted.
ummūletvā.example_1: Taṅkhaṇaṃyeva puratthimādibhedā vātā samuṭṭhahitvā aḍḍhayojanaekayojanadviyojanatiyojanappamāṇāni pabbatakūṭāni padāletvā vanagaccharukkhādīni ummūletvā samantā gāmanigame cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ kātuṃ samatthāpi mahāpurisassa puññatejena vihatānubhāvā bodhisattaṃ patvā cīvarakaṇṇamattampi cāletuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu.
ummūletvā.translation_1: At that very moment, winds from the east and other directions arose, capable of shattering mountain peaks of half a yojana, one yojana, two yojanas, and three yojanas, uprooting forests and trees, and pulverizing surrounding villages and towns; but due to the merit-power of the Great Man, their power was shattered, and upon reaching the Bodhisatta, they could not even move a corner of his robe.
ummūletvā.example_2: Ekaṃ pana aṅgaṇe ṭhitaṃ sākhāviṭapasampannampi mahārukkhaṃ aññehi rukkhehi asambandhattā ummūletvā bhūmiyaṃ pātesi, iminā kāraṇena tumhehipi samaggehi sammodamānehi bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.
ummūletvā.translation_2: But it uprooted and cast to the ground one great tree that stood in an open space, even though it was endowed with branches and twigs, because it was not connected to other trees; for this reason, it is fitting that you too should be united and dwell with mutual appreciation,” he said, and being requested by them, he recounted the past.

bhiṃsetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of the causative bhiṃseti (to terrify), used in the Jātaka story of Māra creating darkness. Root vowel u is nasalised to iṃ.
bhiṃsetvā.example_1: Tato ‘‘ iminā bhiṃsetvā siddhatthaṃ palāpessāmī ’’ ti andhakāraṃ samuṭṭhāpesi.
bhiṃsetvā.translation_1: Then, thinking, “I will terrify him with this darkness and make Siddhattha flee,” he stirred up darkness.

ugghosayuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Third person plural aorist of the causative ugghosayati (u + √ghus). The PEU spelling ugghosayati with ṇaya is doubtful; the commentary form is ugghosayuṃ.
ugghosayuṃ.example_1: Ugghosayuṃ bodhimaṇḍe pamoditā, jayaṃ tadā nāgagaṇā mahesino.
ugghosayuṃ.translation_1: In those days, the host of Nāgas, delighted at the Bodhi-seat, proclaimed this victory of the Great Seer.
ugghosayuṃ.example_2: Ugghosayuṃ bodhimaṇḍe pamoditā, supaṇṇasaṅghāpi jayaṃ mahesino.
ugghosayuṃ.translation_2: In those days, the host of Supaṇṇas, delighted at the Bodhi-seat, proclaimed this victory of the Great Seer.

dvādasakkhattuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Refers to the ten thousand world-systems shaking twelve times. Bahuvrīhi or adv? Text has dvādasakkhattuṃ.
dvādasakkhattuṃ.example_1: Athassa dvādasapadikaṃ paccayākāraṃ vaṭṭavivaṭṭavasena anulomapaṭilomato sammasantassa dasasahassī lokadhātu udakapariyantaṃ katvā dvādasakkhattuṃ sampakampi.
dvādasakkhattuṃ.translation_1: Then, as he contemplated the twelve-factored conditionality in regular and reverse order, through the modes of the round of existence and its cessation, the ten thousand world-systems shook twelve times, down to the water’s edge.

sītādipaṭibāhanatthaṃ.meaning_2: for the purpose of warding off cold and the like; to prevent cold and such things
sītādipaṭibāhanatthaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text, used as an adverbial phrase: 'for the purpose of warding off cold and the like'. The compound contains a verb-derived noun paṭibāhana.
sītādipaṭibāhanatthaṃ.example_1: Tattha sattāhavaddalikāya uppannāya sītādipaṭibāhanatthaṃ mucalindena nāgarājena sattakkhattuṃ bhogehi parikkhitto asambādhāya gandhakuṭiyaṃ viharanto viya vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvediyamāno sattāhaṃ vītināmetvā rājāyatanaṃ upasaṅkami, tatthāpi vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvediyamānoyeva nisīdi.
sītādipaṭibāhanatthaṃ.translation_1: There, when a seven-day rainstorm occurred, to ward off cold and the like, the Nāga King Mucalinda encircled him seven times with his coils, and he sat there for seven days experiencing the happiness of liberation, as if dwelling in a spacious perfumed chamber, after which he went to the Rājāyatana tree, where he sat experiencing the happiness of liberation for another week.

agadaharīṭakaṃ.meaning_2: medicinal myrobalan fruit; healing Terminalia chebula
agadaharīṭakaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text. agada = medicine, remedy; harīṭaka = yellow myrobalan (Terminalia chebula).
agadaharīṭakaṃ.example_1: Sakko devānamindo agadaharīṭakaṃ āharitvā adāsi, satthā taṃ paribhuñji, tenassa sarīravaḷañjaṃ ahosi.
agadaharīṭakaṃ.translation_1: Sakka, the ruler of the devas, brought and gave him a medicinal myrobalan fruit. The Teacher partook of it, and because of that, his bodily system was cleansed.

temitukāmova.meaning_2: wishing to be made wet; wanting to get wet
temitukāmova.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is nominative singular masculine (temitukāmova), taking water as subject: the water wets only one who wishes to be wet. The compound contains the infinitive temituṃ (to be made wet) from √tim.
temitukāmova.example_1: Tambavaṇṇaṃ udakaṃ heṭṭhā viravantaṃ gacchati, temitukāmova temeti, atemitukāmassa sarīre ekabindumattampi na patati.
temitukāmova.translation_1: The reddish water flowed down below with a roar; it wet only those who wished to be wet, but not a single drop fell on the body of one who did not wish to be wet.

atemitukāmassa.meaning_2: not wanting to get wet; not wishing to be drenched
atemitukāmassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text genitive singular, agreeing with sarīre: 'on the body of one who did not wish to be wet'. Negative na + temitu-kāma; cf. temitukāma.
atemitukāmassa.example_1: Tambavaṇṇaṃ udakaṃ heṭṭhā viravantaṃ gacchati, temitukāmova temeti, atemitukāmassa sarīre ekabindumattampi na patati.
atemitukāmassa.translation_1: The reddish water flowed down below with a roar; it wet only those who wished to be wet, but not a single drop fell on the body of one who did not wish to be wet.

mattagajindavilāsitagāmī.meaning_2: walking with the graceful gait of a rutting elephant king; moving with the splendour of a lordly elephant in musth
mattagajindavilāsitagāmī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] An epithet of the Bodhisatta as a lion of men. Compound of matta (rutting, in musth) + gajinda (elephant king) + vilāsita (graceful gait) + gāmī (going). Nominative singular in the text.
mattagajindavilāsitagāmī.example_1: Mattagajindavilāsitagāmī, esa hi tuyhaṃ pitā narasīho.
mattagajindavilāsitagāmī.translation_1: “Walking with the grace of a king of elephants—this Lion of Men is your father.

hiṅgulavaṇṇarattasujivho.meaning_2: having a beautiful red tongue the colour of cinnabar; with a lovely red tongue like vermilion
hiṅgulavaṇṇarattasujivho.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi compound describing the Buddha; nominative singular in the verse, agreeing with the subject. The PEU gives the last member as rattā + sujivhā (fem).
hiṅgulavaṇṇarattasujivho.translation_1: “With a voice deep, sweet, and soft, and a tongue reddish like cinnabar;

osadhipaṇḍarasuddhasuuṇṇo.meaning_2: with a pure white ūrṇā hair (between the eyebrows) like the morning star; (Buddha) whose brow-tuft is bright white like the osadhi star
osadhipaṇḍarasuddhasuuṇṇo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Vocative singular in the text, addressing the Buddha ('esa hi tuyhaṃ pitā narasīho'). The compound describes the white ūrṇā hair between the eyebrows, compared to the osadhi (morning) star; suuṇṇa is likely su + uṇṇa ('well-wooled', i.e. with a fine wool-like curl).
osadhipaṇḍarasuddhasuuṇṇo.example_1: Osadhipaṇḍarasuddhasuuṇṇo, esa hi tuyhaṃ pitā narasīho.
osadhipaṇḍarasuddhasuuṇṇo.translation_1: “With a pure white tuft between the brows like the morning star—this Lion of Men is your father.

avasesetvā.meaning_2: having left over; having left remaining
avasesetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of avaseseti (causative of avasissati); here in the phrase aṭṭhīni avasesetvā, 'leaving only the bones'. Alternative analysis: ava + √sis > avasesa + *e + tvā.
avasesetvā.example_1: Rattibhāgasamanantare yakkhā yakkhanagarato āgantvā sabbepi goṇe ca manusse ca jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā aṭṭhīni avasesetvā agamaṃsu.
avasesetvā.translation_1: In the middle of the night, the demons came from their city, killed all the oxen and men, ate their flesh, left only the bones, and went away.

vijjulatobhāso.meaning_2: glow of a flash of lightning; lightning's radiance
vijjulatobhāso.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The compound is vijjulatā + obhāsa with the initial o- of obhāsa; the PEU split vijjulatā+obhāsa agrees. Nominative singular in the text.
vijjulatobhāso.example_1: ‘‘ Atthi pana vo kenaci vijjulatobhāso diṭṭho ’’ ti?
vijjulatobhāso.translation_1: “Has any one of you seen the glow of a flash of lightning?”

mocāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to be released; having had (them) set free; having had (the carts) unyoked
mocāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of mocāpeti (causative of mucati). In the text it refers to having carts unyoked and to having people released.
mocāpetvā.example_1: So gacchanto yathāpūritāneva pañca sakaṭasatāni goṇamanussānañca hatthaṭṭhikādīni disāvidisāsu vippakiṇṇāni disvā sakaṭāni mocāpetvā sakaṭaparivaṭṭakena khandhāvāraṃ bandhāpetvā kālasseva manusse ca goṇe ca sāyamāsabhattaṃ bhojāpetvā manussānaṃ majjhe goṇe nipajjāpetvā sayaṃ balanāyako hutvā khaggahattho tiyāmarattiṃ ārakkhaṃ gahetvā ṭhitakova aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpesi.
mocāpetvā.translation_1: As he went along, he saw the five hundred carts standing just as they had been loaded, and the bones and other remains of the men and oxen strewn in various directions. He had the carts unyoked, formed a protective circle with them, had his men and oxen eat their evening meal, and after nightfall, had the oxen lie down in the middle with the men around them. He himself, acting as the caravan-leader, kept watch all night long with sword in hand, staying awake until dawn.
mocāpetvā.example_2: Te pana disvā anāthapiṇḍikassa manussā ‘‘ mayaṃ, sāmi, etesaṃ nivāsañca bhattañca paribbayañca jānissāmā ’’ ti vatvā tesaṃ sakaṭāni bahinagare tathārūpe ṭhāne mocāpetvā ‘‘ tumhe idheva vasatha, amhākaṃ vo ghare yāgubhattañca paribbayo ca bhavissatī ’’ ti gantvā dāsakammakare sannipātetvā majjhimayāmasamanantare pañca sakaṭasatāni vilumpitvā nivāsanapārupanānipi nesaṃ acchinditvā goṇe palāpetvā sakaṭāni vicakkāni katvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā cakkānipi gaṇhitvāva agamaṃsu.
mocāpetvā.translation_2: But Anāthapiṇḍika’s workers, seeing them, said, “Sir, we will see to their lodging, food, and expenses,” and having made them unyoke their carts outside the city in such a place, they said, “You stay right here, food and expenses will come to you from our house.” Then, having gone, they gathered the slaves and workers, and at the end of the middle watch, they looted the five hundred carts, stole even the clothes they were wearing, drove the oxen away, removed the wheels from the five hundred carts, left them on the ground, took the wheels, and went off.

āropāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to be loaded; having had (goods) put on
āropāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of āropeti; here with bhaṇḍaṃ, 'having had the goods loaded' onto a cart. The causative sense is passive in English.
āropāpetvā.example_1: Punadivase pana pātova sabbakiccāni niṭṭhāpetvā goṇe bhojetvā dubbalasakaṭāni chaḍḍāpetvā thirāni gāhāpetvā appagghaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ chaḍḍāpetvā mahagghaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ āropāpetvā yathādhippetaṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā diguṇatiguṇena mūlena bhaṇḍaṃ vikkiṇitvā sabbaṃ parisaṃ ādāya puna attano nagarameva agamāsi.
āropāpetvā.translation_1: The next day, after finishing all his tasks early in the morning, he fed the oxen, discarded the weak carts, had the strong ones taken, discarded the low-value goods, had the high-value goods loaded, reached his destination, sold the goods for double or triple their value, and took his entire company back to his own city.

ossajitvā.meaning_2: having given up; having let go; having released
ossajitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Used with vīriyaṃ: 'having given up effort'. The negative form anossajanto (not giving up) appears in the same sentence.
ossajitvā.example_1: Āvuso, ahaṃ maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā alabhitvā ‘‘ abhabbapuggalena mayā bhavitabban ’’ ti vīriyaṃ ossajitvā āgatomhīti.
ossajitvā.translation_1: “Friends, having failed to obtain the path or fruit, I thought ‘I must be a person incapable of realization,’ so I gave up energy and have come back.”
ossajitvā.example_2: ‘‘ Bhante, ayaṃ bhikkhu evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karonto vīriyaṃ ossajitvā āgato ’’ ti āhaṃsu.
ossajitvā.translation_2: “Venerable sir, this bhikkhu, having gone forth in such an emancipating dispensation, while performing the ascetic’s duty, gave up energy and has returned,” they said.

oṇamitvā.meaning_2: having bent down; having stooped; having bowed down
oṇamitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -itvā of the causative oṇameti (ava + nam + *e), used intransitively here: 'having bent down'. Some analyses take it from oṇamati.
oṇamitvā.example_1: Bodhisatto pana ‘‘ imassa pāsāṇassa heṭṭhā udakena bhavitabban ’’ ti otaritvā pāsāṇe ṭhito oṇamitvā sotaṃ odahitvā saddaṃ āvajjento heṭṭhā udakassa pavattanasaddaṃ sutvā uttaritvā cūḷupaṭṭhākaṃ āha –
oṇamitvā.translation_1: But the Bodhisatta, thinking ‘There must be water beneath this rock,’ descended, stood on the rock, stooped down, applied his ear, and listening for the sound, having heard the sound of water flowing beneath, came up and said to his young attendant—

anossajitvā.meaning_2: not having given up; not having let go (of); without relinquishing
anossajitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Negative absolutive (na + ossajitvā) used twice in these sentences: 'not giving up energy' and 'not letting go elsewhere'.
anossajitvā.example_1: Satthāpi dve vatthūni kathetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānetvā dassesi ‘‘ tasmiṃ samaye vīriyaṃ anossajitvā pāsāṇaṃ bhinditvā mahājanassa udakadāyako cūḷupaṭṭhāko ayaṃ ossaṭṭhavīriyo bhikkhu ahosi, avasesaparisā idāni buddhaparisā jātā, satthavāhajeṭṭhako pana ahameva ahosin ’’ ti desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.
anossajitvā.translation_1: The Teacher, too, having told the two matters, having joined the connection, and having connected the birth story, showed: “At that time, the young attendant who, not giving up energy, broke the rock and gave water to the great multitude, was this bhikkhu who gave up energy; the rest of the company has now become the Buddha's company; but the leader of the caravan, that was I myself.” Thus he finished the teaching.
anossajitvā.example_2: Maṇī mamanti sace, samma āḷāra, gacchasiyeva, evaṃ sante mama lohitaṅko dhanahārako sabbakāmadado maṇi saṃvijjati, taṃ uḷāraṃ maṇiratanaṃ ādāya tava gehaṃ gaccha, tattha imassānubhāvena yāvadicchakaṃ dhanaṃ laddhā puna imaṃ maṇiṃ ossajassu, ossajanto ca aññattha anossajitvā attano udakacāṭiyaṃ ossajeyyāsīti vatvā mayhaṃ maṇiratanaṃ upanesīti vadati.
anossajitvā.translation_2: I have a gem (maṇī mamaṃ): “If, friend Āḷāra, you definitely go, if this is so, I possess a red-spotted, wealth-bringing, all-desire-granting gem. Taking that magnificent wondrous Gem, go to your home. There, by its power, having obtained as much wealth as you wish, again, put this gem away. And when putting it away, do not put it away elsewhere, but put it into your own water-pot.” Saying this, he gave me the wondrous Gem, he says.

nivattayīti.meaning_2: turns back; turns away; retreats; desists
nivattayīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Text form is nivattayīti = nivattaya + iti, causative/denominative 3rd singular; treatment follows the PEU (Nivatteti).

saṃkhobhetvā.meaning_2: having shaken; having stirred up; having disturbed thoroughly
saṃkhobhetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of the causative saṃkhobheti (√khubh + *e), 'having caused to shake'. In the text it describes the Elder's roaring shaking the three Piṭakas.
saṃkhobhetvā.example_1: Thero sīhanādaṃ nadanto taruṇasīho viya tīṇi piṭakāni saṃkhobhetvā anumodanaṃ akāsi.
saṃkhobhetvā.translation_1: The Elder, roaring like a young lion, shook the three Pitakas and performed the thanksgiving.

avikkiṇite.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text, used absolutely: 'while my grass is unsold'. The PEU also gives avikkiṇitvā, but here the form is the participle.
avikkiṇite.example_1: So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā tiṇahārake āha ‘‘ ajja mayhaṃ ekekaṃ tiṇakalāpaṃ detha, mayā ca tiṇe avikkiṇite attano tiṇaṃ mā vikkiṇathā ’’ ti.
avikkiṇite.translation_1: Having heard his words, he said to the grass-cutters, “Today, give me a bundle of grass each; and until I have sold my grass, do not sell your own.”

catumāsambhantareyeva.meaning_2: within the interval of four months; within four months
catumāsambhantareyeva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] catumāsambhantare + yeva, with sandhi; the locative catumāsambhantare means "within the interval of four months".
catumāsambhantareyeva.example_1: So ‘‘ tumhehi kathitaupāye ṭhatvā catumāsambhantareyeva laddhan ’’ ti matamūsikaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbaṃ vatthuṃ kathesi.
catumāsambhantareyeva.translation_1: He said, “By abiding in the means told by you, I obtained it within four months,” and starting from the dead mouse, he told the whole story.

lāludāyittherassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A monk's name; the reading lāludāyittherassa is genitive singular. The related entry gives lāludāyitthera = Lāludāyī + thera.
lāludāyittherassa.example_1: Tasmiṃ pātova salākabhattāni uddisamāne lāludāyittherassa kadāci varabhattaṃ pāpuṇāti, kadāci lāmakabhattaṃ.
lāludāyittherassa.translation_1: When he was assigning the ticket-meals in the early morning, sometimes choice rice would fall to the Elder Lāludāyi, and sometimes inferior rice.

lāludāyi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of a bhikkhu, formed of lāla (foolish babbler) + Udāyī. The text has the nominative singular cased as lāludāyi (as addressed in the vocative-like quotation); the PEU headword is lāludāyī.
lāludāyi.example_1: Atha naṃ daharā ca sāmaṇerā ca ‘‘ āvuso lāludāyi tayi salākaṃ dente bhikkhū lābhena parihāyanti, na tvaṃ dātuṃ anucchaviko, gaccha ito ’’ ti salākaggato nikkaḍḍhiṃsu.
lāludāyi.translation_1: Then the boys and novices said to him, “Friend Lāludāyi, when you give out the tickets, the bhikkhus are deprived of their due share; you are not fit to give them out, go away from here,” and they pushed him out of the ticket-room.
lāludāyi.example_2: ‘‘ Ānanda, na idāneva lāludāyi attano bālatāya paresaṃ lābhahāniṃ karoti, pubbepi akāsiyevā ’’ ti āha.
lāludāyi.translation_2: “Ānanda, this is not the only time Lāludāyi has caused the loss of gain to others due to his own foolishness; he has done the same in the past as well,” he said.

nikkaḍḍhāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to be dragged out; having had (someone) removed; having caused (someone) to be expelled
nikkaḍḍhāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of nikkaḍḍhāpeti (causative of nikkaḍḍhati, from ni + √kaḍḍh). The PEU gives 'he was expelled', but the form is an absolutive and in these sentences the king is the one who has others removed. Sometimes written nikkaḍḍhāpetvāna.
nikkaḍḍhāpetvā.example_1: Tasmiṃ kāle rājā lajjito taṃ bālaṃ nikkaḍḍhāpetvā bodhisattasseva agghāpanikaṭṭhānaṃ adāsi.
nikkaḍḍhāpetvā.translation_1: At that time, the king, ashamed, dismissed that foolish man and gave the office of valuer back to the Bodhisatta.
nikkaḍḍhāpetvā.example_2: Rājā ‘‘ nakkhattajānanakena nāma evarūpena bhavitabban ’’ ti sesabrāhmaṇe nikkaḍḍhāpetvā ‘‘ brāhmaṇa, pasannosmi te, varaṃ tvaṃ gaṇhā ’’ ti āha.
nikkaḍḍhāpetvā.translation_2: The king said, “One who knows the stars must be like this,” and after dismissing the other brahmins, said, “Brahmin, I am pleased with you; take a boon.”

yaṃkāraṇā.meaning_2: for the reason that; because of which; on account of which
yaṃkāraṇā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of yaṃ (accusative of ya) and kāraṇā (ablative of kāraṇa, 'reason'). Functions as a causal conjunction meaning 'because; for the reason that'. In the sentence it introduces the reason for the reprimand.
yaṃkāraṇā.example_1: ‘‘ Yaṃkāraṇā jeṭṭhakaṃ ṭhapetvā kaniṭṭhaṃ āṇāpento jeṭṭhāpacāyikakammaṃ na karosī ’’ ti.
yaṃkāraṇā.translation_1: “For the reason that, leaving the elder aside and ordering the youngest to be brought, you do not perform the duty of showing respect to the elder.”

phalāsāva.meaning_2: desire for fruit; aspiration for a result; longing for the reward
phalāsāva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text phalāsāva = phalāsā + eva (sandhi), so the main word is phalāsā. The commentary glosses it as phale āsā, "desire for the fruit". The PEU also gives "desirable benefits", which is doubtful.
phalāsāva.translation_1: 8. “For those who do not hurry, their heart’s desire is fulfilled;
phalāsāva.example_2: Phalāsāva samijjhatīti yathāpatthike phale āsā tassa phalassa nipphattiyā samijjhatiyeva.
phalāsāva.translation_2: Phalāsāva samijjhati means that for whatever fruit is desired, the aspiration for that fruit is indeed fulfilled by its attainment.

avegāyitvā.meaning_2: without hurrying; without making speed; not acting impulsively
avegāyitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A negative absolutive (na + vegāyitvā) used alongside ataritvā to describe acting without haste. The simplex vegāyati is rare; the form is built from vega.
avegāyitvā.example_1: Ataramānānanti paṇḍitānaṃ ovāde ṭhatvā ataritvā avegāyitvā upāyena kammaṃ karontānaṃ.
avegāyitvā.translation_1: Ataramānānaṃ means those who, abiding by the advice of the wise, without haste, without impulsiveness, perform their duties through a proper method.

phalāsāti.meaning_2: desire for fruit; craving for results; (in doctrinal use) desire for benefits
phalāsāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form phalāsāti is likely phalāsa + iti (or phalāsā + ti). If taken as phalā + āsā it is a feminine compound meaning "desire for benefits". The PEU entry reads it as phala + āsā (thī).

tammūlikāya.meaning_2: having that as its basis; rooted in that; caused by that
tammūlikāya.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi compound in the instrumental singular; feminine agreeing with yasasampattiyā, meaning 'based on that (brahmacariya)'.
tammūlikāya.example_1: Vipakkabrahmacariyosmīti ettha cattāri saṅgahavatthūni seṭṭhacariyattā brahmacariyaṃ nāma, tañca tammūlikāya yasasampattiyā paṭiladdhattā vipakkaṃ nāma.
tammūlikāya.translation_1: In the phrase vipakkabrahmacariyosmi, the four means of sustaining a favorable relationship are called brahmacariya because they are noble conduct; and that is called vipakka because it has been obtained due to the glory resulting from them.

pavaṭṭayamāno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative present participle, masculine nominative singular, agreeing with so. Modifies the man who rushes forward as if rolling a stone; cf. the PEU split pa + vaṭṭa + ṇaya + māna.
pavaṭṭayamāno.example_1: So avīmaṃsitvāva selaguḷaṃ pavaṭṭayamāno viya pakkhanditvā ‘‘ gacchatha, imaṃ uppabbājethā ’’ ti āha.
pavaṭṭayamāno.translation_1: Without inquiring, rushing forward like rolling a stone, he said, "Go, expel this woman."

pacchindituṃ.meaning_2: to cut off; to sever; to stop; to prohibit
pacchindituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive form of pacchindati, used with na sakkā (not possible) and vaṭṭati (it is appropriate).
pacchindituṃ.example_1: Tasmā imaṃ kathaṃ pacchindituṃ sarājikāya parisāya majjhe imaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vinicchituṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti.
pacchindituṃ.translation_1: "Therefore, it is appropriate to judge this disciplinary issue in the midst of a company that includes the king."
pacchindituṃ.example_2: Bhariyaṃ āmantetvā ‘‘ bhadde, na sakkā dānaṃ pacchindituṃ, sakalanivesanaṃ vicinitvā kiñci upadhārehī ’’ ti āha.
pacchindituṃ.translation_2: having addressed his wife, said, “Good lady, it is not possible to cut off the giving of alms; search the entire house and look for something.”

vāgurāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is plural in form (vāgurāni), used with ādāya, 'having taken nets'; PEU treats the word as feminine, but the ending here is neuter plural.
vāgurāni.example_1: Te sabbe uyyāne migānaṃ nivāpatiṇāni ropetvā udakaṃ sampādetvā dvāraṃ yojetvā vāgurāni ādāya muggarādinānāvudhahatthā araññaṃ pavisitvā mige pariyesamānā ‘‘ majjhe ṭhite mige gaṇhissāmā ’’ ti yojanamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ parikkhipitvā saṅkhipamānā nigrodhamigasākhamigānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ majjhe katvā parikkhipiṃsu.
vāgurāni.translation_1: They planted food, provided water, blocked the gate, took nets, held various weapons, entered the forest, searched for deer, thought to capture them in the middle, surrounded a league, and enclosed the dwelling place of Kings Nigrodha and Sākha.

sākhamupasaṃvaseti.meaning_2: causes to associate (with); makes cohabit (with); brings into contact (with)
sākhamupasaṃvaseti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Written as one word with sākhaṃ (sākhaṃ + upasaṃvaseti); a compound verb (grammar: pr, comp vb). Causative in form: 'causes to dwell with; makes associate (with)'. 3rd singular present.

upasaṃvase.meaning_2: should dwell near; should associate with; should depend on (for livelihood)
upasaṃvase.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form in the text is upasaṃvase, the optative 3rd singular of upasaṃvasati used in the sense of upagamma saṃvaseyya. Optional optative in -eyya. The commentary glosses na upasaṃvase with na upagamma na saṃvaseyya.
upasaṃvase.example_1: Tattha nigrodhameva seveyyāti tāta tvaṃ vā añño vā attano hitakāmo nigrodhameva seveyya bhajeyya upasaṅkameyya, na sākhamupasaṃvaseti sākhamigaṃ pana na upasaṃvase upagamma na saṃvaseyya, etaṃ nissāya jīvikaṃ na kappeyya.
upasaṃvase.translation_1: In this context, nigrodhameva seveyyāti means: dear child, whether you or another, one who desires their own welfare should keep and associate only with the Banyan deer, not go to the Branch deer; na sākhamupasaṃvaseti means: as for the Branch deer, do not dwell in its vicinity; do not approach or keep company with it, nor should you make your living by relying on it.

kaṇḍinaṃ.meaning_2: having an arrow; with an arrow; arrow-bearer
kaṇḍinaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The word in the verses is the genitive plural or accusative singular of kaṇḍī, a possessive adjective from kaṇḍa ('arrow'). The prose gloss (Kaṇḍamassa atthīti kaṇḍī) explains it as 'one who has an arrow'. The reading of kaṇḍinaṃ in sentence 2 is doubtful; some texts have kaṇḍinaṃ sallaṃ, others kaṇḍinaṃ sallan ti.
kaṇḍinaṃ.example_1: Dhiratthu kaṇḍinaṃ sallanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi.
kaṇḍinaṃ.translation_1: Dhiratthu kaṇḍinaṃ sallanti: while dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching, focusing on the seduction by a former wife.
kaṇḍinaṃ.translation_2: 13. “Shame on the dart of love that pierces a man deeply;

dhiratthūti.meaning_2: shame on!; woe to!; a curse be upon!
dhiratthūti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Indeclinable particle of censure (garahaṇa), used here in the phrase dhiratthūti = dhiratthu + iti. The quoted clause is the gloss of the compound; the exact sandhi splitting of the first element (dhī + ratthu? dhi + iratthu?) is uncertain and left unanalysed.
dhiratthūti.example_1: Nānappakārena kaṇḍena, kumudapattasaṇṭhānathalena ujukagamaneneva sallena ca samannāgataṃ gāḷhavedhinaṃ purisaṃ dhiratthūti ayamettha attho.
dhiratthūti.translation_1: Shame on the man endowed with a dart (salla) of various arrows, a deep-piercer whose tip is shaped like a lotus petal and which travels straight—this is the meaning here.

kaṇḍī.meaning_2: having an arrow; one who has an arrow; arrow-bearer
kaṇḍī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text has kaṇḍī glossed as kaṇḍamassa atthīti, then the accusative kaṇḍinaṃ. The -ī possessive suffix forms a possessive adjective from kaṇḍa, 'having an arrow'.
kaṇḍī.translation_1: He who has an arrow is 'the arrow-bearer' (kaṇḍī); 'that' [is used] for kaṇḍinaṃ.

sallakaṇḍinanti.meaning_2: having a dart-like arrow; with an arrow that is a dart
sallakaṇḍinanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text the compound is sallakaṇḍinaṃ (glossed as kaṇḍinaṃ sallan), quoted with -ti, which is dropped here. Locative or genitive singular.
sallakaṇḍinanti.example_1: Taṃ pana kaṇḍaṃ anupavisanaṭṭhena ‘‘ sallan ’’ ti vuccati, tasmā kaṇḍinaṃ sallanti ettha sallakaṇḍinanti attho.
sallakaṇḍinanti.translation_1: That arrow is called 'a dart' (salla) in the sense of penetrating; therefore, in this passage kaṇḍinaṃ sallanti, the meaning is 'a dart that pierces'.

dhikkitāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form in the text is dhikkitāti = dhikkitā + iti, nominative plural (or singular) of the adjective. Dictionary entry dhikkita is a compound of the interjection dhi and kata (done). The final -ti is the quotation particle iti.

vātamigantiādimāha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the quoted phrase vātamigaṃ iti with ādimāha (ādiṃ + āha), a common commentarial idiom 'he said, beginning with ...'. vātamigaṃ may be an accusative quotation; if preferred, the phrase could be analysed as vātamigaṃ + ādimāha with iti implicit.

uggaṇhāpitoti.meaning_2: causes to learn; has (someone) recite; makes take up
uggaṇhāpitoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form uggaṇhāpitoti is uggaṇhāpito + iti; the awkward cluster -ṇhāpito looks like a doubled causative of uggaṇhāti (also seen as uggāhāpeti). Treated here as causative 3rd singular; the form is doubtful, possibly aorist or absolutive in context.

paṭipaṇāmanena.meaning_2: making retreat; pushing away; driving back
paṭipaṇāmanena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular in the text, paired with abhimukhākaḍḍhanena (pulling towards) and contrasted with it: pushing away. Some editions read paṭipanāmanena.
paṭipaṇāmanena.example_1: Aparo nayo – pādena paṃsuṃ gahetvā abhimukhākaḍḍhanena, paṭipaṇāmanena, ubhosu passesu sañcaraṇena, udaraṃ uddhaṃ pakkhipanena, adho avakkhipanenāti imāhi chahi kalāhi yathā atibhoti,‘‘ mato ayan ’’ ti saññaṃ uppādetvā vañceti, evaṃ taṃ migamāyaṃ uggaṇhāpesinti dīpeti.
paṭipaṇāmanena.translation_1: Another method—by taking soil with his hooves, by pulling it toward him, by pushing it away, by moving on both sides, by throwing his belly upward, and by letting it sag downward—in these six ways, he deceives by causing the perception, 'This one is dead,' and it is shown that I taught him the deer's ruses in this way.

ketakavane.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text: "while dwelling in the Ketaka forest". Name of a forest near the Naḷakapāna lotus pond.
ketakavane.example_1: Disvā padamanuttiṇṇanti idaṃ satthā kosalesu cārikaṃ caramāno naḷakapānagāmaṃ patvā naḷakapānapokkharaṇiyaṃ ketakavane viharanto naḷadaṇḍake ārabbha kathesi.
ketakavane.translation_1: “Having seen the footprints leading down”—The Teacher told this when traveling on tour among the Kosalans, having arrived at the village of Naḷakapāna, while dwelling at the Ketaka forest near the Naḷakapāna lotus pond, referring to the reeds.

kaṇḍi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of one of the horses (or horse-like animals) in the list; nominative singular in the text. Possibly a proper name from kaṇḍa. Uncertain.
kaṇḍi.translation_1: Nigrodha, Lakkhaṇa, Kaṇḍi, Vātamiga, and Kharādiya,

visiṇṇaphalo.meaning_2: with scattered fruit; whose fruit is fallen and scattered
visiṇṇaphalo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Used of a tree whose fruit has been strewn about. Nom sg masc in -o in the text.
visiṇṇaphalo.example_1: Yaṃ tvaṃ sepaṇṇi seyyasīti yaṃ tvaṃ ambho sepaṇṇirukkha purato phalāni pātayamāno seyyasi viseyyasi visiṇṇaphalo hosi, taṃ sabbaṃ kuruṅgamigassa pākaṭaṃ jātaṃ.
visiṇṇaphalo.translation_1: Yaṃ tvaṃ sepaṇṇi seyyasī means: “O Sepanni tree, by causing the fruit to fall in front [of me], you are misbehaving; you have become a tree with scattered fruit; all that is evident to the antelope.”

vacaraṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text vacaraṃ is accusative singular. Probably a rare variant of vacana. The given PEU entries relate to vacana and vacatta, not directly to vacara.
vacaraṃ.translation_1: Having heard the words of the Great Being, the king said:

cātujjātikagandhūpalittāyameva.meaning_2: the anointing with four kinds of perfume; the smearing with four types of fragrance
cātujjātikagandhūpalittāyameva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text the form is cātujjātikagandhūpalittāyameva = cātujjātikagandhupalittāya + eva, locative singular with emphatic eva. The compound is cātujjātika + gandhupalittaya; gandhupalitta is itself gandha + upalitta (pp of upalimpati). Sandhi -a + u- > -ū-. The abstract formation gandhupalitta + ya gives gandhupalittaya; the long ā in the lemma_1 is the locative ending -āya, not part of the stem.
cātujjātikagandhūpalittāyameva.example_1: So satasahassagghanikāya suvaṇṇapātiyaṃyeva nānaggarasasampannaṃ tivassikagandhasālibhojanaṃ bhuñjati, cātujjātikagandhūpalittāyameva bhūmiyaṃ tiṭṭhati, taṃ ṭhānaṃ rattakambalasāṇiparikkhittaṃ upari suvaṇṇatārakakhacitacelavitānaṃ samosaritagandhadāmamālādāmaṃ avijahitagandhatelapadīpaṃ hoti.
cātujjātikagandhūpalittāyameva.translation_1: He consumed fragrant three-year-old rice, rich in various excellent flavors, served only in a golden dish worth a hundred thousand, and stood on ground anointed with the four types of perfumes; that place was enclosed by red wool curtains, with a gold-star-studded star-canopy overhead, clustered with garlands of perfumes and flowers, and illuminated by scented oil lamps that never went out.

attanno.meaning_2: of himself; to himself; for himself
attanno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Attanno = attano, the genitive/dative singular of the reflexive pronoun attan, here meaning 'to him' (referring to the king). The text has the doubled consonant nn by sandhi or scribal variation.
attanno.example_1: Rājā tassa sarīrakiccaṃ kāretvā assārohassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ datvā satta rājāno puna attanno adubbhāya sapathaṃ kāretvā sakasakaṭṭhānāni pesetvā dhammena samena rajjaṃ kāretvā jīvitapariyosāne yathākammaṃ gato.
attanno.translation_1: The King had the body properly tended to, bestowed great honor upon the cavalry warrior, made the seven kings take an oath never to attack him again and sent them to their respective lands, and ruled his kingdom in accordance with the Dhamma, passing away at the end of his life to fare according to his kamma.

nhāpetuṃ.meaning_2: causes to bathe; has (someone) bathed; gives a bath (to)
nhāpetuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of the causative nhāpeti ('to cause to bathe'); here nhāpetuṃ vaṭṭati, 'it is proper to bathe (him)'. Related forms nhāpetha, nhāpetvā.
nhāpetuṃ.example_1: Bodhisatto ‘‘ esa attano sindhavatāya jigucchanto ettha nhāyituṃ na icchati, imaṃ aññatitthe nhāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti tassa āsayaṃ ñatvā ‘‘ bho assagopaka, sappimadhuphāṇitādibhisaṅkhatapāyāsampi tāva punappunaṃ bhuñjantassa titti hoti.
nhāpetuṃ.translation_1: The Bodhisatta, knowing his inclination—that he did not wish to bathe there because of his noble Sindh nature, and that it would be proper to bathe him in another bathing place—said, “My friend horse-keeper, even for one who repeatedly eats porridge prepared with ghee, honey, and molasses, there can be satiety.

paādātave.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is glossed as pa + ā + dātave, with the ā elided by sandhi. The infinitive suffix -tave is added to √ādā with the loss of the initial ā.
paādātave.example_1: Padātaveti paādātave, sandhivasena ākāralopo veditabbo, gahetunti attho.
paādātave.translation_1: Padātave means pa-ā-dātave; the elision of the 'ā' should be understood due to sandhi; the meaning is 'to take'.

nhāpiyamāno.meaning_2: being bathed (by); being made to bathe; being given a bath
nhāpiyamāno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative passive present participle, masculine nominative singular in the text, agreeing with the subject being bathed. Passive of the causative nhāpayati (makes bathe); the -i- is a glide before the passive -ya-. Sometimes analysed as nhāpīyamāna.
nhāpiyamāno.translation_1: Na ghaṃsituṃ means when being bathed, he is not able even to rub his body.

ovijjhanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] 3rd plural present in the text, in a list of verbal abuses (with khuṃsenti, vambhenti). The PEU analysis ava + vidha + ya + anti gives the same sense: piercing with harsh words.
ovijjhanti.example_1: Tasmiñhi samaye chabbaggiyā kalahaṃ karontā pesale bhikkhū khuṃsenti vambhenti ovijjhanti, dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosanti.
ovijjhanti.translation_1: For at that time, the Six-monk group, when quarrelling, would disparage, denigrate, and abuse the good-hearted monks with the ten types of verbal abuse.

pavaṭṭetuṃ.meaning_2: to roll forward; to set in motion; to haul (a load)
pavaṭṭetuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of pavaṭṭeti, used here with sakaṭasataṃ ('a hundred carts'): 'able to set a hundred loaded carts in motion'. The form is pavaṭṭetuṃ, from pa + vaṭṭeti (causative of vaṭṭati).
pavaṭṭetuṃ.example_1: Brāhmaṇo ‘‘ mayhaṃ eko goṇo atibaddhaṃ sakaṭasataṃ pavaṭṭetuṃ samattho atthī ’’ ti āha.
pavaṭṭetuṃ.translation_1: The brahmin said, “I have a bull who is capable of pulling a hundred loaded carts hitched together.”

bhandrāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Unidentified word, no context found. Possibly a sandhi of bhandrā + ti or a quotation ending in -ti; cannot analyse without the sentence.

udaddharīti.meaning_2: took out; pulled out; lifted up; drew out
udaddharīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The -īti at the end is the sandhi of udaddhari + iti, so the entry is for the aorist itself. Aorist 3rd singular, with the same ending as upasaṅkami.

munikaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a pig in a Jātaka story. Accusative singular in the text (munikaṃ).
munikaṃ.example_1: Tassā mātāpitaro ‘‘ kumārikāya vivāhakāle āgatānaṃ pāhunakānaṃ uttaribhaṅgo bhavissatī ’’ ti yāgubhattaṃ datvā munikaṃ nāma sūkaraṃ posesuṃ.
munikaṃ.translation_1: Her parents, thinking, ‘There must be a relish for the guests who come on the day of the maiden’s wedding,’ gave rice gruel and boiled rice to feed a pig named Munika.
munikaṃ.example_2: Tato na cirasseva te manussā āgamiṃsu, munikaṃ ghātetvā nānappakārehi paciṃsu.
munikaṃ.translation_2: Not long after that, those people arrived; they killed Munika and cooked him in many ways.

munikabhāvaṃ.meaning_2: state of being a pig; condition of a munika
munikabhāvaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text. Here munika refers to a pig in the story; the second element bhāva means 'state, condition'.
munikabhāvaṃ.example_1: Tattha mā munikassa pihayīti munikassa bhojane pihaṃ mā uppādayi,‘‘ esa muniko subhojanaṃ bhuñjatī ’’ ti mā munikassa pihayi,‘‘ kadā nu kho ahampi evaṃ sukhito bhaveyyan ’’ ti mā munikabhāvaṃ patthayi.
munikabhāvaṃ.translation_1: Regarding ‘do not envy Munika’, do not give rise to envy regarding Munika’s food; do not be jealous of Munika thinking ‘this pig eats good food’; do not desire to be like Munika thinking ‘when will I too be happy like this’; do not desire the state of Munika.

munikoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form munikoti is munika + iti, so the entry is for the word without the quotation particle. Perhaps a jātaka animal name. The related PEU entry gives the same analysis.

munikasūkaro.meaning_2: Munika the pig; porker named Munika
munikasūkaro.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of a pig in the Jātaka story. Nominative singular in the text. Munika is a proper name, so the compound is not translated word by word.
munikasūkaro.example_1: ‘‘ tadā munikasūkaro ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu ahosi, thullakumārikā esā eva, cūḷalohito ānando, mahālohito pana ahameva ahosin ’’ ti.
munikasūkaro.translation_1: “Munika the pig of those days was the passion-tost bhikkhu, the plump young woman is the same person, Little Red was Ānanda, and Big Red was I myself.”

munikanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi with -ti (munikanti) is not analysed here; the entry is for the name Munika.
munikanti.translation_1: The ford, the face of the elephant, the habitual, the Nandi-Visāla, the Kaṇha, and the Munika.

uragakaroṭipayassa.meaning_2: of the serpents and water-goblins; serpents and water-spirits
uragakaroṭipayassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Variant or misreading of uragakaroṭipayānaṃ (genitive plural), meaning 'of the serpents and the karoṭipāya spirits'; a class of mythical beings alongside Kumbhaṇḍas and Mahārājāno. Treated here as a sandhi or compound form; the final -payassa may be genitive singular or a garbled genitive plural.
uragakaroṭipayassa.example_1: Uragakaroṭipayassa ca hārī, madanayutā caturo ca mahantā ’’ ti.(saṃ. ni. aṭṭha.1.1.247);
uragakaroṭipayassa.translation_1: Nagas, Garuḷas, Kumbhaṇḍas, Goblins, and the Four Great Kings.”

karoṭisaddena.meaning_2: sound of a karoṭi (snake); noise of a karoṭi
karoṭisaddena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular in the text: "by the sound of a karoṭi". karoṭi is a kind of snake, sometimes a mythical creature.

karoṭi.meaning_2: name of a food and drink of the supaṇṇas; food bowl
karoṭi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the Jātaka prose, karoṭi is the name of the supaṇṇas' food and drink, and also their name (karoṭi-saddena). Not a verbal form here; the PEU headword karoṭi is fem.
karoṭi.translation_1: Supaṇṇas are taken by the word 'karoṭi'.
karoṭi.example_2: Tesaṃ kira karoṭi nāma pānabhojanaṃ, tena taṃ nāmaṃ labhiṃsu, dutiyālinde tesaṃ ārakkhā.
karoṭi.translation_2: Their drink and food is called 'karoṭi', thus they got that name; their guard is on the second terrace.

eḷālukoti.meaning_2: cucumber; a kind of cucumber vegetable
eḷālukoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form is eḷālukoti = eḷālukaṃ + iti, with the quotation particle. Often found in the phrase eḷālukoti ("cucumber, it is said"); the PEU also records a homonym eḷāluka 2 meaning cucumber-seller.

ukkaṇṭhāpitoti.meaning_2: caused to be bored; made to be annoyed; caused to be discontented
ukkaṇṭhāpitoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Past participle of the causative ukkaṇṭhāpeti. In the text it carries the quotative -ti, so the entry is for ukkaṇṭhāpita. Normative spelling would be ukkaṇṭhāpita, but the given form has -ā-.

mantiādīsu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] mantiādīsu = mantī + ādīsu (locative plural); variant manti- possible by analogy. The gerundive of √mant (caus.) is also the source of mantī in some analyses.

avattharituṃ.meaning_2: to overwhelm; to spread over; to cover
avattharituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -tuṃ of avattharati (ava + √thar). In these sentences, said of fire that cannot spread over or cover the place where the Buddha stands. Note avattharitvā in PEU.
