avattharituṃ.example_1: Āgantvā tathāgatassa ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ patvā tassa padesassa samantā soḷasakarīsamattaṭṭhānaṃ patto udake opilāpitatiṇukkā viya nibbāyi, vinibbedhato dvattiṃsakarīsamattaṭṭhānaṃ avattharituṃ nāsakkhi.
avattharituṃ.translation_1: Upon reaching the place where the Tathāgata stood, when it arrived within sixteen lengths, it went out like a torch plunged into water; it was unable to sweep over the thirty-two lengths of ground around him.
avattharituṃ.example_2: ‘‘ aho buddhānaṃ guṇā nāma, ayañhi nāma acetano aggi buddhānaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ avattharituṃ na sakkoti, udake tiṇukkā viya nibbāyati, aho buddhānaṃ ānubhāvo nāmā ’’ ti.
avattharituṃ.translation_2: “Oh, how great are the virtues of the Buddhas! For even this senseless fire cannot sweep over the place where the Buddha stands; it goes out like a torch in water. Oh, the power of the Buddhas!”

samparetabbe.meaning_2: to be reached; to be attained; to be gone to; to be approached
samparetabbe.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Potential participle used impersonally in the text: 'samparetabbe' is locative absolute, 'when (the next world) is to be gone to'. The prefix parā is assimilated to para in the spelling samparetabba.
samparetabbe.example_1: Samparāye ca suggatīti samparetabbe imaṃ lokaṃ hitvā gantabbe paralokepi tesaṃ sugatiyeva hotīti.
samparetabbe.translation_1: 'And in the next world a good bourn' means in the future world, which must be gone to after abandoning this world, a good bourn is attained for them.

nikatyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular in the text. The commentary glosses it as vañcanā (deceit). Derived from nikata (deceitful) with an abstract feminine suffix -i.
nikatyā.translation_1: 38. “One whose wisdom is guile does not find happiness through guile;
nikatyā.example_2: Tattha nāccantaṃ nikatippañño , nikatyā sukhamedhatīti nikati vuccati vañcanā, nikatippañño vañcanapañño puggalo tāya nikatyā nikatiyā vañcanāya na accantaṃ sukhamedhati, niccakāle sukhasmiṃyeva patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkoti, ekaṃsena pana vināsaṃ pāpuṇātiyevāti attho.
nikatyā.translation_2: There, regarding the lines “One whose wisdom is guile does not find happiness through guile”: guile is called deceit. An individual whose wisdom is guile is a person whose intelligence is deceptive. Through that guile—that deceit—he does not find happiness, he is unable to remain permanently in happiness; rather, he categorically meets only with ruin. This is the meaning.

āmadāsisaṅkhātāya.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine instrumental singular agreeing with dāsiyā. Compound of āma, dāsī and saṅkhāta (pp of saṅkhāyati).
āmadāsisaṅkhātāya.example_1: Āmajātoti ‘‘ āma, ahaṃ vo dāsī ’’ ti evaṃ dāsabyaṃ upagatāya āmadāsisaṅkhātāya dāsiyā putto.
āmadāsisaṅkhātāya.translation_1: “Low-born” means the son of a female slave who is known as a ‘slave-mother’ because she entered into slavery saying, ‘Yes, I am your slave-woman.’

aṇḍavakucchiyaṃ.meaning_2: the womb of the deep; the belly of the ocean; the ocean floor
aṇḍavakucchiyaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound used to mean the depths of the ocean, the sea floor where the bronze jars rolled. Locative singular in the text.
aṇḍavakucchiyaṃ.example_1: Aññā panassa kulasantakā aṭṭhārasa koṭiyo nadītīre nidahitvā ṭhapitā aciravatodakena nadīkūle bhinne mahāsamuddaṃ paviṭṭhā, tā yathāpihitalañchi tāva lohacāṭiyo aṇḍavakucchiyaṃ pavaṭṭantā vicaranti.
aṇḍavakucchiyaṃ.translation_1: Furthermore, another eighteen crores of ancestral wealth that had been buried on the banks of the Aciravatī river were washed into the great ocean when the riverbank collapsed; and those bronze jars, still sealed and fastened, rolled along and wandered on the floor of the deep.

pavaṭṭantā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle agreeing with lohacāṭiyo (nom pl fem). In the text describing the jars rolling about in the ocean.
pavaṭṭantā.example_1: Aññā panassa kulasantakā aṭṭhārasa koṭiyo nadītīre nidahitvā ṭhapitā aciravatodakena nadīkūle bhinne mahāsamuddaṃ paviṭṭhā, tā yathāpihitalañchi tāva lohacāṭiyo aṇḍavakucchiyaṃ pavaṭṭantā vicaranti.
pavaṭṭantā.translation_1: Furthermore, another eighteen crores of ancestral wealth that had been buried on the banks of the Aciravatī river were washed into the great ocean when the riverbank collapsed; and those bronze jars, still sealed and fastened, rolled along and wandered on the floor of the deep.

tvaṃnti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of tvaṃ + iti; the quotation marker -ti is joined to the preceding word and should be left out of the headword. No sentences were supplied, so the reading is uncertain; the form could also be tvaṃ + anti in a different context.

mandībhūte.meaning_2: become weak; diminished; become low; slackened
mandībhūte.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text, used of dwindling income and low water.
mandībhūte.example_1: Seṭṭhinopi nirantaraṃ dānaṃ dentassa vohāre akarontassa āye mandībhūte dhanaṃ parikkhayaṃ agamāsi.
mandībhūte.translation_1: Since the treasurer gave gifts without cease and did no business, his income dwindled and his wealth went to destruction.
mandībhūte.example_2: So bahuudakakāle nadiyā saddhiṃ ekodako hoti, udake mandībhūte visuṃ hoti.
mandībhūte.translation_2: In the season of much water, it was one with the river; when the water was low, it became separate.

uttāsetvā.meaning_2: having frightened; having terrified; having alarmed; having impaled
uttāsetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of uttāseti. Used literally in the sense of frightening (sentence 2) and of impaling on a stake (sentence 3).
uttāsetvā.example_1: Mahāseṭṭhissa hatthato manussehi paṇṇe āropetvā aṭṭhārasakoṭisaṅkhyaṃ dhanaṃ gahitaṃ atthi, tvaṃ tassa āyuttakavesaṃ gahetvā kañci ajānāpetvā tāni paṇṇāni ādāya katipayehi yakkhataruṇehi parivāritā ekena hatthena paṇṇaṃ, ekena lekhaniṃ gahetvā tesaṃ gehaṃ gantvā gehamajjhe ṭhitā attano yakkhānubhāvena te uttāsetvā ‘‘ idaṃ tumhākaṃ iṇapaṇṇaṃ, amhākaṃ seṭṭhi attano issarakāle tumhe na kiñci āha, idāni duggato jāto, tumhehi gahitakahāpaṇāni dethā ’’ ti attano yakkhānubhāvaṃ dassetvā sabbāpi tā aṭṭhārasa hiraññakoṭiyo sādhetvā seṭṭhissa tucchakoṭṭhake pūretvā aññaṃ aciravatinadītīre nidahitaṃ dhanaṃ nadīkūle bhinne samuddaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ atthi, tampi attano ānubhāvena āharitvā tucchakoṭṭhake pūretvā, aññampi asukaṭṭhāne nāma assāmikaṃ aṭṭhārasakoṭimattameva dhanaṃ atthi, tampi āharitvā tucchakoṭṭhake pūrehi, imāhi catupaññāsakoṭīhi imaṃ tucchakoṭṭhakapūrakaṃ daṇḍakammaṃ katvā mahāseṭṭhiṃ khamāpehīti.
uttāsetvā.translation_1: “There are eighteen crores of debt owed to the treasurer by people recorded in notes. Take the form of his agent, and without letting anyone know, take those notes in the company of some young yakkhas. In one hand hold the note and in the other a stylus, stand in the middle of their houses, and by your yakkha power terrify them, saying, ‘Here is your debt note. Our treasurer did not move in this matter during his time of prosperity, but now he is poor; pay up!’ By showing your power, recover all those eighteen crores and fill the treasurer's empty storehouses. There is another eighteen crores of his that was buried on the riverbank, which collapsed and went into the ocean; recover that by your power and fill the empty storehouses. Further, there is another eighteen crores of unowned wealth in such-and-such a place; recover that as well and fill the empty storehouses. Having performed this atonement of filling the empty storehouses with these fifty-four crores, ask the treasurer to forgive you.”
uttāsetvā.example_2: Bodhisatto manusse āṇāpesi ‘‘ gacchatha tumhe, uyyāne sabbā makkaṭiyo upadhāretha, yassā taṃ piḷandhanaṃ passatha, taṃ uttāsetvā piḷandhanaṃ gaṇhathā ’’ ti.
uttāsetvā.translation_2: The Bodhisatta ordered his men, “You go and keep watch on all the monkeys in the park. If you see the one that has the treasure, frighten it and take the treasure.”

gahitakahāpaṇāni.meaning_2: money to be taken; debts to be collected; borrowed money
gahitakahāpaṇāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text the ending -āni is nominative or accusative plural. The compound may also be read as adj. A lexical entry, not a word of the canon.
gahitakahāpaṇāni.example_1: Mahāseṭṭhissa hatthato manussehi paṇṇe āropetvā aṭṭhārasakoṭisaṅkhyaṃ dhanaṃ gahitaṃ atthi, tvaṃ tassa āyuttakavesaṃ gahetvā kañci ajānāpetvā tāni paṇṇāni ādāya katipayehi yakkhataruṇehi parivāritā ekena hatthena paṇṇaṃ, ekena lekhaniṃ gahetvā tesaṃ gehaṃ gantvā gehamajjhe ṭhitā attano yakkhānubhāvena te uttāsetvā ‘‘ idaṃ tumhākaṃ iṇapaṇṇaṃ, amhākaṃ seṭṭhi attano issarakāle tumhe na kiñci āha, idāni duggato jāto, tumhehi gahitakahāpaṇāni dethā ’’ ti attano yakkhānubhāvaṃ dassetvā sabbāpi tā aṭṭhārasa hiraññakoṭiyo sādhetvā seṭṭhissa tucchakoṭṭhake pūretvā aññaṃ aciravatinadītīre nidahitaṃ dhanaṃ nadīkūle bhinne samuddaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ atthi, tampi attano ānubhāvena āharitvā tucchakoṭṭhake pūretvā, aññampi asukaṭṭhāne nāma assāmikaṃ aṭṭhārasakoṭimattameva dhanaṃ atthi, tampi āharitvā tucchakoṭṭhake pūrehi, imāhi catupaññāsakoṭīhi imaṃ tucchakoṭṭhakapūrakaṃ daṇḍakammaṃ katvā mahāseṭṭhiṃ khamāpehīti.
gahitakahāpaṇāni.translation_1: “There are eighteen crores of debt owed to the treasurer by people recorded in notes. Take the form of his agent, and without letting anyone know, take those notes in the company of some young yakkhas. In one hand hold the note and in the other a stylus, stand in the middle of their houses, and by your yakkha power terrify them, saying, ‘Here is your debt note. Our treasurer did not move in this matter during his time of prosperity, but now he is poor; pay up!’ By showing your power, recover all those eighteen crores and fill the treasurer's empty storehouses. There is another eighteen crores of his that was buried on the riverbank, which collapsed and went into the ocean; recover that by your power and fill the empty storehouses. Further, there is another eighteen crores of unowned wealth in such-and-such a place; recover that as well and fill the empty storehouses. Having performed this atonement of filling the empty storehouses with these fifty-four crores, ask the treasurer to forgive you.”

saṃvaḍḍhiyamāno.meaning_2: being raised; being brought up; growing up; being nurtured
saṃvaḍḍhiyamāno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative passive present participle. Nominative singular agreeing with bodhisatto. The PEU split guesses an extra ṇe; a causative saṃvaḍḍheti with passive -iya is simpler. Sometimes written saṃvaḍḍhamāna.
saṃvaḍḍhiyamāno.example_1: Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto bārāṇasiseṭṭhissa kule nibbattitvā nānappakārehi sukhūpakaraṇehi devakumāro viya saṃvaḍḍhiyamāno anukkamena viññutaṃ patvā soḷasavassakāleyeva sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ patto.
saṃvaḍḍhiyamāno.translation_1: In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the family of the Benares treasurer. He was raised with various luxuries like a prince, and as he gradually reached intelligence, by the age of sixteen, he had perfected all the arts.

losakatissattheraṃ.meaning_2: Elder Losaka Tissa; the elder named Losaka Tissa
losakatissattheraṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a monk in the Jātaka commentary. Accusative singular in the text. The name parts losaka and tissa are themselves names.
losakatissattheraṃ.example_1: Yo atthakāmassāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto losakatissattheraṃ nāma ārabbha kathesi.
losakatissattheraṃ.translation_1: “Yo atthakāmassā” — This Dhamma discourse was taught by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana about the Elder named Losaka Tissa.
losakatissattheraṃ.example_2: Taṃ gahetvā gatā losakatissattheraṃ asaritvā sayameva bhuñjiṃsu.
losakatissattheraṃ.translation_2: Those who took it, forgetting Elder Losaka Tissa, ate it themselves.

losakatissatthero.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of a monk with little merit. Nominative singular in the text.
losakatissatthero.translation_1: Who, then, was this Elder named Losaka Tissa?
losakatissatthero.example_2: So mahallakakāle ‘‘ losakatissatthero ’’ ti paññāyittha appapuñño appalābho.
losakatissatthero.translation_2: In his old age, he was known as Elder Losaka Tissa, having little merit and few gains.

kevaṭṭiyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine form of kevaṭṭa. Instrumental singular in the text (kevaṭṭiyā kucchismiṃ = in the womb of a fisherman's wife).
kevaṭṭiyā.example_1: So kira nibbattaṭṭhānetā cavitvā kosalaraṭṭhe ekasmiṃ kulasahassavāse kevaṭṭagāme ekissā kevaṭṭiyā kucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi.
kevaṭṭiyā.translation_1: They say that upon passing away from his previous place of existence, he took conception in the womb of a fisherman's wife in a fisherman's village of a thousand families in the Kosala country.

losakatissattheroti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of Losakatissatthero + iti. In the text it introduces the name Losaka Tissa Thera; the -ti marks a quotation or thought.

losakassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of Elder Losaka Tissa in the Jātaka commentary. Genitive singular in the text (losakassa).
losakassa.example_1: Theropi ‘‘ imaṃ losakassa dethā ’’ ti laddhāhāraṃ pesesi.
losakassa.translation_1: The Elder sent the food he had obtained, saying, “Give this to Elder Losaka Tissa.”

losakattheraṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of an elder, also called Losaka Tissa. Compound of losaka + thera. Accusative singular in the text.
losakattheraṃ.example_1: Thero ‘‘ hotāvuso, idheva nisīdā ’’ ti losakattheraṃ āsanasālāyaṃ nisīdāpetvā kosalarañño nivesanaṃ agamāsi.
losakattheraṃ.translation_1: The Elder said, “Friend, stay here; sit right there,” and having seated Elder Losaka Tissa in the refectory, he went to the palace of the King of Kosala.

rasaparissāvanakaroṭiṃ.meaning_2: colander; strainer for liquids; filtering cup
rasaparissāvanakaroṭiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text. PEU gives thī (feminine).
rasaparissāvanakaroṭiṃ.example_1: Bhattakārako nānappakāraṃ macchamaṃsavikatiṃ sampādetvā usumanikkhamanatthaṃ bhājanāni thokaṃ vivaritvā rasaparissāvanakaroṭiṃ bhājanamatthake ṭhapetvā bahi nikkhamitvā sedaṃ puñchamāno aṭṭhāsi.
rasaparissāvanakaroṭiṃ.translation_1: The cook prepared various types of fish and meat, opened the pots slightly to let the steam out, placed the colander on top of the vessels, went outside, and stood wiping his sweat.

cuṇṇikamaṃsanti.meaning_2: minced meat; meat cut into small pieces
cuṇṇikamaṃsanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form is cuṇṇikamaṃsanti, i.e. cuṇṇikamaṃsaṃ + iti, with sandhi and the quotative particle. Treated as one compound; alternatively cuṇṇika is an adjective meaning 'powdered, minced'.

cuṇṇikamaṃsena.meaning_2: minced meat; chopped meat; small pieces of meat
cuṇṇikamaṃsena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular in the text (cuṇṇikamaṃsena). The crow contrasts it with mahāmaṃsa, a large piece of meat.
cuṇṇikamaṃsena.example_1: Tasmiṃ khaṇe kāko pacchito sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā bhattagehaṃ olokento tassa nikkhantabhāvaṃ ñatvā ‘‘ ayaṃdāni mayhaṃ manorathaṃ pūretvā maṃsaṃ khādituṃ kālo, kiṃ nu kho mahāmaṃsaṃ khādāmi, udāhu cuṇṇikamaṃsan ’’ ti cintetvā ‘‘ cuṇṇikamaṃsena nāma khippaṃ kucchiṃ pūretuṃ na sakkā, mahantaṃ maṃsakhaṇḍaṃ āharitvā pacchiyaṃ nikkhipitvā khādamāno nipajjissāmī ’’ ti pacchito uppatitvā rasakaroṭiyaṃ nilīyi.
cuṇṇikamaṃsena.translation_1: At that moment, the crow lifted his head from the basket, looked into the kitchen, and knowing he had gone out, thought, “Now is the time for me to fulfill my heart’s desire and eat meat. Should I eat a large chunk or minced meat?” Thinking, “One cannot quickly fill the stomach with minced meat,” he decided, “I will take a large piece of meat, put it in the basket, and lie there eating it,” so he flew up from the basket and alighted on the colander.

rasakaroṭiyaṃ.meaning_2: colander; strainer; spouted vessel; vessel for filtering liquids
rasakaroṭiyaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text (rasakaroṭiyaṃ). A vessel used in the kitchen; the crow perches on it.
rasakaroṭiyaṃ.example_1: Tasmiṃ khaṇe kāko pacchito sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā bhattagehaṃ olokento tassa nikkhantabhāvaṃ ñatvā ‘‘ ayaṃdāni mayhaṃ manorathaṃ pūretvā maṃsaṃ khādituṃ kālo, kiṃ nu kho mahāmaṃsaṃ khādāmi, udāhu cuṇṇikamaṃsan ’’ ti cintetvā ‘‘ cuṇṇikamaṃsena nāma khippaṃ kucchiṃ pūretuṃ na sakkā, mahantaṃ maṃsakhaṇḍaṃ āharitvā pacchiyaṃ nikkhipitvā khādamāno nipajjissāmī ’’ ti pacchito uppatitvā rasakaroṭiyaṃ nilīyi.
rasakaroṭiyaṃ.translation_1: At that moment, the crow lifted his head from the basket, looked into the kitchen, and knowing he had gone out, thought, “Now is the time for me to fulfill my heart’s desire and eat meat. Should I eat a large chunk or minced meat?” Thinking, “One cannot quickly fill the stomach with minced meat,” he decided, “I will take a large piece of meat, put it in the basket, and lie there eating it,” so he flew up from the basket and alighted on the colander.
rasakaroṭiyaṃ.example_2: So bhattakārake macchamaṃsaṃ pacitvā mahānasā nikkhamma sarīrato sedaṃ pavāhente pacchito nikkhamitvā rasakaroṭiyaṃ nilīyitvā ‘‘ kiri kirī ’’ ti saddamakāsi.
rasakaroṭiyaṃ.translation_2: While the cook, having cooked fish and meat, exited the kitchen, letting sweat stream from his body, he [the crow] exited the basket, hid himself in a spice container, and made a “kiri kiri” sound.

lolyaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The PEU entry reads lolya as lola + ṇya (nt). In the sentence it is nominative singular, subject of the clause tañca pana te lolyaṃ nissāya; the variant reading loloyeva shows the adjective lola nearby.
lolyaṃ.example_1: Satthāpi ‘‘ na tvaṃ bhikkhu idāneva lolo, pubbepi loloyeva, tañca pana te lolyaṃ nissāya paṇḍitāpi sakāvāsā parihīnā ’’ ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu anāgāmiphalaṃ patto.
lolyaṃ.translation_1: The Teacher said, “You, bhikkhu, are not greedy only now; you were greedy in the past as well, and because of that greed of yours, the wise were forced to abandon their home,” and having brought forth this discourse, he revealed the Truths; at the end of the Truths, that bhikkhu attained the fruit of non-returning.

veḷukotveva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of veḷukot (locative of veḷukota, probably a place name) + iva; no sentences supplied, so the analysis is uncertain.

siñcituṃ.meaning_2: to pour; to sprinkle; to water
siñcituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of siñcati, used with sakkhissatha, vaṭṭati and sakkā. In the text it refers to pouring or sprinkling water on young trees and on the ground.
siñcituṃ.example_1: Yāvāhaṃ āgacchāmi, tāva imasmiṃ uyyāne rukkhapotakesu udakaṃ siñcituṃ sakkhissathā ’’ ti pucchi.
siñcituṃ.translation_1: He asked, "Will you be able to water the young trees in this park until I return?"
siñcituṃ.example_2: ‘‘ āgametha tāva, udakaṃ nāma sabbakālaṃ dullabhaṃ, taṃ rakkhitabbaṃ, uparopake uppāṭetvā mūlappamāṇaṃ ñatvā dīghamūlakesu bahuṃ, rassamūlakesu appaṃ udakaṃ siñcituṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti.
siñcituṃ.translation_2: 'Wait a moment; water is hard to get at all times. It must be conserved. It is fitting to pull up the saplings, know the length of their roots, and water those with long roots with much water and those with short roots with a little.'

āvahitunti.meaning_2: brings; produces; brings about; brings near
āvahitunti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text joined with the quotative -ti (āvahitunti = āvahituṃ + iti?), but the form is the present 3rd singular āvahati with sandhi; note the passage explains Sukhāvahā, so āvaha means 'bring, produce'.
āvahitunti.example_1: Sukhāvahāti evarūpena anatthakusalena kāyikacetasikasukhasaṅkhātassa atthassa cariyā na sukhāvahā, na sakkā āvahitunti attho.
āvahitunti.translation_1: “Does not bring happiness” means that for such an unskilled person, conduct for the sake of benefit—which is defined as physical and mental happiness—does not bring happiness; it cannot be brought about.

āvahituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive form āvahituṃ in the text ('cannot bring about').
āvahituṃ.example_1: Kapi ārāmiko yathāti yathā ārāme niyutto ārāmarakkhanako makkaṭo ‘‘ atthaṃ karissāmī ’’ ti anatthameva karoti, evaṃ yo koci anatthakusalo, tena na sakkā atthacariyaṃ āvahituṃ, so ekaṃsena atthaṃ hāpetiyevāti.
āvahituṃ.translation_1: “Just as the monkey monastery attendant” signifies that just as a monkey engaged in the monastery, acting as its protector, thinks “I will perform a benefit” but does only what is harmful, in the same way, one who is unskilled in what is worthwhile cannot bring about beneficent conduct; that person categorically omits what is worthwhile.

ullokite.meaning_2: looked up (at); looked towards; having looked up
ullokite.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular ullokite in both sentences: 'in the sky being looked up at' and 'in his own face being looked towards'. Also entry given as nt in PEU.
ullokite.example_1: So kira manto anaggho mahāraho, nakkhattayoge laddhe taṃ mantaṃ parivattetvā ākāse ullokite ākāsato sattaratanavassaṃ vassati.
ullokite.translation_1: They say that this charm is priceless and of great value; when a planetary conjunction is obtained, if one recites that charm and looks up at the sky, a shower of the seven precious things rains down from the sky.
ullokite.example_2: Iti mahāsatto ettakaṃ kālaṃ nandapaṇḍitassa pāṭihāriyāni disvā tasmiṃ pasannacitte te rājāno ñāṇabalena tasmiṃ pasādaṃ bhinditvā attano kathaṃ gāhāpetvā sabbeva attano mukhaṃ ullokite akāsi.
ullokite.translation_2: Thus, the Great Being, seeing Nanda the Wise’s wonders for so long, and with his power of knowledge, shattered the confidence of those kings who had confident minds in Nanda, caused his own words to be accepted, and made everyone look towards him.

pesanakacorā.meaning_2: despatcher robber; robber who sends a captive to fetch ransom money
pesanakacorā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of a class of robbers: they seize two people and send one away to get money. Plural in the text.
pesanakacorā.example_1: Athekadivasaṃ brāhmaṇo bodhisattaṃ ādāya kenacideva karaṇīyena attano gāmā nikkhamitvā cetaraṭṭhaṃ agamāsi, antarāmagge ca ekasmiṃ araññaṭṭhāne pañcasatā pesanakacorā nāma panthaghātaṃ karonti.
pesanakacorā.translation_1: Then one day, the brahmin, taking the Bodhisatta, left his village for some business and went to the Ceti country; and along the way, in a certain forest place, five hundred “Despatcher” robbers were carrying out highway robbery.

pesanakacorāti.meaning_2: kidnapper; one who abducts for ransom
pesanakacorāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] -ti is the quotative enclitic (iti), not part of the word; nominative singular in the text. pesanaka is otherwise unattested and its analysis is uncertain.

pesanakacorātveva.meaning_2: like a messenger thief; as if a thief sent on an errand
pesanakacorātveva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of pesanaka + corā + iva (iva elided to va; the vowel of corā lengthened before it). Alternative division pesanakacorā + iva. No sentence supplied, so the case of the parts cannot be confirmed.

vedabboti.meaning_2: name of a brahmin student; name of a person
vedabboti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text with the quotation marker -ti. Nominative singular here. Probably a proper name; no clear analysis as a common noun.

ajeḷakakukkuṭabhūkarādayo.meaning_2: goats, sheep, chickens, pigs and so on
ajeḷakakukkuṭabhūkarādayo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of ajeḷaka (goat), kakkuṭa (chicken), bhūkara (pig) and ādayo (and so on). Appears as an accusative list of animals slaughtered for sacrifice.
ajeḷakakukkuṭabhūkarādayo.example_1: Tasmiṃ samaye bārāṇasivāsino devatāmaṅgalikā honti, devatā namassanti, bahū ajeḷakakukkuṭabhūkarādayo vadhitvā nānappakārehi pupphagandhehi ceva maṃsalohitehi ca balikammaṃ karonti.
ajeḷakakukkuṭabhūkarādayo.translation_1: At that time, the people of Benares were ‘deity-auspicious,’ they worshipped deities, and having slaughtered many goats, sheep, chickens, pigs, and so forth, performed sacrifices with various kinds of flowers and perfumes, and with flesh and blood.

yedāni.meaning_2: from now on; from today; henceforth
yedāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of ye (relative pronoun, here used indefinitely) + dāni (now), meaning 'from now on; henceforth'. Matches ito paṭṭhāya in the commentary.
yedāni.example_1: Evañca pana vatvā ‘‘ yedāni ito paṭṭhāya dussīlakamme vattissanti, tesaṃ sahassaṃ ghātetvā yaññaṃ yajitvā āyācanato muccissāmī ’’ ti etamatthaṃ pakāsento imaṃ gāthamāha –
yedāni.translation_1: And having said this, declaring this matter, saying, “From now on, those who engage in immoral acts, I will kill one thousand of them, perform a sacrifice, and be released from the vow,” he spoke this verse—

rakkhāpetvā.meaning_2: causes to observe; causes to keep; makes guard; causes to protect
rakkhāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive (abs of rakkhāpeti) in -tvā, from the causative of rakkhati. In the sentence rakkhāpetvā takes sīlaṃ as its object: 'having caused (the people) to observe virtue'. Sometimes written rakkhāpetvāna.
rakkhāpetvā.example_1: Evaṃ bodhisatto ekapuggalampi akilamento sakalaraṭṭhavāsino sīlaṃ rakkhāpetvā sayampi dānādīni puññāni katvā jīvitapariyosāne attano parisaṃ ādāya devanagaraṃ pūrento agamāsi.
rakkhāpetvā.translation_1: In this way, without causing hardship to a single individual, the Bodhisatta caused all the inhabitants of the realm to observe virtue, and having himself performed meritorious deeds such as giving, at the end of his life, he took his company and went on to fill the city of the devas.

losakatissakapota.meaning_2: Losaka, Tissa and Kapota (names of three brothers)
losakatissakapota.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A dvanda compound of three personal names. Applied to three brothers in the Jātaka stories; vocative singular in the text.
losakatissakapota.translation_1: Losaka, Tissa, Kapota, Veḷuka, and Makasa too;

veḷukaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Probably a proper name in this context, perhaps a mountain or place. Accusative singular in the text.
veḷukaṃ.translation_1: Losaka, Tissa, Kapota, Veḷuka, and Makasa too;

ārāmadūsaṃ.meaning_2: temple destroyer; one who destroys a monastery; name of a (mythical?) being
ārāmadūsaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Listed among names (Rohiṇī, Vāruṇīdūsa, Vedabba) in the Jātaka prose; probably a variant of ārāmadūsaka. Accusative singular in the text.

itodāni.meaning_2: from now on; from here onwards; henceforth
itodāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Often followed by paṭṭhāya. Occasionally alternative to ajjatagge / ito paṭṭhāya.
itodāni.example_1: ‘‘ Jīvituṃ asakkontā, devā ’’ ti vutte rājā ‘‘ atha kasmā mama santikaṃ nāgamittha, itodāni paṭṭhāya evarūpaṃ kammaṃ mā karitthā ’’ ti tesaṃ dhanaṃ datvā vissajjesi.
itodāni.translation_1: When they replied, “We are unable to make a living, O King,” the King said, “If so, why did you not come to me? From now on, do not do such an act,” and having given them wealth, he released them.
itodāni.translation_2: 84. “From here now needles (sūciyo) and fish-hooks (baḷisāni) go forth (patāyati);

māgamitthāti.meaning_2: do not go further!; you must not go beyond that!
māgamitthāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the prohibitive particle mā with the aorist gamitthāti (2nd plural of gam, 'you went'), used idiomatically as a strong prohibition. The whole word is quoted with -ti.
māgamitthāti.example_1: Tena hi cakkassa yāva nābhito pathaviṃ paviṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ disvā nivatteyyātha, tato anivattantā purato asanisaddaṃ viya suṇissatha, tamhā ṭhānā nivatteyyātha, tato anivattantā tumhākaṃ rathadhuresu chiddaṃ passissatha, tamhā ṭhānā nivatteyyātha, purato māgamitthāti.
māgamitthāti.translation_1: “If that is so, return when you see carriage-wheel tracks sunk into the earth up to the nave. If you do not return from there, you will hear a noise like a thunderbolt in front of you; return from that place. If you do not return from there, you will see a hole at the front of your carriages; return from that place. Do not go further.”

apabyūhi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text has apabyūhi, which appears to be an aorist or imperative form; it is treated here as present 3rd singular. Root √ūh is not in the given list, so the root fields are uncertain.
apabyūhi.example_1: Sopi siṅgālo maraṇabhayabhīto catūhi pādehi rañño uparibhāge paṃsuṃ apabyūhi, rājā paṃsuno sithilabhāvaṃ ñatvā siṅgālaṃ vissajjetvā nāgabalo thāmasampanno aparāparaṃ sañcaranto ubho hatthe ukkhipitvā āvāṭamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ olubbha vātacchinnavalāhako viya nikkhamitvā ṭhito amacce assāsetvā paṃsuṃ viyūhitvā sabbe uddharitvā amaccaparivuto āmakasusāne aṭṭhāsi.
apabyūhi.translation_1: That jackal, too, terrified by the fear of death, scratched away the earth above the King with its four feet; the King, knowing the earth was loose, released the jackal, and being endowed with the strength of an elephant and full of power, thrashing about, lifted both hands, braced himself against the pit's edge, and exited like a cloud-burst carried by the wind; having stood up, he comforted the ministers, dug up the earth, brought them all out, and surrounded by his ministers, he stood in the cemetery.

āsacchedaṃ.meaning_2: cutting off of hope; loss of hope
āsacchedaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text. In the first sentence, āsacchedaṃ vata akatvā means 'without giving up hope'.
āsacchedaṃ.example_1: Sīlavarājāpi kho alaṅkatapaṭiyatto setacchattassa heṭṭhā sarabhapādake kañcanapallaṅke nisinno attano sampattiṃ oloketvā ‘‘ ayañca evarūpā sampatti amaccasahassassa ca jīvitapaṭilābho mayi vīriyaṃ akaronte na kiñci abhavissa, vīriyabalena panāhaṃ naṭṭhañca imaṃ yasaṃ paṭilabhiṃ, amaccasahassassa ca jīvitadānaṃ adāsiṃ, āsacchedaṃ vata akatvā vīriyameva kattabbaṃ.
āsacchedaṃ.translation_1: King Sīlava, too, adorned and dressed, seated under the white canopy on a golden throne with gazelle-legs, contemplating his own prosperity, thought, “This prosperity and the regaining of the life of a thousand ministers would have amounted to nothing had I not exercised energy; by the strength of energy, I have regained this lost status and have given the gift of life to a thousand ministers; without losing hope, one must exercise energy.
āsacchedaṃ.example_2: Na nibbindeyya paṇḍitoti paṇḍito upāyakusalo yuttaṭṭhāne vīriyaṃ karonto ‘‘ ahaṃ imassa vīriyassa phalaṃ na labhissāmī ’’ ti na ukkaṇṭheyya, āsacchedaṃ kareyyāti attho.
āsacchedaṃ.translation_2: “The learned should not despair” means: a learned person, skilled in strategy, while exercising energy in the appropriate place, should not be depressed—thinking, “I will not obtain the fruit of this energy”—nor should one cut off hope; this is the meaning.

āmapakkāni.meaning_2: unripe and ripe; raw and cooked
āmapakkāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of āma (raw, unripe) and pakka (ripe, cooked). Neuter nominative plural in the text, agreeing with phalāni.
āmapakkāni.example_1: Na kevalaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānatova, gandharasehipissa āmapakkāni phalāni ambaphalasadisāneva, khāditāni pana halāhalavisaṃ viya taṅkhaṇaññeva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpenti.
āmapakkāni.translation_1: Not only in color and shape, but also in scent and taste, its unripe and ripe fruits are identical to mango fruits. However, when eaten, they cause instant death like a deadly poison.

vamāpetvā.meaning_2: having made (them) vomit; having caused to vomit
vamāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of the causative vamāpeti (causative of vamati). In the text it takes an object (tepi) and precedes pāyetvā and akāsi.
vamāpetvā.example_1: Tepi vamāpetvā catumadhuraṃ pāyetvā niroge akāsi.
vamāpetvā.translation_1: he made them vomit, gave them the four sweet foods, and restored them to health.

dakalimakuḷamattā.meaning_2: the size of a plantain bud
dakalimakuḷamattā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes the ogre's tusks. Nominative plural agreeing with dāṭhā; possibly plural in -ā used adjectivally.
dakalimakuḷamattā.example_1: Tasmiṃ aṭavimajjhaṃ sampatte so yakkho tālamatto hutvā kūṭāgāramattaṃ sīsaṃ pattappamāṇāni akkhīni, dakalimakuḷamattā dve dāṭhā ca māpetvā setamukho kabarakucchi nīlahatthapādo hutvā bodhisattassa attānaṃ dassetvā ‘‘ kahaṃ yāsi, tiṭṭha bhakkhosi me ’’ ti āha.
dakalimakuḷamattā.translation_1: When he reached the middle of the forest, that ogre made himself as tall as a palm tree, created a head as big as a house-peak, eyes the size of bowls, and two tusks the size of plantain buds, and having a white face, blotched belly, and blue hands and feet, he showed himself to the Bodhisatta and said, “Where are you going? Stop, you are my food.”

phoṭetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā from the causative phoṭeti (√phuṭ 1). In the sentences it describes shaking off arrows and snapping the fingers.
phoṭetvā.example_1: Yakkho sabbepi te sare phoṭetvā attano pādamūleyeva pātetvā bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkami.
phoṭetvā.translation_1: The ogre shook off all those arrows, dropped them right at his feet, and approached the Bodhisatta.
phoṭetvā.example_2: Sabbe kammārā ‘‘ amhehi ettakaṃ kālaṃ ‘ kammārā nāma edisā hontī ’ ti sutivasenapi na sutapubban ’’ ti aṅguliyo phoṭetvā celukkhepasahassaṃ pavattayiṃsu.
phoṭetvā.translation_2: All the smiths (said): “For so long, we have not even heard by rumour (sutivasena) that smiths are of such a kind (sutapubba)!” They snapped their fingers and caused a thousand cloth-wavings to occur (pavatteti).

kumudiniyo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative plural kumudiniyo in the text, counted with uppaliniyo and paduminiyo. Probably a noun in -inī from kumuda, not a direct root derivation.
kumudiniyo.example_1: Atha naṃ evamāha ‘‘ tāta, ahaṃ mahallako, imaṃ yūthaṃ tuyhaṃ niyyādemi, ajjeva taṃ rājānaṃ karomi, asukasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne saro atthi, tattha dve kumudiniyo, tisso uppaliniyo, pañca paduminiyo ca pupphanti, gaccha, tato pupphāni āharā ’’ ti.
kumudiniyo.translation_1: Then he said to him, “Dear son, I am old; I hand this troop over to you; I will make you king today. In such-and-such a place there is a lake; there, two water-lilies, three lotus-clusters, and five lotus-types are blooming; go, bring flowers from there.”

anibbāyantaṃ.meaning_2: not going out; not being extinguished; burning continuously
anibbāyantaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle in the accusative singular agreeing with aggiṃ; formed with the negative prefix na- and the present participle of nibbāti (√vā + ya, irreg).
anibbāyantaṃ.example_1: Tadā bārāṇasiyaṃ ekasmiṃ brāhmaṇakule puttassa jātadivase aggiṃ gahetvā anibbāyantaṃ ṭhapayiṃsu.
anibbāyantaṃ.translation_1: At that time in Benares, in a certain brahmin family, they had kindled a fire on the day their son was born and kept it without letting it go out.

uggaṇhitabbe.meaning_2: to be learned; should be learned; must be learnt
uggaṇhitabbe.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular agreeing with asātamante; the reading uggaṇhitabbe may also be a locative absolute. Note the irregular -ṇh- from √gah.
uggaṇhitabbe.example_1: ‘‘ Ko pana te asātamante uggaṇhitabbe katvā kathesī ’’ ti?
uggaṇhitabbe.translation_1: “Who told you that you had to learn the Asātamanta?”

aniguhanto.meaning_2: not concealing; not hiding; disclosing openly
aniguhanto.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle with the negative prefix na (an-). Nominative singular masculine in the text, agreeing with the subject addressed. The simplex niguhanta is from ni + √guh; the root sign here is irregular.
aniguhanto.example_1: Yañca te mama mātā katheti, taṃ alajjanto aniguhanto mayhaṃ āroceyyāsi, evaṃ karonto asātamante lacchasi, akaronto na lacchasī ’’ ti āha.
aniguhanto.translation_1: “Whatever my mother says to you, report it to me without shame or concealment. If you do this, you will obtain the Asātamanta; if you do not, you will not.”

dhanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form dhanti with -n- is probably a variant or scribal form of dhati. The PEU analysis as dhanati 'it is complete' does not fit the form well. Alternatively an aorist or present form of dhanati 'sounds', but here treated as a feminine noun.

posāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to nourish; having had (her) brought up
posāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of the causative posāpeti (from √pus); the PEU analysis as 'breast-feed' is doubtful, the sense here is 'brought up, reared'.
posāpetvā.example_1: So ca aṅgavijjāya cheko hoti, athekaṃ duggatitthiṃ gabbhiniṃ disvā ‘‘ dhītaraṃ vijāyissatī ’’ ti ñatvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā paribbayaṃ datvā ghareyeva vasāpetvā vijātakāle dhanaṃ datvā uyyojetvā taṃ kumārikaṃ aññesaṃ purisānaṃ daṭṭhuṃ adatvā itthīnaṃyeva hatthe datvā posāpetvā vayappattakāle taṃ attano vase ṭhapesi.
posāpetvā.translation_1: He was skilled in prognostication; seeing a poor pregnant woman, he knew she would give birth to a girl, summoned her, gave her supplies, had her stay in the house, gave wealth at the time of birth, and after sending her away, he kept that girl in his own control, not letting her be seen by other men, and keeping her only in the hands of women; he raised her and, upon her coming of age, kept her under his own control.

tambūlatakkolakādīni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of tambūlaṃ (or tambūla) + takkola + ādīni; accusative plural in the text, object of adāsi. The compound is tambūlatakkolakādi, with -ādīni as the neuter plural ending.
tambūlatakkolakādīni.example_1: ‘‘ Amma, kiṃ te aññattha gatāya, ito paṭṭhāya mameva santikā harā ’’ ti mūlaṃ aggahetvāva bahūni tambūlatakkolakādīni ceva nānāpupphāni ca adāsi.
tambūlatakkolakādīni.translation_1: “Mother, why go elsewhere? From today, bring them from my place,” he said, and without taking payment, he gave her many betel nuts, bdellium, and various flowers.

nilīyāpetvā.meaning_2: having hidden; having concealed; having made hide
nilīyāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of nilīyāpeti (caus of nilīyati, 'to hide oneself'). In the sentence the woman makes the rogue hide. The PEU analysis gives ṇāpe as the sign.
nilīyāpetvā.example_1: Sā ‘‘ evaṃ hotū ’’ ti dhuttaṃ nilīyāpetvā brāhmaṇe āgate evamāha ‘‘ ahaṃ, ayya, tumhesu vīṇaṃ vādentesu naccituṃ icchāmī ’’ ti.
nilīyāpetvā.translation_1: She said, “So be it,” hid the scamp, and when the brahmin came, said, “Master, I wish to dance while you play the lute.”

āmantakesu.meaning_2: one who can be invited; one who may be summoned; addressable person
āmantakesu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative plural in the text, in the phrase āmantakesu nimantakesu. The PEU links it to √mant with the suffix ṇvu; the -ka suffix is clearer. Sometimes glossed as 'able to be called'; the commentary uses it of men who may be invited.
āmantakesu.example_1: Asaddhammavasena hi āmantakesu nimantakesu vijjamānesu mātugāmo nāma na sakkā rakkhitunti.
āmantakesu.translation_1: For indeed, when those who beckon and invite are present, a woman cannot be guarded.

pothiyamānopi.meaning_2: being beaten; being struck; being tortured
pothiyamānopi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Passive present participle; -pi is joined in the text (pothiyamānopi), meaning 'even while being beaten'. PEU suggests putha + ya + māna; √puth (beat, hurt) fits the sense.
pothiyamānopi.example_1: So pothiyamānopi aññaṃ kiñci avatvā ‘‘ kodhanā akataññū ca, pisuṇā mittabhedikā ’’ ti ettakameva vadati.
pothiyamānopi.translation_1: Even while being beaten, he said nothing else but, “Angry, ungrateful, slanderous, and a breaker of friendships,” saying only this.
pothiyamānopi.example_2: Coro cintesi ‘‘ ayaṃ evaṃ pothiyamānopi aññaṃ kiñci avatvā imāneva cattāri padāni vadati, pucchissāmi nan ’’ ti tassā suttabhāvaṃ ñatvā taṃ pucchi ‘‘ ambho tvaṃ evaṃ pothiyamānopi kasmā etāneva padāni vadasī ’’ ti?
pothiyamānopi.translation_2: The robber thought, “He says only these four words even while being beaten like this; I will ask him,” and knowing the girl was sleeping, he asked, “Friend, why do you say only these words while being beaten like this?”

pothetuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive pothetuṃ in the text. Causative of √puth (beat, hurt); 'began to beat' with ārabhi.
pothetuṃ.example_1: Pabuddho jiṇṇāya surāya puna taṃ pothetuṃ ārabhi, sopi tāneva cattāri padāni vadati.
pothetuṃ.translation_1: Awakening when the liquor had worn off, he began to beat him again, but he said only those four words.
pothetuṃ.example_2: Atha naṃ bandhitvā ‘‘ daṇḍaṃ dehī ’’ ti pothetuṃ ārabhiṃsu.
pothetuṃ.translation_2: Then they bound her and began to beat her, saying, “Pay the fine!”

parihāhisītipi.meaning_2: will fall away (from); will decline; will lose
parihāhisītipi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Likely parihāyissati with the final -ssa- assimilated to -si- before the quotation particle ti: parihāyissatī ti > parihāhisīti. Future 2nd singular; the -pi is an emphatic enclitic.

micchatīti.meaning_2: is wrong; is false; goes wrong
micchatīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Perhaps an artificial denominative from micchā; the -ti is the quotation marker. Doubtful reading.

bhaṇḍito.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular masculine agreeing with so. Here it means he had been quarrelled with / abused (by her), i.e. upset by the dispute; some editions read bhaṇḍito as a past participle of bhaṇḍati.
bhaṇḍito.example_1: So pana pariggaṇhanto tassā dussīlabhāvaṃ ñatvā bhaṇḍito cittabyākulatāya sattaṭṭha divase upaṭṭhānaṃ nāgamāsi.
bhaṇḍito.translation_1: He, watching closely and knowing her immoral character, was upset, and because of his confused mind, did not come to wait on the Teacher for seven or eight days.

mahājambuummūlakavāto.meaning_2: wind capable of uprooting a great jambu tree
mahājambuummūlakavāto.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative of comparison in the text (kismiñcideva gaṇeti). Umbrella-standalone ika formation: mahājambuṃ ummūletuṃ samattho vāto.
mahājambuummūlakavāto.example_1: Na hi sineruuppāṭanakavāto hatthimattaṃ muṇḍapabbataṃ, mahājambuummūlakavāto chinnataṭe virūḷhagacchakaṃ, mahāsamuddaṃ vā pana sosanakavāto khuddakataḷākaṃ kismiñcideva gaṇeti, evaṃ uttamabuddhīnaṃ nāma visuddhacittānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ aññāṇabhāvakarā kilesā tayi kiṃ lajjissanti, visuddhāpi sattā saṃkilissanti, uttamayasasamaṅginopi āyasakyaṃ pāpuṇantī ’’ ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.
mahājambuummūlakavāto.translation_1: The wind that can uproot Mount Sineru does not consider a bare hill the size of an elephant; the wind that can uproot a great Jambu tree does not consider a bush growing on a bank; and the wind that can dry up the great ocean does not consider a tiny pond. If defilements, which create ignorance, can do this to Bodhisattas of supreme wisdom and pure minds, how will they not show contempt for you? Even pure beings become defiled, and those possessed of supreme honor suffer disrepute,” and having said this, he told the story of the past.

sosanakavāto.meaning_2: drying wind; wind that dries up
sosanakavāto.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text. The wind that could dry up the great ocean, paired with other destructive winds in the simile.
sosanakavāto.example_1: Na hi sineruuppāṭanakavāto hatthimattaṃ muṇḍapabbataṃ, mahājambuummūlakavāto chinnataṭe virūḷhagacchakaṃ, mahāsamuddaṃ vā pana sosanakavāto khuddakataḷākaṃ kismiñcideva gaṇeti, evaṃ uttamabuddhīnaṃ nāma visuddhacittānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ aññāṇabhāvakarā kilesā tayi kiṃ lajjissanti, visuddhāpi sattā saṃkilissanti, uttamayasasamaṅginopi āyasakyaṃ pāpuṇantī ’’ ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.
sosanakavāto.translation_1: The wind that can uproot Mount Sineru does not consider a bare hill the size of an elephant; the wind that can uproot a great Jambu tree does not consider a bush growing on a bank; and the wind that can dry up the great ocean does not consider a tiny pond. If defilements, which create ignorance, can do this to Bodhisattas of supreme wisdom and pure minds, how will they not show contempt for you? Even pure beings become defiled, and those possessed of supreme honor suffer disrepute,” and having said this, he told the story of the past.

oṇametvā.meaning_2: having bent down; having bowed; having lowered
oṇametvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā of the causative oṇameti (ava + nam + *e). In the sentence it describes pulling the man's head down. Sometimes written avanametvā; the form here shows the ava > o contraction.
oṇametvā.example_1: Atha naṃ sayane ekato nisinnaṃ dāṭhikāsu gahetvā ‘‘ tava samaṇabhāvaṃ vā brāhmaṇabhāvaṃ vā na jānāsī ’’ ti oṇametvā attano abhimukhaṃ ākaḍḍhi.
oṇametvā.translation_1: Then, as he sat on the bed with her, she took him by the whiskers and, pulling him down, drew him towards her, saying, “Do you not know your ascetic or brahmin state?”

aḷārakkhī.meaning_2: wide-eyed woman; woman with beautiful wide eyes
aḷārakkhī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A feminine bahubbīhi adjective used as a noun for a woman. The form in the text is nominative singular; the PEU entry gives the word as 'aḷārakkhi', an adjective meaning 'having wide, beautiful eyes'. Text has aḷārakkhī, so the commenter may be reinterpreting an underlying aḷārakkhī.
aḷārakkhī.example_1: Yato laddhā aḷārakkhī, icchā icchaṃ vijāyathā ’’ ti.
aḷārakkhī.translation_1: But since I have obtained the wide-eyed one, craving has given birth to craving.”
aḷārakkhī.example_2: Yato pana me ayaṃ aḷārakkhī visālanettā sobhanalocanā laddhā, atha me sā purimikā icchā gehataṇhaṃ upakaraṇataṇhaṃ upabhogataṇhanti uparūpari aññaṃ nānappakāraṃ icchaṃ vijāyatha janesi uppādesi.
aḷārakkhī.translation_2: But since I have obtained this wide-eyed one (aḷārakkhī), with her expansive and beautiful eyes, that initial longing (icchā) has given birth to (vijāyatha) and generated other various types of cravings—craving for a household, craving for possessions, craving for comforts, and so on, one after another.

takkapaṇḍi.meaning_2: Takkapaṇḍi; (the ascetic) wise in reasoning; name of a ascetic who lived on buttermilk; name of one of the six famous ascetics
takkapaṇḍi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of an ascetic in the prose Jātaka. Probably a shortened form or variant of Takkapaṇḍita, 'the wise man who lived by buttermilk'; the PEU gives takkapaṇḍita as the full form. Appears in the nominative singular in the verse.

padahituṃ.meaning_2: to strive; to make an effort; to exert oneself
padahituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of padahati, used with padhānaṃ ("to make an effort"). The root is √dhā with the prefix pa; the base daha is irregular.
padahituṃ.example_1: So evaṃ cintesi ‘‘ ahaṃ neva araññe vasituṃ, na padhānaṃ padahituṃ, na bhikkhācariyāya yāpetuṃ sakkhissāmi, ko me gamanena attho, nivattissāmī ’’ ti so vīriyaṃ ossajitvā te bhikkhū anugantvā nivatti.
padahituṃ.translation_1: He thought, “I will not be able to dwell in the forest, to strive with effort, or to subsist on almsfood. What is the use of my going? I will return.” Thus, giving up his effort, he followed those bhikkhus for a while and then turned back.

avigataniddova.meaning_2: as if without having dispelled sleep; as if still sleepy; as if not free from drowsiness
avigataniddova.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of avigataniddo (adj: not having dispelled sleep) + iva (ind: like, as if). Describes the lazy student as still half-asleep. The form -niddova is -niddo + iva.
avigataniddova.example_1: Kusītamāṇavo uṭṭhāya akkhīni puñchitvā puñchitvā avigataniddova varuṇarukkhaṃ abhiruhitvā sākhaṃ gahetvā attano abhimukhaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā bhañjanto bhijjitvā uṭṭhitakoṭiyā attano akkhiṃ bhindāpetvā ekena hatthena taṃ pidhāya ekena hatthena alladārūni bhañjitvā rukkhato oruyha dārukalāpaṃ bandhitvā ukkhipitvā vegena gantvā tehi pātitānaṃ dārūnaṃ upari pātesi.
avigataniddova.translation_1: The lazy student arose, rubbed his eyes repeatedly, and, still half-asleep, climbed the Varuṇa-tree. He grabbed a branch, pulled it toward himself, and as he broke it, the end snapped up, struck his own eye, and ruined it. Covering that eye with one hand, he used the other hand to break off green Varuṇa-branches. He climbed down, bound the faggot, and hurried away, tossing his load on top of the faggots the others had left.

pasādāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Here pañca pasādāni refers to the five clear sense faculties of the elephant. Nominative plural in the text; the -āni ending is irregular for a masculine, or the word may be read as neuter plural here.
pasādāni.example_1: So mātukucchito nikkhanto sabbaseto ahosi rajatapuñjasannibho, akkhīni panassa maṇiguḷasadisāni, paññāyamānāni pañca pasādāni ahesuṃ, mukhaṃ rattakambalasadisaṃ, soṇḍā rattasuvaṇṇabindupaṭimaṇḍitaṃ rajatadāmaṃ viya, cattāro pādā katalākhārasaparikammā viya.
pasādāni.translation_1: When he emerged from his mother’s womb, he was all white, resembling a heap of silver. His eyes were like beads of gems; his five faculties were clear; his mouth resembled red woolen cloth; his trunk was adorned with red-gold spots, like a pendant of silver; and his four feet seemed as if polished with lac.

mācetukāmo.meaning_2: wishing to release; wanting to free; desiring to set free
mācetukāmo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is nominative singular masculine: so mācetukāmo bhavissati, 'he must wish to release me'. The compound form mā-cetukāma (mā + causative moceti + tuṃ + kāma) is unusual; it means 'desirous to free (from)'.
mācetukāmo.example_1: Bodhisatto puna agamāsi, so puna palāyitvā tassa ṭhitakāle ṭhatvā cintesi ‘‘ ayaṃ vāraṇo mama palāyanakāle tiṭṭhati, ṭhitakāle āgacchati, nāyaṃ mayhaṃ anatthakāmo, imamhā pana maṃ dukkhā mācetukāmo bhavissatī ’’ ti sūro hutvā aṭṭhāsi.
mācetukāmo.translation_1: The Bodhisatta went again, the man ran away again, stopped when the Bodhisatta stopped, and thought, “This elephant stands when I run and comes when I stop. He does not desire my harm; surely he must want to liberate me from this suffering,” and, becoming brave, he stood his ground.

iṇasodhanamattameva.meaning_2: just enough to settle the debt; only sufficient to pay off the debt
iṇasodhanamattameva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of iṇasodhanamattaṃ (nom sg of iṇasodhanamatta, 'just enough to pay the debt') + eva. In the text it is the predicate of jātaṃ. The compound is iṇa + sodhana + matta.
iṇasodhanamattameva.example_1: So taṃ ādāya gantvā vikkiṇitvā tasmiṃ mūle khīṇe puna bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā ‘‘ sāmi, tumhākaṃ dante vikkiṇitvā laddhamūlaṃ mayhaṃ iṇasodhanamattameva jātaṃ, avasesadante dethā ’’ ti āha.
iṇasodhanamattameva.translation_1: He took them, went and sold them, and when that wealth was exhausted, he went to the Bodhisatta again and said, “Lord, the money I received for selling your tusks was only enough to pay my debts. Please give me the rest of the tusks.”

tvevekacciyo.meaning_2: but even some; but a certain
tvevekacciyo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi resolved by the commentary as tu eva ekacciyo, i.e. emphasising na: 'not at all some'. Form of the nominative singular of ekacciya at the end of the quotation.
tvevekacciyo.example_1: Kaṭṭhaṃ niplavitaṃ seyyo, na tvevekacciyo naro ’’ ti.
tvevekacciyo.translation_1: “A log rescued [from the water] is better than some people.”
tvevekacciyo.example_2: Na tvevekacciyo naroti ekacco pana mittadubbhī akataññū pāpapuriso oghena vuyhamāno hatthena gahetvā uttārito na tveva seyyo.
tvevekacciyo.translation_2: Regarding “na tvevekacciyo naro,” it means that some treacherous, ungrateful, evil person who was being swept away by the flood and was rescued by being taken by the hand—that person is not better.

ususattipāsāṇamuggarādippahārehi.meaning_2: with blows from arrows, javelins, stones, clubs and so on
ususattipāsāṇamuggarādippahārehi.construction: usu + satti + pāsāṇa + mugga + ādi + ppahāra + ehi
ususattipāsāṇamuggarādippahārehi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental plural of a long bahubbīhi compound: usu + satti + pāsāṇa + mugga + ādi + ppahāra. Sandhi change: pahāra → ppahāra after ādi. The text omits the usual vuḍḍhi of mugga (muggarādi) but the sense is clear.
ususattipāsāṇamuggarādippahārehi.example_1: Taṃ sutvā khattiyabrāhmaṇādayo nagaravāsino ‘‘ svāyaṃ mittadubbhī rājā evaṃ guṇasampannassa attano jīvitadāyakassa guṇamattampi na jānāti, taṃ nissāya kuto amhākaṃ vuḍḍhi, gaṇhatha nan ’’ ti kupitā samantato uṭṭhahitvā ususattipāsāṇamuggarādippahārehi hatthikkhandhagatameva naṃ ghātetvā pāde gahetvā kaḍḍhitvā parikhāpiṭṭhe chaḍḍetvā bodhisattaṃ abhisiñcitvā rajje patiṭṭhāpesuṃ.
ususattipāsāṇamuggarādippahārehi.translation_1: Hearing this, the nobles, brahmins, and other citizens said, “This treacherous king does not recognize even a measure of the kindness of one so virtuous who gave him his life. Relying on him, how could we ever flourish? Seize him!” Angry, they rose up from all sides, and with blows from arrows, javelins, stones, and clubs, they killed the king while he was still on the elephant, dragged him by the feet, cast him into the moat, and having anointed the Bodhisatta, they established him in the kingdom.

saṃbhaggasākhāviṭapā.meaning_2: with broken branches and twigs; with shattered boughs and foliage
saṃbhaggasākhāviṭapā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi compound modifying rukkhā. Nominative plural in the text. saṃbhagga is the past participle of saṃbhañjati (√bhañj with saṃ-).
saṃbhaggasākhāviṭapā.example_1: Vātassa atibalavatāya daḷhamūlā vanajeṭṭhakarukkhāpi saṃbhaggasākhāviṭapā samūlā nipatiṃsu.
saṃbhaggasākhāviṭapā.translation_1: Due to the extreme strength of the wind, even the forest-lord trees with deep roots, having broken branches and twigs, were uprooted and fell.

araññajā.meaning_2: born in the forest; forest-born; growing in the forest
araññajā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the verse api rukkhā araññajā, nominative plural agreeing with rukkhā (trees). The commentary explains araññe jātarukkhā.
araññajā.example_1: 74. ‘‘ Sādhū sambahulā ñātī, api rukkhā araññajā;
araññajā.translation_1: 74. “United, forest-like, should kinsfolk stand; even trees born in the forest are good;
araññajā.example_2: Api rukkhā araññajāti tiṭṭhantu manussabhūtā, araññe jātarukkhāpi sambahulā aññamaññūpatthambhena ṭhitā sādhuyeva.
araññajā.translation_2: Regarding “api rukkhā araññajā,” let alone those who are human, even trees born in the forest, if they are numerous and stand by mutual support, are indeed excellent.

ajjhottharituṃ.meaning_2: to overwhelm; to overpower; to cover; to dominate
ajjhottharituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -tuṃ of ajjhottharati (adhi + ava + √thar, 'spread over, cover, overwhelm'). Both sentences show the sense 'to overpower, subdue'. The PEU spells it with single -t- (ajjhottharituṃ) but the commentary reads doubled. Sometimes analysed as adhi + o + tharituṃ.
ajjhottharituṃ.example_1: Corā naṃ disvā ‘‘ addhā esa khandhāvārarakkhako bhavissati, imassa niddaṃ okkantakāle vilumpissāmā ’’ ti ajjhottharituṃ asakkontā tattha tattheva aṭṭhaṃsu.
ajjhottharituṃ.translation_1: Seeing him, the robbers thought, “Surely he is the sentry of the camp; we will loot it when he falls asleep,” and being unable to overwhelm him, they stood still in their respective places.
ajjhottharituṃ.example_2: Pattumicchāmi vijetunti imaṃ pathaviṃ dhammena abhibhavituṃ ajjhottharituṃ icchāmi.
ajjhottharituṃ.translation_2: I wish to attain, to conquer (pattumicchāmi vijetuṃ) means I wish to overcome, to overwhelm this earth through righteousness.

ettakevo.meaning_2: this much; this many; so many
ettakevo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text ettakevo = ettake + ivo (eva), 'so many indeed'. Accusative plural modifying core.
ettakevo.example_1: ‘‘ Bhante, ettakevo core disvā bhayaṃ vā sārajjaṃ vā na uppajjī ’’ ti?
ettakevo.translation_1: “Venerable sir, did you not feel fear or suspicion upon seeing so many robbers?”

lābūni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text has lābūni, which is the nominative plural of lābuka (an alternative plural form to lābukāni). The commentary glosses it as 'empty pumpkins'.
lābūni.example_1: Lābūni sīdantīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto soḷasa mahāsupine ārabbha kathesi.
lābūni.translation_1: “Empty pumpkins sink”—the Teacher told this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning sixteen great dreams.
lābūni.example_2: ‘‘ Lābūni sīdanti silā plavanti, maṇḍūkiyo kaṇhasappe gilanti;
lābūni.translation_2: Gourds sink, stones float, and frogs swallow black snakes;

maṇḍūkiyo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative plural maṇḍūkiyo in both sentences. Feminine counterpart of maṇḍūka; glossed in the commentary context as small frogs.
maṇḍūkiyo.example_1: ‘‘ Lābūni sīdanti silā plavanti, maṇḍūkiyo kaṇhasappe gilanti;
maṇḍūkiyo.translation_1: Gourds sink, stones float, and frogs swallow black snakes;
maṇḍūkiyo.example_2: (14) Bhante, khuddakamadhukapupphappamāṇā maṇḍūkiyo mahantamahante kaṇhasappe vegena anubandhitvā uppalanāḷe viya chinditvā chinditvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā gilantiyo addasaṃ, imassa ko vipākoti?
maṇḍūkiyo.translation_2: (14) “Venerable sir, I saw tiny frogs no bigger than minute flowerets pursuing huge black snakes, cutting them up like lotus-stalks, and swallowing them. What is the result of this?”

ossanne.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is a locative absolute with kusale: 'when merit had waned'. Alternatively from √sar (flow), but the PEU derivation ava + sada + ta fits the meaning.
ossanne.example_1: ‘‘ Mahārāja, imassa vipāko neva tava, na mama kāle bhavissati, anāgate pana adhammikānaṃ kapaṇarājūnaṃ adhammikānañca manussānaṃ kāle loke viparivattamāne kusale ossanne, akusale ussanne, lokassa parihāyanakāle devo na sammā vassissati, meghapādā pacchijjissanti, sassāni milāyissanti, dubbhikkhaṃ bhavissati, vassitukāmā viya catūhi disāhi meghā uṭṭhahitvā itthikāhi ātape patthaṭānaṃ vīhiādīnaṃ temanabhayena antopavesitakāle purisesu kuddālapiṭakahatthesu āḷibandhanatthāya nikkhantesu vassanākāraṃ dassetvā gajjitvā vijjulatā nicchāretvā te usabhā viya ayujjhitvā avassitvāva palāyissanti.
ossanne.translation_1: “Great King, the outcome of this dream will not occur in your time or mine. But in the future, in the time of unrighteous, poor kings and unrighteous people, when the world is perverted, merit wanes and demerit waxes, and the world declines—the devas will not rain properly, clouds will break, crops will wither, and famine will occur. Clouds will rise as if to rain, and when women have brought inside the grain spread in the sun for fear of it getting wet, and men have gone out with spades and baskets to bank the water, the clouds will show the appearance of raining, roar, and flash lightning, but they will not rain, they will float away, just like those bulls that showed the appearance of fighting but didn’t.”

parihāyanakāle.meaning_2: time of decline; period of deterioration
parihāyanakāle.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text. parihāyana is from pari + √hā 2 (decrease); the compound means the time when the world declines.
parihāyanakāle.example_1: ‘‘ Mahārāja, imassa vipāko neva tava, na mama kāle bhavissati, anāgate pana adhammikānaṃ kapaṇarājūnaṃ adhammikānañca manussānaṃ kāle loke viparivattamāne kusale ossanne, akusale ussanne, lokassa parihāyanakāle devo na sammā vassissati, meghapādā pacchijjissanti, sassāni milāyissanti, dubbhikkhaṃ bhavissati, vassitukāmā viya catūhi disāhi meghā uṭṭhahitvā itthikāhi ātape patthaṭānaṃ vīhiādīnaṃ temanabhayena antopavesitakāle purisesu kuddālapiṭakahatthesu āḷibandhanatthāya nikkhantesu vassanākāraṃ dassetvā gajjitvā vijjulatā nicchāretvā te usabhā viya ayujjhitvā avassitvāva palāyissanti.
parihāyanakāle.translation_1: “Great King, the outcome of this dream will not occur in your time or mine. But in the future, in the time of unrighteous, poor kings and unrighteous people, when the world is perverted, merit wanes and demerit waxes, and the world declines—the devas will not rain properly, clouds will break, crops will wither, and famine will occur. Clouds will rise as if to rain, and when women have brought inside the grain spread in the sun for fear of it getting wet, and men have gone out with spades and baskets to bank the water, the clouds will show the appearance of raining, roar, and flash lightning, but they will not rain, they will float away, just like those bulls that showed the appearance of fighting but didn’t.”
parihāyanakāle.example_2: Mahārāja, imassāpi vipāko lokassa parihāyanakāle manussānaṃ parittāyukakāle bhavissati.
parihāyanakāle.translation_2: “Great King, the outcome of this also will occur when the world declines, in the time when human life-span is short.”

vijātirājāno.meaning_2: king of low birth; low-caste king; king of inferior lineage
vijātirājāno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative plural in the text: vijātirājāno. The first member is vi + jāti ("low birth"); the PEU treats the whole as vijātirāja.
vijātirājāno.example_1: Anāgatasmiñhi adhammikā vijātirājāno jātisampannānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ āsaṅkāya yasaṃ na dassanti, akulīnānaṃyeva dassanti.
vijātirājāno.translation_1: “In the future, unrighteous, low-caste kings will be suspicious of noble-born sons and will not give them honor, but will give it to those of no caste.”

balipīḷitā.meaning_2: oppressed by taxes; burdened by tribute; crushed by taxation
balipīḷitā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative plural in the text, agreeing with manussā and raṭṭhavāsino. bali here means tax or tribute, not an offering.
balipīḷitā.example_1: Manussā balipīḷitā kiñci dātuṃ asakkontā gāmanigamādayo chaḍḍetvā paccantaṃ gantvā vāsaṃ kappessanti, majjhimajanapado suñño bhavissati, paccanto ghanavāso seyyathāpi pokkharaṇiyā majjhe udakaṃ āvilaṃ pariyante vippasannaṃ.
balipīḷitā.translation_1: Oppressed by these taxes, people will abandon villages, towns, and the like, fleeing to the borders of the realm to settle there. The heart of the land will be desolate, while the borders will be crowded—just as the water in the middle of the pool was muddy, while at the edges it was clear.”
balipīḷitā.example_2: Balipīḷitā raṭṭhavāsino puttadāre ādāya araññe migā viya cariṃsu, gāmaṭṭhāne gāmo nāma nāhosi.
balipīḷitā.translation_2: The inhabitants of the country, oppressed by taxation, taking their children and wives, wandered in the wilderness like animals. There was indeed no village in the place of villages.

apakaḍḍhāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to be dragged away; having had (someone) dragged off
apakaḍḍhāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive: apa + kaḍḍhāpetvā. In the text, part of a series of infinitives/absolutives describing the favourites' threats.
apakaḍḍhāpetvā.example_1: Te rājavallabhā rājānaṃ attano kathaṃ gāhāpetvā vinicchayaṭṭhānādīsu balavanto hutvā kulīnānaṃ paveṇiāgatāni khettavatthādīni ‘‘ amhākaṃ santakāni etānī ’’ ti abhiyuñjitvā tesu ‘‘ na tumhākaṃ, amhākan ’’ ti āgantvā vinicchayaṭṭhānādīsu vivadantesu vettalatādīhi paharāpetvā gīvāyaṃ gahetvā apakaḍḍhāpetvā ‘‘ attano pamāṇaṃ na jānātha, amhehi saddhiṃ vivadatha, idāni vo rañño kathetvā hatthapādacchedanādīni kāressāmā ’’ ti santajjessanti.
apakaḍḍhāpetvā.translation_1: “Those favorites will manipulate the king, hold power in the courts, and seize the ancestral lands and property of the nobles, claiming them as their own. When the nobles come to the courts to dispute this, the favorites will have them beaten with canes, grabbed by the throat, dragged out, and threatened: ‘Do you not know your place? You dare to dispute with us? We shall tell the king and have your hands and feet chopped off.’”

visamakkhimaṇḍalo.meaning_2: with uneven eyes; squint-eyed; with mismatched eye-circles
visamakkhimaṇḍalo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes Illīsa the treasurer along with khañjo and kuṇī. Nominative singular agreeing with seṭṭhi. The compound may be visama + akkhi + maṇḍala ("uneven eye-circle") or visama + akkhimaṇḍala.
visamakkhimaṇḍalo.example_1: Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bārāṇasiyaṃ illiso nāma seṭṭhi ahosi asītikoṭivibhavo purisadosasamannāgato khañjo kuṇī visamakkhimaṇḍalo assaddho appasanno maccharī, neva aññesaṃ deti, na sayaṃ paribhuñjati.
visamakkhimaṇḍalo.translation_1: In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning at Benares, there was a treasurer in Benares named Illīsa who had a fortune of eighty crores. He was possessed of many human defects: he was lame, crippled, squint-eyed, without faith, without devotion, and stingy—he neither gave to others nor used his wealth himself.

gacchantūnti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Form is gacchantuṃ (imperative 3rd plural) plus -ti; -ti is the quotation marker. Lemma is the present 3rd singular.

pacchipasibbakādīni.meaning_2: baskets, sacks and other such things; baskets, sacks and so on
pacchipasibbakādīni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound ending in ādi, functioning as a collective plural; neuter plural accusative in the text, object of gahetvā.
pacchipasibbakādīni.translation_1: A large crowd arrived carrying baskets and sacks and assembled at the house gate.

oṇāmetvā.meaning_2: having bent down; having bowed down; having lowered
oṇāmetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā of oṇamati (ava + namati), with o- representing the dropping of ava-. In sentence 1 the reading oṇāmetvā may be a variant of oṇametvā or onametvā; some editions read onametvā.
oṇāmetvā.example_1: So puna kampamāno uṭṭhāya paṃsuṃ puñchitvā puñchitvā vegena gantvā rathaṃ gaṇhi, gahapatiko rathā otaritvā kesesu gahetvā oṇāmetvā kapparapahārehi koṭṭetvā gale gahetvā āgatamaggābhimukhaṃ khipitvā pakkāmi.
oṇāmetvā.translation_1: The Treasurer rose, trembling, wiped off the dust, and hurried after it to seize the carriage. The yokel climbed down, seized him by the hair, thumped him with his elbows, grabbed him by the throat, threw him toward the road he had come from, and departed.
oṇāmetvā.example_2: Taṃ sutvā kulaputto tuṭṭhamānaso hutvā attano sakalasarīraṃ oṇāmetvā mātāpitaro vanditvā vihāraṃ gantvā bhagavantaṃ pabbajjaṃ yāci.
oṇāmetvā.translation_2: Hearing that, the clansman was joyful, bowed down and worshipped at his parents' feet, went to the Jetavana monastery, worshipped the Blessed One, and requested the going forth.

sañjānanakoti.meaning_2: like someone who knows; as if perceiving
sañjānanakoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of sañjānanako (nom sg of sañjānānaka) + iti, with loss of -o before i-. Not found in the sentences; analysis based on form.

sañjānituṃ.meaning_2: to distinguish; to recognize; to know clearly
sañjānituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive governing sakkomi; the -tuṃ form of the causative-style base sañjānā-. Commentarial prose.
sañjānituṃ.example_1: Bodhisatto dvinnampi sīsaṃ olokento piḷakā disvā ‘‘ mahārāja, dvinnampi sīse piḷakā attheva, nāhaṃ etesu ekassāpi illisabhāvaṃ sañjānituṃ sakkomī ’’ ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –
sañjānituṃ.translation_1: The Bodhisatta, looking at the heads of both, saw the warts, and said, “Great King, there are warts on the heads of both of them. I am unable to distinguish which is the real Illīsa among them,” and he uttered this verse—

vilumpāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to be plundered; having had (the village) robbed
vilumpāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive in -tvā from vilumpāpeti. In the text it describes the headman having the village plundered by thieves.
vilumpāpetvā.example_1: So tasmiṃ gāmabhojake sāyanhasamaye mahājanaparivārena bheriyā vajjamānāya āgacchante ‘‘ ayaṃ duṭṭhagāmabhojako corehi saddhiṃ ekato hutvā gāmaṃ vilumpāpetvā coresu palāyitvā aṭaviṃ paviṭṭhesu idāni upasantūpasanto viya bheriyā vajjamānāya āgacchatī ’’ ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –
vilumpāpetvā.translation_1: Seeing that village headman coming in the evening surrounded by the crowd with drums beating, he said, “This corrupt headman joined with thieves, had the village plundered, and after the thieves ran off and entered the forest, now he comes back acting as if everything is calm, with drums beating,” and he uttered this verse—

kampituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive expressing the action begun by āraddho. From √kamp (shake, tremble).
kampituṃ.translation_1: As soon as Bhīmasena heard the sound of the war drums, he began to tremble.

unnaditvā.meaning_2: having roared; having shouted out; having cried out
unnaditvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -itvā of unnadati (u + √nad). In the text it describes the Bodhisatta roaring before breaking the enemy camp; in the second passage it means giving a loud shout during an ambush. Sometimes analysed as u + √nad + tvā.
unnaditvā.example_1: Evaṃ bodhisatto taṃ garahitvā ‘‘ mā bhāyi, samma, kasmā mayi ṭhite vihaññasī ’’ ti bhīmasenaṃ hatthipiṭṭhito otāretvā ‘‘ nhāyitvā gehameva gacchā ’’ ti uyyojetvā ‘‘ ajja mayā pākaṭena bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti saṅgāmaṃ pavisitvā unnaditvā balakoṭṭhakaṃ bhinditvā sapattarājānaṃ jīvaggāhaṃ gāhāpetvā bārāṇasirañño santikaṃ agamāsi.
unnaditvā.translation_1: In this way, the Bodhisatta having rebuked him, said: “Do not be afraid, friend. Why are you distressed while I am here?” He had Bhīmasena descend from the elephant, and urged him, “Go bathe and then return home.” Then, thinking, “Today it is fitting for me to be clearly recognized,” he entered the battle, roared like a lion, broke through the king’s camp, captured the rival king alive, and went to the presence of the King of Benares.
unnaditvā.example_2: Ajātasattuṃ gaṇhitukāmena asuke nāma pabbatakucchismiṃ dvīsu pabbatabhittīsu manusse ṭhapetvā purato dubbalabalaṃ dassetvā pabbatantaraṃ paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ jānitvā paviṭṭhamaggaṃ occhinditvā purato ca pacchato ca ubhosu pabbatabhittīsu vaggitvā unnaditvā khipe patitamacchaṃ viya antomuṭṭhiyaṃ vaṭṭapotakaṃ viya ca katvā sakkā assa taṃ gahetun ’’ ti.
unnaditvā.translation_2: Wishing to capture Ajātasattu, one should place men at those two mountain walls in that mountain-ravine, show a weak force in front, and knowing he has entered the mountain-pass, block the path he entered by; and by leaping from both mountain walls in front and behind, and shouting, one could capture him like a fish fallen in a basket, or like a quail in the palm of the hand.”

udakadeḍḍūbhakampi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text, with emphatic -pi ('even a water snake'). deḍḍubhaka is a water snake; sandhi pi + udaka optionally gives ...bhakampi.
udakadeḍḍūbhakampi.example_1: ‘‘ Kiṃ panetarahi, bhikkhave, sāgato udakadeḍḍūbhakampi dametuṃ sakkuṇeyyā ’’ ti.
udakadeḍḍūbhakampi.translation_1: “But now, monks, would Sāgata be able to master even a water-snake?”

lāḷentā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle masculine nominative plural; the text has an alternative spelling lāḷentā for lāḷayantā. Refers to wagging hands and feet while dancing.
lāḷentā.translation_1: Anacchimhā means: having drunk that, we danced while wagging our hands and feet.

mākaritthāti.meaning_2: do not do; do not make
mākaritthāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Prohibitive aorist with mā, 2nd person plural: 'you (all) must not do'. The -ti is the quotative enclitic (-iti), not part of the verb.

svāsi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of tvaṃ (pron) and asi (2nd sg of √as 1 'to be'). The PEU lists a separate svāsa entry, but in this sentence the form is best analysed as su + asi, i.e. tvaṃ asi.
svāsi.example_1: Svāsi pāsāṇamāsīno, yasmā jīvaṃ na mokkhasī ’’ ti.
svāsi.translation_1: You are now invested with the stone [wheel], and because of this you shall not be released while still alive.”

anīcatā.meaning_2: non-lowliness; state of not being low; non-inferiority
anīcatā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Abstract noun in -tā. In the text it glosses alīnatā ('non-adherence') as anīcatā, the mind not being low or sluggish. Nominative singular.
anīcatā.translation_1: Alīnatā cā (be diligent) means the non-yielding and non-low state of the mind.

khaṇḍitvā.meaning_2: having broken; having cut; having destroyed
khaṇḍitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The root √khaṇḍ is not in the given root list, though it is standard for 'break'. In the text it agrees with antāni ('the inner organs') and means 'having broken/destroyed'.
khaṇḍitvā.example_1: Kiṃpakkaphalaṃ nāma vaṇṇagandharasasampannaṃ, khāditaṃ pana antāni khaṇḍitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpeti.
khaṇḍitvā.translation_1: The What-fruit is indeed rich in color, scent, and taste, but when eaten, it destroys one’s inner organs and leads to death.

saṃyojayamānā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle of saṃyojayati, used here in the sense of binding or afflicting with suffering. Nominative plural modifying kāmā.
saṃyojayamānā.example_1: Vipākante hananti nanti te kāmā taṃ purisaṃ attano vipākasaṅkhāte ante nirayādīsu uppannaṃ nānappakārena dukkhena saṃyojayamānā hananti.
saṃyojayamānā.translation_1: They slay this person at the time of fruition means those pleasures, at the final time known as their fruit, slay that person born in hell and other realms by binding him with various kinds of suffering.

aḍaṃsanaaviheṭhanamattakena.meaning_2: merely by not biting and not harming; just through the mere fact of neither biting nor hurting
aḍaṃsanaaviheṭhanamattakena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Three-word compound with a- (negation), ḍaṃsana, aviheṭhana and matta, in the instrumental singular, functioning as an adverbial phrase. Related to aḍaṃsanaaviheṭhanamattakena, a negated gerundive of √ḍaṃs (bite) and viheṭhana (harming). Handled as an indeclinable.
aḍaṃsanaaviheṭhanamattakena.example_1: Sīlavāti na haññatīti ghoravisopi samāno aḍaṃsanaaviheṭhanamattakena sīlavāti pasaṃsaṃ labhati, na haññati na vihaññatīti.
aḍaṃsanaaviheṭhanamattakena.translation_1: ‘Behold the deadly snake, which, because it is deemed ‘virtuous,’ is not killed’—even a deadly snake, merely by not biting and not harming, obtains the praise of being called ‘virtuous,’ and it is not killed, not harmed.

kotuhalamaṅgaliko.meaning_2: superstitious; believing in omens and auspicious signs
kotuhalamaṅgaliko.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Spelled kotuhala- in the text (short u), variant of kotūhala. Nominative singular modifying brāhmaṇo.
kotuhalamaṅgaliko.example_1: Rājagahavāsiko kireko brāhmaṇo kotuhalamaṅgaliko tīsu ratanesu appasanno micchādiṭṭhiko aḍḍho mahaddhano mahābhogo, tassa samugge ṭhapitaṃ sāṭakayugaṃ mūsikā khādiṃsu.
kotuhalamaṅgaliko.translation_1: It is said that a brahmin living in Rājagaha was superstitious, lacking faith in the Three Gems, holding wrong views, and very rich, with great wealth and possessions. Mice had gnawed a pair of his clothes kept in a chest.

kotuhalamaṅgalikā.meaning_2: superstitious; believing in auspicious omens and rituals; fond of festivals and ceremonies
kotuhalamaṅgalikā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Text has kotuhalamaṅgalikā (nominative plural) and kotuhalamaṅgalikena (instrumental singular). Often written kotūhala-; the compound means one who engages in kotūhala-maṅgala, i.e. superstitious observances.
kotuhalamaṅgalikā.example_1: Tāpaso ‘‘ amhākaṃ susāne chaḍḍitapilotikā vaṭṭati, na mayaṃ kotuhalamaṅgalikā, kotuhalamaṅgalaṃ nāmetaṃ na buddhapaccekabuddhabodhisattehi vaṇṇitaṃ, tasmā paṇḍitena nāma kotuhalamaṅgalikena na bhavitabban ’’ ti brāhmaṇassa dhammaṃ desesi.
kotuhalamaṅgalikā.translation_1: The ascetic taught the Dhamma to the brahmin, saying, ‘Rags thrown in the charnel ground are appropriate for us; we are not superstitious, and this superstition is not praised by Buddhas, Pacceka Buddhas, or Bodhisattas; therefore, a wise person should not be superstitious.’

kotuhalamaṅgalaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Variant of kotūhalamaṅgala. Nominative singular in the text, with kotuhalamaṅgalikā (adjective, 'superstitious') used just before it.
kotuhalamaṅgalaṃ.example_1: Tāpaso ‘‘ amhākaṃ susāne chaḍḍitapilotikā vaṭṭati, na mayaṃ kotuhalamaṅgalikā, kotuhalamaṅgalaṃ nāmetaṃ na buddhapaccekabuddhabodhisattehi vaṇṇitaṃ, tasmā paṇḍitena nāma kotuhalamaṅgalikena na bhavitabban ’’ ti brāhmaṇassa dhammaṃ desesi.
kotuhalamaṅgalaṃ.translation_1: The ascetic taught the Dhamma to the brahmin, saying, ‘Rags thrown in the charnel ground are appropriate for us; we are not superstitious, and this superstition is not praised by Buddhas, Pacceka Buddhas, or Bodhisattas; therefore, a wise person should not be superstitious.’

kotuhalamaṅgalikena.meaning_2: superstitious; one who believes in auspicious omens; attached to rituals for good luck
kotuhalamaṅgalikena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular in the text (kotuhalamaṅgalikena). Often written kotūhalamaṅgalika; the spelling without the long ū is a metrical or orthographic variant.
kotuhalamaṅgalikena.example_1: Tāpaso ‘‘ amhākaṃ susāne chaḍḍitapilotikā vaṭṭati, na mayaṃ kotuhalamaṅgalikā, kotuhalamaṅgalaṃ nāmetaṃ na buddhapaccekabuddhabodhisattehi vaṇṇitaṃ, tasmā paṇḍitena nāma kotuhalamaṅgalikena na bhavitabban ’’ ti brāhmaṇassa dhammaṃ desesi.
kotuhalamaṅgalikena.translation_1: The ascetic taught the Dhamma to the brahmin, saying, ‘Rags thrown in the charnel ground are appropriate for us; we are not superstitious, and this superstition is not praised by Buddhas, Pacceka Buddhas, or Bodhisattas; therefore, a wise person should not be superstitious.’

bhaṇḍatthāya.meaning_2: for the sake of trade; for merchandise
bhaṇḍatthāya.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Dative of bhaṇḍa + attha, used as an adverbial phrase. In the text it follows gacchantena: going for trade.
bhaṇḍatthāya.example_1: Tadā pana bodhisattena bhaṇḍatthāya paccantaṃ gacchantena tasmiṃ nivesane nivāso gahito hoti.
bhaṇḍatthāya.translation_1: At that time, however, the Bodhisatta, who was going to a border district for the sake of trade, was staying at that residence.

vicakkāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text sakaṭāni vicakkāni katvā means 'having made the carts wheel-less' (i.e. removing the wheels). Vicakkāni = vi (prefix) + cakkāni (nominative/accusative plural neuter of cakka 'wheel'), but it is a sandhi of the prefix vi with the noun cakkāni, not a proper compound headword. Alternatively could be an adjective vi-cakka 'wheel-less' inflected as plural neuter, but DPD convention treats the prefix joined to a full word as sandhi when separable. Accusative plural here.
vicakkāni.example_1: Te pana disvā anāthapiṇḍikassa manussā ‘‘ mayaṃ, sāmi, etesaṃ nivāsañca bhattañca paribbayañca jānissāmā ’’ ti vatvā tesaṃ sakaṭāni bahinagare tathārūpe ṭhāne mocāpetvā ‘‘ tumhe idheva vasatha, amhākaṃ vo ghare yāgubhattañca paribbayo ca bhavissatī ’’ ti gantvā dāsakammakare sannipātetvā majjhimayāmasamanantare pañca sakaṭasatāni vilumpitvā nivāsanapārupanānipi nesaṃ acchinditvā goṇe palāpetvā sakaṭāni vicakkāni katvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā cakkānipi gaṇhitvāva agamaṃsu.
