vicakkāni.translation_1: But Anāthapiṇḍika’s workers, seeing them, said, “Sir, we will see to their lodging, food, and expenses,” and having made them unyoke their carts outside the city in such a place, they said, “You stay right here, food and expenses will come to you from our house.” Then, having gone, they gathered the slaves and workers, and at the end of the middle watch, they looted the five hundred carts, stole even the clothes they were wearing, drove the oxen away, removed the wheels from the five hundred carts, left them on the ground, took the wheels, and went off.

guḷakaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Glossed as a synonym of akkha (die) in the Jātaka commentary; nominative singular in the text.

piḷandhitukāmā.meaning_2: desiring to wear; wanting to put on (an ornament); wishing to adorn oneself
piḷandhitukāmā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of piḷandhati (to wear, put on) + kāma. Feminine nominative singular piḷandhitukāmā in the text, agreeing with the monkey (uyyānamakkaṭī), which wants to wear the queen's pearl necklace.
piḷandhitukāmā.example_1: Athekā uyyānamakkaṭī sākhantare nisinnā deviṃ piḷandhanāni omuñcitvā uttarāsaṅge pakkhipitvā samuggapiṭṭhe ṭhapayamānaṃ disvā tassā muttāhāraṃ piḷandhitukāmā hutvā dāsiyā pamādaṃ olokayamānā nisīdi, dāsīpi taṃ rakkhamānā tahaṃ tahaṃ oloketvā nisinnāyeva niddāyituṃ ārabhi.
piḷandhitukāmā.translation_1: A monkey in the park, sitting in the branches, saw the queen placing her ornaments in the box, and desiring to wear the pearl necklace, waited for the bondswoman to be negligent. The bondswoman was watching, but eventually became drowsy.

niddāyituṃ.meaning_2: to fall asleep; to become drowsy
niddāyituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -tuṃ of niddāyati, used with ārabhi (began to fall asleep). The PEU analysis Ni+dā+ya+tuṃ agrees; √dā 5 is given as 'sleep'. Alternative analysis: denominal from niddā (sleep).
niddāyituṃ.example_1: Athekā uyyānamakkaṭī sākhantare nisinnā deviṃ piḷandhanāni omuñcitvā uttarāsaṅge pakkhipitvā samuggapiṭṭhe ṭhapayamānaṃ disvā tassā muttāhāraṃ piḷandhitukāmā hutvā dāsiyā pamādaṃ olokayamānā nisīdi, dāsīpi taṃ rakkhamānā tahaṃ tahaṃ oloketvā nisinnāyeva niddāyituṃ ārabhi.
niddāyituṃ.translation_1: A monkey in the park, sitting in the branches, saw the queen placing her ornaments in the box, and desiring to wear the pearl necklace, waited for the bondswoman to be negligent. The bondswoman was watching, but eventually became drowsy.

bahivaḷañjo.meaning_2: one who is outside the enclosure; outsider
bahivaḷañjo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Opposite of antovaḷañja. Nominative singular in the text, describing the householder.
bahivaḷañjo.example_1: ‘‘ idaṃ piḷandhanaṃ antovaḷañje naṭṭhaṃ, ayañca gahapatiko bahivaḷañjo, dvārepi balavārakkho, tasmā antovaḷañjanakānampi taṃ gahetvā palāyituṃ na sakkā.
bahivaḷañjo.translation_1: “This treasure was lost in the restricted area, and this householder is an outsider. There is also a strong guard at the gate, so it is impossible for anyone from the restricted area to have taken it and escaped.

temayi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular of the causative temeti; the text has temayi with the same meaning. The PEU entry suggests an alternative analysis as a present form in -i.
temayi.example_1: So yathā rattiṃ abbhokāse himodakena tinto, tatheva divā vanasaṇḍato paggharantehi udakabindūhi temayi.
temayi.translation_1: Just as he was wet with ice-water in the open air at night, so in the day he was drenched by water droplets falling from the forest grove.

sudhotavajirapanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative or nominative singular here; the simile compares the well-set teeth to a line of polished diamonds. Sometimes read as sudhotavajira + panti.
sudhotavajirapanti.example_1: Dvattiṃsa dantā suphusitā sudhotavajirapanti viya khāyanti.
sudhotavajirapanti.translation_1: The thirty-two teeth are well-spaced and look like a row of polished diamonds.

nibbalipalitā.meaning_2: without wrinkles and grey hair; free from wrinkles and grey hair
nibbalipalitā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes a woman who looks young despite her age; nominative singular in the text. Sometimes analysed as ni + valipalita.
nibbalipalitā.example_1: Vīsativassasatikāpi pana samānā soḷasavassuddesikā viya hoti nibbalipalitā.
nibbalipalitā.translation_1: Furthermore, even if she were one hundred and twenty years old, she would appear like a sixteen-year-old girl, with no wrinkles and no grey hair.

pāsāvo.meaning_2: the body; that which flows out; excretion
pāsāvo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is nominative singular, defined as a synonym of pasava in a wordplay on paramapāsāvinī.
pāsāvo.example_1: Pasavo eva pāsāvo, paramo pāsāvo paramapāsāvo, so assā atthīti paramapāsāvinī.
pāsāvo.translation_1: ‘Pasava’ itself is ‘pāsāva’, supreme ‘pāsāva’ is ‘paramapāsāva’; she possesses this, therefore she is ‘paramapāsāvinī’.

paramapāsāvo.meaning_2: supreme animal; best beast; noblest creature
paramapāsāvo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A punning word formation (pasavo + pāsāvo) used to explain paramapāsāvinī. Nominative singular in the text.
paramapāsāvo.example_1: Pasavo eva pāsāvo, paramo pāsāvo paramapāsāvo, so assā atthīti paramapāsāvinī.
paramapāsāvo.translation_1: ‘Pasava’ itself is ‘pāsāva’, supreme ‘pāsāva’ is ‘paramapāsāva’; she possesses this, therefore she is ‘paramapāsāvinī’.

nigaḷāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Appears as plural nigaḷāni in the text, object of chinditvā, meaning 'having cut off the shackles'. Sometimes masculine (nigaḷā).
nigaḷāni.example_1: Atha puriso āgaccheyyāti na attano ruciyā āgaccheyya, ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo – athevaṃ mahājanamajjhe janapadakalyāṇiyā naccamānāya ‘‘ sādhu sādhū ’’ ti sādhukāresu aṅguliphoṭanesu celukkhepesu ca pavattamānesu taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā rājā bandhanāgārato ekaṃ corapurisaṃ pakkosāpetvā nigaḷāni chinditvā samatittikaṃ suparipuṇṇaṃ telapattaṃ tassa hatthe datvā ubhohi hatthehi daḷhaṃ gāhāpetvā ekaṃ asihatthaṃ purisaṃ āṇāpesi ‘‘ etaṃ gahetvā janapadakalyāṇiyā samajjaṭṭhānaṃ gaccha.
nigaḷāni.translation_1: Atha puriso āgaccheyyāti—it does not mean he would come of his own free will; rather, this is the intended meaning: when the Belle of the Land was dancing in the midst of a great crowd, and while applause, snapping fingers, and waving of cloths were going on, the King, having heard of that event, called a criminal from the prison, took off his shackles, placed a full pot of oil in his hand, made him hold it tightly with both hands, and instructed a man armed with a sword: “Take this pot of oil, go to the place where the Belle of the Land is dancing, and if that man, out of negligence, spills even a drop of oil anywhere, strike off his head right there.”

myāyanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Only the form myāyanti is attested and it is doubtful; possibly a Middle Indic passive of √mah or √mā, or a variant of majjanti. The analysis as a present 3rd plural with passive sense is uncertain.

āṇañca.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text āṇañca = āṇaṃ + ca, accusative singular in a compound-like phrase issariyañca āṇañca. Probably from āṇā, authority; cf. āṇatti, āṇatta. One might also consider a masc āṇa, but fem āṇā is more likely.
āṇañca.example_1: Sace tumhe sakalarajje issariyañca āṇañca mayhaṃ dadeyyātha, koci mayhaṃ cittaṃ kopetvā kathetuṃ na sakkhissatī ’’ ti.
āṇañca.translation_1: "If you were to give me power and authority over the whole kingdom, no one would be able to annoy me."
āṇañca.example_2: Iminā kāraṇena na sakkā tuyhaṃ sakalaraṭṭhe vā nagare vā issariyañca āṇañca dātun ’’ ti.
āṇañca.translation_2: "For this reason, it is not possible to give you power and authority over the whole kingdom or the city."

anavasiñcanakaṃ.meaning_2: without remainder; completely; without leaving anything
anavasiñcanakaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text word is Anavasesakan, a gloss on anavasiñcanakaṃ. Anavasesaṃ (without remainder) + kaṃ (adverbial). Also analyzed as anavasesa + ka, but as it stands in the text it is sandhi. The form anavasesakaṃ often functions as an indeclinable meaning 'without exception; completely'.
anavasiñcanakaṃ.translation_1: Anavasesakaṃ means without spilling and without leaking.

nāmasiddhikoyevāti.meaning_2: one who believes that a name alone brings success; one whose luck lies in the name
nāmasiddhikoyevāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of nāmasiddhiko + yeva + iti, with -ya- assimilated as -y-; yeva is emphatic ('just, merely'). In the text nominative singular, ending an utterance.

pothiyamānaṃ.meaning_2: being beaten; being struck; being pounded
pothiyamānaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle passive of potheti. In the text accusative singular modifying a woman. In the second sentence it explains haññamānaṃ.
pothiyamānaṃ.example_1: So antaravīthiyā gacchanto taṃ pothiyamānaṃ disvā ‘‘ kasmā imaṃ pothethā ’’ ti pucchi.
pothiyamānaṃ.translation_1: Walking along the street and seeing her being beaten, he asked, 'Why are you beating her?'

nāmasiddhikoyeva.meaning_2: just one who believes in (the power of) names; merely a believer in name-luck
nāmasiddhikoyeva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of nāmasiddhiko (nominative singular) + eva. Predicate of hoti in the clause, referring to the former pupil who is now the monk. For the separate word see nāmasiddhika.
nāmasiddhikoyeva.example_1: ‘‘ tadā nāmasiddhiko idānipi nāmasiddhikoyeva, ācariyaparisā buddhaparisā, ācariyo pana ahameva ahosin ’’ ti.
nāmasiddhikoyeva.translation_1: “The student who imagined there was a great deal in a name then is the same monk who imagines there is a great deal in a name now; the group of pupils was the Buddha's assembly, and the teacher was I myself.”

bujjhāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to know; having enlightened; having made understand
bujjhāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of bujjhāpeti (from √budh with the causative sign *āpe, with the -jh- assimilation); in the text it describes the Bodhisatta making the ascetics understand the Dhamma.
bujjhāpetvā.example_1: Evaṃ mahāsatto ākāse ṭhitova dhammaṃ desetvā tāpasagaṇaṃ bujjhāpetvā brahmalokameva gato.
bujjhāpetvā.translation_1: In this way, the Great Being, standing in the sky, taught the Dhamma, enlightened the company of hermits, and went to the Brahma realm as before.

ayacakkanti.meaning_2: iron wheel; iron disc; iron circlet
ayacakkanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is joined with the quotation particle -ti (ayacakkanti) and is nominative singular, in apposition with khuradhāraṃ ayacakkaṃ. aya is the stem of ayas (iron).
ayacakkanti.example_1: Pāsāṇacakkaṃ, ayacakkanti imesu dvīsu khuradhāraṃ ayacakkaṃ tassa matthake punappunaṃ patanavasena bhamantaṃ disvā evamāha.
ayacakkanti.translation_1: Seeing the iron circlet—the circlet of fear with a sharp edge—spinning upon his head due to its falling again and again, among the two kinds, the stone circlet and the iron circlet, he spoke thus.

ayacakkaṃ.meaning_2: iron wheel; iron disc; iron circlet
ayacakkaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it refers to the sharp-edged iron wheel that spins on the victim's head; nominative singular in the phrase ayacakkaṃ tassa matthake. Sometimes spelled ayocakka.
ayacakkaṃ.example_1: Pāsāṇacakkaṃ, ayacakkanti imesu dvīsu khuradhāraṃ ayacakkaṃ tassa matthake punappunaṃ patanavasena bhamantaṃ disvā evamāha.
ayacakkaṃ.translation_1: Seeing the iron circlet—the circlet of fear with a sharp edge—spinning upon his head due to its falling again and again, among the two kinds, the stone circlet and the iron circlet, he spoke thus.

idañcidañcāharāti.meaning_2: this and that, bringing; 'I bring this and that' (quoting)
idañcidañcāharāti.construction: idaṃ + ca + idaṃ + ca + āharā + ti
idañcidañcāharāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound sandhi ending in the quotative -ti; the whole is a quotation. Analysis is uncertain: possibly idaṃ + ca + idaṃ + ca + āhara + ti ('bring this and that'), with the final -āti rather than -āti; or āharāti from √har. No sentence context available.

udañcanī.meaning_2: water-drawer; bucket for drawing water from a well; small water-pot
udañcanī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is the subject of pacamānā; the commentary explains it as udakaṃ añcanti etāyāti. The PEU suggests a variant analysis uda + añcana + ī, and also records the sense 'a woman like a small water-pot'.
udañcanī.example_1: 106. ‘‘ Sukhaṃ vata maṃ jīvantaṃ, pacamānā udañcanī;
udañcanī.translation_1: “A happy life was mine, but that water-drawer [a woman who drags and pesters one like a water-pot] keeps me cooking [in distress];
udañcanī.example_2: Udakaṃ añcanti etāyāti udañcanī , cāṭito vā kūpato vā udakaussiñcanaghaṭikāyetaṃ nāmaṃ.
udañcanī.translation_2: Udañcanī is so called because through her, one draws [like water]; it is the name for a small bucket for drawing water from an earthen pot or a well.

añcanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Third person plural in the text (añcanti), used in the explanation of udañcanī; 'draws (water)'.
añcanti.example_1: Udakaṃ añcanti etāyāti udañcanī , cāṭito vā kūpato vā udakaussiñcanaghaṭikāyetaṃ nāmaṃ.
añcanti.translation_1: Udañcanī is so called because through her, one draws [like water]; it is the name for a small bucket for drawing water from an earthen pot or a well.

haṃsapaharanakaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes a bhikkhu who killed a swan. Accusative singular in the text.
haṃsapaharanakaṃ.example_1: Sādhū kho sippakaṃ nāmāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ haṃsapaharanakaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi.
haṃsapaharanakaṃ.translation_1: Sādhū kho sippakaṃ nāmā: The Teacher told this discourse while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a bhikkhu who killed a swan.

abhirādhayitvā.meaning_2: having pleased; having satisfied; having won over
abhirādhayitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā of the causative abhirādhayati; in the text it explains abhirādhayi (aorist).
abhirādhayitvā.translation_1: 'Won the King’s favor' means, having pleased the King, she attained this prosperity.

yathanno.meaning_2: eating according to (the deed); whose food is as (his karma); as one eats
yathanno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of yathā + anna; commentarial gloss yathārūpabhojano hoti. Nominative singular in the text.
yathanno.example_1: Yathanno puriso hotīti idaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto mahāduggataṃ ārabbha kathesi.
yathanno.translation_1: “As fares his worshipper”—this was spoken by the Master while dwelling in Sāvatthī, in reference to a very poor man.
yathanno.example_2: 109. ‘‘ Yathanno puriso hoti, tathannā tassa devatā;
yathanno.translation_2: “As a man eats, so do his devas eat.

vaḍḍhāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to grow; having increased; having heaped up; having made into a ball
vaḍḍhāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive from √vaḍḍh. In the sentence it describes making the kuṇḍaka into a lump or ball before baking. PEU suggests the base vaḍḍha with sign ṇāpe.
vaḍḍhāpetvā.example_1: Tadā paneko paresaṃ bhatikārako duggatamanusso tassaṃ vīthiyaṃ vasamāno cintesi ‘‘ ahaṃ yāguṃ dātuṃ na sakkhissāmi, khajjakaṃ pana dassāmī ’’ ti saṇhasaṇhaṃ kuṇḍakaṃ vaḍḍhāpetvā udakena temetvā akkapaṇṇena veṭhetvā kukkuḷe pacitvā ‘‘ idaṃ buddhassa dassāmī ’’ ti taṃ ādāya gantvā satthu santike ṭhito ‘‘ khajjakaṃ āharathā ’’ ti ekasmiṃ vacane vuttamatte sabbapaṭhamaṃ gantvā taṃ pūvaṃ satthu patte patiṭṭhāpesi, satthā aññehi dīyamānaṃ khajjakaṃ aggahetvā tameva pūvakhajjakaṃ paribhuñji.
vaḍḍhāpetvā.translation_1: At that time, a very poor man who worked for others, living in that street, thought, “I cannot give gruel, but I will give cakes.” He scraped together fine rice powder, kneaded it with water, wrapped it in a swallow-wort leaf, baked it in the embers, and thinking, “I will give this to the Buddha,” he took it and stood near the Master. As soon as the word went out, “Bring along some cakes,” he went before everyone else and placed that cake in the Master’s almsbowl. The Master, not accepting cakes offered by others, ate only the poor man's cake.

naṭṭhoyevāti.meaning_2: as if lost; just like one who is lost
naṭṭhoyevāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of naṭṭhā (past participle of nasati, 'lost; perished') with the emphatic particle yeva. In the Jātaka prose yeva is often weakened to eva with the -i- after -ā-. The form naṭṭhoyevāti can be analysed as naṭṭhā + yeva + ti, the -ā- assimilating before -y-. Uncertain; no sentence context found.

kālarāvī.meaning_2: crowing at the right time; that crows at the proper time
kālarāvī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] An adjective describing a rooster (kukkuṭa) that crows at the proper time. Nominative singular in the text; also analyzable as kāla + √ru + ṇī.
kālarāvī.example_1: Tesaṃ māṇavānaṃ eko kālarāvī kukkuṭo atthi, te tassa vassitasaddena uṭṭhāya sippaṃ sikkhanti.
kālarāvī.translation_1: Among these young brahmins there was a cock that crowed at the right time; they would get up to the sound of its crowing and study their arts.

rucādevatā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a deity in the Jātaka stories. Nominative singular in both sentences. Sometimes written as two words, Rucā devatā.
rucādevatā.example_1: Rucādevatā imāya gāthāya devasaṅghassa dhammaṃ desetvā yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā saddhiṃ kusanāḷidevatāya yathākammaṃ gatā.
rucādevatā.translation_1: The Ruca devatā, having taught the Dhamma to the assembly of gods with this verse, lived out her full lifespan and went according to her kamma along with the Kusanāḷi devatā.
rucādevatā.example_2: ‘‘ tadā rucādevatā ānando ahosi, kusanāḷidevatā pana ahameva ahosin ’’ ti.
rucādevatā.translation_2: 'At that time the Ruca devatā was Ānanda, and the Kusanāḷi devatā was I myself.'

dandhaparisakkano.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it appears as dandhaparisakkano, nominative singular masculine. The second member is probably parisakkana, from the root √sakk, but the exact derivation is uncertain.
dandhaparisakkano.example_1: Satthā āgantvā ‘‘ kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā ’’ ti pucchitvā ‘‘ imāya nāmā ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ na, bhikkhave, lāḷudāyī idāneva dandhaparisakkano yuttāyuttaṃ na jānāti, pubbepi evarūpo ahosi, niccaṃ lāḷakoyeva eso ’’ ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.
dandhaparisakkano.translation_1: The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what are you sitting here discussing?" And when they told him, he said, "Monks, it is not just now that Lāḷudāyi is slow-witted and does not know the proper from the improper; he was just like this in the past as well. He is always one who lets things slip," and he told a story of the past.
dandhaparisakkano.example_2: Tadā tesu māṇavesu eko dandhaparisakkano lāḷako māṇavo dhammantevāsiko hutvā sippaṃ uggaṇhāti, dandhabhāvena pana uggaṇhituṃ na sakkoti.
dandhaparisakkano.translation_2: At that time, among those students, there was one slow-witted, dribbling young student, a resident pupil who learned the arts, but because of his slow-wittedness, he could not master them.

lāḷakoyeva.meaning_2: foolish; silly; one who lets things slip; lālaka
lāḷakoyeva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text lāḷakoyeva = lāḷako + eva, nominative singular of the adjective describing Lāḷudāyi; the reading may be a comic variant of lāḷudāyī.
lāḷakoyeva.example_1: Satthā āgantvā ‘‘ kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā ’’ ti pucchitvā ‘‘ imāya nāmā ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ na, bhikkhave, lāḷudāyī idāneva dandhaparisakkano yuttāyuttaṃ na jānāti, pubbepi evarūpo ahosi, niccaṃ lāḷakoyeva eso ’’ ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.
lāḷakoyeva.translation_1: The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what are you sitting here discussing?" And when they told him, he said, "Monks, it is not just now that Lāḷudāyi is slow-witted and does not know the proper from the improper; he was just like this in the past as well. He is always one who lets things slip," and he told a story of the past.

lāḷako.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes a slow-witted, dribbling pupil. Nominative singular modifying māṇavo in the text.
lāḷako.example_1: Tadā tesu māṇavesu eko dandhaparisakkano lāḷako māṇavo dhammantevāsiko hutvā sippaṃ uggaṇhāti, dandhabhāvena pana uggaṇhituṃ na sakkoti.
lāḷako.translation_1: At that time, among those students, there was one slow-witted, dribbling young student, a resident pupil who learned the arts, but because of his slow-wittedness, he could not master them.

lāḷakaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular masculine in the text, used as a term of abuse for a feeble-minded person; PEU also relates it to laḷa, 'frivolous'.
lāḷakaṃ.example_1: ‘ Ucchu naṅgalīsasadisan ’ ti kathanepi leso atthi,‘ dadhikhīrāni pana niccaṃ paṇḍarāni pakkhittabhājanasaṇṭhānānī ’ ti idha sabbena sabbaṃ upamaṃ na kathesi, na sakkā imaṃ lāḷakaṃ sikkhāpetun ’’ ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –
lāḷakaṃ.translation_1: In saying, 'Sugar cane is like a plough shaft,' there is also a hint; but curds and milk are always white and take the shape of the vessel they are placed in, so here, he did not speak an analogy at all; it is not possible to teach this dribbling one," and he spoke this verse—

lāḷakamāṇavo.meaning_2: foolish young man; drooling youth; Lāḷaka the youth
lāḷakamāṇavo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of a character in the Jātaka story, identified with Lāḷudāyi. Nominative singular in the text. The first element is probably from lāḷaka (foolish; drooling), but the reading lāḷudāyī suggests a name-play; alternatively lāḷa + māṇava.
lāḷakamāṇavo.example_1: ‘‘ tadā lāḷakamāṇavo lāḷudāyī ahosi, disāpāmokkho ācariyo pana ahameva ahosin ’’ ti.
lāḷakamāṇavo.translation_1: 'At that time, the drooling youth was Lāḷudāyi, but I was the world-famed teacher.'

isisatāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text always plural isisatāni (nominative or accusative plural). Often in the stock phrase pañca isisatāni (five hundred hermits).
isisatāni.example_1: Satthā āgantvā ‘‘ kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā ’’ ti pucchitvā ‘‘ imāya nāmā ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepāyaṃ bhikkhu vattasampanno, pubbepetaṃ ekaṃ nissāya pañca isisatāni phalāphalatthāya araññaṃ agantvā eteneva ānītaphalāphalehi yāpesun ’’ ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.
isisatāni.translation_1: The Teacher, having arrived and asked, 'For what topic are you gathered here, monks?', and having been told, 'For this topic,' he replied: 'Monks, this is not the first time; even in the past, this bhikkhu was accomplished in conduct. Even in the past, relying on him, five hundred hermits did not have to go to the forest for fruits, but were sustained by the fruits brought by him,' and he brought forward the past.
isisatāni.example_2: So ‘‘ sādhū ’’ ti mahante mahante cammapasibbake kāretvā rattibhāge bhūmiṃ khaṇitvā dhanacāṭiyo uddharitvā pasibbakesu dhanaṃ pakkhipitvā cāṭiyo tiṇassa pūrāpetvā pañca ca isisatāni aññe ca manusse dhanaṃ gāhāpetvā palāyitvā sāvatthiṃ gantvā sabbe rājayutte gāhāpetvā rajjaṃ gahetvā pākāraaṭṭālakādipaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ kārāpetvā puna sapattaraññā yuddhena aggahetabbaṃ katvā nagaraṃ ajjhāvasati.
isisatāni.translation_2: He said, “Very well.” Then, having caused large leather sacks to be made, in the night-time, he dug the ground, pulled out the treasure pots, put the wealth into the sacks, filled the pots with grass, and having caused five hundred sages and other people to take the wealth, he fled. Having gone to Sāvatthī, he had all the royal officials seized, took the kingdom, and caused the renovation of walls, watchtowers, and so on. Having thus made the city impregnable against attack by enemy kings through battle again, he resided in the city.

lañjetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form lañjetvā is an absolutive of the causative verb lañjeti, from √lañch with the *e sign. The text uses it in the sense of sealing a letter with a seal. The PEU entry suggests lañchetvā as the expected form.
lañjetvā.example_1: So sayameva paṇṇaṃ gahetvā ‘‘ ahaṃ asukaṃ nāma mama puttaṃ tava santikaṃ pahiṇiṃ, āvāhavivāhasambandho nāma mayhañca tayā, tuyhañca mayā saddhiṃ patirūpo, tasmā tvaṃ imassa dārakassa attano dhītaraṃ datvā etaṃ tattheva vasāpehi, ahampi okāsaṃ labhitvā āgamissāmī ’’ ti likhitvā seṭṭhisseva muddikāya lañjetvā yathārucitaṃ paribbayañceva gandhavatthādīni ca gahetvā paccantaṃ gantvā seṭṭhiṃ disvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi.
lañjetvā.translation_1: He himself took a letter and wrote, 'I have sent my son named so-and-so to your presence. A marriage alliance is proper between me and you; therefore, give your daughter to this boy and have him stay right there. I will come when I get the opportunity,' and having sealed it with the treasurer's own seal, taken whatever provisions, perfumes, and clothes he liked, gone to the border, and seen the treasurer, he bowed and stood there.

pisituṃ.meaning_2: to grind; to crush; to pound
pisituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of pisati ('grinds, crushes'), used with gandhaṃ ('perfume') in the sense of grinding perfume ingredients. PEU analyses the base as pisa(pisi).
pisituṃ.example_1: ‘‘ Ime paccantavāsibhāveneva ahatasāṭake vaḷañjituṃ na jānanti, gandhe pisituṃ, pupphāni ganthituṃ na jānantī ’’ ti vatthakammantikādayo garahati.
pisituṃ.translation_1: He would criticize the workers, saying, 'Because they are border-dwellers, they do not know how to use new clothes, do not know how to perfume things, do not know how to string flowers.'
pisituṃ.example_2: Atha sā dakkhiṇahatthato valayaṃ vāmahattheyeva piḷandhitvā dakkhiṇahatthena gandhaṃ saṅkaḍḍhitvā pisituṃ ārabhi, vāmahatthe valayaṃ dutiyaṃ āgamma ghaṭṭiyamānaṃ saddamakāsi.
pisituṃ.translation_2: Then she, having placed the bracelet from her right hand onto her left hand, and having gathered the perfume with her right hand, began to grind. The bracelet on her left hand, rubbing against the second, made a sound.

ganthituṃ.meaning_2: to string; to tie together; to compose
ganthituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of ganthati (to tie, string, weave). Here used of stringing flowers (pupphāni ganthituṃ). The PEU's 'to compose/versify' is a secondary sense; 'to string (flowers)' fits this context.
ganthituṃ.example_1: ‘‘ Ime paccantavāsibhāveneva ahatasāṭake vaḷañjituṃ na jānanti, gandhe pisituṃ, pupphāni ganthituṃ na jānantī ’’ ti vatthakammantikādayo garahati.
ganthituṃ.translation_1: He would criticize the workers, saying, 'Because they are border-dwellers, they do not know how to use new clothes, do not know how to perfume things, do not know how to string flowers.'

paṭiyādāpetha.meaning_2: causes to prepare; has prepared; orders to arrange; gets ready
paṭiyādāpetha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative of paṭiyādeti (paṭi + √yat). Imperative 2nd plural in the text: 'prepare (food)'.
paṭiyādāpetha.example_1: So evaṃ parisaṃ uggaṇhāpetvā bodhisattassa paccantasamīpaṃ āgatakāle sasuraṃ avoca ‘‘ tāta, mama kira pitā tumhākaṃ dassanatthāya āgacchati, tumhe khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ paṭiyādāpetha, ahaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā paṭipathaṃ gamissāmī ’’ ti.
paṭiyādāpetha.translation_1: Having instructed the assembly in this way, when the Bodhisatta arrived near the border, he said to his father-in-law, 'Father, I hear my father, the Benares treasurer, is coming to see you. Prepare food for them, and I will take a present and go meet them.'

ulloketuṃ.meaning_2: to look up (at); to look at
ulloketuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of ulloketi. Used with samattho in the text: 'able to look at'. Spelled ulloketuṃ with sandhi of -tuṃ. The PEU analysis (u + loka + ṇe + tuṃ) treats it as a causative, hence the *e sign here.
ulloketuṃ.example_1: Tato paṭṭhāya kaṭāhakassa mukhaṃ ulloketuṃ samattho nāma nāhosi.
ulloketuṃ.translation_1: From that time on, no one was able to look Kaṭāhaka in the face.

garahituṃ.meaning_2: to criticize; to blame; to condemn; to reproach
garahituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive used with ārabhi and visahi; accusative object bhattaṃ.
garahituṃ.example_1: So ekadivasaṃ seṭṭhidhītāya nānaggarasabhojanaṃ upanetvā kaṭacchuṃ ādāya parivisantiyā bhattaṃ garahituṃ ārabhi.
garahituṃ.translation_1: One day, when the treasurer's daughter had brought and served him an excellent meal with a spoon, he began to criticize the food.
garahituṃ.example_2: Kaṭāhako ‘‘ addhā seṭṭhinā mama kulaṃ ācikkhitvā etissā sabbaṃ kathitaṃ bhavissatī ’’ ti tato paṭṭhāya puna bhattaṃ garahituṃ na visahi, nihatamāno yathāladdhaṃ bhuñjitvā yathākammaṃ gato.
garahituṃ.translation_2: Kaṭāhaka thought, “Surely the treasurer has told her my lineage and must have related the whole story to her.” From that day on, he did not dare to criticize the food anymore; with his pride brought low, he ate whatever he received and departed according to his kamma.

kalaṇḍuko.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a slave in the Jātaka commentary. Nominative singular in the text.
kalaṇḍuko.example_1: Idha panesa bārāṇasiseṭṭhino dāso kalaṇḍuko nāma ahosi.
kalaṇḍuko.translation_1: But in this case, the slave of the treasurer of Benares was named Kalanduka.
kalaṇḍuko.example_2: Tasmiñca kāle kalaṇḍuko nadīkīḷaṃ kīḷitukāmo bahuṃ mālāgandhavilepanañceva khādanīyabhojanīyāni ca gāhāpetvā nadiṃ gantvā seṭṭhidhītāya saddhiṃ nāvaṃ āruyha udake kīḷati.
kalaṇḍuko.translation_2: And at that time, Kalanduka, wishing to engage in river-sports, had a large amount of flowers, perfumes, ointments, as well as hard and soft food brought, and having gone to the river with the merchant's daughter, he got into a boat and played in the water.

kalaṇḍukaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a slave in the Jātaka prose. Accusative singular in both sentences.
kalaṇḍukaṃ.example_1: Tassa palāyitvā paccantavāsiseṭṭhino dhītaraṃ gahetvā mahantena parivārena vasanakāle bārāṇasiseṭṭhi pariyesāpetvāpi tassa gataṭṭhānaṃ ajānanto ‘‘ gaccha, kalaṇḍukaṃ pariyesā ’’ ti attanā puṭṭhaṃ sukapotakaṃ pesesi.
kalaṇḍukaṃ.translation_1: When he had run away and was living with the daughter of a border-merchant, attended by a large retinue, the Benares treasurer, though he had people search for him, could not discover his whereabouts, so he sent a parrot that he had raised himself, saying, “Go, search for Kalanduka.”
kalaṇḍukaṃ.example_2: Sukapotakopi nadītīraṃ gantvā ekissā udumbarasākhāya nisīditvā oloketvā kalaṇḍukaṃ sañjānitvā seṭṭhidhītāya sīse nuṭṭhubhantaṃ disvā ‘‘ are, kalaṇḍuka dāsa, attano jātiñca vasanaṭṭhānañca anussara, khīragaṇḍūsaṃ gahetvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā jātisampannāya sukhasaṃvaḍḍhāya seṭṭhidhītāya sīse mā nuṭṭhubhi, attano pamāṇaṃ na jānāsī ’’ ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –
kalaṇḍukaṃ.translation_2: The parrot, having gone to the riverbank and perched on a branch of a fig tree, looked, recognized Kalanduka, and seeing him spitting onto the head of the merchant's daughter, said, “Hey, slave Kalanduka, remember your own lineage and place of residence; having taken a mouthful of milk and washed your mouth, do not spit on the head of the merchant's daughter, who is well-born and raised in comfort. Do you not know your own measure?” And having said this, he spoke this verse—

kalaṇḍuka.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A proper name of a slave (kalaṇḍuka dāsa) in the Jātaka prose; vocative singular in the text. Possibly from kalaṇḍa (a kind of grain), perhaps meaning "grain-eater".
kalaṇḍuka.example_1: Sukapotakopi nadītīraṃ gantvā ekissā udumbarasākhāya nisīditvā oloketvā kalaṇḍukaṃ sañjānitvā seṭṭhidhītāya sīse nuṭṭhubhantaṃ disvā ‘‘ are, kalaṇḍuka dāsa, attano jātiñca vasanaṭṭhānañca anussara, khīragaṇḍūsaṃ gahetvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā jātisampannāya sukhasaṃvaḍḍhāya seṭṭhidhītāya sīse mā nuṭṭhubhi, attano pamāṇaṃ na jānāsī ’’ ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –
kalaṇḍuka.translation_1: The parrot, having gone to the riverbank and perched on a branch of a fig tree, looked, recognized Kalanduka, and seeing him spitting onto the head of the merchant's daughter, said, “Hey, slave Kalanduka, remember your own lineage and place of residence; having taken a mouthful of milk and washed your mouth, do not spit on the head of the merchant's daughter, who is well-born and raised in comfort. Do you not know your own measure?” And having said this, he spoke this verse—

nuṭṭhubhi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular; the text has both nuṭṭhubhantaṃ (present participle) and mā nuṭṭhubhi (prohibitive).
nuṭṭhubhi.example_1: Sukapotakopi nadītīraṃ gantvā ekissā udumbarasākhāya nisīditvā oloketvā kalaṇḍukaṃ sañjānitvā seṭṭhidhītāya sīse nuṭṭhubhantaṃ disvā ‘‘ are, kalaṇḍuka dāsa, attano jātiñca vasanaṭṭhānañca anussara, khīragaṇḍūsaṃ gahetvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā jātisampannāya sukhasaṃvaḍḍhāya seṭṭhidhītāya sīse mā nuṭṭhubhi, attano pamāṇaṃ na jānāsī ’’ ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –
nuṭṭhubhi.translation_1: The parrot, having gone to the riverbank and perched on a branch of a fig tree, looked, recognized Kalanduka, and seeing him spitting onto the head of the merchant's daughter, said, “Hey, slave Kalanduka, remember your own lineage and place of residence; having taken a mouthful of milk and washed your mouth, do not spit on the head of the merchant's daughter, who is well-born and raised in comfort. Do you not know your own measure?” And having said this, he spoke this verse—

kalaṇḍukāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Iti is attached; the entry is for the noun. Used as a proper name in the Jātaka stories. It could also be read as an ordinary noun, but the PEU gloss supports the name.

kalaṇḍukopi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name. In the text it is joined to the emphatic particle pi (kalaṇḍuko + pi), nominative singular, subject of āha.
kalaṇḍukopi.example_1: Kalaṇḍukopi suvapotakaṃ sañjānitvā ‘‘ maṃ pākaṭaṃ kareyyā ’’ ti bhayena ‘‘ ehi, sāmi, kadā āgatosī ’’ ti āha.
kalaṇḍukopi.translation_1: Kalanduka, also recognizing the parrot, out of fear that it might reveal him, said, “Come, master, when did you arrive?”

musikā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Subject of the clause; nominative singular. Plural sesamūsikā appears in the same sentence. Sometimes spelt mūsikā.
musikā.example_1: Bodhisatto ‘‘ kena nu kho kāraṇena musikā tanuttaṃ gatā ’’ ti cintento siṅgāle āsaṅkaṃ ṭhapetvā ‘‘ vīmaṃsissāmi nan ’’ ti upaṭṭhānakāle sesamūsikā purato katvā sayaṃ pacchato ahosi.
musikā.translation_1: The Bodhisatta, thinking, “For what reason are the rats becoming sparse?” and having developed suspicion about the jackal, thought, “I will test him,” and at the time of attendance, he put the other rats in front and remained at the back himself.

muru.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Onomatopoeic sound word, used twice (muru murū) for the noise of eating in the Jātaka prose. Perhaps related to mura 'crushing, wrapping'.
muru.example_1: Mūsikagaṇo nivattitvā siṅgālaṃ ‘‘ muru murū ’’ ti khāditvā agamāsi.
muru.translation_1: The troop of rats returned, ate the jackal with a 'crunch, crunch,' and left.

murūti.meaning_2: name of a musical instrument; a kind of drum
murūti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Rare form, apparently a variant of muraja, a double-sided drum. No sentence given; the exact meaning is uncertain. If taken as a verb form, it might be an aorist of murati (see PEU), but the noun reading fits the commentary context better.

aṅguṭṭhigaṇanāti.meaning_2: counting on the fingers, it is said; counting with the fingers, thus
aṅguṭṭhigaṇanāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of aṅguṭṭhigaṇanā (finger-counting) with the quotative iti; iti's initial i is elided after the final ā. Compound in -gaṇanā is feminine.

asilakkhaṇakalaṇḍukaṃ.meaning_2: Asilakkhaṇa and Kalaṇḍuka (name of two brothers or ascetics)
asilakkhaṇakalaṇḍukaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A dvanda compound used as a proper name in the Jātaka prose; nominative singular in the text, before the parallel Biḷāraggikosiyaṃ.
asilakkhaṇakalaṇḍukaṃ.translation_1: Asilakkhaṇa and Kalaṇḍuka, Biḷāraggi and Kosiya.

ophunāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to be winnowed; having had threshed and winnowed
ophunāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive in -tvā from ophunāpeti; the text uses it of having rice threshed and winnowed. The PEU gives ava + phuṇa + ṇāpe + tvā.
ophunāpetvā.example_1: Taṃ divasaṃ kira so rattasālīnaṃ sakaṭasahassamattaṃ ophunāpetvā koṭṭhāgāraṃ pūrāpesi, cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ gahetvā āgato akataññū mahācoro sahāyakassa tumbamatte palāpe dāpesi.
ophunāpetvā.translation_1: On that day, they say, he had had a thousand cartloads of red rice threshed and had filled his granary, yet the ungrateful master thief, who had come having taken forty crores of wealth, had a mere tumba of chaff given to his friend.

kalīni.meaning_2: worthless; useless; like chaff; good for nothing
kalīni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text kalībhavanti is glossed by kalīni kāḷakaṇṇisadisāni, i.e. neuter plural agreeing with mittāni; kalī is an adjective meaning 'worthless, chaff-like'. The commentary connects it with kāḷakaṇṇi 'a woeful (hell)'.
kalīni.example_1: Bālassa mittāni kalībhavantīti dandhassa apaññassa mittāni kalīni kāḷakaṇṇisadisāni honti, bhijjantīti attho.
kalīni.translation_1: Bālassa mittāni kalībhavantīti (the friendships of the fool become like chaff) means that for a slow, unintelligent person, friendships become like chaff—like a curse; the meaning is that they are destroyed.

uparavaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text: uparavaṃ akāsi, "made a commotion". Formed from the verb uparavati (upa + √ru, shout).
uparavaṃ.example_1: Kammantadāso ‘‘ hotu, sāmi, mā cintayitthā ’’ ti ubhopi assāsetvā attano gehaṃ netvā gandhodakena nhāpetvā bhojetvā ‘‘ sāmikā, vo āgatā ’’ ti sesadāse sannipātetvā dassetvā katipāhaṃ vītināmetvā sabbe dāse gahetvā rājaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā uparavaṃ akāsi.
uparavaṃ.translation_1: The farm-servant consoled them both saying, “Let it be, sir; do not worry,” and took them to his own house, had them bathed with perfumed water, and fed them. Saying, “Your masters have arrived,” he gathered the remaining slaves, showed them [the couple], and after a few days, having taken all the servants, went to the palace courtyard and made a commotion.

tāvātiādīni.meaning_2: ‘tāva’ and so on; such expressions as ‘tāva’; etc.
tāvātiādīni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of tāva and ātiādīni; a quotation mark after tāva is joined to the end. Probably a neuter plural referring to words like tāva. No sentence was supplied.

pakkudhāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to boil; having boiled thoroughly
pakkudhāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā of the causative pakkudhāpeti (pa + kudh + *e); the text uses it of water being made to boil before smoke and fire are raised.
pakkudhāpetvā.example_1: So kuddhamānaso rattibhāge sabbesaṃ sakuṇānaṃ sannipatitvā rukkhasākhāsu nipannakāle paṭhamaṃ tāva uddhanāropitaṃ viya udakaṃ pakkudhāpetvā dutiyavāre dhūmaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā tatiyavāre tālakkhandhappamāṇaṃ jālaṃ uṭṭhāpesi.
pakkudhāpetvā.translation_1: With an angry mind, during the night-time, when all the birds had gathered and were resting on the tree branches, he first caused the water to boil as if it were placed upon a furnace, secondly he caused smoke to rise, and thirdly he caused a fire as high as a palm-tree to flare up.

bhikkhaniṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text (thullanandaṃ bhikkhaniṃ); commonly written bhikkhunī.
bhikkhaniṃ.example_1: Bhagavā thullanandaṃ bhikkhaniṃ garahitvā ‘‘ bhikkhave, mahiccho puggalo nāma vijātamātuyāpi appiyo hoti amanāpo, appasanne pasādetuṃ, pasannānaṃ vā bhiyyosomattāya pasādaṃ janetuṃ, anuppannaṃ vā lābhaṃ uppādetuṃ, uppannaṃ vā pana lābhaṃ thiraṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti.
bhikkhaniṃ.translation_1: The Blessed One, having rebuked the bhikkhuni Thullanandā, said, “Monks, a person of great desires is displeasing and unlikable even to the mother who bore him; he is not able to placate those without confidence, or to produce confidence in those who have it to an even greater extent, or to give rise to a gain that has not arisen, or to make secure a gain that has already arisen.

tussitabbaṃ.meaning_2: should be content; should be satisfied; should be pleased
tussitabbaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Potential participle from tussati, used impersonally in the commentary glossing tuṭṭhabbaṃ. Nominative singular neuter in the text.
tussitabbaṃ.translation_1: In this, tuṭṭhabbaṃ means one should be content.

vikkiṇāpetvā.meaning_2: causes to sell; has (something) sold; makes (someone) buy
vikkiṇāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā of the causative vikkiṇāpeti; here with maṃsaṃ 'has meat bought'. The causative of vikkiṇāti (√kī with vi-).
vikkiṇāpetvā.example_1: Atha sā mūsikā gocarāya caramānā bodhisattaṃ punappunaṃ passantī uppannasinehā hutvā cintesi ‘‘ mayhaṃ dhanaṃ bahu nikkāraṇena nassissati, iminā saddhiṃ ekato hutvā idaṃ dhanaṃ datvā maṃsaṃ vikkiṇāpetvā khādissāmī ’’ ti.
vikkiṇāpetvā.translation_1: Then that mouse, wandering in search of food, repeatedly seeing the Bodhisatta, felt affection arise and thought, “My wealth will be destroyed for nothing; I shall join with this man, give him this wealth, and have him buy meat for me to eat.”

sopissā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of sā + assā. In the text it functions as the subject of āharati: 'she brought meat'. Alternative analysis: so + assā.
sopissā.example_1: Tato paṭṭhāya imināva niyāmena divase divase bodhisattassa kahāpaṇaṃ deti, sopissā maṃsaṃ āharati.
sopissā.translation_1: From that day on, by this same method, she gave a coin to the Bodhisatta day after day, and he brought meat for her.

nevāraññe.meaning_2: not in the forest; neither in the forest
nevāraññe.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of na + eva + āraññe (locative of ārañña); particle eva strengthens the negation. Occurs in the simile of the firebrand that serves neither in the forest nor in the village. Sometimes analysed as na eva āraññe.
nevāraññe.example_1: Tadā kira dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ ‘‘ āvuso, seyyathāpi nāma chavālātaṃ ubhatopadittaṃ majjhe gūthagataṃ nevāraññe kaṭṭhatthaṃ pharati, na gāme kaṭṭhatthaṃ pharati, evameva devadatto evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā ubhato bhaṭṭho ubhato paribāhiro jāto, gihiparibhogā ca parihīno, sāmaññatthañca na paripūretī ’’ ti.
nevāraññe.translation_1: At that time, the monks in the Hall of Truth raised this subject, saying: “Friends, just as a fire-brand charred at both ends and smeared with excrement in the middle serves no purpose as wood in the forest nor as wood in the village, so Devadatta, having gone forth into such a deliverance-bearing dispensation, has become one who has slipped from both, and is excluded from both; he has fallen away from the enjoyments of a householder and cannot fulfill the goal of monkhood.”

baḷiso.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text. The related PEU entry suggests bala + isa, but the root analysis is uncertain.
baḷiso.translation_1: The hook got stuck on a snag covered by the water.
baḷiso.example_2: Bāḷisiko taṃ ākaḍḍhituṃ asakkonto cintesi ‘‘ ayaṃ baḷiso mahāmacche laggo bhavissati, puttakaṃ mātu santikaṃ pesetvā paṭivissakehi saddhiṃ kalahaṃ kārāpemi, evaṃ ito na koci koṭṭhāsaṃ paccāsīsissatī ’’ ti.
baḷiso.translation_2: The fisherman, being unable to pull it up, thought, “This hook must have caught a large fish. I will send my son to his mother and have her start a quarrel with the neighbors; in this way, no one will hope for a share of this.”

uppīḷayamāno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle masculine nominative singular of uppīḷayati (= uppīḷeti), denoting simultaneous action: 'pressing/rubbing (his eyes)'. The PEU splits U+pīḷa+ṇaya+māna, but the verb is a causative of √pīḷ.
uppīḷayamāno.example_1: So vedanāppatto hutvā hatthena akkhīni uppīḷayamāno gahetvā udakā uttaritvā kampamāno sāṭakaṃ pariyesati.
uppīḷayamāno.translation_1: Suffering pain, clutching his eyes with his hands, he took them, climbed out of the water, trembling, and searched for his robe.

piḷandhitaṃ.meaning_2: put on; adorned with; worn (behind the ear)
piḷandhitaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Agrees with tālapaṇṇaṃ (neuter nominative singular). The word means a palm leaf worn as an ornament behind the ear. The PEU analysis piḷadhi + ta is uncertain.
piḷandhitaṃ.example_1: Atha naṃ ekā sahāyikā evamāha ‘‘ ekasmiṃyeva te kaṇṇe tālapaṇṇaṃ piḷandhitaṃ, ekaṃ akkhi añjitaṃ, piyaputtaṃ viya kukkuraṃ aṅkenādāya gharato gharaṃ gacchasi, kiṃ ummattikāsi jātā ’’ ti.
piḷandhitaṃ.translation_1: Then a female friend said to her, “You have put a palm leaf behind one ear, smeared one eye, and are going from house to house holding a dog as if it were a beloved child; have you gone mad?”

dāpiyati.meaning_2: makes (someone) pay; causes to give; has (a fine) paid
dāpiyati.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Passive-causative form of deti used with daṇḍaṃ: 'has a fine made to be paid'. The text form is plural/impersonal; PEU's 'Dā+ṇāpaya+te' analysis supports a causative-passive. 3rd singular here.
dāpiyati.example_1: Tattha sakhigehe ca bhaṇḍananti sakhī nāma sahāyikā, tassā ca gehe tava bhariyāya bhaṇḍanaṃ kataṃ, bhaṇḍanaṃ katvā bandhitvā pothetvā daṇḍaṃ dāpiyati.
dāpiyati.translation_1: In this, ‘in the friend’s house there is a quarrel’ means: sakhī (a friend) is a companion, and in the house of that friend, a quarrel has been made by your wife; having caused a quarrel, she has him tied and beaten and made to pay a fine.

vīhikoṭṭikadāsī.meaning_2: slave woman who husks rice; female servant employed in husking paddy
vīhikoṭṭikadāsī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of vīhi (rice), koṭṭika (husker, from √kuṭṭ) and dāsī (slave woman). Nominative singular in the text.
vīhikoṭṭikadāsī.example_1: Tasmiṃ kāle ekā bhatiyā vīhikoṭṭikadāsī vīhiṃ gehadvāre ātape pattharitvā rakkhantī nisinnāva niddaṃ okkami.
vīhikoṭṭikadāsī.translation_1: At that time, a certain grain-husking slave-woman had spread out rice in the sun near the house door and was sitting watching it when she fell asleep.

ghaṃsi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular, used intransitively for an animal rubbing its own body against something; also spelled ghasi in some texts. Alternative analysis: aorist of ghaṃsati from √ghaṃs (rub, grind).
ghaṃsi.example_1: So sarīre jhāyante ‘‘ aggiṃ nibbāpessāmī ’’ ti vegena gantvā hatthisālāya samīpe ekissā tiṇakuṭiyā sarīraṃ ghaṃsi, sā pajjali.
ghaṃsi.translation_1: With its body burning, thinking “I shall extinguish the fire,” it ran with speed and rubbed its body against a thatched shed near the elephant stable, and that caught fire.
ghaṃsi.example_2: Athekadivasaṃ ekissā vīhikoṭṭikāya dāsiyā ātape pasāritavīhiṃ khādanto eko eḷako ummukkena pahāraṃ labhitvā ādittasarīro palāyanto ekissā hatthisālaṃ nissāya tiṇakuṭiyā kuṭṭe sarīraṃ ghaṃsi.
ghaṃsi.translation_2: Then one day, one ram, eating rice that a female slave pounding rice had spread out in the sun, having received a blow with a firebrand, fled with his body ignited, rubbing himself on the wall of a grass-hut near an elephant stable.

gahitukāmo.meaning_2: wanting to catch; desiring to seize
gahitukāmo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of the infinitive gahituṃ (from gaṇhāti) and kāma. Nominative singular in the text, agreeing with manusso.
gahitukāmo.example_1: Atha naṃ eko manusso gahitukāmo ahosi.
gahitukāmo.translation_1: Then a certain man wanted to catch him.

ghatāsanajhānasodhaṃ.meaning_2: Ghaṭāsana and Jhānasodha; Ghaṭa, Āsana, and Jhānasodha
ghatāsanajhānasodhaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of two proper names in a verse listing persons; obscure, possibly names of deities or ascetics. Accusative singular in the text.

saloṇakaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular modifying aggibhagavantaṃ. Derived from saha + loṇa with the suffix ka; the initial sa- is the sandhi form of saha.
saloṇakaṃ.example_1: Athassa etadahosi ‘‘ idha loṇaṃ natthi, aggibhagavā aloṇaṃ khādituṃ na sakkhissati, gāmato loṇaṃ āharitvā aggibhagavantaṃ saloṇakaṃ khādāpessāmī ’’ ti.
saloṇakaṃ.translation_1: Then he thought, “There is no salt here; the Fire-lord will not be able to eat it without salt. I will fetch salt from the village and let the Fire-lord eat it with salt.”

kosiyāyanī.meaning_2: woman of the Kosiya clan; brahmin lady of the Kosiya family
kosiyāyanī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A feminine clan name (Kosiya + āyana + ī). The text glosses it as kosiyāyanī brāhmaṇī, a brahmin woman of the Kosiya family, nominative singular.
kosiyāyanī.example_1: Virattā kosiyāyaneti mātā no kosiyāyanī brāhmaṇī virattā amhākaṃ pitari nippemā jātā.
kosiyāyanī.translation_1: ‘Virattā kosiyāyane’ means: our mother, the brahmin lady of the Kosiya clan, has become indifferent and devoid of affection toward our father.

vaṭṭakkhīni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Kākā are described as praising the crow-hen's round eyes. Neuter plural of a bahubbīhi compound in -akkhi. PEU gives vaṭṭakkhi as na; the text's -ī reflects the plural ending of the compound adjective.
vaṭṭakkhīni.example_1: Evañca pana vatvā sabbepi te kākā ‘‘ tassā kākiyā evarūpaṃ nāma tuṇḍaṃ ahosi, evarūpāni vaṭṭakkhīni, evarūpaṃ chavisaṇṭhānaṃ, evarūpo madhurasaddo.
vaṭṭakkhīni.translation_1: And having said this, all those crows lamented much, saying, “The crow-hen had such a beak, such round eyes, such a complexion, and such a sweet voice.

obhañjāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to be folded; having had (the cloth) pressed
obhañjāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of the causative verb obhañjāpeti (√bhañj, 'break, fold'). In the sentence it describes pressing/folding cloth before it is pleated (satavalikaṃ sahassavalikaṃ).
obhañjāpetvā.example_1: So taṃ sudhotaṃ dhovāpetvā obhañjāpetvā satavalikaṃ sahassavalikaṃ kāretvā ṭhapesi.
obhañjāpetvā.translation_1: He washed them, pressed them, and had them made into a hundred or a thousand creases and kept them.

tuṇhehi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental plural tuṇhehi in the text. The PEU entry glosses tuṇha as 'one who is silent', but in these Jātaka sentences it clearly means 'beak': crows peck with beaks, and the nāga youths strike with their mouths. Doubtful derivation; possibly connected with tuṇḍa (beak, snout).
tuṇhehi.example_1: Balavavedanā pavattanti, kākā sīse nilīyitvā kaṇayaggasadisehi tuṇhehi akkhīni vijjhanti.
tuṇhehi.translation_1: Intense pains arose, and crows perched on his head and pecked out his eyes with beaks like the points of daggers.
tuṇhehi.example_2: Tepi cattāro nāgamāṇavakā ‘‘ dehī ’’ ti tuṇhehi sīsaṃ paharantā viya dāṭhā vivaritvā passasantā aṭṭhaṃsu.
tuṇhehi.translation_2: Those four Nāga youths also stood there, opening their fangs and hissing as if striking the head with their mouths, saying, “Give her.”

avamaññituṃ.meaning_2: to despise; to slight; to look down on
avamaññituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of avamaññati used with na vaṭṭati ('should not'). The doubled ññ is due to the *ya sign of √man.
avamaññituṃ.example_1: Anto uppannakileso hi ‘ parittako ’ ti avamaññituṃ na vaṭṭati, kileso nāma paccāmittasadiso.
avamaññituṃ.translation_1: For a defilement that has arisen within should not be slighted as ‘a little thing’; a defilement is like an enemy.

pajahitabbo.meaning_2: to be abandoned; to be given up; to be relinquished
pajahitabbo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Potential participle of pajahati, used impersonally with a subject understood (e.g. kilesa).
pajahitabbo.example_1: Uppannuppannakkhaṇeyeva paṭisaṅkhānabalena bhāvanābalena yathā muhuttampi hadaye aṭṭhatvā paduminipattā udakabindu viya vivaṭṭati, evaṃ pajahitabbo.
pajahitabbo.translation_1: At the very moment it arises, by the power of discrimination and the power of development, it should be abandoned so that it does not stay in the heart even for a moment, but rolls off like a water droplet from a lotus leaf.

porāṇakapaṇḍi.meaning_2: ancient wise man; sage of old
porāṇakapaṇḍi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text has porāṇakapaṇḍi, probably a contraction or variant of porāṇakapaṇḍita. Nominative singular, subject of āhari.
porāṇakapaṇḍi.example_1: Porāṇakapaṇḍi tāpi appamattakampi kilesaṃ garahitvā yathā puna abbhantare nuppajjati, evaṃ niggaṇhiṃsū ’’ ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.
porāṇakapaṇḍi.translation_1: The wise of old also, having criticized even a small defilement, suppressed it so that it would not arise within again,” and having said this, he related the past.

sampaggahito.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Past participle used as participle. In the sentence it modifies matabyaggho: 'supported by the gift of life'. The related PEU entry suggests a sandhi analysis saṃ + paggahita; here treated as the regular past participle of sampaggaṇhāti.
sampaggahito.example_1: Byaggho sañjīviko yathāti, yathā sañjīvena māṇavena mantaṃ parivattetvā matabyaggho sañjīviko jīvitasampadānena sampaggahito attano jīvitadāyakaṃ sañjīvameva jīvitā voropetvā tattheva pātesi, evaṃ aññopi yo asantapaggahaṃ karoti, so dussīlo taṃ attano sampaggāhakameva vināseti.
sampaggahito.translation_1: “Just as the tiger did to Sañjīva” (byaggho sañjīviko yathā) means: just as the dead tiger, which the student Sañjīva had restored to life by reciting a mantra and which was supported by the gift of life, ended up killing the very person who gave it life and letting him fall down dead right there, so too, whoever else supports the wicked—that immoral person destroys the very person who supports him.

sampadāno.meaning_2: name of a country; (the land of) Sampadāna
sampadāno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is part of a list of place names (Litta, Parosata, Haṃci, Kusanāḷā, Sampadāna); the form looks nominative but may be an accusative in -aṃ with sandhi, or a locative/ablative; the commentary PeU treats it as a derivable noun (saṃ + pa + dā + yu).
sampadāno.translation_1: Litta, Parosata, Haṃci, Kusanāḷi, and Asampadāna,

dubbinicchayaṃ.meaning_2: difficult to judge; hard to decide; difficult to settle
dubbinicchayaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Qualifies aḍḍa (lawsuit) in the text; accusative singular. du- becomes dub- before v-.
dubbinicchayaṃ.example_1: Ekasmiṃ pana divase kosalarājā ekaṃ agatigataṃ dubbinicchayaṃ aḍḍaṃ vinicchinitvā bhuttapātarāso allahatthova alaṅkatarathaṃ abhiruyha satthu santikaṃ gantvā phullapadumasassirikesu pādesu nipatitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi.
dubbinicchayaṃ.translation_1: Now, one day the king of Kosala had finished judging a difficult lawsuit involving a wrong course of action, and with his hands still wet [from eating], he mounted his adorned carriage, went to the presence of the Teacher, fell at his feet which were beautiful like an open lotus, and having venerated the Teacher, sat down to one side.
dubbinicchayaṃ.example_2: ‘‘ Bhante, ajja ekaṃ agatigataṃ dubbinicchayaṃ aḍḍaṃ vinicchinanto okāsaṃ alabhitvā idāni taṃ tīretvā bhuñjitvā allahatthova tumhākaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ āgatomhī ’’ ti.
dubbinicchayaṃ.translation_2: “Venerable sir, today I had to judge a difficult lawsuit involving a wrong course of action, and not finding an opportunity, I have only now finished it, eaten, and while my hands are still wet, I have come to your presence.”

kūṭaḍḍakārakā.meaning_2: false litigant; dishonest plaintiff; one who brings a fraudulent lawsuit; maker of a false case
kūṭaḍḍakārakā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominal compound (kūṭa + aḍḍa + kāraka), not a root derivative, so root fields are left empty. Nominative plural in both sentences, with the distributive nāma and negated ahesuṃ ('there were none'). The PEU analysis kūṭa + aḍḍa + kāraka is followed; aḍḍa here means 'lawsuit, case', not 'half'.
kūṭaḍḍakārakā.example_1: Vohāresu dhammena vinicchayamānesu kūṭaḍḍakārakā nāma nāhesuṃ, tesaṃ abhāvā aḍḍatthāya rājaṅgaṇe uparavo pacchijji.
kūṭaḍḍakārakā.translation_1: Since lawsuits were judged in accordance with Dhamma, there were no false litigants; because of their absence, the clamor in the palace courtyard for lawsuits ceased.
kūṭaḍḍakārakā.translation_2: While he was living, there were no so-called false accusers.

aḍḍatthāya.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Here the form is aḍḍa + atthāya, the dative of purpose, meaning 'for the sake of lawsuits'. The word aḍḍa in the sense of 'lawsuit' is found in compounds such as this and in the sentence's aḍḍakārakā.
aḍḍatthāya.example_1: Vohāresu dhammena vinicchayamānesu kūṭaḍḍakārakā nāma nāhesuṃ, tesaṃ abhāvā aḍḍatthāya rājaṅgaṇe uparavo pacchijji.
aḍḍatthāya.translation_1: Since lawsuits were judged in accordance with Dhamma, there were no false litigants; because of their absence, the clamor in the palace courtyard for lawsuits ceased.

uparavo.meaning_2: clamour; uproar; shouting; noise (of a crowd)
uparavo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text. In these sentences it refers to the hubbub of litigants in the palace courtyard, which ceased (pacchijji) when no disputes arose.
uparavo.example_1: Vohāresu dhammena vinicchayamānesu kūṭaḍḍakārakā nāma nāhesuṃ, tesaṃ abhāvā aḍḍatthāya rājaṅgaṇe uparavo pacchijji.
uparavo.translation_1: Since lawsuits were judged in accordance with Dhamma, there were no false litigants; because of their absence, the clamor in the palace courtyard for lawsuits ceased.
uparavo.example_2: ‘‘ mayi dhammena rajjaṃ kārente vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchantā nāma natthi, uparavo pacchijji, vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ chaḍḍetabbabhāvaṃ pattaṃ, idāni mayā attano aguṇaṃ pariyesituṃ vaṭṭati ‘ ayaṃ nāma me aguṇo ’ ti sutvā taṃ pahāya guṇesuyeva vattissāmī ’’ ti.
uparavo.translation_2: “Because I rule the kingdom in accordance with Dhamma, there is no one coming to the judgment hall; the clamor has ceased, and the judgment hall has reached a state of being abandoned. Now, it is appropriate for me to search for my own fault; having heard ‘this is my fault,’ I will abandon it and live only in goodness.”

antovaḷañjakādīsu.meaning_2: inside the palace courtyard and so on; within the inner apartments and elsewhere
antovaḷañjakādīsu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative plural in the text, agreeing with a person: 'among those inside the palace courtyard and so on'. A compound of anto (inside) and vaḷañjaka (courtyard, inner enclosure) with ādi (etc.).
antovaḷañjakādīsu.example_1: Tasmiṃ pana kāle balliko nāma kosalarājāpi dhammena rajjaṃ kārento aguṇakathaṃ gavesanto hutvā antovaḷañjakādīsu aguṇavādiṃ adisvā attano guṇakathameva sutvā janapadaṃ pariggaṇhanto taṃ padesaṃ agamāsi.
antovaḷañjakādīsu.translation_1: At that very time, Mallika, the king of Kosala, was also ruling his kingdom in accordance with Dhamma. He too was searching for his own faults, and finding no fault-finder among those within his palace and so on, and hearing only praise, he investigated the countryside and arrived at that very spot.

abhinādayi.meaning_2: makes resound; causes to echo; fills with sound
abhinādayi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist abhinādayi in the text; causative of abhinadati. The commentary glosses it as ekaninnādaṃ akāsi.
abhinādayi.example_2: Daddaraṃ abhinādayīti tena asanipātasaddasadisena bheravatarena sīhanādena taṃ rajatapabbataṃ abhinādayi ekaninnādaṃ akāsi.
abhinādayi.translation_2: “Made the silver mountain resound” means that with that fearful lion’s roar, resembling the sound of a thunderbolt, he made that silver mountain resound with one unified roar.

abhinādayīti.meaning_2: makes a loud noise; sounds out; resounds; roars
abhinādayīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative of abhinadati. The -ti of abhinādayīti is the sandhi quotation ending, i.e. abhinādaya + iti; the form is 3rd singular present. The related entry reads abhinādayati.

āvedhikāya.meaning_2: offering; presentation; formal submission of a question or case
āvedhikāya.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Only the instrumental singular āvedhikāya occurs, in the phrase āvedhikāya vā nivedhikāya vā, paired in contrast with nivedhika. Probably a compound with ā-, but the second element and the exact sense are uncertain; the translation is contextual.
āvedhikāya.example_1: ‘‘ sacāhaṃ imissā parisāya majjhe sāriputtaṃ āluḷento pañhaṃ pucchissāmi, ayaṃ me parisā ‘ bahussuto ayan ’ ti ñatvā sakkārasammānaṃ karissatī ’’ ti parisantarā uṭṭhāya theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā ekamantaṃ ṭhatvā ‘‘ āvuso sāriputta, mayampi taṃ ekaṃ pañhaṃ pucchāma, amhākampi okāsaṃ karohi, dehi me vinicchayaṃ āvedhikāya vā nivedhikāya vā niggahe vā paggahe vā visese vā paṭivisese vā ’’ ti āha.
āvedhikāya.translation_1: “If I ask Sāriputta a question while harassing him in the midst of this assembly, this assembly, knowing that ‘he is a learned one,’ will offer him respect and honors.” So, rising from the midst of the assembly, he approached the Elder, stood to one side, and said: “Friend Sāriputta, I too have a question for you; allow me an opportunity. Give me a judgment in refutation or in acceptation, in restraint or in exertion, in distinction or in counter-distinction.”

paṭivisese.meaning_2: in counter-distinction; in contrast; in differentiation
paṭivisese.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular of paṭivisesa used adverbially, paired with visese. Alternative reading: locative of paṭivisesa from paṭi + vi + √sis.
paṭivisese.example_1: ‘‘ sacāhaṃ imissā parisāya majjhe sāriputtaṃ āluḷento pañhaṃ pucchissāmi, ayaṃ me parisā ‘ bahussuto ayan ’ ti ñatvā sakkārasammānaṃ karissatī ’’ ti parisantarā uṭṭhāya theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā ekamantaṃ ṭhatvā ‘‘ āvuso sāriputta, mayampi taṃ ekaṃ pañhaṃ pucchāma, amhākampi okāsaṃ karohi, dehi me vinicchayaṃ āvedhikāya vā nivedhikāya vā niggahe vā paggahe vā visese vā paṭivisese vā ’’ ti āha.
paṭivisese.translation_1: “If I ask Sāriputta a question while harassing him in the midst of this assembly, this assembly, knowing that ‘he is a learned one,’ will offer him respect and honors.” So, rising from the midst of the assembly, he approached the Elder, stood to one side, and said: “Friend Sāriputta, I too have a question for you; allow me an opportunity. Give me a judgment in refutation or in acceptation, in restraint or in exertion, in distinction or in counter-distinction.”

yujjitukāmosi.meaning_2: wishing to fight; wanting to do battle
yujjitukāmosi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text asi is attached to the cpd (yujjitukāmo + asi, 2nd sg. of √as 1), so the form is yujjitukāmosi. The first member is the inf. yujjituṃ (of yujjhati, √yudh) used with kāma in the sense 'wishing to ...'.
yujjitukāmosi.example_1: Sace yujjitukāmosi, jayaṃ samma dadāmi te ’’ ti.
yujjitukāmosi.translation_1: If you wish to fight, friend, I grant you the victory.”

jīvapaṭijīvaṃ.meaning_2: exchange of "long life!" greetings; mutual wishing of long life; the custom of saying "may you live long"; (as name) the "Long Life" exchange
jīvapaṭijīvaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Occurs in the phrase jīvapaṭijīvaṃ nāma, referring to a customary exchange of "jīva!" greetings in a past story (jātaka). Neuter nominative/accusative singular; sometimes taken as the name of that custom. The PEU analysis gives the meaning as words meaning "may you live long".
jīvapaṭijīvaṃ.example_1: ‘‘ bhante, jīvapaṭijīvaṃ nāma kadā uppannan ’’ ti?
jīvapaṭijīvaṃ.translation_1: “Venerable sir, when did the ‘long life’ exchange arise?”
jīvapaṭijīvaṃ.example_2: Satthā ‘‘ bhikkhave, jīvapaṭijīvaṃ nāma porāṇakāle uppannan ’’ ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.
jīvapaṭijīvaṃ.translation_2: The Teacher said, “Bhikkhus, the ‘long life’ exchange arose in the olden days,” and he told the story of the past.

paṭijīvāti.meaning_2: lives off; subsists on; depends on for a living
paṭijīvāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Form is 3rd singular present with -ti (text variant for -ti). Paṭi- prefix with jīvati; not in the given sentences.

jīvapaṭijīvabhāṇino.meaning_2: one who says 'may you live' and 'may you live too'; exchanging long-life greetings
jīvapaṭijīvabhāṇino.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The compound is jīvapaṭijīva + bhāṇī; the first part refers to the greetings 'jīvā' and 'paṭijīvā'. In the text it is accusative plural.
jīvapaṭijīvabhāṇino.example_1: Tattha adhivattho yakkho dvādasa vassāni vessavaṇaṃ upaṭṭhahitvā taṃ sālaṃ labhanto ‘‘ imaṃ sālaṃ paviṭṭhamanussesu yo khipite ‘ jīvā ’ ti vadati, yo ca ‘ jīvā ’ ti vutte ‘ paṭijīvā ’ ti vadati, te jīvapaṭijīvabhāṇino ṭhapetvā avasese khādeyyāsī ’’ ti labhi.
jīvapaṭijīvabhāṇino.translation_1: The yakkha dwelling there, having served Vessavaṇa for twelve years, had received this building with the boon: “Of the humans who enter this building, if anyone, when someone sneezes, says ‘Long life to you,’ and if anyone, when ‘Long life to you’ is said, says ‘May you live long too,’ you may eat all those who are not those who exchange ‘long life.’”
jīvapaṭijīvabhāṇino.translation_2: “Except for those who say ‘Long life to you,’ I eat the rest.” (‘‘ Jīvapaṭijīvabhāṇino ṭhapetvā avasese khādāmī ’’ ti.)

cuṇṇo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text, though the form cuṇṇo looks like a masculine nominative; possibly written for cuṇṇaṃ. Subject of āgantvā pāvisi.
cuṇṇo.example_1: So ‘‘ bodhisattassa pitaraṃ khipāpessāmī ’’ ti attano ānubhāvena sukhumacuṇṇaṃ vissajjesi, cuṇṇo āgantvā tassa nāsapuṭe pāvisi.
cuṇṇo.translation_1: He thought, “I will make the Bodhisatta’s father sneeze,” and by his own magic power he let down fine dust, and the dust came and entered his nostrils.

khipāpito.meaning_2: made to sneeze; caused to sneeze; thrown (down); caused to be thrown
khipāpito.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative passive participle of khipati. In sentence 1 the sense is 'made to sneeze' (from the sneezing omen), while in sentence 2 it means 'caused to be thrown (down)'. Nominative singular in both.
khipāpito.example_1: Bodhisatto taṃ otarantaṃ disvā ‘‘ iminā me pitā khipāpito bhavissati, ayaṃ so khipite ‘ jīvā ’ ti avadantaṃ khādakayakkho bhavissatī ’’ ti pitaraṃ ārabbha paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –
khipāpito.translation_1: The Bodhisatta, seeing him descend, thought, “He must have made my father sneeze; this yakkha must be one who eats those who do not say ‘Long life to you,’” and regarding his father, he spoke the first stanza –
khipāpito.example_2: Atha naṃ rājā ‘‘ tāta, mayā tvaṃ gambhīre papāte khipāpito, kathaṃ sajīvitosī ’’ ti pucchanto navamaṃ gāthamāha –
khipāpito.translation_2: Then the king, asking, “Dear child, by me you were thrown down a deep precipice; how are you still alive?” spoke the ninth stanza—

paṭijīvaṃ.meaning_2: may you live long too; long-life exchange
paṭijīvaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of paṭi (indeclinable, 'in return; back') and jīvaṃ (1st singular of jīvati, 'I live'). The phrase paṭijīvaṃ karissāmi means 'I will make the return greeting' or 'I will perform the long-life exchange'. Alternative analysis: a quotation formula paṭi + jīvāmi with sandhi, but the context demands the first person singular. Also occurs as paṭijīvā in direct speech.
paṭijīvaṃ.example_1: ‘‘ ayaṃ so ‘ paṭijīvā ’ ti abhaṇantānaṃ khādakayakkho bhavissati, paṭijīvaṃ karissāmī ’’ ti.
paṭijīvaṃ.translation_1: “This must be the yakkha who eats those who do not say ‘May you live long too’; I will perform the long-life exchange.”

uṭṭhahituṃ.meaning_2: to rise; to get up; to stand up; to rise up (against)
uṭṭhahituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive used with samattho and nādāsi in the sense of rising up (against someone).
uṭṭhahituṃ.example_1: Tato paṭṭhāya sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ bodhisattassa hatthagatameva jātaṃ, añño paṭisattu nāma uṭṭhahituṃ samattho nāhosi.
uṭṭhahituṃ.translation_1: From that day on, the kingdom of the whole of Jambudīpa was firmly in the Bodhisatta's hands, and no other rival was able to rise against him. (Tato paṭṭhāya sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ bodhisattassa hatthagatameva jātaṃ, añño paṭisattu nāma uṭṭhahituṃ samattho nāhosi.)
uṭṭhahituṃ.example_2: Corajeṭṭhako purisalakkhaṇakusalo, so taṃ oloketvāva ‘‘ uttamapuriso ayan ’’ ti ñatvā ekassapi uṭṭhahituṃ nādāsi.
uṭṭhahituṃ.translation_2: The chief of robbers was skilled in reading men’s characteristics. Just by looking at him, he recognized, “This is a supreme person,” and did not allow even one of them to rise up.

nassituṃ.meaning_2: to be destroyed; to perish; to be lost
nassituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive following 'na labbhati' meaning 'is not allowed to be destroyed'. Passive sense. The PEU split 'nasa+ya+tuṃ' is doubtful; the infinitive suffix is -ituṃ.
nassituṃ.example_1: ‘‘ Bhante, tumhākaṃ dinnaṃ yāva pādapuñchanāpi nassituṃ na labbhatī ’’ ti?
nassituṃ.translation_1: “Venerable sir, even a foot towel given to you is not allowed to be destroyed?”
nassituṃ.example_2: ‘‘ Āma, mahārāja, amhākaṃ dinnaṃ nassituṃ na labbhati, paribhogameva hotī ’’ ti.
nassituṃ.translation_2: “Yes, Great King, it is not allowed to be destroyed; it only serves as an item of use.”

ovijjhitvā.meaning_2: having torn apart; having pierced through; having mangled
ovijjhitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā from a passive/impersonal stem ovijjhiya (√vidh 'pierce' with ava). In the first sentence it describes the lion tearing flesh with its fangs; in the second, elephants tearing each other apart.
ovijjhitvā.example_1: So muhuttaṃ vissamitvā saraṃ oruyha kaddamaṃ dhovitvā nhāyitvā darathaṃ paṭippassambhetvā ekaṃ mahiṃsaṃ vadhitvā dāṭhāhi ovijjhitvā maṃsaṃ ubbattetvā ‘‘ khāda, sammā ’’ ti siṅgālassa purato ṭhapetvā tena khādite pacchā attanā khādi.
ovijjhitvā.translation_1: The lion rested for a moment, went down to the lake, washed off the mud, bathed, calmed his agitation, killed a buffalo, tore up the flesh with his fangs, and placed it before the jackal, saying, “Eat, friend!” and after the jackal had eaten, he himself ate afterwards.
ovijjhitvā.example_2: Tepi hatthī sīhanādaṃ sutvā maraṇabhayatajjitā aññamaññaṃ ovijjhitvā tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, ṭhapetvā sīhe sesāpi migasūkarādayo sasabiḷārapariyosānā sabbe catuppādā tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu.
ovijjhitvā.translation_2: Those elephants, too, hearing the lion’s roar, were tormented by the fear of death, attacked one another, and perished right there; with the exception of the lions, all other animals—swine, deer, and so on, down to rabbits and cats—all perished right there.

sīhiyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular sīhiyā in the text ("with a lioness", "for the lioness"). The common form is sīhinī; sīhī is its shortened variant.
sīhiyā.example_1: Sīho ‘‘ gaṇhāhī ’’ ti vatvā sayampi sīhiyā atthāya maṃsaṃ gaṇhitvā ‘‘ ehi, samma, amhākaṃ pabbatamuddhani ṭhatvā sakhiyā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gamissāmā ’’ ti vatvā tattha gantvā maṃsaṃ khādāpetvā siṅgālañca siṅgāliñca assāsetvā ‘‘ ito paṭṭhāya idāni ahaṃ tumhe paṭijaggissāmī ’’ ti attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ netvā guhāya dvāre aññissā guhāya vasāpesi.
sīhiyā.translation_1: The lion said, “Take it.” And having taken meat for the lioness as well, he said, “Come, friend, let us go to my place on the mountain top and to your friend’s dwelling.” Having gone there and fed the lioness, he reassured the jackal and his mate, saying, “From now on, I will provide for you.” And he took them to his own place, and had them live in a cave near his own.
sīhiyā.translation_2: One day, a thought occurred to the lioness—

sīhiñca.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text sīhiñca is sīhaṃ + ca, with the accusative singular ending -aṃ assimilated before c: the lion (sīhaṃ) is the object of ṭhapetvā, and it is joined with siṅgāliṃ by ca. The PEU entry sīhinī (lioness) is a related feminine form, not this word.
sīhiñca.example_1: Te tato paṭṭhāya gocarāya gacchantā sīhiñca siṅgāliñca ṭhapetvā siṅgālena saddhiṃ gantvā nānāmige vadhitvā ubhopi tattheva maṃsaṃ khāditvā itarāsampi dvinnaṃ āharitvā denti.
sīhiñca.translation_1: From that time on, when they went to search for food, leaving the lioness and the jackaless behind, he would go with the jackal, kill various prey, and both would eat the meat there, and bring some back for the two others.

sīhī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine of sīha. Nominative singular in all three sentences, subject of vijāyi and of viheṭheti/tajjeti. The PEU cross-refers to sīhinī.
sīhī.example_1: Evaṃ kāle gacchante sīhī dve putte vijāyi, siṅgālīpi dve putte vijāyi.
sīhī.translation_1: In this way, as time passed, the lioness gave birth to two cubs, and the jackaless also gave birth to two.
sīhī.example_2: ‘‘ sāmi, ciraṃ amhehi tumhākaṃ santike nivutthaṃ, aticiraṃ vasantā nāma appiyā honti, amhākaṃ gocarāya pakkantakāle sīhī siṅgāliṃ viheṭheti ‘ imasmiṃ ṭhāne kasmā vasatha, palāyathā ’ ti tajjeti, sīhapotakāpi siṅgālapotake tajjenti.
sīhī.translation_2: “Master, we have lived in your presence for a long time; those who stay too long are not welcome. When we are away searching for food, the lioness plagues the jackaless, saying, ‘Why do you stay in this place? Run away!’ and the lion cubs also frighten the jackal cubs.”

sīhiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form sīhiṃ is the accusative singular of sīhinī (sīha + inī, fem). The PEU entry gives sīhinī as a variant of sīhī; the accusative singular sīhiṃ occurs in the sentence 'sīho sīhiṃ āha' (the lion spoke to the lioness).
sīhiṃ.example_1: Tassa vacanaṃ sutvā sīho sīhiṃ āha –
sīhiṃ.translation_1: Hearing his words, the lion spoke to the lioness—

mātimaññitthoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of mā + atimaññittho ti? Or mā + maññittho? Unclear; possibly maññati with mā and quotative -ti, so mā maññittho 'do not consider'. Verify against the text.

yaṃgocaro.meaning_2: whose range is whatever; having whatever as range; of whatever scope
yaṃgocaro.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Relative-correlative compound (yaṃ ... taṃ ...) in the gloss; nominative singular agreeing with soṇo.
yaṃgocaro.example_1: Suhanūpi tādisoyeva , yo soṇassa sagocaroti yādiso soṇo, suhanupi tādisoyeva, yo soṇassa sagocaro yaṃgocaro soṇo, sopi taṃgocaroyeva.
yaṃgocaro.translation_1: Suhanūpi tādisoyeva, yo soṇassa sagocaro means: just as Soṇa is, so too is Suhanu; the scope Soṇa has, Suhanu also has that same scope.

nāluḷessati.meaning_2: will not agitate; will not disturb
nāluḷessati.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] na + āluḷessati, future 3rd singular of āluḷeti (causative of √luḷ); the negative of the verb in a rhetorical question.
nāluḷessati.example_1: Atha naṃ satthā ‘‘ bhikkhu mātugāmo nāma kasmā tumhādisānaṃ cittaṃ nāluḷessati, porāṇakapaṇḍitānampi hi mātugāmassa saddaṃ sutvā satta vassasatāni asamudāciṇṇakilesā okāsaṃ labhitvā khaṇeneva samudācariṃsu.
nāluḷessati.translation_1: Then the Teacher said to him, “Bhikkhu, why wouldn’t womankind disturb the mind of someone like you? Even the wise men of old, on hearing the sound of a woman, with defilements that had not arisen for seven hundred years, having found an opening, they would arise in a single moment.

aṇḍakālepi.meaning_2: at the time of the egg; while still in the egg
aṇḍakālepi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative of aṇḍakāla used adverbially, with -pi in the text. The form aṇḍakālepi is aṇḍakāle + pi.
aṇḍakālepi.example_1: Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto morayoniyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā aṇḍakālepi kaṇikāramakuḷavaṇṇaaṇḍakoso hutvā aṇḍaṃ bhinditvā nikkhanto suvaṇṇavaṇṇo ahosi dassanīyo pāsādiko pakkhānaṃ antare surattarājivirājito, so attano jīvitaṃ rakkhanto tisso pabbatarājiyo atikkamma catutthāya pabbatarājiyā ekasmiṃ daṇḍakahiraññapabbatatale vāsaṃ kappesi.
aṇḍakālepi.translation_1: In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta took conception in a peacock species; even while in the egg, he became one with an eggshell as yellow as a kaṇikāra bud, and when he broke the egg and emerged, he was golden-hued, attractive, graceful, and adorned with red lines between his wings. To preserve his life, he traversed three mountain ranges, and on the fourth mountain range, he took up residence on a golden mountain plateau of Daṇḍaka.

moriṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine counterpart of mora (peacock). Accusative singular in the text (moriṃ).
moriṃ.example_1: So gantvā bodhisattena akkantaṭṭhānepi pāsassa asañcaraṇabhāvaṃ, attano parittaṃ katvā gocarabhūmigamanabhāvañcassa ñatvā paccantaṃ otaritvā ekaṃ moriṃ gahetvā yathā hatthatāḷasaddena naccati, accharāsaddena ca vassati, evaṃ sikkhāpetvā taṃ ādāya gantvā morena paritte akate pātoyeva pāsayaṭṭhiyo ropetvā pāse oḍḍetvā moriṃ vassāpesi.
moriṃ.translation_1: He went, and having known that the snare did not function even where the Bodhisatta stepped, and knowing that it went to its feeding ground after performing its protection, he went to a border region, caught a peahen, and trained it to dance at the sound of hand-clapping and to cry at the sound of snapping fingers; then, taking it along, he went, and early in the morning, before the peacock had performed its protection, he planted the snare sticks, set the snares, and made the peahen cry.
moriṃ.example_2: Atha naṃ pariggaṇhanto sāyaṃpātaṃ parittaṃ karontaṃ disvā ‘‘ imasmiṃ ṭhāne añño moro natthi, iminā brahmacārinā bhavitabbaṃ, brahmacariyānubhāvena ceva parittānubhāvena cassa pādo pāse na bajjhatī ’’ ti nayato pariggahetvā paccantajanapadaṃ gantvā ekaṃ moriṃ bandhitvā yathā sā accharāya pahaṭāya vassati, pāṇimhi pahaṭe naccati, evaṃ sikkhāpetvā ādāya gantvā bodhisattassa parittakaraṇato puretarameva pāsaṃ oḍḍetvā accharaṃ paharitvā moriṃ vassāpesi.
moriṃ.translation_2: Then, observing him reciting the protective chant morning and evening, he saw that in that place there was no other peacock, and thought, "This must be a celibate; because of the power of his celibacy and the power of his protective chant, his foot is not caught in the snare," and having realized this by logic, he went to a border country, bound a peahen, trained her to utter a note when fingers were snapped and to dance when hands were clapped, and taking her, he went to the Bodhisattva, set the snare before the peacock could perform his protective chant, snapped his fingers, and made the peahen call out.

maṅgalapokkharaṇito.meaning_2: auspicious lotus pond; royal bathing pond; ceremonial lotus lake
maṅgalapokkharaṇito.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Ablative singular in both sentences (maṅgalapokkharaṇiyā is the usual form; maṅgalapokkharaṇito appears here, with -to as the ablative ending).
maṅgalapokkharaṇito.example_1: ‘‘ Mahārāja, ahaṃ cakkavattikāle ratanamaye rathe nisīditvā ākāse vicariṃ, so me ratho maṅgalapokkharaṇiyā antobhūmiyaṃ nidahāpito, taṃ maṅgalapokkharaṇito ukkhipāpehi, so me sakkhi bhavissatī ’’ ti.
maṅgalapokkharaṇito.translation_1: 'Great King, in the time of my being a Wheel-turning Monarch, I traveled in the sky seated in a car made of jewels; that car of mine is buried beneath the auspicious royal lake. Have it raised from the auspicious lake, and that will be my witness.'
maṅgalapokkharaṇito.example_2: Kepuketi kepukaṃ vuccati udakaṃ, maṅgalapokkharaṇito udakaṃ nīharāpetvā nidhiṃ dassesi.
maṅgalapokkharaṇito.translation_2: Regarding the treasure in the water, ‘water’ is called ‘kepuka’; he had the water drawn out of the ceremonial lotus pond and revealed the treasure.
