pokkharaṇito.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Ablative singular in the text (pokkharaṇito); the -ī stem takes -to in the ablative. The pond here is the one from which water and lotus leaves are brought.
pokkharaṇito.example_1: Rājā ‘‘ sādhū ’’ ti paṭissuṇitvā pokkharaṇito udakaṃ harāpetvā rathaṃ nīharāpetvā bodhisattassa saddahi.
pokkharaṇito.translation_1: The king said, 'Very well,' and having acknowledged this, had the water removed from the lake, had the chariot raised, and believed the Bodhisatta.
pokkharaṇito.translation_2: Navehi pattehi means ‘with fresh lotus leaves brought from the pond at that very moment’ (taṅkhaṇaññeva pokkharaṇito ābhatehi allapaduminipattehi).

paṭiniyyādetvā.meaning_2: having handed back; having returned; having restored; having entrusted
paṭiniyyādetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā of the causative paṭiniyyādeti, 'causes to be given back'. In both sentences with rajjaṃ, 'handed the kingdom back (to)'. PEU suggests √yata (yata + ṇe + tvā), which would suit √yat 1 or √yam 1; the root here is uncertain.
paṭiniyyādetvā.example_1: So rajjaṃ tasseva paṭiniyyādetvā katipāhaṃ vasitvā ‘‘ appamatto hohi, mahārājā ’’ ti ovaditvā ākāse uppatitvā daṇḍakahiraññapabbatameva agamāsi.
paṭiniyyādetvā.translation_1: He restored the kingdom to him, and having stayed for a few days, exhorted him, 'Be diligent, Great King,' rose up in the sky, and went back to the golden mountain of Daṇḍaka.
paṭiniyyādetvā.example_2: Bodhisattopi rajjaṃ amaccānaṃ paṭiniyyādetvā himavantapadesaṃ gantvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.
paṭiniyyādetvā.translation_2: The Bodhisatta also, having returned the kingdom to the ministers, went to the Himalayan region, went forth into the ascetic life, and without his absorption having declined, was destined for the Brahma world.

adayhīti.meaning_2: burns; is burnt; is consumed (by fire)
adayhīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text as adayhīti = a + dayhi + iti; dayhi is the aorist 3rd singular of dahati/ḍayhati, 'it did not burn; it was not burnt'. The PEU entry points to dayhati/ḍayhati. Doubtful whether the aorist base is dah or ḍah; here treated as √ḍah with the aorist dayhi.

lehantiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine accusative singular lehantiṃ agreeing with sāmamigiṃ; present participle of lehati (licks).
lehantiṃ.example_1: So evaṃ vatvā ‘‘ na me tayā mittadubbhinā attho ’’ ti taṃ aggiṃ udakena nibbāpetvā sākhāhi pothetvā antohimavantaṃ pavisitvā ekaṃ sāmamigiṃ sīhassa ca byagghassa ca dīpino ca mukhaṃ lehantiṃ disvā ‘‘ sappurisehi saddhiṃ santhavā paraṃ seyyo nāma natthī ’’ ti cintetvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –
lehantiṃ.translation_1: Having said this, thinking, “I have no use for you, traitor,” he quenched the fire with water, beat it with sticks, entered deep into the Himalayas, and seeing a golden hind licking the faces of a lion, a tiger, and a panther, he thought, “There is nothing better than association with true people,” and uttered the second verse—

tavīmeti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] tava is the genitive singular of tvaṃ, meaning "your, of you"; the enclitics me and ti are appended in the given form.

biladvāre.meaning_2: opening of a hole; mouth of a burrow; entrance of a den
biladvāre.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text (biladvāre). Refers to the mouth of the mongoose's hole or the ant-heap in the story.
biladvāre.example_1: Atha sappassa bahinikkhantakāle nakulo caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ vammikassa biladvāre sīsaṃ nīharitvā mukhaṃ vivaritvā nipanno assasanto passasanto niddaṃ upagañchi.
biladvāre.translation_1: Then, at a time when the snake had gone out, the mongoose came to the entrance of the ant-heap at the edge of the cloistered walk, opened its mouth, lay down facing the opening, and fell asleep, breathing in and out.

upasāḷakanāmānīti.meaning_2: named Upasāḷaka; whose name is Upasāḷaka
upasāḷakanāmānīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of upasāḷakanāmāni + iti, with -āni contracted to -ānī before the quotation particle. Neuter nominative plural in the text. The word upasāḷaka is a proper name; nāma means 'named'.

upasāḷakaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A proper name. Accusative singular in the text; the compound Upasāḷakanāmāni is the title of the story.
upasāḷakaṃ.example_1: Upasāḷakanāmānīti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto ekaṃ upasāḷakaṃ nāma susānasuddhikaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi.
upasāḷakaṃ.translation_1: The Teacher told this story, Upasāḷakanāmāni, while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning a brahmin named Upasāḷaka who was fastidious about cemeteries.

upasāḷako.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A proper name (yādicchakanāma). Nominative singular in the text.
upasāḷako.example_1: Atīte imasmiññeva rājagahe ayameva upasāḷako brāhmaṇo ayamevassa putto ahosi.
upasāḷako.translation_1: In the past, in this very Rājagaha, this very brahmin Upasāḷaka and this very son of his existed.

upasāḷakoyeva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name in the Jātaka story, nominative singular joined with emphatic eva (koyeva). Although the word occurs within a compound sentence, here it is a sandhi of two words, not a compound.
upasāḷakoyeva.example_1: Bodhisatto imināva niyāmena pucchitvā māṇavassa vacanaṃ sutvā ‘‘ ehi, tava pitarā ācikkhitaṭṭhānassa ucchiṭṭhabhāvaṃ vā anucchiṭṭhabhāvaṃ vā jānissāmā ’’ ti tehi saddhiṃ pabbatamatthakaṃ āruyha ‘‘ idaṃ tiṇṇaṃ pabbatānaṃ antaraṃ anucchiṭṭhaṭṭhānan ’’ ti māṇavena vutte ‘‘ māṇava, imasmiṃyeva ṭhāne jhāpitakānaṃ pamāṇaṃ natthi, taveva pitā imasmiṃyeva rājagahe brāhmaṇakuleyeva nibbattitvā upasāḷakoyeva nāma hutvā imasmiṃyeva pabbatantare cuddasa jātisahassāni jhāpito.
upasāḷakoyeva.translation_1: The Bodhisatta, having asked in this same way and heard the young man's words, said, “Come, let us know whether the place pointed out by your father is previously used or not,” and having ascended the peak with them, when the young man said, “This space between the three hills is an unused place,” he said, “Young man, there is no count of those cremated in this very place; your own father, born in this very Rājagaha in a brahmin family, being Upasāḷaka by name, has been cremated in this very mountain-cleft for fourteen thousand births.

antaradhāpetabboti.meaning_2: causes to disappear; makes vanish; destroys
antaradhāpetabboti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative of antaradhāyati. Fused with quotative -ti; optative or potential sense possible in the commentary, but present indicative is the default analysis.

virādhetuṃ.meaning_2: lets fail; misses; loses; causes to go wrong; neglects
virādhetuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of the causative virādheti in the text (virādhetuṃ na vaṭṭati: 'it is not right to let it fail/be lost'). The PEU gives the root as radh; √rādh 1 (succeed, please) with the causative sign *e. Also analysed as virādhayati.
virādhetuṃ.example_1: Satthā āgantvā ‘‘ kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā ’’ ti pucchitvā ‘‘ imāya nāmā ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ bhikkhave, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi ‘ uppanno kalyāṇasaddo virādhetuṃ na vaṭṭatī ’ ti pabbajiṃsuyevā ’’ ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.
virādhetuṃ.translation_1: The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what topic are you gathered here now?” and when they said, “For this topic,” he said, “Monks, even the wise men of old went forth saying ‘it is not right to let a lucky word that has arisen disappear,’” and he brought forth the past.

ghuramādiyanti.meaning_2: takes up the yoke; takes up the burden (of restraint)
ghuramādiyanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound verb ghuramādiyati = ghuraṃ + ādiyati
ghuramādiyanti.example_1: Tasmā na hiyyetha naro sapañño, hiriyāpi santo ghuramādiyanti.
ghuramādiyanti.translation_1: a wise person should not fall away from that; virtuous ones take up the yoke out of moral shame and fear of wrongdoing.

kaṇṭakuraṇḍakavaṇṇaṃ.meaning_2: the colour of a kaṇṭakuraṇḍaka flower; the colour of the thorny barleria blossom
kaṇṭakuraṇḍakavaṇṇaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes the colour of a monk's robe (kāsāva); accusative singular agreeing with kāsāvaṃ. The PEU treats kaṇṭa as the first member; the usual word is kaṇṭaka (thorn).
kaṇṭakuraṇḍakavaṇṇaṃ.example_1: So kaṇṭakuraṇḍakavaṇṇaṃ kāsāvaṃ nivāsetvā kaṇikārapupphavaṇṇaṃ cīvaraṃ pārupitvā saṅghamajjhaṃ pavisitvā there vanditvā alaṅkataratanamaṇḍape paññattavaradhammāsanaṃ abhiruhitvā citrabījaniṃ gahetvā ‘‘ sarabhāṇaṃ bhaṇissāmī ’’ ti nisīdi, tāvadevassa sarīrā sedā mucciṃsu, sārajjaṃ okkami, pubbagāthāya paṭhamaṃ padaṃ udāharitvā anantaraṃ na passi.
kaṇṭakuraṇḍakavaṇṇaṃ.translation_1: He robed himself in his ocher robe the color of a trumpet-flower, wrapped himself in a robe the color of a kaṇikāra blossom, entered the midst of the Saṅgha, venerated the Elders, ascended the excellent preaching seat arranged in the decorated jeweled pavilion, and taking a variegated fan, he sat down thinking, ‘I will recite the scriptures.’ At that very moment, beads of sweat started out all over his body, timidity overcame him, and having repeated the first word of the first verse, he could not see what came next.

abhinādeti.meaning_2: makes resound; causes to echo; fills with sound
abhinādeti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Third person singular causative in -eti; in the text it governs daddaraṃ and is glossed as ekanādaṃ karoti, 'makes (the mountain) resound with a single roar'.
abhinādeti.example_1: 43. ‘‘ Ko nu saddena mahatā, abhinādeti daddaraṃ;
abhinādeti.translation_1: “Who is it with a mighty cry makes Daddara resound?
abhinādeti.example_2: Tattha abhinādeti daddaranti daddaraṃ rajatapabbataṃ ekanādaṃ karoti.
abhinādeti.translation_2: In that context, abhinādeti daddaran means he makes the silver mountain Daddara resound with a single roar.

accantīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Quotation form of accanti, 3rd plural present of acchati (√as 1), with iti joined. The commentary explains accantīti as attho, glossing samaccare.
accantīti.example_1: Tattha samaccareti santi upasaggamattaṃ, accantīti attho, tuṇhī hutvā nisīdantīti vuttaṃ hoti.
accantīti.translation_1: In that context, samaccare, the san is merely a particle, meaning ‘they stay,’ which is to say they sit in silence.

visibbanto.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle masculine nominative singular of visibbati; the simplex sibbati means 'sews', so the form is usually taken in the sense 'warming oneself' as in the text. Some editions may read visibbento.
visibbanto.example_1: So ekadivasaṃ vassānakāle deve vassante sāradārūni aggiṃ jāletvā visibbanto phalakatthare nipajji, puttopissa tāpasakumārako pitu pāde sambāhantova nisīdi.
visibbanto.translation_1: One day during the rainy season, as the devas poured down rain, he kindled a fire with dry wood and lay down on a wooden pallet to warm himself, while his son, the young ascetic, sat by him chafing his feet.

dubbhiyamakkaṭajātakaṇṇanā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Title heading in the Jātaka commentary; nominative singular. The compound is probably dubbhiya + makkaṭa + jātaka + aṇṇanā (= vaṇṇanā with elision).

uhannanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form uhannanti is present 3rd plural. The PEU entry uhanna is likely a past participle of the same verb; the root is uncertain.

vuḍḍi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine i-stem noun. In the text nominative singular in a conditional clause. Sometimes spelled vuḍḍhi or vaḍḍhi.
vuḍḍi.example_1: Sace pana vuḍḍi bhavissati, tuṇhī bhavissatī ’’ ti.
vuḍḍi.translation_1: But if there is to be benefit, he will remain silent.”

paṭissaraṇaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text, in the phrase natthi no aññaṃ paṭissaraṇaṃ aññatra vānarindena. The double s is sandhi for paṭi + saraṇa.
paṭissaraṇaṃ.example_1: Asītisahassavānarā manusse disvā maraṇabhayatajjitā ‘‘ natthi no aññaṃ paṭissaraṇaṃ aññatra vānarindenā ’’ ti tassa santikaṃ gantvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –
paṭissaraṇaṃ.translation_1: The eighty thousand monkeys, seeing the humans, were terrified by the fear of death, and thinking, “We have no other refuge besides the monkey king,” they went to his presence and recited the first stanza:

janittaṃ.meaning_2: context of birth; source of one's existence; place where one is born; birthplace
janittaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] From the refrain "janittaṃ me bhavittaṃ me". The commentary explains it in the sense of the place and circumstances where one comes into being; "birthplace" is the traditional rendering. The nominative singular is janittaṃ in the text.
janittaṃ.example_1: Janittaṃ me bhavittaṃ meti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ahivātakarogamuttaṃ ārabbha kathesi.
janittaṃ.translation_1: “That is one’s birthplace and one’s home”—the Teacher told this story while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, concerning a man who had been freed from cholera.
janittaṃ.example_2: 55. ‘‘ Janittaṃ me bhavittaṃ me, iti paṅke avassayiṃ;
janittaṃ.translation_2: “This is my birthplace, this is my home; for this reason I settled in the mud.

piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍenāti.meaning_2: exchanging alms (for food); swapping alms; giving food given as alms and receiving food in return
piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍenāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is followed by -āti (= -ā + iti), so the form is the instrumental singular piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍena. Listed as one of the wrong livelihoods of bhikkhus. Sometimes treated as a single dvanda compound.
piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍenāti.example_1: Ekasmiñhi kāle bahū bhikkhū vejjakammena dūtakammena pahiṇakammena jaṅghapesanikena piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍenāti evarūpāya ekavīsatividhāya anesanāya jīvikaṃ kappesuṃ.
piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍenāti.translation_1: At one time, many bhikkhus were earning a living by means of the twenty-one types of wrong livelihood, such as practicing medicine, acting as a go-between, running errands, serving as a foot-runner, or exchanging alms.

cāpanāḷiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text. The second member nāḷi ("tube, stalk") is an ī-stem, so the compound is declined like an ī-fem; meaning "the tube of the bow", i.e. the quiver.
cāpanāḷiṃ.example_1: Bodhisatto antosāṇiṃ pavisitvā uparinivatthaṃ setavatthaṃ haritvā ekaṃ rattapaṭaṃ nivāsetvā kacchaṃ bandhitvā ekaṃ rattapaṭaṃ udare bandhitvā pasibbakato sandhiyuttaṃ khaggaṃ nīharitvā vāmapasse sannayhitvā suvaṇṇakañcukaṃ paṭimuñcitvā cāpanāḷiṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ sannayhitvā sandhiyuttameṇḍakamahādhanuṃ ādāya pavāḷavaṇṇaṃ jiyaṃ āropetvā uṇhīsaṃ sīse paṭimuñcitvā tikhiṇakhurappaṃ nakhehi parivattayamāno sāṇiṃ dvidhā katvā pathaviṃ phāletvā alaṅkatanāgakumāro viya nikkhamitvā sarakhipanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā khurappaṃ sannayhitvā rājānaṃ āha –
cāpanāḷiṃ.translation_1: The Bodhisatta entered inside the curtain, discarded his outer white garment, dressed in a red loincloth, fastened his waistband, put on a red garment around his belly, drew from his bag a sword with joints, fastened it to his left side, put on a golden mailcoat, fastened his bow-case behind his back, took his ramshorn great-bow with joints, fixed the coral-colored bowstring, put the turban on his head, twirling the sharp razor-tipped arrow with his nails, split the curtain in two, tore open the earth, and emerged like a decorated Naga prince, went to the place for shooting the arrow, fixed the razor-tipped arrow to the string, and said to the king—

vidhūnati.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative of √dhū with vi-. In the text aṅguliyo vidhūnati: 3rd singular, active, 'waves (his) fingers'. Sometimes written vidhunāti.
vidhūnati.example_1: Mahājano taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā ‘‘ na no evarūpaṃ diṭṭhapubban ’’ ti mahāpurisaṃ pasaṃsati unnadati apphoṭeti aṅguliyo vidhūnati, celukkhepasahassāni pavatteti.
vidhūnati.translation_1: Seeing that miracle, the great crowd praised the Great Being, shouting, clapping, snapping their fingers, waving thousands of cloths, saying, “We have never seen anything like this before!”

gatapubbosi.meaning_2: you have gone before; you have previously travelled
gatapubbosi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of gatapubba (pp of gacchati, 'gone before') + asi ('you are', from √as 1). In the text it occurs in the question Himavantacārikaṃ gatapubbosi nandā, 'Nanda, have you travelled in the Himalayas before?'.
gatapubbosi.translation_1: “Nanda, have you ever traveled in the Himalaya?”

hattikkhandhavaragato.meaning_2: gone onto the excellent elephant's shoulder; mounted on the noble elephant's back
hattikkhandhavaragato.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound used of a king seated on his state elephant; nominative singular in the text, agreeing with the subject.
hattikkhandhavaragato.example_1: Sapattarājā maṅgalahatthiṃ vammena chādetvā sayampi vammaṃ paṭimuñcitvā hattikkhandhavaragato tikhiṇaṃ aṅkusaṃ ādāya ‘‘ nagaraṃ bhinditvā paccāmittaṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā rajjaṃ hatthagataṃ karissāmī ’’ ti hatthiṃ nagarābhimukhaṃ pesesi.
hattikkhandhavaragato.translation_1: The rival king had his state elephant armored, donned his own armor, ascended the best of elephants, took a sharp goad, and sent the elephant towards the city, thinking, “I will break down the city, destroy the enemy, and make the kingdom mine.”

avamadda.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Given as a gloss for omaddā in the commentary; imperative avamadda in the text means 'trample down'. Possibly a causative or denominative of √madd.

tāvamadhuraphalo.meaning_2: having previously had sweet fruit; whose fruit was once sweet
tāvamadhuraphalo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi compound, descriptive of the mango (ambo). Note the sandhi tāvaṃ + madhura > tāvamadhura. Nominative singular in the text.
tāvamadhuraphalo.example_1: Tena asātaamadhurasaṃsaggena tāvamadhuraphalo ambo tittako jāto nimbapaṇṇasadisaraso, ambaphalānaṃ tittakabhāvaṃ ñatvā uyyānapālo palāyi.
tāvamadhuraphalo.translation_1: Because of that association with the unpleasant and non-sweet, the mango tree, which had been sweet, became bitter, tasting like nimb leaves; knowing the mangoes had become bitter, the gardener fled.

kakkāretvā.meaning_2: having cleared the throat; having coughed; having spat out
kakkāretvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā of a causative verb; the text describes spitting out (niṭṭhubhi). The PEU connects it with √kar but the formation looks like an imitative causative (cf. kakkāra 'sound' as 'katt').
kakkāretvā.example_1: Dadhivāhano uyyānaṃ gantvā ambaphalaṃ khādanto mukhe paviṭṭhaṃ ambarasaṃ nimbakasaṭaṃ viya ajjhoharituṃ asakkonto kakkāretvā niṭṭhubhi.
kakkāretvā.translation_1: Dadhivāhana went to the park, and while eating a mango fruit, he was unable to swallow the mango juice that had entered his mouth, as it was like nimb juice, so he spat it out.

amboyaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound with udaka/uda in the final member; nominative singular in -aṃ in the verse, referring to the mango's juice or the mango-and-water drink.
amboyaṃ.translation_1: 71. “Endowed with colour, scent, and taste, this mango was (sweet) in the past;

naditukāmo.meaning_2: wanting to roar; desiring to make a sound
naditukāmo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text, agreeing with sopi (the jackal). Compound of the infinitive nadituṃ (from nadati) and kāma.
naditukāmo.example_1: Athekadivasaṃ deve vassitvā vigate sīhesu naditvā sīhakīḷaṃ kīḷantesu sopi tesaṃ antare naditukāmo hutvā siṅgālikaṃ nādaṃ nadi.
naditukāmo.translation_1: One day, when the rain had fallen and cleared, and the lions were roaring and playing the lion-sport, that son of the jackal, desiring to roar among them, uttered a jackal-cry.

nadituṃ.meaning_2: to roar; to make a sound
nadituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive after ussahi ("dared"); the creature no longer dared to roar.
nadituṃ.example_1: Imañca pana ovādaṃ sutvā puna so nadituṃ nāma na ussahi.
nadituṃ.translation_1: Having heard this advice, that creature never again attempted to roar.

osīdituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is the infinitive osīdituṃ (to sink), after ārabhiṃsu: 'the feet began to sink'. Infinitive of osīdati, formed with -tuṃ.
osīdituṃ.example_1: Athassa buddhārammaṇā pīti mandā jātā, pādā osīdituṃ ārabhiṃsu, so puna buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ daḷhaṃ katvā udakapiṭṭheneva gantvā jetavanaṃ pavisitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi.
osīdituṃ.translation_1: Then his rapture focused on the Buddha became weak and his feet began to sink. He again made his rapture focused on the Buddha firm and, walking on the surface of the water, he reached Jetavana, entered, venerated the Teacher, and sat to one side.

alaññeva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of alaṃ + yeva; alaṃ with the instrumental purāṇiyā means 'no need of, enough with'. Sentence quote marker -ti follows.
alaññeva.example_1: Aññaṃ jiyaṃ karissāmi, alaññeva purāṇiyā ’’ ti.
alaññeva.translation_1: I will make another bowstring; I have no need for that Purāṇī.”

niṭṭhubhantī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] It seems to be niṭṭhubhati, present 3rd singular participle niṭṭhubhantī in the text. There is no caus; the form is active and transitive. It takes an accusative object (bahalakheḷaṃ) and an upari phrase. The PEU glosses are partly wrong.
niṭṭhubhantī.example_1: Bhariyā panassa ‘‘ evarūpaṃ nāma dussīlaṃ kuṇṭhaṃ gaṅgāya āvāhetvā paṭijagganto vicaratī ’’ ti vatvā taṃ kuṇṭhaṃ jigucchamānā niṭṭhubhantī vicarati.
niṭṭhubhantī.translation_1: But his wife said, “He is living by nursing such an evil, limbless wretch cast adrift in the Ganges,” and she went around spitting in disgust at the wretch.
niṭṭhubhantī.example_2: Sā attano dhammatāya vicarantī uyyānaṃ gantvā kisavacchatāpasaṃ disvā ‘‘ ayaṃ kāḷakaṇṇī bhavissati, imassa sarīre kaliṃ pavāhetvā nhatvā gamissāmī ’’ ti dantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā sabbapaṭhamaṃ tassūpari bahalakheḷaṃ niṭṭhubhantī kisavacchatāpasassa jaṭantare niṭṭhubhitvā dantakaṭṭhampissa sīseyeva khipitvā sayaṃ sīsaṃ nhāyitvā gatā.
niṭṭhubhantī.translation_2: As was her custom, she wandered about. Having gone to the park, she saw the ascetic Kisavaccha and thought, “This one must be Misfortune. I shall wash away my bad luck on his body, then bathe, and go!” So, biting her toothpick, first of all, spitting thick phlegm on him, she spat into the ascetic Kisavaccha’s matted hair, threw her toothpick right on his head, and then washed her own head and departed.

saṃviruḷhesu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Used in a locative absolute construction (saṃviruḷhesu) meaning 'when ... had healed'. The root √ruh with saṃ vi takes the form viruḷha (with ḷ).
saṃviruḷhesu.example_1: Bodhisatto tassa vaṇesu saṃviruḷhesu bhariyāya saddhiṃ taṃ assamapadeyeva ṭhapetvā aṭavito phalāphalāni āharitvā tañca bhariyañca posesi.
saṃviruḷhesu.translation_1: When the wretch's wounds had healed, the Bodhisatta kept him in the ashram with his wife, and he brought fruits from the forest to feed both the wretch and his wife.

vadhitabbā.meaning_2: should be killed; to be executed
vadhitabbā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Potential participle, nominative singular feminine agreeing with itthiyo. In the commentary vajjhā and vadhitabbā are glossed together; the form is passive causative in sense.
vadhitabbā.translation_1: “Women deserve to die” means women are indeed those who should be killed, who deserve to be executed.

dubbhituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive form dubbhituṃ in the text. DPD lemma form given as present 3rd singular.
dubbhituṃ.example_1: Atha naṃ satthā ‘‘ upakārako te, mahārāja, so ca amacco sā ca itthī piyā ’’ ti pucchitvā ‘‘ āma, bhante, ativiya upakārako sakalaṃ rājakulaṃ sandhāreti, sāpi me itthī piyā ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ mahārāja,‘ attano upakārakesu sevakesu piyāsu ca itthīsu dubbhituṃ na sakkā ’ ti pubbepi rājāno paṇḍitānaṃ kathaṃ sutvā majjhattāva ahesun ’’ ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.
dubbhituṃ.translation_1: Then the Teacher asked him, “Great King, is that minister very helpful to you, and is that woman dear to you?” When he replied, “Yes, venerable sir, he is exceedingly helpful and manages the entire royal household, and that woman is also dear to me,” the Teacher said, “Great King, when servants are helpful and women are dear, one cannot harm them. In the past, too, kings, having heard the words of the wise, remained indifferent,” and having said this, he told the story of the past at the king’s request.
dubbhituṃ.translation_2: “Yet they desire to harm even those like that, Great King;

apaiti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Probably apa + eti (√i with -e-), 3rd singular. No example sentences were supplied, so the reading is uncertain. If it is a sandhi form it should be split and analysed separately.

itthikuttahāvabhāvavilāsehi.meaning_2: allurements and charms of women; feminine wiles and dalliances
itthikuttahāvabhāvavilāsehi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi-like compound describing the goblins' wiles; instrumental plural in the text. Possibly to be read as itthi + kutta + hāva + bhāva + vilāsa.
itthikuttahāvabhāvavilāsehi.example_1: tumhepi vāṇijāyeva, mayaṃ tumhākaṃ pādaparicārikā bhavissāmā ’’ ti vatvā te vāṇije itthikuttahāvabhāvavilāsehi palobhetvā yakkhanagaraṃ netvā sace paṭhamagahitā manussā atthi, te devasaṅkhalikāya bandhitvā kāraṇaghare pakkhipanti, attano vasanaṭṭhāne bhinnanāve manusse alabhantiyo pana parato kalyāṇiṃ orato nāgadīpanti evaṃ samuddatīraṃ anusañcaranti.
itthikuttahāvabhāvavilāsehi.translation_1: You too are merchants; we will be your wives.’ Having said this, they enticed the merchants with feminine wiles and dalliances and took them to the goblin city; then, if they had any previously captured men, they bound them with magic chains and cast them into a dungeon, while for those who found no shipwrecked men in their own place, they searched the seacoast as far as the Kalyāṇi river on one side and Nāgadīpa on the other.

umhayate.meaning_2: smiles; laughs; shows a happy face
umhayate.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text as umhayate (3rd singular middle, -e ending) in the phrase na naṃ umhayate disvā; commented as na hasitaṃ karoti, pahaṭṭhākāraṃ na dasseti. Root uncertain; the PEU suggests u + mhi + a, but no suitable root fits.
umhayate.example_1: Na naṃ umhayate disvāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi.
umhayate.translation_1: “He does not smile on seeing,” etc.—The Teacher told this story while dwelling at Jetavana, regarding a certain bhikkhu.
umhayate.example_2: 93. ‘‘ Na naṃ umhayate disvā, na ca naṃ paṭinandati;
umhayate.translation_2: “He smiles not when he sees him, and does not welcome him in return;

upakūthito.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Past participle used adverbially in the simile 'mummure upakūthito' (burnt up in the hot ashes/embers), referring to Poṭṭhapāda lying in the embers (kukkuḷe jhāmo).
upakūthito.translation_1: One should lie like Poṭṭhapāda, burnt up in the hot ashes.”
upakūthito.example_2: Aniyyānikañca saccaṃ bhaṇanto sayetha poṭṭhapādova , mummure upakūthito , yathā poṭṭhapādo kukkuḷe jhāmo sayati, evaṃ sayeyyāti.
upakūthito.translation_2: ‘And one who speaks truth that is non-beneficial, let him lie like Poṭṭhapāda, burnt up in the hot ashes; just as Poṭṭhapāda lies burnt in the embers, so let him lie.’

upakūdhitotipi.meaning_2: one whose drum has been beaten too; even with the (war) drum beaten
upakūdhitotipi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of upakūdhito (nominative singular of upakūdhita, 'whose drum has been beaten; drummed') + iti, before a quotation. The -pi/ti at the end is uncertain; likely iti, possibly iti + pi.

soyevāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of so (nominative of ta) with yeva and the quotative iti; -ti marks the end of a quotation. Written soyevāti in the text.

sarīradabyaṃ.meaning_2: having a beautiful body; of handsome appearance
sarīradabyaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of sarīra (body) and dabya (from √dabb? 'fitting, handsome'). Neuter singular in the verse, agreeing with the list of qualities. The PEU gives 'a beautiful body or a state of beautiful appearance'.
sarīradabyaṃ.translation_1: 99. “One has beauty, one has years, one is well-born, and one is virtuous;

sojaccaṃ.meaning_2: good birth; noble birth; nobility of lineage
sojaccaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Formed from sujāti with the secondary suffix ṇya (sojātya > sojacca). Nominative singular in the text; some editions read sujacca.
sojaccaṃ.translation_1: 99. “One has beauty, one has years, one is well-born, and one is virtuous;
sojaccaṃ.translation_2: One has noble birth, the perfection of lineage.

sādhusīliyaṃ.meaning_2: good conduct; virtue; state of having good moral behaviour; perfection of virtue
sādhusīliyaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Abstract noun from sādhusīla (virtuous). Subject in both sentences: nominative singular in the verse, neuter singular in the prose gloss (sundarasīlabhāvo sīlasampadā).
sādhusīliyaṃ.translation_1: 99. “One has beauty, one has years, one is well-born, and one is virtuous;
sādhusīliyaṃ.translation_2: One has good conduct, the state of having beautiful moral behavior, the perfection of virtue.

kannu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Interrogative pronoun with the sandhi -nnu (possibly from kaṃ nu) in the question kannu tesaṃ vanimhase. In the commentary this is glossed with kaṃ. The form is accusative singular used as the object of vanimhase; sometimes analysed as kannu or kaṃ + nu.
kannu.example_1: Brāhmaṇaṃ teva pucchāma, kannu tesaṃ vanimhase ’’ ti.
kannu.translation_1: I ask you, brahmin, which of these is best?”
kannu.example_2: Kannu tesaṃ vanimhaseti tesaṃ catunnaṃ janānaṃ kaṃ vanimhase, kaṃ icchāma, kassa tā kumārikā dadāmāti pucchati.
kannu.translation_2: “Which of these is best?”: among those four, which one should we take as a son-in-law? Which one do we desire? To which one should we give these maidens? he asks.

sarīradabyavirahitopi.meaning_2: even if devoid of bodily beauty; though lacking physical beauty
sarīradabyavirahitopi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of sarīradabyavirahita (adj, comp: sarīradabya + virahita) and the emphatic api. Concessive in sense: 'although devoid of bodily beauty'. The form is a nominative singular used of a person; the PEU split gives sarīradabya + virahita.
sarīradabyavirahitopi.example_1: Sīlavā hi ācārasampanno sarīradabyavirahitopi pujjo pāsaṃsoti.
sarīradabyavirahitopi.translation_1: For a virtuous person, endowed with good conduct, even if devoid of bodily beauty, is worthy, praised, and wise.

ruhakaṃ.meaning_2: name of a court brahmin (in the Ruhaka Jātaka)
ruhakaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name; accusative singular in the verse. The commentary explains it as a brahmin who officiates at royal ceremonies; the PEU's gloss "hole" may be a guess from ruhira/ruhaka.

ratthibhāge.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text, meaning 'in the middle of the night'. The first member is from ratti (night), with the stem-final i assimilated to the following bh.
ratthibhāge.example_1: So tassā anācikkhitvā ratthibhāge uṭṭhāya palāyi.
ratthibhāge.translation_1: He rose in the middle of the night without telling her and fled.

sīthilaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes a bond (bandhana) in the verse; neuter nominative singular agreeing with bandhanaṃ, same form as the masculine accusative.
sīthilaṃ.example_1: 102. ‘‘ Etaṃ daḷhaṃ bandhanamāhu dhīrā, ohārinaṃ sīthilaṃ duppamuñcaṃ;
sīthilaṃ.translation_1: 102. “Steadfast ones call that a strong bond—encircling, loose, and difficult to be freed from.

saṃparivattakādikīḷaṃ.meaning_2: tumbling and other games; rolling-around and similar play
saṃparivattakādikīḷaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of saṃparivattaka (tumbling, rolling) + ādi (etc.) + kīḷa (play). Accusative singular in the text, object of kīḷāpeti.
saṃparivattakādikīḷaṃ.example_1: Tadā brahmadattassa jiṇṇaṃ jarāppattaṃ hatthiṃ vā assaṃ vā goṇaṃ vā dassetuṃ na sakkā, keḷisīlo hutvā tathārūpaṃ disvāva anubandhāpeti, jiṇṇasakaṭampi disvā bhindāpeti, jiṇṇamātugāme disvā pakkosāpetvā udare paharāpetvā pātāpetvā puna uṭṭhāpetvā bhāyāpeti, jiṇṇapurise disvā laṅghake viya bhūmiyaṃ saṃparivattakādikīḷaṃ kīḷāpeti, apassanto ‘‘ asukaghare kira mahallako atthī ’’ ti sutvāpi pakkosāpetvā kīḷati.
saṃparivattakādikīḷaṃ.translation_1: At that time, Brahmadatta could not stand the sight of any elephant, horse, or ox that was old or decrepit. Being of a playful nature, whenever he saw such things, he would have them chased away. Even old carts he had broken up. Old women he had called, beaten on the belly, made to fall, then stood up again, only to frighten them. Old men he had made to roll on the ground like acrobats. If he did not see any, but heard that in such and such a house there was an old man, he would have him brought and play with him.

upaṭṭhahitunti.meaning_2: to take care of; to attend on; to nurse; to serve
upaṭṭhahitunti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The -ti at the end is the quotation particle, so the word is upaṭṭhahituṃ (infinitive). Alternative analysis with the present base upaṭṭhaha-.

uparī.meaning_2: above; over; on top (of); as a name: Ubarī
uparī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text 'uparī' is the name of a chief queen, not the adverb 'above'; the adverb would normally be written 'upari'. The word is therefore best treated as a proper name in these sentences.
uparī.example_1: Tassa uparī nāma aggamahesī piyā ahosi manāpā abhirūpā dassanīyā pāsādikā atikkantā mānusavaṇṇaṃ, apattā dibbavaṇṇaṃ.
uparī.translation_1: His chief queen, named Ubarī, was dear to him, agreeable, handsome, attractive, and inspiring; she surpassed the appearance of humans but did not reach the appearance of goddesses.
uparī.example_2: Bhante ‘‘‘ uparī nāma gomayapāṇakayoniyaṃ nibbattissatī ’ ti na saddahāmahan ’’ ti.
uparī.translation_2: “Venerable sir, I do not believe that Ubarī has been reborn as a dung-worm.”

metehi.meaning_2: belonging to friendliness; of benevolence; (in the phrase) enough of those ...
metehi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text 'metehi' = metta + ihi, instrumental plural, 'with those ...'. Part of the idiom 'alaṃ me ...' = enough of those ...'.
metehi.example_1: Alaṃ metehi ambehīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto devadattassa vadhāya parisakkanaṃ ārabbha kathesi.
metehi.translation_1: The Teacher told this story while dwelling at Jetavana, focusing on Devadatta's attempt to murder him.
metehi.example_2: 115. ‘‘ Alaṃ metehi ambehi, jambūhi panasehi ca;
metehi.translation_2: 115. “Enough of those mangoes, rose-apples, and jackfruits,

viakāsi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist form of viakaroti, "to distort, alter, misrepresent." In the text, an explanation of Byākāsi, meaning "he answered that memory in a distorted way." Also analyzed by the commentary as vi + akāsi, with vikāraṃ āpādesi as gloss.
viakāsi.example_1: Byākāsi saññaṃ parisaṃ vigayhāti atha ca pana parisaṃ vigāhitvā taṃ saññaṃ viakāsi vikāraṃ āpādesi, parivattesīti attho.
viakāsi.translation_1: “But once he entered the assembly, he answered something else” means: But instead, upon entering the assembly, he answered that memory in a twisted way, causing a transformation; this is the meaning.

vuḍḍhitabhattena.meaning_2: with heaped-up rice; with rice piled high
vuḍḍhitabhattena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular. vuḍḍhita, past participle of vuḍḍheti (heap up, pile up); bhatta (rice, boiled rice). The text explains: the rice at the top should be cold, at the bottom hot.
vuḍḍhitabhattena.example_1: Kiṃ heṭṭhā kiñca upparīti vuḍḍhitabhattena nāma upari sītalena, heṭṭhā uṇhena bhavitabbaṃ, idañca pana na tādisaṃ, tena taṃ pucchāmi –
vuḍḍhitabhattena.translation_1: Regarding “what is at the bottom and what is at the top?”: when rice has been heaped up, that at the top should be cold and that at the bottom should be hot; but this is not like that, so I ask about it—

bharuraṭṭhe.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text. Name of the kingdom of King Bharu.
bharuraṭṭhe.example_1: Atīte bharuraṭṭhe bharurājā nāma rajjaṃ kāresi.
bharuraṭṭhe.translation_1: In the past, a king named Bharu reigned in the kingdom of Bharu.
bharuraṭṭhe.translation_2: “King of Bharu” means the king in the kingdom of Bharu.

bharurājā.meaning_2: king of Bharu; the Bharu king
bharurājā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of the country name Bharu and rāja. Nominative singular in the text; the commentary glosses it as bharuraṭṭhe rājā.
bharurājā.example_1: Atīte bharuraṭṭhe bharurājā nāma rajjaṃ kāresi.
bharurājā.translation_1: In the past, a king named Bharu reigned in the kingdom of Bharu.
bharurājā.translation_2: “King of Bharu” means the king in the kingdom of Bharu.

bharunagaraṃ.meaning_2: Bharu city; the city of Bharu
bharunagaraṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of a city. Accusative singular in the text (patvā). PEU treats it as feminine/neuter; the -a stem is neuter here.
bharunagaraṃ.example_1: Tadā bodhisatto pañcābhiñño aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī gaṇasatthā tāpaso hutvā himavantapadese ciraṃ vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya pañcasatatāpasaparivuto himavantā otaritvā anupubbena bharunagaraṃ patvā tattha piṇḍāya caritvā nagarā nikkhamitvā uttaradvāre sākhāviṭapasampannassa vaṭarukkhassa mūle nisīditvā bhattakiccaṃ katvā tattheva rukkhamūle vāsaṃ kappesi.
bharunagaraṃ.translation_1: At that time, the Bodhisatta was a hermit who had acquired the five supernatural faculties and the eight attainments, and was the teacher of a group of hermits. He dwelt for a long time in the Himalaya region, and for the sake of salt and seasoning, he descended from the Himalaya with five hundred hermits in his following. Gradually arriving at the city of Bharu, he went for alms, came out of the city, and sat at the foot of a banyan tree at the northern gate, which was covered with branches and twigs. Having eaten, he took up his abode there at the foot of the tree.

bharuraṭṭhaṃ.meaning_2: kingdom of Bharu; Bharu country; the realm of Bharu
bharuraṭṭhaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of a kingdom in the Bharu Jātaka. Accusative singular in the text (bharuraṭṭhaṃ samuddaṃ ubbattetvā).
bharuraṭṭhaṃ.example_1: Sakalabharuraṭṭhavāsino devatā ekato hutvā ‘‘ sīlavante kalahaṃ karontena raññā ayuttaṃ katan ’’ ti bharurañño kujjhitvā tiyojanasatikaṃ bharuraṭṭhaṃ samuddaṃ ubbattetvā araṭṭhamakaṃsu.
bharuraṭṭhaṃ.translation_1: The devas dwelling in the entire kingdom of Bharu gathered together, and being angry with the King of Bharu, thinking, “It is improper for the king to have caused the virtuous hermits to quarrel,” they made the three-hundred-league kingdom of Bharu uninhabitable by submerging it in the sea.

jeṭṭhakaisi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text jeṭṭhakaisi is a compound (jeṭṭhaka + isi, 'chief hermit'), nominative singular; this entry covers the first member jeṭṭhaka.
jeṭṭhakaisi.example_1: ‘‘ ahaṃ tena samayena jeṭṭhakaisi ahosin ’’ ti, rājā tathāgatassa bhattakiccaṃ katvā gatakāle manusse pesetvā titthiyārāmaṃ viddhaṃsāpesi, titthiyā appatiṭṭhā ahesuṃ.
jeṭṭhakaisi.translation_1: “At that time, I was the head of the hermits.” The king, having finished the meal for the Tathāgata, at the time of his departure sent men and had the sectarians’ park destroyed, and the sectarians were left without a place.

tyāgatoti.meaning_2: from sacrifice; from giving up; from generosity
tyāgatoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Tappurisa compound with the ablative ending -to; same as tyāgā. Possible sandhi of tyāgā + ito? Not likely here. Meaning depends on context.

cūpatapeti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it appears as cūpatapeti, a sandhi of ca + upatapeti; the commentary glosses upatāpeti (causative) with kilameti viheṭheti. The reading upatapeti is also found.
cūpatapeti.example_1: 132. ‘‘ So maṃ dahati rāgaggi, cittaṃ cūpatapeti maṃ;
cūpatapeti.translation_1: 132. “That fire of passion burns me, and my mind torments me;
cūpatapeti.example_2: Cittaṃ cūpatapeti manti rāgasampayuttakaṃ mama cittameva ca maṃ upatāpeti kilameti viheṭheti.
cūpatapeti.translation_2: ‘And my mind torments me’ means: my mind, connected with passion, torments me, exhausts me, and harasses me.

seggu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A proper name, used in the vocative singular in both sentences. The context is a brahmin named Seggu.
seggu.example_1: 133. ‘‘ Sabbo loko attamano ahosi, akovidā gāmadhammassa seggu;
seggu.translation_1: 133. “All the world’s on pleasure bent, Seggu, you know not the ways of the village;
seggu.example_2: Tena tvaṃ pana, amma, seggu akovidā gāmadhammassa, imasmiṃ gāmadhamme vasaladhamme akusalāsīti vuttaṃ hoti.
seggu.translation_2: Therefore, O Seggu, since you are not skilled in the ways of the village, it is said that you are unskilled in this village-way, this low-minded way.

seggūti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Word appears with a quotation or enclitic (seggūti = seggu + iti); likely a Prakritism or variant form, possibly a misreading. No sentences were supplied, so the meaning is uncertain.

ayaphāle.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative plural in the text: 'in the iron ploughshares'. Part of a humorous simile.
ayaphāle.example_1: ‘‘ kulalā dārake gahetvā ākāse gantuṃ na sakkonti, mūsikā pana ayaphāle khādantī ’’ ti.
ayaphāle.translation_1: ‘If hawks cannot carry off children into the sky, then do mice eat iron ploughshares?’

paṭisāṭheyyaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominal formation paṭi + sāṭheyya (deceitfulness, from saṭha). Nominative singular in both sentences, referring to the Bodhisatta's counter-plot against the rogue.
paṭisāṭheyyaṃ.example_1: Bodhisatto ‘‘ saṭhassa paṭisāṭheyyaṃ katvā jinissāmīti iminā cintitaṃ bhavissatī ’’ ti ñatvā ‘‘ suṭṭhu te cintitan ’’ ti vatvā imā gāthā avoca –
paṭisāṭheyyaṃ.translation_1: The Bodhisatta, knowing, ‘He intends to defeat the rogue with his own trickery,’ and thinking, ‘He must have planned this,’ said, ‘Well thought!’ and uttered these verses —
paṭisāṭheyyaṃ.example_2: Sāṭheyyamidaṃ sucintitanti idaṃ paṭisāṭheyyaṃ cintentena tayā suṭṭhu cintitaṃ.
paṭisāṭheyyaṃ.translation_2: Sāṭheyyamidaṃ sucintitan (This trickery is well-thought-out) means: this counter-trick was well-conceived by you as you planned it.

sāṭheyyamiṃda.meaning_2: indeed the trickery; truly the deceit
sāṭheyyamiṃda.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of sāṭheyyaṃ (nominative singular of sāṭheyya, 'trickery') + ida (emphatic particle, variant of idaṃ/ida). In the text: sāṭheyyamiṃda = sāṭheyyaṃ + ida. Some editions may read sāṭheyyaṃ ida.
sāṭheyyamiṃda.example_1: 135. ‘‘ Saṭhassa sāṭheyyamiṃda sucintitaṃ, paccoḍḍitaṃ paṭikūṭassa kūṭaṃ;
sāṭheyyamiṃda.translation_1: 135. “Well thought out is the trickery of the rogue; the rogue has been tricked by a counter-trick.”

paṭikūṭassa.meaning_2: counter-rogue; rogue in return; one who cheats a cheat; counter-trick
paṭikūṭassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Genitive singular in the text (paṭikūṭassa kūṭaṃ = the counter-rogue's trick). Kūṭa here means 'rogue, cheat'. It is used as a noun in this verse.
paṭikūṭassa.example_1: 135. ‘‘ Saṭhassa sāṭheyyamiṃda sucintitaṃ, paccoḍḍitaṃ paṭikūṭassa kūṭaṃ;
paṭikūṭassa.translation_1: 135. “Well thought out is the trickery of the rogue; the rogue has been tricked by a counter-trick.”
paṭikūṭassa.example_2: Paccoḍḍitaṃ paṭikūṭassa kūṭanti kūṭassa puggalassa tayā paṭikūṭaṃ suṭṭhu paccoḍḍitaṃ, paṭibhāgaṃ katvā oḍḍitasadisameva katanti attho.
paṭikūṭassa.translation_2: Paccoḍḍitaṃ paṭikūṭassa kūṭan (The rogue's trick has been countered by a trick) means: for the rogue, you have effectively countered it with a trick; the meaning is that you have acted in a manner identical to the way he ensnared you, having created a corresponding object.

paṭikūṭaṃ.meaning_2: counter-cheating; returning the trick; cheater in return
paṭikūṭaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text paṭikūṭassa is genitive/dative singular and paṭikūṭaṃ (before suṭṭhu) is the neuter accusative, glossed with paccoḍḍitaṃ. A non-canonical word, probably from the commentary's etymology pati + kūṭa.
paṭikūṭaṃ.example_1: Paccoḍḍitaṃ paṭikūṭassa kūṭanti kūṭassa puggalassa tayā paṭikūṭaṃ suṭṭhu paccoḍḍitaṃ, paṭibhāgaṃ katvā oḍḍitasadisameva katanti attho.
paṭikūṭaṃ.translation_1: Paccoḍḍitaṃ paṭikūṭassa kūṭan (The rogue's trick has been countered by a trick) means: for the rogue, you have effectively countered it with a trick; the meaning is that you have acted in a manner identical to the way he ensnared you, having created a corresponding object.

kūṭapaṭikūṭānaṃ.meaning_2: cheat the cheat; cheater of cheaters; rogue who cheats the cheats
kūṭapaṭikūṭānaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Genitive plural in the text, glossed kūṭassa kūṭā / kūṭassa paṭikūṭā. It is a reduplicative type formation; kūṭa here means 'rogue, cheat'.
kūṭapaṭikūṭānaṃ.example_1: Kūṭassa hi santi kūṭakūṭāti tvaṃ ‘‘ ahameva mūsikāhi phāle khādāpitapuriso kūṭo ’’ ti maññasi, tādisassa pana kūṭassa imasmiṃ loke bahū kūṭā santi, kūṭassa kūṭāti kūṭapaṭikūṭānaṃ etaṃ nāmaṃ, kūṭassa paṭikūṭā nāma santīti vuttaṃ hoti.
kūṭapaṭikūṭānaṃ.translation_1: Kūṭassa hi santi kūṭakūṭā (For there exist those who cheat the cheat) means: you think, ‘I alone am a rogue because I have made the man have the ploughshare eaten by mice,’ but there are many such rogues in this world; ‘cheat the cheat’ is a name for those who cheat the cheaters; it is said that those who cheat the cheats indeed exist.

paṭikūṭā.meaning_2: cheat the cheat; one who cheats the cheater; a rogue who out-rogues another
paṭikūṭā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative plural in kūṭapaṭikūṭānaṃ / kūṭassa paṭikūṭā; explained in the commentary as kūṭassa kūṭā. The PEU entry gives the stem paṭikūṭa as an adjective, but here it is used as a masculine noun.
paṭikūṭā.example_1: Kūṭassa hi santi kūṭakūṭāti tvaṃ ‘‘ ahameva mūsikāhi phāle khādāpitapuriso kūṭo ’’ ti maññasi, tādisassa pana kūṭassa imasmiṃ loke bahū kūṭā santi, kūṭassa kūṭāti kūṭapaṭikūṭānaṃ etaṃ nāmaṃ, kūṭassa paṭikūṭā nāma santīti vuttaṃ hoti.
paṭikūṭā.translation_1: Kūṭassa hi santi kūṭakūṭā (For there exist those who cheat the cheat) means: you think, ‘I alone am a rogue because I have made the man have the ploughshare eaten by mice,’ but there are many such rogues in this world; ‘cheat the cheat’ is a name for those who cheat the cheaters; it is said that those who cheat the cheats indeed exist.

nikatyāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form in the text is a quotation followed by iti; the -ti belongs to the quotation marker. Ablative or instrumental case.

vañcanakapuggalassa.meaning_2: deceitful person; fraudulent person; person who is a deceiver
vañcanakapuggalassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Genitive singular in the text, qualifying vañcanakapuriso. vañcanaka is a gerundive-type adjective from √vañc 1 (be bent, deceive).
vañcanakapuggalassa.example_1: Bhavati cāpi nikatino nikatyāti nikatino nekatikassa vañcanakapuggalassa nikatyā aparo nikatikārako vañcanakapuriso bhavatiyeva.
vañcanakapuggalassa.translation_1: Bhavati cāpi nikatino nikatyā (And those given to guile also exist, having been caught through guile) means: by the guile of another deceitful and fraudulent person, the fraudulent person also comes to be caught.

vañcanakapuriso.meaning_2: deceitful man; fraudulent person; cheating man
vañcanakapuriso.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text; glosses vañcanakapuggala.
vañcanakapuriso.example_1: Bhavati cāpi nikatino nikatyāti nikatino nekatikassa vañcanakapuggalassa nikatyā aparo nikatikārako vañcanakapuriso bhavatiyeva.
vañcanakapuriso.translation_1: Bhavati cāpi nikatino nikatyā (And those given to guile also exist, having been caught through guile) means: by the guile of another deceitful and fraudulent person, the fraudulent person also comes to be caught.

paṭivinicchinitvā.meaning_2: having decided again; having judged again; having re-examined (a case)
paṭivinicchinitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is the absolutive of the verb paṭivinicchināti ("decides again; re-judges"), here governing aḍḍaṃ, "having re-judged the case". Related to vinicchināti and vicināti.
paṭivinicchinitvā.example_1: Mahājano sannipati, bodhisatto taṃ aḍḍaṃ paṭivinicchinitvā sāmikaññeva sāmikaṃ akāsi.
paṭivinicchinitvā.translation_1: A great crowd gathered; the Bodhisatta re-judged the case and gave the judgment for the one who was the rightful owner.

dubbinicchito.meaning_2: wrongly judged; badly decided; poorly settled
dubbinicchito.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Used of a legal case (aḍḍa) wrongly decided. Nominative singular masculine in the text; also agrees with aḍḍa (masc).
dubbinicchito.example_1: ‘‘ Deva, dhammadhajapaṇḍitena dubbinicchito aḍḍo suvinicchito, tatresa sādhukārasaddo ’’ ti.
dubbinicchito.translation_1: “Great King, a case wrongly judged by the general has been well resolved by the wise Dhammadhaja; that is the sound of applause there.”
dubbinicchito.example_2: Sace dubbinicchito hoti, pādukā aññamaññaṃ paṭihaññanti.
dubbinicchito.translation_2: If a case was decided wrongly, the sandals struck against each other.

dubbinicchitaṃ.meaning_2: badly decided; wrongly judged; poorly adjudicated
dubbinicchitaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Qualifies aḍḍaṃ (case) in the text; accusative singular neuter agreeing with aḍḍaṃ. du- becomes dub- before v.
dubbinicchitaṃ.example_1: ‘‘ Āma, mahārāja, kāḷakena dubbinicchitaṃ aḍḍaṃ vinicchinin ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ ito dāni paṭṭhāya tumheva aḍḍaṃ vinicchinatha, mayhañca kaṇṇasukhaṃ bhavissati lokassa ca vuḍḍhī ’’ ti vatvā anicchantampi taṃ ‘‘ sattānuddayāya vinicchaye nisīdathā ’’ ti yācitvā sampaṭicchāpesi.
dubbinicchitaṃ.translation_1: When it was said, “Yes, Great King, I have resolved a case wrongly judged by Kāḷaka,” the king said, “From this day on, you yourself shall judge the cases; it will be a joy for my ears and a prosperity for the world,” and he requested him, though unwilling, saying, “In pity for beings, sit in judgment,” and won his consent.

nisnehako.meaning_2: free from affection; without attachment; indifferent
nisnehako.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes a person without affection or attachment; nominative singular in the text.
nisnehako.example_1: Nisnehako ahaṃ deva, akkodhanaṃ adhiṭṭhito ’’ ti.
nisnehako.translation_1: —am indifferent, and I am established in the practice of non-anger,” he said, “I am endowed with four qualities.”

bhūtapūbbo.meaning_2: having been before; that has existed before; former; previous
bhūtapūbbo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is nominative singular masculine (na bhūtapūbbo): 'there has not been (such a thing) before'. Compound of bhūta (been) + pubba (before).
bhūtapūbbo.example_1: ‘‘ Mayhañhi, mahārāja, usūyā nāma natthi, majjaṃ me na pivitapubbaṃ, paresu me sneho vā kodho vā na bhūtapūbbo.
bhūtapūbbo.translation_1: “This is true, Great King. For me, there is no jealousy; liquor has never been drunk by me; regarding others, there has never been love or anger.”

khādayiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] First person singular aorist of khādati; the form is anomalous. In the text the son-eater confesses he ate his son's flesh.
khādayiṃ.translation_1: “I was drunk, Great King, and I ate the flesh of my son;”

amaṃsakabhattampi.meaning_2: and a meatless meal too; even a meal without meat
amaṃsakabhattampi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text the sandhi joins amaṃsakabhattaṃ (nominative/accusative singular of amaṃsakabhatta, 'meatless meal') with the enclitic pi; the nasal of bhattaṃ assimilates to pi. Split as amaṃsakabhattaṃ + pi; the entry for the main word is amaṃsakabhatta.
amaṃsakabhattampi.example_1: Ahaṃ, mahārāja, pubbe tādiso bārāṇasirājā hutvā majjena vinā vattituṃ nāsakkhiṃ, amaṃsakabhattampi bhuñjituṃ nāsakkhiṃ.
amaṃsakabhattampi.translation_1: Great King, formerly I was a Bārāṇasī king like you, and I could not live without liquor, and I could not eat a meal without meat.

amaṃsakabhojanaṃ.meaning_2: meal without meat; food without meat
amaṃsakabhojanaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text, object of upanāmetuṃ. The cook uses it when no meat is available on the uposatha day.
amaṃsakabhojanaṃ.example_1: Bhattakārako uposathadivase maṃsaṃ alabhitvā rañño nānaggarasabhojanaṃ pacitvā pāsādaṃ āropetvā upanāmetuṃ asakkonto deviṃ upasaṅkamitvā ‘‘ devi, ajja me maṃsaṃ na laddhaṃ, amaṃsakabhojanaṃ nāma upanāmetuṃ na sakkomi, kinti karomī ’’ ti āha.
amaṃsakabhojanaṃ.translation_1: Unable to obtain meat on the Uposatha day, the cook, unable to serve the fine, varied food he had prepared for the king, approached the queen and said, “My Lady, today I did not obtain meat, and I am unable to serve a meal without meat; what shall I do?”

kandituṃ.meaning_2: to cry; to weep; to lament
kandituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive used alongside rodituṃ and kathetuṃ after samattho; the form is kandituṃ (cf. PEU Kanda+tuṃ).
kandituṃ.example_1: Rañño bhayena ekopi kandituṃ vā rodituṃ vā kathetuṃ vā samattho nāma nāhosi.
kandituṃ.translation_1: For fear of the king, not a single person was able to weep, cry, or speak.

nisneho.meaning_2: free from affection; without love; without attachment
nisneho.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Prefix ni + sneha. Nominative singular in the text: nisneho jāto 'became free from affection'. Commentary glosses as 'without love (for)'. Could also be masc in the abstract sense, but here it functions as an adjective.
nisneho.example_1: Atha naṃ rājā ‘‘ kiṃ pana, samma chattapāṇi, ārammaṇaṃ disvā nisneho jātosī ’’ ti pucchi.
nisneho.translation_1: Then the king asked him, “But friend Chattapāṇi, what object did you see that made you become one who is without love?”
nisneho.example_2: Pattaṃ bhinditvā cavito, nisneho tassa kāraṇā ’’ ti.
nisneho.translation_2: “Because he broke the bowl, he passed away; I am without love for that reason.”

upavaditvā.meaning_2: having criticised; having insulted; having slandered
upavaditvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā of upavadati (upa + √vad). In the sentence it describes the commander's action of slandering the wise man before trying to have him killed.
upavaditvā.example_1: Taṅkhaṇaññeva amaccā ca brāhmaṇagahapatikādayo ca uṭṭhahitvā ‘‘ are lañjakhādaka duṭṭhacora, tvaṃ lañjaṃ alabhitvā paṇḍitaṃ upavaditvā māretukāmo jāto ’’ ti kāḷakaṃ senāpatiṃ hatthapādesu gahetvā rājanivesanā otāretvā gahitagahiteheva pāsāṇamuggarehi sīsaṃ bhinditvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā pādesu gahetvā kaḍḍhantā saṅkāraṭṭhāne chaḍḍesuṃ.
upavaditvā.translation_1: At that very moment, the ministers, brahmins, householders, and others arose, saying, “Hey, bribe-eating, wicked thief! You were unable to obtain bribes, so you became someone wanting to kill a wise man by slandering him,” and they seized the commander Kāḷaka by hand and foot, dragged him from the royal residence, and with whatever stone or club they could get hold of, they smashed his head, caused him to perish, and dragging him by the feet, they threw him into a dunghill.

kacchapamacchaseggu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A compound of three animal names at the head of a verse; seggu is rare (cf. Skt sṛga 'bird', perhaps a pheasant or stork). Nominative singular in the text; taken as a dvanda, though it may be a list of separate words joined in sandhi.
kacchapamacchaseggu.translation_1: Kacchapa, Maccha, Seggu, Kūṭavāṇija, and Garahita;

sibbāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of sibbāpeti, causative of sibbati. The text has the -tvā form in a series of causative absolutives: chindāpetvā, sibbāpetvā, rajāpetvā.
sibbāpetvā.example_1: Devadatto tassa dasā chindāpetvā ovaṭṭikaṃ sibbāpetvā rajāpetvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭavaṇṇaṃ katvā pārupi.
sibbāpetvā.translation_1: Devadatta had the hem cut, the seams sewn, and it was dyed to look like a gold-leaf color, and so he wore it.

paṭisīsakaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text; worn as part of a false Pacceka-Buddha disguise.
paṭisīsakaṃ.example_1: So āvudhaṃ ādāya kāsāvavatthavasano paccekabuddhavesaṃ gaṇhitvā paṭisīsakaṃ paṭimuñcitvā hatthivīthiyaṃ ṭhatvā āvudhena hatthiṃ māretvā dante ādāya bārāṇasiyaṃ vikkiṇanto jīvikaṃ kappesi.
paṭisīsakaṃ.translation_1: That poor man took a weapon, dressed in ocher robes, assumed the appearance of a Pacceka-Buddha, put on a head-covering, stood in the path of the elephants, slew an elephant with his weapon, took the tusks, and sold them in Benares, thus making his living.

āharaṇakavānarā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative plural in the text (āharaṇakavānarā). Refers to monkeys that fetch fruit.
āharaṇakavānarā.example_1: Āharaṇakavānarā tassā na denti, sā khudāpīḷitā aṭṭhicammāvasesā kisā ahosi.
āharaṇakavānarā.translation_1: The carrier monkeys did not give them to the blind mother, and she became thin, mere skin and bone, from hunger.

giliyamāno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle passive of gilati. Masculine nominative singular in the text: 'so ... giliyamāno'.
giliyamāno.example_1: So pathaviyā giliyamāno ācariyassa ovādaṃ saritvā ‘‘ imaṃ vata kāraṇaṃ disvā pārāsariyabrāhmaṇo mayhaṃ ovādamadāsī ’’ ti paridevamāno imaṃ gāthādvayamāha –
giliyamāno.translation_1: As he was swallowed by the earth, he remembered his teacher’s advice and, wailing: “Indeed, seeing this matter, the Brahmin Pārāsariya gave me that advice,” he spoke these two verses:

nisnehova.meaning_2: without affection; free from love; unloving
nisnehova.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form nisnehova is nisneha + eva; the lemma is nisneha. Used predictively of a person in the text.
nisnehova.example_1: ‘‘ Upāsike, niccakālampi tvaṃ etassa hitakāmā sasnehā, ayaṃ pana nisnehova.
nisnehova.translation_1: “Lay sister, you are always loving and kind toward him, but he is indeed loveless toward you.

paṭinameyya.meaning_2: should bend back; should bow back; should return (a greeting); should reciprocate
paṭinameyya.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Optative 3rd singular in -eyya; the text uses it for returning a bow or greeting. Formed with paṭi + √nam; the root appears as nam- here.
paṭinameyya.example_1: Tattha name namantassa bhaje bhajantanti yo attano namati, tasseva paṭinameyya.
paṭinameyya.translation_1: In regard to that, name namantassa bhaje bhajantaṃ (one should bow to him who bows, and associate with him who associates) means one should reciprocate bowing to whoever bows to oneself.
paṭinameyya.example_2: Tattha name namantassāti yo attani muducittena namati, tasseva paṭinameyya.
paṭinameyya.translation_2: There, “one should bow to one who bows” (name namantassa) means that to one who bows with a gentle heart towards oneself, one should bow back to him.

dussanakapuriso.meaning_2: wicked man; bad person; man of bad character
dussanakapuriso.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of dussanaka (bad, wicked) + purisa (man). Nominative singular in the text; a benefactor described as a wrongdoer.
dussanakapuriso.example_1: Tassattho – amhākampi rājūnaṃ sataṃ ediso bahūpakāro agāre dussanakapuriso atthi, so ca kho idha vijjati, idānipi idheva saṃvijjati, mayaṃ rājānopi samānā tassa bahūpakārataṃ sandhāya adhivāsema, tuyhaṃ pana araññopi sato adhivāsanabhāro jāto.
dussanakapuriso.translation_1: The meaning of that is: for us kings also, there exists in the house such a very helpful man who is a transgressor, and he is found right here; he exists right here at this very moment. Being kings, we forgive him, bearing in mind his helpfulness, but for you who are not a king, the burden of forgiveness has arisen.

nākāle.meaning_2: not out of season; not at the wrong time
nākāle.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of na + akāle. In the text, nākāle is glossed by akāle pana. It functions as an adverbial phrase, the opposite of kāle.
nākāle.example_1: 151. ‘‘ Kāle nikkhamanā sādhu, nākāle sādhu nikkhamo;
nākāle.translation_1: “Departure in season is good, departure out of season is not good;
nākāle.example_2: Nākāle sādhu nikkhamoti akāle pana attano vasanaṭṭhānato aññattha gantuṃ nikkhamo nāma nikkhamanaṃ vā parakkamanaṃ vā na sādhu.
nākāle.translation_2: ‘Departure out of season is not good’ means that when it is not the right time, departing from one’s dwelling to go elsewhere—either departing or making an effort—is not good.

saṃcuṇṇento.meaning_2: crushing to powder; pulverising; smashing to pieces
saṃcuṇṇento.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative present participle, nominative singular masculine used adverbially in both sentences. PEU splits the word as saṃ + cuṇṇa + ṇe + anta.
saṃcuṇṇento.example_1: Atha naṃ ‘‘ kathemi te pañhan ’’ ti ekappahāreneva pātetvā aṭṭhīni saṃcuṇṇento viya pothetvā gūthaṃ mukhe pakkhipitvā ‘‘ ito dāni paṭṭhāya imaṃ gāmaṃ āgataṃ kañci bhikkhuṃ pañhaṃ pucchitakāle jānissāmī ’’ ti santajjetvā pakkāmi.
saṃcuṇṇento.translation_1: Then, saying, ‘I will answer your question,’ he felled him with a single blow as if crushing his bones, put filth in his mouth, and threatened him, ‘From now on, I will know [how to deal with you] if you ask questions of any monk who comes to this village!’ and he went away.
saṃcuṇṇento.example_2: Hatthīpi bhagavantaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā manusse tāsento gehāni viddhaṃsento sakaṭāni saṃcuṇṇento soṇḍaṃ ussāpetvā pahaṭṭhakaṇṇavālo pabbato viya ajjhottharanto yena bhagavā tenābhidhāvi.
saṃcuṇṇento.translation_2: The elephant, on seeing the Blessed One approaching, ran towards where the Blessed One was, frightening the people, destroying houses, crushing wagons to powder, and raising its trunk with its ears and tail erect like a moving mountain.

tīhacatūhaccayena.meaning_2: after three or four days; when three or four days had passed
tīhacatūhaccayena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental of tīhacatūhaccaya, used adverbially as a time expression. Alternative resolution: tīhi catūhi accayena.
tīhacatūhaccayena.example_1: Tato tīhacatūhaccayena sakko āvajjamāno tassa taṃ ābādhaṃ ñatvā ‘‘ tikicchissāmi nan ’’ ti brāhmaṇavaṇṇena āgantvā dvāre ṭhatvā ‘‘ vejjabrāhmaṇo tumhākaṃ tikicchanatthāya āgato ’’ ti ārocāpesi.
tīhacatūhaccayena.translation_1: Three or four days later, Sakka, reflecting and knowing of his illness, thought, “I will cure him.” He came in the guise of a brahmin, stood at the door, and had it announced: “A brahmin physician has arrived to cure you.”

jayāpetvā.meaning_2: having greeted; having wished victory; having paid respects
jayāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of the causative jayāpeti (to cause to conquer; to greet respectfully). In the Jātaka prose, it commonly means 'having paid respects / wished victory' before taking a seat or standing aside. The 'tvā' is the absolutive termination added to the causative base. In example 3 it is a condensed rendering of the greeting before the formal speech.
jayāpetvā.example_1: Sakko pavisitvā jayāpetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi, rājā ‘‘ tvaṃ maṃ tikicchasī ’’ ti āha.
jayāpetvā.translation_1: Sakka entered, wished him victory, and stood to one side. The king said, “You are going to cure me?”
jayāpetvā.example_2: Tassa jayāpetvā ṭhitakāle rañño rathaṃ dassesuṃ.
jayāpetvā.translation_2: When he was standing after his greeting, they showed the chariot to the king.

nibyādhitaṃ.meaning_2: state of being free from illness; freedom from disease; health
nibyādhitaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text (nibyādhitaṃ pāpuṇi, 'attained freedom from illness'). Probably an abstract noun formed from byādhi with the negative prefix ni-, rather than a past participle; related entry nibyādhi is given as an adjective.
nibyādhitaṃ.example_1: Rājāpissa dhammaṃ sutvā vigatasoko hutvā tāvadeva nibyādhitaṃ pāpuṇi.
nibyādhitaṃ.translation_1: The king, too, hearing his discourse, became free of grief and in that very moment attained a state of being free from illness.

tenaṃ.meaning_2: by that; therefore; on account of that
tenaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of tena (instrumental of ta) with aṃ (probably etaṃ or aṃ). In the text it seems to serve as an indeclinable meaning 'therefore' or 'on that account'. Alternatively could be analysed as tena + imaṃ but the sandhi is irregular.
tenaṃ.example_1: So ‘‘ takkasilaṃ gaṇhissāmī ’’ ti mahantena balakāyena gantvā nagarato avidūre ṭhatvā ‘‘ iminā niyāmena hatthī pesetha, iminā asse, iminā rathe, iminā pattī, evaṃ dhāvitvā āvudhehi paharatha, evaṃ ghanavassavalāhakā viya saravassaṃ vassathā ’’ ti tenaṃ vicārento imaṃ gāthādvayamāha –
tenaṃ.translation_1: He thought, “I will capture Takkasilā,” and having gone with a great army, stood not far from the city. Planning to direct his army, saying, “Send the elephants according to this plan, send the horses according to this, send the chariots according to this, send the infantry according to this; run and strike with weapons in this way; shower them with a rain of arrows like clouds pouring forth rain,” he uttered this pair of verses:

rathūmijātehi.meaning_2: of surging seas of chariots; whose chariot-hosts are like great waves
rathūmijātehi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A poetic compound describing an army of chariots like rising waves. In the text it is instrumental plural, agreeing with the army.
rathūmijātehi.translation_1: 157. “With elephants like storm-clouds, with noble steeds of lineage, with surging seas of chariots, with showers of arrows,

vadantibhi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Irregular form: vadantibhi = vadanti + bhi, an instrumental plural of the present participle vadanta ('speaking'), agreeing with the elephants vināditā. The final -i ismetri causa. Not from the finite verb vadanti.
vadantibhi.example_1: 158. ‘‘ Abhidhāvatha cūpadhāvatha ca, vividhā vināditā vadantibhi;
vadantibhi.translation_1: 158. “Rush against them, fall upon them, with various outcries and trumpeting elephants;

rathūmijātehīti.meaning_2: ‘because a crowd of chariots has arisen’
rathūmijātehīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of rathūmijātehi (instrumental plural of rathūmijāta) and the quotative iti; the vowels coalesce and -ti is the result. The word is a compound ratha + ūmi + jāta, but sandhi rules require the sandhi analysis here.

sañjātarathūmīhi.meaning_2: with arisen chariots like wave-surges; with rising chariot forces
sañjātarathūmīhi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A rare compound in the commentary explaining rathūmijātehi; instrumental plural in the text, qualifying sāgarasalilehi. ūmi means 'wave'.
sañjātarathūmīhi.example_1: Rathūmijātehīti sañjātaūmivegehi sāgarasalilehi viya sañjātarathūmīhi, rathānīkehīti attho.
sañjātarathūmīhi.translation_1: ‘With surging seas of chariots’ means: like sea-waters with rising wave-surges, with chariot-warriors arising [in battle], the chariot forces.

vinaditā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is nominative plural (vinaditā) used as a predicate with bhavatha; the commentary explains it as nānāvirava, full of various cries. Could also be analysed as a past participle of vinadati, but the gloss here treats it as an adjective.
vinaditā.example_1: Vividhā vināditā vadantibhīti varavāraṇehi saddhiṃ vividhā vinaditā bhavatha, selitagajjitavāditehi nānāviravā hothāti attho.
vinaditā.translation_1: ‘With various outcries and trumpeting elephants’ means: be various outcries with the noble elephants; be full of different noises with the shouting and clashing sounds.

selitagajjitavāditehi.meaning_2: resounding with the cries of the selita and the trumpeting (of elephants); full of the sounds of clashing and trumpeting
selitagajjitavāditehi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental plural agreeing with varavāraṇehi. A compound of sound-words: selita (clashing/roaring) + gajjita (trumpeting) + vādita (sounding).
selitagajjitavāditehi.example_1: Vividhā vināditā vadantibhīti varavāraṇehi saddhiṃ vividhā vinaditā bhavatha, selitagajjitavāditehi nānāviravā hothāti attho.
selitagajjitavāditehi.translation_1: ‘With various outcries and trumpeting elephants’ means: be various outcries with the noble elephants; be full of different noises with the shouting and clashing sounds.

kumbhilaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text, the name of a Jātaka story. The related entry kumbhika is a different word (from kumbha + ṇika).
kumbhilaṃ.translation_1: The Yellow Robe, Cūḷanandiya, the Puta-rice, and the Crocodile;

osakkituṃ.meaning_2: to step back; to draw back; to retreat
osakkituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -tuṃ used after sikkhāpetvā with other infinitives (gantuṃ, nipajjituṃ, ṭhātuṃ); the elephant is taught to back up on command.
osakkituṃ.example_1: So taṃ ‘‘ gacchā ’’ ti vutte osakkituṃ,‘‘ osakkā ’’ ti vutte gantuṃ,‘‘ tiṭṭhā ’’ ti vutte nipajjituṃ,‘‘ nipajjā ’’ ti vutte ṭhātuṃ,‘‘ gaṇhā ’’ ti vutte ṭhapetuṃ,‘‘ ṭhapehī ’’ ti vutte gaṇhituṃ sikkhāpetvā punadivase taṃ hatthiṃ abhiruhitvā rājaṅgaṇaṃ agamāsi.
osakkituṃ.translation_1: He taught it to back when told to go, to go when told to back, to lie down when told to stand, to stand when told to lie down, to drop when told to pick up, and to pick up when told to drop, then the next day mounted the elephant and went to the palace courtyard.

talasā.meaning_2: sole (of the foot); surface; flat ground
talasā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text talasā is instrumental singular ('pained by the sole of the foot' per the gloss pādatalena ca pīḷitā); the commentary explains tala as the foot-sole, though the instrumental is unusual and the word could also be read as an adjective. Related PEU entry talati is a different root.
talasā.example_1: Ghammābhitattā talasā papīḷitā, tasseva pāde purisassa khādare.
talasā.translation_1: If they chafe the feet until they are burning and sore, they torment the feet of that very man.
talasā.example_2: Ghammābhitattā talasā papīḷitāti ghammena abhitattā pādatalena ca pīḷitā.
talasā.translation_2: Ghammābhitattā talasā papīḷitā means scorched by the heat and pained in the soles of the feet.

papīḷitā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Past participle used adjectivally, nominative plural agreeing with the subject in the verse. The gloss explains it as pīḷitā.
papīḷitā.example_1: Ghammābhitattā talasā papīḷitā, tasseva pāde purisassa khādare.
papīḷitā.translation_1: If they chafe the feet until they are burning and sore, they torment the feet of that very man.
papīḷitā.example_2: Ghammābhitattā talasā papīḷitāti ghammena abhitattā pādatalena ca pīḷitā.
papīḷitā.translation_2: Ghammābhitattā talasā papīḷitā means scorched by the heat and pained in the soles of the feet.

papīḷitāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The -ti is the quotation particle; the entry is for the main word. Separated in the PEU as pa + pīḷa + ta, a past participle used adjectivally in the commentary.

tammoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of taṃ + iti, the quotation particle -ti joined to the end of a sentence. Tentative: the related entries (tammaya, tammāka) do not fit and no context sentences were supplied; likely a sandhi resolve of taṃ + iti.

tammāko.meaning_2: teacher; one who cultivates various crafts; name for a teacher
tammāko.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A rare word explained in a commentary: taṃ taṃ manatīti 'tammo' ti vattabbe tammāko. It means one who minds/cultivates this or that craft, and is a name for a teacher. Nominative singular in the text.
tammāko.example_1: Tammāka vijjañca sutañca ādiyāti ettha taṃ taṃ manatīti ‘‘ tammo ’’ ti vattabbe tammāko, taṃ taṃ sippaṃ āsevati parivattetīti attho, ācariyassetaṃ nāmaṃ.
tammāko.translation_1: Regarding tammāka vijjañca sutañca ādiyā: here, because one 'minds' or 'thinks' about this and that, it is said to be 'tammāka'—meaning that they cultivate and revolve in their minds this or that craft; this is a name for a teacher.

tammākā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Uncertain. Perhaps a shortened form of an indeclinable or a pronoun, or a quotation of a grammatical word. The sentence is a comment on metre.
tammākā.example_1: Tasmā tammākā, gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ panassa rassabhāvo kato.
tammākā.translation_1: Therefore, from 'tammāka', for the sake of the ease of the verse's meter, a shortening (rassa) has been made.

saṅgantumarahasīti.meaning_2: to meet; to come together; to assemble
saṅgantumarahasīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form in the text is saṅgantum + arahasi + iti, joined by sandhi. The main word is the infinitive saṅgantum, from saṅgacchati.

saṅgantuṃ.meaning_2: to associate (with); to go together (with); to be a partner (to)
saṅgantuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive used with arahati ('is fit to') and its negative nārahati; the text glosses it with saha gantuṃ. Constructed as saṃ + gantuṃ (inf of gacchati).
saṅgantuṃ.example_1: Na hi khujjena vāmena , bhoti saṅgantumarahasīti iminā hi khujjena vāmanattā vāmena bhoti tvaṃ mahākule jātā abhirūpā dassanīyā saṅgantuṃ saha gantuṃ nārahasīti.
saṅgantuṃ.translation_1: Na hi khujjena vāmena, bhoti saṅgantumarahasī: Because he is crooked, being a hunchback, it is not fitting for you, born into a great family, shapely and attractive, to associate or go together with him.

khujjamakāmayiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 1st singular of kāmayati (= kāmesiṃ). The form kāmayiṃ is sandhi for kāmayi + aṃ. In the text it is combined with khujjaṃ; the word is separated from it.
khujjamakāmayiṃ.translation_1: 164. “Thinking him a handsome man, I clung to the hunchback;

thuṇāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text reads thuṇāti with a retroflex ṇ, probably a scribal variant of thunāti (√thu 1 moan).

akāmayiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 1st singular of kāmeti, used here in the sense 'I became enamoured (of)'. Variant reading akāmayiṃ.
akāmayiṃ.example_1: Tassattho – ahaṃ, ayya, ekaṃ usabhaṃ disvā ‘‘ gunnaṃ jeṭṭhakassa piṭṭhiyaṃ kakudhaṃ hoti, imassapi taṃ atthi, imināpi purisūsabhena bhavitabban ’’ ti evamahaṃ khujjaṃ purisūsabhaṃ maññamānā akāmayiṃ.
akāmayiṃ.translation_1: The meaning: ‘Master, seeing one handsome man, I thought, “A hump is found on the back of the leader of the herd; he too has that, so this one too must be a handsome man.” Thinking of the hunchback as a handsome man in this way, I became enamored.’

vikaṇṇakajātakavaṇṇanā.meaning_2: commentary on the Vikaṇṇaka Birth Story
vikaṇṇakajātakavaṇṇanā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Title heading in the Jātaka commentary; nominative singular.
vikaṇṇakajātakavaṇṇanā.translation_2: The third Vikaṇṇaka Birth Story is concluded.

haññatī.meaning_2: is killed; is harmed; is destroyed
haññatī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Passive of hanati. In the text haññatī is the sandhi form before ti.
haññatī.example_1: Passa ghoraviso nāgo, sīlavāti na haññatī ’’ ti.
haññatī.translation_1: Behold the deadly snake, which, because it is deemed ‘virtuous,’ is not killed.”
haññatī.example_2: Sīlavāti na haññatīti ghoravisopi samāno aḍaṃsanaaviheṭhanamattakena sīlavāti pasaṃsaṃ labhati, na haññati na vihaññatīti.
haññatī.translation_2: ‘Behold the deadly snake, which, because it is deemed ‘virtuous,’ is not killed’—even a deadly snake, merely by not biting and not harming, obtains the praise of being called ‘virtuous,’ and it is not killed, not harmed.

paṭisandhituṃ.meaning_2: to be reborn; to link (to a new existence); to reconnect
paṭisandhituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -tuṃ. In the text with na sakkā: 'cannot be reunited / reborn'. The related adjective is appaṭisandhika, 'not subject to rebirth'.
paṭisandhituṃ.example_1: Soyaṃ appaṭisandhikoti so pana kāmo idāni appaṭisandhiko jāto, na sakkā paṭisandhituṃ.
paṭisandhituṃ.translation_1: “This desire is now incapable of reunion” means: “That desire is now incapable of reunion; it cannot be reunited.”

nānīhamānassa.meaning_2: for one not striving; of him who does not exert himself
nānīhamānassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of na + īhamānassa, dative/genitive singular of the present participle īhamāna (√īh). Part of the verse gharā nānīhamānassa.
nānīhamānassa.translation_1: 170. “There is no house for one who does not strive, there is no house for one who does not speak falsehood;

nābhaṇato.meaning_2: for one who does not speak; from not speaking (falsehood)
nābhaṇato.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of na + bhaṇato, genitive/dative of the negative present participle bhaṇanta, here with the reading nābhaṇato musā ('not speaking falsehood'), possibly a sandhi written nā- for na. The gloss gives nābhaṇato quite literally as amusābhaṇatopi.
nābhaṇato.translation_1: 170. “There is no house for one who does not strive, there is no house for one who does not speak falsehood;
nābhaṇato.example_2: Gharā nābhaṇato musāti khettavatthuhiraññasuvaṇṇādīnaṃ atthāya amusābhaṇatopi gharā nāma natthi.
nābhaṇato.translation_2: “There is no house for one who does not speak falsehood” means: for the sake of wealth, gold, and silver, there is no house even for one who does not speak falsehood.

nānīhamānassāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text this is nānīhamāna + ti (quotative), sandhi -assa + ti. The verb is a negated ānīhati/ānayati 'brings, takes away'. The -nīha- form is irregular.

upapāditaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Agrees with sīlena (neuter) in the verse; here glossed 'fulfilled, accomplished'. Could also be read as a causative passive participle.
upapāditaṃ.translation_1: When that is joined with virtuous behavior (sīlena) and fulfilled with patience,

saññuttantiādimāha.meaning_2: he said (starting with) 'saññuttaṃ iti' and so on
saññuttantiādimāha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of a quoted neuter form with iti, adi and the aorist āha. Tentative segmentation; saññuttaṃ may be 'perception; notion'.

kumīnāni.meaning_2: fish trap; wicker fish-trap; fish basket
kumīnāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative plural in the text, object of oḍḍesuṃ. Sometimes explained as ku + mīna, 'bad fish', or from √kam in the sense of 'where fish enter'.
kumīnāni.example_1: Tadā manussā nadīkandarādīsu tattha tattha macche gahaṇatthāya kumīnāni oḍḍesuṃ.
kumīnāni.translation_1: At that time, people set wicker fish-traps in rivers and streams here and there to catch fish.

vilumpitunti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text this is vilumpituṃ followed by the quotative ti, written vilumpitunti. Infinitive after sakkoti.
vilumpitunti.example_1: ‘‘ Yāva so upakappatī ’’ tipi pāṭho, yattakaṃ kālaṃ so puriso sakkoti vilumpitunti attho.
vilumpitunti.translation_1: There is also a reading, “As long as he can compass it,” meaning: for as long a time as that person is able to rob.

lañjantūti.meaning_2: shut up!; block it!; be silent!
lañjantūti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Imperative 3rd plural (lañjantu) with the quotation particle -ti joined: lañjantūti. The PEU entry suggests a causative-like sense 'shut up; block it' from √lajj?; doubtful, the root is uncertain.

lañji.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Rare verb; the sentence means the people blocked their ears with bean-flour paste. Perhaps related to √rañj (colour, smear); the PEU reading 'blocked' fits the context.
