lañji.example_1: Mahājano bheriyā āṇaṃ sutvā antamaso biḷāle upādāya sabbacatuppadānañceva attano ca kaṇṇacchiddāni yathā parassa saddaṃ sotuṃ na sakkā, evaṃ māsapiṭṭhena lañji.
lañji.translation_1: The people heard the order of the drum and, down to their very cats, they all, together with their four-footed animals, sealed their ear-cavities with bean-flour in such a way that it was impossible to hear anyone else's sound.

gaddūlena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Found only in the compound gaddūlena in the text; instrumental singular. The related PEU entry gives the headword gaddūla; the meaning 'strap; thong' fits the context of tying a dog.
gaddūlena.example_1: Athekadivasaṃ eko gāmavāsī puriso taṃ ṭhānaṃ patto sunakhaṃ disvā pānīyahārakānaṃ uttarisāṭakañca kahāpaṇañca datvā gaddūlena bandhitvā taṃ ādāya pakkāmi.
gaddūlena.translation_1: Then one day, a certain villager arrived at that place, saw the dog, gave an upper garment and a coin to the water-carriers, tied the dog with a strap, took him, and went away.

gaddūlaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text (gaddūlaṃ mocesi, he loosened the strap). PEU points to the Tipiṭaka passage about the dog let loose from its leash.
gaddūlaṃ.example_1: Atha so puriso ‘‘ ayaṃ idāni maṃ piyāyatī ’’ ti gaddūlaṃ mocesi, so vissaṭṭhamatto ekavegena āsanasālameva gato.
gaddūlaṃ.translation_1: Then the man thought, “He is now fond of me,” and loosened the strap. As soon as he was set free, the dog went off in a single dash back to the assembly hall.

saṃcuṇṇetvā.meaning_2: having crushed to powder; having pounded to pieces; having smashed
saṃcuṇṇetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Formed from the causative saṃcuṇṇeti (PEU: saṃ + cuṇṇa + ṇe + ti, Curādi); sometimes analysed as saṃ + cuṇṇa + etvā with the ṇe as part of the base. Absolutive of saṃcuṇṇeti, used with pāsāṇadaṇḍādīhi ('with rocks and staves') of beating Mūsila to death.
saṃcuṇṇetvā.example_1: Tasmiṃ khaṇe rājā mahājanassa iṅgitasaññaṃ adāsi, mahājano uṭṭhāya ‘‘ tvaṃ ācariyena saddhiṃ virujjhitvā ‘ samakāraṃ karomī ’ ti vāyamasi, attano pamāṇaṃ na jānāsī ’’ ti mūsilaṃ tajjetvā gahitagahiteheva pāsāṇadaṇḍādīhi saṃcuṇṇetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā pāde gahetvā saṅkāraṭṭhāne chaḍḍesi.
saṃcuṇṇetvā.translation_1: At that moment, the king gave a signal to the great crowd; the crowd arose and cried out against Mūsila, “You tried to compete with your teacher, claiming ‘I will make them equal,’ you do not know your measure!” and with rocks and staves they beat him to death, seized his feet, and threw him on a dust heap.

bhūtapacaniṃ.meaning_2: craving that cooks beings; that which torments beings
bhūtapacaniṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text (bhūtapacaniṃ). Stands for craving (taṇhā) that "cooks" beings in the lower realms; the commentary glosses it with taṇhā. Alternative analysis bhūta + paca + yu + ī (agent noun).
bhūtapacaniṃ.example_1: Yo ca kālaghaso bhūto, sa bhūtapacaniṃ pacī ’’ ti.
bhūtapacaniṃ.translation_1: But the one who has consumed time, they have cooked the cooker of beings.”
bhūtapacaniṃ.example_2: Sa bhūtapacaniṃ pacīti so yāyaṃ taṇhā apāyesu bhūte pacati, taṃ ñāṇagginā paci dahi bhasmamakāsi, tena ‘‘ bhūtapacaniṃ pacī ’’ ti vuccati.
bhūtapacaniṃ.translation_2: ‘They have cooked the cooker of beings’ means: the craving that cooks beings in the lower realms, they have cooked and burned with the fire of knowledge, turning it into ashes; therefore it is said, ‘they have cooked the cooker of beings’.

pajanintipi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Text form is pajaninti + pi, presumably a variant or typo of pajānanti with -pi. Treated as the present 3rd plural of pajānāti.

lālo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes a dull, idle prince; nominative singular lālo in both sentences. PEU also records lāla as 'very foolish'.
lālo.example_1: Rañño pādañjalī nāma putto lālo dandhaparisakkano ahosi.
lālo.translation_1: The king had a son named Pādañjali, who was an idle, lazy loafer.
lālo.example_2: Bodhisatto pana ‘‘ ayaṃ kumāro lālo dandhaparisakkano, pariggahetvā naṃ abhisiñcissāmā ’’ ti āha.
lālo.translation_2: The Bodhisatta, however, said, “This prince is an idle, lazy loafer; we should test him before consecrating him.”

lālabhāvaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text. Literally 'state of a lāla', perhaps from lāla (foolish, childish).
lālabhāvaṃ.example_1: Amaccā pādañjalikumārassa lālabhāvaṃ ñatvā bodhisattaṃ rajje abhisiñciṃsu.
lālabhāvaṃ.translation_1: The ministers, having realized Prince Pādañjali's foolishness, consecrated the Bodhisatta as king.

isivesenāgantvā.meaning_2: having come in the guise of a sage; having arrived in the form of an ascetic
isivesenāgantvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of isivesa (ascetic's appearance, disguise) and āgantvā (having come, absolutive of āgacchati). The whole phrase means 'having come in the disguise of a sage'. Occurs in a Jātaka prose story about a monkey posing as an ascetic.
isivesenāgantvā.example_1: So makkaṭo ekassa matatāpasassa santakāni vakkalāni nivāsetvā ca pārupitvā ca ajinacammaṃ aṃse katvā kājakamaṇḍaluṃ ādāya isivesenāgantvā paṇṇasāladvāre aggissa kāraṇā kuhakakammaṃ katvā aṭṭhāsi.
isivesenāgantvā.translation_1: That monkey had put on the robes belonging to a dead ascetic, thrown a black antelope skin over his shoulder, taken a pole and waterpot, and coming in the guise of an ascetic to the door of the hut, he performed a hypocritical act for the sake of the fire and stood there.

sinerukampanakavāto.meaning_2: wind that can shake Mount Sineru; wind capable of shaking Mount Meru
sinerukampanakavāto.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text. A vivid simile for the power of defilement; the compound is a bahubbīhi describing the wind.
sinerukampanakavāto.example_1: Sinerukampanakavāto purāṇapaṇṇakasaṭaṃ kiṃ na kampessati, bodhitale nisīditvā abhisambujjhanakasattaṃ ayaṃ kileso āloḷesi, tādisaṃ kiṃ na āloḷessatī ’’ ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.
sinerukampanakavāto.translation_1: Does not the wind that can shake Mount Sineru scatter a heap of old leaves? This defilement troubled the Being who, seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, was about to realize the Truths; why would it not trouble someone like you?” Having said this, he told the past tale at their request.

ohīyituṃ.meaning_2: to stay behind; to remain; to be left
ohīyituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of ohīyati (Passive of ava + √hā 1). In the sentence, the queen is told she should stay behind in the city while the king goes to suppress the disturbance.
ohīyituṃ.example_1: So tassa vūpasamanatthāya gantukāmo deviṃ āmantetvā ‘‘ bhadde, tayā nagare ohīyituṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti āha.
ohīyituṃ.translation_1: Desiring to go to suppress it, he called the queen and said, “Good lady, you should stay here in the city.”

āvedhañca.meaning_2: and the wound; and the piercing wound
āvedhañca.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi (āvedhaṃ + ca) resolving the text's āvedhañca, which the commentary glosses with vaṇa at the place of piercing; accusative singular before na passāmi.
āvedhañca.translation_1: 3. I see no wound from which blood might flow;
āvedhañca.example_2: Āvedhañca na passāmīti viddhaṭṭhāne vaṇañca na passāmi.
āvedhañca.translation_2: Āvedhañca na passāmīti means 'I do not see the wound in the place where it was pierced'.

āvedhato.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is the present participle āvedhato (genitive plural agreeing with me) from √vidh, causative. The commentary glosses it with pagghareyya, so it means 'flowing, gushing'.
āvedhato.example_1: Yato ruhiramassaveti yato me āvedhato lohitaṃ pagghareyya, taṃ na passāmīti attho.
āvedhato.translation_1: Yato ruhiramassaveti means 'from which wound blood might flow; I do not see that place'.

anutāḷayi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist anutāḷayi in the text, from the causative stem anutāḷaya-. Object in accusative (maṃ), instrument in instrumental (laṭṭhiyā); anutāḷento is the present participle.
anutāḷayi.translation_1: Seized me by the arm and beat me with a stick.”
anutāḷayi.example_2: Yaṃ maṃ tvaṃ tilamuṭṭhiyā kāraṇā anutāḷayi, anutāḷento ca maṃ bāhāya gahetvā anutāḷayi, taṃ anutāḷanaṃ ajjāpi me manasīti ayañhettha attho.
anutāḷayi.translation_2: It means: for the reason that you beat me for a handful of sesame seeds—and while beating me, you seized me by the arm and beat me—that act of beating is on my mind even today; this is the meaning here.

anutāḷayīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The -ti is the quotative iti joined by sandhi; the headword is the verb. Doubtful: the PEU entry suggests anu + taḷa + ṇaya, but the usual analysis is causative of √taḷ 'to beat, strike', i.e. 'beats (a drum) in accompaniment'.

tiṇaparighāsanti.meaning_2: remnant of grass; leftover grass; grass spike left over
tiṇaparighāsanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of tiṇa (grass) + parighāsa (remnant). In the text the final -a is elided before the quotative -ti (tiṇaparighāsanti = tiṇaparighāso iti), so the entry is for the nominative singular tiṇaparighāso. The meaning given in the source is uncertain.

vaḷañjetvā.meaning_2: having used; having employed; having spent
vaḷañjetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Used in the text in the phrase kahāpaṇe vaḷañjetvā, 'having used the coins'. The absolutive of the causative vaḷañjeti. The PEU gloss 'Look' appears to be an error.
vaḷañjetvā.example_1: Tesu rājā passenadī kosalo taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā tassā sāṭakena ceva sahassatthavikāya ca saddhiṃ bhattabhājanāni pahiṇi ‘‘ mayhaṃ ayyaṃ parivisamānā imaṃ sāṭakaṃ nivāsetvā ime kahāpaṇe vaḷañjetvā theraṃ parivisatū ’’ ti.
vaḷañjetvā.translation_1: Among them, king Pasenadi of Kosala, hearing that news, sent her food together with a wrap garment and a purse of one thousand coins, saying, ‘When you are entertaining my noble one, put on this wrap, use these coins, and entertain the Elder.’

ākirāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to be poured; having had poured (into)
ākirāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive in -tvā; here construed with doṇiyaṃ 'into the trough'.
ākirāpetvā.example_1: Bodhisatto punadivase assapotakassa piṇḍarasabhojanaṃ sajjetvā ‘‘ vīmaṃsissāmi tāva naṃ, jānāti nu kho attano balaṃ, udāhu na jānātī ’’ ti doṇiyaṃ kuṇḍakayāguṃ ākirāpetvā dāpesi.
ākirāpetvā.translation_1: The next day, the Bodhisatta, having prepared delicious food for the foal, thought, ‘I will test him for a moment; does he know his own strength or not?’ and had rice-powder gruel poured into a trough and given to him.

pāyituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of the causative pāyati 'causes to drink; gives to drink', used here simply as 'to drink'. Subject of the negated verb na icchi.
pāyituṃ.example_1: So ‘‘ nāhaṃ imaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjissāmī ’’ ti taṃ yāguṃ pāyituṃ na icchi.
pāyituṃ.translation_1: He, saying, ‘I will not eat this food,’ did not wish to drink that gruel.

parighāsaṃ.meaning_2: leftover food; leavings; remnant food (of grass); moss
parighāsaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text, glossed with vighāsatiṇa (leftover grass) and glossed by the commentary with khāditāvasesa. Maybe pari + √ghas with the prefix pari in its 'around, about' sense.
parighāsaṃ.example_1: Tattha bhutvā tiṇaparighāsanti tvaṃ pubbe mahallikāya dinnaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ khāditāvasesaṃ vighāsatiṇasaṅkhātaṃ parighāsaṃ bhuñjitvā vaḍḍhito.
parighāsaṃ.translation_1: In regard to the words “having eaten grass-scum,” this means: In the past, you grew up having eaten the grass-residue—that is, the leftovers of grass left by other horses—which that old woman gave you.

ratthapaṭaṃ.meaning_2: carriage cloth; cloth for a chariot
ratthapaṭaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text; the following sentence explains it with rattapaṭa. Could also be rattha + paṭa, a type of cloth.
ratthapaṭaṃ.example_1: Puna ratthapaṭaṃ udare parikkhipitvā vissajjesi, rattapaṭameva passiṃsu.
ratthapaṭaṃ.translation_1: Again, he wrapped a red cloth around his belly and released him; they saw only the red cloth.

aposayi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Desiderative-like formation from poseti (posayati); third person singular aorist. The sentence has mātarañca aposayi, 'and nourished his mother.'
aposayi.translation_1: So long did he attain a long life, and he nourished his mother.”

aposayīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Third person singular of the causative verb; in the text it appears as aposayīti, an aorist or causative form with the quotative particle -iti. The related entry aposayi points to poseti.
aposayīti.translation_1: Regarding “And he nourished his mother,” this is just a heading for the discourse; the meaning is that he also nourished his mother and father.

ayādīni.meaning_2: iron and so on; iron, etc.
ayādīni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of aya (neut. nominative/accusative plural of ayas, iron) + ādīni (neuter plural of ādi, beginning, etc.). Object of labhiṃsu. Could also be analysed as a compound aya + ādi. Variant reading ayāni is possible.
ayādīni.example_1: Tattha te vāṇijā ‘‘ pānīyaṃ pivissāmā ’’ ti taṃ udapānaṃ khaṇantā paṭipāṭiyā bahūni ayādīni labhiṃsu.
ayādīni.translation_1: There, the merchants said: “We shall drink water,” and as they dug that well, they gradually found much iron and so on.

leḍḍūsū.meaning_2: clod of earth; lump of earth; stone
leḍḍūsū.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative plural in the text (leḍḍūsu), with the following paṃsūsu: 'on clods and dust falling'. Also found as feminine and neuter in some dictionaries.
leḍḍūsū.example_1: So ca udapāno nāgapariggahito, athassa heṭṭhā vasanakanāgarājā attano vimāne bhijjante leḍḍūsū ca paṃsūsu ca patamānesu kuddho ṭhapetvā bodhisattaṃ avasese sabbepi nāsikavātena paharitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā nāgabhavanā nikkhamma sakaṭāni yojetvā sabbaratanānaṃ pūretvā bodhisattaṃ sukhayānake nisīdāpetvā nāgamāṇavakehi saddhiṃ sakaṭāni yojāpento bodhisattaṃ bārāṇasiṃ netvā gharaṃ pavesetvā taṃ paṭisāmetvā attano nāgabhavanameva gato.
leḍḍūsū.translation_1: And that well was under the authority of a nāga. Then, the Nāga king who dwelt beneath it, seeing his palace being destroyed and clods and earth falling, became angry. Leaving the Bodhisatta aside, he struck all the rest with the breath of his nostrils, causing their death. He emerged from the nāga world, harnessed the carts, filled them with all the treasures, seated the Bodhisatta in a comfortable carriage, and while having the nāga-youths drive the carts together with the Bodhisatta, he took him to Benares, entered his house, stored the treasure, and returned to his own nāga world.

akhāṇisuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] 3rd plural aorist with the prefix a-; the text has akhāṇisuṃ for khāṇiṃsu. The simplex √khaṇ gives khāṇati.
akhāṇisuṃ.example_1: 17. ‘‘ Te ca tena asantuṭṭhā, bhiyyo bhiyyo akhāṇisuṃ;
akhāṇisuṃ.translation_1: 17. “But those merchants were not content with that, and they dug ever deeper and deeper.

abhisiñcituṃ.meaning_2: to anoint; to consecrate; to make king
abhisiñcituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -tuṃ after abhi + sic; used of royal consecration (rajje abhisiñcituṃ).
abhisiñcituṃ.example_1: Amaccā mahantena sakkārena rañño sarīrakiccaṃ katvā matakadānaṃ datvā sattame divase rājaṅgaṇe sannipatitvā ‘‘ kumāro atidaharo, na sakkā rajje abhisiñcituṃ, vīmaṃsitvā naṃ abhisiñcissāmā ’’ ti ekadivasaṃ nagaraṃ alaṅkārāpetvā vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ sajjetvā pallaṅkaṃ paññapetvā kumārassa santikaṃ gantvā ‘‘ vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ, deva, gantuṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti āhaṃsu.
abhisiñcituṃ.translation_1: The ministers performed the king's funeral rites with great honor, gave offerings for the dead, and on the seventh day they gathered in the palace court and deliberated: “The prince is too young; he cannot be inaugurated as king. We will test him and then inaugurate him.” One day, they decorated the city, prepared the judgment hall, set up a throne, and went to wait upon the prince, saying, “Great King, it is proper to go to the judgment hall.”
abhisiñcituṃ.example_2: ‘‘ Sace amhe disvā na pabbajissasi, atha taṃ rajje abhisiñcituṃ āgatāmhā ’’ ti.
abhisiñcituṃ.translation_2: “If you did not renounce the world upon seeing us, we have come to anoint you as king.”

nicittako.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes a monkey as mindless (nicittako vānaro); nominative singular masculine. The prefix ni- here has a privative sense.
nicittako.example_1: Kumāro taṃ oloketvā ‘‘ cittavato manussassa lomaṃ nāma evarūpaṃ na hoti, ayaṃ nicittako vānaro vinicchayakammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkhissatī ’’ ti ñatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –
nicittako.translation_1: The prince looked at him and knew that a fully formed human with a mind does not have such hair; even this must be a thoughtless monkey who cannot perform the task of judging cases. Reflecting thus, he said the second stanza—

bilapassāni.meaning_2: sides of the hole; edges of the burrow
bilapassāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative plural of bila + passāni (sides, edges). Text form in -i. Could also be analysed as a plural of bila + passa.
bilapassāni.example_1: Atha naṃ tato parabhāge mahāmaggasamīpe ekasmiṃ vammike vasanto sappo disvā ‘‘ gāmaṇicanda, kahaṃ yāsī ’’ ti pucchitvā ‘‘ rājānaṃ passitun ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ rājā kira paṇḍito, sāsanaṃ me harā ’’ ti vatvā ‘‘ ahaṃ gocaratthāya gamanakāle chātajjhatto milātasarīro vammikato nikkhamanto sarīrena bilaṃ pūretvā sarīraṃ kaḍḍhento kicchena nikkhamāmi, gocaraṃ caritvā āgato pana suhito thūlasarīro hutvā pavisanto bilapassāni aphusanto sahasāva pavisāmi, tattha kiṃ kāraṇanti rājānaṃ pucchitvā mayhaṃ katheyyāsī ’’ ti āha.
bilapassāni.translation_1: Then, further on, near the highway, a snake living in a termite mound saw him and asked, “Uncle Gāmaṇicanda, where are you going?” When he replied, “To see the king,” he said, “The king is said to be wise; take my message,” and said: “When I go out to search for food, I am hungry and emaciated, and as I exit the termite mound, I fill the hole with my body and drag myself out with difficulty. But when I return satisfied, with a full body, I enter quickly without touching the sides of the hole. Ask the king the reason for this and tell me.”

aniyyāditattā.meaning_2: state of not having been returned; failure to return; not having handed back
aniyyāditattā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Ablative singular in the text: aniyyāditattā, 'because of not having been returned'. Formed from the negated past participle niyyādita (√ni + √yād? no; √yā?) with the abstract suffix -tta.
aniyyāditattā.example_1: ‘‘ Bho canda, goṇānaṃ aniyyāditattā goṇā tava gīvā, ayaṃ pana puriso disvāva ‘ na passāmī ’ ti sampajānamusāvādaṃ bhaṇi, tasmā tvaññeva kammiko hutvā imassa ca purisassa pajāpatiyāya cassa akkhīni uppāṭetvā sayaṃ goṇamūlaṃ catuvīsati kahāpaṇe dehī ’’ ti.
aniyyāditattā.translation_1: “My friend Canda, because you failed to return the oxen, you are liable for them. But this man, having seen them, spoke a deliberate lie saying he did not see them. Therefore, you yourself shall act as the official: pluck out the eyes of this man and his wife, and pay him twenty-four pieces of money as the price of the oxen.”

ajīrāpetvā.meaning_2: without completing; without breaking off; without exhausting; not having finished
ajīrāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of na + jīrāpetvā, the negative absolutive of the causative jīrāpeti (from √jīr). In the text it expresses doing something without first completing or settling the earlier obligation.
ajīrāpetvā.example_1: Navamaṃ sutvā ‘‘ sā gaṇikā pubbe ekassa hatthato bhatiṃ gahetvā taṃ ajīrāpetvā aññassa hatthato na gaṇhāti, tenassā pubbe bahuṃ uppajji.
ajīrāpetvā.translation_1: Having heard the ninth, he said: “That courtesan formerly took payment from one hand and did not take from another without completing the first; because of that, she earned much.”

ajīrāpetvāva.meaning_2: without completing; without finishing; without exhausting
ajīrāpetvāva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text, the absolutive is joined to ca/va (ajīrāpetvāva = ajīrāpetvā + eva?); the entry is for the form without the enclitic. It is a negative absolutive of the causative of √jīr ('cause to finish, complete').
ajīrāpetvāva.example_1: Idāni pana attano dhammataṃ vissajjetvā ekassa hatthato gahitaṃ ajīrāpetvāva aññassa hatthato gaṇhāti, purimassa okāsaṃ akatvā pacchimassa karoti, tenassā bhati na uppajjati, na keci naṃ upasaṅkamanti.
ajīrāpetvāva.translation_1: “But now, having abandoned her own nature, she takes from another’s hand without completing the one from the first; not providing the opportunity for the first, she takes the opportunity for the last, because of which payment does not arise for her, and no one visits her.”
ajīrāpetvāva.example_2: Iminā kāraṇena sā ‘‘ ahaṃ gahitabhatiṃ ajīrāpetvāva aññena dīyamānāya bhatiyā hatthaṃ pasāresiṃ, iminā kāraṇena maṃ sīlaṃ nārādheti, tena vo dātuṃ na sakkā ’’ ti paṭikkhipi.
ajīrāpetvāva.translation_2: For this reason, she refused, saying, “Before I had finished with the wage I had already taken, I stretched out my hand for a wage offered by another. For this reason, my virtue does not please me; therefore, I cannot give it to you.”

mandhātuṃ.meaning_2: Mandhātu; name of a legendary king
mandhātuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a mythical king (Mandhātā). Accusative singular mandhātuṃ in the text, object of netvā. PEU analyses it as a compound (maṃ + dhā + tu), which may be folk etymology; the form is best treated as a proper name.
mandhātuṃ.example_1: Sakko mandhātuṃ tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ netvā devatā dve koṭṭhāse katvā attano devarajjaṃ majjhe bhinditvā adāsi.
mandhātuṃ.translation_1: Sakka took Mandhātā to the abode of the Thirty-three, divided the gods into two parts, and having broken his own divine rule in the middle, gave it to him.

āpāsūti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text āpā is followed by the single-word quotation iti (sandhi āpā + iti → āpāsūti). The form is probably āpā + ā (ablative of āpa, 'from the water'), but this is uncertain; it may also be a misreading of āpasūti (āpa + su + iti) or a similar sandhi.

vesāyī.meaning_2: name of Yama; Yama, the one with a domain
vesāyī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Vesāyī is glossed in the text as vesāyī vuccati yamo, 'Yama is called vesāyī', derived from vesāyino visayā. Nom. sg. in -ī.
vesāyī.example_1: Vesāyino visayāti vesāyī vuccati yamo, tassa visayā.
vesāyī.translation_1: “From the domain of Yama” means Yama is called the one with the domain; from his domain.

alaṅkarāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to be decorated; having had (it) adorned
alaṅkarāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of alaṅkaroti, used transitively with an object of the thing adorned. Formed from alaṃ + √kar with the causative sign *āpe and the absolutive -tvā.
alaṅkarāpetvā.example_1: Bhuñjanto pana antogehe na bhuñjati, attano bhojanavidhānaṃ olokentaṃ mahājanaṃ puññaṃ kāretukāmatāya rājadvāre ratanamaṇḍapaṃ kāretvā bhojanavelāya taṃ alaṅkarāpetvā kañcanamaye samussitasetacchatte rājapallaṅke nisīditvā khattiyakaññāhi parivuto satasahassagghanikāya suvaṇṇapātiyā sabbarasabhojanaṃ bhuñjati.
alaṅkarāpetvā.translation_1: However, he did not eat inside the house; wishing to confer merit upon the great mass of people watching his manner of eating, he had a jewel pavilion built at the palace gate. At mealtime, he had it decorated, and sitting upon a golden royal dais under a white parasol, surrounded by princesses, he ate food of all flavors from a gold dish worth a hundred thousand pieces.

allīyāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to cling; having made stick fast; having pressed (against)
allīyāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of allīyāpeti, from √lī with the causative sign; used of pressing an elephant against a wall and of animals standing head to head. Sometimes analysed as ā + lī + ṇāpe + tvā.
allīyāpetvā.example_1: So ‘‘ ayaṃ dāni rājadhītāya vuttadivaso ’’ ti vāraṇaṃ abhiruhitvā muduhatthakaṃ cūḷupaṭṭhākaṃ hatthipiṭṭhe nisīdāpetvā gantvā rājanivesanassa ākāsaṅgaṇābhimukhe ṭhāne hatthiṃ mahābhittiyaṃ allīyāpetvā vātapānasamīpe temento aṭṭhāsi.
allīyāpetvā.translation_1: Thinking, “This is the day the king's daughter mentioned,” he mounted the elephant, seated the soft-handed page boy on its back, went to the place opposite the open courtyard of the royal residence, pressed the elephant against the great wall, and stood near the window getting drenched.
allīyāpetvā.example_2: Te ekadivasaṃ gocaraṃ gahetvā ekasmiṃ rukkhamūle sīsena sīsaṃ, siṅgena siṅgaṃ, tuṇḍena tuṇḍaṃ allīyāpetvā romanthayamāne ṭhite disvā eko luddako sattiṃ khipitvā ekappahāreneva jīvitā voropesi.
allīyāpetvā.translation_2: One day, while ruminating at the root of a tree, having obtained pasture, they stood with head to head, horn to horn, and mouth to mouth; a hunter saw them, shot a javelin, and killed both in a single blow.

mañcātimañcāni.meaning_2: bed upon bed; tier upon tier of platforms; scaffold of stacked stages
mañcātimañcāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Neuter in -a. Plural nominative/accusative in the text (mañcātimañcāni), paired with cakkāticakkāni describing tiers of platforms erected between mansions.
mañcātimañcāni.example_1: Tasmiṃ khaṇe ‘‘ kumārassa yasaṃ passissāmā ’’ ti sakalanagaraṃ saṅkhubhi, pāsādantare cakkāticakkāni mañcātimañcāni bandhanti.
mañcātimañcāni.translation_1: At that moment, the entire city was agitated, thinking, “We will go to see the youth's fortune,” and they tied circles within circles and tiers upon tiers between the mansions.
mañcātimañcāni.example_2: ‘‘ aññasmiṃ kāle mayi pāsādato pāsādaṃ gacchante sakalanagaraṃ saṅkhubhati, cakkāticakkāni mañcātimañcāni bandhanti, ajja pana ṭhapetvā mayhaṃ manusse añño koci natthi, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇan ’’ ti.
mañcātimañcāni.translation_2: “In other times, when I am traveling from one mansion to another, the entire city is agitated; they tie circles within circles and tiers upon tiers. But today, besides my own people, there is no one else. What could be the reason?”

samāluharitāmayoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Probably a text corruption or a very rare compound; the final -ti is taken as the quotation particle, so the headword is samāluharitāmaya, nominative singular samāluharitāmayo. No sentences were supplied, so the analysis is uncertain.

nibbhacchesi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The PEU entry is unreliable. Probably from ni + √bhakkh with the -e causative, meaning 'to drive away (by scolding)'. Here 3rd singular present in the sentence.
nibbhacchesi.example_1: Atha naṃ hatthagahaṇādivasena keḷiṃ kātuṃ āraddhaṃ hatthe gahetvā ‘‘ apehi apehi, na me tayā attho ’’ ti nibbhacchesi.
nibbhacchesi.translation_1: Then, as he reached out to dally with her by holding her hand and so on, she grabbed his hand and scolded him, saying, “Go away, go away, I have no need for you!”

ādikenevātiāditova.meaning_2: from the beginning; at once; straight away
ādikenevātiāditova.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text has ādikena eva ādi-to va joined by sandhi. Ādikena is instrumental of ādi in an adverbial idiom; ādito is ablative 'from the beginning'. The whole runs as two emphatic words, probably 'just from the very start'. Sandhi of ādikena + eva + ādito + va.

āḷiṅgaṃ.meaning_2: name of a small drum with tapering ends
āḷiṅgaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text (āḷiṅgaṃ ... mudiṅgaṃ). Variant of āliṅga. PEU suggests a derivation ā + √ligi + ṇa, but it is uncertain; left empty.
āḷiṅgaṃ.example_1: Tesu eko samuddaṃ pāvisi, ekaṃ dasabhātikarājāno udake kīḷamānā labhitvā āḷiṅgaṃ nāma mudiṅgaṃ akaṃsu.
āḷiṅgaṃ.translation_1: Of them, one entered the sea, and the ten royal brothers, while playing in the water, found the other and made a drum called Āḷiṅga.

vinindāmi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present 3rd singular in the text. The prefix vi- strengthens the meaning: 'especially blame; reproach'.
vinindāmi.example_1: 54. ‘‘ Nāhaṃ tumhe vinindāmi, ye caññe vānarā vane;
vinindāmi.translation_1: 54. "I do not criticize you, nor the other monkeys in the forest;

nevassā.meaning_2: not his; there is no (duty) for him; not to him
nevassā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text nevassā is likely a sandhi of na evassa (na + eva + assa), meaning 'she has no (duty) towards...'. The final -ā could be a sandhi with a following word, but the sentence reads nevassā sassusasurasāmikavattaṃ atthi; compare the meaning 'she has no duty towards her parents-in-law and husband'. The form may also be analysed as na + eva + assā (f. dat./gen. of ayaṃ), 'not to her', but the sense is the same. No root applies because it is a sandhi compound.
nevassā.example_1: Esā, bhante, kulasuṇhā agāravā, nevassā sassusasurasāmikavattaṃ atthi, assaddhā appasannā ahorattaṃ kalahaṃ kurumānā vicaratīti.
nevassā.translation_1: The great merchant replied, "Venerable sir, this daughter-in-law of the family is without respect; she has no duties towards her parents-in-law and husband, she is faithless and unbelieving, and goes about day and night causing quarrels."

ujjhātuṃ.meaning_2: to reproach; to insult; to blame; to censure
ujjhātuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text ujjhātuṃ is the infinitive of this causative verb (u + jhā + tuṃ), used with na arahasi: 'you should not censure'. The simplex ujjhati is not recorded separately; the causative ujjhāti is the usual form.
ujjhātuṃ.example_1: Na taṃ ujjhātumarahasīti taṃ amhākaṃ paveṇiāgataṃ dhammaṃ sabhāvaṃ tvaṃ ujjhātuṃ na arahasi, na yuttaṃ te ettha kujjhitunti.
ujjhātuṃ.translation_1: You should not censure that (na taṃ ujjhātumarahasī) means: you should not censure or destroy that custom of ours that has come down through our lineage; it is not suitable for you to be angry in this matter. This is the meaning.

kujjhitunti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text kujjhituṃ is the infinitive of this verb, with the quotation particle -ti added: kujjhituṃ + ti. The sentence means 'it is not suitable for you to be angry here'.
kujjhitunti.example_1: Na taṃ ujjhātumarahasīti taṃ amhākaṃ paveṇiāgataṃ dhammaṃ sabhāvaṃ tvaṃ ujjhātuṃ na arahasi, na yuttaṃ te ettha kujjhitunti.
kujjhitunti.translation_1: You should not censure that (na taṃ ujjhātumarahasī) means: you should not censure or destroy that custom of ours that has come down through our lineage; it is not suitable for you to be angry in this matter. This is the meaning.

vihiyyati.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Text form vihiyyati is a passive/denominative-looking variant standing for vihaññati (√han, passive); the meaning in the verse is 'is lost, falls away'. If taken at face value it could be from √hi 1 or √hā 1, but the sense here fits vihaññati. Present 3rd singular, passive.
vihiyyati.translation_1: 64. “Through association with a friend whereby one’s freedom from bondage falls away;

vihiyyatīti.meaning_2: is left; is abandoned; is deprived (of)
vihiyyatīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Passive of vijahati (√hā 1). Quotative -iti added; entry is for vihiyyati. Reading uncertain.

māhesu.grammar: pr, 3rd plural, opt of atthi; sandhi of mā + ahesuṃ
māhesu.meaning_2: let them not be; may they not be
māhesu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of mā + ahesuṃ (aorist 3rd plural of atthi); the sandhi form māhesu is glossed in the commentary as mā ahesuṃ. Alternative analysis: mā + hes-suṃ, an aorist of √as. Printed as māhesu.
māhesu.example_1: Mā vanaṃ chindi nibyagghaṃ, byagghā māhesu nibbanā ’’ ti.
māhesu.translation_1: Do not let the forest be cut down, being bereft of tigers; let not the tigers be homeless.”
māhesu.example_2: Byagghā māhesu nibbanāti tumhādisā ca byaggharājāno attano vasanaṭṭhānā palāyitattā nibbanā vasanaṭṭhānabhūtena vanena virahitā mā ahesuṃ.
māhesu.translation_2: Byagghā māhesu nibbanā means let not tiger-kings like yourselves, having fled from your own dwelling place, be homeless, bereft of the forest that served as your dwelling.

uddhitabhattovāti.meaning_2: with the rice removed; whose rice has been taken away; with the food lifted off
uddhitabhattovāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound uddhita (removed; lifted off) + bhatta (rice; meal). Followed by the quotation marker vā + ti, written together in the text; the entry is for the compound alone. No sentences supplied, so the meaning and case are uncertain; if the reading is nominative singular, lemma_2 is uddhitabhatto.

rasakaroṭimatthake.meaning_2: on the edge of the rim of the cooking pot
rasakaroṭimatthake.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Dictionary form is uncertain: could also be rasakaroṭimaṭṭhaka or a bahubbīhi 'having its head at the edge of the pot'. Locative singular in the text.
rasakaroṭimatthake.example_1: Kāko ‘‘ ayaṃ idāni kālo maṃsaṃ khāditun ’’ ti gantvā rasakaroṭimatthake nisīdi.
rasakaroṭimatthake.translation_1: The crow thought, “Now is the time to eat the meat,” and went and sat on the rim of the cooking pot.

sikhinī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine of sikhī; in the text it agrees with balākā. DPD would probably list sikhī, but sikhinī is the form in the text.
sikhinī.example_1: Kāyaṃ balākā sikhinīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ lolabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi.
sikhinī.translation_1: Kāyaṃ balākā sikhinīti—the Teacher told this story while dwelling at Jetavana, referring to a greedy bhikkhu.
sikhinī.translation_2: 70. Who is this tufted crane, a thief with clouds for grandfathers?

punapāpajjasī.meaning_2: again you will incur; again you will come to (something bad)
punapāpajjasī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of puna + āpajjasi (2nd singular future of āpajjati). The commentary glosses punapi evarūpaṃ āpajjissasi; printed in the text with an extra m in sammāti.
punapāpajjasī.translation_1: 72. You will come to grief again, friend, for your moral conduct is just like that.
punapāpajjasī.example_2: Tattha punapāpajjasī sammāti samma vāyasa, punapi tvaṃ evarūpaṃ dukkhaṃ paṭilabhissaseva, natthi te ettakena mokkho.
punapāpajjasī.translation_2: In that passage, ‘punapāpajjasī sammā’ means: “Friend crow, you will certainly come to grief again; there is no deliverance for you from such misery.”

tulayimha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] First person plural aorist; in the text paired with nimimha, meaning 'we compared, considered'.
tulayimha.example_1: Aparo nayo – tava saddhañca sīlaguṇasaṅkhātaṃ vaṇṇañca sutvā ‘‘ uḷāraguṇo rājā jīvitampi yācito dadeyya, pageva tiracchānagataṃ nāgan ’’ ti evaṃ kāliṅgassa santike iminā añjanavaṇṇena tava vaṇṇaṃ nimimhase nimimha tulayimha, tenamhā idhāgatāti.
tulayimha.translation_1: Another interpretation: Having heard of your faith and virtue, we thought, “A king of such great merit would give even his own life if asked, so what need to speak of a mere animal, this elephant?” Thus, we came here to exchange—that is, to compare—the gold we brought with this black elephant to take to the King of Kalinga.

gopayitvā.meaning_2: having protected; having guarded; having kept safe
gopayitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of the causative gopeti (√gup 2 + *aya), meaning 'having guarded, having taken care of'. In the sentence it describes the charioteer guarding the chariot before waiting at the palace gate.
gopayitvā.example_1: Sārathipi rathaṃ gopayitvā punadivase pātova taṃ ādāya rājadvāre tiṭṭhati.
gopayitvā.translation_1: The driver would guard the chariot, and in the morning, he would wait at the palace door.

nikkhantukāmo.meaning_2: wishing to leave; desiring to go out
nikkhantukāmo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text, nominative singular modifying a subject; alternative analysis nikkhanta + kāma.
nikkhantukāmo.example_1: Sace taṅkhaṇaññeva nikkhantukāmo hoti, rasmiyo ca patodañca antoratheyeva ṭhapetvā rājupaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati.
nikkhantukāmo.translation_1: If the viceroy wished to leave then, he would leave the reins and goad inside the chariot and go to serve the king.

nikkhantuṃ.meaning_2: to go out; to leave; to depart
nikkhantuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -tuṃ (cf. nikkhamitvā, nikkhanta). The commentary glosses it as 'to go out'. The text's nikkhantuṃ shows the common assimilation of -mi- to -n- before t; the standard form is nikkhamituṃ. Here it is the object of nādāsi: 'did not allow him to leave'.
nikkhantuṃ.example_1: Rājā ‘‘ devo vassatī ’’ ti tassa nikkhantuṃ nādāsi, so tattheva bhuñjitvā sayi.
nikkhantuṃ.translation_1: The king said, 'It is raining,' and did not let him leave. He ate and slept there.

bilamajjhaṃ.meaning_2: middle of the hole; inside the burrow
bilamajjhaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text, the destination of pāpuṇi ("reached"). Compound of bila (hole) and majjha (middle).
bilamajjhaṃ.example_1: Sopi ekadivasaṃ janapade khettaṃ minanto rajjuṃ daṇḍake bandhitvā ekaṃ koṭiṃ khettasāmikena gaṇhāpetvā ekaṃ attanā aggahesi, tena gahitarajjukoṭiyā baddhadaṇḍako ekassa kakkaṭakassa bilamajjhaṃ pāpuṇi.
bilamajjhaṃ.translation_1: One day, while surveying land in the country, he tied a cord to a stake, had the landowner hold one end, and he held the other. The stake tied to his end reached a crab's hole.

ghaṭetuṃ.meaning_2: to connect; to join together; to mend; to support; to strive (for); to make an effort
ghaṭetuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of ghaṭeti, used with na sakkomi in the sense 'cannot support (my life)' and 'cannot mend (them)'. The PEU's Ghaṭa+ṇe+tuṃ is not standard; the form is ghaṭeti + tuṃ.
ghaṭetuṃ.example_1: ‘‘ mayhaṃ sahassaṃ datvā gatapurisassa tīṇi saṃvaccharāni anāgacchantassa duggatā jātā, jīvitavuttiṃ ghaṭetuṃ na sakkomi, ito dāni paṭṭhāya mayā vinicchayamahāmattānaṃ ārocetvā paribbayaṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti.
ghaṭetuṃ.translation_1: She thought, “It has been three years since the man who gave me a thousand pieces left. I have become poor and cannot support my life. From today on, I must report to the judges and take my wage.”
ghaṭetuṃ.example_2: Sā vinicchayaṃ gantvā ‘‘ sāmi, paribbayaṃ datvā gatapurisassa me tīṇi saṃvaccharāni, matabhāvampissa na jānāmi, jīvitaṃ ghaṭetuṃ na sakkomi, kiṃ karomi, sāmī ’’ ti āha.
ghaṭetuṃ.translation_2: She went to the court and said, “Sir, it has been three years since the man who gave me a wage left. I do not know if he is dead or alive. I cannot support my life. What should I do, sir?”

tedānīti.meaning_2: at that time thus; 'then' so it was said
tedānīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of tedāni (then) + iti; the -ti is a quotation marker, often used in commentarial glosses.

nibbati.meaning_2: is reborn; comes into existence; arises
nibbati.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the sentence, nibbati is 3rd singular present of ni + √vatt, meaning 'is reborn' (as a jackal). Probably a variant or textual form of nibbattati; the PTS form is uncertain.
nibbati.example_1: Athassa mātā kālakiriyaṃ katvā puttasinehena tassa āgamanamagge opapātikasiṅgālī hutvā nibbati.
nibbati.translation_1: After she died, due to her love for her son, she was reborn as a supernatural jackal on the road her son was coming along.

occhindamānā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine nominative singular agreeing with siṅgālī in the text; the form is one who repeatedly crosses the road to block it.
occhindamānā.example_1: Atha sā siṅgālī putte aṭavīmukhaṃ sampatte ‘‘ tāta, mā aṭaviṃ abhiruhi, corā ettha ṭhitā, te taṃ māretvā kahāpaṇe gaṇhissantī ’’ ti punappunaṃ maggaṃ occhindamānā nivāreti.
occhindamānā.translation_1: Then that jackal, as her son reached the entrance to the forest, repeatedly crossed the road, blocking it, and tried to stop him, saying, “Dear, do not enter the forest! Robbers are staying there; they will kill you and take the kahāpaṇas.”

occhindatīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The -ti is the quotative particle (iti), so the entry is for the verb alone; 3rd singular present.

occhinditvā.meaning_2: having blocked; having cut off; having obstructed
occhinditvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of occhindati (ava + √chid); the initial o- is the sandhi form of ava-. In the text it means blocking a path (maggaṃ occhinditvā).
occhinditvā.example_1: ‘‘ Mātā te tayi nikkhante kālaṃ katvā puttasinehena siṅgālī hutvā tava maraṇabhayabhītā maggaṃ te occhinditvā taṃ vāresi, taṃ tvaṃ tajjetvā palāpesi, satapattasakuṇo pana te paccāmitto.
occhinditvā.translation_1: “Your mother died after you left, and due to her love for her son, she was reborn as a jackal, and fearing for your life, she blocked your path and tried to stop you. You harassed and chased her away. But the crane is your enemy.
occhinditvā.example_2: Ajātasattuṃ gaṇhitukāmena asuke nāma pabbatakucchismiṃ dvīsu pabbatabhittīsu manusse ṭhapetvā purato dubbalabalaṃ dassetvā pabbatantaraṃ paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ jānitvā paviṭṭhamaggaṃ occhinditvā purato ca pacchato ca ubhosu pabbatabhittīsu vaggitvā unnaditvā khipe patitamacchaṃ viya antomuṭṭhiyaṃ vaṭṭapotakaṃ viya ca katvā sakkā assa taṃ gahetun ’’ ti.
occhinditvā.translation_2: Wishing to capture Ajātasattu, one should place men at those two mountain walls in that mountain-ravine, show a weak force in front, and knowing he has entered the mountain-pass, block the path he entered by; and by leaping from both mountain walls in front and behind, and shouting, one could capture him like a fish fallen in a basket, or like a quail in the palm of the hand.”

dūsa.meaning_2: name of a king (one of the ten kings in the Kurudhamma Jātaka); Dūsa
dūsa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is part of a list of ten kings; probably a proper name rather than a common noun. The PEU entry gives a different derivation (dusa + a, 'to be destroyed'), possibly connected with √dū or √dus.
dūsa.example_1: Sujanādhipa romaka dūsa puna, satapattavaro puṭakamma dasāti.
dūsa.translation_1: Kurudhamma, Romaka, Dūsa, Satapatta, Puṭadusa; these are the ten.

attapariccāgī.meaning_2: sacrificing oneself; self-sacrificing; one who gives up oneself
attapariccāgī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi in -ī (possessive suffix) meaning 'one who has given up oneself'. Nominative singular in the verses; glossed by the commentary as kāye ca jīvite ca nirapekkho hutvā attānaṃ pariccajanto.
attapariccāgī.translation_1: As a hero sacrificing himself, I shall be one who obtains that.”
attapariccāgī.example_2: Attapariccāgīti kāye ca jīvite ca nirapekkho hutvā tassa tividhassapi bhattu atthāya attānaṃ pariccajanto.
attapariccāgī.translation_2: Attapariccāgī means: having become unconcerned with body and life, sacrificing oneself for the sake of that threefold master.

attapariccāgīti.meaning_2: one who gives up oneself; one who sacrifices oneself
attapariccāgīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text with the quotation-marking enclitic -ti: attapariccāgī ti = attapariccāgī + iti. The final -ī is the possessive suffix -ī; the compound is bahubbīhi.

suyevāti.meaning_2: it is surely well heard; certainly well heard
suyevāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of suyeva (su + eva) with iti. No sentence context was found; analysis is tentative.

yuddho.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Written yuddho in the text by sandhi for yuddhaṃ before nāma (or as nominative singular in an older form).
yuddho.example_1: ‘‘ bhante, yuddho nāma tividho – padumabyūho, cakkabyūho, sakaṭabyūhoti.
yuddho.translation_1: “Venerable sir, there are three kinds of war: the lotus array, the wheel array, and the wagon array.

vaggitvā.meaning_2: having shouted; having cried out; having roared
vaggitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive used of shouting or roaring, often in combination with gajjitvā (as in the text). The root √vagg 1 (dance, jump) is uncertain; the PPED gives Vaggati. Sometimes read as a form of vagga (group) but the sense here is clearly vocal.
vaggitvā.example_1: Ajātasattuṃ gaṇhitukāmena asuke nāma pabbatakucchismiṃ dvīsu pabbatabhittīsu manusse ṭhapetvā purato dubbalabalaṃ dassetvā pabbatantaraṃ paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ jānitvā paviṭṭhamaggaṃ occhinditvā purato ca pacchato ca ubhosu pabbatabhittīsu vaggitvā unnaditvā khipe patitamacchaṃ viya antomuṭṭhiyaṃ vaṭṭapotakaṃ viya ca katvā sakkā assa taṃ gahetun ’’ ti.
vaggitvā.translation_1: Wishing to capture Ajātasattu, one should place men at those two mountain walls in that mountain-ravine, show a weak force in front, and knowing he has entered the mountain-pass, block the path he entered by; and by leaping from both mountain walls in front and behind, and shouting, one could capture him like a fish fallen in a basket, or like a quail in the palm of the hand.”
vaggitvā.example_2: Baladevo taṃ disvā ‘‘ na naṃ hatthena chupissāmī ’’ ti hatthisālato mahantaṃ hatthiyottaṃ āharitvā vaggitvā gajjitvā yottaṃ khipitvā cāruraṃ udare veṭhetvā dve yottakoṭiyo ekato katvā vattetvā ukkhipitvā sīsamatthake bhametvā bhūmiyaṃ pothetvā bahi akkhavāṭe khipi.
vaggitvā.translation_2: Baladeva, seeing him, thought, “I will not touch him with my hand,” and fetching a thick elephant-yoke strap from the elephant stable, shouting and roaring, he cast the strap, wound it around Cānura’s belly, joined the two ends together, twisted them, lifted him up, whirled him around over his head, struck him down on the ground, and threw him outside the ring.

paṭioloketha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text the word is written as 'paṭioloketha' and glossed as an imperative plural 'look back at him', while the following clause has the aorist 'paṭiolokesuṃ'. The lemma is the present 3rd singular, causative of paṭiolokati. The initial 'o' may stand for 'ava' (ava + loketi), but here it is treated as part of the causative base.
paṭioloketha.example_1: Vaḍḍhakīsūkaro ‘‘ paṭioloketha nan ’’ ti sūkarānaṃ saññaṃ adāsi, te paṭiolokesuṃ.
paṭioloketha.translation_1: Vaḍḍhakīsūkaro gave a sign to the boars, “Look back at him,” and they looked back.

paṭiolokesuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text reads paṭiolokesuṃ (with elided vowel) for paṭiolokesuṃ; 3rd plural aorist of paṭioloketi. Some editions read paṭilokesuṃ.
paṭiolokesuṃ.example_1: Vaḍḍhakīsūkaro ‘‘ paṭioloketha nan ’’ ti sūkarānaṃ saññaṃ adāsi, te paṭiolokesuṃ.
paṭiolokesuṃ.translation_1: Vaḍḍhakīsūkaro gave a sign to the boars, “Look back at him,” and they looked back.

dummaddayā.meaning_2: hard to crush; difficult to suppress
dummaddayā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Predicative in the text, agreeing with sūkarā (nominative plural); glossed duppasahā dummaddayā.
dummaddayā.example_1: Ayaṃ pana saṅkhepattho – ime sūkarā pubbe maṃ disvā bhayena aṭṭitā pīḷitā attano leṇagavesino puthū visuṃ visuṃ hutvā disodisaṃ yanti , taṃ taṃ disaṃ abhimukhā palāyanti, te dāni sabbepi samāgantvā ekato vasanti tiṭṭhanti, tañca bhūmisīsaṃ upagatā, yattha ṭhitā duppasahā dummaddayā ajja ime mayāti.
dummaddayā.translation_1: But this is the concise meaning: In the past, these boars, on seeing me, were racked and oppressed by fear; they went in all directions, each seeking its own refuge, fleeing headlong to one side or the other. But now, all of them have assembled, standing together in one group; they have approached this terrain where, standing there, they are today difficult for me, difficult to crush.”

iṅghitaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Variant spelling of iṅgita. Accusative singular in the text (tesaṃ iṅghitaṃ disvā).
iṅghitaṃ.example_1: Vaḍḍhakīsūkaro tesaṃ iṅghitaṃ disvā ‘‘ kiṃ nu kho tumhe na tussathā ’’ ti āha.
iṅghitaṃ.translation_1: The Carpenter's Boar, seeing their behavior, asked, “Why are you not satisfied?”

taruṇasūkariṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine in the text: taruṇasūkariṃ (accusative singular of taruṇasūkarī), a young sow, made chief queen.
taruṇasūkariṃ.example_1: Parivāretvā ṭhitasūkarā kūṭajaṭilaṃ bhūmiyaṃ pātetvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ katvā yāva aṭṭhito khāditvā vaḍḍhakīsūkaraṃ udumbarakhandheyeva nisīdāpetvā kūṭajaṭilassa paribhogasaṅkhena udakaṃ āharitvā abhisiñcitvā rājānaṃ kariṃsu, ekañca taruṇasūkariṃ tassa aggamahesiṃ akaṃsu.
taruṇasūkariṃ.translation_1: The boars standing guard knocked the fraudulent hermit to the ground, tore him into pieces, ate him right down to the bones, seated the Carpenter's Boar on the tree trunk, brought water in the hermit's own conch shell, consecrated him as king, and made a young sow his chief queen.

gatvā.meaning_2: having gone; having gone (to); having reached
gatvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of gacchati; gantvā → gatvā by consonant assimilation. Used in both sentences to mean 'having gone (to)'.
gatvā.example_1: ‘‘ anāthapiṇḍiko duggato hutvā puna issaro jāto, yaṃnūnāhaṃ taṃ daṭṭhukāmo viya gatvā tassa gharato siriṃ thenetvā āgaccheyyan ’’ ti.
gatvā.translation_1: “Anāthapiṇḍika was poor and then became wealthy; what if I go as if to see him and steal his good luck?”
gatvā.example_2: Evarūpassa hi kalahavaḍḍhanaṃ nāma ayuttaṃ, tasmā ito gatvā attano pitaraṃ bhūtādhipaṃ sakkameva pucchatha, sace attano uttamaṃ adhamañca na jānāthāti.
gatvā.translation_2: Indeed, for such a noble one, to cause a quarrel is improper. Therefore, if you do not know your own highest and lowest, go from here and ask Sakka, your father and the Lord of Beings, himself.”

lakkhivā.meaning_2: lucky; fortunate; endowed with good fortune
lakkhivā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form lakkhivā is the nominative singular masculine of the possessive adjective lakkhivant (lakkhī + vant). It agrees with puriso in the commentarial gloss. Sippavanto asippā ca lakkhivā tāni bhuñjati.
lakkhivā.example_1: Sippavanto asippā ca, lakkhivā tāni bhuñjati.
lakkhivā.translation_1: Both skilled and unskilled equally obtain / Should fortune’s favor grant them lucky gain.”
lakkhivā.example_2: Lakkhivā tāni bhuñjatīti tāni ‘‘ bahuṃ dhanan ’’ ti vuttāni dhanāni puññavā puriso attano puññaphalaṃ paribhuñjanto kiñci kammaṃ akatvāpi paribhuñjati.
lakkhivā.translation_2: ‘The lucky one enjoys them’: those riches mentioned as ‘much wealth’ are enjoyed by the lucky person—the one full of merit—who consumes the fruit of his own merit, enjoying them even without performing any specific work.

vevāhikapuriso.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text. Compound of vevāhika (relating to a wedding) and purisa (man).
vevāhikapuriso.example_1: Idāni katipāhasseva so vevāhikapuriso mahatiyā parisāya yutto yuttasevako idha atithi hutvā āgato bhavissati, athetaṃ sālūkaṃ musalasadisena uttaroṭṭhena samannāgatattā musaluttaraṃ māritaṃ sayantaṃ dakkhasīti.
vevāhikapuriso.translation_1: Now, in a few days, that wedding guest will arrive here, being a guest accompanied by a large assembly, and then you will see that Sālūka, because of being endowed with an upper lip like a pestle, is the flat-snouted one (musaluttaraṃ), being killed and lying there.

vevāhikesu.meaning_2: wedding guest; member of a wedding party
vevāhikesu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative plural in the text (vevāhikesu āgatesu). Derived from vivāha (marriage) with the suffix -ika and the lengthened first syllable.
vevāhikesu.example_1: Tato katipāhasseva vevāhikesu āgatesu sālūkaṃ māretvā uttaribhaṅgamakaṃsu.
vevāhikesu.translation_1: A few days later, when the wedding guests had arrived, they killed Sālūka and made him into the main course.

sālūko.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a pig in this Jātaka; nominative singular in the text, identified with the discontented bhikkhu. Also a common noun meaning 'lotus root'.
sālūko.example_1: ‘‘ Tadā kumārikā etarahi thullakumārikā ahosi, sālūko ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu, cūḷalohito ānando, mahālohito pana ahameva ahosin ’’ ti.
sālūko.translation_1: “At that time the girl was the fat girl of today; Sālūka was the discontented bhikkhu; Little Redcoat was Ānanda; and Big Redcoat was I myself.”

nānaṭoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Probably na + anaṭoti (√aṭ, roam) or na + aññathā ti; no sentence available to confirm. The PEU entry nānaṭṭha (nānā + attha) is unrelated.

anaṭo.meaning_2: not an actor; not a dancer; not behaving like an actor
anaṭo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text. na + naṭa with the vowel contracted; some editions may read annaṭa. Compare the related anaṭṭha.
anaṭo.example_1: Yo evaṃ anaṭo, so mūḷhesu lābhaṃ na labhati.
anaṭo.translation_1: Whoever is not an actor in this way does not obtain gain among the foolish.

kutūhalo.meaning_2: chatterer; one who speaks of scattered things; one who talks of this and that
kutūhalo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is nominative singular and is defined as a person of scattered speech (vippakiṇṇavācā). The related PEU entry derives it from ku + tula + a with the sense of 'commotion' or 'curiosity'. The first sentence is a word analysis of nākutūhalo (na + kutūhalo).
kutūhalo.translation_1: Nākutūhalo means a chatterer is one whose speech is scattered.
kutūhalo.example_2: Tattha sesesu akathentesuyeva yo uṭṭhahitvā ‘‘ asuko ca asuko ca nāmā ’’ ti vadati, ayaṃ kutūhalo nāma.
kutūhalo.translation_2: Among them, while the others remain silent, whoever gets up and says, “So-and-so and so-and-so did this,” is called a chatterer.

gilāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā of the causative gilāpeti; in the text it means 'having caused (a fish) to swallow'.
gilāpetvā.example_1: ‘‘ ahaṃ iminā dinnapattiṃ anumoditvā dibbayasena vaḍḍhitvā etassa santakaṃ rakkhissāmī ’’ ti attano ānubhāvena taṃ bhaṇḍikaṃ ekaṃ mahāmacchaṃ gilāpetvā sayaṃ ārakkhaṃ gaṇhi.
gilāpetvā.translation_1: “Having rejoiced at the merit given by this man and having grown in celestial glory, I will protect his property,” and by her own power, she made a large fish swallow that package, and took it under her own protection.
gilāpetvā.example_2: Bodhisatto ‘‘ imassa rañño byādhi natthi, bhariyaṃ pana apassanto cetasikarogena phuṭṭho, upāyena taṃ tikicchissāmī ’’ ti āyurañca pukkusañcāti dve rañño paṇḍitāmacce āmantetvā ‘‘ rañño deviyā adassanena cetasikaṃ rogaṃ ṭhapetvā añño rogo natthi, bahūpakāro ca kho pana amhākaṃ rājā, tasmā upāyena naṃ tikicchāma, rājaṅgaṇe samajjaṃ kāretvā asiṃ gilituṃ jānantena asiṃ gilāpetvā rājānaṃ sīhapañjare katvā samajjaṃ olokāpessāma, rājā asiṃ gilantaṃ disvā ‘ atthi nu kho ito aññaṃ dukkarataran ’ ti pañhaṃ pucchissati.
gilāpetvā.translation_2: The Bodhisatta thought, “This king has no illness, but not seeing his wife, he is touched by mental sickness; I will cure him by a means.” So, having addressed the two wise ministers of the king, Āyura and Pukkusa, he said, “There is no other sickness for the king, except for mental sickness due to not seeing the queen; and indeed, the king is very helpful to us, therefore we will cure him by a means. We will make a gathering in the royal courtyard, and having caused a man who knows how to swallow a sword to swallow a sword, we will place the king on the lion-balcony and cause him to observe the gathering. The king, seeing the man swallowing a sword, will ask the question, ‘I wonder if there is anything more difficult than this?’”

udukkhalaṃbhikaṅkhatīti.meaning_2: wishing (for) a mortar; longing (for) a mortar
udukkhalaṃbhikaṅkhatīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of udukkhalaṃbhikaṅkhati (udukkhalaṃ + abhikaṅkhati, 'wishes for a mortar') + iti. Alternative analysis: udukkhalaṃ + abhikaṅkhatīti; the word occurs in a Jātaka prose story.

yañcetanti.meaning_2: and thinking whatever...; whatever one thinks, that...
yañcetanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of yaṃ ci (or ce) with the 3rd singular of tanoti? Uncertain segmentation; no sentence context, so the exact analysis is a guess.

vīmaṃsitukāmatāyāti.meaning_2: desire to examine; wish to investigate; state of wanting to test
vīmaṃsitukāmatāyāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The -ti is the quotative particle iti sandhied to the end (āya + iti > āyāti); the headword drops it. Instrumental singular in the text.

pottho.meaning_2: rag; tattered garment; one clothed in rags
pottho.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the verse pottho is nominative singular, paired with naggo (naked) and explained in the commentary as one wearing a tattered garment (potthakapilotikā).
pottho.example_1: Tadā naggo ca pottho ca, pacchā bālo vihaññati.
pottho.translation_1: Then, naked and in rags, the fool is tormented later on.
pottho.example_2: Naggo ca pottho cāti kadāci naggo, kadāci potthakapilotikāya nivatthattā pottho.
pottho.translation_2: Naggo ca pottho ca means: sometimes naked, sometimes clothed in rags because of wearing a tattered garment.

pariggaṇhāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to be examined; having had investigated; having made (someone) examine
pariggaṇhāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of pariggaṇhāpeti (causative of parigaṇhāti), used in the text with purise pesetvā of the king sending men to have the matter investigated. Could also be analysed as a form of pariggaṇhāpeti meaning 'to cause to take possession of, to have apportioned'.
pariggaṇhāpetvā.example_1: Rājā purise pesetvā pariggaṇhāpetvā tato paṭṭhāya theriyā tathārūpaṃ bhattaṃ adāsi.
pariggaṇhāpetvā.translation_1: The King sent messengers to investigate, and from then on gave such food to the Theri.

dhiratthumaṃ.meaning_2: fie upon!; shame on!; woe on!
dhiratthumaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Indeclinable expressing scorn or disgust. In the text dhiratthumaṃ = dhiratthu + imaṃ, 'fie upon this'. Variant of dhiratthū. Not a verbal root derivative, so root fields are left empty.
dhiratthumaṃ.example_1: 129. ‘‘ Dhiratthumaṃ āturaṃ pūtikāyaṃ, jegucchiyaṃ assuciṃ byādhidhammaṃ;
dhiratthumaṃ.translation_1: 129. “Fie upon this diseased, rotten body, loathsome, impure, and subject to illness;

paṭipasaṃsanto.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular of the present participle agreeing with kāko. The prefix pati- here carries the sense 'in return, back'.
paṭipasaṃsanto.example_1: Atha naṃ kāko paṭipasaṃsanto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –
paṭipasaṃsanto.translation_1: Then the crow, praising him in return, uttered the second stanza:

tyatthūti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of tyattha (tatra + attha, 'there, in that matter') and the quotation particle iti. No sentences supplied, so the analysis is uncertain; the form may also be treated as tyattha + ū + iti (with emphatic ū) in the commentary's prose.

tāvakharampi.meaning_2: even that much pain; even to that extent of suffering
tāvakharampi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of tāvakharaṃ (as much pain, so great suffering) + api (even). The PEU splits as tāva + khara 'that serious, that much'. In the text it is the object of agaṇetvā: 'disregarding even that pain'. It could also be analysed as an adverb; here treated as a sandhi compound.
tāvakharampi.example_1: So tattha nisinno ākāsena gacchantaṃ ekaṃ kākaṃ disvā tāvakharampi taṃ vedanaṃ agaṇetvā piyabhariyāya sāsanaṃ pesetuṃ kākaṃ āmantento imā gāthā āha –
tāvakharampi.translation_1: Seated there, he saw a crow flying through the air; disregarding even that intense pain, he called to the crow to send a message to his dear wife and uttered these verses:

māsitoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The word in the text is māsita + ti (quotation particle). Uncertain; possibly related to √mā (measure) or a denominative. No sentences were supplied, so the meaning is a guess.

pāsādathupikaṃ.meaning_2: palace pinnacle; spire of a palace
pāsādathupikaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of the pinnacle or spire on top of a palace. The compound is pāsāda + thupikā (feminine); the text has the accusative singular form pāsādathupikaṃ.
pāsādathupikaṃ.example_1: Thero ākāse uppatitvā pādaṅguṭṭhakena pāsādathupikaṃ paharitvā yāva udakapariyantā pāsādaṃ kampesi.
pāsādathupikaṃ.translation_1: The Elder rose into the sky, struck the pinnacle of the palace with his big toe, and shook the palace to the very edge of the ocean.

aṭṭhaṃsū.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] 3rd person plural aorist of tiṭṭhati; the initial a- is the augment. Alternate reading aṭṭhaṃsu is sometimes treated as a sandhi of atthaṃsu.
aṭṭhaṃsū.example_1: Te bhikkhū maraṇabhayabhītā nikkhamitvā bahi aṭṭhaṃsū.
aṭṭhaṃsū.translation_1: Those monks, terrified of death, went out and stood outside.

mukhamakkaṭikakīḷāsaṅkhātāni.meaning_2: called monkey-face play; known as grimacing like a monkey
mukhamakkaṭikakīḷāsaṅkhātāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound adjective qualifying mukhavikārāni; neuter nominative plural in the text (-āni). Gloss of makkaṭiyā in the commentary.
mukhamakkaṭikakīḷāsaṅkhātāni.translation_1: “Monkey-like grimaces” means facial distortions known as monkey-like facial play.

lohitapo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Commentary glosses lohitapo as lohitapāyī. Nominative singular in the verse; the second sentence quotes the word and explains it.
lohitapo.translation_1: The observer of purity, having come near, the blood-drinker broke his fervor.”
lohitapo.translation_2: “Blood-drinker” means the one who drinks blood.

lohitapoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Uncertain. Possibly a tree name (lohita + poti/pāṭī), red-sapped or red-coloured. No sentences given; if the reading is lohitapotī, the headword would be fem.

avadhārikā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name in the Jātaka story of Saccaka; nominative singular in the text. Possibly an agent noun from avadharati (ava + √dhar).
avadhārikā.example_1: Dārikānaṃ ‘‘ saccā, lolā, avadhārikā, paṭicchādā ’’ ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu, dārakassa ‘‘ saccako ’’ ti.
avadhārikā.translation_1: They named the daughters Saccā, Lolā, Avadhārikā, and Paṭicchādā, and the boy Saccaka.

piḷandhi.example_1: Devīpi kāsikavatthañceva ābharaṇāni ca apanetvā tena ābhatavatthaṃ nivāsetvā ābharaṇāni piḷandhi.
piḷandhi.translation_1: The queen also, having removed her Kasi garments and ornaments, put on the garment that he had brought and wore her ornaments.
piḷandhi.example_2: Purohito ‘‘ ahaṃ etehi guṇehi samannāgato ’’ ti vatvā tānipi āharāpetvā piḷandhi.
piḷandhi.translation_2: The chaplain, having said, “I am possessed of these qualities,” had those too brought and wore them.

sodānīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Emphatic form with -ti in the text; from so + dāni.

sampatthitā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine nominative singular modifying khantī and tapo (as a collective); the commentary glosses it with icchitā and abhikaṅkhitā. The prefix saṃ- is used in place of paṭi- (cf. patthita).
sampatthitā.example_1: 10. ‘‘ Pubbeva khantī ca tapo ca mayhaṃ, sampatthitā dubbhisena ahosi;
sampatthitā.translation_1: “Already, O Dubbhisena, forbearance and asceticism were desired by me;
sampatthitā.translation_2: Desired (sampatthitā) means longed for and wished for.

sampatthitāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The -ti is the quotation particle (iti), so the main word is sampatthita. Used here as a past participle meaning 'longed for'. If it is instead taken as a finite verb, it could be a 3rd singular aorist, but the iti-closing position shows a quoted word.

passsantassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Genitive singular of passanta (passantassa) in sandhi with preceding kassaci. Written passsantassa; siya passantassa.
passsantassa.example_1: ‘‘ Tumhe na kassaci passsantassa ābhataṃ gaṇhatha, ahaṃ pana pāpakaraṇe raho nāma na passāmī ’’ ti dīpento imā dve gāthā āha –
passsantassa.translation_1: “You do not accept what is brought if anyone sees it, but I do not see any such thing as secrecy in wrongdoing,” explaining thus, he spoke these two verses:

sohāyasmā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of so (nominative singular of ta, 'that') and āyasmā ('venerable'). In the text it refers to the elder, probably Mahākassapa, and is the subject of parodi.
sohāyasmā.example_1: Sohāyasmā ‘‘ ajja rattiyā paccūsasamaye satthā parinibbāyissatī ’’ ti ñatvā ‘‘ ahañcamhi sekkho sakaraṇīyo, satthu ca me parinibbānaṃ bhavissati, pañcavīsati vassāni satthu kataṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ nipphalaṃ bhavissatī ’’ ti sokābhibhūto uyyānaovarake kapisīsaṃ ālambitvā parodi.
sohāyasmā.translation_1: That venerable one, knowing, 'Today, at the approach of dawn, the Teacher will attain final Nibbāna,' thought, 'I am still a trainee with much to do, and my Teacher's final Nibbāna will occur; the twenty-five years of service rendered to the Teacher will be fruitless.' Overwhelmed with sorrow, he leaned on the door-lintel in the garden storeroom and wept.

vibhāyi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Common idiom ratti vibhāyi 'the night dawned'. Aorist 3rd singular; the root aorist of vibhāti is irregular.
vibhāyi.translation_1: While he was doing so, the night dawned.
vibhāyi.example_2: Deviyā sādhukāraṃ datvā dhammaṃ suṇantiyā dhammassavanena atittāya eva ratti vibhāyi.
vibhāyi.translation_2: While the queen, giving her approbation, was listening to the Dhamma, and was indeed not yet satisfied with listening to the Dhamma, the night dawned.

saṅkitabbāni.meaning_2: to be suspected; to be distrusted; to be feared
saṅkitabbāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Potential participle of saṅkati (doubt, suspect); neuter plural agreeing with the following clause in the verse. Sometimes spelled saṅkitabba with a single k.
saṅkitabbāni.translation_1: 44. “One should suspect what is to be suspected; one should guard against the danger yet to come;

vissāmetvā.meaning_2: causes to rest; lets rest; gives rest (to)
vissāmetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative of vissamati. Absolutive in -tvā in both sentences; takes the elder(s) as object.
vissāmetvā.example_1: Daharabhikkhu jetavanassa āsannaṭṭhāne ‘‘ sāmaṇera tvaṃ theraṃ vissāmetvā āneyyāsi, ahaṃ puretaraṃ gantvā pariveṇaṃ paṭijaggissāmī ’’ ti jetavanaṃ pāvisi.
vissāmetvā.translation_1: When they were near Jeta’s Grove, the young monk said, “Novice, you should bring the elder after letting him rest, while I go ahead and prepare the cell.” Having said this, he entered Jeta’s Grove.
vissāmetvā.example_2: So te dvepi vissāmetvā saṇikaṃ ānesi.
vissāmetvā.translation_2: He, having let both of them rest, brought them slowly.

uppīḷento.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle of uppīḷeti (causative of pīḷ). Nominative singular masculine in the text, used with sīsena and daṇḍena ('pressing with the head/staff').
uppīḷento.example_1: Sāmaṇero punappunaṃ sīsena uppīḷento viya ‘‘ gaccha, bhante, gaccha, bhante ’’ ti taṃ balakkārena neti.
uppīḷento.translation_1: The novice, as if repeatedly pressing him with his head, saying, “Go, venerable sir, go, venerable sir,” led him by force.
uppīḷento.example_2: Khuddakatāpaso pitarā saddhiṃ saṇikaṃ gacchanto taṃ kaṭippadese sīsena uppīḷento viya gaccha gacchāti taṃ balakkārena neti.
uppīḷento.translation_2: The young ascetic, going slowly with his father, as if repeatedly pressing him in the hip region with his head, saying, “Go, go,” led him by force.

mandībhāvena.meaning_2: state of being dull; dullness; immaturity; youthfulness
mandībhāvena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular in the text (mandībhāvena), glossed by the commentary as taruṇatāya "due to youthfulness". The i is lengthened before bhāva.
mandībhāvena.translation_1: ‘From immaturity’ means due to dullness, due to youthfulness.

sandhātuṃ.meaning_2: to reconcile; to make friends (with); to restore (friendship); to connect
sandhātuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -tuṃ of sandahati. The sandhi in the second sentence (sakhiñca mittañcāti) belongs to a quotation, not to this word. Both sentences have arahati, 'is worthy to ...'.
sandhātuṃ.example_1: Sayaṃ sandhātumarahatīti tesu akhamāpentesupi ‘‘ ehi, bhadramukha, uddesaṃ gaṇha, aṭṭhakathaṃ suṇa, bhāvanamanuyuñja, kasmā paribāhiro hosī ’’ ti evaṃ sayaṃ sandhātuṃ arahati mittabhāvaṃ ghaṭeti, eso evarūpo mettāvihārī uttaritaro mittabhārassa mittadhurassa ca vahanato ‘‘ bhāravaho ’’ti ‘‘ dhuraddharo ’’ti ca saṅkhaṃ gacchatīti.
sandhātuṃ.translation_1: ‘Who is worthy to reconcile himself’ means that even among those not asking for forgiveness, he is worthy to reconcile himself (by saying), “Come, dear boy, take up recitation, listen to the commentary, devote yourself to meditation, why are you deprived (of the Dhamma)?” In this way, he himself forms friendship. Such a one, dwelling in loving-kindness, is superior, and because he bears the burden of friendship and the yoke of friendship, he is called ‘bearer of the burden’ and ‘carrier of the yoke’.”
sandhātuṃ.example_2: Sakhiñca mittañcāti sakhibhāvañca mittabhāvañca tathārūpena kulajātena tittena akapaṇena amaccharinā saddhiṃ paṇḍito sandhātuṃ puna ghaṭetuṃ arahati, tayā pana kapaṇena ahituṇḍikena saddhiṃ ko mittabhāvaṃ puna ghaṭetunti attho.
sandhātuṃ.translation_2: 'Friendship and alliance' means that a wise one is worthy to form friendship and camaraderie, and to restore it again, with a high-born person who is content, not wretched, and ungrudging. But with you, the wretched snake-charmer, who would restore friendship again? – that is the meaning.

kujjhitukāmā.meaning_2: desiring to be angry; wanting to get angry
kujjhitukāmā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive kujjhituṃ (from kujjhati) + kāma. Nominative plural in the text, agreeing with tumhe.
kujjhitukāmā.example_1: Tasmiṃ gate senāpati bodhisattassa sarīrato lohitaṃ puñchitvā hatthapādakaṇṇanāsakoṭiyo sāṭakakaṇṇe katvā bodhisattaṃ saṇikaṃ nisīdāpetvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā ‘‘ sace, bhante, tumhe kujjhitukāmā, tumhesu katāparādhassa raññova kujjheyyātha, mā aññesan ’’ ti yācanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –
kujjhitukāmā.translation_1: When that [king] was gone, the commander-in-chief wiped off the blood from the Bodhisatta’s body, and using a corner of his garment for the extremities of his hands, feet, ears, and nose, he gently seated the Bodhisatta. Having venerated him, and sitting to one side, he requested, saying, “Venerable sir, if you are desirous of being angry, you should be angry only with the king who committed an offense against you, not with others.” Thus requesting, he uttered the first verse:

manujesvapekkhiya.meaning_2: having looked upon (the unstable pleasure and pain) among human beings
manujesvapekkhiya.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the locative plural manujesu and the absolutive apekkhiya (from apekkhati, 'having regarded'). Here manujesu depends on apekkhiya: 'having regarded ... among human beings'.
manujesvapekkhiya.translation_1: 67. Having regarded pleasure and pain among human beings as thus unstable and unestablished—

gañchi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular of gacchati in the text, taking the destination in the accusative (gehaṃ gañchi = went to the house).
gañchi.example_1: So taṃ gahetvā nagaraguttikassa gehaṃ gañchi.
gañchi.translation_1: He, taking it, went to the city guard’s house.

gītakaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Diminutive of gīta (sung; song). Accusative singular in all three sentences (imaṃ gītakaṃ, ekaṃ naṃ gītakaṃ, tava gītakaṃ).
gītakaṃ.example_1: Te tattha samajjaṃ karontā paṭhamameva imaṃ gītakaṃ gāyiṃsu –
gītakaṃ.translation_1: They, making a gathering there, first of all sang this song—
gītakaṃ.example_2: Athassa bhariyā cintesi ‘‘ mayhaṃ sāmiko idāni marissati, ekaṃ naṃ gītakaṃ yācitvā parisamajjhe taṃ gāyantī jīvikaṃ kappessāmī ’’ ti cintetvā ‘‘ sāmi, tvaṃ udake nimujjasi, ekaṃ me gītakaṃ dehi, tena jīvikaṃ kappessāmī ’’ ti vatvā gāthamāha –
gītakaṃ.translation_2: Then his wife thought, ‘My husband will die now. Having entreated him for a song, I will make a livelihood by singing that in the midst of an assembly.’ Having thought this, she said, ‘My lord, you are sinking in the water. Give me one song, and I will make a livelihood by it!’ Having said this, she uttered the verse:

cajituṃ.meaning_2: to give up; to abandon; to let go
cajituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -tuṃ from the root √caj; used with sakkuṇeyya ('able') in the sentence.
cajituṃ.example_1: Tattha succajaṃ vatāti sukhena cajituṃ sakkuṇeyyampi na caji.
cajituṃ.translation_1: Regarding this, succajaṃ vata means ‘he did not give up even what could be given up easily’.

sabbissariyamadāsi.meaning_2: all sovereignty; overlordship of everything; supreme power
sabbissariyamadāsi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text sabbissariyamadāsi is a compound verb: sabbissariyaṃ + adāsi, 'gave (her) all sovereignty'. Compound of sabba + issariya, joined by sandhi.
sabbissariyamadāsi.example_1: Rājā tassa vacanena deviyā guṇaṃ saritvā ‘‘ paṇḍita, tava kathāyāhaṃ deviyā guṇaṃ anussarin ’’ ti vatvā tassā sabbissariyamadāsi.
sabbissariyamadāsi.translation_1: The king, remembering the queen’s virtues by his words, said, “Wise man, by your words I recollected the queen’s virtues,” and having said this, he gave her full sovereignty.

sarāpitoti.meaning_2: causes to remember; reminds; makes recollect
sarāpitoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form in the text is sarāpitoti = sarāpito + iti, a past participle (pp of sarāpeti, 'reminded; caused to remember'), nominative singular masculine. The headword here is the causative verb.

aditvā.meaning_2: not having seen; not seeing; not having found
aditvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Negative absolutive of dassati (√dis 1). In the text aditvā means 'not seeing' or 'not finding'; adi- is a sandhi of na + di-. Used of water, meat, and a person.
aditvā.example_1: Thero ‘ nhāyissāmī ’’ ti tena saddhiṃyeva āgantvā koṭṭhake udakaṃ aditvā ‘‘ kahaṃ udakan ’’ ti pucchi.
aditvā.translation_1: The Elder, (thinking) ‘I will take a bath,’ came together with him. Not finding water in the storage room, he asked, ‘Where is the water?’
aditvā.example_2: Bhattakārako taṃ maṃsaṃ aditvā kahāpaṇamuṭṭhiṃ ādāya carantopi maṃsaṃ uppādetuṃ asakkonto ‘‘ sace amaṃsakabhattaṃ upanāmessāmi, jīvitaṃ me natthi, kiṃ nu kho karissāmī ’’ ti cintetvā ‘‘ attheso upāyo ’’ ti vikāle āmakasusānaṃ gantvā muhuttamatassa purisassa ūrumaṃsaṃ āharitvā supakkaṃ pacitvā bhattaṃ upanāmesi.
aditvā.translation_2: The cook, not finding that meat, and being unable to procure meat even after taking a handful of coins and going around, thought, “If I offer a meal without meat, my life is forfeit. What indeed shall I do?” But then thinking, “There is a way,” in the evening he went to an open-air cemetery. Having brought the thigh-flesh of a man who had just died a short while ago, he cooked it well and offered the meal.

uḷuṅkasaddakotveva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Likely a sandhi of uḷuṅkasaddako (nominative singular; the cry of an uḷuṅka, an unknown bird) with iti eva, with -o dropped before i-. No sentences were supplied, so the segmentation and meaning are uncertain; the compound is probably uḷuṅka + sadda, with -ka.

sīliyanti.meaning_2: is virtuous; conducts oneself well; observes moral conduct
sīliyanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] 3rd person plural present of a causative/denominative verb from sīla. The reading is uncertain; sīlenti is the expected causative form. Could also be a denominative in -iya. No sentence context available.

paṭirodati.meaning_2: weeps in return; cries back; weeps in response
paṭirodati.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The prefix pati- becomes paṭi- before r. The commentary explains it as the answer to another's weeping: 'natthī' ti vadanto paṭirodati nāma. Present 3rd singular in the text.
paṭirodati.example_1: So ekadivasaṃ rājānaṃ uyyānaṃ āgantvā vanditvā nisinnaṃ disvā ‘‘ upāhanañca chattañca yācissāmī ’’ ti cintetvā puna cintesi ‘‘ paraṃ ‘ imaṃ nāma dehī ’ ti yācanto rodati nāma, paropi ‘ natthī ’ ti vadanto paṭirodati nāma,‘ mā kho pana maṃ rodantaṃ mahājano addasa, mā rājānan ’’ ti raho paṭicchannaṭṭhāne ubhopi roditvā tuṇhī bhavissāmā ’’ ti.
paṭirodati.translation_1: One day, he came to the royal park, and seeing the king seated, he venerated him and thought, “I will ask for a pair of sandals and an umbrella.” Then he thought again, “Indeed, when one requests, saying, ‘Give me this or that,’ one weeps, and the other, when refusing, saying, ‘There is none,’ weeps in return. Let not the great mass of people see me weeping, nor the king. We both will weep in a secret, private place, and then become silent.”
paṭirodati.example_2: ‘‘ Mahārāja,‘ imaṃ nāma me dehī ’ ti yācanto rodati nāma,‘ natthī ’ ti vadanto paṭirodati nāma.
paṭirodati.translation_2: “Great King, when one requests, saying, ‘Give me this or that,’ one weeps, and when one refuses, saying, ‘There is none,’ one weeps in return.

roditapaṭiroditaṃ.meaning_2: mutual weeping; weeping and wailing; crying back and forth
roditapaṭiroditaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is accusative singular agreeing with taṃ. Probably a dvanda compound of rodita and paṭirodita, used idiomatically for mutual weeping.
roditapaṭiroditaṃ.example_1: ‘ Sace tvaṃ mayā yācito na dadeyyāsi, taṃ no roditapaṭiroditaṃ nāma mahājano mā passatū ’ ti etadatthaṃ raho paccāsīsāmī ’’ ti vatvā ādito tisso gāthā abhāsi –
roditapaṭiroditaṃ.translation_1: ‘If you, having been requested by me, were not to give it, may the great mass of people not see that mutual weeping of ours.’ For this reason, I wished to speak privately.” Having said this, he declared these three verses from the beginning.

paṭirodanaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominal compound of paṭi + rodana (weeping). The text defines it as one who refuses a request. Nominative singular in the sentence.
paṭirodanaṃ.translation_1: and whoever refuses a request—that they call counter-weeping.”

paṭirodantaṃ.meaning_2: weeping in response; crying back; crying against
paṭirodantaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text, agreeing with an implied object; the quotation mark after raho suggests verse. Sometimes analysed as pati + rudanta.
paṭirodantaṃ.example_1: Tuvaṃ vā paṭirodantaṃ, tasmā icchāmahaṃ raho ’’ ti.
paṭirodantaṃ.translation_1: nor you counter-weeping. Therefore, I wish to be in private.”

paṭirodananti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Form is uncertain; possibly 3rd plural present or part of a sandhi. The related noun paṭirodana means crying in response.

ahāliddaṃ.meaning_2: not like turmeric dye; fast; lasting; not fickle
ahāliddaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is neuter nominative singular agreeing with cittaṃ. The commentator explains it as 'not fading quickly like turmeric dye', i.e. firm. The PEU gives it as a ti adjective.
ahāliddaṃ.example_1: 103. ‘‘ Yassa cittaṃ ahāliddaṃ, saddhā ca avirāginī;
ahāliddaṃ.translation_1: 103. “The one whose mind is not fickle, and whose faith is not transient;
ahāliddaṃ.example_2: Tassattho – yassa puggalassa cittaṃ ahāliddaṃ haliddirāgo viya khippaṃ na virajjati, thirameva hoti.
ahāliddaṃ.translation_2: Its meaning is: For the person whose mind is not fickle (ahāliddaṃ), meaning it does not become dispassionate quickly like a turmeric stain, but is indeed firm.

samuddāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Plural here (satta samuddāni), the object of atari and atikkamitvā. The PEU entry samuddānita is a different word and not relevant.
samuddāni.example_1: Kathaṃ satta samuddāni, kathaṃ simbalimāruhī ’’ ti.
samuddāni.translation_1: How did you cross the seven oceans? How did you climb the Simbali tree?”
