samuddāni.example_2: Tassattho – tvaṃ imaṃ jambudīpasamuddaṃ tassa parato kepukaṃ nāma nadiṃ pabbatantaresu ṭhitāni satta samuddāni ca kathaṃ atari, kenupāyena tiṇṇo satta samuddāni atikkamitvā ṭhitaṃ amhākaṃ bhavanaṃ simbalirukkhañca kathaṃ āruhīti.
samuddāni.translation_2: The meaning of that is: “How did you cross this ocean of Jambudīpa, the river called Kepuka on that side of it, and the seven oceans situated between mountains? By what means did you overcome them? How did you climb the Simbali tree, our abode, which is situated beyond the seven oceans?”

sammillahāsinītissā.meaning_2: of Tissā, the smiling girl; of smiling Tissā
sammillahāsinītissā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Probably a sandhi of sammillahāsinī (smiling, laughing; fem. of sammillahāsin) with the name Tissā, in the genitive or as the first member of a name compound. No sentence is available; the analysis is uncertain.

sammillahāsinī.grammar: fem, comp, name of a person
sammillahāsinī.meaning_2: name of a girl; Samillahāsinī; (perhaps) she who smiles gently when speaking
sammillahāsinī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a brahmin's daughter, later identified with Rāhula's mother. The reading varies between sammillahāsinī and sammillabhāsinī in the texts; the second element is uncertain (perhaps hāsinī 'smiling' or bhāsinī 'speaking'). Nominative singular in the sentences.
sammillahāsinī.example_1: Tasmiṃ pana kāle eko puññavā satto brahmalokato cavitvā kāsiraṭṭheyeva nigamagāme asītikoṭivibhavassa brāhmaṇassa gehe kumārikā hutvā nibbatti,‘‘ sammillahāsinī ’’ tissā nāmaṃ akaṃsu.
sammillahāsinī.translation_1: But at that time, a certain meritorious being, having descended from the Brahma-world, was reborn as a girl in the house of a brahmin with eighty crores of wealth, in a market-town village within the Kasi kingdom. They called her Sammillabhāsinī (sammillahāsinī).
sammillahāsinī.example_2: Tattha manussā taṃ disvā ‘‘ asukabrāhmaṇassa dhītā sammillahāsinī kiṃkāraṇā idha ṭhitā ’’ ti āhaṃsu.
sammillahāsinī.translation_2: There, the people, on seeing it, said, “For what reason is Sammillabhāsinī, the daughter of such-and-such a brahmin, standing here?”

sammillahāsiniyā.meaning_2: Sammillahāsinī; name of a princess who speaks with a smile
sammillahāsiniyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of a princess, the Bodhisatta's wife. Instrumental singular in the text. The commentary glosses milla as 'smiling' (Millamocane), so the name means 'she who speaks with a smile'.
sammillahāsiniyā.example_1: Bodhisattassa ca sammillahāsiniyā ca ubhinnampi anicchantānaññeva maṅgalaṃ kariṃsu.
sammillahāsiniyā.translation_1: And they performed the wedding ceremony for both the Bodhisatta and Sammillabhāsinī, though both were unwilling.

brāhmāno.meaning_2: brahmin; a member of the priestly caste
brāhmāno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text reads brāhmāno, a rare spelling of brāhmaṇo, nominative plural here (dve brāhmāno viya). Normally brāhmaṇā in the plural; the -āno ending may be a scribal variant or archaic form.
brāhmāno.example_1: Te ekagabbhe vasamānā ekasmiṃ sayane sayantāpi na aññamaññaṃ kilesavasena olokayiṃsu, dve bhikkhū dve brāhmāno viya ca ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vasiṃsu.
brāhmāno.translation_1: Dwelling in the same room and even sleeping on the same bed, they did not look at one another with thoughts due to defilements. They dwelt in one place like two monks or two brahmins.

byāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] 3rd singular present of byāti; used absolutely with nimisati in the sense of blinking.
byāti.example_1: Yāva byāti nimisati, tatrāpi rasatī vayo.
byāti.translation_1: even in the time of a blink, one’s youth wanes.”

mekantipi.meaning_2: not even; not so much as; don't (with quotation)
mekantipi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of mā, iti and pi; the -e- replaces the -ā + i contraction. No sentences were supplied, so the exact nuance is uncertain and the analysis is provisional.

byātīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form adds the quotative -iti; the entry is for the verb byāti. The given analysis suggests prefix byā + root a + ti, but the root is uncertain.

tirīṭino.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Genitive/dative singular in the first sentence, commenting on tirīṭino in the verse; the gloss tirīṭavatthanivatthassa equates it with wearing tirīṭa-cloth. The form is a possessive adjective from tirīṭa (bark-cloth).
tirīṭino.translation_1: When you, with sword belted on, in armour clad and wearing bark-cloth,
tirīṭino.translation_2: “Wearing bark-cloth” (tirīṭino) means wearing bark-cloth at the time of traveling on the path.

tirīṭinoti.meaning_2: with a fragrant bark garland; wearing tirīṭi blossoms
tirīṭinoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Unclear form: likely an instrumental of tirīṭin 'having tirīṭi bark' (tirīṭi + -in suffix), with -ti perhaps a sandhi or grammatical ending. No occurrences found in the canon; possibly a scribal variant.

cīdha.meaning_2: whoever here; whoever in this world
cīdha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of ci (interrogative/relative particle) + idha. Occurs in verse (Jātaka 140, etc.). Sometimes analysed as yo ci idha.
cīdha.example_1: 140. ‘‘ Yo cīdha kammaṃ kurute pamāya, thāmabbalaṃ attani saṃviditvā;
cīdha.translation_1: “But the one who does his work here after measuring, having understood the power and strength within himself,
cīdha.example_2: Yo cīdha tacchaṃ paviceyya gaṇhati, sa ve naro seṭṭhamupeti ṭhānan ’’ ti.
cīdha.translation_2: The person who examines and takes what is accurate here reaches the highest state.”

saṃviditvā.meaning_2: having known well; having understood; having perceived
saṃviditvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā of saṃvidati; the commentary glosses it as understanding or knowing fully. Both occurrences are locative constructions (attani, jīvitaṃ) meaning 'having understood'.
saṃviditvā.example_1: 140. ‘‘ Yo cīdha kammaṃ kurute pamāya, thāmabbalaṃ attani saṃviditvā;
saṃviditvā.translation_1: “But the one who does his work here after measuring, having understood the power and strength within himself,
saṃviditvā.example_2: So ittaraṃ jīvitaṃ saṃviditvā, asassataṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ.
saṃviditvā.translation_2: he, having understood that life is ephemeral, not eternal, and subject to change,

parikkhavā.meaning_2: discerning; endowed with discernment; possessing the requisite equipment
parikkhavā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Formed from parikkhā (discernment; requisite) + vant. The commentary glosses it as parikkhāsampanno, 'endowed with discernment'. In the text it is nominative singular used in a verse; the -vā is the regular -vantu ending.
parikkhavā.example_1: Jappena mantena subhāsitena, parikkhavā so vipulaṃ jinātī ’’ ti.
parikkhavā.translation_1: By chanting, by consultation, and by well-spoken words, being discerning, he wins abundance.”

pīṭhamadāyimhāti.meaning_2: we did not give you a seat, thus; 'we gave you no seat', iti
pīṭhamadāyimhāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of pīṭhaṃ + adāyimhā + iti (with -ṃ assimilated to -m- before the vowel). The quoted words form the title of a story in the Jātaka commentary; the whole phrase is the citation form in the sentence.
pīṭhamadāyimhāti.example_1: Na te pīṭhamadāyimhāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi.
pīṭhamadāyimhāti.translation_1: The Teacher, while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, spoke this, beginning with “We offered thee no seat” (Na te pīṭhamadāyimhā), referring to a certain bhikkhu.

nevābhisajjāmi.meaning_2: not attached; not obsessed; one does not cling
nevābhisajjāmi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of na + eva + abhisajjāmi (√saj, present 1st singular). The PEU analysis reads neva + abhi + sajja + a + mi. See abhisajjati.
nevābhisajjāmi.example_1: 146. ‘‘ Nevābhisajjāmi na cāpi kuppe, na cāpi me appiyamāsi kiñci;
nevābhisajjāmi.translation_1: 146. “I am not attached, nor do I become angry, nor was anything unpleasant to me;

nevābhisajjāmīti.grammar: pr, neg of abhisajjati; sandhi with na
nevābhisajjāmīti.meaning_2: does not cling (to); is not obsessed (with); is not attached
nevābhisajjāmīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of na + eva + abhisajjāmi, ending -iti. The DPD entry should perhaps be for abhisajjati; here the negative form is given as it appears.

phālāpetvā.meaning_2: causes to split; causes to be cut open; has (something) opened
phālāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive (gerund) of the causative phālāpeti, used here with satthena: 'having had (his knee) cut open with a knife'. From √phal 1 in the sense of splitting; the PEU spelling phala is a variant.
phālāpetvā.example_1: Rājā ‘‘ sace mama putto maṃ māretvā rajjaṃ gaṇhissati, ko ettha doso ’’ ti dakkhiṇajāṇuṃ satthena phālāpetvā lohitaṃ suvaṇṇataṭṭakena gāhāpetvā deviyā pāyesi.
phālāpetvā.translation_1: The king [thought], “If my son will kill me and seize the kingdom, what fault is there in that?” Having caused his right knee to be opened with a scalpel, and having caused the blood to be collected in a golden dish, he gave it to the queen to drink.

nikaṇṇikavasena.meaning_2: by way of whispering; in a whisper; secretly
nikaṇṇikavasena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Adverbial phrase in -vasena meaning 'by way of whispering / secretly'. In the text it describes the ministers conspiring in the park. The word before it, 'mantayamānā', supports the sense of whispered consultation.
nikaṇṇikavasena.example_1: Te tato paṭṭhāya uyyāne paṭicchannā hutvā nikaṇṇikavasena mantayamānā ‘‘ attheko upāyo, khaggaṃ sannayhitvā mahāupaṭṭhānaṃ gatakāle amaccānaṃ antare ṭhatvā rañño pamattabhāvaṃ ñatvā khaggena paharitvā māretuṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti vavatthapesuṃ.
nikaṇṇikavasena.translation_1: From then on, they, having concealed themselves in the park, consulting with each other by way of whispering, decided, “There is one means: having girded on a sword, when it is time to go to the great assembly, having stood amongst the ministers, and having known the king’s heedlessness, it is proper to kill him by striking with the sword.”

nikaṇṇikā.meaning_2: whispering; speaking into the ear; private counsel
nikaṇṇikā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is nominative singular. The commentary glosses it as kaṇṇamūle mantanā, counsel at the ear, i.e. secret whispering.
nikaṇṇikā.example_1: 150. ‘‘ Yā mantanā araññasmiṃ, yā ca gāme nikaṇṇikā;
nikaṇṇikā.translation_1: 150. “The counsel in the forest wilderness, and the whispering in the village;

cīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is a quotative word (iti cīti ca). Perhaps a contamination of iti and cintā or a Sanskritising citi; not in PEU. Stands as the object of karaṇaṃ.
cīti.example_1: Yañcetaṃ iti cīti ca, etampi viditaṃ mayā ’’ ti.
cīti.translation_1: And this scheming of yours—this too is known to me.”
cīti.example_2: Yañcetaṃ iti cīti cāti yañca etaṃ idāni mama paharaṇokāsapariyesanaṃ.
cīti.translation_2: And this scheming of yours (yañcetaṃ iti cīti ca) means, “and this current searching for an opportunity to strike me.”

nikaṇṇikāti.meaning_2: near the ear; at the ear
nikaṇṇikāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form is nikaṇṇikāti = nikaṇṇikā + iti, so the entry is for the main word nikaṇṇika. The PEU adds a sense of whispering or discussion at someone's ear; nikaṇṇika here is feminine (nikaṇṇikā) and possibly a noun in that sense. Cf. kaṇṇika.

uppāṭāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to be pulled out; having had extracted; having caused to be plucked out
uppāṭāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of uppāṭāpeti (causative of uppāṭeti, 'causes to be pulled out'). In the text used of having fruit and eyes extracted.
uppāṭāpetvā.example_1: Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā araññe jāto makkaṭo attano yūthapariharaṇaṃ āsaṅkanto taruṇassa makkaṭapotakassa dantehi phalaṃ chinditvā purisabhāvaṃ nāseti, tathā tava atirajjakāmassa phalāni uppāṭāpetvā purisabhāvaṃ nāsessāmīti.
uppāṭāpetvā.translation_1: This means: “Just as a monkey born in the wilderness, fearing for the maintenance of his own troop, having cut off the fruit (testicles) of a young monkey son with its teeth, destroys its manhood; so too, you who are excessively desirous of the kingdom, I will cause your ‘fruits’ (testicles) to be extracted and will destroy your manhood.”
uppāṭāpetvā.example_2: Na kevalañca idāneva, pubbepesa khattiyasahassānaṃ akkhīni uppāṭāpetvā māretvā tesaṃ maṃsena balikammaṃ kāresī ’’ ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.
uppāṭāpetvā.translation_2: And not only now, but in the past too he had the eyes of a thousand khattiyas extracted, killed them, and had an offering made with their flesh.” Having said this, he recounted a story of the past.

pavesāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to enter; having put (into); having had (him) put (in)
pavesāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of pavesāpeti, from the causative base of pa + √vis. In the text it takes bandhanāgāraṃ as its object: 'having had (him) put into the prison house'. The double causative force matches bandhāpetvā before it.
pavesāpetvā.example_1: Rājā ‘‘ na mayhaṃ koci kammaṃ jānātīti tvaṃ cintesī ’’ ti taṃ tajjetvā saṅkhalikabandhanena bandhāpetvā bandhanāgāraṃ pavesāpetvā ārakkhaṃ ṭhapesi.
pavesāpetvā.translation_1: The king, rebuking him, “You thought, ‘No one knows my actions,’ ” had him bound with chains and put into the prison house, and placed a guard over him.

nuppajjatī.meaning_2: does not arise; does not appear; is not born
nuppajjatī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of na + uppajjati (na + u > nu). Third person singular present in the text; -ī is a metrical lengthening before buddho.
nuppajjatī.translation_1: 155. Until the Buddha, the Dhamma-king, the light-bringer, arises,

pamussituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of pamussati in the text, used with na icchāmi: 'I do not wish to forget/neglect giving'. Formed with -tuṃ; the double -ss- is from the √mus with the ya sign.
pamussituṃ.example_1: Adadanto hi dānaṃ pamajjati nāma na sarati na sallakkheti, ahaṃ pana jīvamāno dānaṃ pamussituṃ na icchāmi, tasmā dānaṃ dassāmiyevāti dīpeti.
pamussituṃ.translation_1: Indeed, one who does not give is called negligent, does not remember, does not reflect. But I, while living, do not wish to neglect giving. Therefore, I will indeed give gifts—this is what it declares.

nimujjāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to plunge; having caused to sink; having drowned; having submerged
nimujjāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of nimujjāpeti; takes an object (the thing made to sink), as kapiṃ and nāvaṃ in the sentences.
nimujjāpetvā.example_1: So ‘‘ taṃ kapiṃ udake nimujjāpetvā māretvā hadayamaṃsaṃ gahetvā saṃsumāriyā dassāmī ’’ ti cintetvā mahāsattaṃ āha –
nimujjāpetvā.translation_1: He, having thought, “I will cause that monkey to plunge into the water and kill him, and having taken his heart-meat, I will give it to the female crocodile,” spoke to the Great Being.
nimujjāpetvā.example_2: Bodhisatto anantaragāthāya tassa nāmaṃ ācikkhitvā ‘‘ tātā, imaṃ balavāmukhasamuddaṃ patvā nivattituṃ samatthā nāvā nāma natthi, ayaṃ sampattanāvaṃ nimujjāpetvā vināsaṃ pāpetī ’’ ti āha.
nimujjāpetvā.translation_2: The Bodhisatta, having declared its name with the following verse, said: “Friends, once a ship has reached this Valabhāmukha Sea, there is no ship capable of returning. This Valabhāmukha Sea sinks the arriving ship and causes it to perish.”

alametehi.meaning_2: enough with these; away with these
alametehi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of alaṃ (enough) with the instrumental plural demonstrative etehi; the whole phrase means "enough with these …". Verse context, so the metre requires the sandhi.
alametehi.translation_1: Enough with these mangoes, rose-apples, and jackfruits;
alametehi.example_2: Alametehi ambehi, jambūhi panasehi cā ’’ ti.(jā.1.2.115)–
alametehi.translation_2: ‘Enough with these mangoes, rose-apples, and jackfruits!’”

murāmurāpetvā.meaning_2: having made a crunching sound; having gnashed; having munched noisily
murāmurāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The word is a reduplicative onomatopoeic formation, probably a causative absolutive from a sound-imitative base (murāmurā), not a standard root. Appears in the tiger-eating-children story in the Jātaka commentary; no finite verb is attested in the corpus for this form.
murāmurāpetvā.example_1: Sāpi sakuṇikā tehi saddhiṃ gantvā ‘‘ yathā imehi mama puttakā māritā, tatheva ne karissāmī ’’ ti te dārake gahetvā byagghassa pādamūle khipi, byaggho murāmurāpetvā khādi.
murāmurāpetvā.translation_1: She also, having gone with them, thinking, “Just as these (children) killed my young ones, I will do the same to them,” took those children and threw them at the tiger’s feet. The tiger, crunching them noisily, ate them.

kuntinī.meaning_2: type of bird; Sarus crane; female of the kunti bird
kuntinī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it refers to a female bird kept at the royal palace; nominative singular.
kuntinī.example_1: Taṃ kāraṇaṃ sutvā bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ ‘‘ āvuso, rājakule kira asukā nāma kuntinī sakuṇikā ye hissā potakā māritā, te dārake byagghassa pādamūle khipitvā himavantameva gatā ’’ ti.
kuntinī.translation_1: Hearing that matter, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: “Friends, they say that a Kuntinī bird named So-and-so in the royal palace, whose young ones were killed, having thrown those children at the tiger’s feet, went to the Himalayas itself.”
kuntinī.example_2: Tassa nivesane ekā kuntinī sakuṇikā dūteyyahārikāti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva.
kuntinī.translation_2: In his residence, a Kuntinī bird was a messenger—all was just the same as before.

paṭikibbise.meaning_2: retaliatory wrongdoing; harm done in return; counter-wickedness
paṭikibbise.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the verses it is written paṭikibbise, which can be read as locative singular ("in retaliatory harm") or as a sandhi-contracted form of paṭikibbisaṃ. The commentary glosses it with paṭikate, so the sense is harm done back to one who has harmed.
paṭikibbise.example_1: 166. ‘‘ Yo ve kate paṭikate, kibbise paṭikibbise;
paṭikibbise.translation_1: “Whoever indeed, for harm done, does retaliatory harm,
paṭikibbise.example_2: Tassattho – yo puggalo parena kate kibbise attano puttamāraṇādike dāruṇe kamme kate puna attano tassa puggalassa paṭikate paṭikibbise ‘‘ paṭikataṃ mayā tassā ’’ ti jānāti.
paṭikibbise.translation_2: Its meaning is: whatever person, when a cruel wicked deed such as the killing of one's own child has been committed by another, and one then commits a retaliatory wicked deed against that person, knows, “I have retaliated against her.”

kuntini.meaning_2: name of a female crane; Kuntinī
kuntini.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Vocative singular in the text, addressed in a verse quoted in the commentary. Name of a bird (sarus crane), used as a form of address.
kuntini.example_1: Evaṃ taṃ sammatī veraṃ, vasa kuntini māgamā ’’ ti.
kuntini.translation_1: in this way that enmity is appeased. Dwell, Kuntinī, do not go!”
kuntini.example_2: Evaṃ taṃ sammatī veranti ettakena taṃ veraṃ sammati vūpasantaṃ hoti, tasmā vasa kuntini māgamāti.
kuntini.translation_2: Evaṃ taṃ sammatī veraṃ means, 'by so much, that enmity is appeased and quelled. Therefore, dwell, Kuntinī, do not go!'

māgamāti.meaning_2: do not go; do not come
māgamāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the prohibitive particle mā with āgamāti (ā + gamāti, 3rd singular of āgamati, 'comes; goes'). In the text māgamāti is addressed to Kuntinī: 'do not go!' or 'do not come!'
māgamāti.example_1: Evaṃ taṃ sammatī veranti ettakena taṃ veraṃ sammati vūpasantaṃ hoti, tasmā vasa kuntini māgamāti.
māgamāti.translation_1: Evaṃ taṃ sammatī veraṃ means, 'by so much, that enmity is appeased and quelled. Therefore, dwell, Kuntinī, do not go!'
māgamāti.example_2: Dhīrānañhi metti bhinnāpi puna ghaṭīyati, bālānaṃ pana sakiṃ bhinnā bhinnāva hoti, tasmā vasa kuntini māgamāti.
māgamāti.translation_2: Indeed, the friendship of the wise, even if broken, is reconciled again. But for the foolish, once broken, it remains broken. Therefore, Kuntinī, do not go, but stay!”

upapīḷitassa.root_base: upa + pīḷ + a > upapīḷe (caus); upapīḷe + ta
upapīḷitassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Past participle used as an adjective qualifying puggalassa (genitive singular in the text). The prefix upa- intensifies pīḷita.
upapīḷitassa.example_1: Tattha na katassa ca kattā cāti katassa ca abhibhūtassa upapīḷitassa puggalassa, idāni vibhattivipariṇāmaṃ katvā yo kattā tassa cāti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ puggalānaṃ puna mittabhāvo nāma na sandhīyati na ghaṭīyatīti attho.
upapīḷitassa.translation_1: Therein, na katassa ca kattā ca: the meaning is that friendship between the one who was harmed (the overwhelmed, oppressed person) and the one who committed the harm (the perpetrator) indeed is not mended again, nor is it reconciled.

vilumbite.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Formed from √lup with the vi- prefix and the *a sign; variant stem of vilumpita (√lup with the *a sign). Locative plural agreeing with corehi in the text: 'as if plundered by thieves'.
vilumbite.example_1: Tadā sakko devarājā ‘‘ ke nu kho loke mātāpitaro upaṭṭhahanti, kule jeṭṭhāpacayanakammaṃ karonti, dānaṃ denti, sīlaṃ rakkhanti, uposathakammaṃ karonti, ke pabbajitā samaṇadhamme yuttapayuttā viharanti, ke anācāraṃ carantī ’’ ti lokaṃ volokento imaṃ ambagopakaṃ anācāraṃ kūṭajaṭilaṃ disvā ‘‘ ayaṃ kūṭajaṭilo kasiṇaparikammādiṃ attano samaṇadhammaṃ pahāya ambavanaṃ rakkhanto vicarati, saṃvejessāmi nan ’’ ti tassa gāmaṃ bhikkhāya paviṭṭhakāle attano ānubhāvena ambe pātetvā corehi vilumbite viya akāsi.
vilumbite.translation_1: Then Sakka, king of the gods, surveying the world, thought, “Who, I wonder, in the world supports their mothers and fathers, performs the act of honoring elders in the family, gives gifts, keeps ethical conduct, performs Uposatha observance? Who among those gone forth abide diligently practicing the qualities of recluses? Who behave ill-behaved?” And seeing this ill-behaved mango-watcher, the matted-hair cheat, he thought, “This matted-hair cheat, having abandoned his own monk’s life, such as kasiṇa meditation practice and so on, dwells watching the mango grove. I will agitate him.” So, at the time he entered the village for alms, Sakka, by his own power, made the mangoes fall and made it seem as if they had been plundered by thieves.

palibuddhi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] From palibuddhati (pari + √budh), 'to obstruct, harass'. Aorist 3rd singular; the commentary glosses it as stopping the boys.
palibuddhi.example_1: Kūṭajaṭilo tā disvā ‘‘ tumhehi me ambāni khāditānī ’’ ti palibuddhi.
palibuddhi.translation_1: The matted-hair cheat, seeing them, stopped them and said, “My mangoes have been eaten by you.”

maṇḍayati.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the verse nīliyaṃ maṇḍayati means 'dyes the hair dye' i.e. applies dark dye to grey hair; the prose gloss explains nīlaphalādīni yojetvā kataṃ nīliyaṃ maṇḍayati. 3rd singular present.
maṇḍayati.translation_1: 169. “Whoever dyes his hair, is tormented with tweezers;
maṇḍayati.example_2: Tassattho – yo puriso palitānaṃ kāḷavaṇṇakaraṇatthāya nīlaphalādīni yojetvā kataṃ nīliyaṃ maṇḍayati, nīlakesantare ca uṭṭhitaṃ palitaṃ uddharanto saṇḍāsena vihaññati kilamati, tassa evarūpassa mahallakassa sā vasaṃ anvetu, tathārūpaṃ patiṃ labhatu, yā te ambe avāharīti.
maṇḍayati.translation_2: Its meaning is: “She who carried away your mangoes, desiring a husband, having become a woman going to a tryst for the purpose of going to meet him, alone and without a second, let her go a long journey, a distance of one or two leagues. And even having gone there, at that trysting place where it was appointed, saying, ‘You should come to such and such a place,’ may she not find that husband.”

pacalaka.meaning_2: waddler; totterer; one who sways or staggers
pacalaka.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Used as a vocative term of address in the Jātaka prose; probably a nickname mocking the person's unsteady gait. The reading pacalaka may also be analysed as pa + cala + ka ("swayer").
pacalaka.example_1: Kathaṃ karosi pacalaka, evaṃ dandhaparakkamo ’’ ti.
pacalaka.translation_1: How will you manage, waddler, so slow in your striving?”

pacalakoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Unidentified. Not found in the sentences supplied and not in any dictionary entry given; the PEU entry pacalaka (a personal name, perhaps pa + cala + ka) may be related, but there is no evidence for the final -ti here. Possibly a proper name or an error in the text; needs checking against the Jātaka passage.

brāmhaṇakule.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Form with br- is a common orthographic variant of brāhmaṇakula. Locative singular in the text.
brāmhaṇakule.example_1: Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe brāmhaṇakule nibbatti,‘‘ kappakumāro ’’ tissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu.
brāmhaṇakule.translation_1: In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling the kingdom in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born in a brahmin family in the Kasi kingdom; they gave him the name “Prince Kappa.”

ohiyi.meaning_2: remains behind; stays behind; is left behind
ohiyi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular of ohīyati, the passive of ava + √hā 1; here active in sense, 'he stayed behind'. The text has ohiyi with a short i.
ohiyi.example_1: So ‘‘ sādhū ’’ ti jeṭṭhantevāsikena saddhiṃ te himavantaṃ pesetvā sayaṃ ekakova ohiyi.
ohiyi.translation_1: He said, “Very well,” and sent them to the Himalayas together with the chief disciple, while he himself remained behind all alone.

pakkāsāpetvā.meaning_2: causes to be declared; has announced; summons by proclamation
pakkāsāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative of pakāsati. In the sentence it is an absolutive (pakkāsāpetvā) meaning 'having had (Nārada) summoned/declared'. The form is 3rd singular present in the lemma.
pakkāsāpetvā.example_1: ‘‘ Sādhu, bhante ’’ ti rājā nāradaṃ nāma amaccaṃ pakkāsāpetvā ‘‘ nārada, amhākaṃ bhadantaṃ gahetvā vanacarakehi saddhiṃ himavantaṃ yāhī ’’ ti pesesi.
pakkāsāpetvā.translation_1: The king, saying, “Very well, Venerable sir,” summoned a minister named Nārada and sent him, saying, “Nārada, take our venerable one and go to the Himalayas with the forest dwellers.”

vakkhāti.meaning_2: will say; will speak; will tell
vakkhāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Future 3rd singular of vadati/vacati (irregular future formation, vakkhati). Related forms in the text: vakkhāhi (imperative) and vakkhāma (future 1st plural).

rājidha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Vocative singular used in address; a poetical compound of rāja + idha, perhaps 'the king here'. Alternatively may be a sandhi of rāja + idha. Compare rājiddhi.
rājidha.example_1: 182. ‘‘ Dūto ahaṃ rājidha rakkhasānaṃ, vadhāya tuyhaṃ pahitohamasmi;
rājidha.translation_1: “O king, I am a messenger of the Rakkhasas, sent here for your harm;

vibhiṃsikaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text uses the accusative singular vibhiṃsikaṃ; as a noun it refers to the frightening display made by the yakkhas.
vibhiṃsikaṃ.example_1: Mahatī sā vibhiṃsikāti yaṃ panete yakkhā sannipatitvā vibhiṃsikaṃ dassenti, sā mahatī vibhiṃsikā bhayakāraṇadassanamattameva mayhaṃ, na panāhaṃ bhāyāmīti attho.
vibhiṃsikaṃ.translation_1: That is great intimidation (mahatī sā vibhiṃsikā) means that the great intimidation which these yakkhas show after gathering together is merely a terrifying display for me, but I am not afraid, is the meaning.

vibhiṃsikā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Appears with mahatī, 'a great intimidation'. In the commentary explained as bhayakāraṇadassana, a display that causes fear. Nominative singular in the text.
vibhiṃsikā.example_1: Nālaṃ pisācā yuddhāya, mahatī sā vibhiṃsikā ’’ ti.
vibhiṃsikā.translation_1: these goblins are not able to fight; that is great intimidation.”
vibhiṃsikā.example_2: Mahatī sā vibhiṃsikāti yaṃ panete yakkhā sannipatitvā vibhiṃsikaṃ dassenti, sā mahatī vibhiṃsikā bhayakāraṇadassanamattameva mayhaṃ, na panāhaṃ bhāyāmīti attho.
vibhiṃsikā.translation_2: That is great intimidation (mahatī sā vibhiṃsikā) means that the great intimidation which these yakkhas show after gathering together is merely a terrifying display for me, but I am not afraid, is the meaning.

mettibhindanakajano.meaning_2: person who breaks loving-kindness; one who destroys friendship; mischief-maker
mettibhindanakajano.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of metti, bhindanaka (from bhindati) and jana. Nominative singular in the text, describing the slanderer.
mettibhindanakajano.example_1: Ekasmiṃ kira samaye satthā ‘‘ chabbaggiyā bhikkhū pesuññaṃ upasaṃharantī ’’ ti sutvā te pakkosāpetvā ‘‘ saccaṃ kira tumhe, bhikkhave, bhikkhūnaṃ bhaṇḍanajātānaṃ kalahajātānaṃ vivādāpannānaṃ pesuññaṃ upasaṃharatha, tena anuppannāni ceva bhaṇḍanāni uppajjanti, uppannāni ca bhiyyobhāvāya saṃvattantī ’’ ti pucchitvā ‘‘ saccan ’’ ti vutte te bhikkhū garahitvā ‘‘ bhikkhave, pisuṇā vācā nāma tikhiṇasattipahārasadisā, daḷho vissāsopi tāya khippaṃ bhijjati, tañca pana gahetvā attano mettibhindanakajano sīhausabhasadiso hotī ’’ ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.
mettibhindanakajano.translation_1: Once, it is said, the Teacher, hearing that “the bhikkhus of the group of six were spreading slander”, having summoned them, asked, “Is it true, monks, that you spread slander among bhikkhus who are quarreling, fighting, and disputing, and because of that, quarrels that had not arisen, arise, and quarrels that had arisen, conduce to increasing?” When they said, “It is true,” he rebuked those bhikkhus, saying, “Monks, divisive speech is like a blow from a sharp spear. Even a strong intimacy is quickly broken by it. And whoever takes it up—that person who breaks friendship—becomes like the lion and the strong bull.” Having said this, he recounted a story of the past.

kuṭidūso.meaning_2: destroyer of huts; one who spoils a dwelling; name of a character in a Jātaka
kuṭidūso.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text, a variant of kuṭidūsaka; listed as a name in the verse.
kuṭidūso.translation_1: The Kuṭidūsa, the Duddabha, the Brahmadattacammasāṭaka;

duddabhāyo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a dog in the Jātaka prose. Nom sg in the text. The word is a compound, so root fields are empty.
duddabhāyo.translation_1: The Kuṭidūsa, the Duddabha, the Brahmadattacammasāṭaka;

kinnarīvānarakuntinī.meaning_2: kinnarī (female kinnara) and vānara and kuntinī; the Kinnarī, the Vānara, the Kuntinī
kinnarīvānarakuntinī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A string of four names in a verse list; nominative singular forms joined by sandhi. Might also be analysed as two compounds (kinnarīvānara + kuntinī).
kinnarīvānarakuntinī.translation_1: The Kinnarī, the Vānara, the Kuntinī, the Ambahārī, the Gajakumbha;

lunitvā.meaning_2: having cut; having cut off; having shaved; having reaped
lunitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive glossed in the commentary as lāyitvā; same root √lū. Root sign nā is uncertain (√lū not in the provided root list).

nevayyakassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the verse nevayyakassa is a sandhi of na + ayyakassa; the prose gloss takes it as a single word meaning 'of the grandfather' (ayyakassa). Genitive singular in the text.
nevayyakassa.translation_1: “But my grandfather’s head and hands and feet are not to be seen;
nevayyakassa.example_2: Nevayyakassa sīsañcāti ayyakassa pana sīsañca hatthapādā ca na dissanti.
nevayyakassa.translation_2: Nevayyakassa sīsañca means ‘but my grandfather’s head and hands and feet are not seen’.

uppāṭāpesi.meaning_2: caused to be extracted; had (someone) tear out; caused to be pulled out; had (eyes) removed
uppāṭāpesi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative aorist 3rd singular of uppāṭāpeti; in both sentences the king has the artisan's eyes put out (akkhīni uppāṭāpesi). The form is 3rd singular with the object in the plural.
uppāṭāpesi.example_1: Kārāpetvā ca pana ‘‘ ayaṃ vaḍḍhakī aññassapi rañño evarūpaṃ pāsādaṃ kareyyā ’’ ti maccharāyanto tassa akkhīni uppāṭāpesi.
uppāṭāpesi.translation_1: And indeed, having had it built, he, being envious, thinking ‘this artisan might build such a palace for another king as well,’ had his eyes extracted.
uppāṭāpesi.example_2: Tasmā bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ ‘‘ āvuso, bodhirājakumāro kira tathārūpassa vaḍḍhakino akkhīni uppāṭāpesi, aho kakkhaḷo pharuso sāhasiko ’’ ti.
uppāṭāpesi.translation_2: Therefore, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall, saying, “Friends, Prince Bodhi indeed had the eyes of such an artisan extracted! Alas, what a harsh, savage, and reckless person he is!”

bhinnanāvo.meaning_2: with a broken boat; whose boat is wrecked; broken boat
bhinnanāvo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Kammadhāraya compound used adjectivally of a person (like a wrecked boat); the related PEU entry treats it as ti. Nominative singular in the text.
bhinnanāvo.example_1: Bodhisatto aṅgavijjāvasena tassa kakkhaḷapharusasāhasikabhāvaṃ ñatvā ‘‘ tāta, tvaṃ kakkhaḷo pharuso sāhasiko, pharusena nāma laddhaṃ issariyaṃ aciraṭṭhitikaṃ hoti, so issariye vinaṭṭhe bhinnanāvo viya samudde patiṭṭhaṃ na labhati, tasmā mā evarūpo ahosī ’’ ti taṃ ovadanto dve gāthā abhāsi –
bhinnanāvo.translation_1: The Bodhisatta, having known his harsh, savage, and reckless nature by means of prognostication, admonishing him, declared these two verses: “Dear child, you are harsh, savage, and reckless. Indeed, lordship obtained harshly is not long-lasting. When that lordship is destroyed, he, like a broken boat in the sea, does not find a footing. Therefore, do not be such a person.”
bhinnanāvo.example_2: Atthaccayeti so tvaṃ aniccatāvasena issariye vigate attano atthassa accaye yathā nāma bhinnaplavo bhinnanāvo manusso sāgaramajjhe patiṭṭhaṃ alabhanto sampamūḷho hoti, evaṃ mā ahu sampamūḷho.
bhinnanāvo.translation_2: Atthaccaye means ‘when that sovereignty of yours has vanished due to impermanence, and when your own welfare has passed away, just as a man with a broken raft or a broken boat, not finding a footing in the middle of the sea, becomes utterly deluded, so do not be utterly deluded’.

balibheriṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text. PEU notes the word at Ja 3.148 is corrupt for balabherī; both analyses give the same sense.
balibheriṃ.example_1: Rājā ‘‘ sādhū ’’ ti paṭissuṇitvā antosāṇiyaṃ mahābale malle ṭhapetvā ekamekaṃ rājānaṃ pakkosāpetvā nippīḷanena visaññaṃ kāretvā akkhīni uppāṭetvā māretvā maṃsaṃ ādāya kaḷevarāni gaṅgāyaṃ pavāhetvā vuttappakāraṃ balikammaṃ kāretvā balibheriṃ ākoṭāpetvā yuddhāya gato.
balibheriṃ.translation_1: The king, having answered, “Very well,” and having placed strong wrestlers inside the curtain, summoned each king one by one. Having made them unconscious by crushing, he had their eyes extracted, killed them, and taking their flesh, caused their corpses to be floated away in the Gaṅgā. Having then made the aforementioned offering and having caused the sacrificial drum to be beaten, he went for battle.

ākoṭāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to be beaten; having had (a drum) struck
ākoṭāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of ākoṭāpeti (causative of ākoṭeti). In the text it governs balibheriṃ: 'having had the sacrificial drum beaten'. PEU splits it as ā + kuṭa + ṇāpe + tvā.
ākoṭāpetvā.example_1: Rājā ‘‘ sādhū ’’ ti paṭissuṇitvā antosāṇiyaṃ mahābale malle ṭhapetvā ekamekaṃ rājānaṃ pakkosāpetvā nippīḷanena visaññaṃ kāretvā akkhīni uppāṭetvā māretvā maṃsaṃ ādāya kaḷevarāni gaṅgāyaṃ pavāhetvā vuttappakāraṃ balikammaṃ kāretvā balibheriṃ ākoṭāpetvā yuddhāya gato.
ākoṭāpetvā.translation_1: The king, having answered, “Very well,” and having placed strong wrestlers inside the curtain, summoned each king one by one. Having made them unconscious by crushing, he had their eyes extracted, killed them, and taking their flesh, caused their corpses to be floated away in the Gaṅgā. Having then made the aforementioned offering and having caused the sacrificial drum to be beaten, he went for battle.

paṭiāgataṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Neuter nominative singular agreeing with dukkhaṃ. The prefix pair paṭi + ā is unusual; cf. paccāgata.
paṭiāgataṃ.example_1: Tameva dukkhanti yaṃ mayā paresaṃ akkhiuppāṭanadukkhaṃ kataṃ, idaṃ me tatheva paṭiāgataṃ, idāni no ācariyassa vacanaṃ matthakaṃ pattanti paridevati.
paṭiāgataṃ.translation_1: That very suffering (tameva dukkhaṃ) means: the suffering of having eyes gouged out, which was done by me to others, this has similarly returned to me. Now our teacher’s word has reached its climax; thus he laments.

anavhitoti.meaning_2: not to be called; not to be addressed; not to be apologized to
anavhitoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form adds the quotation -ti. The PEU entry connects avhita to ā + √vhe + ta with the prefix na; possibly a variant of anabbhita.

paṭipākatitaṃ.meaning_2: restored to the original state; back to its former condition
paṭipākatitaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is accusative singular in the phrase paṭipākatikaṃ kātuṃ ('to restore'). Some editions read paṭipākatikaṃ; the word is a compound of paṭi and pākatika ('original').
paṭipākatitaṃ.example_1: Tassattho – yathā nāma udakakumbho ukkhipiyamāno patitvā sattadhā bhinno puna tāni kapālāni paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapetvā saṃvidahitvā paṭipākatikaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, yo petamanusocati, tassapi etamanusocanaṃ evaṃnipphattikameva hoti, matassa puna jīvāpetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā iddhimato vā iddhānubhāvena bhinnaṃ kumbhaṃ saṃvidahitvā udakassa pūretuṃ sakkā bhaveyya, kālakato pana iddhibalenāpi na sakkā paṭipākatitaṃ kātunti.
paṭipākatitaṃ.translation_1: Its meaning is: Just as a water-jar, when lifted and dropped, broken into seven pieces, cannot be restored to its original state by placing its fragments back in order and reassembling them; for one who grieves for the departed, this grieving brings about the same result, because it is impossible to bring the dead back to life. Or, it might be possible for one with supernormal power to reassemble a broken jar and fill it with water through his supernormal power, but a departed one cannot be restored to their original state even with psychic power.

nālamekotipi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] No sentences were supplied, so the form cannot be analysed with certainty. It looks like a sandhi of na + alaṃ + eko + api or na + alaṃ + ekoti + api ('not even one is enough'), but this is a guess and needs checking.

yidhatthoti.meaning_2: this is the welfare; the good; the benefit
yidhatthoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] No sentences supplied; likely idaṃ + attho + ti or idha + attho + ti, quoted with ti.

sānūni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text sānūni is nominative/accusative plural. The commentary glosses it with paṃsupabbate ca silāpabbate ca, i.e. mounds of earth and rock. The PEU entries sānaṃ1 and sānaṃ2 are unrelated homographs.
sānūni.example_1: Vikiriya sānūni ca pabbatāni ca, tasmā silaṃ dariyā pakkhipāmī ’’ ti.
sānūni.translation_1: Leveling the ridges and the mountains, therefore I throw the stone into the cave.’’
sānūni.example_2: Sānūni ca pabbatāni cāti paṃsupabbate ca silāpabbate ca.
sānūni.translation_2: Sānūni ca pabbatāni cā means: ‘‘mounds of earth and rock mountains.’’

meko.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Grammarians' sandhi of mayā + eko (or me + eko) in the verse phrase karaṇāya meko; the commentary glosses it as eko. Not a dictionary word of its own.
meko.example_1: 36. ‘‘ Nayimaṃ mahiṃ arahati pāṇikappaṃ, samaṃ manusso karaṇāya meko;
meko.translation_1: 36. ‘‘This earth, not by one human alone, is able to be made level like the palm of a hand;
meko.example_2: Tattha karaṇāya mekoti karaṇāya eko kātuṃ na sakkotīti dīpeti.
meko.translation_2: There, karaṇāya meko means: ‘‘One is not able to make (it),’’ thus he declares.

mekoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi: final o + ti. The word before the quotative ti may be meko or another form; not found in the supplied sentences.

saṃsāramocakādayo.meaning_2: the liberators from the round of rebirth and others; Saṃsāramocaka and the rest
saṃsāramocakādayo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Subject of the sentence; nominative plural. The first member is an adjective (saṃsāramocaka, 'liberating from the round of rebirth') used as a noun here.
saṃsāramocakādayo.example_1: Saṃsāramocakādayo panettha kusalasaññino, te tvaṃ kathaṃ ānayissasi, tasmā diṭṭhadiṭṭhānaṃ sīlaṃ adatvā yācantānaññeva dehīti.
saṃsāramocakādayo.translation_1: And in this regard, there are those who perceive even such acts as leading to liberation as wholesome. How will you bring them (to your view)? Therefore, without giving ethical conduct to whomever you see, give it only to those who ask.’’

papothayeyyanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Optative 1st singular papothayeyyaṃ with -ti of quotation attached; the sentential context is missing.

parigaḷitvā.meaning_2: having slipped down; having rolled down; having fallen off; having slid off
parigaḷitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -itvā of a verb pari + √gal (drip, flow, fall). Used of an elephant, a man and a jewel slipping or rolling down. Variant reading parigalitvā.
parigaḷitvā.example_1: Vāraṇo ‘‘ ettha pānīyaṃ bhavissatī ’’ ti papātābhimukho gacchanto parigaḷitvā pabbatapāde patitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi.
parigaḷitvā.translation_1: The elephant thought, ‘‘There will be drinking water here,’’ and going towards the precipice, he rolled down, fell at the foot of the mountain, and died.
parigaḷitvā.example_2: So tattha disāmūḷho hutvā sattāhaṃ nirāhāro vicaranto ekaṃ tindukarukkhaṃ disvā abhiruyha phalāni khādanto tindukarukkhato parigaḷitvā saṭṭhihatthe narakapapāte pati.
parigaḷitvā.translation_2: There, having lost his way and wandering for seven days without food, he saw a tiṇḍuka tree and climbed it; while eating the fruit, he slipped off the tiṇḍuka tree and fell sixty cubits into a hell-like abyss.

kaḍḍhāpetvā.meaning_2: causes to be dragged; has (someone) dragged; causes to drag
kaḍḍhāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive kaḍḍhāpetvā in both sentences: 'having had (him) dragged'. Causative of kaḍḍhati; the sign may also be analysed as *āpe.
kaḍḍhāpetvā.example_1: Khantīvādījātake (jā.1.4.49 ādayo) dvīhipi kasāhi pahārasahassehi tāḷāpetvā hatthapāde ca kaṇṇanāsañca chedāpetvā jaṭāsu gahetvā kaḍḍhāpetvā uttānakaṃ nipajjāpetvā ure pādena paharitvā gato.
kaḍḍhāpetvā.translation_1: In the Khantīvādī Jātaka, he had him beaten with two thousand whip-strokes with both whips, and caused his hands and feet and ears and nose to be cut off, and having seized him by the matted hair, caused him to be dragged, and having laid him down face-up, struck him on the chest with his foot, and went away.
kaḍḍhāpetvā.example_2: So tassa kujjhitvā ‘‘ ayaṃ kūṭajaṭilo ettakaṃ kālaṃ nāgarānaṃ santike mamaññeva aguṇaṃ kathesi maññe, hotu jānissāmī ’’ ti cintetvā ‘‘ sve amhākaṃ gharadvāraṃ āgaccheyyāthā ’’ ti nimantetvā punadivase purāṇagūthassa cāṭiyo paripūrāpetvā tāpasesu āgatesu tesaṃ bhikkhābhājanāni gūthassa pūrāpetvā dvāraṃ pidahāpetvā musalāni ca lohadaṇḍe ca gāhāpetvā isīnaṃ sīsāni bhindāpetvā jaṭāsu gāhāpetvā kaḍḍhāpetvā sunakhehi khādāpetvā tattheva bhinnaṃ pathaviṃ pavisitvā sunakhamahāniraye nibbattati, tatrassa tigāvutappamāṇasarīraṃ ahosi.
kaḍḍhāpetvā.translation_2: He, having become angry with him, thought, “This matted-hair cheat has, for so long, only spoken of my lack of virtue in the vicinity of the citizens, I suppose. Let it be, I will know (what to do to him)!” and having invited him, saying, “May you come to our house door tomorrow,” on the next day, having caused pots to be filled with old feces, when the ascetics arrived, he caused their alms bowls to be filled with feces, had the door closed, had pestles and iron clubs taken, had the heads of the sages broken, had them grabbed by their matted hair, had them dragged, had them eaten by dogs, and right there, having entered the split earth, he was reborn in the great dog hell, where his body was three gāvutas in size.

karomī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] First person singular karomi, written karomī before the quotation ti (karomī ti). Occurs in all three sentences, in the sense of doing or making, e.g. pabbājessāmi 'I will make him the owner'.
karomī.example_1: Tato bhagavā cintesi ‘‘ yaṃ ayaṃ pitu santakaṃ dhanaṃ icchati, taṃ vaṭṭānugataṃ savighātaṃ, handassa bodhimaṇḍe paṭiladdhaṃ sattavidhaṃ ariyadhanaṃ demi, lokuttaradāyajjassa naṃ sāmikaṃ karomī ’’ ti āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ āmantesi ‘‘ tena hi, tvaṃ sāriputta, rāhulakumāraṃ pabbājehī ’’ ti.
karomī.translation_1: Then the Blessed One thought: “The wealth that he asks for, which belongs to his father, leads to the cycle of rebirth and entails suffering. Come, I will give him the sevenfold noble wealth I obtained at the Bodhi-seat. I will make him the owner of a supramundane inheritance,” and he addressed Venerable Sāriputta: “Sāriputta, in that case, ordain Prince Rāhula.”
karomī.example_2: ‘‘ Sādhu karomī ’’ ti sahassena abbhutaṃ akāsi.
karomī.translation_2: “Very well, I will do it,” and he made a wager of a thousand pieces.

paṭipāṭetvā.meaning_2: having put in order; having arranged in sequence; having joined in order
paṭipāṭetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā; the text describes sinew, flesh and skin being joined back in order.
paṭipāṭetvā.example_1: Iti taṃ ālapitvā puna ‘‘ tvañca eso cāpi mahāmigoti dvepi janā sukhī niddukkhā hothā ’’ ti taṃ samassāsetvā luddako bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā vāsiyā cammapāsaṃ chinditvā pāde laggapāsakaṃ saṇikaṃ nīharitvā nhārunā nhāruṃ, maṃsena maṃsaṃ, cammena cammaṃ paṭipāṭetvā pādaṃ hatthena parimajji.
paṭipāṭetvā.translation_1: Thus, having addressed her, and again comforting her with the words, “You and that great stag, both people, be happy and free from suffering,” the hunter, having gone to the Bodhisatta’s presence, cut the leather snare with an axe, and carefully removed the small snare stuck to his foot, rejoining sinew with sinew, flesh with flesh, and skin with skin, and stroked his foot with his hand.

vaṭatīti.meaning_2: is; happens; is proper; is fit
vaṭatīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form is vaṭati + iti (vaṭatīti), the quotative particle being attached by sandhi. The PEU entry is uncertain and offers several unrelated senses; the usual sense of vaṭati is 'is proper, is fit'. No reliable root is given in the available list.

sedumadīpo.meaning_2: name of an island; Sedumadi Island
sedumadīpo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of an island in the Jātaka. Nominative singular in the text. Possibly the first element relates to seda (sweat); uncertain.
sedumadīpo.example_1: Tadā bodhisatto supaṇṇayoniyaṃ nibbatti, tasmiṃ kāle nāgadīpo sedumadīpo nāma ahosi.
sedumadīpo.translation_1: Then the Bodhisatta was reborn in the Garuḍa species. At that time, Nāga Island was named Sedumadi Island.

nāvo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular; the form nāvo is irregular (expected nāvā). In the text it means the merchants' ship.
nāvo.example_1: ‘‘ Ahaṃ ce gandhabbaṃ kareyyaṃ, mayi pana gandhabbaṃ karonte macchā calissanti, atha vo nāvo bhijjissatī ’’ ti.
nāvo.translation_1: He [replied], “If I were to perform celestial music, then while I am performing celestial music, the fish will be agitated, and your ship will break.”

ghosavā.meaning_2: noisy; resounding; making a loud sound
ghosavā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the verse it describes the small sea as noisy. The gloss ghosavāti mahāravo explains it as 'having a great sound'. Nominative singular.
ghosavā.example_1: 55. ‘‘ Vāti gandho timirānaṃ, kusamuddo ca ghosavā;
ghosavā.translation_1: 55. “The fragrance of the timira trees wafts, and the small sea is noisy;

sedumanti.meaning_2: having pure conduct; of pure character
sedumanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Possibly a compound of seda/cedu (pure) + mant; exact meaning uncertain as no sentences were provided. If correct, nominative singular is sedumā.

sedumadīpaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text, glossing the adjective seduma (sedumā). The name of an island.

phalakenāhamaplaviṃ.meaning_2: by means of a plank; on a plank
phalakenāhamaplaviṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of phalakena (instrumental of phalaka, 'plank') and ahaṃ ('I'); the -a of phalakena absorbs ahaṃ, giving phalakenāhaṃ. Final -aplaviṃ is the verb aplaviṃ (aorist of plavati, 'I floated').
phalakenāhamaplaviṃ.translation_1: the ship was broken by sea monsters, and I floated on a plank.

uddharī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular (or 1st singular) of uddharati, sandhi of uddhara + i; here with aṅgena, 'lifted with the arm'. The PEU lists uddhara as the base.
uddharī.example_1: Aṅgena uddharī bhaddā, mātā puttaṃva orasaṃ.
uddharī.translation_1: the lovely one lifted me up with her arms, like a mother her own son.

mandakkhī.meaning_2: of gentle gaze; with soft eyes
mandakkhī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The commentary glosses it as mandadassanī, 'one whose nature is to look gently'. Used as a feminine epithet of a woman; nominative singular in the text.
mandakkhī.example_1: Attanāpi ca mandakkhī, evaṃ tamba vijānahī ’’ ti.
mandakkhī.translation_1: And with herself, the maiden of gentle gaze—thus, Tamba, understand this.”
mandakkhī.example_2: Mandakkhīti mandadassanī, mudunā ākārena olokanasīlāti vuttaṃ hoti.
mandakkhī.translation_2: The word mandakkhī (mandakkhī) means ‘of gentle gaze’, which is to say ‘one whose nature is to look with a gentle manner’.

mandadassanī.meaning_2: of gentle gaze; with soft, gentle eyes
mandadassanī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Glossed in the commentary as 'mudunā ākārena olokanasīlā'. Nominative singular in the text.
mandadassanī.example_1: Mandakkhīti mandadassanī, mudunā ākārena olokanasīlāti vuttaṃ hoti.
mandadassanī.translation_1: The word mandakkhī (mandakkhī) means ‘of gentle gaze’, which is to say ‘one whose nature is to look with a gentle manner’.

saṃvāsamabhirocaye.meaning_2: approves of; consents to; wishes for
saṃvāsamabhirocaye.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of saṃvāsaṃ + abhirocaye (accusative object + verb, not a true compound); 1st singular optative ending -eyya is written -e in verse. The verb is abhiroceti (causative of abhirocati), 'to approve of, consent to'; here with saṃvāsaṃ, 'to consent to living together with'.
saṃvāsamabhirocaye.translation_1: I will not wish to dwell in communion with you.

setī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Used in the text as present 3rd singular of √sī (to lie, sleep). The form setī occurs before ti (quotative), representing seti.
setī.example_1: Sa ve rāja sukhaṃ setīti mahārāja so puggalo eko adutiyo pavivitto kāyikacetasikasukhasamaṅgī hutvā sukhaṃ seti.
setī.translation_1: “He, indeed, O king, sleeps happily” means, Great King, that person, being alone without a companion, secluded, and possessed of bodily and mental happiness, sleeps happily.
setī.example_2: Kapotakassa vacanaṃ akatvā, amittahatthatthagatova setī ’’ ti.
setī.translation_2: He lies having fallen into the hands of an enemy, like the crow who did not heed the pigeon’s word.”

abhirocaye.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Negated in the text: na abhirocaye, 1st singular present of abhirocayati, 'I do not desire'. The PEU entry gives the base abhirocayati but the form here is 1sg -e; also analysed as causative in -aya of abhirocati.
abhirocaye.example_1: Dubbhasīti yadi evaṃ tayā saddhiṃ samaggavāsaṃ vasantaṃ maṃ siṅgālassa kathaṃ gahetvā tvaṃ dubbhasi hanituṃ icchasi, ito dāni paṭṭhāya ahaṃ tayā saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ na abhirocaye.
abhirocaye.translation_1: Regarding “speak ill of”, (the meaning is:) ‘If, having taken the jackal’s words, you speak ill of me, who am dwelling in harmonious communion with you, or you wish to harm (me), then from now on I will not desire to dwell in communion with you.’

tavāhamasmī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of tava, ahaṃ and asmi. Occurs in the verse and is glossed tavāhaṃ mitto ti in the prose. Optional chandasi form; the usual order is ahaṃ tava asmi.
tavāhamasmī.example_1: 70. ‘‘ Hiriṃ tarantaṃ vijigucchamānaṃ, tavāhamasmī iti bhāsamānaṃ;
tavāhamasmī.translation_1: 70. “One who transgresses the sense of shame, who loathes [you] in friendship,
tavāhamasmī.example_2: Tavāhamasmīti ‘‘ tava ahaṃ mitto ’’ ti kevalaṃ vacanamatteneva bhāsamānaṃ.
tavāhamasmī.translation_2: ‘I am yours’ (tavāhamasmī) means one who merely speaks, “I am your friend,” by mere words.

ghaṭetunti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text ghaṭetuṃ is an infinitive ('to restore') and ghaṭetunti is ghaṭetuṃ + iti with sandhi; the headword here is the present 3rd singular. Causative of ghaṭati in the sense of joining or uniting.
ghaṭetunti.example_1: Sakhiñca mittañcāti sakhibhāvañca mittabhāvañca tathārūpena kulajātena tittena akapaṇena amaccharinā saddhiṃ paṇḍito sandhātuṃ puna ghaṭetuṃ arahati, tayā pana kapaṇena ahituṇḍikena saddhiṃ ko mittabhāvaṃ puna ghaṭetunti attho.
ghaṭetunti.translation_1: 'Friendship and alliance' means that a wise one is worthy to form friendship and camaraderie, and to restore it again, with a high-born person who is content, not wretched, and ungrudging. But with you, the wretched snake-charmer, who would restore friendship again? – that is the meaning.

maraṇamaccuveso.meaning_2: disguise of Death; appearance of the Death-deity
maraṇamaccuveso.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text glosses it as maraṇamaccuveso, dwelling in the cavity of the body (sarīraguhāya vasanako).
maraṇamaccuveso.translation_1: Death in disguise dwelling in the cave of the heart means the disguise of Death (Māra) as death, dwelling in the cave of the body.

sāḷiyachāpotīti.meaning_2: young rice plants, it is said; young rice shoots, so it is said
sāḷiyachāpotīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of sāḷiyachāpotī (nominative plural of sāḷiyachāpota, 'young rice plant') + iti, marking a quotation. The -ī before iti is shortened to -i.

sāḷiyachāpaṃ.meaning_2: young sāḷiya bird; young grackle; young myna
sāḷiyachāpaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text. sāḷiya is a bird (grackle/myna); chāpa means the young of an animal. The doctor uses it to trick the Bodhisatta.
sāḷiyachāpaṃ.example_1: Tadā eko dubbalavejjo gāme kiñci alabhitvā nikkhamanto taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā ekaṃ sappaṃ viṭapabbhantarena sīsaṃ nīharitvā niddāyantaṃ disvā ‘‘ mayā gāme kiñci na laddhaṃ, ime dārake vañcetvā sappena ḍaṃsāpetvā tikicchitvā kiñcideva gaṇhissāmī ’’ ti cintetvā bodhisattaṃ āha ‘‘ sace sāḷiyachāpaṃ passeyyāsi, gaṇheyyāsī ’’ ti.
sāḷiyachāpaṃ.translation_1: Then, a poor doctor, not finding anything in the village, going out and having arrived at that place, saw a snake sleeping with its head protruding through the fork of a branch. Having thought, “I have obtained nothing in the village; having deceived these children, and having caused them to be bitten by the snake, and having cured them, I will get something,” he spoke to the Bodhisatta, “If you were to see a young hedgehog, would you seize it?”

ohanitvā.meaning_2: having struck down; having beaten down; having knocked down
ohanitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -itvā of ohanati (ava + √han). In the text it is paired with ohacca as a gloss on the same action: 'having struck down and hurled down'.
ohanitvā.example_1: Yaṃ meti yena pāpena mama sirasmiṃ ohacca ohanitvā idaṃ khuracakkaṃ mama matthake bhamati, taṃ kiṃ nāmāti?
ohanitvā.translation_1: [Regarding] “That for me…”, it means: “By which evil, having struck down, this razor-sharp wheel spins upon my head — what is that called?”

ramaṇakādīsu.meaning_2: name of a type of gem or palace; beginning with the ramaṇaka (gem); (to be confirmed)
ramaṇakādīsu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form ramaṇakādīsu is a locative plural of ramaṇaka used in an -ādi compound (ramaṇaka + ādi) meaning 'beginning with ramaṇaka'. The exact referent is uncertain; the commentary apparently lists celestial palaces, so it may denote a kind of gem or mansion. Locative plural in the text.
ramaṇakādīsu.example_1: Kenatthenāti tvaṃ etesu ramaṇakādīsu catasso aṭṭha soḷasa dvattiṃsāti etā devadhītaro pahāya te pāsāde atikkamitvā kena kāraṇena idha āgatoti.
ramaṇakādīsu.translation_1: [Regarding] “For what reason have you come here?” it means: “Having left behind these four, eight, sixteen, and thirty-two divine maidens in these palaces beginning with the palace of crystal, and having surpassed those palaces, for what reason have you come here?”

nipisamānaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Neuter singular nominative agreeing with khuracakkaṃ. The text is corrupt; it may be nippisamānaṃ.
nipisamānaṃ.example_1: Mittavindakaṃ pana kathentameva nipisamānaṃ taṃ khuracakkaṃ bhassi, tena so puna kathetuṃ nāsakkhi.
nipisamānaṃ.translation_1: But while Mittavindaka was still speaking, that razor-sharp wheel fell, crushing him, and because of that, he was unable to speak again.

āsaṅkituṃ.meaning_2: to suspect; to be suspicious (of); to be apprehensive (about)
āsaṅkituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Occurs in the stock phrase āsaṅkitabbayuttakaṃ āsaṅkituṃ vaṭṭati. Infinitive of āsaṅkati; the form may also be analysed as āsaṅketuṃ.
āsaṅkituṃ.example_1: Haṃsarājā taṃ disvā rukkhadevataṃ āmantetvā ‘‘ samma palāsa, nigrodho nāma yamhi rukkhe jāyati, vaḍḍhanto taṃ nāseti, imassa vaḍḍhituṃ mā deti, vimānaṃ te nāsessati, paṭikacceva naṃ uddharitvā chaḍḍehi, āsaṅkitabbayuttakaṃ nāma āsaṅkituṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti palāsadevatāya saddhiṃ mantento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –
āsaṅkituṃ.translation_1: The king of geese, seeing that, having addressed the tree deva, said, “Friend Palāsa, a banyan, indeed, on which tree it is born, growing, it destroys that tree. Do not let this (shoot) grow, it will destroy your mansion. Indeed, pull it up and throw it away beforehand. Indeed, it is proper to suspect what should be suspected.” Advising thus with the Palāsa tree deva, he uttered the first verse:
āsaṅkituṃ.example_2: Idhāpi satthā antokoṭisanthāre kāmavitakkābhibhūte pañcasate bhikkhū disvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā ‘‘ bhikkhave, āsaṅkitabbayuttakaṃ nāma āsaṅkituṃ vaṭṭati, kilesā nāma vaḍḍhantā vane nigrodhādayo viya rukkhaṃ, purisaṃ bhañjanti, teneva pubbepi koṭasimbaliyaṃ nibbattadevatā ekaṃ sakuṇaṃ nigrodhabījāni khāditvā attano rukkhassa sākhantare vaccaṃ pātentaṃ disvā ‘ ito me vimānassa vināso bhavissatī ’ ti bhayappattā ahosī ’’ ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.
āsaṅkituṃ.translation_2: Here, too, the Teacher, seeing five hundred monks overwhelmed by sensual thoughts within the golden pavement, having assembled the community of bhikkhus, said: “Monks, it is proper to be suspicious of what is fit to be suspected. Defilements, like banyan trees and the like growing in a forest, destroy a man. For this very reason, even in the past, a deity born in the Koṭasimbali tree, seeing a certain bird that had eaten banyan seeds dropping excrement among the branches of her tree, became frightened and trembling, thinking, ‘From this, my mansion will be destroyed!’” Having said this, he recounted a story of the past.

āmanta.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Used in the formula āmanta kho taṃ gacchāmi 'I bid you farewell, I am leaving'. Variant for āmantayitvā; the PEU entry treats it as a verb 'make him know, call him'.
āmanta.example_1: Āmanta kho taṃ gacchāma, vuḍḍhi massa na ruccatī ’’ ti.
āmanta.translation_1: I bid you farewell, I am leaving; its growth is not what I prefer.”
āmanta.example_2: Āmanta kho tanti tasmā mayaṃ taṃ āmantetvā jānāpetvā gacchāma.
āmanta.translation_2: Regarding āmanta kho taṃ (āmanta kho taṃ), it means: therefore, having addressed and informed you, we are leaving.

massāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text with the quotation particle -ti (massāti = massu + iti), so the headword is massu. The form massā is likely nominative/accusative plural or a sandhi variant; -ā for u-stems is unusual.

āsaṅkitvā.meaning_2: having suspected; having feared; having anticipated
āsaṅkitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -itvā from āsaṅkati. Paired with the potential participle āsaṅkitabbaṃ in the text.
āsaṅkitvā.example_1: Idhāpi satthā tatheva rājānaṃ sakiṃ puttena saddhiṃ kīḷamānaṃ sakiṃ dhammaṃ suṇantaṃ disvā ‘‘ taṃ nissāya rañño bhayaṃ uppajjissatī ’’ ti ñatvā ‘‘ mahārāja, porāṇakarājāno āsaṅkitabbaṃ āsaṅkitvā attano puttaṃ ‘ amhākaṃ dhūmakāle rajjaṃ kāretū ’ ti ekamante akaṃsū ’’ ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.
āsaṅkitvā.translation_1: Here too, the Teacher, seeing the king at one time playing with his son and at another time listening to the Dhamma, and knowing that “danger will arise for the king through him,” said: “Great King, ancient kings, having suspected what was to be suspected, kept their sons in confinement, saying, ‘Let them rule the kingdom after our bodies have been cremated.’” Having said this, he recounted a story of the past.

adhīyitabbamevāti.meaning_2: but must be learned;  indeed is to be studied; such is...
adhīyitabbamevāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of adhīyitabbaṃ eva iti. adhīyitabba is a potential participle of adhīyati (√i 2, study, recite). eva is emphatic. iti marks the end of a quotation or gloss.
adhīyitabbamevāti.example_1: Hīnamukkaṭṭhamajjhimanti hīnaṃ vā hotu uttamaṃ vā majjhimaṃ vā, sabbaṃ adhīyitabbamevāti dīpeti.
adhīyitabbamevāti.translation_1: Hīnamukkaṭṭhamajjhiman means: “Whether it is low, high, or middling, all should indeed be learned,” it declares.

tāvesā.meaning_2: indeed she; she indeed; certainly she
tāvesā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of tāva (indeed) + esā (she). In the text it emphasizes that this very woman killed her husband.
tāvesā.example_1: Corajeṭṭhako ‘‘ kuladattiyaṃ tāvesā sāmikaṃ māresi, aññaṃ panekaṃ disvā mampi evamevaṃ karissati, imaṃ chaḍḍetuṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti cintetvā gacchanto antarāmagge ekaṃ kunnadiṃ uttānatalaṃ taṅkhaṇodakapūraṃ disvā ‘‘ bhadde, imissaṃ nadiyaṃ susumārā kakkhaḷā, kiṃ karomā ’’ ti āha.
tāvesā.translation_1: The chief of robbers thought, “This woman indeed killed her husband, given by her family. If she sees another man, she will do just so to me too. It is proper to abandon her.” Thinking thus, as he went along the way, he saw a small, shallow-bottomed river, full of water at that moment, and said, “Good lady, fierce alligators are in this river. What should we do?”

kambojigumbe.meaning_2: Kamboji thicket; thicket of cassia (Cassia tora) trees
kambojigumbe.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text; glossed by eḷagalāgumba as a thicket of cassia trees.
kambojigumbe.translation_1: In the cassia thicket (eḷagalāgumbe) means in the cassia thicket.

dānī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Encouraging particle meaning 'now' or 'then'; often follows another word in the clause, as in suṇāhi dāni and karomi dāni.
dānī.example_1: Athassa taṃ sutvā bodhisatto ‘‘ mahāseṭṭhi, tvaṃ aññāṇatāya kāmagiddho hutvā gharāvāsassa guṇaṃ, pabbajjāya ca aguṇaṃ kathesi, gharāvāsassa te aguṇaṃ kathessāmi, suṇāhi dānī ’’ ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –
dānī.translation_1: Then, having heard that, the Bodhisatta said, “Great treasurer, you, being greedy for sensual pleasures due to ignorance, speak of the virtues of the household life and the defects of the going forth. I will speak to you of the defects of the household life; listen now,” and uttered the second verse—
dānī.example_2: Asocamāno adhivāsayeyya, kammaṃ daḷhaṃ kinti karomi dānī ’’ ti.
dānī.translation_2: Without grieving, one should endure, [thinking,] ‘My kamma is strong; what can I do now?’”

koraṇḍi.meaning_2: name of a female goat; Koraṇḍi
koraṇḍi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is the name of a goat (or animal in Jātaka 503?) listed along with Ghaṭa, Laṭukī, etc.; the machine translation treats it as a proper name. Other possible analyses: locative of koraṇḍa 'a genus of plant, the Kurchi tree' (Barleria), but the names of the other animals favor a name. The text form is nominative singular, likely a Sanskritic -i stem, not declined here.
koraṇḍi.example_1: Ghaṭaṃ koraṇḍi laṭuki, dhammapālaṃ migaṃ tathā.
koraṇḍi.translation_1: Ghaṭa, Koraṇḍi, Laṭukī, Dhammapāla, and Miga;

laṭuki.meaning_2: Laṭukī; name of a female character (in a list of names)
laṭuki.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Probably a proper name (cf. laṭuka, laṭukikā). Occurs in a list of names in a verse in the Jātaka commentary.
laṭuki.example_1: Ghaṭaṃ koraṇḍi laṭuki, dhammapālaṃ migaṃ tathā.
laṭuki.translation_1: Ghaṭa, Koraṇḍi, Laṭukī, Dhammapāla, and Miga;

khajjopanaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a mythical serpent king (nāgarāja) in the Jātaka list; the Pali English Ultimate glosses it as 'firefly, glow-worm'. In the text nominative singular; varies with khajjopanaka.

sāḷiyaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name in a list of names in the Jātaka prose. Appears as sāḷiyaṃ, which may be accusative singular; if the list is nominative, read it as a sandhi or scribal variant of sāḷiyo.

ulloḷaṃ.meaning_2: commotion; uproar; disturbance; tumult; great noise
ulloḷaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Used adverbially in the phrases ulloḷaṃ katvā and ulloḷaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā, 'making a commotion'. Accusative singular, agreeing with the neuter abstract noun. The PEU analysis takes the prefix u- with loḷa (from √luḷ, 'to agitate'); alternatively it may be read as a verbal noun from uḷuḷ (cf. ulloleti).
ulloḷaṃ.example_1: So kujjhitvā ‘‘ ehi re samaṇa, vahāmī ’’ ti theraṃ nāvaṃ āropetvā ujukaṃ agantvā heṭṭhā nāvaṃ netvā ulloḷaṃ katvā tassa pattacīvaraṃ temetvā kilametvā tīraṃ patvā andhakāravelāyaṃ uyyojesi.
ulloḷaṃ.translation_1: He, having become angry, said, ‘Come, recluse, I will take you!’ and having placed the Elder in the boat, not going straight but leading the boat downwards, he made a commotion, thereby wetting his bowl and robe and troubling him. Having arrived at the bank, he dismissed him at the time of darkness.
ulloḷaṃ.example_2: Atha tumhe ‘ ṭhapetvā brahmadattaṃ añño amhākaṃ rañño uttaritaro idha natthī ’ ti kalahaṃ vaḍḍhetvā amhākaṃ rañño āsanamattampi alabhantā ‘ na dāni vo suraṃ pātuṃ macchamaṃsaṃ khādituṃ dassāmā ’ ti nadantā vaggantā mahāghosaṃ karontā tesaṃ santāsaṃ janentā mahantehi leḍḍudaṇḍehi sabbacāṭiyo bhinditvā macchamaṃsaṃ vippakiritvā aparibhogaṃ katvā javena senāya antaraṃ pavisitvā devanagaraṃ paviṭṭhā asurā viya ulloḷaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā ‘ mayaṃ mithilanagare mahosadhapaṇḍitassa purisā, sakkontā amhe gaṇhathā ’ ti tumhākaṃ āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā āgacchathā ’’ ti pesesi.
ulloḷaṃ.translation_2: 'Then you should escalate the quarrel by saying, 'Excluding Brahmadatta, there is no one here superior to our king.' When you are not even given a seat for our king, shout, 'We will not let you drink wine or eat fish and meat today!' creating a great uproar, and smash all the wine jars with large stones and sticks, scatter the fish and meat, and render it unfit for consumption; then, with speed, penetrate the army, enter the city like Asuras who have entered the city of the gods, stir up great commotion, announce your arrival by saying, 'We are the men of Mahosadha the learned man from Mithila city; if you dare, catch us,' and return.'

kujjhatuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of kujjhati used after na vaṭṭati in the sentence raññā nāma kujjhatuṃ na vaṭṭati; the related form kujjha is imperative.
kujjhatuṃ.example_1: Māsu kujjha rathesabhāti evamevāhaṃ taṃ anusāsāmi, raññā nāma kujjhatuṃ na vaṭṭati.
kujjhatuṃ.translation_1: ‘Do not be angry, lord of chariots (māsu kujjha rathesabhā)’ means: ‘Thus I counsel you, for it is not proper for a king to become angry.’

āyāpāyaṃ.meaning_2: gain and loss; profit and loss; advantage and disadvantage
āyāpāyaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of āya (gain) and apāya (loss), with the initial vowel of the second member lengthened (āya + apāya > āyāpāya). Accusative singular in the text: 'na attano āyāpāyaṃ jānāti' (does not know his own gain and loss).
āyāpāyaṃ.example_1: So bālo neva guṇavantānaṃ guṇaṃ jānāti, na attano āyāpāyaṃ jānāti, so gaṅgaṃ taritukāmaṃ janaṃ paṭhamaṃ tāretvā pacchā vetanaṃ yācati, vetanaṃ adentehi saddhiṃ kalahaṃ karonto akkosappahāreyeva bahū labhati, appaṃ lābhaṃ, evarūpo andhabālo.
āyāpāyaṃ.translation_1: He was a fool, neither knowing the virtues of the virtuous nor understanding his own gain and loss. He would first ferry people across the Ganges who wished to cross, and then ask for the fare. When they did not give the fare, he would quarrel with them, and would get many insults and blows, but little gain. Such a blind fool was he.

saoiti.meaning_2: this connection 'sa-oiti'; the words sa and oiti
saoiti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The word as it stands, in a grammatical rule describing the sandhi of 'sa' with 'oiti'; nominative singular subject in the sentence.
saoiti.example_1: Sa-oiti imesaṃ padānañhi sūti sandhi hoti.
saoiti.translation_1: For these words, sa-o, there is a euphonic combination of ‘sū’.

oiti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Grammatical term naming the sandhi of -o with a following i-. Quoted form in the text; treated as a compound of the letter o and iti.
oiti.example_1: Sa-oiti imesaṃ padānañhi sūti sandhi hoti.
oiti.translation_1: For these words, sa-o, there is a euphonic combination of ‘sū’.

uddālajātake.meaning_2: Uddāla Jātaka; the Jātaka of the Uddāla tree
uddālajātake.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of a Jātaka story, quoted by its title. Locative singular in the text.
uddālajātake.example_1: Mā tāta kujjhi na hi sādhu kodhoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kuhakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi, paccuppannavatthu uddālajātake (jā.1.14.62 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.
uddālajātake.translation_1: ‘Dear child, do not be angry; certainly, anger is not good’ (Mā tāta kujjhi na hi sādhu kodho) — the Teacher spoke this while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, referring to a deceitful bhikkhu. The present story will be clearly set forth in the Uddāla Jātaka (Jā.1.14.62, etc.).

onametvā.meaning_2: having bent down; having bowed; having lowered
onametvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of the causative onameti (ava + nam + *e), 'having made bend down, having bowed down'. In the text it describes the caṇḍāla forcing the other man down.
onametvā.example_1: Caṇḍālo ‘‘ nāhaṃ taṃ etaṃ disaṃ pucchāmi, tvaṃ ettakampi ajānanto mama sarīre pahaṭavātaṃ jigucchasī ’’ ti taṃ khandhaṭṭhike gahetvā onametvā attano pādantarena gamesi.
onametvā.translation_1: The outcast said, ‘I am not asking you about that kind of direction. You, not knowing even this much, detest the wind that has struck my body!’ and taking him by the shoulders, bent him down and made him go between his feet.

karitva.meaning_2: having done; having performed; having committed
karitva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā of karoti (√kar + *tvā); the final long ā is often written short in manuscripts, hence 'karitva' in the text. Takes the object pāpāni kammāni here.
karitva.example_1: 11. ‘‘ Pāpāni kammāni karitva rāja, bahussuto ce na careyya dhammaṃ;
karitva.translation_1: 11. “Even if one who is learned, O king, were to do evil deeds and not practice the Dhamma;

parimuñcituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -ituṃ of parimuñcati (pari + muc). The object is expressed with the ablative (lobhajātaṃ ... parimuñcituṃ = to free oneself from this greed).
parimuñcituṃ.example_1: Evaṃ anatthakārakaṃ pana imaṃ guṇaparidhaṃsakaṃ lobhajātaṃ kasmā sattā parimuñcituṃ na sakkontīti?
parimuñcituṃ.translation_1: But why are beings unable to free themselves from this greed, which thus causes harm and destroys virtue?

catukuṭṭikanirayoti.meaning_2: Catukuṭṭika hell; hell with four corners; the womb as a four-cornered hell
catukuṭṭikanirayoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The -ti is the quotative particle iti, attached by sandhi; the entry is for the main word. The compound means the mother's womb, a hell with four corners, as described in the stories. Nominative singular in -ti.

catukuṭṭikanirayo.meaning_2: four-cornered hell; the hell of the four corners (i.e. the mother's womb)
catukuṭṭikanirayo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A commentarial expression for the mother's womb, where a being is confined on all four sides (Jātaka commentary). Nominative singular in the text; kuṭṭika is otherwise unrecorded and may be a variant of koṭṭha/kuṭṭa "corner".
catukuṭṭikanirayo.example_1: Mātukucchi hi nirassādaṭṭhena idha ‘‘ nirayo ’’ ti vutto,‘‘ catukuṭṭikanirayo ’’ ti vuccati.
catukuṭṭikanirayo.translation_1: Indeed, the mother’s womb is called “hell” here because it has no satisfaction; it is called a “four-cornered hell.”
catukuṭṭikanirayo.example_2: ‘‘ Catukuṭṭikanirayo nāma kataro ’’ ti vutte mātukucchimeva vattuṃ vaṭṭati.
catukuṭṭikanirayo.translation_2: When asked, “Which is called the four-cornered hell?” it is appropriate to say “just the mother’s womb.”

catukoṭena.meaning_2: four corners; four points; (in the womb) with four limbs drawn in
catukoṭena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular catukoṭena in the text ("with four corners"). Describes the cramped posture in the womb; related catukoṭika is an adjective meaning "four-cornered".
catukoṭena.example_1: Avīcimahāniraye nibbattasattassa hi aparāparaṃ ādhāvanaparidhāvanaṃ hotiyeva, tasmā taṃ ‘‘ catukuṭṭikanirayo ’’ ti vattuṃ na labbhati, mātukucchiyaṃ pana nava vā dasa vā māse catūhipi passehi ito cito ca dhāvituṃ nāma na sakkā, atisambādhe okāse catukoṭena catusaṅkuṭiteneva hutvā acchitabbaṃ, tasmā esa ‘‘ catukuṭṭikanirayo ’’ ti vuccati.
catukoṭena.translation_1: Indeed, for a being reborn in the great Avīci purgatory, running continually hither and thither certainly occurs; therefore, it is not possible to call that a “four-cornered hell.” But in the mother’s womb, for nine or ten months, one is certainly unable to run hither and thither by all four sides; one must stay, having become contracted in four ways with four limbs in a very confined place. Therefore, this is called a “four-cornered hell.”

visatiṃvase.meaning_2: dwelling with twenty; residence with twenty (monks); living in a community of twenty
visatiṃvase.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text. Compound of visati (twenty) and vasa (dwelling), referring to a residence of twenty monks.
visatiṃvase.translation_1: or where there is honour for the lowly and immoral, one should not dwell in such a residence.

āsīsatevātiādimāha.grammar: sandhi, pr + ind + ind + masc + pr
āsīsatevātiādimāha.meaning_2: he said 'āsīsate vā' etc.; and so on, saying 'āsīsate'
āsīsatevātiādimāha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A quotation compound in the commentary; the quoted word is āsīsati from the root √is.

sereyyakasseva.meaning_2: of the sereyyaka flower, as if; like of the sereyyaka plant
sereyyakasseva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of sereyyakassa (genitive singular of sereyyaka, a fragrant plant) with iva, contracted to -eva. The compound mālā sereyyakasseva = 'a garland of sereyyaka flowers, as it were'. In the text sereyyaka is used adjectivally with mālā, though formally the genitive singular.
sereyyakasseva.translation_1: Like a garland of sereyyaka flowers, which are beautiful but scentless.

sampesīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Third person singular present of a causative (saṃ + √pis 1 + *e), with ṇe/ī endings as in the related PEU entry sampesesi. In -ti form here; final -īti is sandhi with iti, so the headword is sampeseti not sampesīti.

sereyyakassāti.meaning_2: fragrant reed; a kind of scented grass
sereyyakassāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text the -ti is the quotative particle: sereyyakassa + ti, genitive singular, 'of the fragrant reed'. The -ka is a diminutive/attributive suffix; sereyya is the plant name.

sereyyakādīnaṃ.meaning_2: name of a plant (Barleria cristata or similar); sereyyaka flower
sereyyakādīnaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form sereyyakādīnaṃ is sereyyaka + ādīnaṃ, 'sereyyaka and other (flowers)', a genitive plural in -ānaṃ with the stem-final a lengthened before ādi. In the Jātaka commentary the sereyyaka is a fragrant flower; the passage says it pleases by sight but lacks fragrance.
sereyyakādīnaṃ.example_1: Vaṇṇavantā agandhikāti yathā sereyyakādīnaṃ mālā vaṇṇavantatāya dassanena tappeti, agandhatāya gandhena na tappeti, evaṃ tvampi dassanena piyavacanena ca santappesi, na kammunāti dīpeti.
sereyyakādīnaṃ.translation_1: Vaṇṇavantā agandhikā (beautiful and scentless) means that just as a garland of sereyyaka flowers and so on pleases by sight due to its beauty, but does not please by scent due to its lack of fragrance, in the same way, you too pleased by sight and pleasant words, but not by deeds—thus he explains.

yaṃnāmasmi.meaning_2: by which name I am called; by whatever name I am (known)
yaṃnāmasmi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Verse in the Jātaka commentary. Probably yaṃ (relative pronoun) + nāmasmi, asmi being the 1st singular of √as; alternatively yaṃ + nāma + asmi, or a sandhi of yannāmasmi. No finite form sammi exists, so nāmasmi is unlikely as a single word.
yaṃnāmasmi.example_1: 33. ‘‘ Etadeva hi me nāmaṃ, yaṃnāmasmi rathesabha;
yaṃnāmasmi.translation_1: “This indeed is my name, O lord of chariots, by which name I am called;

yaṃnāmā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the relative pronoun yaṃ with the instrumental nāma (nāmā) in the phrase yaṃnāmā ahaṃ asmi, 'by whatever name I am'; likely a printer's or editorial misreading for yaṃ nāma. No verbal root, so the root fields are empty.
yaṃnāmā.example_1: Tassattho – yaṃnāmā ahaṃ asmi, taṃ etaṃ āsaṅkātveva mama nāmanti.
yaṃnāmā.translation_1: The meaning of that is: ‘The name by which I am called, that indeed is my name, Āsaṅkā.’”

apanandagijjho.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of the vulture into which the Bodhisatta was reborn. Nominative singular in the text.
apanandagijjho.example_1: Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto gijjhayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā apanandagijjho nāma ahosi.
apanandagijjho.translation_1: In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling the kingdom at Benares, the Bodhisatta, having been reborn in the vulture species, was named Apanandagijjha.

atuccaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of ati + uccaṃ; usually written atiuccaṃ, as the gloss shows. Adverbial accusative; used as a prefix compound with patati ('flies too high').
atuccaṃ.example_1: Atuccaṃ tāta patasi, abhūmiṃ tāta sevasi.
atuccaṃ.translation_1: Dear child, you fly too high; dear child, you frequent a region that is not yours.”
atuccaṃ.example_2: Atuccaṃ tāta patasīti tāta, tvaṃ aññesaṃ gijjhānaṃ sīmaṃ atikkamitvā atiuccaṃ gacchasi.
atuccaṃ.translation_2: Atuccaṃ tāta patasi (Dear child, you fly too high) means: ‘Dear child, you go too high, surpassing the boundary of the other vultures.’”

gijjhovātītasāsano.meaning_2: one who disregards the instruction; one who has overstepped the teaching; heedless of the norm
