gijjhovātītasāsano.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of gijjha and atītasāsana; the -u- is a compound linker vowel. In the text it modifies a person (nominative singular); 'like the vulture' is the English rendering of gijjha, instr. here would be gijjhena, but the Pāḷi reads gijjho.
gijjhovātītasāsano.translation_1: Wandering beyond the boundary, arrogant, like the vulture who disregards instruction,

apanando.meaning_2: name of a king of vultures; Apananda
apanando.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name, nominative singular in the text. The PEU reads it as Apa + nanda; the commentary perhaps plays on na nandati ('does not rejoice') because the vulture king is contrasted with the unruly Migālopa.
apanando.example_1: ‘‘ tadā migālopo dubbacabhikkhu ahosi, apanando pana ahameva ahosin ’’ ti.
apanando.translation_1: “Then Migālopa was the unruly monk; but Apananda was I myself.”

nāyituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -ituṃ, written with n- for nh-, as commonly in manuscripts (nhāyituṃ). Used with yuttā ('fitting') in the text.
nāyituṃ.example_1: Kāḷakaṇṇī ‘‘ ahaṃ lokaṃ pālemi vicāremi, tasmā paṭhamaṃ nāyituṃ yuttāmhī ’’ ti vadati.
nāyituṃ.translation_1: Kāḷakaṇṇī said, “I protect and administer the world; therefore, I am fitting to bathe first.”

sārambhī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes a person who is argumentative or creates conflict. Nominative singular in the text, in a list of negative qualities.
sārambhī.example_1: 43. ‘‘ Makkhī paḷāsī sārambhī, issukī maccharī saṭho;
sārambhī.translation_1: 43. “The contemptuous, the insolent, the rivalrous, the envious, the avaricious, the deceitful;

khudhañca.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of khudhā (fem, instrumental or ablative singular) with the enclitic ca. Occurs in a list of hardships (sīta, uṇha, vātātapa, khudhā, pipāsā).
khudhañca.example_1: Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo mahāseṭṭhi sīte vā uṇhe vā vātātape vā ḍaṃsasarīsape vā sati etehi sītādīhi pīḷiyamānopi etāni ceva sītādīni khudhañca pipāsañcāti sabbampetaṃ parissayaṃ abhibhuyya abhibhavitvā tiṇaṃ viya agaṇetvā rattindivaṃ kasivaṇijjādīsu ceva dānasīlādīsu ca satataṃ attano kammesu niyutto attānaṃ yojetvā vattati.
khudhañca.translation_1: This means: that great merchant, even when there is cold or heat, wind and sun, or flies and reptiles—even though afflicted by these conditions like cold etc.—having overcome and overpowering all these dangers, such as cold etc., hunger, and thirst, disregarding them like grass, constantly dedicated himself and engaged himself day and night in his own work, such as agriculture and trade, and giving and morality.

lolabiḷārī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is a simile for women who entice and ruin men. Nominative singular in -ī. PEU splits lola + biḷāra and gives the feminine form lolabiḷārī.
lolabiḷārī.example_1: Tañhi bhikkhuṃ satthā ‘‘ kasmā ukkaṇṭhitosī ’’ ti pucchitvā ‘‘ ekaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ itthiṃ disvā kilesavasena, bhante ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ bhikkhu itthiyo nāma vañcetvā upalāpetvā attano vasaṃ gatakāle vināsaṃ pāpenti, lolabiḷārī viya hontī ’’ ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.
lolabiḷārī.translation_1: The Teacher, having asked that bhikkhu, “Why are you dissatisfied?”—when he was told, “Venerable sir, it is due to defilements, having seen a certain adorned and prepared woman,”—having said, “Bhikkhu, women, having deceived and enticed (men), cause them to fall into ruin when they come under their power; they are like greedy cats,” he recounted a story of the past.

biḷāriṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular biḷāriṃ in the text, referred to by migī; the commentary word is probably read as biḷāriṃ (< biḷārī).
biḷāriṃ.translation_1: In this regard, migī refers to the cat.

lohitape.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Vocative singular in the text, addressed to a she-goat (or similar creature). Literally 'blood-drinker'; compare lohitapāyī/lohitapāyinī. Alternate form of lohitapā.
lohitape.translation_1: “O corpse-eater, blood-drinker, thief, slayer of cocks;

kukkuṭapothini.meaning_2: slayer of cocks; killer of chickens
kukkuṭapothini.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Vocative singular in the text, an insult addressed to a female. Possibly kukkuṭa + pothinī, from √puth (beat, hurt) with the *in suffix, as in the PEU's kukkuṭapotha.
kukkuṭapothini.translation_1: “O corpse-eater, blood-drinker, thief, slayer of cocks;

biḷārī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominal feminine of biḷāra with the suffix -ī. Nominative singular in the text; in the simile of the cat luring the rooster.
biḷārī.example_1: Nenti saṇhāhi vācāhi, biḷārī viya kukkuṭaṃ.
biḷārī.translation_1: Lead him with smooth words, like the cat (leads) the rooster.
biḷārī.example_2: Biḷārī viyāti yathā sā biḷārī taṃ kukkuṭaṃ netuṃ vāyamati, evaṃ aññāpi nāriyo nentiyeva.
biḷārī.translation_2: Biḷārī viyā means ‘just as that cat endeavors to lead that rooster, so too other women indeed lead (men under their power)’.

biḷāriyāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] biḷāriyā + ti (quotation); the sandhi portion is left out. Feminine of biḷāra formed with -iyā; vocative or nominative singular in the text.

biḷārito.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Ablative singular biḷārito, meaning 'from the cat' in the sentence: the rooster was freed from the cat. The spelling may also be analysed as biḷāra + ito, with the ablative ending written as -ito.
biḷārito.example_1: Kukkuṭovāti yathā so ñāṇasampanno kukkuṭo biḷārito mutto, evaṃ sattusambādhato muccatīti attho.
biḷārito.translation_1: Kukkuṭovā means ‘just as that wise rooster was freed from the cat, so too one is freed from the enemy’s trap’—that is the meaning.

gāmanigamāsu.meaning_2: village and market town; villages and towns
gāmanigamāsu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative plural in the text (gāmanigamāsu), glossed by the commentary as gāmesu ca nigamesu ca. The compound is treated as a dvanda.
gāmanigamāsu.example_1: Dhammadhajo gāmanigamāsu sādhu, dujjāno purisena bālisena.
gāmanigamāsu.translation_1: Taking the Dhamma as his standard, he is esteemed in villages and market towns; he is hard for a foolish person to know.”
gāmanigamāsu.example_2: Gāmanigamāsu sādhūti gāmesu ca nigamesu ca sādhu bhaddako sambhāvito.
gāmanigamāsu.translation_2: “‘Esteemed in villages and market towns’ means good, blessed, and esteemed in villages and market towns.”

bālisena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The instrumental singular bālisena in the text ('dujjāno purisena bālisena') agrees with purisena; in the gloss it is explained as aññāṇena ('ignorant'). Possibly a passive/kitaka formation from √is ('wish, seek') in the sense 'one whose desire is childish', but this is uncertain; treated here as a compound.
bālisena.example_1: Dhammadhajo gāmanigamāsu sādhu, dujjāno purisena bālisena.
bālisena.translation_1: Taking the Dhamma as his standard, he is esteemed in villages and market towns; he is hard for a foolish person to know.”
bālisena.example_2: Dujjānoti ayaṃ evarūpo dussīlo paṭicchannakammanto bālisena aññāṇena purisena na sakkā jānituṃ.
bālisena.translation_2: “‘Hard to know’ means, such an immoral one, secretive in his actions, cannot be known by a foolish, ignorant person.”

migavittakova.meaning_2: like deer meat + indeed; deer-meat lover + indeed
migavittakova.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of migavittako (nom sg of migavittaka, 'deer-meat lover') + iva, 'like; as it were'. Alternatively analysed as migavittaka + eva, 'indeed'; the sentence context favours iva. The compound migavittaka is itself miga + vitta + ka.
migavittakova.translation_1: Then, the Kosala king was indeed a deer hunter.

porakkhaṇiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Probably a distortion of pokkharaṇī. Accusative singular in the text.
porakkhaṇiṃ.example_1: Manussā sannipatitvā ‘‘ ayyā, ayaṃ rājā amhākaṃ kammacchedaṃ karoti, gharāvāsopi nassati, yaṃnūna mayaṃ ajjunavanaṃ uyyānaṃ parikkhipitvā dvāraṃ yojetvā porakkhaṇiṃ khaṇitvā tiṇāni āropetvā daṇḍamuggarādihatthā araññaṃ pavisitvā gumbe paharantā mige nīharitvā parivāretvā gorūpāni viya vajaṃ uyyānaṃ pavesetvā dvāraṃ pidahitvā rañño ārocetvā attano kammaṃ kareyyāmā ’’ ti mantayiṃsu.
porakkhaṇiṃ.translation_1: The people gathered together and consulted, “Sirs, this king is destroying our work, and even our household life is perishing. Let us then enclose the Ajjuna forest park, construct a gate, dig a tank, and plant grasses. Then, with sticks, clubs, and so on in hand, let us enter the forest, striking the thickets, expel the deer, surround them, and like cattle into a pen, force them into the park. Then, let us close the gate, tell the king, and go about our own work.”

muccesi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text reads muccesi, the present 2nd singular. The context is 'why do you not release (the arrow)?', so it is causative in sense.
muccesi.example_1: Mahāsatto ‘‘ kiṃ, mahārāja, saraṃ na muccesi, muñcāhī ’’ ti āha.
muccesi.translation_1: The Great Being said, “Great King, why do you not release the arrow? Release it!”

vastanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Form vastanti is accusative singular or nominative/accusative plural. The PEU entry suggests derivation from Vatta+ṇa, but this is uncertain; alternatively from √vas 2 'to wear, clothe'.

uppilāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to float; having floated
uppilāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of uppilāpeti; in the text it describes making a needle float on water.
uppilāpetvā.example_1: Bodhisatto taṃ sutvā savanasaṃsaggena bajjhitvā ‘‘ pādaparicārikaṃ naṃ karissāmī ’’ ti uttamajātikaṃ ayaṃ gahetvā ekaṃ sukhumaṃ ghanaṃ sūciṃ katvā pāse vijjhitvā udake uppilāpetvā aparampi tathārūpameva tassā kosakaṃ katvā pāse vijjhi.
uppilāpetvā.translation_1: The Bodhisatta, hearing that and becoming entangled by merely hearing (of her), thought: “I will make her my wife (pādaparicārikā).” So, taking iron of the best kind (uttamajātika), he made a single fine, strong (ghana) needle. Having made it pierce dice, he made it float (uppilāpeti) on water. He then made another sheath (kosaka) of the same kind for it and pierced dice with it.

paṭithaddhaṃ.meaning_2: hard; firm; rigid; not soft; stiffened
paṭithaddhaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes a needle in the Jātaka verse; accusative singular agreeing with sūciṃ. The root is uncertain; pati + √ṭhā (or √thambh) is likely.
paṭithaddhaṃ.example_1: Ghanaghātimaṃ paṭithaddhaṃ, ko sūciṃ ketumicchatī ’’ ti.
paṭithaddhaṃ.translation_1: Strong enough to pierce an anvil (ghanaghātimaṃ), very hard (paṭithaddhaṃ)? Who desires to buy such a needle (sūciṃ)?”

paṭithaddhanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The -ti in the text is the quotation particle; the entry is for the past participle. The PEU derivation has √thabhi for √thambh, with the usual assimilation mbh > ddh.

itodānīti.meaning_2: from here now, thus: 'ito dāni'; from this time on
itodānīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of ito, dāni and the quotative iti, common in commentary glosses; the final -ti marks the end of a quoted phrase.

koyanti.meaning_2: ko + yanti: 'who are they?' or 'what do they go to?'; (sandhi of ko and yanti)
koyanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the interrogative pronoun ko and the present verb yanti. In the Jātaka prose this form introduces a question about a group. The exact reading depends on context, but this analysis is the most likely. Alternatives: ko + ayanti, or a textual variant.

yañcatthaññaṃ.meaning_2: and whatever else exists there; and whatever other (wealth) there is
yañcatthaññaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of yaṃ + ca + attha + aññaṃ; yaṃ is the neuter pronoun agreeing with dhanaṃ, attha (= atthi, 'there is') is glossed by the commentary. Occurs in the refrain yañcatthaññaṃ ghare dhanaṃ.
yañcatthaññaṃ.example_1: Tayā ca maṃ nimanteyya, yañcatthaññaṃ ghare dhanan ’’ ti.
yañcatthaññaṃ.translation_1: He would invite me, and with you, he would offer whatever other wealth (dhanaṃ) exists in the house (ghare).”
yañcatthaññaṃ.example_2: Yañcatthaññaṃ ghare dhananti yañca aññaṃ saviññāṇakaṃ vā aviññāṇakaṃ vā ghare dhanaṃ atthi, tena maṃ nimanteyya.
yañcatthaññaṃ.translation_2: And whatever other wealth exists in the house means: whatever other wealth, animate or inanimate, exists in the house, by that he would invite me.

yañcassaññantipi.meaning_2: and whatever of it is without consciousness; and what of it is senseless
yañcassaññantipi.construction: yaṃ + ca + assa + aññaṃ + iti + pi
yañcassaññantipi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of yaṃ ca assa aññaṃ iti pi. Context is unclear since no sentence was supplied; 'aññaṃ' is taken as 'añña' (other; without consciousness) agreeing with 'yaṃ', and 'assa' as genitive/dative singular of 'ima'. If the underlying word is 'saññaṃ' or 'saññā', another analysis is yaṃ + ca + assa + saññaṃ + iti + pi.

sūkarī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nom sg in the text. From sūkara + feminine suffix ī; sūkara itself is doubtful, perhaps sū + √kar.
sūkarī.translation_1: When the sow was full-term pregnant, she gave birth to two young.
sūkarī.example_2: Sūkarī taṃ saddaṃ sutvā maraṇabhayena puttake chaḍḍetvā palāyi.
sūkarī.translation_2: The sow, having heard that sound, fled out of fear of death, abandoning her young.

mahātuṇḍilo.meaning_2: name of a pig; literally 'great-snouted one'
mahātuṇḍilo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name given by an old woman to the elder of two piglets she raised as her own children (Mahātuṇḍila Jātaka). Nominative singular in the text.
mahātuṇḍilo.example_1: Mahallikā sūkarapotake disvā puttasaññaṃ paṭilabhitvā pacchiyaṃ pakkhipitvā gharaṃ netvā jeṭṭhakassa mahātuṇḍilo, kaniṭṭhassa cūḷatuṇḍiloti nāmaṃ karitvā te puttake viya posesi.
mahātuṇḍilo.translation_1: The old woman, having seen the young pigs, developed the perception of them as her children; she put them in her basket, took them home, and, having named the elder Mahātuṇḍila and the younger Cūḷatuṇḍila, she cared for them like her own children.
mahātuṇḍilo.example_2: Taṃ sutvā mahātuṇḍilo ‘‘ ettakaṃ kālaṃ mama mātarā cūḷatuṇḍilassa saddo na dinnapubbo, maṃyeva paṭhamaṃ saddāyati, avassaṃ ajja amhākaṃ bhayaṃ uppannaṃ bhavissatī ’’ ti aññāsi.
mahātuṇḍilo.translation_2: Mahātuṇḍila, having heard that, knew: “All this time, my mother has never called Cūḷatuṇḍila before; she always calls me first. Surely, danger must have arisen for us today.”

cūḷatuṇḍiloti.meaning_2: Cūḷatuṇḍila; Little-Snout; name of a young pig
cūḷatuṇḍiloti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of the younger of two pigs in the Jātaka story. In the text it is cūḷatuṇḍilo + ti, the -ti being the quotative particle; the nominative singular is cūḷatuṇḍilo.
cūḷatuṇḍiloti.example_1: Mahallikā sūkarapotake disvā puttasaññaṃ paṭilabhitvā pacchiyaṃ pakkhipitvā gharaṃ netvā jeṭṭhakassa mahātuṇḍilo, kaniṭṭhassa cūḷatuṇḍiloti nāmaṃ karitvā te puttake viya posesi.
cūḷatuṇḍiloti.translation_1: The old woman, having seen the young pigs, developed the perception of them as her children; she put them in her basket, took them home, and, having named the elder Mahātuṇḍila and the younger Cūḷatuṇḍila, she cared for them like her own children.

mahātuṇḍilaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A proper name, the name of a horse in the Jātaka story. Accusative singular in the text. Tuṇḍila is otherwise unattested as a common adjective; the compound is analysed as 'great Tuṇḍila'.
mahātuṇḍilaṃ.example_1: Sā kahāpaṇe gahetvā ‘‘ tātā, mahātuṇḍilaṃ dātuṃ na sakkomi.
mahātuṇḍilaṃ.translation_1: She took the coins and said, “My children, I cannot give you Mahātuṇḍila.

cūḷatuṇḍilaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a pig in the Jātaka stories; accusative singular in the text.

cūḷatuṇḍila.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a pig in the Jātaka prose. Used as a vocative in the text, though the commentarial context treats it as a name. Cūḷa means 'small'; tuṇḍila is of uncertain meaning, perhaps 'snouty'.
cūḷatuṇḍila.example_1: Mahallikā ‘‘ tāta, cūḷatuṇḍila, ehī ’’ ti tassa saddamakāsi.
cūḷatuṇḍila.translation_1: The old woman called out to him, “Dear child, Cūḷatuṇḍila, come!”
cūḷatuṇḍila.example_2: Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto ‘‘ tāta cūḷatuṇḍila, mama kira mātā ettheva sūkare posentī nāma yadatthaṃ poseti, svāssā attho ajja matthakaṃ patto, tvaṃ mā cintayī ’’ ti vatvā madhurena sarena buddhalīḷāya dhammaṃ desento dve gāthā abhāsi –
cūḷatuṇḍila.translation_2: Having heard that, the Great Being said, “Dear child Cūḷatuṇḍila, the purpose for which my mother nourishes these pigs has today indeed reached its culmination. Do not worry,” and, with a sweet voice and the grace of a Buddha, teaching the Dhamma, he declared two verses:

cūḷatuṇḍilassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A proper name of a pig in the Jātaka story. Genitive singular in the text (cūḷatuṇḍilassa).
cūḷatuṇḍilassa.example_1: Taṃ sutvā mahātuṇḍilo ‘‘ ettakaṃ kālaṃ mama mātarā cūḷatuṇḍilassa saddo na dinnapubbo, maṃyeva paṭhamaṃ saddāyati, avassaṃ ajja amhākaṃ bhayaṃ uppannaṃ bhavissatī ’’ ti aññāsi.
cūḷatuṇḍilassa.translation_1: Mahātuṇḍila, having heard that, knew: “All this time, my mother has never called Cūḷatuṇḍila before; she always calls me first. Surely, danger must have arisen for us today.”
cūḷatuṇḍilassa.translation_2: The Great Being began a discourse on the Dhamma for Cūḷatuṇḍila in the midst of the great assembly.

thambhituṃ.meaning_2: to be stiff; to be paralysed; to steady oneself
thambhituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive used with na sakkoti: 'was unable to steady himself'. From thambhati, 'is stiff, is rigid'. The PEU entry treats it as a noun (thambha + tuṃ) meaning stiffness; the context is better served by the infinitive.
thambhituṃ.example_1: So gacchā nikkhamitvā bhattadoṇisamīpe tesaṃ ṭhitabhāvaṃ disvā ‘‘ ajja me maraṇaṃ uppannan ’’ ti maraṇabhayatajjito nivattitvā kampamāno bhātu santikaṃ āgantvā thambhituṃ nāsakkhi, kampamāno paribbhami.
thambhituṃ.translation_1: Having gone out, he saw them standing near the food trough. Thinking, “Today death has arisen for me,” he was tormented by the fear of death. He turned back, trembling, and came to his brother. He was unable to steady himself, and he reeled about, trembling.

svāssā.meaning_2: that (purpose) for him; that for him
svāssā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text printed as svāssā before attho; the final -ā belongs to the following word (attho) or is a sandhi vowel. So = nominative singular of ta, assa = dative/genitive singular of ta: 'that purpose for him'. Could also be analysed as svā + assa. Not related to svāsa ('asthma').
svāssā.example_1: Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto ‘‘ tāta cūḷatuṇḍila, mama kira mātā ettheva sūkare posentī nāma yadatthaṃ poseti, svāssā attho ajja matthakaṃ patto, tvaṃ mā cintayī ’’ ti vatvā madhurena sarena buddhalīḷāya dhammaṃ desento dve gāthā abhāsi –
svāssā.translation_1: Having heard that, the Great Being said, “Dear child Cūḷatuṇḍila, the purpose for which my mother nourishes these pigs has today indeed reached its culmination. Do not worry,” and, with a sweet voice and the grace of a Buddha, teaching the Dhamma, he declared two verses:

tuṇḍila.meaning_2: name of a pig; name of a man (brother of the courtesan Kāḷī)
tuṇḍila.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name in the Jātaka prose. In the first sentence the pig addresses himself; in the second the merchant's son speaks to the man Tuṇḍila.
tuṇḍila.example_1: Appossukko bhuñja tuṇḍila, maṃsatthāya hi positāmhase.
tuṇḍila.translation_1: Have no fear, eat, O Tuṇḍila, for we have been nourished for the sake of our flesh.
tuṇḍila.example_2: Atheko seṭṭhiputto niccakālaṃ kāḷiyā sahassaṃ āharāpento disvā ‘‘ kasmā tuṇḍila rodasī ’’ ti pucchi.
tuṇḍila.translation_2: Then a certain merchant's son, who constantly had a thousand pieces of money brought to Kālī, seeing him, asked, “Why are you weeping, Tuṇḍila?”

cūḷatuṇḍilo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of a pig in the Jātaka commentary; in the text it also stands for a bhikkhu in the identification of the characters. Nominative singular in both sentences.
cūḷatuṇḍilo.example_1: Taṃ sutvā cūḷatuṇḍilo ‘‘ mayhaṃ bhātā evaṃ vadeti, amhākañca vaṃse pokkharaṇiṃ otaritvā nahānaṃ, sarīrato sedamalapavāhanaṃ, purāṇavilepanaṃ hāretvā navavilepanagahaṇañca kismiñci kāle natthi, kiṃ nu kho sandhāya bhātā maṃ eva māhā ’’ ti pucchanto catutthaṃ gāthamāha –
cūḷatuṇḍilo.translation_1: Cūḷatuṇḍila, having heard that, asked, “My brother says this, but in our lineage, bathing after descending into a pond, washing away sweat and stains from the body, and removing old ointment to take new ointment never occurs at any time. Referring to what, I wonder, did my brother say this to me?” and uttered the fourth verse:
cūḷatuṇḍilo.example_2: Tadā rājā ānando ahosi, cūḷatuṇḍilo maraṇabhīruko bhikkhu, parisā buddhaparisā, mahātuṇḍilo pana ahameva ahosinti.
cūḷatuṇḍilo.translation_2: Then the king was Ānanda, Cūḷatuṇḍila was the bhikkhu who was in fear of death, the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly, and Mahātuṇḍila was I indeed.

māhāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Variant (m-) of āha, aorist 3rd singular of brūti; -ti is the quotative particle. The form without -ti is māha.

cūḷatuṇḍilena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of a pig, companion of the Bodhisatta. Instrumental singular in the text: "saddhiṃ cūḷatuṇḍilena" (together with Cūḷatuṇḍila).
cūḷatuṇḍilena.example_1: Mahāsatto tassa sarīraparihāraṃ kāretvā vinicchaye potthake likhāpetvā ‘‘ imaṃ potthakaṃ oloketvā aḍḍaṃ tīreyyāthā ’’ ti vatvā mahājanassa dhammaṃ desetvā appamādena ovādaṃ datvā sabbesaṃ rodantānaṃ paridevantānaññeva saddhiṃ cūḷatuṇḍilena araññaṃ pāvisi.
cūḷatuṇḍilena.translation_1: The Great Being, having performed the funeral rites for his body, and having had a book of judgments written, said, “You should decide law-suits by contemplating this book.” Then, having taught the Dhamma to the great populace and given them advice with diligence, he entered the wilderness with Cūḷatuṇḍila, while all of them wept and lamented.

sālindiyo.meaning_2: Sālindiya; name of a brahmin village
sālindiyo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a village; the text's -o is the nominative ending, so the name itself is sālindiya. Sometimes written sālindiyo in compounds.
sālindiyo.example_1: Atīte rājagahassa pubbapasse sālindiyo nāma brāhmaṇagāmo hoti.
sālindiyo.translation_1: In the past, on the eastern side of Rājagaha, there was a brahmin village named Sālindiya.

micche.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Metrically shortened form of micchā (or possibly micchā with -e ending) at the end of the verse line; it means 'wrongly'; 'vainly', and modifies the verb hiṃsituṃ.
micche.example_1: 98. ‘‘ Mamañca disvāna pavaddhakāyaṃ, sabbo jano hiṃsitumeva micche;
micche.translation_1: And seeing my grown body, all people would surely wish to harm me;

disva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā (loss of the final root consonant before tvā). Text spelling 'disva' represents disvā. From the root √dis 'see'.
disva.example_1: Sāduñca thūlañca muduñca maṃsaṃ, kākāpi maṃ disva viheṭhayeyyun ’’ ti.
disva.translation_1: Thinking my meat is sweet, fat, and tender, even crows, seeing me, would torment me.”

anāvamiyamānaṃ.meaning_2: not being drawn out; not being removed; not being vomited up
anāvamiyamānaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Negative potential participle used passively (kamma) of āvamati 'draws out, lets out, vomits'. Agrees with maccaṃ (accusative singular masculine) in the text; -mānaṃ is the accusative singular ending here, not the lemma form.
anāvamiyamānaṃ.example_1: Pure visaṃ gāḷhamupeti maccanti imañhi maccaṃ mayā anāvamiyamānaṃ visaṃ gāḷhaṃ balavaṃ hutvā upagaccheyya, taṃ yāva na upagacchati, tāvadeva amhe dvepi jane khippaṃ muñcāti.
anāvamiyamānaṃ.translation_1: Before the poison deeply reaches the mortal (pure visaṃ gāḷhamupeti maccaṃ) means that if the poison is not drawn out by me, it would become deeply strong and reach this mortal. As long as it does not reach him, just until then, quickly release both of us people.

sañcarituṃ.meaning_2: to move about; to wander; to go around
sañcarituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of sañcarati, used with sakkoti ('is able to move about').
sañcarituṃ.example_1: Taṃ sutvā kakkaṭako cintesi ‘‘ ayaṃ ekenupāyena maṃ dvepi jane vissajjāpetvā palāyitukāmo, mayhaṃ upāyakosallaṃ na jānāti, ahaṃ dāni yathā sappo sañcarituṃ sakkoti, evaṃ aḷaṃ sithilaṃ karissāmi, kākaṃ pana neva vissajjessāmī ’’ ti evaṃ cintetvā sattamaṃ gāthamāha –
sañcarituṃ.translation_1: Hearing that, the crab thought, “This one, by some stratagem, desires to make me release both of them and then flee; he does not know my skill in device. Now I will loosen my claw so that the snake can move about, but I will certainly not release the crow.” Having thus thought, he uttered the seventh verse –

paṭibandhakoti.meaning_2: one who obstructs; opposer; one who binds; insurer
paṭibandhakoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text the quotation particle -ti is attached; the entry is for the main word. Doubtful reading; PEU gives paṭibandhaka as a masculine agent noun.

āvamitvā.meaning_2: having drawn out; having sucked out; having spat out
āvamitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -itvā of āvamati (ā + √vam). In the text it describes the snake drawing the poison out of the Great Being's body. The PEU entry gives the infinitive āvamituṃ with the sense 'to suck up'.
āvamitvā.example_1: Sappo visaṃ āvamitvā mahāsattassa sarīraṃ nibbisaṃ akāsi.
āvamitvā.translation_1: The snake, having drawn out the poison, made the Great Being’s body free from poison.

sālindiyagāmameva.meaning_2: to Sālindiya village indeed; just to Sālindiya village
sālindiyagāmameva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of sālindiyagāmaṃ (accusative singular of sālindiyagāma, 'Sālindiya village', a place name in the Jātaka stories) + eva. The -ṃ of the accusative becomes -m- before eva.
sālindiyagāmameva.example_1: Suvaṇṇakakkaṭakaṃ sobbhe vissajjetvā nhatvā sālindiyagāmameva gato.
sālindiyagāmameva.translation_1: Having released the golden crab in the pool, and having bathed, he went to Sālindiya village.

mayhakoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the bird's cry mayhakaṃ ('mine') + iti. No sentences were supplied; the form is inferred from the PEU entry for mayhaka, a bird whose call sounds like 'it's mine'. Alternative split mayhaṃ + iti is also possible.

vipphaliṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text itself glosses it as pipphali (figs), from pipphalī. Form seems to be a quotation or verse remnant; possibly an accusative or a free-standing accusative used adverbially.
vipphaliṃ.example_1: Bhutvāna vipphaliṃ yantīti taṃ pipphalirukkhaṃ paribhuñjitvā aññaṃ phalasampannaṃ rukkhaṃ gacchanti.
vipphaliṃ.translation_1: Having eaten the figs, they go (bhutvāna vipphaliṃ yantī) means having partaken of that fig tree, they go to another tree laden with fruit.

teso.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of te (nominative plural of ta) and eso (nominative singular of eta). In the verse Seyyo nu teso, the commentary explains eso virūpo pabbajito, so the sense is 'this one', though the form may be read as te + eso or teso alone. DPD may prefer tesa.
teso.example_1: Seyyo nu teso udavā sarikkho, nāmaṃ parassattano cāpi brūhī ’’ ti.
teso.translation_1: Is he your better or your equal, say, tell us his name and your own.”
teso.example_2: Seyyo nu tesoti eso virūpo pabbajito kiṃ nu tayā uttaritaro, udāhu sarikkho.
teso.translation_2: Is he your better? (Seyyo nu teso) means, ‘Is this ill-formed renunciant superior to you, or equal?’

tesoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Unclear sandhi form, perhaps te + so or te + iti with the final element obscure; no sentence context is available. Tentative only.

lapituṃ.meaning_2: to speak; to utter; to say
lapituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive used with na labbhati (is not possible). The same infinitive serves for both samaṇā and nāmaṃ lapituṃ.
lapituṃ.example_1: Atha naṃ sakko ‘‘ mahārāja, samaṇā nāma garuṭṭhāniyā, tena me nāmaṃ lapituṃ na labbhati, mayhaṃ pana te nāmaṃ kathessāmī ’’ ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –
lapituṃ.translation_1: Then Sakka, having said to him, “Great King, ascetics are indeed venerable ones, therefore it is not possible for me to utter his name. But I will tell you my own name,” uttered the second verse.

sakkohamasmī.meaning_2: I am Sakka; Sakka am I
sakkohamasmī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Quotation of Sakka identifying himself; ahaṃ asmī contracted to -hamasmī. Treated here as a set phrase rather than a true sandhi of two words.
sakkohamasmī.example_1: Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakko ‘‘ nāhaṃ, mahārāja, illiso, sakkohamasmī ’’ ti mahatiyā sakkalīlāya ākāse aṭṭhāsi.
sakkohamasmī.translation_1: At that moment, Sakka stood in the sky with great celestial majesty, saying, “Great King, I am not Illisa; I am Sakka.”

saṃvejayamānā.meaning_2: agitating; alarming; stirring up; causing a sense of urgency
saṃvejayamānā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle of the causative saṃvejeti (to agitate, to stir). Feminine nominative singular agreeing with devadhītā in the text.
saṃvejayamānā.example_1: Atha naṃ ekā devadhītā rukkhakkhandhavivare ṭhatvā saṃvejayamānā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –
saṃvejayamānā.translation_1: Then a certain devī, standing in a hollow in a tree trunk and agitating him, uttered the first verse:

saṃvejento.meaning_2: agitating; alarming; stirring up; causing a sense of urgency
saṃvejento.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Masculine nominative singular agreeing with Sakka; causative of √vij, here in the sense of frightening or stirring someone to a sense of urgency.
saṃvejento.example_1: Sakko devarājā ‘‘ ime saṃvejessāmī ’’ ti suko hutvā tesaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā ekasmiṃ rukkhe nilīyitvā te saṃvejento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –
saṃvejento.translation_1: Sakka, the king of the gods, thinking, “I will agitate them,” became a parrot, came to their dwelling place, and hiding in a tree, he agitated them and uttered the first verse:

vanibbinoti.meaning_2: causes to split; makes burst open; takes away
vanibbinoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Rare form; no sentences found in the source, so the analysis is uncertain. Possibly a denominative or causative verb; could also be a sandhi (vani + bbinoti) or a misreading.

hārayinti.meaning_2: causes to remove; causes to take away
hārayinti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Probably hāraya + ti with -nti sandhi, or an emphatic -i ending; 3rd singular present causative, first person aorist also possible (hārayiṃ).

massuyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular massuyā in the text, referring to the crow's beard; the related entry gives the same gender (na).
massuyā.example_1: 139. ‘‘ Tvaññeva maṇinā channo, sukatāya ca massuyā;
massuyā.translation_1: “You indeed are suited by that gem and by that well-trimmed beard;
massuyā.example_2: Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – samma vāyasa, tvaññeva imassa maṇino anucchaviko imissā ca sukatāya massuyā, mama pana tava adassanameva piyaṃ, tasmā taṃ āmantayitvā gacchāmīti.
massuyā.translation_2: This was said: ‘Indeed, friend crow, you yourself are appropriate for this gem and for this well-done beard; but for me, your absence is pleasant, therefore, having addressed you, I go.’

tuṇḍilaṃ.meaning_2: Tuṇḍila; name of a pig; name of a man
tuṇḍilaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text, listed among names of persons or beings. Formed from tuṇḍa with the suffix -ila (one with a good snout).

sāhasiyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Variant of sāhasika; feminine instrumental singular sāhasiyā in the text, modifying taṇhāya.
sāhasiyā.example_1: Evanti evaṃ paṇḍito rājāpi asāhasaṃ sāhasiyā taṇhāya vasaṃ agacchanto agatigamanaṃ pahāya raṭṭhaṃ apīḷetvā upacikānaṃ vammikavaḍḍhananiyāmena madhukarānaṃ reṇuṃ gahetvā madhukaraṇaniyāmena ca dhanaṃ saṅgharanto –
sāhasiyā.translation_1: “So too” means that a wise king, not falling under the power of aggressive craving without violence, having abandoned wrong paths, and without oppressing the realm, collecting wealth by the method of ants growing their anthill, and by the method of bees taking pollen to make honey—

saravaraveganiddhutanti.meaning_2: pierced by the speed of the arrow; struck by the swiftness of the shaft
saravaraveganiddhutanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The printed text and the guide read niddhutanti = niddhuta + anti, the -nt present participle of niddhunāti; lemma_1 follows the masculine -nta stem. The guide's analysis treats sara as 'blade reed' and vara as the adjective 'excellent', but here sara is more likely 'arrow' in a compound describing speed.

konāmosīti.meaning_2: what is your name?; who are you named?
konāmosīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of ko nāma asi, with -ti (iti) enclitic in the text. Interrogative asking a person's name.

sūpitaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text, agreeing with bhikkhaṃ. From sūpa (curry) with the kicca suffix -ita; Peu leaves the root unstated.
sūpitaṃ.translation_1: 16. “Come inside, young man, taking your seasoned food;

sūpitanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Occurs as sūpitanti = sūpitaṃ + iti in the commentary, with the final consonant doubled before -ti. The PEU entry connects it with sūpa (sauce, curry) and compares it to pupphita; it is probably a past participle meaning 'seasoned, cooked with sauce'.

palibujjhitvā.meaning_2: having been entangled; having got caught; having twisted around
palibujjhitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive from palibujjhati (pari + √bhuj 2, passive sense 'to be entangled, be twisted'). The prefix pari appears as pali- by assimilation. Describes the feet caught in a creeper.
palibujjhitvā.example_1: Siṅgālo ‘‘ appossukkā hohi, āharissāmi te ’’ ti nadītīre caranto valliyā pāde palibujjhitvā anutīrameva agamāsi.
palibujjhitvā.translation_1: The jackal said: ‘Be at ease, I will bring it to you.’ Walking on the river bank, having entangled his feet with a creeper, he went along the bank.

āyurañca.meaning_2: Āyura; name of one of the king's wise ministers
āyurañca.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name. In the text āyurañca = āyuraṃ + ca, accusative singular in sandhi. Not to be confused with āyura as a form of āyus (life).
āyurañca.example_1: Bodhisatto ‘‘ imassa rañño byādhi natthi, bhariyaṃ pana apassanto cetasikarogena phuṭṭho, upāyena taṃ tikicchissāmī ’’ ti āyurañca pukkusañcāti dve rañño paṇḍitāmacce āmantetvā ‘‘ rañño deviyā adassanena cetasikaṃ rogaṃ ṭhapetvā añño rogo natthi, bahūpakāro ca kho pana amhākaṃ rājā, tasmā upāyena naṃ tikicchāma, rājaṅgaṇe samajjaṃ kāretvā asiṃ gilituṃ jānantena asiṃ gilāpetvā rājānaṃ sīhapañjare katvā samajjaṃ olokāpessāma, rājā asiṃ gilantaṃ disvā ‘ atthi nu kho ito aññaṃ dukkarataran ’ ti pañhaṃ pucchissati.
āyurañca.translation_1: The Bodhisatta thought, “This king has no illness, but not seeing his wife, he is touched by mental sickness; I will cure him by a means.” So, having addressed the two wise ministers of the king, Āyura and Pukkusa, he said, “There is no other sickness for the king, except for mental sickness due to not seeing the queen; and indeed, the king is very helpful to us, therefore we will cure him by a means. We will make a gathering in the royal courtyard, and having caused a man who knows how to swallow a sword to swallow a sword, we will place the king on the lion-balcony and cause him to observe the gathering. The king, seeing the man swallowing a sword, will ask the question, ‘I wonder if there is anything more difficult than this?’”

āyura.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name, vocative singular in the text (samma āyura).
āyura.example_1: Taṃ samma āyura, tvaṃ ‘ asukaṃ nāma dadāmīti vacanaṃ ito dukkarataran ’ ti byākareyyāsi, tato samma pukkusa, taṃ pucchissati, athassa tvaṃ ‘ mahārāja, dadāmīti vatvā adadato sā vācā aphalā hoti, tathārūpaṃ vācaṃ na keci upajīvanti na khādanti na pivanti, ye pana tassa vacanassānucchavikaṃ karonti, yathāpaṭiññātamatthaṃ dentiyeva, idaṃ tato dukkarataran ’ ti evaṃ byākareyyāsi, ito paraṃ kattabbaṃ ahaṃ jānissāmī ’’ ti vatvā samajjaṃ kāresi.
āyura.translation_1: “Friend Ayura, you should answer, ‘The statement, “I give such and such a thing,” is more difficult than this.’ Then, friend Pukkusa, he will ask you, and you should answer him, ‘Great King, for one who says, “I give,” but does not give, that word is fruitless; no one lives, nor eats, nor drinks by such a word. But those who act in accordance with that word and indeed give the thing as promised, this is more difficult than that.’ Having said, ‘After this, I will know what is to be done,’ he arranged a gathering.

āyuraṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A proper name (Yādicchakanāma). Accusative singular in the text: the king questions Āyura.
āyuraṃ.example_1: Rājā taṃ disvā ‘‘ ayaṃ puriso etaṃ asiṃ gilati,‘ atthi nu kho ito aññaṃ dukkarataran ’ ti ime paṇḍite pucchissāmī ’’ ti cintetvā āyuraṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –
āyuraṃ.translation_1: The king, seeing him, thought, “This man is swallowing this sword. ‘I wonder if there is anything more difficult than this?’ I will ask these wise ones.” Having thought this, inquiring from Ayura, he uttered the first verse:

āyuro.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a man in the Jātaka commentary. Nominative singular in the text.
āyuro.example_1: 41. ‘‘ Byākāsi āyuro pañhaṃ, atthaṃ dhammassa kovido;
āyuro.translation_1: “Ayura answered the question, skilled in the meaning of the Dhamma;
āyuro.translation_2: “Āyura answered the question, and Pukkusa the man too;

parisaṇṭhāsi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist used in the text: parisaṇṭhāsi, meaning 'settled down' (referring to the stomach). Third person singular.
parisaṇṭhāsi.example_1: Tassevaṃ cintentassa padumapatte udakabindu viya sabbasoko nivattitvā gato, taṅkhaṇaññevassa kucchi parisaṇṭhāsi.
parisaṇṭhāsi.translation_1: As he thought thus, all his grief departed, rolling away like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. At that very moment, his stomach settled down.

pasannapañcapasādāni.meaning_2: with pure fivefold confidence; whose five senses are clear
pasannapañcapasādāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of pasanna + pañcapasādi (neuter plural accusative) or a compound with an added -āni ending; in the text it qualifies akkhīni (eyes).
pasannapañcapasādāni.example_1: Tasmiṃ khaṇe mahāsatto pasannapañcapasādāni akkhīni ummīletvā samantato parisaṃ olokento taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ disvā cintesi ‘‘ ettakā parisā somanassajātā sādhukāraṃ datvā dhammaṃ suṇanti, ayaṃ paneko brāhmaṇo domanassappatto rodati, etassa abbhantare assujananasamatthena sokena bhavitabbaṃ, tamassa ambilena paharitvā tambamalaṃ viya padumapalāsato udakabinduṃ viya vinivattetvā ettheva naṃ nissokaṃ tuṭṭhamānasaṃ katvā dhammaṃ desessāmī ’’ ti.
pasannapañcapasādāni.translation_1: At that moment, the Great Being, opening his eyes, clear with the five graces, surveyed the assembly all around. Seeing that brahmin, he thought: “This entire assembly, overcome with joy, gives applause and listens to the Dhamma. But this one brahmin, having attained dejection, is crying. There must be sorrow within his interior capable of producing tears. I will teach him the Dhamma, making him free from grief and with a pleased mind, by striking that sorrow with an acid-like teaching, distinguishing it like copper rust, or like a drop of water from a lotus leaf.”

vettanaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Glossed as vettanaṃ in the text. The sentence discusses the reading vetanan (vettanaṃ), so this may be a variant spelling of vetana; accusative singular in the text.
vettanaṃ.translation_1: Regarding this, vetanam means wage, or this is indeed the reading.

aṭṭhisenajātakavaṇṇanā.meaning_2: commentary on the Aṭṭhisena birth story
aṭṭhisenajātakavaṇṇanā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Title heading a section of the Jātaka commentary; nominative singular. Name of the eighth jātaka commentary in this collection.
aṭṭhisenajātakavaṇṇanā.translation_1: 8. Commentary on the Aṭṭhisena Birth Story
aṭṭhisenajātakavaṇṇanā.translation_2: The Commentary on the Aṭṭhisena Jātaka is the eighth.

aṭṭhisena.meaning_2: Aṭṭhisena; name of a brahmin (a former birth of the Buddha)
aṭṭhisena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name, used in direct address (vocative) in all three sentences. Analyzed as aṭṭhi + sena, though the name's origin is uncertain.
aṭṭhisena.example_1: 54. ‘‘ Yeme ahaṃ na jānāmi, aṭṭhisena vanibbake;
aṭṭhisena.translation_1: 54. ‘‘Aṭṭhisena, those beggars whom I do not know,
aṭṭhisena.example_2: Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ayya, aṭṭhisena, yeme vanibbake ahaṃ nāmagottajātikulappadesena ‘‘ ime nāmete ’’ tipi na jānāmi, te maṃ samāgantvā icchiticchitaṃ yācanti, tvaṃ pana kasmā maṃ kiñci na yācasīti.
aṭṭhisena.translation_2: This was stated thus: ‘‘Master Aṭṭhisena, those beggars, whom I do not know by name, clan, birth, family, or region (thinking, ‘These are their names’), they come together to me and ask for whatever they desire. But you, why do you not ask me for anything?’’

nāmetetipi.meaning_2: causes to bend; bends; makes bow
nāmetetipi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The -ti is doubled in nāmetetipi (nāmeti + iti + pi); the sandhi adds iti and the emphatic pi. Causative of namati.

vedituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of the causative vedeti, used with jānituṃ and arahati. The sandhi form veditumarahati = vedituṃ + arahati.
vedituṃ.example_1: Dhīro ca veditumarahatīti upaṭṭhāko pana dhīro paṇḍito gilānakāle ca agilānakāle ca yena yenattho, taṃ sabbaṃ sayameva vedituṃ jānituṃ arahati.
vedituṃ.translation_1: And a wise one should know what is appropriate (dhīro ca veditumarahati) means: but a wise, astute attendant should himself know and understand everything that is needed, both when sick and when not sick.
vedituṃ.example_2: ‘‘ yopi suhadayo mitto vā amitto vā appañño sappaññopi vā yo anatthavā anatthacaro, sopi guyhaṃ vedituṃ nārahate ’’ ti.
vedituṃ.translation_2: “Whether it be a good-hearted friend or an enemy, an unwise person or even a wise one, if they bring harm or act for what is not worthwhile, they are not worthy to know a secret.”

ekadoṇikanāvappamāṇaṃ.meaning_2: of the size of a single-hulled boat; as big as a one-hulled canoe
ekadoṇikanāvappamāṇaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it occurs in the accusative (masc and nt) agreeing with attabhāvaṃ, sarīraṃ and sappavaṇṇaṃ. doṇikā is a small trough-shaped boat; ekadoṇikā nāvā is a boat with a single hull. Some editions read ekaṃ doṇināvaṃ pamāṇaṃ.
ekadoṇikanāvappamāṇaṃ.example_1: Gaṅgeyyo nāgarājā ‘‘ ime ucchiṭṭhakaṃ mama upari khipantī ’’ ti kujjhitvā ‘‘ sabbe te jane gahetvā gaṅgāya osīdāpessāmī ’’ ti mahantaṃ ekadoṇikanāvappamāṇaṃ attabhāvaṃ māpetvā udakaṃ bhinditvā phaṇaṃ dhārayamāno tesaṃ abhimukho pāyāsi.
ekadoṇikanāvappamāṇaṃ.translation_1: The Nāga king Gaṅgeyyo, angered that “these people are throwing their leftovers upon me,” and thinking, “I will take all these people and make them sink in the Ganges,” created a huge body the size of a single-hulled boat, broke through the water, raised his hood, and advanced facing them.
ekadoṇikanāvappamāṇaṃ.example_2: Bodhisattassa sarīraṃ mahantaṃ ekadoṇikanāvappamāṇaṃ vaṭṭetvā ṭhapitasumanapupphadāmaṃ viya jiñjukaphalasannibhehi akkhīhi jayasumanapupphasadisena ca sīsena samannāgataṃ ativiya sobhati.
ekadoṇikanāvappamāṇaṃ.translation_2: The Bodhisatta’s body was large, the size of a single trough-shaped canoe, and having coiled itself, it was exceedingly beautiful, like a placed jasmine garland, endowed with eyes resembling crab’s eye berries and a head like an oleander flower.

ahosīnti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Form is ahosi + iti, the quotative particle joined by sandhi. 3rd singular aorist of hoti.

abbhañjāpetvā.grammar: caus of abbhañjati; abs of abbhañjāpeti
abbhañjāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to be anointed; having had (someone) smear (with oil)
abbhañjāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive (gerund) form of the causative verb abbhañjāpeti. In the sentence it is part of a series of absolutives describing the king's actions: he had the monkey's body anointed with oil. The base verb is abbhañjati, 'anoints, smears', from abhi + √añj 2. The ṇāpe sign marks the causative. The Dictionary of Pāli gives abbhañjāpetvā as an absolutive of abbhañjāpeti, a causative of abbhañjati.
abbhañjāpetvā.example_1: So pabhātāya rattiyā mahāsattassa tussitvā ‘‘ na yuttaṃ imaṃ kapirājānaṃ nāsetuṃ, upāyena naṃ otāretvā paṭijaggissāmī ’’ ti antogaṅgāya nāvāsaṅghāṭaṃ ṭhapetvā tattha aṭṭakaṃ bandhāpetvā saṇikaṃ mahāsattaṃ otārāpetvā piṭṭhiyaṃ kāsāvavatthaṃ pattharāpetvā gaṅgodakena nhāpetvā phāṇitodakaṃ pāyetvā parisuddhasarīraṃ sahassapākatelena abbhañjāpetvā sayanapiṭṭhe eḷakacammaṃ santharāpetvā saṇikaṃ tattha nipajjāpetvā attanā nīce āsane nisīditvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –
abbhañjāpetvā.translation_1: When the night had dawned, he, having been pleased with the Great Being, thought, “It is not suitable to destroy this king of monkeys. I will bring him down by some means and take care of him.” Thus, having placed the rafts of boats inside the Ganges, and having caused a platform to be bound there, he gently caused the Great Being to come down, had a yellow robe spread on his back, caused him to be bathed with Ganges water, caused him to drink sugared water, had his cleansed body anointed with oil refined a thousand times, caused a goat skin to be spread on the bedding, and gently caused him to lie down there. He himself, sitting on a low seat, uttered the first verse:

bhaggavi.meaning_2: Bhaggavī; name of a female potter; (vocative) O Bhaggavī
bhaggavi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A feminine counterpart of bhaggava (potter), used as a vocative address in the Jātaka verse. The form as it stands is vocative singular; treatment as an indeclinable vocative would be an alternative.
bhaggavi.example_1: Ahampi eko carissāmi bhaggavi, hitvāna kāmāni yathodhikānī ’’ ti.
bhaggavi.translation_1: I too, Bhaggavi, will wander alone, having abandoned sensual desires as they are.’’

atiloṇakaṃ.meaning_2: with too much salt; over-salted; too salty
atiloṇakaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular neuter agreeing with bhattaṃ (rice) in the list of ways it was cooked. The -ka is a secondary suffix; the simplex atiloṇa has the same meaning.
atiloṇakaṃ.example_1: Aparabhāge tesu thokaṃ vaḍḍhitvā attano ayānayajānanasamatthataṃ sampattesu tesaṃ vīmaṃsanatthaṃ ekadivasaṃ bhattaṃ pacanto thokaṃ uttaṇḍulaṃ paci, ekadivasaṃ thokaṃ kilinnaṃ, ekadivasaṃ supakkaṃ, ekadivasaṃ atikilinnaṃ, ekadivasaṃ aloṇakaṃ, ekadivasaṃ atiloṇakaṃ.
atiloṇakaṃ.translation_1: After a time, when they had grown a little and reached the ability to know what was proper and improper for themselves, for the purpose of examining them, one day, while cooking rice, he cooked a little raw, one day a little sodden, one day well-cooked, one day excessively sodden, one day devoid of salt, and one day with too much salt.

atiloṇakanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form in the text has the quotation or clause marker -ti (atiloṇakan-ti), which is left out. Means 'too salty', possibly a bahubbīhi adjective rather than a neuter noun.

āmapakkaloṇikaatiloṇikāni.meaning_2: knowing (the difference between) raw and cooked, salted and over-salted; able to judge raw and cooked, salted and too salty food
āmapakkaloṇikaatiloṇikāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A dvanda compound of four adjectives used as a neuter plural substantive: 'things raw and cooked, salted and over-salted' (āma + pakka + loṇika + atiloṇika). Accusative plural in the text. The children can tell raw food from cooked and salted from over-salted, i.e. they know their way around food.
āmapakkaloṇikaatiloṇikāni.example_1: Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto ‘‘ āma, tātā ’’ ti vatvā cintesi ‘‘ ime dārakā idāni āmapakkaloṇikaatiloṇikāni jānanti, attano dhammatāya jīvituṃ sakkhissanti, mayā pabbajituṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti.
āmapakkaloṇikaatiloṇikāni.translation_1: Having heard that, the Bodhisatta said, ‘‘Yes, my children,’’ and thought, ‘‘These children now know what is raw and cooked, salty and excessively salty. They will be able to live by their own nature. It is proper for me to go forth.’’

sallakkhāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to observe; having made consider; having caused to perceive
sallakkhāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive from the causative of sallakkheti. In the text it means 'having made (Udena) consider (my virtues)'.
sallakkhāpetvā.example_1: Idāni pana me mahallakakāle kammaṃ nittharituṃ asamatthakāle sabbaṃ taṃ parihāraṃ acchindi, anāthā nippaccayā hutvā araññe ketakāni khādantī jīvāmi, aññaṃ mayhaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ natthi, udenaṃ mama guṇaṃ sallakkhāpetvā porāṇakaparihāraṃ me paṭipākatikaṃ kāretha bhagavā ’’ ti paridevamānā tathāgataṃ yāci.
sallakkhāpetvā.translation_1: Now, however, in my old age, when I am unable to perform service, he has taken back all those honors. Having become unprotected and without support, I live in the wilderness eating ketaka fruits. I have no other refuge. Blessed One, please make Udena consider my virtues and restore my former honors to me!’ Thus, lamenting, she pleaded with the Tathāgata.

oṭṭhibyādhi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A yādicchakanāma (arbitrary proper name); nominative singular in the text. Sometimes written as two words oṭṭhi byādhi; here the elephant is called by the ailment she once had.
oṭṭhibyādhi.example_1: Tadā tassa rañño ekā oṭṭhibyādhi hatthinī thāmabalasampannā mahabbalā ahosi.
oṭṭhibyādhi.translation_1: Then that king had a certain she-elephant afflicted with a lip disease, endowed with vigor and strength, and of great might.
oṭṭhibyādhi.example_2: Rājā tassa kathaṃ sutvā ‘‘ amhākaṃ oṭṭhibyādhi kahan ’’ ti pucchi.
oṭṭhibyādhi.translation_2: The king, hearing that talk, asked, ‘Where is our she-elephant with the lip disease?’

nittharantī.meaning_2: accomplishes; carries out; completes; gets through
nittharantī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present 3rd plural nittharantī in the text, glossing vahantī together with it; from nī + √tar, with the t doubled after the prefix.
nittharantī.example_1: Tattha vahantīti dūteyyaharaṇaṃ saṅgāme balakoṭṭhakabhindanaṃ taṃ taṃ kiccaṃ vahantī nittharantī.
nittharantī.translation_1: Here, vahantī means carrying and accomplishing such duties as carrying messages and breaking down strongholds in battle.

nārādhayiṃ.meaning_2: did not please; did not satisfy; failed to win over
nārādhayiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Negated aorist 1st singular of ārādheti, with na joined by sandhi; parallel to paritosesiṃ in the sentence.
nārādhayiṃ.example_1: Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sace sāmi, ahaṃ imāni kiccāni karontī rañño daḷhadhammassa cittaṃ nārādhayiṃ na paritosesiṃ, ko dāni añño tassa cittaṃ ārādhayissatīti.
nārādhayiṃ.translation_1: This is said to be the meaning: ‘If, my lord, while performing these duties, I did not please or satisfy King Daḷhadhamma, then who else will now please his mind?’

pavīṇati.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text confined to the verse yāvatāsīsati tāvadeva pavīṇati and glossed bhajati sevati; 3rd singular present. The commentary derivation pa + vī + nā is doubtful.
pavīṇati.translation_1: 101. “As long as a person expects a return, just so long he serves (him);
pavīṇati.example_2: Tattha paṭhamagāthāya tāva attho – idhekacco aññāṇajātiko poso yāvatāsīsatī , yāva ‘‘ idaṃ nāma me ayaṃ kātuṃ sakkhissatī ’’ ti paccāsīsati, tāvadeva taṃ purisaṃ pavīṇati bhajati sevati, tassa pana atthāpāye vaḍḍhiyā apagamane parihīnakāle taṃ nānākiccesu patthitaṃ posaṃ ekacce bālā imaṃ oṭṭhibyādhiṃ ayaṃ khattiyo viya jahanti.
pavīṇati.translation_2: Here, the meaning of the first verse is this: a certain foolish person serves or cultivates that man just so long as he expects, ‘This one will be able to do this for me.’ But upon the cessation of benefit, at the decline of gain and the time of its deterioration, certain foolish people abandon that person, who was desired for various tasks, just like this aristocrat (abandoned) the Lip-disease (elephant).

oṭṭhibyādhiṃva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is accusative singular, oṭṭhibyādhiṃ, with the particle va (like) added: oṭṭhibyādhiṃva. The compound means literally 'lip-disease'. The story explains that the king abandoned the elephant when it became useless, like a man abandoning an elephant afflicted with a disease of the lip.
oṭṭhibyādhiṃva.translation_1: Upon the cessation of benefit, they abandon him, like an aristocrat (abandons) the Lip-disease (elephant).

manubujjhati.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is 3rd singular present. The sandhi is mano + bujjhati, with the vowel shortened before the verb; the meaning is 'understands, realises'.
manubujjhati.translation_1: 103. “Whoever, having previously received kindness and achieved his purpose, realizes (it);

abhipatthikā.meaning_2: longed for; desired; worthy of longing
abhipatthikā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the verse the form could also be read as nominative plural (patthikā as agreement with the relative ye). Here listed as the feminine/plural adjective from abhipatthita.
abhipatthikā.example_1: Atthā tassa pavaḍḍhanti, ye honti abhipatthikā.
abhipatthikā.translation_1: His benefits increase, all those that are longed for.

oṭṭhibyādhiṃ.meaning_2: lip-disease; name of a female elephant
oṭṭhibyādhiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of an elephant (yādicchakanāma) in the Jātaka commentary; accusative singular in the text.
oṭṭhibyādhiṃ.example_1: Tattha paṭhamagāthāya tāva attho – idhekacco aññāṇajātiko poso yāvatāsīsatī , yāva ‘‘ idaṃ nāma me ayaṃ kātuṃ sakkhissatī ’’ ti paccāsīsati, tāvadeva taṃ purisaṃ pavīṇati bhajati sevati, tassa pana atthāpāye vaḍḍhiyā apagamane parihīnakāle taṃ nānākiccesu patthitaṃ posaṃ ekacce bālā imaṃ oṭṭhibyādhiṃ ayaṃ khattiyo viya jahanti.
oṭṭhibyādhiṃ.translation_1: Here, the meaning of the first verse is this: a certain foolish person serves or cultivates that man just so long as he expects, ‘This one will be able to do this for me.’ But upon the cessation of benefit, at the decline of gain and the time of its deterioration, certain foolish people abandon that person, who was desired for various tasks, just like this aristocrat (abandoned) the Lip-disease (elephant).

oṭṭhibyādhiyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular in the text: "because of Oṭṭhibyādhi". A proper name of an elephant, not a literal illness; the feminine gender comes from the word's use as a name.
oṭṭhibyādhiyā.example_1: Taṃ sutvā rājā oṭṭhibyādhiyā yasaṃ paṭipākatikaṃ akāsi.
oṭṭhibyādhiyā.translation_1: Hearing that, the king restored the honors of the Lip-disease (elephant).

vacchitoti.meaning_2: will live; will dwell; will stay
vacchitoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text as vacchitoti = vacchati + iti, with -ti added twice through sandhi of the quotation particle. The PEU note suggests vacchita is a faulty form; the likely reading is the future of vasati. Could also be read as vacchita + iti if a participle is intended.

pavellati.meaning_2: sways; sways to and fro; moves gently
pavellati.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Occurs as the present participle pavellamānā (fem nom sg) in the text, describing a creeper swaying in a gentle breeze; the simplex vellati is also found.
pavellati.example_1: Kāḷappavāḷāva pavellamānāti yathā nāma taruṇakāle susamuggatā kāḷavallī pavāḷā vā hutvā mandavāteritā ito cito ca pavellati, evaṃ pavellamānā itthivilāsaṃ dassayamānā kumārikā palobhayantīva naresu gacchati.
pavellati.translation_1: Swaying like a black sprout (kāḷappavāḷāva pavellamānā) means, 'just as a well-grown black creeper or sprout in its youth, moved by a gentle breeze, sways hither and thither, so a maiden, swaying thus and displaying feminine charm, moves among men as if enticing them (palobhayantīva naresu gacchati).'

rajjuvālambanī.meaning_2: like a hanging rope; comparable to a dangling rope
rajjuvālambanī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A simile describing delight for one dwelling at home. Feminine nominative singular in the text, referring to rati.
rajjuvālambanī.example_1: 120. ‘‘ Rajjuvālambanī cesā, yā gehe vasato rati;
rajjuvālambanī.translation_1: “And this delight for one dwelling at home is like a hanging rope;
rajjuvālambanī.example_2: Rajjuvālambanī cesāti ca-kāro nipātamatto, ālambanarajju viya esāti attho.
rajjuvālambanī.translation_2: And this is like a hanging rope (rajjuvālambanī cesā): the particle ‘ca’ is merely a particle, and the meaning is, 'this is like a supporting rope.'

koṭasimbaliyaṃ.meaning_2: in the Koṭasimbali tree; at the Koṭasimbali (silk-cotton) tree
koṭasimbaliyaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular of koṭasimbali (nt) in the text; the final -aṃ is the locative ending, written here joined to the noun. Could also be read as koṭasimbali + iṃ.
koṭasimbaliyaṃ.example_1: Idhāpi satthā antokoṭisanthāre kāmavitakkābhibhūte pañcasate bhikkhū disvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā ‘‘ bhikkhave, āsaṅkitabbayuttakaṃ nāma āsaṅkituṃ vaṭṭati, kilesā nāma vaḍḍhantā vane nigrodhādayo viya rukkhaṃ, purisaṃ bhañjanti, teneva pubbepi koṭasimbaliyaṃ nibbattadevatā ekaṃ sakuṇaṃ nigrodhabījāni khāditvā attano rukkhassa sākhantare vaccaṃ pātentaṃ disvā ‘ ito me vimānassa vināso bhavissatī ’ ti bhayappattā ahosī ’’ ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.
koṭasimbaliyaṃ.translation_1: Here, too, the Teacher, seeing five hundred monks overwhelmed by sensual thoughts within the golden pavement, having assembled the community of bhikkhus, said: “Monks, it is proper to be suspicious of what is fit to be suspected. Defilements, like banyan trees and the like growing in a forest, destroy a man. For this very reason, even in the past, a deity born in the Koṭasimbali tree, seeing a certain bird that had eaten banyan seeds dropping excrement among the branches of her tree, became frightened and trembling, thinking, ‘From this, my mansion will be destroyed!’” Having said this, he recounted a story of the past.
koṭasimbaliyaṃ.example_2: Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto koṭasimbaliyaṃ rukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti.
koṭasimbaliyaṃ.translation_2: In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling the kingdom at Benares, the Bodhisatta became a tree deity born in the Koṭasimbali tree.

koṭasimbaliyā.meaning_2: of the Koṭasimbali tree; in the Koṭasimbali tree (a type of silk-cotton tree)
koṭasimbaliyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is a locative or ablative-type form used with sākhantare ('among the branches') — locative in sense. The compound is koṭa + simbali; the PEU gloss treats koṭasimbali as a kind of silk-cotton tree. The final -yā looks like the ā-stem oblique ending attached to the compound, but no full paradigm fits cleanly; the sandhi/derivation should be checked against a proper koṭasimbali entry.
koṭasimbaliyā.example_1: Tasmiṃ pana nigrodhe ekā sakuṇikā atthi, sā nigrodharukkhe vissaṭṭhe uppatitvā koṭasimbaliyā sākhantare nisīdi.
koṭasimbaliyā.translation_1: But in that banyan tree, there was a certain female bird. When the banyan tree was thrown away, she flew up and sat down among the branches of the Koṭasimbali tree.

pavedhantiyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine instrumental singular of the present participle. The form pavedhantiyā modifies tassā (she). Alternative analysis: present participle from pavedhati, with -ntī feminine ending.
pavedhantiyā.example_1: Tassā pavedhantiyā koṭasimbalīpi yāva mūlā pavedhi.
pavedhantiyā.translation_1: As she trembled, even the Koṭasimbali tree trembled down to its roots.

nivātajā.meaning_2: born in a wind-sheltered place; grown in shelter from the wind
nivātajā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the verse the form is the nominative plural nivātajā, referring to trees growing at the speaker's side, sheltered from the wind by its branches. The commentary explains it as nivāte jātā.
nivātajā.example_1: 124. ‘‘ Te rukkhā saṃvirūhanti, mama passe nivātajā;
nivātajā.translation_1: Those trees will grow at my sides, born in shelter from the wind.
nivātajā.example_2: Nivātajāti mama sākhāhi vātassa nivāritattā nivāte jātā.
nivātajā.translation_2: Born in shelter from the wind (nivātajā) means born in a wind-sheltered place because the wind is warded off by my branches.

saṃviruhissanti.meaning_2: will grow; will increase; will sprout
saṃviruhissanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Future 3rd plural of saṃvirūhati (compare the gloss saṃviruhissanti vaḍḍhissanti); the lemma is the present 3rd singular and lemma_2 repeats lemma_1 for the future verb.
saṃviruhissanti.translation_1: Will grow (saṃvirūhanti) means they will grow, they will increase.

pahūtaindhano.meaning_2: having much fuel; with plenty of firewood
pahūtaindhano.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of pahūta + indhano; glossed by pahūtejo and pahūtedho in the commentary. Nom sg describing aggī.
pahūtaindhano.translation_1: Therein, having much fuel (pahūtejo) means having much firewood.
pahūtaindhano.translation_2: Having much fuel (pahūtedho) means having much firewood/fuel.

makasaḍḍitāti.meaning_2: bitten by mosquitoes; tormented by mosquitoes
makasaḍḍitāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form makasaḍḍitāti is makasaḍḍitā + iti, nominative singular (or plural) of the adjective used as a noun. aḍḍita is past participle of aḍḍati (√add, afflict).

aniddāyitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Negative absolutive of niddāyati (√nid + āya). In the sentence it describes the lay follower keeping awake.
aniddāyitvā.example_1: Satthā ‘‘ na kho, upāsaka, tvaṃyeva aniddāyitvā jagganto visesaṃ labhi, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi jaggantā visesaṃ guṇaṃ labhiṃsū ’’ ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.
aniddāyitvā.translation_1: The Teacher, having said, 'Indeed, lay follower, it is not you alone who, keeping awake without sleeping, received a special state; ancient wise men too, keeping awake, obtained a special state, a virtue,' and being requested by him, recounted a story of the past.

nisnehāya.meaning_2: free from affection; without attachment; oil-less; dry
nisnehāya.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Glosses Sukkhāyā (dry) in the commentary. Dative singular in the text.

nisīdetvāti.meaning_2: having sat down; having taken a seat
nisīdetvāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form nisīdetvāti is nisīdetvā + iti; the entry is for the absolutive itself. Probably a variant or caus./denom. spelling of nisīditvā (from nisīdati); the -e- may reflect nisīdeti.

ukkhitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of ukkhipati (u + √khip + tvā, with the root-final p assimilated to t). The related entry ukkhitta is the past participle of the same verb. In the text it is part of an instruction: having lifted (them) up and hung (them), place (them).
ukkhitvā.translation_1: “Lift them up and hang them there.”

anikkhamitvā.meaning_2: not having gone out; not having exited; without coming out
anikkhamitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Negative absolutive of nikkhamati. Used in prose to express 'without going out'. Appears in all three sentences with the same sense.
anikkhamitvā.example_1: So ‘‘ sādhu, devā ’’ ti mahāsatto parisaṃ gahetvā sapattarañño ṭhitadvārena anikkhamitvā aññaṃ dvāraṃ vivaritvā nikkhami.
anikkhamitvā.translation_1: That Great Being, saying, “Very well, Sire,” took his assembly and, without exiting by the gate where the hostile king was positioned, opened another door and departed.
anikkhamitvā.example_2: So ‘‘ idheva me annapānañca sayanañca nipphannaṃ, aññattha kiṃ karissāmī ’’ ti cintetvā tattheva abhirato bahi anikkhamitvā antokucchiyaṃyeva vasi.
anikkhamitvā.translation_2: He thought, “Here indeed my food, drink, and bedding are perfectly supplied; what would I do elsewhere?” Delighting in that very place, he did not come out, but lived inside the belly.

vaṅgītipi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Form is vaṅgīti + pi (enclitic) → vaṅgītipi; entry is for the main word. Compound of unclear history, possibly vaṅga + iti ('so the song'), sometimes written vaṅgīti. Feminine ī-stem; here nominative or accusative.

vippaṭipajjitvā.meaning_2: having behaved wrongly (towards); having misconducted oneself (towards); having acted improperly (towards)
vippaṭipajjitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of vippaṭipajjati; in the text with "mātari", meaning "having misconducted himself towards your mother".
vippaṭipajjitvā.example_1: ‘‘ Ayaṃ me pitā ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ nāyaṃ tava pitā, pitā pana te bārāṇasirājā, ayaṃ tumhākaṃ dāso, so mātari te vippaṭipajjitvā imasmiṃ ṭhāne tava pitaraṃ māretvā nikhaṇī ’’ ti aṭṭhīni nīharitvā dassesi.
vippaṭipajjitvā.translation_1: When told, “This is my father,” he said, “This is not your father; your father was the king of Benares. This man is your slave; having acted wrongly toward your mother, he killed and buried your father in this place,” and he pulled out the bones and showed them to him.

ismiṃyeva.meaning_2: in this very; in this exact
ismiṃyeva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the locative singular of ima with the emphatic eva. Locative in the text, modifying titthe.
ismiṃyeva.example_1: ‘‘ Yaṃ te ismiṃyeva titthe pitu tena kataṃ, taṃ karohī ’’ ti sabbaṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhitvā kumāraṃ katipāhaṃ tharugaṇhanaṃ sikkhāpesi.
ismiṃyeva.translation_1: “Do to him what he did to your father at this very bathing place,” he said; and having told the whole story, he taught the prince how to grasp a sword-hilt for a few days.

sākhamakampayi.meaning_2: that matter was declared by the one who shook the bough
sākhamakampayi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of sākhaṃ (nt, acc sg of sākha) + akampayi (aor of kampati, caus). The aorist form akampayi causes the bough to shake. Quote from verse; the word is the second person singular aorist.
sākhamakampayi.example_1: Akkhātaṃ nūna taṃ tena, yo taṃ sākhamakampayi.
sākhamakampayi.translation_1: Surely that matter was declared by the one who shook the bough.

vissāsetvā.meaning_2: having made confident; having reassured; having gained the trust of
vissāsetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of vissāseti; in the sentence it takes pitaraṃ as object. Also spelt vissāsayitvā in other texts.
vissāsetvā.example_1: Avañci pitaraṃ mamāti tvaṃ mama pitaraṃ ‘‘ nhāyituṃ gacchāmā ’’ ti vissāsetvā nhāyantaṃ māretvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chinditvā nikhaṇitvā ‘‘ sace koci jānissati, mayhampi evarūpaṃ bhayaṃ āgacchissatī ’’ ti vañcesi, idaṃ kho pana maraṇabhayaṃ idāni tavāgatanti.
vissāsetvā.translation_1: The phrase ‘you deceived my father’ (avañci pitaraṃ mamā) means that you deceived my father by making him confident, saying, ‘‘Let us go to bathe,’ and while he was bathing, you killed him, cut him into pieces, buried him, [and thought], ‘If anyone finds out, such fear will come to me too.’ But now this fear of death has come to you.

ujjhāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to find fault; having irritated; having provoked; having startled
ujjhāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of ujjhāpeti (from √jhā with the causative *āpe and the prefix u). In the first sentence it means 'having provoked, having irritated'; in the second, 'having startled, having alarmed' the deities.
ujjhāpetvā.example_1: ‘‘ imaṃ mahallikaṃ ujjhāpetvā puttassa paṭikūlaṃ kāressāmī ’’ ti.
ujjhāpetvā.translation_1: ‘‘I will irritate this old woman and make her disagreeable to her son.’
ujjhāpetvā.example_2: Evañca pana vatvā paṇḍito māṇavo pitaraṃ attano vacanaṃ gāhāpetuṃ asakkonto mahantena saddena devatā ujjhāpetvā ‘‘ evarūpena pāpakārinā saddhiṃ na gamissāmī ’’ ti pitu passantasseva palāyitvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmaloke uppajji.
ujjhāpetvā.translation_2: And having spoken thus, the wise youth, unable to make his father accept his words, startled the deities with a loud voice, and saying, “I will not go with such a sinner,” fled away in his father's sight, entered the Himalayas, went forth, developed direct knowledge and attainments, and without losing his jhāna, was reborn in the Brahma world.

uposako.meaning_2: lay follower who observes the uposatha precepts; one keeping the sabbath
uposako.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text. Denotes one who observes the eight precepts on uposatha days.
uposako.example_1: Athekadivasaṃ so uposako dhammassavanatthāya jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi.
uposako.translation_1: Then one day, that lay follower, having gone to Jeta’s Grove to hear the Dhamma, saluted the Teacher and sat down to one side.

miyyatī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Third person singular present of marati with passive/irregular -īya- stem; occurs in verse. The sandhi -tī dhammavaro shows the following word begins with dh-.
miyyatī.example_1: Sahassanetto atulānubhāvo, na miyyatī dhammavaro kadācī ’’ ti.
miyyatī.translation_1: The thousand-eyed one of incomparable power—the noble Right never dies.”

nivutthaghuṇapāṇako.meaning_2: woodworm living in (a hole); insect dwelling in (dry wood)
nivutthaghuṇapāṇako.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text (kaṇṇikāyaṃ ... nivutthaghuṇapāṇako); the compound describes a worm lodging in the pinnacle of the palace. nivuttha = past participle of nivāseti/nivisati, 'dwelt in; lodged'.
nivutthaghuṇapāṇako.example_1: Tadā bārāṇasirājā sirisayane nisinno aḍḍharattasamaye aṭṭha sadde assosi – paṭhamaṃ rājanivesanasāmantā uyyāne eko bako saddamakāsi, dutiyaṃ tasmiṃ sadde anupacchinneyeva hatthisālāya toraṇanivāsinī kākī saddamakāsi, tatiyaṃ rājagehe kaṇṇikāyaṃ nivutthaghuṇapāṇako saddamakāsi, catutthaṃ rājagehe posāvaniyakokilo saddamakāsi, pañcamaṃ tattheva posāvaniyamigo saddamakāsi, chaṭṭhaṃ tattheva posāvaniyavānaro saddamakāsi, sattamaṃ tattheva posāvaniyakinnaro saddamakāsi, aṭṭhamaṃ tasmiṃ sadde anupacchinneyeva rājanivesanamatthakena uyyānaṃ gacchanto paccekabuddho ekaṃ udānaṃ udānento saddamakāsi.
nivutthaghuṇapāṇako.translation_1: Then, the King of Benares, seated on a royal couch at midnight, heard eight sounds: First, a crane in a garden near the royal residence made a sound (saddamakāsi). Second, without interruption (anupacchinneyeva) after that sound, a female crow residing on the archway of the elephant stables made a sound (saddamakāsi). Third, a woodworm (ghuṇapāṇako) residing in the pinnacle (kaṇṇikāyaṃ) of the royal palace made a sound (saddamakāsi). Fourth, a tame (posāvaniya) cuckoo in the royal palace made a sound (saddamakāsi). Fifth, a tame (posāvaniya) deer in the same place made a sound (saddamakāsi). Sixth, a tame (posāvaniya) monkey there made a sound (saddamakāsi). Seventh, a tame (posāvaniya) kinnara (kinnaro) there made a sound (saddamakāsi). Eighth, without interruption (anupacchinneyeva) after that sound, a private Buddha, passing over the roof of the royal residence to the garden, made a sound (saddamakāsi) by making an inspired utterance.

ghuṇapāṇako.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text. ghuṇa is a woodworm or weevil, pāṇaka a (small) living being.
ghuṇapāṇako.example_1: ‘‘ Pāsādakaṇṇikāya pana te, mahārāja, eko ghuṇapāṇako vasati.
ghuṇapāṇako.translation_1: ‘‘But, Great King, on the pinnacle of your palace, a certain woodworm dwells.

ghuṇoti.meaning_2: eats away; bores into (wood); destroys (like woodworm)
ghuṇoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] No sentences available; form not in the related entries. Probably a denominative of ghuṇa (woodworm, insect in wood). The only PEU entry related is the noun ghuṇa, and its English is confused; this entry is a guess and needs checking against the text.

phegguyā.meaning_2: softwood; sapwood; the soft outer wood of a tree
phegguyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine instrumental singular phegguyā in the text ('as far as the extent of that softwood'). Treated here as a neuter u-stem; some sources class it as masculine.
phegguyā.example_1: Tattha yāva tassā gatī ahūti yāva tassā phegguyā nipphatti ahosi, sā sabbā khāditā.
phegguyā.translation_1: In this regard, ‘as far as its reach extended’ (yāva tassā gatī ahu) means, ‘as far as the extent of that softwood was, all of it was eaten.’

bāhikoti.meaning_2: foreigner; one living in another country
bāhikoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The -ti in the text is the quotative enclitic; the entry is for bāhika. The PEU treats it as an adjective; here taken as a masculine noun.

āvajissaṃ.meaning_2: will return (to); will go back (to); will resort (to)
āvajissaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] First person singular āvajissaṃ (future of āvajjati, negated with na: 'I shall not return'). Thematic class; the future stem is āvajissa-.
āvajissaṃ.example_1: Tassattho – jātiyā khayantasaṅkhātassa nibbānassa diṭṭhattā jātikhayantadassī ahaṃ asaṃsayaṃ puna gabbhaseyyaṃ na āvajissaṃ, ayaṃ me antimā jāti, pacchimā gabbhaseyyā, khīṇo me punabbhavāya khandhapaṭipāṭisaṅkhāto saṃsāroti.
āvajissaṃ.translation_1: Its meaning is: “Because I have seen Nibbāna, which is called the end of birth, I am one who sees the end of birth (jātikhayantadassī); I shall without a doubt (asaṃsayaṃ) not return again to conception in a womb. This is my final birth, my last conception in a womb; for me, saṃsāra—which is the succession of the aggregates—is exhausted for any future existence.”

āṇisadaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text (āṇisadaṃ paharitvā, struck him on the hip); uncertain first element, possibly āṇi (nail, pin) with sada (seat). PEU suggests āṇi + sada + a.
āṇisadaṃ.example_1: Coro rajjuṃ kūpe otāresi, atha naṃ onamitvā udakaṃ osiñcantaṃ mahabbaladāsī ubhohi hatthehi āṇisadaṃ paharitvā kūpe khipitvā ‘‘ na tvaṃ ettakena marissasī ’’ ti ekaṃ mahantaṃ iṭṭhakaṃ matthake āsumbhi.
āṇisadaṃ.translation_1: The thief let down the rope into the well. Then, as he was bending down to draw the water, the very strong bondswoman struck him on the hip and pushed him into the well. “You will not die by so much,” she said, and let a large brick fall (āsumbhi) on his head.

sulasāya.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a courtesan. Genitive singular in the text (sulasāya = "of Sulasā"). The PEU suggests the name means "she who has fine reddish cloth". The second meaning in PEU, a courtesan of Bārāṇasī, is probably a different story; here the Rājagaha Sulasā is meant.
sulasāya.example_1: Coro tiṇṇaṃ catunnaṃ māsānaṃ accayena cintesi ‘‘ ahaṃ imasmiṃyeva ṭhāne vasituṃ na sakkhissāmi, tucchahatthena palāyitumpi na sakkā, sulasāya piḷandhanabhaṇḍaṃ satasahassaṃ agghati, sulasaṃ māretvā idaṃ gaṇhissāmī ’’ ti.
sulasāya.translation_1: After three or four months, the thief thought, “I will not be able to stay in this one place; it is also not possible to flee empty-handed. Sulasā’s ornaments are worth a hundred thousand. I will kill Sulasā and take this.”

balipātiṃ.meaning_2: offering bowl; sacrificial dish; plate for oblations
balipātiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text (balipātiṃ). Compound of bali (offering) + pāti (bowl, dish).
balipātiṃ.example_1: So tāya ‘‘ sādhū ’’ ti sampaṭicchito taṃ balipātiṃ ukkhipāpetvā sayaṃ sannaddhapañcāvudho hutvā pabbatamatthakaṃ abhiruhitvā ekaṃ sataporisapapātaṃ nissāya jātarukkhamūle balibhājanaṃ ṭhapāpetvā ‘‘ bhadde, nāhaṃ balikammatthāya āgato, taṃ pana māretvā piḷandhanaṃ te gahetvā gamissāmīti āgatomhi, tava piḷandhanaṃ omuñcitvā uttarasāṭakena bhaṇḍikaṃ karohī ’’ ti āha.
balipātiṃ.translation_1: Having received her agreement, he had the offering-platter carried up, while he himself, well-equipped with five weapons, climbed to the mountaintop. Near a precipice a hundred times as high as a man, he placed the offering-vessel at the foot of a tree and said: “Good lady, I have not come for the sake of an offering. I have come with the intention of killing you, taking your adornments, and going away. Having taken off your adornments, make a bundle (bhaṇḍikaṃ) with your upper garment (uttarasāṭakena).”

vicintikāti.meaning_2: having nothing to think about; free from worry
vicintikāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Formed with the negative prefix vi- and the suffix -ika; the text form vicintikāti is vicintika + iti. The reading is doubtful.

avekkhiya.meaning_2: having looked at; having considered; having discerned
avekkhiya.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -iya (variant of -tvā) of avekkhati. In the text it is used absolutely in the sense of having considered or discerned something for oneself.
avekkhiya.example_1: Tadāyamatthoti sayaṃ avekkhiya, athassa daṇḍaṃ sadisaṃ nivesaye.
avekkhiya.translation_1: then, having discerned for himself, ‘This indeed is the meaning [of the matter],’ he should then impose a punishment appropriate to the offense.
avekkhiya.translation_2: 18. “Himself, with people in the family well-managed, having looked at his own wealth,

upāyaso.meaning_2: by skilful means; through strategy; by method
upāyaso.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text upāyaso is glossed by upāyakosallena. Appears alongside ñāyena; the form looks like an adverbial ending -so from upāya. Perhaps sandhi of upāyaso with a following word, but it is entered here as an indeclinable.
upāyaso.example_1: 35. ‘‘ Evaṃ sunītena subhāsitena, dhammena ñāyena upāyaso nayaṃ;
upāyaso.translation_1: 35. ‘‘Thus, by proper guidance and well-spoken words, by Dhamma, by justice, and by skillful means, guiding [the kingdom],

upāyasoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The -ti is the quotative particle (iti), not part of the word; it sandhi-joins to the final -o. The form in the text is nominative singular.

ajjuposathiko.meaning_2: observing the Uposatha today; having today's Uposatha observance
ajjuposathiko.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of ajja (today) and uposathika (observing the Uposatha); the sandhi ajju- stands for ajja-u-. Nominative singular in the quotation, addressed to the Bodhisatta.
ajjuposathiko.example_1: Bodhisatto kālasseva uṭṭhāya kammantaṃ agamāsi,‘‘ ajjuposathiko bhaveyyāsī ’’ ti tassa koci nārocesi.
ajjuposathiko.translation_1: The Bodhisatta rose early and went to work. No one had informed him, ‘You should observe the Uposatha today.’

kasāvarattanivāsano.meaning_2: wearing a reddish-brown garment; wearing a dyed (kasāya) cloth
kasāvarattanivāsano.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Descriptive bahubbīhi compound of kasāvaratta + nivāsana, used of Nāgabala. Nominative singular in the text.
kasāvarattanivāsano.example_1: Nāgabalo bhatiko cha yojanāni atikkamma majjhanhikasamaye vītaccikaṅgārasanthataṃ viya uṇhaṃ vālukaṃ maddanto dhanalobhena haṭṭhapahaṭṭho kasāvarattanivāsano kaṇṇe tālapaṇṇaṃ piḷandhitvā ekena āyogavattena gītaṃ gāyanto rājaṅgaṇena pāyāsi.
