kasāvarattanivāsano.translation_1: The wage-earner, strong as an elephant, having passed over six leagues at midday, treading on hot sand that was like coals spread without flame, overjoyed by greed for wealth, wearing a reddish-brown garment and a palm-leaf in his ear, went along the royal courtyard, singing a song in pursuit of his purpose.

laṅghituṃ.meaning_2: to leap; to fly; to traverse (the sky)
laṅghituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of laṅghati. In the text it depends on na sakkhissasi: 'you will not be able to leap into the sky'.
laṅghituṃ.example_1: Tattha bhūmiyaṃ tiṭṭhāti bhūmiyaṃyeva patiṭṭha, puna ākāsaṃ laṅghituṃ na sakkhissasīti attho.
laṅghituṃ.translation_1: Here, stay on the ground (bhūmiyaṃ tiṭṭha) means, ‘Be established solely on the ground; you will not be able to traverse the sky again.’

patva.meaning_2: having reached; having arrived (at); having attained; having come to
patva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the verse the sandhi form patva stands for patvā before pariyāyaṃ; the gloss explains it as kālapariyāyaṃ patvā. Alternative analysis as absolutive of a hypothetical pappoti/pāpuṇāti.
patva.example_1: Pāvekkhi pathaviṃ cecco, hīnatto patva pariyāyaṃ.
patva.translation_1: That wretch entered the earth, reduced to a base state, having reached his appointed time.”
patva.example_2: Patva pariyāyanti attano kālapariyāyaṃ patvā pathaviṃ pāvisīti attho.
patva.translation_2: “Having reached his appointed time” (patva pariyāyaṃ) means having reached his own appointed time, he entered the earth.

jhāmasukkhakūro.meaning_2: burnt dry food; scorched dry crust
jhāmasukkhakūro.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text, listed among poor quality foods. The third element is doubtful; possibly a variant of kūla or a word for a morsel or scrap.
jhāmasukkhakūro.example_1: Āhāropi uḷuṅkapiṭṭhena ghaṭṭitā bhinnasitthakayāgu vā pūtisukkhakhajjakaṃ vā jhāmasukkhakūro vā pāpuṇāti, yāpanapamāṇaṃ na hoti.
jhāmasukkhakūro.translation_1: His food, too, was either gruel of broken rice grains scooped by the back of a ladle, or putrid dry hard food, or burnt dry food bits. It was not enough for sustenance.

meṇḍissaro.meaning_2: Meṇḍissara; name of a sage; name of a former birth of Kassapa
meṇḍissaro.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a sage (isi) in the Jātaka commentary, identified with Kassapa. Nominative singular in the text.
meṇḍissaro.example_1: Meṇḍissaro nāma isi pajjotakapañcālarañño vijite kalabbacūḷakaṃ nāma nigamaṃ nissāya anekasahassaisiparivāro vasi.
meṇḍissaro.translation_1: A sage named Meṇḍissara dwelt near a town called Kalabbacūḷaka, in the realm of King Pajjotapañcāla, surrounded by countless thousands of sages.
meṇḍissaro.example_2: Tadā nārado ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu ahosi, nagarasobhiṇī purāṇadutiyikā, sālissaro sāriputto, meṇḍissaro kassapo, pabbato anuruddho, kāḷadevilo kaccāyano, anupiyo ānando, kisavaccho mahāmoggallāno, sarabhaṅgo pana ahameva ahosinti.
meṇḍissaro.translation_2: At that time, Nārada was the discontented bhikkhu. The city’s beauty was the former wife. Sālissara was Sāriputta. Meṇḍissara was Kassapa. Pabbata was Anuruddha. Kāḷadevala was Kaccāna. Anupiya was Ānanda. Kisavaccha was Mahāmoggallāna. And Sarabhaṅga was I indeed.”

kalabbacūḷakaṃ.meaning_2: name of a town; name of a village
kalabbacūḷakaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text, the object of nissāya. The first element kalabba is uncertain.
kalabbacūḷakaṃ.example_1: Meṇḍissaro nāma isi pajjotakapañcālarañño vijite kalabbacūḷakaṃ nāma nigamaṃ nissāya anekasahassaisiparivāro vasi.
kalabbacūḷakaṃ.translation_1: A sage named Meṇḍissara dwelt near a town called Kalabbacūḷaka, in the realm of King Pajjotapañcāla, surrounded by countless thousands of sages.

meṇḍissaraṃ.meaning_2: name of a person; name of an ascetic
meṇḍissaraṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a companion of the Bodhisatta at the Kapiṭṭhaka hermitage. Accusative singular in the text.
meṇḍissaraṃ.example_1: So ‘‘ netaṃ pahātuṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti sālissaraṃ ānesi, meṇḍissaraṃ ānesi, pabbatampi ānesi.
meṇḍissaraṃ.translation_1: He thought, “It is not proper to abandon him.” So he brought Sālissara, he brought Meṇḍissara, and he also brought Pabbata.
meṇḍissaraṃ.example_2: Bodhisatto meṇḍissaraṃ āmantetvā,‘‘ meṇḍissara, tvaṃ imaṃ isigaṇaṃ ādāya suraṭṭhajanapadassa sīmantare sātodikā nāma nadī atthi, tassā tīre vasāhī ’’ ti uyyojesi, puna kapiṭṭhakaassamo paripūri.
meṇḍissaraṃ.translation_2: The Bodhisatta addressed Meṇḍissara, saying, “Meṇḍissara, taking this company of ascetics, dwell on the bank of the Sātodikā River, which is located in the border region of Suraṭṭha country.” He dismissed him, and again the Kapiṭṭhaka hermitage was filled.

paṭihanitukāmo.meaning_2: wishing to prevent; wanting to obstruct; desiring to ward off
paṭihanitukāmo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive paṭihanituṃ (to prevent; to obstruct) + kāma (desire). Nominative singular agreeing with the addressee; in the text it qualifies taṃ (you).
paṭihanitukāmo.example_1: Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – nārada, na heva vatthukāmapatthanāya dhammā cavitumarahasi, ekasmiṃ anatthe uppanne taṃ paṭihanitukāmo nānatthā na atthenapi kāraṇabhūtena dhammā cavitumarahasi,‘‘ asuko nāma me attho uppajjissatī ’’ ti evampi atthakāraṇāpi na dhammā cavitumarahasi, kataṃ pana nipphāditaṃ jhānasukhaṃ niraṃkatvā vināsetvā neva dhammā cavitumarahasīsi.
paṭihanitukāmo.translation_1: This means, Nārada, you should not indeed fall from righteousness for the aspiration for sensual objects. When a certain harm arises, even if desiring to overcome it, you should not fall from righteousness for unbeneficial things, nor even for a reason of benefit. Even for a reason of benefit, thinking “such and such a benefit will arise for me,” you should not fall from righteousness. And having discarded and destroyed the accomplished jhāna-happiness, you should certainly not fall from righteousness.

analasyachekakusalabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ.meaning_2: called the state of being diligent, expert, and skilful
analasyachekakusalabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Long bahubbīhi compound describing dakkhaṃ in the Jātaka prose; accusative singular agreeing with dakkhaṃ.
analasyachekakusalabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ.example_1: Tattha dakkhaṃ gahapatīti nārada gharāvāsaṃ vasantānaṃ gahapatīnaṃ bhoguppādanatthāya analasyachekakusalabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ dakkhaṃ nāma sādhu, dakkhabhāvo bhaddako.
analasyachekakusalabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ.translation_1: In this regard, the phrase skill for a householder means, Nārada, that the skill—which is the state of being unlazy, expert, and proficient—is good for householders dwelling in the household life for the purpose of producing wealth. The state of being skillful is auspicious.

māmiva.meaning_2: like me; as (you would do) to me
māmiva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of maṃ (accusative of ahaṃ) with iva. Alternative split: mama + iva. In the verse māmiva depends on pappoti, 'comes to (destruction) like me'.
māmiva.translation_1: 66. “O Sivi, you will come to destruction, just like me, as if falling into the hands of enemies.

māmivāti.meaning_2: like me, just as (I); so to me
māmivāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of maṃ (me, accusative of amhaṃ) + iva (like, as) + iti (quotation particle). Alternative analysis: mā + iva + iti. No context was supplied, so the analysis is uncertain; the -āti suggests a following -iti rather than the word mā.

nagarasobhiṇī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of nagara and the feminine agent noun sobhiṇī (from √subh). Used for a beautiful courtesan. Nominative singular in the text.
nagarasobhiṇī.example_1: Tadā nārado ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu ahosi, nagarasobhiṇī purāṇadutiyikā, sālissaro sāriputto, meṇḍissaro kassapo, pabbato anuruddho, kāḷadevilo kaccāyano, anupiyo ānando, kisavaccho mahāmoggallāno, sarabhaṅgo pana ahameva ahosinti.
nagarasobhiṇī.translation_1: At that time, Nārada was the discontented bhikkhu. The city’s beauty was the former wife. Sālissara was Sāriputta. Meṇḍissara was Kassapa. Pabbata was Anuruddha. Kāḷadevala was Kaccāna. Anupiya was Ānanda. Kisavaccha was Mahāmoggallāna. And Sarabhaṅga was I indeed.”
nagarasobhiṇī.example_2: Bārāṇasiyañca ekā nagarasobhiṇī vaṇṇadāsī abhirūpā ahosi sobhaggappattā.
nagarasobhiṇī.translation_2: And in Benares, there was a certain city courtesan who was shapely and possessed of beauty and charm.

nagarasobhiṇiyāyeva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form is nagarasobhiṇiyā (a feminine ā-stem instrumental/dative/genitive singular) + yeva, with the sandhi -ā + y- > -āy-. The sentence means 'I will go to the city courtesan's house itself.'
nagarasobhiṇiyāyeva.example_1: So rājakulā nikkhamitvā ‘‘ idāni gehaṃ gantvā āgamanavelā natthi, nagarasobhiṇiyāyeva gehaṃ gamissāmī ’’ ti upaṭṭhāke uyyojetvā ekakova tassā gehaṃ pāvisi.
nagarasobhiṇiyāyeva.translation_1: He, having exited the royal palace, thought, “Now there is no time to go home and return; I shall go to the city courtesan’s house itself,” and having sent away his attendants, he entered her house all alone.

nagarasobhiṇiyāpi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The word in the text is nagarasobhiṇiyā + api with sandhi. It is instrumental singular.
nagarasobhiṇiyāpi.translation_1: And the city courtesan’s deeds became public throughout the city.

kumudinī.meaning_2: lotus-pond; pond full of kumuda lotuses; water-lily lake
kumudinī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the Jātaka verse the Ganges is called kumudinī, a pond covered with kumuda lotuses (compare kumudasarā in the prose explanation). Nominative singular in the text.
kumudinī.example_1: Gaṅgā kumudinīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi.
kumudinī.translation_1: The Teacher, dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, related this discourse, referring to a certain dissatisfied bhikkhu, beginning with the words: “Ganges, a lotus-tank...”
kumudinī.example_2: 77. ‘‘ Gaṅgā kumudinī santā, saṅkhavaṇṇā ca kokilā;
kumudinī.translation_2: “When the Ganges is a calm lotus-tank, and cuckoos are conch-coloured;

gaṇacāriṇī.meaning_2: moving in a group; swarming; frequenting a group
gaṇacāriṇī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine form of gaṇacārī, used as an adjective describing makkhikā (flies) in the text. Alternative construction gaṇa + cara + ṇī.
gaṇacāriṇī.translation_1: “When swarms of flies, having drunk a pot of liquor;

kulakoti.meaning_2: beginning of a family; first generation of a family
kulakoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Not in the provided sentences; PEU gives thī (feminine). Locative singular or other case form may appear as kulakoṭiyā etc. Sometimes the compound may be interpreted as masc.

vipphandatova.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text vipphandatova = vipphandati + eva, 'even while quivering'; the -ti has become -to before the emphatic eva, and the form describes the panther's writhing while trying to catch the ewe. The related PEU entry connects it to √phand with vi, but the DPD sign *e or other analyses are also possible.
vipphandatova.example_1: Sāpi ito cito ca olokentī taṃ disvā ‘‘ esa maṃ māretvā khāditukāmatāya ṭhito, sace nivattitvā palāyissāmi, jīvitaṃ me natthi, ajja mayā purisakāraṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti cintetvā siṅgāni ukkhipitvā tassa abhimukhaṃ vegena pakkhanditvā dīpikassa ‘‘ ito gaṇhissāmi, ito gaṇhissāmī ’’ ti vipphandatova gahaṇaṃ anupagantvā vegena palāyitvā eḷakānaṃ antaraṃ pāvisi.
vipphandatova.translation_1: She, looking hither and thither, saw him and thought: “This one is standing here with the desire to kill and eat me. If I turn back and flee, my life is lost. Today it is proper for me to act heroically.” Having thought thus, she lifted up her horns and swiftly leaped towards him. Without falling into the panther’s grasp, even as he was quivering with the thought “I will seize her here, I will seize her here,” she swiftly fled and entered among the goats.

sāmhīti.meaning_2: I am (one) who is calm; I am a self-controlled person
sāmhīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of samo + asmi, with -ti appended; possibly a quotation or word-play in the text. Uncertain segmentation; the final -iti is taken as the quotative particle.

sabbhiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental plural of santa (sabbhi is the contracted form sadbhi/sabbhi). The gloss in the text is sundaraṃ subhāsitaṃ, but contextually it means the virtuous.
sabbhiṃ.example_1: Nikkamaṃ duṭṭhe yuñjetha, so ca sabbhiṃ na rañjatī ’’ ti.
sabbhiṃ.translation_1: One should apply effort against the wicked, for he does not delight in the virtuous.”
sabbhiṃ.example_2: So ca sabbhiṃ na rañjatīti so pana puggalo sabbhiṃ sundaraṃ subhāsitaṃ na rañjati, na piyāyatīti attho.
sabbhiṃ.translation_2: ‘For he does not delight in the virtuous’ (so ca sabbhiṃ na rañjatī) means that person does not delight in beautiful, well-spoken words with the virtuous, nor does he desire them – that is the meaning.

anvāvamaddīti.meaning_2: crushes by stepping on; tramples down; crushes and kills
anvāvamaddīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Ends in -ti, which may be the quotation particle -ti rather than part of the verb; if so the headword is anvāvamaddi, aorist 3rd singular of anvāvamaddati. The PEU guide analyses it as a causative (anu + ā + ava + madda + a + ti) meaning 'to crush by stepping on, bite and kill'.

papātī.meaning_2: flying high; one who leaps high; falling from a height
papātī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is an accusative singular qualifying jānaṃ? Actually variant of papātinaṃ; explained as 'ucce papātī ayaṃ'. The same passage has papātin, so papātī may be a feminine or a scribal variant.
papātī.example_1: Jānaṃ uccaṃ papātinanti ‘‘ putto te atiuccaṃ ṭhānaṃ laṅghatī ’’ ti sutvā ‘‘ ucce papātī ayan ’’ ti jānanto.
papātī.translation_1: Knowing him to be one who flies to great heights (jānaṃ uccaṃ papātinaṃ) means knowing “this one flies high” after hearing “your son jumps to a very high place.”

acchanditvā.meaning_2: having been unwilling (to); having no desire (for); having renounced the will (to)
acchanditvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the sentence brahmadattena ... rajjaṃ acchanditvā: 'Brahmadatta, having no desire for (i.e. having taken by force) the kingdom'. The PEU analysis (na + chanda + ita) supports the privative reading; the form appears to be a negative absolutive in -itvā.
acchanditvā.example_1: Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatto nāma kāsirājā ahosīti brahmadattena dīghītissa kosalarañño rajjaṃ acchanditvā aññātakavesena vasantassa māritabhāvañceva dīghāvukumārena attano jīvite dinne tato paṭṭhāya tesaṃ samaggabhāvañca kathetvā ‘‘ tesañhi nāma, bhikkhave, rājūnaṃ ādinnadaṇḍānaṃ ādinnasatthānaṃ evarūpaṃ khantisoraccaṃ bhavissati.
acchanditvā.translation_1: “Once upon a time, monks, there was a king of Kāsī named Brahmadatta at Benares”—having told how Brahmadatta, having usurped the kingdom of King Dīghīti of Kosala, and killed him while he was dwelling in an unknown form, and how from that time on they were in concord when Prince Dīghāvu gave his life to him—“indeed, monks, for such kings, who had taken up rods and taken up weapons, there will be such patience and gentleness.

yime.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the relative pronoun ye with the demonstrative ime; in the text na yime sukarā means 'these are not easy'. Alternatively could be read as ye + ime or as the demonstrative ime with an attached particle; the relative sense fits the context.
yime.example_1: Idha kho taṃ, bhikkhave, sobhetha, yaṃ tumhe evaṃ svākkhāte dhammavinaye pabbajitā samānā khamā ca bhaveyyātha soratā cā ’’ ti ovaditvā dutiyampi tatiyampi ‘‘ alaṃ, bhikkhave, mā bhaṇḍanan ’’ ti vāretvā anoramante disvā ‘‘ pariyādiṇṇarūpā kho ime moghapurisā, na yime sukarā saññāpetun ’’ ti pakkamitvā punadivase piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto gandhakuṭiyā thokaṃ vissamitvā senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā attano pattacīvaramādāya saṅghamajjhe ākāse ṭhatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –
yime.translation_1: Here, indeed, monks, it would be fitting for you, having gone forth in such a well-proclaimed Dhamma and discipline, to be tolerant and gentle”—having thus exhorted them, and having stopped them a second time and a third time saying, “Enough, monks, no quarreling!” and seeing that they did not cease, he departed, saying, “Indeed, these foolish men are like those possessed, they are not easy to convince.” On the next day, when he had come back again from his round for alms, having rested a little while in his perfumed chamber, and having put his lodging in order, taking his own bowl and robe, having stood in the sky in the midst of the Saṅgha, he declared these verses:

rākārassa.meaning_2: the syllable rā; the letter rā
rākārassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Grammatical term used in the commentary on the shortening of rā to ra. Genitive singular in the text.
rākārassa.example_1: Vācāgocarabhāṇinoti rā-kārassa rassādeso kato, vācāgocarā ca na satipaṭṭhānādiariyadhammagocarā, bhāṇino ca.
rākārassa.translation_1: Speaking only what they want to say (vācāgocarabhāṇino) means that the ‘rā’ syllable has been shortened; they are speakers (only) within the range of speech, and not within the range of noble Dhamma like mindfulness and so on.

mantiādikaṃ.meaning_2: beginning with the consultation; starting with the counsel
mantiādikaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound with the suffix ādika ('beginning with'). Accusative singular neuter in the text, agreeing with a neuter noun. No sentence context provided, so the meaning is inferred from the compound parts; manti is likely the noun 'consultation, counsel'; less likely a sandhi of manta + ādika.

ākoṭiyamāno.meaning_2: being beaten; being struck; being buffeted; being hammered
ākoṭiyamāno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Passive causative present participle, masculine nominative singular agreeing with rukkho. Describes the stump being beaten by the wind.
ākoṭiyamāno.example_1: Rukkho khāṇukamatto hutvā chiddāvachiddo vāte paharante ākoṭiyamāno viya aṭṭhāsi.
ākoṭiyamāno.translation_1: The tree, having become a mere stump, full of holes, stood as if being buffeted when the wind was blowing.

sākhavā.meaning_2: having branches; endowed with branches; full of branches
sākhavā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Vocative singular in the verse, glossed by the commentary as sākhasampanno. Some editions read sākhāvā.
sākhavā.example_1: So sākhavā phalimā saṃvirūḷho, madhutthiko tiṭṭhatu sobhamāno ’’ ti.
sākhavā.translation_1: may that tree, rich in branches and fruit, grown luxuriantly, and full of honey-sweet fruit, stand shining.”
sākhavā.translation_2: In that regard, sākhavā means “endowed with branches.”

upabhuñjimhā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 1st person plural of upabhuñjati (upa + bhuñjati). The reading upabhuñjimhā is unusual; the standard aorist 1st plural would be upabhuñjimha. The PEU lists it under upabhuñjimhā but the form in the text is upabhuñjimhā.
upabhuñjimhā.translation_1: 31. “We have enjoyed its fruit for many countless years;

opattamaphalaṃ.meaning_2: without leaves and fruit; leafless and fruitless
opattamaphalaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Commentarial compound, accusative singular qualifying rukkhaṃ; variant of opattaphalita. o + patta (fallen) with a- linking and phala.
opattamaphalaṃ.translation_1: 32. “The dry tree, withered, devoid of leaves and fruitless;

pañhapaṭipañhāpi.meaning_2: question and counter-question; questions and answers
pañhapaṭipañhāpi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it carries the emphatic -pi (pañhapaṭipañhāpi) and is nominative plural, subject of veditabbā; the related entry treats it as an adjective meaning 'asking and answering'.
pañhapaṭipañhāpi.example_1: Pañhapaṭipañhāpi atthopi purimanayeneva veditabbā, anuttānapadameva pana vaṇṇayissāma.
pañhapaṭipañhāpi.translation_1: Both the questions and answers, and the meaning, should be known in the same way as the previous method; but we will explain only the unclear words.

opattanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Probably ava + patati with vowel assimilation (o-). Related PEU entry opatta seems to be a different, adjective analysis (ava + patta, 'without leaves'); the verb reading fits opattanti in a prose Jātaka.

abhisiñcayīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Form abhisiñcayi (aorist 3rd singular) + iti. The context and gloss confirm the meaning 'sprinkled'. 3rd singular aorist.
abhisiñcayīti.example_1: Amatamādāyāti attano ānubhāvena ṭhito gaṅgodakaṃ gahetvā abhisiñcayīti attho.
abhisiñcayīti.translation_1: Amatamādāyā means, “standing by his own power, taking Ganges water, he sprinkled.”

anuvicinituṃ.meaning_2: to search for; to investigate; to examine
anuvicinituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive expressing purpose after vaṭṭati. The form is from anuvicināti (anuvicināti); the PEU split anu + vi + ci + nā + tuṃ supports this. The sandhi anuvicinituṃ for anuvicinātuṃ is common.
anuvicinituṃ.example_1: Rājā ajānanto viya hutvā bodhisattaṃ pakkosāpetvā ‘‘ tāta, rājanivesanato bahuratanabhaṇḍaṃ haṭaṃ, handa naṃ anuvicinituṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti āha.
anuvicinituṃ.translation_1: The king, having pretended as if not knowing, summoned the Bodhisatta and said, ‘Dear child, much jewel-treasure has been taken from the royal residence. Come, it is proper to search for it.’

parigantvā.meaning_2: having gone around; having circled; having traversed
parigantvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of parigacchati (pari + √gam). In the text it describes circling the royal compound and the pond three times. The form is parigantvā (with -tvā suffix, -tvāna variant).
parigantvā.example_1: So ‘‘ sādhu, devā ’’ ti vatvā mātaraṃ vanditvā mantaṃ parivattetvā mahātale ṭhitova ‘‘ mahārāja, dvinnaṃ corānaṃ padaṃ paññāyatī ’’ ti vatvā rañño ca purohitassa ca padānusārena sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā tato nikkhamitvā pāsādā oruyha rājanivesanantare tikkhattuṃ parigantvā padānusāreneva pākārasamīpaṃ gantvā pākāre ṭhatvā ‘‘ mahārāja, imasmiṃ ṭhāne pākārato muccitvā ākāse padaṃ paññāyati, nisseṇiṃ attharāpetvā dethā ’’ ti nisseṇiṃ pākāramatthakena otaritvā padānusāreneva vinicchayasālaṃ gantvā puna rājanivesanaṃ āgantvā nisseṇiṃ attharāpetvā pākāramatthakena oruyha pokkharaṇiṃ gantvā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā ‘‘ mahārāja, corā imaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ otiṇṇā ’’ ti vatvā attanā ṭhapitaṃ viya bhaṇḍikaṃ nīharitvā rañño datvā ‘‘ mahārāja, ime dve corā abhiññātamahācorā iminā maggena rājanivesanaṃ abhiruḷhā ’’ ti āha.
parigantvā.translation_1: He said, ‘Very well, Great King!’ and venerated his mother. Having recited the charm, he stood on the great platform and said, ‘Great King, the tracks of two robbers are evident!’ Then, following the tracks of both the king and the priest, he entered the royal closet. Exiting from there, he descended from the palace, circled three times within the royal compound by following the tracks, and then went to the vicinity of the wall. Standing on the wall, he said, ‘Great King, in this place, leaving the wall, tracks are evident in the sky. Have a ladder set up and give it to me!’ Having had a ladder set up over the top of the wall, he descended by it, and by following the very tracks, he went to the judgment hall. Again, returning to the royal residence, he had a ladder set up over the top of the wall and descended by it. Having gone to the pond, he circumambulated it three times and said, ‘Great King, the robbers descended into this pond!’ Then, drawing out the bundle as if he had placed it there himself, he gave it to the king and said, ‘Great King, these two robbers are well-known great robbers who ascended the royal residence by this path.’

vāditvā.meaning_2: having played (a musical instrument); having made sound; having caused to sound
vāditvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of the causative vādeti, 'to play (an instrument)'; in the text paired with naccitvā and gāyitvā.
vāditvā.example_1: So ekasmiṃ ussavadivase bhariyamādāya bārāṇasiṃ pavisitvā naccitvā vīṇaṃ vāditvā gāyitvā dhanaṃ labhitvā ussavapariyosāne bahuṃ surābhattaṃ gāhāpetvā attano gāmaṃ gacchanto nadītīraṃ patvā navodakaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā bhattaṃ bhuñjanto suraṃ pivanto nisīditvā matto hutvā attano balaṃ ajānanto ‘‘ mahāvīṇaṃ gīvāya bandhitvā nadiṃ uttaritvā gamissāmī ’’ ti bhariyaṃ hatthe gahetvā nadiṃ otari.
vāditvā.translation_1: On a certain festival day, taking his wife, he entered Benares. Having danced, played the lute, and sung, he received money. At the end of the festival, having obtained much liquor and food, he was going to his own village. Having arrived at the river bank, he saw fresh water coming, and sat down eating the meal and drinking the liquor. Having become drunk and not knowing his own strength, he said, ‘I shall go, having tied my great lute around my neck and having crossed the river!’ Then, taking his wife by the hand, he descended into the river.

nipīḷeti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Third person singular present, causative/transitive in form. In the sentence the subject (a goddess?) is crushing the speaker's head. Some eds. read nippīḷeti.
nipīḷeti.example_1: Sā me sīsaṃ nipīḷeti, jātaṃ saraṇato bhayan ’’ ti.
nipīḷeti.translation_1: That crushes my head; fear has arisen from my refuge.”

nipīḷetīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form has the quotative -ti attached (nipīḷeti + iti); the entry is for the verb. Causative in form, active 3rd singular.

yāpanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] 3rd person plural present of causative yāpeti, from √yā. In the text, yāpanti means 'they sustain life' (by that food).
yāpanti.translation_1: “By which, when eaten, many brahmins and khattiyas maintain life;

sampiyāyitvā.meaning_2: having treated kindly; having shown affection (to); having made friends (with)
sampiyāyitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The prefix saṃ- before p- doubles to samp- with the conjunct appearing as piyāy-; the text has ¬tvā (absolutive) formed from the denominative/causative sampiyāyati. In the sentence it governs sassuṃ in the accusative: 'having shown affection to her mother-in-law'.
sampiyāyitvā.example_1: Sā pubbabhāge sassuṃ sampiyāyitvā pacchā puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhamānā taṃ nīharitukāmā ahosi.
sampiyāyitvā.translation_1: She, at first having shown affection to her mother-in-law, later, as her sons and daughters grew up, desired to drive her away.

paribhinditvā.meaning_2: having broken; having split; having shattered; having slandered; having defamed
paribhinditvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of paribhindati in -itvā. Used figuratively in both sentences in the sense of slandering or defaming someone to another (with the dative/genitive).
paribhinditvā.example_1: Sā sāmikassa santike sassuyā nānappakāraṃ dosaṃ vatvā paribhinditvā ‘‘ ahaṃ te mātaraṃ posetuṃ na sakkomi, mārehi nan ’’ ti vatvā ‘‘ manussamāraṇaṃ nāma bhāriyaṃ, kathaṃ naṃ māremī ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ niddokkamanakāle naṃ mañcakeneva saddhiṃ gahetvā susumāranadiyaṃ khipissāma, atha naṃ susamārā khādissantī ’’ ti āha.
paribhinditvā.translation_1: She, having spoken various kinds of fault concerning her mother-in-law in the presence of her husband, and having slandered her, said, “I am not able to support your mother; kill her!” And when he was told, “Killing a human is indeed a serious matter; how shall I kill her?” she said, “At the time of falling asleep, we will take her together with the bed itself and throw her into the crocodile river. Then the alligators will eat her.”
paribhinditvā.example_2: ‘‘ bodhiparibbājakassa vinicchinanakālato paṭṭhāya mayaṃ kiñci na labhāma, handa naṃ ‘ rājaveriko ’ ti vatvā rañño antare paribhinditvā mārāpessāmā ’’ ti.
paribhinditvā.translation_2: "From the time Bodhi the wandering ascetic began judging, we get nothing at all. Come, having called him 'the king's enemy' and slandered him to the king, we will cause him to be killed."

susamārā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text susamārā is a variant spelling of susumārā, nominative plural acting as the subject of khādissanti. The related PEU entries susamaṇa and susama are unrelated.
susamārā.example_1: Sā sāmikassa santike sassuyā nānappakāraṃ dosaṃ vatvā paribhinditvā ‘‘ ahaṃ te mātaraṃ posetuṃ na sakkomi, mārehi nan ’’ ti vatvā ‘‘ manussamāraṇaṃ nāma bhāriyaṃ, kathaṃ naṃ māremī ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ niddokkamanakāle naṃ mañcakeneva saddhiṃ gahetvā susumāranadiyaṃ khipissāma, atha naṃ susamārā khādissantī ’’ ti āha.
susamārā.translation_1: She, having spoken various kinds of fault concerning her mother-in-law in the presence of her husband, and having slandered her, said, “I am not able to support your mother; kill her!” And when he was told, “Killing a human is indeed a serious matter; how shall I kill her?” she said, “At the time of falling asleep, we will take her together with the bed itself and throw her into the crocodile river. Then the alligators will eat her.”

paribbajanaṃ.meaning_2: wandering; homeless wandering (of an ascetic); mendicant life
paribbajanaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text, glossing the life of a pabbajita. Compare paribbājaka; here the -j- (not -jj-) suggests derivation from paribbajati.
paribbajanaṃ.example_1: Sāyeva jīvikāti pabbajitassa mattikāpattaṃ ādāya paragharāni upasaṅkamitvā āhārapariyesanajīvikāva yasadhanalābhato sataguṇena sahassaguṇena varatarāti attho api rajjena taṃ varanti taṃ anagārassa sato aññaṃ avihiṃsantassa paribbajanaṃ sakalajambudīparajjenapi varanti attho.
paribbajanaṃ.translation_1: Sāyeva jīvikā means that the livelihood of seeking food by taking a clay bowl and approaching others’ houses for one who has gone forth is a hundred times, a thousand times better than the gain of fame and wealth. And api rajjena taṃ varaṃ means that the wandering of one who is homeless and does not harm another is better even than the kingship of the entire Jambudīpa.

ayājayīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The -ti is the quotative enclitic, split off in the entry as ayājayi. Third singular aorist of the causative yājati (to cause to sacrifice, to officiate at a sacrifice); the sentence is not available, so the form is identified from the word alone.

viddhaṃsāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to be destroyed; having caused to be demolished; having caused to be ruined
viddhaṃsāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of viddhaṃsāpeti (causative of viddhaṃsati). In the text it refers to causing a sacrificial pit and alms-halls to be destroyed. The form is indeclinable.
viddhaṃsāpetvā.example_1: So evaṃ vatvā kasiṇaṃ samannāharitvā naṭṭhaṃ visesaṃ uppādetvā ākāse pallaṅkena nisīditvā rañño dhammaṃ desetvā ‘‘ appamatto hohī ’’ ti ovaditvā yaññāvāṭaṃ viddhaṃsāpetvā mahājanassa abhayadānaṃ dāpetvā rañño yācantasseva uppatitvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gantvā yāvajīvaṃ ṭhatvā āyupariyosāne brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.
viddhaṃsāpetvā.translation_1: Having said thus, he concentrated on the kasiṇa, re-established the special state he had lost, sat cross-legged in the sky, taught the Dhamma to the king, exhorted him saying “Become diligent!”, caused the sacrificial pit to be destroyed, caused a gift of fearlessness to be given to the great populace, and even while the king was still requesting, he leapt up and went to his very dwelling place. Having remained there all his life, at the end of his life he was destined for the Brahma world.
viddhaṃsāpetvā.example_2: Taṃ pavattiṃ rucāya dhātiyo sutvā rājadhītāya ārocayiṃsu ‘‘ ayye, pitarā kira te ājīvakassa kathaṃ sutvā micchādassanaṃ gahitaṃ, so kira catūsu nagaradvāresu dānasālāyo viddhaṃsāpetvā parapariggahitā itthiyo ca kumārikāyo ca pasayhakārena gaṇhituṃ āṇāpeti, rajjaṃ na vicāreti, kāmamattoyeva kira jāto ’’ ti.
viddhaṃsāpetvā.translation_2: When the nurses heard that news, they informed the princess: ‘Lady, it is said that your father has heard the discourse of a charlatan and adopted wrong views; he has ordered the destruction of alms-halls at the four city gates, and he is ordering the seizure of women and maidens by force; he does not govern the kingdom, it is said he has become engrossed in sensual pleasure.’

loṇiyateliyāni.meaning_2: prepared with salt and oil; seasoned with salt and oil; cooked with salt and oil
loṇiyateliyāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Neuter nominative plural in the text, agreeing with annāni. The PEU suggests comparison with salt and oil ("compared with salt and oil"); the sense in the Jātaka verse is more likely food seasoned or dressed with salt and oil. Doubtful formation; loṇiya and teliya may be adjectives from loṇa and tela.
loṇiyateliyāni.example_1: 74. ‘‘ Ahampi maṃsāni phalāni bhuñje, annāni ca loṇiyateliyāni;
loṇiyateliyāni.translation_1: 74. ‘‘I too eat flesh and fruits, and grains with salt and oil;

loṇiyateliyānīti.meaning_2: salty ghee and oil; ghee and oil mixed with salt
loṇiyateliyānīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Variant of loṇiya-telāni, neuter nominative/accusative plural. Analysed as sandhi of loṇiyatela + iyāni (or loṇiya + teliyāni); iti is attached at the end.

tussasī.meaning_2: is satisfied (with); is content (with); is pleased (with)
tussasī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] 2nd singular present of tussati in the text: 'na tussasī' = 'you are not satisfied'. The final -i is elided before the vowel of the next word.
tussasī.example_1: Na tussasī rukkhaphalehi dhaṅka, maṃsāni vā yāni susānamajjhe.
tussasī.translation_1: Crow, you are not satisfied with tree fruits, or with whatever flesh there is in the middle of the cemetery.

cakkavākī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine counterpart of cakkavāka. Nominative singular in the text, paired with cakkavāko.
cakkavākī.example_1: Tadā kāko lolabhikkhu ahosi, cakkavākī rāhulamātā, cakkavāko pana ahameva ahosinti.
cakkavākī.translation_1: Then the crow was the greedy bhikkhu, the female ruddy goose was Rāhula’s mother, and the (male) ruddy goose was I myself.

accupasevato.meaning_2: associates excessively (with); keeps too close company (with); attends on too much
accupasevato.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is an absolutive-like genitive singular of the present participle accupasevanta ('of one associating too much'), from ati + upa + sevati; the glossed form bālaṃ accupasevato = 'of one associating too much with a fool'. Kept as the verb here.
accupasevato.translation_1: 85. ‘Dear child, harms increase by associating too much with a fool;
accupasevato.translation_2: ‘By associating too much with a fool’ means: ‘by associating too much with an unwise fool.’

accupasevatoti.meaning_2: associates with too much; frequents excessively; is too closely involved with
accupasevatoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Quotative form (--ti) in the commentary; lemma is the form without the enclitic ti. acc + upa + sevati, with sandhi u. 3rd singular present.

uggilitvā.meaning_2: having vomited up; having spat out
uggilitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā of uggilati; u- + √gil (swallow). Used of bringing up a casket from the belly. Some manuscripts and editions may read uggilatvā.
uggilitvā.example_1: So ekadivasaṃ nhāyitukāmatāya ekaṃ saraṃ gantvā karaṇḍakaṃ uggilitvā taṃ tato nīharitvā nhāpetvā vilimpetvā alaṅkāretvā ‘‘ thokaṃ tava sarīraṃ utuṃ gaṇhāpehī ’’ ti taṃ karaṇḍakasamīpe ṭhapetvā sayaṃ nhānatitthaṃ otaritvā taṃ anāsaṅkamāno thokaṃ dūraṃ gantvā nhāyi.
uggilitvā.translation_1: One day, desiring to bathe, he went to a certain lake, vomited up the casket, and having removed her from it, bathed, anointed, and adorned her. (Then he said), ‘Let your body get a little air,’ and having placed her near the casket, he himself descended into the bathing place. Not suspecting her, he went a little distance and bathed.
uggilitvā.example_2: Taṃ sutvā dānavo ‘‘ vijjādharā nāma bahumāyā honti, sacassa khaggo hatthagato bhavissati, kucchiṃ me phāletvāpi palāyissatī ’’ ti bhītatasito hutvā khippaṃ karaṇḍakaṃ uggilitvā purato ṭhapesi.
uggilitvā.translation_2: Hearing that, the titan thought, ‘Masters of knowledge are indeed very cunning. If his sword should be in his hand, he will even rip open my belly and escape!’ Having become terrified and trembling, he quickly vomited up the casket and placed it in front [of him].

alaṅkāretvā.meaning_2: having adorned; having decorated; having dressed up
alaṅkāretvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -etvā from the causative of karoti with the prefix alaṃ. Used of adorning a woman before presenting her.
alaṅkāretvā.example_1: So ekadivasaṃ nhāyitukāmatāya ekaṃ saraṃ gantvā karaṇḍakaṃ uggilitvā taṃ tato nīharitvā nhāpetvā vilimpetvā alaṅkāretvā ‘‘ thokaṃ tava sarīraṃ utuṃ gaṇhāpehī ’’ ti taṃ karaṇḍakasamīpe ṭhapetvā sayaṃ nhānatitthaṃ otaritvā taṃ anāsaṅkamāno thokaṃ dūraṃ gantvā nhāyi.
alaṅkāretvā.translation_1: One day, desiring to bathe, he went to a certain lake, vomited up the casket, and having removed her from it, bathed, anointed, and adorned her. (Then he said), ‘Let your body get a little air,’ and having placed her near the casket, he himself descended into the bathing place. Not suspecting her, he went a little distance and bathed.
alaṅkāretvā.example_2: Te taṃ suvaṇṇarūpakaṃ sakalajambudīpaṃ parihārāpetvā tathārūpaṃ itthiṃ alabhantā udayabhaddaṃ alaṅkāretvā tassa santike ṭhapesuṃ.
alaṅkāretvā.translation_2: They had that golden image taken throughout all Jambudīpa, and not finding a woman of that kind, they decorated Udayabhaddā and placed her near it.

iseti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative of √is? Perhaps a variant spelling of īseti? Not found in the extracts; perhaps related to issā. Third person singular present.

aññamabhippamodayi.meaning_2: delighted in another; gave joy to another
aññamabhippamodayi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of aññaṃ (accusative of añña, 'another') + abhippamodayi, aorist 3rd singular of abhippamodayati (abhi + pa + √mud + *aya, caus). The corrupt woman rejoiced in another man. Printed as one word in the text.
aññamabhippamodayi.example_1: Yathā have pāṇarivettha rakkhitā, duṭṭhā mayī aññamabhippamodayi.
aññamabhippamodayi.translation_1: Just as here, this one was protected by me as if my own life, yet being corrupt towards me, she delighted in another man.

jotirivā.meaning_2: like a flame; like a fire
jotirivā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of joti (flame; fire) and iva (like). The commentary glosses it aggi viya, 'like a fire'. Alternative sandhi resolution joti + ivā.
jotirivā.example_1: 92. ‘‘ Divā ca ratto ca mayā upaṭṭhitā, tapassinā jotirivā vane vasaṃ;
jotirivā.translation_1: 92. ‘By me she was attended to, day and night, like a flame by an ascetic dwelling in a forest.
jotirivā.example_2: Jotirivā vane vasanti vane vasantena tapassinā aggi viya mayā upaṭṭhitā paricaritā.
jotirivā.translation_2: Jotirivā vane vasan means ‘she was attended to and cared for by me, like a fire by an ascetic dwelling in the forest.’

abhipatthetabbaṃ.meaning_2: to be aspired to; to be longed for; to be desired
abhipatthetabbaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Neuter nominative singular agreeing with sivaṃ; passive potential participle of abhipattheti. The root √patth is not in the given root list, so root fields are probable.
abhipatthetabbaṃ.example_1: Etaṃ sivanti yadetaṃ mātugāmato nissaṭānaṃ visaṃsaṭṭhānaṃ caraṇaṃ, etaṃ jhānasukhameva sivaṃ khemaṃ uttamaṃ abhipatthetabbaṃ, etaṃ patthayamāno mātugāmehi saddhiṃ santhavaṃ na kareyyāti.
abhipatthetabbaṃ.translation_1: Etaṃ sivan means ‘whatever practice of isolated dwelling belongs to those who have escaped from women, this very pleasure of jhāna should be aspired to as peaceful, safe, and supreme. Aspiring to this, one should not engage in intimacy with women.’

paṭigacchantiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle (fem accusative singular) modifying meṇḍamātaraṃ; the reading is paṭigacchantiṃ, not *paṭigacchanti*.
paṭigacchantiṃ.translation_1: She broods over Meṇḍamātā, who has come but is now retreating.”
paṭigacchantiṃ.example_2: Atha naṃ sā idāni āgataṃ mama santikaṃ anāgantvāva paṭigacchantiṃ meṇḍamātaraṃ pajjhāyati anusocatīti.
paṭigacchantiṃ.translation_2: And then she broods and sorrows after Meṇḍamātā, who, having just come (near), is now retreating without even reaching my presence.

sañjīvito.meaning_2: brought back to life; revived; restored to life; (of one who was thought dead) come back to life
sañjīvito.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Past participle of sañjīvati (saṃ + √jīv). In the text nominative singular in agreement with pati; the commentary glosses it with uṭṭhito and arogo, so 'revived; risen; healthy'.
sañjīvito.example_1: Pati sañjīvito mayhaṃ, eyyāsi piyapucchikā ’’ ti.
sañjīvito.translation_1: My husband has been brought back to life; come, you who ask after my loved one.”
sañjīvito.example_2: Pati sañjīvito mayhanti mama sāmiko sañjīvito uṭṭhito arogoti attho.
sañjīvito.translation_2: My husband has been brought back to life (pati sañjīvito mayhaṃ) means: ‘my husband is brought back to life, risen, and healthy’.

āḷino.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Vocative singular āḷi in the gloss; the text form āḷino is genitive or dative singular, 'to/for your friend'. Not related to āḷinda (portico).
āḷino.example_1: Ārogyaṃ āḷino vajjaṃ, idheva vasa māgamā ’’ ti.
āḷino.translation_1: I will tell your friend the news of well-being; dwell right here, do not come.”
āḷino.example_2: Tassattho – āḷi, tava gehe bahubhaṇḍakaṃ atthi, taṃ te nikkhantāya agārasmā anārakkhaṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ vinassati, ahameva te āḷino sahāyakassa ārogyaṃ vajjaṃ vadissāmi, tvaṃ idheva vasa māgamāti.
āḷino.translation_2: The meaning of that is: ‘Friend, there are many goods in your house. For you who depart from the house, that unprotected property will perish. I indeed will tell your friend, your companion, the news of well-being. You dwell right here, do not come.’

ghurughurāyanto.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle masculine nominative singular, used adverbially of the ascetic in the Jātaka prose.
ghurughurāyanto.example_1: Tāpaso pātova bhattaṃ pacitvā dve godhāputtake māretvā khādi, divā tittirapaṇḍitañca vacchakañca māretvā khādi, sāyaṃ dhenuṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā tampi māretvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā rukkhamūle nipajjitvā ghurughurāyanto niddaṃ okkami.
ghurughurāyanto.translation_1: Early in the morning, the ascetic, having cooked his rice, killed and ate the two young lizards. During the day, he killed and ate the wise partridge and the calf. In the evening, seeing the cow coming, he killed that too, and having eaten the flesh, he lay down at the root of a tree, snoring, and fell asleep.

nipātaye.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Optative 3rd singular used in the text; the root is √pat with the causative suffix *e.
nipātaye.example_1: Padesaṃ taṃ na passāmi, yattha dāṭhaṃ nipātaye.
nipātaye.translation_1: I do not see that spot where I could strike my fangs.

kānissa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Rare sandhi of kāni (neuter plural of ka) + assa (dative/genitive singular of idaṃ). In the text, part of a question about someone's occupations.
kānissa.translation_1: 110. “What would be his life-paths, by which his way of life is known?

sañcaritabbo.meaning_2: to be traversed; to be walked through; to be wandered about
sañcaritabbo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Potential participle in the gloss explaining vettācaro ('one who is carried along by canes'); the word is glossed as the place/thing traversed, so the passive sense 'to be traversed (with)' fits.
sañcaritabbo.translation_1: Vettācaro means that which is traversed with canes.

kulīkāti.meaning_2: name of a bird (perhaps a hawk or falcon)
kulīkāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Word appears in the form kulīkāti, i.e. kulīkā + iti. The bird is mentioned in the Jātaka stories.

cūḷasūvaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of a bird in a list of birds. Accusative singular in the text. Sūva probably means 'parrot' (compare suva).
cūḷasūvaṃ.translation_1: Gijjha, Kosambī, and Suva, Cūḷasūva, Harittaca;

gīyiṃsu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Passive aorist 3rd plural, 'were sung' or 'sang'; the sentence subject gītikārakā, 'the composers', sang them.
gīyiṃsu.translation_1: In the Jātaka’s Ninth Nipāta, the composers sang them.

oruddhapaṭiruddhosmi.meaning_2: obstructed and blocked; hemmed in and trapped
oruddhapaṭiruddhosmi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of the past participles oruddha and paṭiruddha (both from √rudh 1); in the text with the present tense of √as, oruddhapaṭiruddhosmi = oruddhapaṭiruddho + asmi, 1st person singular.
oruddhapaṭiruddhosmi.translation_1: I am hemmed in and trapped; what bad deed have I committed?

oruddhapaṭiruddhosmīti.meaning_2: I am obstructed and blocked, iti; 'I am hemmed in and blocked'
oruddhapaṭiruddhosmīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of oruddha + paṭiruddho + asmi + iti; oruddha and paṭiruddha are past participles of rundhati (with o- and paṭi-). Quotation phrase in a Jātaka story.

abhinihato.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Past participle of abhihanati (abhi + ni + √han). In the text it occurs in the definition cakkena abhinihato, explaining cakkābhinihato; the form is nominative singular masculine.
abhinihato.translation_1: Cakkābhinihato (struck by the circlet) means struck by the circlet.

aticchaṃ.meaning_2: excessively greedy; full of excessive craving; insatiably desirous
aticchaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text aticchaṃ agrees with cakkaṃ in the verse, but the prose gloss takes it as referring to the person (aticcho pāpapuggalo), so it is a bahubbīhi adjective. Alternative analysis ati + icchati.
aticchaṃ.translation_1: “And from sixteen to thirty-two, reaching the circlet through excessive craving;
aticchaṃ.example_2: Aticchaṃ cakkamāsadoti atha tvaṃ yathāladdhena asantuṭṭho ‘‘ atra uttaritaraṃ labhissāmī ’’ ti evaṃ laddhaṃ laddhaṃ atikkamanalobhasaṅkhātāya aticchāya samannāgatattā aticcho pāpapuggalo tassa uposathakammassa khīṇattā dvattiṃsa itthiyo atikkamitvā imaṃ petanagaraṃ āgantvā tassa mātupahāradānaakusalassa nissandena idaṃ khuracakkaṃ sampattosi.
aticchaṃ.translation_2: Aticchaṃ cakkamāsado (reaching the circlet through excessive craving) means: then, because you were dissatisfied with whatever you obtained, thinking “I will obtain something better here,” you became an excessively greedy person—a bad person—who, because of your insatiable greed, attained thirty-two heavenly maidens; but when that Uposatha kamma was exhausted, you left them, came to this hell-city, and due to the fruition of the bad kamma of striking your mother, you reached this razor-wheel.

aticcho.meaning_2: excessively greedy; insatiably desirous; wanting too much
aticcho.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text aticcho is nominative singular, an adjective describing pāpapuggalo; the commentary glosses it with aticchāya samannagatattā, greed that keeps wanting more. PEU compares atriccha, atricchā.
aticcho.example_1: Aticchaṃ cakkamāsadoti atha tvaṃ yathāladdhena asantuṭṭho ‘‘ atra uttaritaraṃ labhissāmī ’’ ti evaṃ laddhaṃ laddhaṃ atikkamanalobhasaṅkhātāya aticchāya samannāgatattā aticcho pāpapuggalo tassa uposathakammassa khīṇattā dvattiṃsa itthiyo atikkamitvā imaṃ petanagaraṃ āgantvā tassa mātupahāradānaakusalassa nissandena idaṃ khuracakkaṃ sampattosi.
aticcho.translation_1: Aticchaṃ cakkamāsado (reaching the circlet through excessive craving) means: then, because you were dissatisfied with whatever you obtained, thinking “I will obtain something better here,” you became an excessively greedy person—a bad person—who, because of your insatiable greed, attained thirty-two heavenly maidens; but when that Uposatha kamma was exhausted, you left them, came to this hell-city, and due to the fruition of the bad kamma of striking your mother, you reached this razor-wheel.

māviddhaṃ.meaning_2: do not let it be pierced; may it not be fixed (on)
māviddhaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of mā + viddhaṃ, past participle of vijjhati. In the text mā with the participle gives a prohibition: 'let it not be pierced/fixed'. The alternative analysis mā + āviddhaṃ ('not pierced through') is possible.
māviddhaṃ.example_1: Cakkaṃ te sirasi māviddhaṃ, na taṃ jīvaṃ pamokkhasī ’’ ti.
māviddhaṃ.translation_1: The circlet is fixed upon your head; you shall not be released from it while alive.”

nisnehanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Possibly a sandhi of nisneha + iti, or an indeclinable/verb form in -ti; no sentence was available to confirm the analysis.

nisnehaṃ.meaning_2: free from affection; without attachment; free from greed
nisnehaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Attested in the commentary as an explanatory gloss; in the text it is accusative singular (nisnehaṃ). The compound is glossed as apagatalobha.
nisnehaṃ.example_1: Nisnehanti puttadhītādīsu vā saviññāṇakesu dhanadhaññādīsu vā aviññāṇakesu attano santakesupi nisnehaṃ apagatalobhaṃ.
nisnehaṃ.translation_1: “Nisnehan” means: being without affection for children, wives, etc., who have consciousness, or for wealth, grain, etc., which have no consciousness, even for those that are one's own, and being without greed.

āsaṅgī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the verses it describes kodha as clinging and troublesome; the gloss āsaṅgakaraṇo confirms the sense 'causing attachment'. Sometimes analysed as ā + sañj + ṇī.
āsaṅgī.example_1: Āsaṅgī bahupāyāso, tasmā kodhaṃ na rocaye.
āsaṅgī.translation_1: it clings and causes great distress; therefore, I do not desire anger.

pariṇamitvā.meaning_2: having changed; having transformed; having digested
pariṇamitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of pariṇamati in -itvā. The text has parivattitvā just before, in the same sense.
pariṇamitvā.example_1: Doso kodhasamuṭṭhānoti yathā anambilaṃ takkaṃ vā kañjikaṃ vā pariṇāmavasena parivattitvā ambilaṃ hoti, taṃ ekajātikampi samānaṃ ambilaṃ anambilanti nānā vuccati, tathā pubbakāle kodho pariṇamitvā aparabhāge doso hoti.
pariṇamitvā.translation_1: Doso kodhasamuṭṭhāno (hatred arises from anger) means: just as buttermilk or sour gruel, when changed by the process of digestion, becomes sour—though it is of the same origin, the sour and the non-sour are referred to differently—in the same way, anger, having changed in the aftermath, becomes hatred.

saṅgathitā.meaning_2: tied together; bound together; strung together; joined
saṅgathitā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text glosses it with ghaṭitā and baddhā. The PEU notes that the root is doubtful, reading it as a variant of saṅganthita (√ganth); the spelling with single -th- is unusual. Nominative plural here, agreeing with ganthā.
saṅgathitā.example_1: Snehasaṅgathitā ganthāti ārammaṇesu allīyanalakkhaṇena snehena saṅgathitā punappunaṃ uppādavasena ghaṭitā suttena pupphāni viya baddhā nānappakāresu ārammaṇesu pavattamānā abhijjhākāyaganthā.
saṅgathitā.translation_1: Snehasaṅgathitā ganthā (affection-knots are bound by attachment) means: knots—such as the knot of covetousness—that are bound by the affection which has the nature of clinging to objects, and which, like flowers tied with string, are joined together by repeated arising and manifest in various objects.

maṃkate.meaning_2: because of me; on my account; by reason of me
maṃkate.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of maṃ (accusative of amhaṃ, 'me') + kate (locative of kata, 'done', here 'on account of'). The commentary glosses it mama kāraṇā. Locative absolute. The hyphen in maṃ-kate is editorial.
maṃkate.example_1: Na mano vā sarīraṃ vā, maṃ-kate sakka kassaci;
maṃkate.translation_1: May no creature, because of me, Sakka, ever be harmed
maṃkate.translation_2: ‘Because of me’ means on my account.

maṃkateti.meaning_2: caused by me; on account of me; referring to me
maṃkateti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular maṃkateti (maṃkate + iti) in the text; the -e form before -iti suggests an alternative stem in -e or a sandhi of maṃkate. Formed from the pronoun maṃ (me) + kata (done, made).

moḷinī.meaning_2: name of a city (an old name of Bārāṇasī); Moḷinī
moḷinī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of Bārāṇasī in the Saṅkhabrāhmaṇa Jātaka; nominative singular in the text, used as a place name. The English translation calls it "Molinī".
moḷinī.example_1: Atīte ayaṃ bārāṇasī moḷinī nāma ahosi.
moḷinī.translation_1: In the past, this Benares was named Molinī.
moḷinī.example_2: Ayañhi bārāṇasī udayajātake (jā.1.11.37 ādayo) surundhananagaraṃ nāma jātā, cūḷasutasomajātake (jā.2.17.195 ādayo) sudassanaṃ nāma, soṇanandajātake (jā.2.20.92 ādayo) brahmavaḍḍhanaṃ nāma, khaṇḍahālajātake (jā.2.22.982 ādayo) pupphavatī nāma, saṅkhabrāhmaṇajātake (jā.1.10.39 ādayo) moḷinī nāma, imasmiṃ pana yudhañcayajātake rammanagaraṃ nāma ahosi.
moḷinī.translation_2: For this Benares is named Surundhana City in the Udaya Birth, Sudassana in the Cūḷasutasoma Birth, Brahmavaddhana in the Soṇananda Birth, Pupphavatī in the Khaṇḍahāla Birth, Moḷinī in the Saṅkhabrāhmaṇa Birth, but in this Yudhañjaya Birth it was named Ramma City.

moḷininagare.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text (moḷininagare). Moḷinī is the name of the city; the compound is probably moḷiniyā nagara with the final -ā contracted.
moḷininagare.example_1: Moḷininagare brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente saṅkho nāma brāhmaṇo aḍḍho mahaddhano mahābhogo pahūtavittupakaraṇo pahūtadhanadhaññasuvaṇṇarajato catūsu nagaradvāresu nagaramajjhe nivesanadvāre cāti chasu ṭhānesu cha dānasālāyo kāretvā devasikaṃ chasatasahassāni vissajjento kapaṇaddhikānaṃ mahādānaṃ pavattesi.
moḷininagare.translation_1: While Brahmadatta reigned in Molinī, a brahmin named Saṅkha, wealthy, of great wealth, possessed of great property, with abundant money, grain, gold, and silver, built almshouses in six places—at the four city gates, in the city center, and at his own house door—and daily distributed six hundred thousand, performing a great gift for travelers and beggars.

ussiñcituṃ.meaning_2: to bail out; to draw out; to scoop up
ussiñcituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of ussiñcati (ud + √sic, to sprinkle out), used with nāsakkhiṃsu; the water could not be bailed.
ussiñcituṃ.example_1: Athassa mahāsamuddaṃ paṭipannassa sattame divase nāvā vivaraṃ adāsi, udakaṃ ussiñcituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu.
ussiñcituṃ.translation_1: When he was on the high sea, on the seventh day the boat sprang a leak, and they could not bail out the water.

paṭipādayī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular of the causative paṭipādayati, sometimes spelt paṭipādesi, as the gloss confirms. The form is resolved as paṭipādayī in the text; the final -ī is the aorist ending, not the root vowel.
paṭipādayī.example_1: Paṭipādayī saṅkha upāhanāni, sā dakkhiṇā kāmaduhā tavajjā ’’ ti.
paṭipādayī.translation_1: who had blistered feet, was thirsty, and weary; that gift is your Cow of Plenty today.”
paṭipādayī.translation_2: Paṭipādayīti means he provided; the meaning is that he endowed him with them.

paṭipādayīti.meaning_2: makes proceed; carries out; arranges; gives; hands over; causes to be accepted
paṭipādayīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The -ti is the quotative iti, so the form is paṭipādayī (aorist 3rd singular of the causative) + iti. The PEU entry analyses it as a causative of pada; the aorist 3rd singular paṭipādayi is also possible here.

moḷiniṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text: 'take me to Moḷinī'. Probably moḷi + -nī, or a proper name of unknown derivation.
moḷiniṃ.example_1: Aññassa yānassa na hettha bhūmi, ajjeva maṃ moḷiniṃ pāpayassū ’’ ti.
moḷiniṃ.translation_1: there is no place here for another vehicle; this very day take me to Moḷinī.”

moḷininagaraṃ.meaning_2: Moḷinī city; the city of Moḷinī
moḷininagaraṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a city in the Jātaka prose. Accusative singular in the text as the goal of pāpayassu and netvā.
moḷininagaraṃ.example_1: Tassattho – devate, evaṃ sante mayhaṃ ekaṃ nāvaṃ māpehi, khuddakaṃ pana ekadoṇikanāvaṃ māpehi, yaṃ nāvaṃ māpessasi, sā hotu nāvā bahūhi susibbitehi phalakehi upapannā, udakapavesanassābhāvena anavassutā, erakena sammā gahetvā gacchantena vātena yuttā, ṭhapetvā dibbanāvaṃ aññassa yānassa ettha bhūmi natthi, tāya pana dibbanāvāya ajjeva maṃ moḷininagaraṃ pāpayassūti.
moḷininagaraṃ.translation_1: Its meaning: ‘O deity, if that is the case, create a ship for me; but create a small, single-canoe ship. The ship that you create should be built of planks well-joined together, impervious due to being unable to let in water, and driven by the wind that correctly seizes and moves it. Leaving aside a celestial ship, there is no place here for any other vehicle; by that celestial ship, however, take me today to the city of Moḷinī.’
moḷininagaraṃ.example_2: Atha naṃ nāvaṃ moḷininagaraṃ netvā brāhmaṇassa ghare dhanaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva agamāsi.
moḷininagaraṃ.translation_2: Then, having taken the ship to the city of Moḷinī, she deposited the wealth in the brahmin's house and returned to her own dwelling place.

patiṭṭhayi.meaning_2: stands firm; takes a stand; becomes obstinate; persists
patiṭṭhayi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular patiṭṭhayi (= patiṭṭhahi), from patiṭṭhāti; in the text the last in a series of angry reactions, glossed 'grow obstinate'.
patiṭṭhayi.example_1: So kira bhikkhu niyyānike buddhasāsane pabbajitvāpi kodhaṃ niggahetuṃ nāsakkhi, kodhano ahosi upāyāsabahulo, appampi vutto samāno abhisajji kuppi byāpajji patiṭṭhayi.
patiṭṭhayi.translation_1: It is said that this monk, even after going forth in the emancipating Buddha's teaching, was unable to control his anger; he was irritable, easily exasperated, and even if spoken to only slightly, he would take offense, get angry, become bitter, and grow obstinate.

saṃrāgavasena.meaning_2: because of passion; due to lust; on account of intense passion
saṃrāgavasena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental of saṃrāgavasa (saṃrāga + vasa); used adverbially in the text.
saṃrāgavasena.example_1: Ubhinnaṃ panetesaṃ kilesasamudācāro nāma na bhūtapubbo, saṃrāgavasena aññamaññassa olokanaṃ nāma nāhosi, supinepi methunadhammo nāma na diṭṭhapubbo, evaṃ parisuddhasīlā ahesuṃ.
saṃrāgavasena.translation_1: For these two, however, the arising of defilements had never happened before. Due to intense passion, they did not even look at one another, and they had never even seen sexual intercourse in their dreams; in this way, they were pure in virtue.

saṃmhitabhāsiniṃ.meaning_2: pleasant-spoken; speaking sweetly; whose speech is pleasant (?)
saṃmhitabhāsiniṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Verse context; accusative singular agreeing with piyaṃ. The compound / sandhi is uncertain: probably saṃmhita (pp of saṃmhā?) + bhāsiniṃ, 'speaking pleasantly', but the first member may be an irregular or scribal form (cf. saṇha, saṃhita).
saṃmhitabhāsiniṃ.example_1: 49. ‘‘ Yo te imaṃ visālakkhiṃ, piyaṃ saṃmhitabhāsiniṃ;
saṃmhitabhāsiniṃ.translation_1: “You who previously boasted, appearing as though you were strong,

saṃmhitabhāsininti.meaning_2: speaking in verse; reciting verses; one who speaks in song
saṃmhitabhāsininti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Vocative singular, with -ti (iti) attached in the text. The word may be a compound (saṃmhita + bhāsinī); a vocative ending in -i can stand for -ī. Meaning uncertain: possibly 'speaking in verse/couplets'.

matthiyamāne.meaning_2: being rubbed; being churned; being twirled (fire-sticks)
matthiyamāne.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular matthiyamāne in the text, glossing matthamānasmiṃ; the commentary explains it as araṇīsahitena matthiyamāne, i.e. fire-sticks being rubbed together. Alternative reading maddamānasmiṃ.
matthiyamāne.example_1: Kaṭṭhasmiṃ matthamānasminti araṇīsahitena matthiyamāne,‘‘ maddamānasmin ’’ tipi pāṭho.
matthiyamāne.translation_1: “In grass and sticks” (kaṭṭhasmiṃ matthamānasmiṃ) means while being rubbed with fire-sticks; there is also a reading, “maddamānasmiṃ” (in being crushed).

anindhano.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is the nominative singular anindhano agreeing with aggi; the gloss explains anedho as anindhano aggi viya. The PEU lists it as a ti (adjective).
anindhano.translation_1: “Like a fire without fuel” (anedho dhūmaketūvā) means like a fire without fuel.

chaṭṭetvā.meaning_2: having thrown away; having abandoned; having discarded
chaṭṭetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā of the denominative chaṭṭeti. In both sentences it takes the thing thrown down as object: bhaṇḍikaṃ chaṭṭetvā (having dropped the bundle) and puttaṃ chaṭṭetvā (having abandoned the child). The PEU analysis chaṭṭa + ṇe + tvā also points to a causative/denominative formation.
chaṭṭetvā.example_1: Athekadivasaṃ eko coro antonagare corikaṃ katvā dhanasāraṃ ādāya nikkhanto ‘‘ coro ’’ ti ñatvā paṭibuddhehi gharassāmikehi ceva ārakkhamanussehi ca anubaddho niddhamanena nikkhamitvā vegena susānaṃ pavisitvā tāpasassa paṇṇasāladvāre bhaṇḍikaṃ chaṭṭetvā palāyi.
chaṭṭetvā.translation_1: One day, a thief committed robbery inside the city, took valuable goods, and emerged; the householders and guards, awakened by the realization that it was a “thief,” followed him. He escaped through a drain, emerged, and running swiftly toward the charnel ground, entered it, abandoned his bundle of goods at the ascetic’s hut, and fled.
chaṭṭetvā.example_2: Athekadivasaṃ tasmiṃ satthe ekā duggatitthī rattiyā ekasmiṃ nigrodhamūle puttaṃ vijāyitvā pātova satthe gacchante ‘‘ ahaṃ vinā satthena gantuṃ na sakkhissāmi, sakkā kho pana jīvantiyā puttaṃ labhitun ’’ ti nigrodhamūlajāle jalābuñceva gabbhamalañca attharitvā puttaṃ chaṭṭetvā agamāsi.
chaṭṭetvā.translation_2: Then, one day, a poor woman in that caravan gave birth to a son under a banyan tree during the night; and in the morning, as the caravan was moving on, she thought, “I cannot go without the caravan, but if I live, I might get a child,” so she spread out the afterbirth and the filth of pregnancy in the banyan roots, abandoned the son, and went away.

ārogaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is used in the phrase 'puttakaṃ no ārogaṃ karotha' (make our son healthy), where it is the object complement agreeing with puttakaṃ; the form is masculine accusative singular, though it could agree as neuter. Related nominal form is ārogya (health).
ārogaṃ.example_1: Athassa mātāpitaro sappena ḍaṭṭhabhāvaṃ ñatvā kumārakaṃ ukkhipitvā tāpasassa santikaṃ ānetvā pādamūle nipajjāpetvā ‘‘ bhante, pabbajitā nāma osadhaṃ vā parittaṃ vā jānanti, puttakaṃ no ārogaṃ karothā ’’ ti āhaṃsu.
ārogaṃ.translation_1: His parents, having known he was bitten by the snake, picked up the boy, brought him to the ascetic, laid him at his feet, and said, “Venerable sir, those gone forth know either medicine or charms; please make our son healthy.”

bilarā.meaning_2: from a hole; from the burrow; out of a cleft
bilarā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The commentary glosses bilarā as vivarā ('holes; from holes'), so it is likely an ablative/instrumental plural of bila with a suffix -ra. Ablative sense 'from the hole' fits the serpent rising from the ant-hill hole.
bilarā.example_1: 64. ‘‘ Āsīviso tāta pahūtatejo, yo taṃ aḍaṃsī bilarā udicca;
bilarā.translation_1: 64. “The serpent, dear one, is of great power, which bit you having risen from the ant-hill hole;
bilarā.translation_2: Bilarā means [emerging from] holes; this is the reading.

bilarāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text has the sandhi form bilarāti (bilara + iti) or similar; the entry is for the main word bilara. Not verified in the given sentences.

tānayinti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Probably sandhi of tāni + iti, though the ending -yinti is unusual and the analysis is uncertain; no sentences were supplied to confirm. If the word is rather a verb form, the entry would need a different analysis.

khamyataṃ.grammar: pr, caus of khamati; imp 3rd sg
khamyataṃ.meaning_2: may it be forgiven; let it be tolerated; may (you) pardon
khamyataṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Imperative 3rd singular causative (or passive-looking form) in the text: 'taṃ khamyataṃ' = 'may that be forgiven'. PEU gives khamyataṃ as [Khamu+ya+taṃ] 'let him be patient', suggesting a passive/impersonal imperative from √kham with -ya. Alternative sandhi of khamayataṃ (causative imperative) is possible.
khamyataṃ.example_1: 71. ‘‘ Maṇḍabya bhāsiṃ yamabhāsaneyyaṃ, taṃ khamyataṃ puttakahetu majja;
khamyataṃ.translation_1: 71. “Maṇḍabya, I have spoken what should not be said; may it be forgiven today for the sake of the son;

khamyatanti.meaning_2: is endured; is borne; is patient; is forgiven
khamyatanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form is khamyatanti, i.e. khamyataṃ + ti (imperative passive 3rd singular with the quotative -ti). The PEU entry takes khamyataṃ as an imperative 'let him be patient'. The main word is therefore the passive verb khamyati, not khamati itself; cf. khamayatu.

pottikoti.meaning_2: name of a female spirit; name of a she-devil
pottikoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Attested in some readings as a reading for potthaka- variants; uncertain form; the ending -ti in the text's pottikoti suggests sandhi with iti.

pottikassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of an instructor in the Jātaka story, in a genitive that follows pottikassa santike. The derivation from potta is uncertain.
pottikassa.example_1: Nigrodhakumāro pottikassa attano santike sippaṃ paṭṭhapesi.
pottikassa.translation_1: Nigrodha-Kumāra provided Pottika with an education under his own care.

pottiko.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a character in the Jātaka stories. Nominative singular in the text.
pottiko.example_1: Taṃ divasaññeva seṭṭhiṃ nissāya vasantassa tunnakārassa bhariyāpi pilotikantare puttaṃ vijāyi, tassa ‘‘ pottiko ’’ ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu.
pottiko.translation_1: On that same day, the wife of a tailor who served the merchant gave birth to a son among some cloth scraps, and they named him Pottika (Dollie).
pottiko.example_2: Tesupi sahāyesu rukkhamūle nipajjitvā niddāyantesu pottiko paccūsakāle uṭṭhāya nigrodhakumārassa pāde parimajjanto nisīdi.
pottiko.translation_2: While the three comrades were sleeping under the tree, Pottika awoke at dawn and sat rubbing Nigrodha-Kumāra’s feet.

pottikopi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name. In the text pottikopi = pottiko + pi, nominative singular of pottika with the emphatic particle pi.
pottikopi.example_1: So rajjaṃ patvā sākhassa senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ datvā mahantena sakkārena nagaraṃ pāvisi, pottikopi tehi saddhiññeva agamāsi.
pottikopi.translation_1: Having attained the kingship, he gave the position of commander-in-chief to Sākha and entered the city with great honors, and Pottika accompanied them.

pottikaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in both sentences, referring to a man named Pottika.
pottikaṃ.translation_1: Then he ordered Pottika to do it.
pottikaṃ.example_2: Atha naṃ rājā ‘‘ sākha imaṃ pottikaṃ sañjānāsī ’’ ti pucchi.
pottikaṃ.translation_2: Then the king asked him, “Sākha, do you recognize this Pottika?”

akataññuna.meaning_2: ungrateful; not recognising what has been done (for one)
akataññuna.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular in the verse, agreeing with dummatinā and dubbhinā. Compound of na + kata + ññu ("not knowing the done").
akataññuna.translation_1: “Such is the wretched one, the fool, the ungrateful and treacherous one;

labbhitā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The PEU gives the same analysis (labha + ya + ta). Feminine nominative plural labbhitā agreeing with iddhī in the sentence, but the form could also be read as a feminine nominative singular. Compare the more common labbha/laddha.
labbhitā.example_1: Tayāmā labbhitā iddhī, ettha me natthi saṃsayo.
labbhitā.translation_1: We have obtained this prosperity through you; in this I have no doubt.”

pottika.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name used in direct address (vocative singular) in the Jātaka prose. PEU lists pottha as a separate word; the name may be derived from it, but the connection is uncertain.
pottika.example_1: Sakhīnaṃ sājīvakaroti samma, pottika tvaṃ sahāyakānaṃ suājīvakaro jīvikāya uppādetā.
pottika.translation_1: 'Source of livelihood for friends' means, friend Pottika, you are one who brings about a pleasant livelihood for friends; you are the one who produces their sustenance.

paṭiānayāti.meaning_2: leads back; brings back; takes back
paṭiānayāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Text form paṭiānayāti shows the causative -aya- with a lengthened -ā- before the ti, giving the present 3rd singular of paṭiāneti (cf. PEU paṭiānaya). Could also be read as a corruption of paṭinayāti; no sentence context available.

paṭiānetuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinite form paṭiānetuṃ in the text, glossed as 'to bring back'. The simplex āneti is also causative in form with the meaning 'bring'.
paṭiānetuṃ.example_1: Na paṭiānayāti matassa nāma pāṇā paṭiānetuṃ na sakkā.
paṭiānetuṃ.translation_1: 'Hard to bring back' means it is not possible to bring back the life of one who is dead.

pottikasseva.meaning_2: Pottika's own; just for Pottika; Pottika's indeed
pottikasseva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of pottikassa (masc genitive singular, a stem, proper name) + eva. In the text usually written pottikass'eva; the gemination is phonetic. = Pottika's own / just for Pottika.
pottikasseva.example_1: Rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā sākhassa khami, senāpatiṭṭhānampi pottikasseva dātukāmo ahosi, so pana na icchi.
pottikasseva.translation_1: Hearing his words, the king forgave Sākha, and wanted to bestow the position of commander-in-chief upon Pottika, but he did not wish for it.

kaḷambāni.meaning_2: young shoot of the toddy palm; palm sprout (eaten as a vegetable)
kaḷambāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Plural nominative/accusative in the verse. Possibly a dialectal variant of kaḍamba (cf. kaḷamba ~ kaḍamba), a palm shoot eaten as food; listed among edible plants (takkalā, ālu, biḷāli).
kaḷambāni.example_1: 82. ‘‘ Na takkalā santi na āluvāni, na biḷāliyo na kaḷambāni tāta;
kaḷambāni.translation_1: “No bulbs are here, no herbs for cooking meet, no catmint, nor no other plant to eat, dear;

āluvakandā.meaning_2: edible tuber; a kind of yam or potato; (commentary) āluva bulb
āluvakandā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Explained in the commentary as āluvakandā, the bulb or tuber of the āluva plant. Nominative singular in the definition; plural in the quotation.

biḷārivallikandā.meaning_2: creeper root of the biḷāri plant; root-tuber of the catmint creeper
biḷārivallikandā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Glossed in the text as biḷārīnaṃ vallīnaṃ kando, the root-tuber of the biḷāri creepers. Explanatory compound in -kandā; the ending is nominative singular neuter, not feminine.

kaḷambānīti.meaning_2: kaḷamba vegetables, it is said; kaḷamba greens, thus
kaḷambānīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of kaḷambāni (neuter plural, 'kaḷamba vegetables/greens') and iti. The reading may be uncertain; if the word is really kaḷambāni alone, it is the nominative/accusative plural of kaḷamba.

pītaraṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Irregular r-stem noun; accusative singular pītaraṃ (with lengthened stem vowel) is used in the quoted passage: ‘pītaraṃ dukkhā pamocessāmī’.
pītaraṃ.example_1: Tassattho – tāta, tvaṃ ‘‘ pītaraṃ dukkhā pamocessāmī ’’ ti maraṇadukkhena yojento etaṃ pāpakaṃ saṅkappaṃ paṭiladdhā tassa ca saṅkappavasena hitaṃ atikkamma ṭhitattā accāhitaṃ kammaṃ karosi luddanti.
pītaraṃ.translation_1: The meaning is: “Dear, thinking, ‘I will free my father from suffering,’ you are conceiving this evil thought while yoking him with the suffering of death, and because you are beyond what is benevolent, you are doing a reckless, savage kamma.”

paṭilacchase.meaning_2: will get; will receive; will obtain; will attain
paṭilacchase.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] 2nd singular future of paṭilabhati in the text (tuvaṃ ... paṭilacchase), not the present. Formed with the future sign -ssa- plus the 2sg ending -se.
paṭilacchase.example_1: ‘‘ Mayāpi tāta paṭilacchase tuvaṃ, etādisaṃ kamma jarūpanīto;
paṭilacchase.translation_1: “I too, when you are old, will get such a kamma; when you have reached old age,
paṭilacchase.example_2: Tassattho – tāta, ahampi etasmiṃ sobbhe taṃ mahallakakāle nikhaṇissāmi, iti kho tāta, mayāpi kate imasmiṃ sobbhe tuvaṃ jarūpanīto etādisaṃ kammaṃ paṭilacchase, yaṃ etaṃ tayā pavattitaṃ kulavattaṃ, taṃ anuvattamāno vayappatto bhariyāya saddhiṃ vasanto ahampi taṃ nikhaṇissāmi sobbheti.
paṭilacchase.translation_2: The meaning is: “Dear, I too will bury you in this pit when you are old; so, dear, having been brought to old age in this pit that I have dug, you will receive just such a kamma. Following that family tradition initiated by you, when I have reached adulthood and am living with a wife, I too will bury you in a pit.”

vārayituṃ.meaning_2: to stop; to restrain; to prevent; to prohibit
vārayituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of the causative vāreti (from √var 1, 'cover, restrain'). Used with arahāmi and ussahe in the text.
vārayituṃ.example_1: Pāpañca taṃ kamma pakubbamānaṃ, arahāmi no vārayituṃ tato.
vārayituṃ.translation_1: But regarding that evil kamma you are committing, I am able to stop you from that.”
vārayituṃ.example_2: Tamariyamaggaṃ paṭipajjamānaṃ, na ussahe vārayituṃ kumāran ’’ ti.
vārayituṃ.translation_2: I do not dare to restrain the prince who is following that noble path.”

aniggayhamānā.meaning_2: not being restrained; not being controlled
aniggayhamānā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle (negative), nominative plural feminine agreeing with itthiyo (women).
aniggayhamānā.example_1: Taṃ sutvā kumāro ‘‘ tāta, itthiyo nāma uppanne dose aniggayhamānā punappunaṃ pāpaṃ karonti, mama mātā yathā puna evarūpaṃ na karoti, tathā naṃ paṇāmetuṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti navamaṃ gāthamāha –
aniggayhamānā.translation_1: Hearing this, the boy, thinking, “Dear, women, when they have committed a fault and are not restrained, commit evil again and again; it is right to rebuke her so that my mother does not do such a thing again,” recited the ninth stanza:

amhākāñhi.meaning_2: for us indeed; for us truly
amhākāñhi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of amhākaṃ (genitive/dative plural of amhaṃ) and hi. In the text: amhākāñhi kule, 'in our family indeed'.
amhākāñhi.example_1: Etāni eḷakassa vā sunakhassa vā bhavissanti, mayhaṃ pana putto na marati, amhākāñhi kule yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā taruṇakāle matapubbā nāma natthi, tvaṃ musā bhaṇasīti.
amhākāñhi.translation_1: “These must be a goat's or a dog's, but my son has not died. Indeed, in our family, for seven generations, there has never been a case of death in tender youth. You are speaking falsely.”

dāsyoti.meaning_2: slavery; servitude; the state of being a slave
dāsyoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form dāsyoti is dāsyaṃ + iti (nominative/accusative singular with sandhi to -y before the quotation ti). The quoted form dāsyanti would normally be a future of dāti, but in this context the PEU reading dāsya is more likely.

paṭirakkhati.meaning_2: protects again; protects (in return); guards (one who guards it)
paṭirakkhati.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] From paṭi + √rakkh with the present ending -ti; third person singular in the text.
paṭirakkhati.example_1: Tattha rakkhatīti dhammo nāmeso rakkhito attano rakkhitaṃ paṭirakkhati.
paṭirakkhati.translation_1: Regarding that, rakkhati means this Dhamma itself, being protected, protects the one who protects it.
paṭirakkhati.translation_2: “Guards” means it protects the one by whom it is practiced.

nāsīde.meaning_2: does not approach; does not draw near; should not approach
nāsīde.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Negative of āsīdati, formed with na. In the text the na joins with āsīde under sandhi. Second sentence glosses it with na upagaccheyya.
nāsīde.translation_1: Do not approach such hollow men, in whom no gratitude is found.
nāsīde.translation_2: ‘Nāsīde’ means one should not approach; one should not draw near to such people.

bilapaṭicchannaāsīvisasadise.meaning_2: like a snake concealed in a hole; like a viper hidden in its den
bilapaṭicchannaāsīvisasadise.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi compound describing a deceitful person (kuhakapuggala); locative singular in the text. The image is of a snake lurking unseen in a burrow.
bilapaṭicchannaāsīvisasadise.example_1: Atisanteti anto upasame avijjamāneyeva ca bahi upasamadassanena atisante viya paṭicchannakammantepi bilapaṭicchannaāsīvisasadise kuhakapuggale.
bilapaṭicchannaāsīvisasadise.translation_1: ‘Atisante’ refers to a fraudulent person, like a snake hidden in a hole, who shows calmness on the outside even when there is no genuine inner peace, and who conceals their true actions.

nāsīdeti.meaning_2: does not cause to sit; should not approach; should not resort to
nāsīdeti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative of nisīdati with negative na- and ā-; used figuratively in the commentary to mean 'should not approach'. 3rd singular present.
nāsīdeti.example_1: Yasmiṃ natthīti yasmiñca puggale kataññutā natthi, tampi nāsīdeti attho.
nāsīdeti.translation_1: ‘Yasmiṃ natthī’ means one should not approach even a person in whom there is no gratitude.

samuñchakanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Third person plural present in the text. Related noun: samuñchaka.

karoṭiyaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text. PEU lists karoṭiya as 'helmet-wearer', but the context (filling, cow-fodder) points to a container; the form may be karoṭi + iya or a variant spelling.
karoṭiyaṃ.example_1: ‘‘ Tena hi tesaṃ karoṭiyaṃ vaḍḍhetvā gobhattaṃ dehī ’’ ti.
karoṭiyaṃ.translation_1: “In that case, fill a pot for them and give them cow-fodder.”
karoṭiyaṃ.example_2: Sā tesaṃ karoṭiyaṃ vaḍḍhetvā mahāgoṇānaṃ pakkabhattaṃ āharitvā adāsi.
karoṭiyaṃ.translation_2: She filled a pot with the cooked cow-fodder prepared for the cattle and brought it to them.

laggāpetvā.meaning_2: having made stick; having caught (in the throat); having attached; having brought to a stop
laggāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of laggāpeti, from laggati. In the text used of food sticking in the throat and of bringing a ship to a standstill.
laggāpetvā.example_1: Pañcapi janā kabaḷe vaḍḍhetvā mukhe pakkhipitvā gale laggāpetvā akkhīni parivattetvā vissaṭṭhasaññā matā viya nipajjiṃsu.
laggāpetvā.translation_1: All five of them made lumps, put them in their mouths, let it stick in their throats and choke them, rolled their eyes, became senseless, and lay down as if dead.
laggāpetvā.example_2: Seṭṭhi antarapīthiṃ paṭipannamanusse pakkosāpetvā ‘‘ ahaṃ mama bhuñjananiyāmena etesaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ bhattaṃ dāpesiṃ, ete lobhena mahante piṇḍe katvā bhuñjamānā gale laggāpetvā matā, mama niddosabhāvaṃ jānāthā ’’ ti vatvā parisaṃ sannipātesi.
