laggāpetvā.translation_2: The treasurer summoned the people passing by in the road, and when he had gathered a crowd, he said, “I gave these brahmins food according to my own manner of eating; they were greedy and made large lumps, and as they ate, it stuck in their throats and they died; I call you to witness that I am blameless.”

karoṭikesu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative plural in the text, referring to the bowls from which food is taken. The related entry gives karoṭika as masculine or neuter; here it is masculine.
karoṭikesu.example_1: ‘‘ khippaṃ gantvā etesaṃ karoṭikesu bhattaṃ haritvā nānaggarasaṃ sālibhattaṃ vaḍḍhehī ’’ ti.
karoṭikesu.translation_1: “Quickly go, take the food from their bowls, and fill them with the finest rice.”

antarapīthiṃ.meaning_2: along the street; on the road
antarapīthiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Probably a compound of antara (between; along) + pīthi (street, road, open space), occurring only in the phrase antarapīthiṃ paṭipanna; accusative singular in the text. Syntax unclear; antarapīthi may be an indeclinable or an alternative spelling of antarāpaṇa or a similar street word.
antarapīthiṃ.example_1: Seṭṭhi antarapīthiṃ paṭipannamanusse pakkosāpetvā ‘‘ ahaṃ mama bhuñjananiyāmena etesaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ bhattaṃ dāpesiṃ, ete lobhena mahante piṇḍe katvā bhuñjamānā gale laggāpetvā matā, mama niddosabhāvaṃ jānāthā ’’ ti vatvā parisaṃ sannipātesi.
antarapīthiṃ.translation_1: The treasurer summoned the people passing by in the road, and when he had gathered a crowd, he said, “I gave these brahmins food according to my own manner of eating; they were greedy and made large lumps, and as they ate, it stuck in their throats and they died; I call you to witness that I am blameless.”

anāsāpetvā.meaning_2: not having caused to bring; not having sent for
anāsāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the sentence anāsāpetvā is joined with porāṇakulavaṃsaṃ; it looks like a causative absolutive of √sā (complete) with the negative na + ā, but is uncertain. The meaning is guessed from context: not letting the ancient family lineage be exhausted.
anāsāpetvā.example_1: Bilārakosiyo sirasmiṃ añjaliṃ patiṭṭhapetvā ‘‘ deva, ahaṃ ito paṭṭhāya porāṇakulavaṃsaṃ anāsāpetvā dānaṃ pavattessāmi, ajja ādiṃ katvā antamaso udakadantaponaṃ upādāya attano laddhāhāraṃ parassa adatvā na khādissāmī ’’ ti sakkassa paṭiññaṃ adāsi.
anāsāpetvā.translation_1: Biḷārikosiya placed his hands together in reverence and gave a promise to Sakka: “Lord, from this day on, I will not destroy my ancient family custom, but will perform giving. From this day forward, I will not eat without sharing with others my own food, even down to the water and the tooth-cleaner I use.”

loṇiyateliyaṃ.meaning_2: prepared with salt and oil; seasoned with salt and oil; sprinkled with salt and oil
loṇiyateliyaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of loṇiya (salty; prepared with salt) and teliya (made with oil). Accusative singular neuter in the text, agreeing with an understood food item.
loṇiyateliyaṃ.translation_1: For I, friend, eat in the village what is prepared with salt and oil.

ghasasī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] 2nd singular present ghasasi, written ghasasī before ti in the text; glossed bhuñjasi.
ghasasī.example_1: Utrasto ghasasī bhīto, tena vaṇṇo tavediso.
ghasasī.translation_1: You eat in fear and trembling; therefore your complexion is such.

maṃmiva.meaning_2: like me; as (you are dear) to me
maṃmiva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the pronoun maṃ (me) and iva (like). The commentary reads piyo hohisi maṃ iva, 'you will be dear like me'. Doubt: the doubled mm is unusual; it may also be analysed as maṃ + iva with assimilation.
maṃmiva.example_1: Ahiṃsāya cara loke, piyo hohisi maṃmiva.
maṃmiva.translation_1: Walk in the world with harmlessness; then you will be beloved, just as I am.”

koliniyā.meaning_2: of good family; of good lineage; well-born
koliniyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine adjective agreeing with sīlavatī and patibbatā. Instrumental singular in the text: koliniyā. PEU splits as kulina + iya; the form is probably a feminine in -inī from kula.
koliniyā.example_1: Koliniyā sīlavatī patibbatā, dāresu ve sotthānaṃ tadāhu.
koliniyā.translation_1: Of good lineage, virtuous, and faithful—that, they say, is safety regarding one’s wife.

sippavā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nom. sg. of the possessive adjective sippavant. The commentary glosses it as attano kule sikkhitabbasippena samannāgato.
sippavā.example_1: Tattha sahapaṃsukīḷitā sahāyā nāma, dasa dvādasa vassāni ekato vutthā sahāyamattā nāma, te sabbepi ‘‘ ahaṃ sippavā, ime nisippā ’’ ti evaṃ sippena vā ‘‘ ahaṃ kulīno, ime na kulīnā ’’ ti evaṃ kulasampattisaṅkhātāhi kulyāhi vā,‘‘ ahaṃ aḍḍho, ime duggatā ’’ ti evaṃ dhanena vā,‘‘ ahaṃ jātisampanno, ime dujjātā ’’ ti evaṃ jaccā vā nāvajānāti.
sippavā.translation_1: There, those who played together in the dust are called 'friends', while those who have lived together for ten or twelve years are called 'associates'. He does not despise them by thinking, ‘I am skilled, these are unskilled,’ or by citing the excellence of lineage, or wealth, or birth.
sippavā.example_2: 1499. ‘‘ Vinīto sippavā danto, katatto niyato mudu;
sippavā.translation_2: 1499. “Disciplined (vinīto), skilled (sippavā), tamed (danto), possessed of purpose, assured, and malleable (mudū);

nisippāti.meaning_2: unskilled; without skill; lacking a craft
nisippāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Text form nisippāti = nisippa + iti; the -ti is the quotative, not part of the word. The PEU entry gives masculine-ish 'one without skill', but taken as a bahubbīhi adjective here.

sambūlajātaka.meaning_2: Sambūla Birth Story; the Jātaka of Sambūla (Jā 16)
sambūlajātaka.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of a Jātaka tale, listed among stories about safety through a virtuous woman. Appears in a compound in the text (sambūlajātaka-), joined with maṇicorajātaka and khaṇḍahālajātaka.
sambūlajātaka.example_1: Tattha sīlavantaṃ mātugāmaṃ nissāya sotthibhāvo maṇicorajātaka- (jā.1.2.87 ādayo) sambūlajātaka- (jā.1.16.297 ādayo) khaṇḍahālajātakehi (jā.2.22.982 ādayo) kathetabbo.
sambūlajātaka.translation_1: In this case, safety based on a virtuous woman should be told through the Maṇicorajātaka, Sambūlajātaka, and Khaṇḍahālajātaka.

andhakaveṇḍo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a slave, the husband of the woman in the story. Nominative singular in the text. The related PEU entry suggests the first element is andhaka and records Sanskrit and canonical variants such as Andhakaviṇha.
andhakaveṇḍo.example_1: Andhakaveṇḍo nāma dāso tassā sāmiko ārakkhamakāsi.
andhakaveṇḍo.translation_1: Her husband, a slave named Andhakaveṇḍa, performed the watching.

upasāgaro.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of the son of king Sāgara (and brother of Sāgara) in the Jātaka prose. Nominative singular in the text. Sometimes analysed as upa + sāgara 'near the ocean', but here it is a personal name.
upasāgaro.example_1: Tassa sāgaro, upasāgaro cāti dve puttā ahesuṃ.
upasāgaro.translation_1: He had two sons, Sāgara and Upasāgara.
upasāgaro.example_2: Tesu pitu accayena sāgaro rājā ahosi, upasāgaro uparājā.
upasāgaro.translation_2: Upon the passing of their father, Sāgara became king and Upasāgara was viceroy.

upasāgarassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A personal name in the Jātaka prose. Genitive singular in the text (upasāgarassa).
upasāgarassa.example_1: Sā pakatiyāva tasmiṃ paṭibaddhacittā taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā ‘‘ sādhū ’’ ti sampaṭicchitvā nandigopā upasāgarassa saññaṃ datvā rattibhāge taṃ pāsādaṃ āropesi.
upasāgarassa.translation_1: She, being by nature captivated by him, having heard those words and saying “Very well,” agreed; Nandagopā gave a sign to Upasāgara, and at nightfall had him enter the palace.
upasāgarassa.example_2: So maraṇabhayabhīto rājānaṃ abhayaṃ yācitvā ‘‘ deva, ete na mayhaṃ puttā, upasāgarassa puttā ’’ ti taṃ antaraṃ ārocesi.
upasāgarassa.translation_2: He, fearing death, sought freedom from fear from the king and reported the secret, [saying], “Sire, they are not my sons, they are Upasāgara’s sons.”

upasāgarasseva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of the husband of Devagabbhā in the story of the Andhaka-Venhuputtas. In the text upasāgarasseva = upasāgarassa + eva, dative/genitive singular; the entry is for the main word without the emphatic particle.
upasāgarasseva.example_1: Te sutvā ‘‘ bhaginiṃ nāsetuṃ na sakkā, sace dhītaraṃ vijāyissati, tampi na nāsessāma, sace pana putto bhavissati, nāsessāmā ’’ ti cintetvā devagabbhaṃ upasāgarasseva adaṃsu.
upasāgarasseva.translation_1: They, having heard it, thought, “We cannot destroy our sister; if she gives birth to a daughter, we will not destroy her either, but if it is a son, we will destroy [him],” and they gave Devagabbhā to Upasāgara as a wife.

andhakaveṇḍadāsaputtā.meaning_2: son of the Andhakaveṇḍa slave; the ten brethren, sons of a slave named Andhakaveṇḍa
andhakaveṇḍadāsaputtā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of the ten brother-kings in the Jātaka stories. Nominative plural in the text: andhakaveṇḍadāsaputtā. Andhakaveṇḍa is the name of the slave; dāsaputta is a compound with putta as its last member.
andhakaveṇḍadāsaputtā.example_1: Te andhakaveṇḍadāsaputtā dasa bhātikā ceṭakāti pākaṭā ahesuṃ.
andhakaveṇḍadāsaputtā.translation_1: They became known as the ten brethren, the sons of the Andhakaveṇḍa slave.
andhakaveṇḍadāsaputtā.example_2: Manussā sannipatitvā ‘‘ andhakaveṇḍadāsaputtā dasa bhātikā raṭṭhaṃ vilumpantī ’’ ti rājaṅgaṇe upakkosiṃsu.
andhakaveṇḍadāsaputtā.translation_2: The people gathered and proclaimed in the king’s court, “The ten brethren, the sons of the Andhakaveṇḍa slave, are plundering the realm!”

andhakaveṇḍaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a person in the Jātaka commentary; accusative singular in the text. The PEU suggests the compound may contain Andhaka + Veṇḍa/Veṇhu, possibly a name for Krishna or a descendant of Andhaka.
andhakaveṇḍaṃ.example_1: Rājā andhakaveṇḍaṃ pakkosāpetvā ‘‘ kasmā puttehi vilopaṃ kārāpesī ’’ ti tajjesi.
andhakaveṇḍaṃ.translation_1: The king had Andhakaveṇḍa summoned and threatened him, [saying], “Why do you allow your sons to plunder?”

bhametvā.meaning_2: having whirled around; having spun; having rotated
bhametvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of the causative bhāmeti. In the sentence it describes whirling someone around over the head before throwing him down.
bhametvā.example_1: Baladevo taṃ disvā ‘‘ na naṃ hatthena chupissāmī ’’ ti hatthisālato mahantaṃ hatthiyottaṃ āharitvā vaggitvā gajjitvā yottaṃ khipitvā cāruraṃ udare veṭhetvā dve yottakoṭiyo ekato katvā vattetvā ukkhipitvā sīsamatthake bhametvā bhūmiyaṃ pothetvā bahi akkhavāṭe khipi.
bhametvā.translation_1: Baladeva, seeing him, thought, “I will not touch him with my hand,” and fetching a thick elephant-yoke strap from the elephant stable, shouting and roaring, he cast the strap, wound it around Cānura’s belly, joined the two ends together, twisted them, lifted him up, whirled him around over his head, struck him down on the ground, and threw him outside the ring.

viravituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of viravati. In the text the donkey says it cannot bray. From vi + √ru.
viravituṃ.example_1: Gadrabho ‘‘ na sakkā na viravituṃ, tumhe pana paṭhamataraṃ āgantvā cattāro janā mahantāni ayanaṅgalāni gahetvā catūsu nagaradvāresu mahante ayakhāṇuke bhūmiyaṃ ākoṭetvā nagarassa uppatanakāle naṅgalāni gahetvā naṅgalabaddhaṃ ayasaṅkhalikaṃ ayakhāṇuke bandheyyātha, nagaraṃ uppatituṃ na sakkhissatī ’’ ti āha.
viravituṃ.translation_1: The donkey said, “I cannot [do] not bray. But you, first of all, come, four of you take great iron ploughs, strike great iron stakes into the ground at the four city gates, and at the time the city rises, you take the ploughs and tie the chain bound to the plough to the stakes. The city will not be able to rise.”

ayakhāṇuke.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative plural in the text (ayakhāṇuke). PEU gives neuter as well as masculine.
ayakhāṇuke.example_1: Gadrabho ‘‘ na sakkā na viravituṃ, tumhe pana paṭhamataraṃ āgantvā cattāro janā mahantāni ayanaṅgalāni gahetvā catūsu nagaradvāresu mahante ayakhāṇuke bhūmiyaṃ ākoṭetvā nagarassa uppatanakāle naṅgalāni gahetvā naṅgalabaddhaṃ ayasaṅkhalikaṃ ayakhāṇuke bandheyyātha, nagaraṃ uppatituṃ na sakkhissatī ’’ ti āha.
ayakhāṇuke.translation_1: The donkey said, “I cannot [do] not bray. But you, first of all, come, four of you take great iron ploughs, strike great iron stakes into the ground at the four city gates, and at the time the city rises, you take the ploughs and tie the chain bound to the plough to the stakes. The city will not be able to rise.”

manusocasīti.meaning_2: you sorrow; you grieve; you worry
manusocasīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is manusocasī ti, i.e. the 2nd singular present of manusocati plus the quotation particle iti, contracted by sandhi to manusocasīti. The prefix manu- is doubtful; possibly a false sandhi of maṃ ('me') + anusocati, or a misreading of anusocasīti.

masūrakaṃ.meaning_2: pillow; cushion; padded roll; leather mattress
masūrakaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text, used for something bound round the belly to fake pregnancy, and something crushed underfoot. Probably a stuffed or leather pad; the sense of a lentil-shaped (masūra) roll is possible.
masūrakaṃ.example_1: Te ekaṃ daharakumāraṃ alaṅkaritvā gabbhiniākārena dassetvā udare masūrakaṃ bandhitvā tassa santikaṃ netvā ‘‘ bhante, ayaṃ kumārikā kiṃ vijāyissatī ’’ ti pucchiṃsu.
masūrakaṃ.translation_1: They adorned a young boy, made him look as if he were pregnant by binding a pillow around his belly, brought him into the ascetic’s presence, and asked, “Venerable sir, when will this girl be delivered?”
masūrakaṃ.example_2: Atha naṃ osadhamantaṃ katvā naṅguṭṭhe gahetvā heṭṭhāsīsaṃ katvā sañcāletvā gahitabhojanaṃ chaḍḍāpetvā bhūmiyaṃ dīghato nipajjāpetvā masūrakaṃ maddanto viya pādehi madditvā aṭṭhīni cuṇṇiyamānāni viya ahesuṃ.
masūrakaṃ.translation_2: Then, having applied the medicine, he seized him by the tail, hung him head-down, shook him, made him vomit the food he had taken, laid him at full length on the ground, and trampled him with his feet as if crushing a reed, so that his bones were as if being crushed to powder.

kaṇhuposo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name in a list of kings in the Jātaka commentary. Nominative singular in the text.
kaṇhuposo.translation_1: Catudvāra, Kaṇhuposa, Saṅkha, Bodhi, and Dīpāyana;

takkala.meaning_2: name of a tree; (or) name of a plant (Dioscorea); name of one of the Nigrodha brothers' companions
takkala.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the Jātaka verse it is a proper name in a list (Nigrodha, Takkala, Dhammapāla, Kukkuṭa, Kuṇḍalī); nominative singular. Elsewhere takkala means a resin or a kind of yam (Dioscorea), sometimes neuter; the split takka + ala is uncertain.
takkala.translation_1: Nigrodha, Takkala, Dhammapāla, Kukkuṭa, and Kuṇḍalī;

bilāra.meaning_2: cat; name of a star or lunar mansion (Bilāra)
bilāra.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Appears in a list of names (perhaps stars or lunar mansions) in the Jātaka prose. Possibly a variant of bilāla (cat).
bilāra.example_1: Bilāra cakka bhūri ca, maṅgala ghaṭa soḷasa.
bilāra.translation_1: Bilāra, Cakka, and Bhūri, along with Maṅgala and the sixteenth, Ghaṭa.

koṭṭiyamānopi.meaning_2: being pounded; being pierced; being struck
koṭṭiyamānopi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present passive participle used adverbially with api; the Bodhisatta is 'even while being struck with spears'. Alternative analysis of the PEU: koṭṭa + iya + māna.
koṭṭiyamānopi.example_1: Bodhisattopi hatthācariyaṃ disvā ‘‘ idaṃ bhayaṃ na aññato uppannaṃ, tassa purisassa santikā uppannaṃ bhavissati, ahaṃ kho pana mahābalo hatthisahassampi viddhaṃsetuṃ samattho homi, kujjhitvā saraṭṭhakaṃ senāvāhanaṃ nāsetuṃ, sace pana kujjhissāmi, sīlaṃ me bhijjissati, tasmā ajja sattīhi koṭṭiyamānopi na kujjhissāmī ’’ ti adhiṭṭhāya sīsaṃ nāmetvā niccalova aṭṭhāsi.
koṭṭiyamānopi.translation_1: The Bodhisatta, seeing the elephant trainer, thought, “This danger has not arisen from elsewhere, it must have come from that man. I am indeed of great strength; I am capable of destroying even a thousand elephants, [or] destroying a whole kingdom’s army and transport [of elephants] if I were to become angry. But if I become angry, my virtue will be broken. Therefore, even if pierced today with spears, I will not be angry,” and having made this determination, he lowered his head and remained motionless.

kavacamabhihessati.meaning_2: will strike; will attack; will assail
kavacamabhihessati.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of kavacaṃ + abhihessati in the text. The verb is a future (with -ssa-) of the causative-type abhiheṭheti; the root √hiṃs (hurt) is not in the supplied root list, so the root fields may need adjusting.
kavacamabhihessati.example_1: Yattha rājā rājakumāro vā, kavacamabhihessati achambhito ’’ ti.
kavacamabhihessati.translation_1: Where a king or prince, fearless, will strike against the armor [of an enemy].”

kavacamabhihessatīti.meaning_2: will strike; will hit; will attack
kavacamabhihessatīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] kavacam-abhihessati-ti: kavacaṃ + abhihessati + iti. The -ti is the quotative particle, so the entry is for abhihessati; kavacaṃ is a separate word. Future 3rd singular of abhihanati.

nūnasā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of nūna (indeed, surely) + sā (she). The commentary glosses sā nūnasā as nūna sā esā. Quoted as a compound in the verse.
nūnasā.translation_1: 4. “She is a miserable one, blind and without a guide;
nūnasā.example_2: Tattha sā nūnasāti mahārāja, nūna sā esā.
nūnasā.translation_2: Regarding that, sā nūnasā means ‘Great King, surely she is this one.’

nūnasāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Possibly corrupt or sandhi (nūna + sa- or nūnasa + -ti). No occurrence found in the text; needs verification before entry.

tyāhamatrajo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi in the verse: tyāhaṃ = tyaṃ (te, 'your') + ahaṃ ('I') with change of final ṃ; atrajo = atra + ja ('born of her, i.e. legitimate'). Alternative analysis: tyāhaṃ atrajo = tyāhaṃ (ti + ahaṃ?) is less likely. Nominative singular functioning as a sentence.
tyāhamatrajo.example_1: 11. ‘‘ Uṭṭhehi amma kiṃ sesi, āgato tyāhamatrajo;
tyāhamatrajo.translation_1: 11. “Rise, mother! Why do you lie there? I, your legitimate son, have arrived;

āpūratī.meaning_2: is full; is filled; becomes complete
āpūratī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text reads āpūratī, following the very common eastern form -ti with place of articulation doubled before the variant ending -i; the final -i probably belongs to the preceding word, tathāhaṃ (tathā + ahaṃ), tayāpi (tayā + api), laddho (laddha) + iti. Third person singular present in a verse quoted in the commentary.
āpūratī.example_1: Āpūratī kāsipatī tathāhaṃ, tayāpi me saṅgamo ajja laddho ’’ ti.
āpūratī.translation_1: I am filled, O Lord of Kasi, in that way; today I have gained an association with you.”

atibalo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it qualifies saccanikkamo (nominative singular) in a verse of the Pāyāsi story.
atibalo.example_1: Pāyāsi vitto abhiruyha sandanaṃ, maggeneva atibalo saccanikkamo.
atibalo.translation_1: Traveled on joyful, having mounted his chariot, the one of great strength and true resolution [proceeded] by the path alone.

abhisiñcitukāmo.meaning_2: desiring to anoint; wishing to consecrate (as king)
abhisiñcitukāmo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Desiderative compound of abhisiñcituṃ (infinitive of abhisiñcati, to sprinkle; anoint) + kāma (desire). Nominative singular modifying rājā and pitā in the text; the object of the anointing is the prince in the accusative (puttaṃ, naṃ).
abhisiñcitukāmo.example_1: Rājā puttaṃ rajje abhisiñcitukāmo ‘‘ kumārassa idāni rajjasukhasevanakālo, nāṭakāpissa paccupaṭṭhāpessāmī ’’ ti sāsanaṃ pesesi.
abhisiñcitukāmo.translation_1: The King, desiring to sprinkle the prince as king, sent a message: “For the prince, this is now the time to enjoy royal pleasures; I shall provide him with dancers.”
abhisiñcitukāmo.example_2: Atha naṃ pitā rajje abhisiñcitukāmo hutvā ‘‘ sahāyassa kira me bārāṇasirañño dhītā atthi, tamevassa aggamahesiṃ karissāmī ’’ ti tassā atthāya bahuṃ paṇṇākāraṃ datvā amacce pesesi.
abhisiñcitukāmo.translation_2: Then his father, wishing to consecrate him as king, thought, “I hear my friend, the King of Benares, has a daughter; I will make her my son's chief queen.” For her sake, he gave many gifts and sent ministers.

parihārāpetvā.meaning_2: causes to carry around; has taken around; causes to be conveyed
parihārāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive (causative) of parihāreti, the causative of pariharati. In the sentence it governs suvaṇṇarūpakaṃ: 'having had the golden image carried around'. The form is -tvā, so stem and pattern are left empty.
parihārāpetvā.example_1: Te taṃ suvaṇṇarūpakaṃ sakalajambudīpaṃ parihārāpetvā tathārūpaṃ itthiṃ alabhantā udayabhaddaṃ alaṅkāretvā tassa santike ṭhapesuṃ.
parihārāpetvā.translation_1: They had that golden image taken throughout all Jambudīpa, and not finding a woman of that kind, they decorated Udayabhaddā and placed her near it.

yaṃhetu.meaning_2: for the sake of which; because of which
yaṃhetu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of yaṃ (accusative of ya) + hetu (masc). Used relatively: 'for the sake of which'.
yaṃhetu.example_1: 42. ‘‘ Yā sā rati uttamā kāmabhoginaṃ, yaṃhetu sattā visamaṃ caranti;
yaṃhetu.translation_1: 42. “That joy which is best for those who enjoy sense-pleasures, for the sake of which beings perform evil deeds;

sāhanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Difficult form; probably a 3rd singular present from √sah with sā- (cf. sāhasa, sahasā). The text has no sentence to confirm the reading. Could also be an aorist or a sandhi.

vijigucchiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form vijigucchiṃ is 1st person singular aorist (or imperfect) of vijigucchati; the entry is given under the present stem. The PEU analysis vi+gupa+cha is uncertain; the double -gg- points to a formation from √gup.
vijigucchiṃ.example_1: Tena pacchā vijigucchiṃ, taṃ pāpaṃ pakataṃ mayā;
vijigucchiṃ.translation_1: Loathing the evil I had done, I felt disgust for it afterwards.

yevānucchavikāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of yevā (eva with sandhi) + anucchavikā (feminine adjective meaning suitable) + iti quotation particle. No sentences found for this occurrence.

surāmerayamādhukāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Part of the fifth precept phrase surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā. Here the -ti is the quotative enclitic: surāmerayamādhukā ti. Ends in -ā because it is a feminine compound of surā; the text's -āti is the sandhi of the final -ā with ti.

niggahitabboyevāti.meaning_2: should be restrained; should be rebuked; ought to be suppressed
niggahitabboyevāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Written as niggahitabbā + yeva + iti with sandhi; final -ā of the potential participle is lost before yeva. The full form is niggahitabbā yeva iti.

patanakaussavabindūni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative plural in the text. The form kaussava is unusual (probably dissimilation of ussava); the commentary glosses it as dew-drops falling in the cold season.
patanakaussavabindūni.example_1: Evaṃ gacchante kāle bodhisatto ekadivasaṃ pātova rathavaramāruyha mahantena sirivibhavena uyyānakīḷaṃ gacchanto rukkhaggatiṇaggasākhaggamakkaṭakasuttajālādīsu muttājālākārena laggitaussavabindūni disvā ‘‘ samma sārathi, kiṃ nāmetan ’’ ti pucchitvā ‘‘ ete deva, himasamaye patanakaussavabindūni nāmā ’’ ti sutvā divasabhāgaṃ uyyāne kīḷitvā sāyanhakāle paccāgacchanto te adisvāva ‘‘ samma sārathi, kahaṃ nu kho ete ussavabindū, na te idāni passāmī ’’ ti pucchi.
patanakaussavabindūni.translation_1: As time passed in this way, one day the Bodhisatta mounted his splendid chariot early in the morning and, going to sport in the park with great majesty and glory, he saw dew-drops hanging like strings of pearls on tree-tips, grass-tips, branch-tips, spider-webs, and the like. He asked, “Friend charioteer, what is this called?” and upon hearing, “My lord, these are called dew-drops that fall in the cold season,” he spent the day sporting in the park. As he was returning in the evening, he did not see them and asked, “Friend charioteer, where are those dew-drops? I do not see them now.”

nipāletuṃ.meaning_2: to keep; to protect; to preserve; to look after
nipāletuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of nipāleti, meaning 'to keep' or 'to protect'. The PEU entry suggests ni + pāla + ṇe + tuṃ, but the causative stem is pāle. Appears in a verse about a person unable to keep something.
nipāletuṃ.example_1: 86. ‘‘ Yaṃ na sakkā nipāletuṃ, posena lapataṃ bahuṃ;
nipāletuṃ.translation_1: “When a person can never keep a thing, though they may cry loudly,

nipāletunti.meaning_2: protects; guards; takes care of; watches over
nipāletunti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form nipāletunti = nipāletuṃ + ti (quotation), the infinitive of nipāleti. The PEU entry reads it as a single infinitive. Doubtful: whether the ending belongs to the verb itself or to a following ti.

saṃbhaggavibhaggā.meaning_2: broken and shattered; divided and scattered
saṃbhaggavibhaggā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is masculine nominative plural agreeing with sattā, meaning 'broken and shattered (at the mouth of death)'. It is a dvanda compound of two past participles (saṃbhagga from saṃ + bhañj, vibhagga from vi + bhaj).
saṃbhaggavibhaggā.example_1: Daharā cāti gāthā ‘‘ maccu nāmesa tāta bharata, neva suvaṇṇarūpakasadisānaṃ daharānaṃ khattiyakumārakādīnaṃ, na vuddhippattānaṃ mahāyodhānaṃ, na bālānaṃ puthujjanasattānaṃ, na buddhādīnaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ, na cakkavattiādīnaṃ issarānaṃ, na niddhanānaṃ daliddādīnaṃ lajjati, sabbepime sattā maccuparāyaṇā maraṇamukhe saṃbhaggavibhaggā bhavantiyevā ’’ ti dassanatthaṃ vuttā.
saṃbhaggavibhaggā.translation_1: The stanza Daharā cā was spoken to show: “Dear Bharata, this ‘death’ does not show respect for golden, young princes and the like, nor for aged, great warriors, nor for foolish, ordinary beings, nor for wise ones like the Buddhas, nor for masters like the Wheel-turning Monarchs, nor for the destitute and poor; all these beings are destined for death, appearing as broken and shattered at the mouth of death.”

metiādīhi.meaning_2: with 'me' and the like; by 'me' etc.
metiādīhi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the quotation me (my; me) plus iti plus ādīhi (with the like, instrumental plural of ādi). Possible alternative split: me + ti + ādīhi. No sentence context supplied.

suvaṇṇāḷiṅgasadisagīvo.meaning_2: whose neck is like a golden drum; golden-drum-necked
suvaṇṇāḷiṅgasadisagīvo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Explains the epithet kambugīva; nominative singular in the text. Probably suvaṇṇa + āḷiṅga (golden drum) rather than suvaṇṇā + liṅga.
suvaṇṇāḷiṅgasadisagīvo.translation_1: In it, 'golden-necked' means his neck resembled a golden drum.

uppātitaṃ.meaning_2: driven out; raised; caused to arise; expelled (of wind)
uppātitaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Past participle used as an adjective of akālavātaṃ (nom. sg. nt.) in the sentence, meaning a violent or out-of-season wind that has been stirred up or released. PEU suggests a link with uppātika/uppāteti.
uppātitaṃ.example_1: Nāvā satta divasāni nirupaddavā agamāsi, tato akālavātaṃ uppātitaṃ uppajji, nāvā cattāro māse pakatisamuddapiṭṭhe vicaritvā khuramālīsamuddaṃ nāma pattā.
uppātitaṃ.translation_1: The ship went for seven days without mishap, but then an unseasonable wind arose; the ship wandered for four months on the surface of the natural ocean and arrived at the ocean called Khuramāli.

pavāḷussanno.meaning_2: abounding in coral; full of coral; covered with coral
pavāḷussanno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Qualifies samuddo in the text (nominative singular). Perhaps a bahubbīhi for a sea rich in coral; the second member is from ussanna (pp of ussīdati / ussanna, 'overflowing, abundant').
pavāḷussanno.example_1: Veḷūti pana pavāḷassetaṃ nāmaṃ, so ca samuddo pavāḷussanno rattobhāso ahosi, tasmā ‘‘ yathā naḷova veḷuvā ’’ ti pucchiṃsu.
pavāḷussanno.translation_1: Now, by ‘bamboo’ (veḷu), this is a name for coral, and that ocean was abundant in coral and was red-hued; therefore they asked, “Just as an ocean like reeds, like bamboo, is seen.”

kūṭaḍḍaparājitā.meaning_2: defeated by a false judgement; beaten by a rigged lawsuit
kūṭaḍḍaparājitā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Kūṭa + aḍḍa + parājita, 'defeated by false judgment'. Nominative plural here, agreeing with manussā; DPD may prefer the split kūṭa + aḍḍa + parājita.
kūṭaḍḍaparājitā.example_1: Athekadivasaṃ vinicchaye kūṭaḍḍaparājitā manussā bandhulaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā mahāravaṃ viravantā vinicchayaamaccānaṃ kūṭaḍḍakāraṇaṃ tassa ārocesuṃ.
kūṭaḍḍaparājitā.translation_1: One day, some men who had been defeated in court by false judgment, seeing Bandhula approach, raised a great outcry and informed him of the judges' corruption.

kūṭaḍḍakāraṇaṃ.meaning_2: case of a false judgment; matter of a crooked court decision; corruption in judgment
kūṭaḍḍakāraṇaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] kūṭaḍḍa is itself a compound (kūṭa + aḍḍa, 'crooked/false lawsuit'); accusative singular in the text, object of ārocesuṃ.
kūṭaḍḍakāraṇaṃ.example_1: Athekadivasaṃ vinicchaye kūṭaḍḍaparājitā manussā bandhulaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā mahāravaṃ viravantā vinicchayaamaccānaṃ kūṭaḍḍakāraṇaṃ tassa ārocesuṃ.
kūṭaḍḍakāraṇaṃ.translation_1: One day, some men who had been defeated in court by false judgment, seeing Bandhula approach, raised a great outcry and informed him of the judges' corruption.

ussisakapasse.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Only in compound ussisakapassa, locative singular 'at the pillow'; ussisaka 'pillow'. But uncertain, perhaps ussīsaka; so the entry may need revision.
ussisakapasse.example_1: Vimānapariyantikameva mama ñātīnaṃ devatānampi jīvitaṃ, na kho pana maṃ tathā attano vināso bādhati, yathā ñātīnaṃ, tasmā nesaṃ mayā jīvitaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti cintetvā aḍḍharattasamaye dibbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito rañño sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā sakalagabbhaṃ ekobhāsaṃ katvā ussisakapasse rodamāno aṭṭhāsi.
ussisakapasse.translation_1: “The life of my kin-deities is also as long as their dwellings; but it is not my own destruction that hurts me, but that of my kin. Therefore, I must give them life.” With this thought, at midnight, adorned in divine splendor, he entered the king's royal chamber, filled it with a singular radiance, and stood by the king's pillow, weeping.

tyāssūni.meaning_2: by what are thy tears; why do your tears flow
tyāssūni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of tava (or te) + assūni, with -a + a- > -ā-. The commentary (Kena tyāssūni vattantīti ... tava assūni vattanti) resolves it as tava assūni. Occurs in the verse 'Kena tyāssūni vattanti'.
tyāssūni.example_1: Kena tyāssūni vattanti, kuto taṃ bhayamāgatan ’’ ti.
tyāssūni.translation_1: Whence come thy fears, and why do thy tears flow?”
tyāssūni.example_2: Kena tyāssūni vattantīti kena kāraṇena tava assūni vattanti.
tyāssūni.translation_2: Kena tyāssūni vattantī means: for what reason do your tears flow?

chedayīti.meaning_2: causes to cut; has cut; has cut down
chedayīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form in the text is chedayīti, which is chedayati joined with ti. It is imperative 2nd singular in sense, negative with mā: 'do not have (it) cut'.
chedayīti.example_1: Yathevāti tasmā yatheva te porāṇakarājāno maṃ pūjayiṃsu, ekopi imaṃ rukkhaṃ na chindāpesi, tvañcāpi maṃ tatheva pūjaya, mā me rukkhaṃ chedayīti.
chedayīti.translation_1: Yathevā means: therefore, just as those ancient kings worshipped me and none of them had this tree cut down, so too should you worship me; do not have my tree cut down.

tepihaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Text is uncertain (verse); possibly te + pi + ihaṃ, 'these, too, here', or te + ihaṃ, 'these here'. Analysed as sandhi by the sandhi rules; if treated as te + pi + ahaṃ the pos would differ.
tepihaṃ.translation_1: These I should crush by one huge fall,—and great would be their woe.”

saṃbhaggavimāne.meaning_2: with shattered heavenly mansions; whose celestial palaces are destroyed
saṃbhaggavimāne.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi compound describing the deities (devasaṅgha): their vimānas are saṃbhagga 'shattered'. The form in the text is used adverbially as part of the phrase saṃbhaggavimāne karonto 'destroying (their) heavenly mansions'. The PEU analysis treats it as a ti adjective.
saṃbhaggavimāne.example_1: Ñātī meti mama bhaddasālarukkhassa chāyāya sukhasaṃvaddhā mama passe taruṇasālarukkhesu nibbattā mayā katavātaparittāṇattā nivātajā mama ñātakā devasaṅghā atthi, te ahaṃ visālasākhaviṭapo mūle chinditvā patanto upahiṃseyyaṃ, saṃbhaggavimāne karonto vināseyyanti attho.
saṃbhaggavimāne.translation_1: Ñātī me means: in the shade of my Lucky Tree, my relatives, the host of deities who have arisen among the young sal trees in my vicinity and who live in the shelter from the wind that I provide, are present; if I, with my spreading branches, were to be cut at the root and fall, I would crush them, destroying them by shattering their heavenly mansions.

uttarāpetvā.meaning_2: causes to rise; causes to overflow; causes to flood; makes arise
uttarāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative of uttarati. In the text it is an absolutive (uttarāpetvā, 'having caused to rise/overflow') in the phrase mahāsamuddaṃ uttarāpetvā, 'having caused the great ocean to rise'.
uttarāpetvā.example_1: Devatā ‘‘ ime amhākaṃ kīḷāmaṇḍalaṃ paṭikūlaṃ karontī ’’ ti kujjhitvā ‘‘ mahāsamuddaṃ uttarāpetvā dīpakadhovanaṃ karissāmā ’’ ti mantetvā ‘‘ ayaṃ kāḷapakkho, ajja amhākaṃ samāgamo ca bhinno, ito dāni pannarasame divase puṇṇamīuposathadivase candassuggamanavelāya samuddaṃ ubbattetvā sabbepime ghātessāmā ’’ ti divasaṃ ṭhapayiṃsu.
uttarāpetvā.translation_1: The deities, thinking, “They are making our playground disgusting,” got angry and plotted, “We will bring up the great ocean and cleanse the island. Today is the dark fortnight, our assembly is broken; now, on the fifteenth day, the full moon, at the time of the moon's rising, we will bring up the ocean and kill them all,” and fixed the day.

tipañcarattūpagatamhi.meaning_2: having arrived at the third night (of the fortnight); reached on the fifteenth night
tipañcarattūpagatamhi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text (tipañcarattūpagatamhi). Probably tīhi pañcahi rattīhi upagata, i.e. arrived at the third (fifteenth) night; the split ti + pañca + ratti is uncertain.
tipañcarattūpagatamhi.example_1: 26. ‘‘ Tipañcarattūpagatamhi cande, vego mahā hehiti sāgarassa;
tipañcarattūpagatamhi.translation_1: 26. “When the moon has reached the third night [of the fortnight], the ocean will have a great current;

āputtaputtehi.meaning_2: children and grandchildren; sons and grandsons; descendants
āputtaputtehi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is instrumental plural: 'together with children and grandchildren'. Sometimes written as āputtāputta or āputtapaṇaputtaka. The initial ā is a prefix meaning 'up to, including'.
āputtaputtehi.example_1: Na vo bhayaṃ paṭipassāmi kiñci, āputtaputtehi pamodathavho ’’ ti.
āputtaputtehi.translation_1: I see no fear for you at all; rejoice together with your children and sons.”

āputtaputtehīti.meaning_2: with sons and daughters; with children and grandchildren
āputtaputtehīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Likely part of the sandhi āputtamāputtehi + iti, only the pronoun-like portion is opaque; the meaning is uncertain without context.

paviceyya.meaning_2: should examine; should investigate; should discern
paviceyya.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Optative 3rd singular used in the sense of examining and discriminating between statements. The PEU analysis as an absolutive (pa + vi + ci + tvā) does not fit the syntax here; the two sentences require a finite verb. The form overlaps with the absolutive paviceyya but is best treated as optative of a causative pavicet 1.
paviceyya.example_1: Yo cīdha tacchaṃ paviceyya gaṇhati, sa ve naro seṭṭhamupeti ṭhānan ’’ ti.
paviceyya.translation_1: The person who examines and takes what is accurate here reaches the highest state.”
paviceyya.example_2: Yaṃ pana sotavisayaṃ āpāthagataṃ hoti, taṃ āpāthagataṃ gahetvā yo idha paṇḍitapuriso purimavacanañca pacchimavacanañca paviceyya vicinitvā tīretvā upaparikkhitvā tacchaṃ gaṇhāti, yaṃ tathaṃ saccaṃ sabhāvabhūtaṃ, tadeva paccakkhaṃ katvā gaṇhāti.
paviceyya.translation_2: But whatever comes within the range of hearing, a wise person here, having taken that which has come within the range of hearing, having examined, investigated, and weighed the first and later statements, takes what is accurate—that which is true, factual, and based on nature—taking that as the evident truth.

byadhesi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text has byadhesi, which is the aorist (or the 2sg present) of byadheti; the commentary glosses byadheti. The root is √badh (bind, tie), which gives byādhati, and the causative byādh- > byadh-.
byadhesi.example_1: 36. ‘‘ Anāgataṃ paṭikayirātha kiccaṃ,‘ mā maṃ kiccaṃ kiccakāle byadhesi ’;
byadhesi.translation_1: 36. “One should do the work of the future beforehand, ‘lest the work distress me at the time of work’;
byadhesi.example_2: Mā maṃ kiccaṃ kiccakāle byadhesi , pure kattabbañhi pure akayiramānaṃ pacchā paccuppannabhāvappattaṃ attano kiccakāle kāyacittābādhena byadheti, taṃ maṃ mā byadhesīti paṭhamameva naṃ paṇḍito kareyya.
byadhesi.translation_2: Mā maṃ kiccaṃ kiccakāle byadhesi: For work that should be done beforehand, when not done, distresses one through physical and mental suffering at the time when that work becomes present; a wise person should perform that work at the very beginning so that it does not distress me.

byadhetīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The quoted -iti is dropped from lemma_1. Causative present, 3rd singular, preceded by an explanatory quotation in the commentary.

byadheti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative of byadhati (to pierce; to afflict). Occurs as an aorist/prohibitive form byadhesi in the text; here glossed as present 3rd singular. 2nd sg in 'mā ... byadhesi'.
byadheti.example_1: Mā maṃ kiccaṃ kiccakāle byadhesi , pure kattabbañhi pure akayiramānaṃ pacchā paccuppannabhāvappattaṃ attano kiccakāle kāyacittābādhena byadheti, taṃ maṃ mā byadhesīti paṭhamameva naṃ paṇḍito kareyya.
byadheti.translation_1: Mā maṃ kiccaṃ kiccakāle byadhesi: For work that should be done beforehand, when not done, distresses one through physical and mental suffering at the time when that work becomes present; a wise person should perform that work at the very beginning so that it does not distress me.
byadheti.example_2: Taṃ kiccaṃ kiccakāleti anāgataṃ kiccaṃ kayiramānaṃ pacchā paccuppannabhāvappattaṃ attano kiccakāle kāyacittābādhakāle tādisaṃ purimaṃ na byadheti na bādhati.
byadheti.translation_2: Taṃ kiccaṃ kiccakāle means that future work, when it is being done and has reached the state of being present, does not distress—does not torment—such a person at the time of work, at the time of physical and mental suffering.

koṭāpemi.meaning_2: causes to cut; has cut; fells; clears (a site); has (a field) cleared
koṭāpemi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] 1st person singular present of a causative verb; the PEU entry suggests koṭṭheti (√kuṭ 'cut') as the base verb.
koṭāpemi.example_1: Satthā tassa upanissayaṃ disvā sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pavisanto maggā okkamma tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā ‘‘ kiṃ karosi brāhmaṇā ’’ ti vatvā ‘‘ khettaṭṭhānaṃ koṭāpemi bho, gotamā ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ sādhu, brāhmaṇa, kammaṃ karohī ’’ ti vatvā agamāsi.
koṭāpemi.translation_1: The Teacher, seeing his potential for growth, while entering Sāvatthī for alms, stepped out of the road and spoke kindly to him, saying, “Brahmin, what are you doing?” When he replied, “Master Gotama, I am felling the site for a field,” the Teacher said, “It is good, brahmin, carry on with the work,” and went on.

taṇhāvase.meaning_2: power of craving; control of craving; sway of craving
taṇhāvase.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text (taṇhāvase), in the phrase taṇhāvase na pavattati, 'does not act under the power of craving'. Related taṇhāvasika is a derivative adjective.
taṇhāvase.example_1: Na kurute vasanti tādisañhi purisaṃ taṇhā vase vattetuṃ na sakkoti, sveva pana taṇhāya ādīnavaṃ disvā sarabhaṅgamāṇavo viya ca aḍḍhamāsakarājā viya ca taṇhāvase na pavattatīti attho.
taṇhāvase.translation_1: Na kurute vasaṃ means craving cannot bring such a person under its power, but having seen the danger of craving, just like the student Sarabhaṅga and the half-weight king, they do not act under the power of craving; this is the meaning.

iccassuhātipi.meaning_2: this is also a reading; iti ca assu hā ti pi
iccassuhātipi.construction: iti + ca + assu + hā + ti + pi
iccassuhātipi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A commentary compound of iti, ca, assu, hā, ti, and pi, citing an alternative reading (pāṭho).

pesuññakāraṇo.meaning_2: one who causes tale-bearing; one who sows discord
pesuññakāraṇo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Glosses pisuṇa in the commentary. Nominative singular in the text.

posituṃ.meaning_2: to nourish; to support; to bring up; to foster
posituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of poseti used with samattho in the sense of being able to support. Alternative root analysis √pu + *s > posa.
posituṃ.example_1: Pahu santoti dhanabalenāpi kāyabalenāpi posituṃ samattho paṭibalo samāno.
posituṃ.translation_1: Pahu santoti: being capable of supporting them with the strength of wealth and the strength of the body.

uposakā.meaning_2: observer of the fast day; one who keeps the uposatha precepts; lay devotee observing the sabbath
uposakā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative plural in the text. Denotes a lay person (here male) who observes the uposatha; often contrasted with upāsaka, the ordinary lay follower.
uposakā.example_1: Bhikkhū bhikkhudhammaṃ, bhikkhuniyo bhikkhunidhammaṃ, uposakā upāsakadhammaṃ, upāsikā upāsikadhammaṃ, brāhmaṇā brāhmaṇadhammaṃ vissajjesuṃ.
uposakā.translation_1: Monks, nuns, lay followers, and brahmins all abandoned their respective duties.

parivaṭṭento.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle masculine nominative singular in the text (parivaṭṭento), from parivaṭṭeti; here used of twirling an arrow and of rolling on the ground.
parivaṭṭento.example_1: Tadā sakko devarājā nave nave deve apassanto manussalokaṃ oloketvā manussānaṃ apāyesu nibbattitabhāvaṃ ñatvā satthu sāsanaṃ osakkitaṃ disvā ‘‘ kiṃ nu karissāmī ’’ ti cintetvā ‘‘ attheko upāyo, mahājanaṃ tāsetvā bhītabhāvaṃ ñatvā pacchā assāsetvā dhammaṃ desetvā osakkitaṃ sāsanaṃ paggayha aparampi vassasahassaṃ pavattanakāraṇaṃ karissāmī ’’ ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā mātalidevaputtaṃ mocappamāṇadāṭhaṃ catūhi dāṭhāhi viniggatarasmiyā bhayānakaṃ katvā gabbhinīnaṃ dassaneneva gabbhapātanasamatthaṃ ghorarūpaṃ ājāneyyappamāṇaṃ kāḷavaṇṇaṃ mahākaṇhasunakhaṃ māpetvā pañcabandhanena bandhitvā rattamālaṃ kaṇṭhe piḷandhitvā rajjukoṭikaṃ ādāya sayaṃ dve kāsāyāni nivāsetvā pacchāmukhe pañcadhā kese bandhitvā rattamālaṃ piḷandhitvā āropitapavāḷavaṇṇajiyaṃ mahādhanuṃ gahetvā vajiragganārācaṃ nakhena parivaṭṭento vanacarakavesaṃ gahetvā nagarato yojanamatte ṭhāne otaritvā ‘‘ nassati loko, nassati loko ’’ ti tikkhattuṃ saddaṃ anusāvetvā manusse uttāsetvā nagarūpacāraṃ patvā puna saddamakāsi.
parivaṭṭento.translation_1: Then Sakka, the king of the gods, not seeing any new deities, looked upon the human world, learned that humans were being born in states of suffering, and seeing the decline of the Buddha’s Dispensation, he thought, ‘What shall I do?’ Having decided, ‘There is one way; I will terrify the multitude, and when I know they are frightened, I will then console them, teach the Dhamma, uphold the declined Dispensation, and ensure it lasts for another thousand years,’ he transformed Mātali into a great black hound with tusks the size of banana buds, with a horrific, terrifying form, capable of causing miscarriage in pregnant women just by being seen, bound it with fivefold chains, and led it by a cord. He himself put on two robes, bound his hair in five knots at the back, wore a red wreath, took a great bow with a string the color of coral, twirled a diamond-tipped arrow with his finger, assumed the guise of a hunter, descended one league from the city, cried out three times, ‘The world will perish! The world will perish!’ to terrify the humans, reached the city outskirts, and sounded the cry again.
parivaṭṭento.example_2: Taṃ gahetvā mahājano bhūmiyaṃ parivaṭṭento parivaṭṭento paridevi.
parivaṭṭento.translation_2: Taking that, the great populace lamented, rolling over and over on the ground.

usīnakarājāpi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a king; the -pi is the enclitic 'also' and is not part of the headword. Nominative singular in the text.
usīnakarājāpi.translation_1: King Usīnara also took his household and went up to the palace terrace.

jambudipe.meaning_2: Jambudīpa; the island of the rose-apple tree; the southern continent; India
jambudipe.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text (jambudipe, with the stem vowel shortened by sandhi). Name of the southern continent of Buddhist cosmology.
jambudipe.example_1: Vidhurajātake (jā.2.22.1346 ādayo) hi puṇṇakayakkharañño, kusajātake (jā.2.20.1 ādayo) kusarañño, bhūridattajātake (jā.2.22.784 ādayo) sudassananāgarañño, imasmiṃ mahākaṇhajātake ayaṃ saddoti ime cattāro saddā jambudipe mahāsaddā nāma ahesuṃ.
jambudipe.translation_1: In the Vidhura Jātaka, it was the sound of Puṇṇaka; in the Kusa Jātaka, the sound of King Kusa; in the Bhūridatta Jātaka, the sound of the snake-king Sudassana; and this sound in this Mahākaṇha Jātaka—these four are the great sounds in Jambudīpa.

adhiyitvā.meaning_2: having studied; having learned by heart; having recited
adhiyitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of adhiyāti (adhi + √i 2, study, recite). Used with sāvittiṃ, 'having studied the Sāvittī hymn'.

adhiyitvāti.meaning_2: having studied; having learned; having mastered
adhiyitvāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Attached to -ti, so the word is adhiyitvā; it is the absolutives adhiyitvā of adhiyāti, glossed with adhiyitvā ti attho.
adhiyitvāti.translation_1: “Sacrificial rites” means the ritual texts; having studied the sacrificial texts, this is the meaning.

bharituṃ.meaning_2: to bear; to support; to maintain; to bring up
bharituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive from √bhar (carry, support), used with samatthā as 'capable of supporting'; glossed by posetuṃ in the text.
bharituṃ.translation_1: “Being able” means being capable of supporting and maintaining [them].

vito.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text: devaloko tuccho viya vito, 'the heaven-world has become as if empty'. Possibly a rare form of vitta ('empty, void') or a sandhi. Uncertain; not in standard dictionaries.
vito.example_1: So tato mahājanassa utrastakāle sunakhaṃ rajjuyā ākaḍḍhitvā ṭhapitaṃ viya katvā luddakavesaṃ vijahitvā attano ānubhāvena ākāse jalamāno ṭhatvā ‘‘ mahārāja, ahaṃ sakko devarājā,‘ ayaṃ loko vinassatī ’ ti āgato, pamattā hi mahājanā, adhammaṃ vattitvā matamatā sampati apāye pūrenti, devaloko tuccho viya vito, ito paṭṭhāya adhammikesu kattabbaṃ ahaṃ jānissāmi, tvaṃ appamatto hohi, mahārājā ’’ ti catūhi satārahagāthāhi dhammaṃ desetvā manussānaṃ dānasīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā osakkitasāsanaṃ aññaṃ vassasahassaṃ pavattanasamatthaṃ katvā mātaliṃ ādāya sakaṭṭhānameva gato.
vito.translation_1: Then, at the time the great crowd was terrified, he pulled the hound back with the leash, acted as if it were fixed in place, shed the disguise of a hunter, and standing in the sky, radiant through his own power, said: “Great King, I am Sakka, King of the Gods. I have come because ‘this world is being destroyed.’ For the great crowd is negligent; living by non-Dhamma, the people who die are currently filling the four states of woe. The heaven-world has become as if empty. From this day forward, I will know how to deal with those who follow non-Dhamma. You, Great King, be diligent.” Having declared the Dhamma in four noble stanzas, established the people in merit such as giving and virtue, and strengthened the waning Dispensation so that it was capable of lasting for another thousand years, he took Mātali and returned to his own place.

nipparādhohamasmīti.meaning_2: I am without fault, I am blameless, thus
nipparādhohamasmīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of nipparādho ahaṃ asmi iti. No sentences given; the analysis follows the spelling. The -ti marks the end of a quotation. nipparādho agrees with ahaṃ as a nominative singular adjective.

saṃkhubbhitvā.meaning_2: having been agitated; having been disturbed; having become tumultuous
saṃkhubbhitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of saṃkhubbhati (passive sense, 'having been shaken/agitated'). Alternative reading saṅkhubbhitvā; some analyses take khubha as a separate base.
saṃkhubbhitvā.example_1: Sakalanagaraṃ saṃkhubbhitvā ‘‘ rājā kira mātugāmassa vacanaṃ gahetvā mahāpadumakumāraṃ ghātāpesī ’’ ti sannipatitvā rājakumārassa pādamūle nipatitvā ‘‘ idaṃ te sāmi, ananucchavikan ’’ ti mahāsaddena paridevi.
saṃkhubbhitvā.translation_1: The whole city was in turmoil, and they gathered, saying, “They say the king, believing the woman's word, is having Prince Mahāpaduma killed,” and falling at the prince's feet, they lamented with a loud noise, “Master, this is not worthy of you!”

daṇḍiyañca.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is daṇḍiyaṃ, joined to ca by sandhi (daṇḍiyaṃ + ca). It contrasts with adaṇḍiya in the same line. Another analysis takes it from the root √daṇḍ with the suffix -iya.
daṇḍiyañca.translation_1: 108. “He punishes one who should not be punished, and does not punish one who should be punished;
daṇḍiyañca.example_2: Adaṇḍiyanti yo adaṇḍiyaṃ adaṇḍapaṇetabbañca daṇḍetvā daṇḍiyañca daṇḍapaṇetabbaṃ adaṇḍetvā attano rucimeva karoti, so andho viya visamaṃ maggaṃ paṭipanno, na jānāti samāsamaṃ, tato pāsāṇādīsu pakkhalanto andho viya catūsu apāyesu mahādukkhaṃ pāpuṇātīti attho.
daṇḍiyañca.translation_2: Adaṇḍiyan: He who punishes one who should not be punished and does not punish one who should be punished, but acts according to his own desire—he is like a blind man following an uneven path; he does not know the even from the uneven. Consequently, like a blind man who stumbles on rocks and the like and reaches great suffering, so too does he reach great suffering in the four states of deprivation.

veravā.meaning_2: hostile; having enemies; full of enmity
veravā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text nominative singular, used of a king (so veravā nāma hoti). The commentary glosses it as 'one who has enmity', from vera + vant (with vā by sandhi or māgadhī influence).
veravā.example_1: 111. ‘‘ Paribhūto mudu hoti, atitikkho ca veravā;
veravā.translation_1: 111. “The malleable one is disdained, and the overly severe one has wrath;
veravā.example_2: Veravāti atitikkhassa pana sabbepi raṭṭhavāsino verino hontīti so veravā nāma hoti.
veravā.translation_2: Veravā: For the overly severe king, all the inhabitants of the realm become enemies; he is called one who has enmity.

adaṇḍapaṇetabbañca.meaning_2: not to be punished; not deserving punishment
adaṇḍapaṇetabbañca.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi with ca: adaṇḍapaṇetabbaṃ + ca. Part of the pair adaṇḍiya ... adaṇḍapaṇetabba, explained by adaṇḍiyanti in the commentary. Negative of daṇḍapaṇetabba; cf. PEU adaṇḍapaṇetabba.
adaṇḍapaṇetabbañca.example_1: Adaṇḍiyanti yo adaṇḍiyaṃ adaṇḍapaṇetabbañca daṇḍetvā daṇḍiyañca daṇḍapaṇetabbaṃ adaṇḍetvā attano rucimeva karoti, so andho viya visamaṃ maggaṃ paṭipanno, na jānāti samāsamaṃ, tato pāsāṇādīsu pakkhalanto andho viya catūsu apāyesu mahādukkhaṃ pāpuṇātīti attho.
adaṇḍapaṇetabbañca.translation_1: Adaṇḍiyan: He who punishes one who should not be punished and does not punish one who should be punished, but acts according to his own desire—he is like a blind man following an uneven path; he does not know the even from the uneven. Consequently, like a blind man who stumbles on rocks and the like and reaches great suffering, so too does he reach great suffering in the four states of deprivation.

daṇḍetvā.meaning_2: having punished; having inflicted punishment (on); having tortured
daṇḍetvā.example_1: Adaṇḍiyanti yo adaṇḍiyaṃ adaṇḍapaṇetabbañca daṇḍetvā daṇḍiyañca daṇḍapaṇetabbaṃ adaṇḍetvā attano rucimeva karoti, so andho viya visamaṃ maggaṃ paṭipanno, na jānāti samāsamaṃ, tato pāsāṇādīsu pakkhalanto andho viya catūsu apāyesu mahādukkhaṃ pāpuṇātīti attho.
daṇḍetvā.translation_1: Adaṇḍiyan: He who punishes one who should not be punished and does not punish one who should be punished, but acts according to his own desire—he is like a blind man following an uneven path; he does not know the even from the uneven. Consequently, like a blind man who stumbles on rocks and the like and reaches great suffering, so too does he reach great suffering in the four states of deprivation.

adaṇḍetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Negative absolutive; appears in the definition of adaṇḍiya in the commentary.
adaṇḍetvā.example_1: Adaṇḍiyanti yo adaṇḍiyaṃ adaṇḍapaṇetabbañca daṇḍetvā daṇḍiyañca daṇḍapaṇetabbaṃ adaṇḍetvā attano rucimeva karoti, so andho viya visamaṃ maggaṃ paṭipanno, na jānāti samāsamaṃ, tato pāsāṇādīsu pakkhalanto andho viya catūsu apāyesu mahādukkhaṃ pāpuṇātīti attho.
adaṇḍetvā.translation_1: Adaṇḍiyan: He who punishes one who should not be punished and does not punish one who should be punished, but acts according to his own desire—he is like a blind man following an uneven path; he does not know the even from the uneven. Consequently, like a blind man who stumbles on rocks and the like and reaches great suffering, so too does he reach great suffering in the four states of deprivation.

pharāpetvā.meaning_2: having spread; having pervaded; having suffused; having infused
pharāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of pharāpeti (causative of pharati). In the text it describes spreading a divine touch (dibbasamphassaṃ) over the body. The PEU entry splits it as phara + ṇāpe + tvā.
pharāpetvā.example_1: Athassa mettānubhāvena pabbate adhivatthā devatā ‘‘ mā bhāyi mahāpadumā ’’ ti taṃ samassāsetvā ubhohi hatthehi gahetvā hadaye ṭhapetvā dibbasamphassaṃ pharāpetvā otaritvā pabbatapāde patiṭṭhitanāgarājassa phaṇagabbhe ṭhapesi.
pharāpetvā.translation_1: Then, by the power of his loving-kindness, the devatā haunting the mountain comforted him, saying, “Do not fear, Mahāpaduma!” and catching him with both hands, pressed him to his heart, infused him with a divine thrill, and descending, placed him in the hood of the snake-king dwelling at the foot of the mountain.
pharāpetvā.example_2: Samphusitvāti suṭṭhu phusitvā attano hatthasamphassaṃ mama sarīre pharāpetvā.
pharāpetvā.translation_2: Samphusitvā means “having thoroughly touched, having spread the touch of his hand over my body.”

labheyyito.meaning_2: may he receive from here; may he get from this
labheyyito.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the optative labheyya (3rd singular of labhati) and the indeclinable ito. The commentary glosses it as labheyya ito; the whole is a wish, 'may he too receive from here'.
labheyyito.example_1: Tato naṃ nānukampati, aho sopi labheyyito.
labheyyito.translation_1: Because of that, he does not sympathize with him, [thinking] ‘Alas, may he also receive it!’
labheyyito.example_2: Tato naṃ anukampati, aho sopi labheyyito.
labheyyito.translation_2: Because of that, he sympathizes with him, [thinking] ‘Alas, may he also receive it!’

kelāyito.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Past participle used adjectivally of a person: kelāyito hoti, 'he is affectionate'. In the gloss it is explained by kelāyati, mamāyati, pattheti, piheti, icchati.
kelāyito.translation_1: Then he becomes affectionate, and welcomes him with kind words.
kelāyito.example_2: Kelāyitoti kelāyati mamāyati pattheti piheti icchatīti attho.
kelāyito.translation_2: ‘Affectionate’ (kelāyito) means he cherishes, calls it his own, longs for, loves, and desires it—this is the meaning.

labheyyitoti.meaning_2: would get; would receive; would obtain
labheyyitoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Optative 3rd singular with -iti and -to appended in the text (-eyyito ti); the -ti is the quotative particle, so the entry is for labhati.

kelāyitoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi kelāyito + ti; ending -īti is the 3rd singular, possibly with the emphatic -ti clitic to be removed. The related kelāyita is a past participle built with -ta on the same base.

nikkhimitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text has nikkhimitvā, a variant spelling of nikkhamitvā (absolutive of nikkhamati). The meaning here is 'having gone out from'.
nikkhimitvā.example_1: So pātova vuṭṭhāya kājaṃ ādāya tato gāmā nikkhimitvā araññe ekaṃ ambarukkhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā sattapadamatthake ṭhito taṃ mantaṃ parivattetvā ambarukkhaṃ ekena udakapasatena paharati.
nikkhimitvā.translation_1: He would rise early in the morning, take his carrying-pole, go out from that village, approach a certain mango tree in the forest, and standing at a distance of seven paces, he would recite that charm and strike the mango tree with a handful of water.

guyhittho.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Passive sense with caus form; often in manto guyhati. Not to be confused with guyha as pp 'secret'. In the text the form is guyhittho, possibly a corrupted or variant spelling.
guyhittho.example_1: Mā cassu me pucchito nāmagottaṃ, guyhittho atthaṃ vijaheyya manto.
guyhittho.translation_1: He said, ‘Do not conceal your name and lineage from me when asked; a concealed hymn would lose its benefit.’
guyhittho.example_2: Pakatiñca saṃsīti ‘‘ mā me pucchito nāmagottaṃ guyhittho, sace gūhasi, mantā te nassissantī ’’ ti tesaṃ nassanapakatiñca mayhaṃ saṃsi.
guyhittho.translation_2: Pakatiñca saṃsī means: He told me their nature of disappearing, saying, “Do not conceal your name and lineage when asked by me; if you conceal it, they will be ruined.”

micchāya.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the sentence micchāya is the instrumental of the adverb used as a noun ('by falsehood'), referring to the lie 'brāhmaṇassāti'; the related entry micchāyasa is a separate compound (micchā + yasa).
micchāya.example_1: Brāhmaṇassāti micchāti ‘‘ brāhmaṇassa santike mayā ime mantā gahitā ’’ ti micchāya abhaṇiṃ, tena me te mantā naṭṭhā, svāhaṃ pahīnamanto idāni kapaṇo rudāmīti.
micchāya.translation_1: Brāhmaṇassāti micchā means: “These hymns were learned by me from a brahmin,” I lied falsely; because of that, those hymns were lost to me. So I, having lost the hymn, now weep, wretched.

paccakkhitvā.meaning_2: having rejected; having abandoned; having renounced; having disavowed
paccakkhitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -itvā of paccakkhāti (pati + ā + khā). In the sentence the teacher is the object renounced.
paccakkhitvā.example_1: So mahāsattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno ‘‘ kiṃkāraṇā āgatosī ’’ ti puṭṭho ‘‘ ācariya, musāvādaṃ katvā ācariyaṃ paccakkhitvā mahāvināsaṃ pattomhī ’’ ti vatvā accayaṃ dassetvā puna mante yācanto –
paccakkhitvā.translation_1: He approached the Great Being, venerated him, and seated himself to one side. When asked, “For what reason have you come?” he said, “Teacher, having spoken a lie and renounced my teacher, I have reached great ruin,” and having shown his transgression, and asking for the hymns again –

upakkhandhamhāti.meaning_2: upper shoulder; region of the shoulder
upakkhandhamhāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi with -ti; ablative singular in the text (upakkhandhamhā + ti). Variant reading of upakhandha.

javituṃ.meaning_2: to run; to race; to move quickly
javituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -tuṃ from the root √ju (be fast) with the a-sign. Used with na sakkhissati (will not be able to race). Appears twice in these sentences.
javituṃ.example_1: ‘‘ Tātā, sūriyajavo nāma sīgho, sūriyena saddhiṃ javituṃ na sakkhissatha, antarāva vinassissatha, mā gamitthā ’’ ti.
javituṃ.translation_1: ‘My dears, the sun’s speed is swift; you will not be able to race with the sun; you will perish in the middle of the way. Do not go.’
javituṃ.example_2: Mahāsatto te adisvā ‘‘ kahaṃ nu kho gatā ’’ ti pucchitvā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā cintesi ‘‘ te sūriyena saddhiṃ javituṃ na sakkhissanti, antarāva vinassissanti, jīvitaṃ tesaṃ dassāmī ’’ ti.
javituṃ.translation_2: The Great Being, not seeing them, asked ‘Where have they gone?’ and having heard the situation, he thought, ‘They will not be able to race with the sun; they will perish in the middle of the way. I will give them [the gift of] their lives.’

vicārituṃ.meaning_2: to manage; to administer; to look after
vicārituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of vicāreti, used with gehaṃ in the sense of managing or administering a household. PEU gives vi+cara+ṇe+tuṃ.
vicārituṃ.example_1: Athekadivasaṃ mahāupāsikā tassa savanapathe ṭhatvā ‘‘ imasmiṃ gehe upabhogaparibhogamattā atthi, tathārūpo pana me putto vā jāmātā vā gehaṃ vicārituṃ samattho natthī ’’ ti āha.
vicārituṃ.translation_1: One day, the great lay follower, standing in his earshot, said: “In this house there are sufficient possessions for use and enjoyment, but there is no such son or son-in-law capable of managing the household.”

kaḍḍhetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā of kaḍḍhati; part of a series of absolutives (pothetvā ... gahetvā ... kaḍḍhetvā) describing the father's actions.
kaḍḍhetvā.example_1: ‘‘ ayaṃ taruṇadārako na kiñci jānāti, pitarā panassa mahallakakāle pabbajitena bhavitabbaṃ, so āgantvā ‘ idha kiṃ karosī ’ ti maṃ pothetvā pāde gahetvā kaḍḍhetvā araññe khipissati, tasmiṃ anāgateyeva palāyissāmī ’’ ti.
kaḍḍhetvā.translation_1: “This young lad knows nothing. His father must have gone forth in his old age. When he comes and asks, ‘What are you doing here?’ he will beat me, seize me by the feet, drag me, and throw me into the forest. I will flee before he comes.”

parigalantaṃ.meaning_2: falling away (from); slipping down (from); dropping off
parigalantaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular present participle agreeing with pakkaṃ (vaṇṭā parigalantaṃ pakkaṃ = ripe fruit falling from its stalk). Could be read as parigalanta, nt acc., dependent on the fruit's dropping.
parigalantaṃ.example_1: Thero ‘‘ sādhū ’’ ti sampaṭicchitvā ākāsena bodhimaṇḍaṃ gantvā vaṇṭā parigalantaṃ pakkaṃ bhūmiṃ asampattameva cīvarena sampaṭicchitvā gahetvā ānandattherassa adāsi.
parigalantaṃ.translation_1: The Elder, agreeing, went through the air to the Bo-mandala, caught a ripe Bo-fruit slipping from its stalk with his robe before it touched the ground, took it, and gave it to the Elder Ānanda.

mupayanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Only the 3rd plural mupayanti is found in the text; the lemma is a guess, as mupa- is not a standard prefix. Probably a false reading or a very rare variant of an approach verb. The verb is plural, as are the subject nāgā.
mupayanti.example_1: Ettāvatā padesaṃ te, nāgā neva mupayanti.
mupayanti.translation_1: They do not approach this much of the area.”

sampesito.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Past participle of sampeseti (causative of √pis). In the verse sampesito agrees with nāgo, nominative singular; the commentary probably glosses it as 'sent by the king'.
sampesito.example_1: 75. ‘‘ Sampesito ca raññā, nāgo koñcova abhinaditvāna;
sampesito.translation_1: 75. “Pierced by the king, the elephant trumpeted like a heron,

abhinaditvāna.meaning_2: having trumpeted; having sounded; having cried out
abhinaditvāna.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Form with the rare absolutive suffix -tvāna instead of -tvā; simplex naditvāna is also found. Used of an elephant's trumpeting in the verse.
abhinaditvāna.example_1: 75. ‘‘ Sampesito ca raññā, nāgo koñcova abhinaditvāna;
abhinaditvāna.translation_1: 75. “Pierced by the king, the elephant trumpeted like a heron,

koṭṭiyamānāpi.meaning_2: being beaten; being pounded; being hammered
koṭṭiyamānāpi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle passive of koṭṭeti, used adverbially with api ('even when being beaten'). The PEU analysis Koṭṭa+ya+māna is doubtful; the root is √kuṭ (knock, beat).
koṭṭiyamānāpi.example_1: Ettāvatāti sabbepi te ettakaṃ padesaṃ neva upayanti, koṭṭiyamānāpi na upagacchantiyeva.
koṭṭiyamānāpi.translation_1: ‘This much’ means all of them do not approach this much of the area; even when beaten, they do not approach.

abhinaditvānāti.meaning_2: having shouted; having roared; having made a loud sound
abhinaditvānāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text as abhinaditvānāti, sandhi of the absolutive abhinaditvāna with the quotation particle ti; lemma is the absolutive without ti.

bhumyā.meaning_2: on the ground; on the earth
bhumyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular form of bhūmi, spelled bhumyā here; the locative ending -yā is irregular for an i-stem feminine. The sentence means the elephant fell right on the ground.
bhumyā.example_1: Saṅkanteva raññe nāgo, tattheva pati bhumyā;
bhumyā.translation_1: As soon as the king had moved, the elephant fell right there on the ground,

sannipātayi.meaning_2: gathered; assembled; collected together; caused to meet
sannipātayi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular of the causative sannipāteti (cf. PEU sannipātayī). Used in the text for gathering flowers and assembling ministers.
sannipātayi.translation_1: “He gathered sixty thousand cartloads of flowers,
sannipātayi.example_2: Tassa sattaratanamayā vedikā kāresi, ratanamissakaṃ vālukaṃ okirāpetvā pākāraparikkhittaṃ kāresi, sattaratanamayaṃ dvārakoṭṭhakaṃ kāresi, devasikaṃ pupphānaṃ saṭṭhivāhasahassāni sannipātayi, evaṃ bodhimaṇḍaṃ pūjesi.
sannipātayi.translation_2: He had a railing made of seven gems for it, had sand mixed with gems scattered, had it surrounded by a wall, had a gateway made of seven gems, and every day he gathered sixty thousand cartloads of flowers; in this way he worshipped the Bodhi-mandala.

kāvīrapaṭṭanasamīpe.meaning_2: near Kāvīrapaṭṭana; in the vicinity of the port of Kāvīra
kāvīrapaṭṭanasamīpe.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative of samīpa in a bahubbīhi compound functioning as an adverb; sandhi of samīpa + e. The text reads kāvīrapaṭṭana-; the PEU gives Kāvīrapaṭṭana.
kāvīrapaṭṭanasamīpe.example_1: Atha mahāsatto ‘‘ ayaṃ lābhasakkāro mahā, parivāropi mahanto, mayā ekakeneva viharituṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti cintetvā avelāya antamaso bhaginimpi ajānāpetvā ekakova nikkhamitvā anupubbena damiḷaraṭṭhaṃ patvā kāvīrapaṭṭanasamīpe uyyāne viharanto jhānābhiññāyo nibbattesi.
kāvīrapaṭṭanasamīpe.translation_1: Then the Great Being thought, ‘This gain and honor is great, and the company is great; I should dwell alone.’ Having thought this, at an unexpected time, without even letting his sister know, he left alone, and traveling progressively, reached the Tamil kingdom, where, dwelling in a park near the harbor city of Kāvīra, he generated the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and the supernormal faculties.

vīmiṃsissāmi.meaning_2: will examine; will test; will investigate
vīmiṃsissāmi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Irregular future in -issati of the desiderative verb vīmiṃsati (from √mīl + *e iya). First person singular in the text, used by Sakka of testing the ascetic.
vīmiṃsissāmi.example_1: Sakko ‘‘ ko nu kho maṃ ṭhānā cāvetukāmo ’’ ti āvajjento akittipaṇḍitaṃ disvā ‘‘ kimatthaṃ esa tāpaso sīlāni rakkhati, sakkattaṃ nu kho pattheti, udāhu aññaṃ, vīmiṃsissāmi naṃ.
vīmiṃsissāmi.translation_1: Sakka, reflecting, ‘Who is trying to move me from my place?’ saw Akitti the Wise and thought, ‘For what purpose does this ascetic guard his virtues? Is he aspiring to the status of Sakka, or for some other reason? I will test him.

adoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Probably not a dictionary word but ado + iti, i.e. the pronoun ado with the quotative iti. Occurs in the Jātaka commentary prose; no context supplied, so the identification is uncertain. If instead it is a verb, compare deti / dadāti.

tuṇḍilo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of Kālī's brother, a gambler and drunkard, in the Jātaka commentary. Nominative singular in the text. The PEU gloss 'one who has a good mouth' is a late folk etymology; the name is from tuṇḍa + ila.
tuṇḍilo.example_1: Pubbe kira bārāṇasiyaṃ kāḷī nāma gaṇikā ahosi, tassā tuṇḍilo nāma bhātā.
tuṇḍilo.translation_1: Once, they say, there was a courtesan in Benares named Kālī, and she had a brother named Tuṇḍila.
tuṇḍilo.example_2: Tuṇḍilo pana itthidhutto surādhutto akkhadhutto ahosi.
tuṇḍilo.translation_2: Tuṇḍila, however, was a debauchee in sex, a debauchee in drink, and a debauchery in gambling.

tuṇḍilassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a man, younger brother of the prostitute Kāḷī. Genitive singular in the text. PEU also gives the sense 'one who has a good mouth'.
tuṇḍilassa.example_1: Tāya ca dāsiyo āṇattā honti ‘‘ tuṇḍilassa āgatakāle kiñci adatvā gīvāyaṃ naṃ gahetvā nīhareyyāthā ’’ ti.
tuṇḍilassa.translation_1: Kālī had instructed her maids, “When Tuṇḍila comes, give him nothing, but seize him by the throat and cast him out.”
tuṇḍilassa.example_2: Tasmā so seṭṭhiputto tāya dinnavatthāni nivāsetvā attano sāṭake tuṇḍilassa dāpesi.
tuṇḍilassa.translation_2: Therefore, that merchant's son put on the clothes provided by her and had his own garments given to Tuṇḍila.

tuṇḍilamanupucchiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the accusative proper name tuṇḍilaṃ and the aorist anupucchiṃ (1st singular of anupucchati), in a verse. See tuṇḍila and anupucchati.
tuṇḍilamanupucchiṃ.example_1: 106. ‘‘ Kimevahaṃ tuṇḍilamanupucchiṃ, kareyya saṃ bhātaraṃ kāḷikāyaṃ;
tuṇḍilamanupucchiṃ.translation_1: 106. Why did I ask of Tuṇḍila? I should have cared for the brother of Kālī; stripping me of my pair of garments, I myself am naked, and this meaning is just like that.

accupatī.meaning_2: flies up to; flies across to; flies over
accupatī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Third person singular in the text; non-doubled sandhi form of ati-upa-paṭati/accupatati. The commentary glosses it as atigantvā uppati. The spelling accupatī is unusual.
accupatī.translation_1: 107. The fork-tail that flies between two fighting rams without being part of the fight;
accupatī.example_2: Accupatīti atigantvā uppati, ākāse sīsānaṃ vemajjhe aṭṭhāsīti attho.
accupatī.translation_2: Accupatī means: having gone beyond, it flew; it stood in the middle of the heads in the air, this is the meaning.

kuliṅgo.meaning_2: fork-tailed drongo; a bird that flies between fighting rams
kuliṅgo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the verse. The commentary glosses it as a bird that hovers between two fighting rams; the PE(U) derivation ku + liṅga is uncertain.
kuliṅgo.translation_1: 107. The fork-tail that flies between two fighting rams without being part of the fight;

accupatīti.meaning_2: runs up to; rushes towards; goes beyond
accupatīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text written accupatīti, i.e. accupati + iti. The prefix here is accu- (from acc-), and pati- is a prefix. Verb of motion in the 3rd singular present; exact nuance uncertain without the passage.

avakkhipantī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle of avakkhipati; feminine nominative singular avakkhipantī in the verse. Commentarial gloss: kīḷamānā pacchimapāde khipantī.
avakkhipantī.example_1: 109. ‘‘ Ajā yathā veḷugumbasmiṃ baddhā, avakkhipantī asimajjhagacchi;
avakkhipantī.translation_1: 109. As a she-goat bound in a bamboo clump, kicking, met a knife;
avakkhipantī.translation_2: In this context, avakkhipantī means frisking and kicking with the hind legs.

paricitto.meaning_2: having a mind (of); endowed with thoughts; with mind filled (with)
paricitto.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the verse paricitto contrasts with aticitto: "the whole world has a mind, has an over-mind"; the commentary explains it as pāṇātipātādicittena (with a mind of killing and so on), so paricitta means "with mind (of such a kind)". Nominative singular in the text.
paricitto.example_1: 115. ‘‘ Sabbo loko paricitto aticitto, sabbo loko cittavā samhi citte;
paricitto.translation_1: 115. The whole world is full of different minds, the whole world has a mind in the mind;
paricitto.example_2: Sabbo loko paricittoti mahārāja, asappuriso nāma pāṇātipātādicittena, sappuriso pāṇātipātā veramaṇi ādicittena aticittoti, evaṃ sabbo loko paricitto aticittoti attho.
paricitto.translation_2: Sabbo loko paricitto means: O King, a bad person has a mind for killing and so on, a good person has a mind for abstaining from killing and so on; thus, the whole world is of one way or another.

cittavā.meaning_2: having a mind; possessed of mind; endowed with mind
cittavā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Vocative/possessive form in -vā of cittavant, used predicatively ("sabbo loko cittavā"). The commentary glosses it as cittena cittavā, i.e. having mind. Related to cittavasa, cittavasī.
cittavā.example_1: 115. ‘‘ Sabbo loko paricitto aticitto, sabbo loko cittavā samhi citte;
cittavā.translation_1: 115. The whole world is full of different minds, the whole world has a mind in the mind;
cittavā.example_2: Cittavā samhi citteti sabbo pana loko attano hīnena vā paṇītena vā cittena cittavā nāma.
cittavā.translation_2: Cittavā samhi citte means: the whole world is possessed of a mind, whether it be low or refined.

paricittoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] No sentences found; the word is unattested in the supplied context. Form appears to be paricitta + ti, likely an error or an enclitic -ti (quotation) joined to the end; if so the entry should be made for paricitta. Analysis uncertain.

māhaṃsu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd plural of brūti, irregular base māha-. In the verse māhaṃsu is the verb of the quotation, 'they said'. Some editions read māhu.
māhaṃsu.example_1: 123. ‘‘ Saccaṃ kireva māhaṃsu, narā ekacciyā idha;
māhaṃsu.translation_1: 123. People here speak truly, it is said;

yamuddhariṃ.meaning_2: rescued; pulled out; drew out; saved
yamuddhariṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Here in the sandhi yaṃ + uddhariṃ; 1st person singular aorist, 'I rescued', with the relative pronoun yaṃ agreeing with the rescued one.
yamuddhariṃ.example_1: 125. ‘‘ Yamuddhariṃ vāhane vuyhamānaṃ, mahodake salile sīghasote;
yamuddhariṃ.translation_1: 125. The one I rescued, carried by the current in the great, swift-flowing water,
yamuddhariṃ.translation_2: which I rescued from the great water while it was being carried by the current.

paṭisedhatūti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the sentence it is part of the quotation paṭisedhatūti = paṭisedhatu + iti, an imperative 3rd singular in -tu, so the form in the text is paṭisedhatu, not the present indicative. The entry is given under the present 3rd singular paṭisedhati according to the lemma rule. The commentary explains taṃ devo as 'let the king prevent that herd of deer', so the meaning here is 'prohibits; prevents; restrains'.
paṭisedhatūti.example_1: Tattha taṃ devoti taṃ migagaṇaṃ devo paṭisedhatūti.
paṭisedhatūti.translation_1: In that stanza, taṃ devo means: “Let the King prevent that herd of deer.”

kaṇḍambarukkhamūleti.meaning_2: at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree (iti)
kaṇḍambarukkhamūleti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the locative kaṇḍambarukkhamūle with the quotative iti; ti marks the end of a quoted phrase. The compound is kaṇḍamba + rukkhamūla, the mango tree grown by the gardener Kaṇḍamba (Ja prose).

gubbhaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Rare word; the commentary glosses it as a dense thicket (gahanavanasaṇḍa). Accusative singular in the text, object of anuparigantvā.
gubbhaṃ.example_1: Paṭhamameva sarabhamigo uṭṭhāya tikkhattuṃ gubbhaṃ anuparigantvā palāyanokāsaṃ olokento sesadisāsu manusse bāhāya bāhaṃ dhanunā dhanuṃ āhacca nirantare ṭhite disvā rañño ṭhitaṭṭhāneyeva okāsaṃ addasa.
gubbhaṃ.translation_1: The Sarabha-deer was the first to spring up, and after circling the thicket three times and looking for a place to escape, he saw men standing in the other directions—arm to arm, bow to bow, with no gaps—and he perceived an opening only where the king was standing.

ummīlitesu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative plural in the text (ummīlitesu akkhīsu = with the eyes open). The pp of ummīleti is shown here with the prefix u-.
ummīlitesu.example_1: So ummīlitesu akkhīsu vālukaṃ khipamāno viya rājānaṃ abhimukho agamāsi.
ummīlitesu.translation_1: He rushed toward the king, as if casting sand into his wide-open eyes.

konena.meaning_2: by what?; with what?; by whom?
konena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of kiṃ + ena, instrumental of the interrogative pronoun kiṃ. Written konena in the text. The king's statement is being mocked.
konena.example_1: ‘‘ Rājā ‘ viddho me ’ ti vadati, konena viddho, nibbirajjho bho amhākaṃ rājā, bhūminena viddhā ’’ ti te nānappakārena raññā saddhiṃ keḷiṃ kariṃsu.
konena.translation_1: "The king claims, 'I hit him,' but what did he hit? Our king is hopeless, friends; did he hit the earth?" They mocked the king in many ways.

nibbirajjho.meaning_2: without defect; without deficiency; blameless; faultless; hopeless
nibbirajjho.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Used mockingly of the king in the sentence. Nominative singular used as a predicate, agreeing with rājā. The PEU gloss treats it as 'one who has no defect'.
nibbirajjho.example_1: ‘‘ Rājā ‘ viddho me ’ ti vadati, konena viddho, nibbirajjho bho amhākaṃ rājā, bhūminena viddhā ’’ ti te nānappakārena raññā saddhiṃ keḷiṃ kariṃsu.
nibbirajjho.translation_1: "The king claims, 'I hit him,' but what did he hit? Our king is hopeless, friends; did he hit the earth?" They mocked the king in many ways.

sañjātakāruñño.meaning_2: filled with compassion; whose compassion has arisen; compassionate
sañjātakāruñño.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes Sarabha the deer in the Jātaka prose. Nominative singular in -o; the compound is bahubbīhi on sañjāta (arisen) + kāruñña (compassion).
