sañjātakāruñño.example_1: Sarabho tassa padasaddaṃ asuṇanto nivattitvā taṃ apassanto ‘‘ narakāvāṭe patito bhavissatī ’’ ti ñatvā āgantvā olokento taṃ gambhīraudake apatiṭṭhaṃ kilamantaṃ disvā tena kataṃ aparādhaṃ hadaye akatvā sañjātakāruñño ‘‘ mā mayi passanteva rājā nassatu, imamhā dukkhā naṃ mocessāmī ’’ ti āvāṭatīre ṭhito ‘‘ mā bhāyi, mahārāja, mahantā dukkhā taṃ mocessāmī ’’ ti vatvā attano piyaputtaṃ uddharituṃ ussāhaṃ karonto viya tassuddharaṇatthāya silāya yoggaṃ katvāva ‘‘ vijjhissāmī ’’ ti āgataṃ rājānaṃ saṭṭhihatthā narakā uddharitvā assāsetvā piṭṭhiṃ āropetvā araññā nīharitvā senāya avidūre otāretvā ovādamassa datvā pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpesi.
sañjātakāruñño.translation_1: The Sarabha-deer, hearing no sound of his footsteps, turned back, and seeing no one, realized, "He must have fallen into the pit." He came back, looked, and saw him struggling in the deep, water-filled pit; yet, bearing no grudge in his heart for the injury the king had done him, he was filled with compassion, thinking, "May the king not perish before my eyes! I will save him from this suffering." Standing at the edge of the pit, he cried, "Do not fear, Great King, I will deliver you from this great suffering." Then, exerting as much effort as if he were trying to save his own beloved son, he braced himself against the rocks and pulled the king out of the sixty-cubit pit, comforted him, placed him on his back, led him out of the forest, set him down not far from his army, gave him instruction, and established him in the Five Virtues.

āsacchedakakammaṃ.meaning_2: act of cutting off hope; deed of severing expectation
āsacchedakakammaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text. The compound is āsa + chedaka + kamma; the commentarial gloss explains it as 'not cutting off hope'.
āsacchedakakammaṃ.example_1: Tattha āsīsetheva purisoti āsacchedakakammaṃ akatvā attano kammesu āsaṃ karotheva na ukkaṇṭheyya.
āsacchedakakammaṃ.translation_1: In that, “A man should surely hope,” means one should certainly hold onto hope in one’s own affairs without cutting off that hope, and should not be dejected.

etadakkhā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of etaṃ + akkhā (aorist 3rd singular of dadāti? no, of √akkh 'see'?). Actually from √akkh 'see', aorist akkhā. Used in dialogue verses.
etadakkhā.example_1: 142. ‘‘ Kiṃ tvaṃ nu tattheva tadā ahosi, udāhu te koci naṃ etadakkhā;
etadakkhā.translation_1: 142. “Were you there at that time, O brahmin, or did someone else tell you about it?
etadakkhā.example_2: 143. ‘‘ Na cevahaṃ tattha tadā ahosiṃ, na cāpi me koci naṃ etadakkhā;
etadakkhā.translation_2: 143. “I was neither there at that time, nor did anyone else tell me about it;

paricāriyanto.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle of the causative paricāreti; the -nta- is passive in sense, 'being attended (by)'. The reading is paricāriyanto; nominative singular masculine in the text, agreeing with the addressee.
paricāriyanto.example_1: Nārīgaṇehi paricāriyanto, modassu raṭṭhe tidiveva vāsavo.
paricāriyanto.translation_1: Attended by groups of maidens, rejoice in the kingdom like Vasava in the heaven of the thirty-three.”

sāliddiyo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a village in the Jātaka stories; nominative singular in the text (sāliddiyo nāma brāhmaṇagāmo). The English 'Sālindiya' is a different spelling.
sāliddiyo.example_1: Tadā nagarato pubbuttaradisāya sāliddiyo nāma brāhmaṇagāmo ahosi.
sāliddiyo.translation_1: At that time, there was a brahmin village named Sālindiya to the north-east of the city.

sāliddiyavāsī.meaning_2: living in Sāliddiya; resident of Sāliddiya
sāliddiyavāsī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sāliddiya may be a village name; vāsī is an agent noun meaning 'dwelling in'. The form is nominative singular modifying brāhmaṇo.
sāliddiyavāsī.example_1: Tassa pubbuttaradisāya magadhakhettaṃ atthi, tattha kosiyagotto nāma sāliddiyavāsī brāhmaṇo sahassakarīsamattaṃ khettaṃ gahetvā sāliṃ vapāpesi.
sāliddiyavāsī.translation_1: To the north-east of that village there was a Magadha field; there, a brahmin named Kosiyagotta, living in Sālindiya, took a field of one thousand karīsas and had rice sown.

sāliddiyagāmaṃ.meaning_2: Sālindiya village; name of a village
sāliddiyagāmaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text. Village name; spelling varies (sālindiya-).
sāliddiyagāmaṃ.example_1: Atha so puriso ‘‘ sace ime aññaṃ katipāhaṃ evaṃ khādissanti, kiñci na bhavissati, brāhmaṇo sāliṃ agghāpetvā mayhaṃ iṇaṃ karissati, gantvā tassa ārocessāmī ’’ ti sālimuṭṭhinā saddhiṃ tathārūpaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā sāliddiyagāmaṃ gantvā brāhmaṇaṃ passitvā vanditvā paṇṇākāraṃ datvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito ‘‘ kiṃ, bho purisa, sampannaṃ sālikhettan ’’ ti puṭṭho ‘‘ āma, brāhmaṇa, sampannan ’’ ti vatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –
sāliddiyagāmaṃ.translation_1: Then that man thought, “If these parrots eat like this for a few more days, there will be nothing left; the brahmin will have the rice valued and make me pay the debt; I will go and tell him,” and taking a handful of rice and a corresponding gift, went to the brahmin village, saw the brahmin, bowed, gave the gift, stood at one side, and when asked, “What, my good man, is the rice field prosperous?” replied, “Yes, brahmin, it is prosperous,” and spoke two verses—
sāliddiyagāmaṃ.example_2: Khettapālo suvarājassa baddharavaṃ suvānañca ākāse pakkhandanasaddaṃ sutvā ‘‘ kiṃ nu kho ’’ ti kuṭiyā oruyha pāsāṭṭhānaṃ gantvā suvarājānaṃ disvā ‘‘ yasseva me pāso oḍḍito, sveva baddho ’’ ti tuṭṭhamānaso suvarājānaṃ pāsato mocetvā dve pāde ekato bandhitvā daḷhaṃ ādāya sāliddiyagāmaṃ gantvā suvarājaṃ brāhmaṇassa adāsi.
sāliddiyagāmaṃ.translation_2: The watchman, hearing the parrot-king’s cry and the sound of the other parrots rushing through the sky, thought, “What is this?” Coming out of his hut and going to the snare, he saw the parrot-king and thought, “The very bird I set the snare for is bound!” Delighted, he released the parrot-king from the snare, tied both his feet together, and taking him firmly, went to Sālindiya village and gave him to the brahmin.

rattatuṇḍo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi compound describing a bird (a peacock) in the Jātaka commentary; glossed lohitatuṇḍa. Nominative singular in the text.
rattatuṇḍo.example_1: Sabbasundaroti sabbehi koṭṭhāsehi sundaro rattatuṇḍo jiñjukasannibhaakkhi rattapādo tīhi rattarājīhi parikkhittagīvo mahāmayūrapamāṇo so yāvadatthaṃ sāliṃ khāditvā aññaṃ tuṇḍena gahetvā gacchatīti.
rattatuṇḍo.translation_1: Sabbasundaro means one who is excellent in every part: red-beaked, eyes like jiñjuka seeds, red-footed, with a neck encircled by three red stripes, the size of a great peacock; he eats rice until satisfied, then takes some more in his beak and leaves.
rattatuṇḍo.translation_2: “Ruddy beak” (lohitatuṇḍako) means having a red beak, possessing beauty.

iṇadānaṃ.meaning_2: granting of a loan; lending money; debt settlement
iṇadānaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of iṇa (debt) and dāna (giving). Nominative singular in the text. Commentaries gloss it as lending money at interest.
iṇadānaṃ.example_1: 8. ‘‘ Kīdisaṃ te iṇadānaṃ, iṇamokkho ca kīdiso;
iṇadānaṃ.translation_1: “What is your granting of a loan, and what is your release from debt?
iṇadānaṃ.example_2: 12. ‘‘ Īdisaṃ me iṇadānaṃ, iṇamokkho ca īdiso;
iṇadānaṃ.translation_2: 12. “Such is my granting of a loan, and such is release from debt;

iṇadānanti.meaning_2: thus: debt settlement; (said) the granting of a loan
iṇadānanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Form of iṇadāna + iti, with the final -a elided before iti. The commentary reads it as a neuter compound iṇa + dāna meaning debt settlement or the granting of a loan at interest; if taken as a quotation, -ti belongs to the following clause.

hātūna.meaning_2: having taken; having carried; having brought
hātūna.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Rare absolutive in -tūna (= -tvāna) of harati; note the lengthened ū. The PEU entry hātuna (= hara + tuna) glosses the same form 'having carried'. Verse, metrically lengthened.
hātūna.example_1: Tesaṃ tuṇḍena hātūna, muñce pubbakataṃ iṇaṃ.
hātūna.translation_1: Bringing food for them in my beak, I pay the debt incurred in the past.”

santappayi.grammar: aor of santappati; caus of tapati
santappayi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular of the causative santappeti (the -ayi ending). Also analysed as saṃ + tapa + ṇaya + ī. Used transitively here: 'satisfied ascetics and brahmins with food and drink'.
santappayi.example_1: Annena pānena pasannacitto, santappayi samaṇabrāhmaṇe cā ’’ ti.
santappayi.translation_1: With a pleased mind, through food and drink, he satisfied ascetics and brahmins.”

santappayīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The ṇ in ṇaya is the vikaraṇa sign; the form is 3rd singular causative. The text form santappayīti is santappayi + iti, with mutated i before iti.

vārāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to be requested; having had (her) asked for (in marriage); having arranged (the marriage)
vārāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of vāreti (< √var 2, 'wish, choose'); here in the sense 'having had (a girl) asked for in marriage'. The form is vārāpetvā, not vāretvā.
vārāpetvā.example_1: So kira sāvatthiyaṃ parijiṇṇassa kulassa putto sahāyaṃ pesetvā aññataraṃ kuladhītaraṃ vārāpetvā ‘‘ atthi panassa uppannakiccaṃ nittharaṇasamattho mitto vā sahāyo vā ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ natthī ’’ ti vatvā ‘‘ tena hi mitte tāva bandhatū ’’ ti vutte tasmiṃ ovāde ṭhatvā paṭhamaṃ tāva catūhi dovārikehi saddhiṃ mettiṃ akāsi, athānupubbena nagaraguttikagaṇakamahāmattādīhi saddhiṃ mettiṃ katvā senāpatināpi uparājenāpi saddhiṃ mettiṃ akāsi.
vārāpetvā.translation_1: It is said that this man, who was the son of a decayed family in Sāvatthī, sent a companion to arrange a marriage with a certain young woman of good family. When he was asked, “Does he have any friend or companion capable of disposing of any urgent matter that might arise?” and replied “No,” they told him, “Then you must first make some friends.” Following this advice, he first struck up a friendship with the four gatekeepers, and then, by degrees, made friends with the town warders, the accountants, the chief ministers, and so forth, and eventually also with the commander-in-chief and the viceroy.

senasakuṇo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sena is probably a shortening of senaka/sena, hawk; sakuṇa means bird. Nominative singular in the text.
senasakuṇo.example_1: Tassa dakkhiṇapasse eko senasakuṇo, pacchimapasse ekā senasakuṇī, uttarapasse sīho migarājā, pācīnapasse ukkusasakuṇarājā vasati.
senasakuṇo.translation_1: On its southern shore lived a male hawk, on the western shore a female hawk, on the northern shore a lion, king of beasts, and on the eastern shore an osprey, king of the birds.

senasakuṇī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine form senasakuṇī is used for the female hawk; masculine senasakuṇo for the male. In the text senasakuṇī is nominative singular.
senasakuṇī.example_1: Tassa dakkhiṇapasse eko senasakuṇo, pacchimapasse ekā senasakuṇī, uttarapasse sīho migarājā, pācīnapasse ukkusasakuṇarājā vasati.
senasakuṇī.translation_1: On its southern shore lived a male hawk, on the western shore a female hawk, on the northern shore a lion, king of beasts, and on the eastern shore an osprey, king of the birds.
senasakuṇī.example_2: Senasakuṇī attano putte oloketvā ‘‘ mitte nissāya amhehi dārakā laddhā ’’ ti sukhanisinnasamaye senena saddhiṃ sallapantī mittadhammaṃ pakāsamānā cha gāthā abhāsi –
senasakuṇī.translation_2: The female hawk, looking at her young, thought, “Through friends we have recovered our little ones,” and while conversing happily with her mate, wishing to manifest the practice of friendship, she declared six verses:

manthetvā.meaning_2: having rubbed; having churned; having kindled (by friction)
manthetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā of the causative mantheti; used of rubbing a fire-drill (araṇiṃ manthetvā) to kindle fire.
manthetvā.example_1: Tesaṃ pakkhesu asañjātesuyeva ekadivasaṃ te jānapadā divasaṃ araññe caritvā kiñci alabhitvā ‘‘ na sakkā tucchahatthena gharaṃ gantuṃ, macche vā kacchape vā gaṇhissāmā ’’ ti saraṃ otaritvā taṃ dīpakaṃ gantvā tassa kadambassa mūle nipajjitvā makasādīhi khajjamānā tesaṃ palāpanatthāya araṇiṃ manthetvā aggiṃ nibbattetvā dhūmaṃ kariṃsu.
manthetvā.translation_1: Before the wings of the young had grown, one day those country folk, having wandered in the forest all day and found nothing, thought, “We cannot return home empty-handed; we will catch fish or tortoises.” They went down to the lake, reached that little island, and lay down at the base of the kadamba tree; and being tormented by gnats and mosquitoes, they kindled a fire by rubbing a fire-drill to drive them away, and made smoke.

cilācāti.meaning_2: stands; is situated; lives (in a village)
cilācāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Rare verb; the related PEU entry glosses cilāca as a village-dweller and cilācati as 'stands'. The text form cilācāti may reflect a variant reading or sandhi.

cilācānaṃ.meaning_2: of the country people; of the villagers and forest-dwellers
cilācānaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Probably cilātānaṃ (or cilācānānaṃ), genitive plural of a compound like cilā-cāna, 'country folk', glossed by the commentary as villagers and forest-dwellers. The machine translation 'climb' is wrong: abhiruhanaṃ olokento is 'watching the climbing'.
cilācānaṃ.example_1: Ukkusarājāpi gantvā kadambassa avidūre cilācānaṃ abhiruhanaṃ olokento ekasmiṃ rukkhagge nisīditvā ekassa cilācassa abhiruhanakāle tasmiṃ kulāvakassa avidūraṃ abhiruḷhe sare nimujjitvā pakkhehi ca mukhena ca udakaṃ āharitvā ukkāya upari āsiñci, sā nibbāyi.
cilācānaṃ.translation_1: The osprey king also came, and watching for the country folk to climb near the kadamba tree, he sat on a tree-top. Just as one of the country folk was climbing and reached near the bird's nest, the osprey dived into the lake, brought water in his wings and beak, and poured it over the torch, and it went out.

cilācassa.meaning_2: person living in a village; villager; country folk
cilācassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Rare word, apparently a village-dweller (cf. PEU cilāca). Genitive plural cilācānaṃ in the first occurrence; genitive singular cilācassa in the second. Meaning uncertain; possibly related to cīlā/cilāta.
cilācassa.example_1: Ukkusarājāpi gantvā kadambassa avidūre cilācānaṃ abhiruhanaṃ olokento ekasmiṃ rukkhagge nisīditvā ekassa cilācassa abhiruhanakāle tasmiṃ kulāvakassa avidūraṃ abhiruḷhe sare nimujjitvā pakkhehi ca mukhena ca udakaṃ āharitvā ukkāya upari āsiñci, sā nibbāyi.
cilācassa.translation_1: The osprey king also came, and watching for the country folk to climb near the kadamba tree, he sat on a tree-top. Just as one of the country folk was climbing and reached near the bird's nest, the osprey dived into the lake, brought water in his wings and beak, and poured it over the torch, and it went out.

senapotakehi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental plural in the text; part of the idiom kiṃ no senapotakehi, 'what do we need with the young hawks?'.
senapotakehi.example_1: Cilācā ‘‘ kiṃ no senapotakehi, imaṃ kāḷakacchapaṃ parivattetvā māressāma, ayaṃ no sabbesaṃ pahossatī ’’ ti valliyo uddharitvā jiyā gahetvā nivatthapilotikāpi mocetvā tesu tesu ṭhānesu bandhitvā kacchapaṃ parivattetuṃ na sakkonti.
senapotakehi.translation_1: The country folk thought, “Why bother about the young hawks? We will roll over this black tortoise and kill him; he will be enough for all of us,” and they pulled up creepers, took bowstrings, and even took off their worn clothes and tied them in various places, but they could not roll the tortoise over.

nosi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the enclitic pronoun no (genitive/dative of amhaṃ) with the verb asi, 'you are'. The form often follows pāda-position; the analysis as no + asi fits the sense 'you are ours' ('tvaṃ no asi').
nosi.example_1: Puttā mamaṭṭā gatimāgatosmi, tvaṃ nosi rājā bhava me sukhāyā ’’ ti.
nosi.translation_1: My young in danger, straight I fly to thee: Thou art our king, and therefore I am here.
nosi.example_2: 209. ‘‘ Tvaṃ nosi ñāti purimāsu jātisu, so maccharī rosako pāpadhammo;
nosi.translation_2: “You were our kindred in former births, that avaricious, harassing person of bad character;

disasamūhaṃ.meaning_2: multitude of enemies; host of foes
disasamūhaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Explained in the gloss as paccatthikagaṇa. Accusative singular in the text (taṃ disasamūhaṃ).
disasamūhaṃ.example_1: Tattha taṃ disatanti taṃ disasamūhaṃ, taṃ tava paccatthikagaṇanti attho.
disasamūhaṃ.translation_1: Therein, taṃ disataṃ means that troop of enemies, that host of your adversaries.

kocoti.meaning_2: who is that?; who is he?
kocoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of ko and iti; the -ti is the quotative particle, so the whole is a question meaning 'who is he?'. Alternatively the final syllable could be the quotation clitic attached to ko alone.

sampannasakho.meaning_2: having perfected companions; endowed with friends; possessing true friends
sampannasakho.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text, qualifying a person. The PEU entry treats it as an adjective meaning one who has the conduct of a true friend; sakha is a member of the sakhi declension, so the compound's final element is somewhat irregular.
sampannasakho.example_1: Bhavanti heteti yo ca sampannasakho paripuṇṇamittadhammo, tassa ete sahāyā bhavanti.
sampannasakho.translation_1: Regarding “for these exist,” whoever has perfected companions and is endowed with the practice of friendship, for that person these companions exist.

asmiṃdhaloketi.meaning_2: in this world; here in this world
asmiṃdhaloketi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the locative pronoun asmiṃ and the locative noun loke; the -ti quoted in the text is the quotation particle iti, not part of the word.

uddālo.meaning_2: golden shower tree (Cassia fistula); a tree so named
uddālo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text, used as the source of the name Uddālaka. The suggested U+dala+ṇa analysis is uncertain.
uddālo.example_1: So ‘‘ vaṇṇadāsiyā kucchimhi nibbattattā na sakkā kulanāmaṃ kātun ’’ ti cintetvā ‘‘ bhadde, ayaṃ vātaghātarukkho uddālo nāma, idha paṭiladdhattā ‘ uddālako ’ tissa nāmaṃ kareyyāsī ’’ ti vatvā aṅgulimuddikaṃ adāsi.
uddālo.translation_1: He, thinking “Because he is born in the womb of a prostitute, it is not fitting to give him a family name,” said, “Good lady, this wind-breaking tree is called an uddāla. Because he was conceived here, you should give him the name ‘Uddālaka,’” and having said this, he gave her a finger-ring.

bhayasantikaraṃ.meaning_2: making the end of danger; bringing peace from danger
bhayasantikaraṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular modifying nibbānaṃ in the text. PEU splits as bhayasantikara; santi here is the noun 'end, cessation' (cf. santika).
bhayasantikaraṃ.example_1: Santiṃ puṇātīti samāpattisaṅkhātena caraṇena danto bhayasantikaraṃ nibbānaṃ pāpuṇātīti.
bhayasantikaraṃ.translation_1: Santiṃ puṇātī means: The tamed one attains Nibbāna, which brings peace from dangers, through the practice defined as the attainments.

evaṃkaro.meaning_2: one who acts like this; one who does thus
evaṃkaro.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it appears as evaṃkaro, the nominative singular masculine. The PEU treats it as an adjective formed from evaṃ and kara.
evaṃkaro.example_1: Evaṃkaro brāhmaṇo hoti khemī, dhamme ṭhitaṃ tena amāpayiṃsū ’’ ti.
evaṃkaro.translation_1: One who does this is a brahmin and is peaceful; they said he is firm in Dhamma.”
evaṃkaro.example_2: Dhammaṃ care samaṇabrāhmaṇesu, evaṃkaro saggamupeti ṭhānan ’’ ti.
evaṃkaro.translation_2: a learned person should practice the Dhamma among renunciants and brahmins; one who does thus goes to a heavenly state.”

abhisecanakakammaṃ.meaning_2: act of sprinkling; anointing ceremony; consecration rite
abhisecanakakammaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is the nominative singular of the pronoun 'there' compound in apposition to siñcaṃ etc. The first member abhisecana is a kamma-made noun (sprinkling).
abhisecanakakammaṃ.example_1: Āpo siñcaṃ yajaṃ usseti yūpanti abhisecanakakammaṃ karonto sammāpāsaṃ vā vājapeyyaṃ vā niraggaḷaṃ vā yajanto suvaṇṇayūpaṃ ussāpeti.
abhisecanakakammaṃ.translation_1: Āpo siñcaṃ yajaṃ usseti yūpan means performing the act of sprinkling, sacrificing with a sammāpāsa, a vājapeyya, or a niraggaḷa, he erects a golden sacrificial pole.

upapurohitaṃ.meaning_2: deputy chaplain; subordinate court priest; second-ranking purohita
upapurohitaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text, in the phrase upapurohitaṃ karotha, "make him the deputy chaplain".
upapurohitaṃ.example_1: ‘‘ sabbe ete, mahārāja, kuhakā sakalajambudīpe kohaññeneva nāsenti, uddālakaṃ uppabbājetvā upapurohitaṃ karotha, sese uppabbājetvā phalakāvudhāni datvā sevake karothā ’’ ti.
upapurohitaṃ.translation_1: “Great King, all these hermits are deceivers; they ruin the whole of Jambudīpa through deceit. Dismiss Uddālaka and make him the deputy chaplain; dismiss the rest, give them shields and weapons, and make them your servants.”

upakañcanakumārotissa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] No sentences supplied, so the analysis is uncertain. The form looks like a personal name, a compound of upakañcana + kumāra + utissa, but the segmentation and meaning cannot be confirmed without context. If it is a compound, a compound entry or a sandhi analysis may be more suitable.

thenanaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text the word occurs in the phrase 'bhisamattaṃ thenanaṃ nāma appatirūpaṃ', 'stealing even a lotus-fibre is unseemly'; nominative singular neuter.
thenanaṃ.example_1: Ete bhisakoṭṭhāse tumhe ‘‘ karimhā ’’ ti vadatha, ahaṃ na labhāmi, etesaṃ thenetvā khādakaṃ ñātuṃ vaṭṭati, kāme pahāya pabbajitānaṃ bhisamattaṃ thenanaṃ nāma appatirūpanti.
thenanaṃ.translation_1: You say you have made these portions of lotus fibers for me; I do not receive them. It is fitting to find out who stole and ate them. For those who have gone forth abandoning sensual pleasures, stealing even a lotus fiber is unseemly.”

upakañcanatāpaso.meaning_2: Upakañcana the hermit; the ascetic named Upakañcana
upakañcanatāpaso.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of the Bodhisatta's younger brother in this story. Nominative singular in the text.
upakañcanatāpaso.example_1: Tasmiṃ khaṇeva bodhisattassa kaniṭṭho upakañcanatāpaso uṭṭhāyāsanā bodhisattaṃ vanditvā sesānaṃ apacitiṃ dassetvā ‘‘ ācariya, ahaṃ aññe apaṭṭhapetvā attānaññeva sodhetuṃ labhāmī ’’ ti pucchi.
upakañcanatāpaso.translation_1: At that very moment, the Bodhisatta’s younger brother, Upa-Kañcana the hermit, rose from his seat, saluted the Bodhisatta, showed reverence to the rest, and asked, “Teacher, may I clear myself without considering the others?”

gharamāvasātu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of gharaṃ + āvasati, but treated here as a compound verb (gharaṃ + āvasati). 3rd singular present in the sentence; imperative sense in the translation is uncertain.
gharamāvasātu.example_1: Vayaṃ apassaṃ gharamāvasātu, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.
gharamāvasātu.translation_1: Not seeing his own decay, may he dwell in his house, he who stole your lotus-roots, Brahmin.

mahimāvasātu.meaning_2: may he rule the earth; may he dwell ruling the earth
mahimāvasātu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of mahī (earth) + avasātu (imperative of avasati, dwell; rule). Feminine accusative mahim in the text.
mahimāvasātu.example_1: Sa cāturantaṃ mahimāvasātu, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.
mahimāvasātu.translation_1: May he dwell ruling the earth to its four boundaries, he who stole your lotus-roots, Brahmin.

carātu.meaning_2: may wander; may roam; may go about; let her wander
carātu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Imperative 3rd singular active of carati used as a blessing or curse in these verses. The form is carātu, not caratu, by metrical lengthening of the stem vowel.
carātu.example_1: Carātu lābhena vikatthamānā, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yā ahāsi.
carātu.translation_1: May she wander boasting of her gains, she who stole your lotus-roots, Brahmin.
carātu.example_2: Sakacchabandho visikhaṃ carātu, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsī ’’ ti.
carātu.translation_2: Wearing a waist-band, may he wander the streets, he who stole your lotus-roots, Brahmin.

bajjhatū.meaning_2: may he be bound; may he be tied; may he be caught
bajjhatū.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Imperative 3rd singular in -tū (bajjhatū) in the verse; passive of √badh with -ya and assimilation dh > jjh. PEU wrongly connects it with bādhīyati.
bajjhatū.example_1: 89. ‘‘ So bajjhatū pāsasatehi chabbhi, rammā vanā niyyatu rājadhāniṃ;
bajjhatū.translation_1: May he be bound with six hundred snares, and be led from the pleasant forest to the royal capital;

sampannakasikammo.meaning_2: one who has accomplished farming; one whose ploughing work is complete; one with successful farming
sampannakasikammo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi compound describing a farmer; nominative singular in the text, glossing kasimā. The PEU analysis sampanna + kasi + kamma is confirmed by the commentary.
sampannakasikammo.translation_1: In regard to that, in the verse spoken by the third brother, “engaged in farming” (kasimā) means one who has successful farming.

parigalite.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in both sentences, in the phrase issariye parigalite; the form is a past participle used absolutely ('when ... has faded').
parigalite.example_1: Idaṃ so ‘‘ issarānaṃ nāma issariye parigalite mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajjatī ’’ ti rajje dosaṃ dassento kathesi.
parigalite.translation_1: He spoke this, showing the faults of royalty, thinking, “For those who have power, when that power fades, great suffering arises.”
parigalite.example_2: Idaṃ so ‘‘ purohitassa purohitaṭṭhāne parigalite mahantaṃ domanassaṃ uppajjatī ’’ ti dassetuṃ kathesi.
parigalite.translation_2: He spoke this to show that “when the position of the family priest fades away, great dejection arises.”

carātūti.meaning_2: you move indeed; you walk indeed; you behave indeed
carātūti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Cara is the 2nd singular present of carati (√car 1), with -ti the quotative iti joined by sandhi; the final -ti is what remains before the quotation begins. No sentences were supplied, so the analysis rests on the form alone.

vupatthambha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text, in the phrase kismiṃ vupatthambha. Probably vi + upatthambha with elision of the initial vowel (v-upatthambha), rather than a separate simplex.
vupatthambha.example_1: Kismiṃ vupatthambha sahassanetta, isīhi tvaṃ kīḷasi devarājā ’’ ti.
vupatthambha.translation_1: Neither relatives nor friends of yours; on what support, thousand-eyed one, do you, O king of gods, play with the ascetics?”

isivesena.meaning_2: ascetic's guise; appearance of a hermit; form of a sage
isivesena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular in the text: "in the guise of a sage". Often in the phrase isivesena gantvā / āgantvā, of a deity in disguise.
isivesena.example_1: Sakko tassa paṭiññaṃ gahetvā isivesena rājuyyānaṃ gantvā tāsaṃ itthīnaṃ upari ākāse caṅkamanto attānaṃ dassetvā ‘‘ kassāhaṃ puttavaraṃ dammi, kā puttavaraṃ gaṇhissatī ’’ ti āha.
isivesena.translation_1: Sakka, having obtained his promise, went to the royal park in the guise of a sage, walked in the air above those women, showed himself, and said, “To whom shall I give the blessing of a son? Who will accept the blessing of a son?”
isivesena.example_2: Manojarājā pana taṃ ramaṇīyena isivesena tathā āgacchantaṃ disvā gāthamāha –
isivesena.translation_2: But King Manoja (manojarājā), seeing (disvā) him (taṃ) thus (tathā) approaching (āgacchantaṃ) in a delightful (ramaṇīyena) ascetic's guise (isivesena), uttered the verse (gāthamāha):

samañchitvā.meaning_2: having stretched out; having extended; having bent
samañchitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of samañchati; in the text it describes raising and stretching out the hands. The PEU gives 'saṃ + achi + tvā'.
samañchitvā.example_1: Tā ukkhittahatthe samañchitvā ‘‘ sace sīlavatiyā dātukāmo, sumedhāya santikaṃ gacchāhī ’’ ti vadiṃsu.
samañchitvā.translation_1: They folded their raised hands and said, “If you wish to give to a virtuous woman, go to Sumedhā.”

dummīti.meaning_2: with evil eyes; having bad eyes
dummīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Only the quotation marker -ti is attached in the text; the headword is dummī. The PEU gloss relates the eye to the 'control of the viewing sense' (cakkhundriya), so the word may describe someone with an uncontrolled or harmful eye. No sentence was supplied, so the case cannot be confirmed.

rāgādikilesaniggahatthaṃ.meaning_2: for the purpose of subduing defilements such as lust
rāgādikilesaniggahatthaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Commentary word; the form is a compound with -atthaṃ (for the sake of), functioning as an adverbial phrase. The final -aṃ is the accusative ending of attha. Alternative spelling rāgādikilesaniggahāya.
rāgādikilesaniggahatthaṃ.example_1: Tadā hi satthā dhammasabhāyaṃ catuparisamajjhe alaṅkatabuddhāsane nisīditvā muducittena parisaṃ oloketvā ‘‘ ajja upāsakānaṃ kathaṃ paṭicca desanā samuṭṭhahissatī ’’ ti ñatvā upāsake āmantetvā ‘‘ uposathikattha upāsakā ’’ ti pucchitvā ‘‘ āma, bhante ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ sādhu vo kataṃ, uposatho nāmesa porāṇakapaṇḍitānaṃ vaṃso, porāṇakapaṇḍitā hi rāgādikilesaniggahatthaṃ uposathavāsaṃ vasiṃsū ’’ ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.
rāgādikilesaniggahatthaṃ.translation_1: At that time, the Teacher, sitting on a glorious Buddha-seat in the middle of the Hall of Truth, surrounded by the four assemblies, looked upon the assembly with a gentle heart. Knowing, “Today, the teaching will arise owing to the affairs of the lay followers,” he addressed them, asking, “Lay followers, are you keeping the Uposatha?” When they replied, “Yes, venerable sir,” he said, “You have done well. This observance of the Uposatha is the lineage of the wise men of old; indeed, the wise men of old observed the Uposatha in order to subdue defilements such as lust.” And, requested by them, he brought forth the past.

kapotiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine of kapota. In the text kapotiṃ is accusative singular: 'a pigeon (female)'.
kapotiṃ.example_1: Tassa pacchato gacchantiṃ kapotiṃ eko seno gahetvā palāyi.
kapotiṃ.translation_1: A hawk seized the pigeon’s mate, who was following behind, and flew off.
kapotiṃ.example_2: Athaggahī sākuṇiko kapotiṃ, akāmako tāya vinā ahosiṃ.
kapotiṃ.translation_2: But then a hawk snatched my mate away; unwillingly, I was left separated from her.”

aniggahetvā.meaning_2: without subduing; without restraining; not having suppressed
aniggahetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Negated absolutive of niggaṇhāti (ni + √gah); the na is written an- before the vowel. Occurs three times in these sentences with rāga, kodha and lobha as objects.
aniggahetvā.example_1: Kapoto tāya viyogena rāgapariḷāhena pariḍayhamāno cintesi ‘‘ ayaṃ rāgo maṃ ativiya kilameti, na idāni imaṃ aniggahetvā gocarāya pakkamissāmī ’’ ti.
aniggahetvā.translation_1: Tormented by the fever of lust due to that separation from his mate, the pigeon thought, “This lust torments me exceedingly; I will not go forth to forage until I have subdued this lust.”
aniggahetvā.example_2: Sappo tesaṃ gatakāle nikkhamitvā ‘‘ ahaṃ kodhaṃ nissāya imaṃ jīvitā voropetvā mahājanassa hadaye sokaṃ pavesesiṃ, na dāni imaṃ kodhaṃ aniggahetvā gocarāya pakkamissāmī ’’ ti cintetvā nivattitvā taṃ assamaṃ gantvā kodhaniggahāya uposathaṃ samādiyitvā ekamantaṃ nipajji.
aniggahetvā.translation_2: When they had gone, the snake emerged and thought, “Because of anger, I have deprived this being of life and brought sorrow to the hearts of many people. From now on, I will not go out to forage without subduing this anger.” Having decided this, he returned, went to the hermitage, undertook the Uposatha to subdue anger, and lay down to one side.

pothesuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] 3rd plural aorist in -uṃ; the commentary glosses it as pelting with bows and sticks. Alternative spelling of pothesuṃ is posthesuṃ. Could also be analysed as aorist of potheti (√puth, caus.).
pothesuṃ.example_1: So mahājanena parivāritabhāvaṃ ñatvā nikkhamitvā palāyi, palāyantameva taṃ dhanūhi ceva daṇḍādīhi ca pothesuṃ.
pothesuṃ.translation_1: Realizing he was surrounded by the crowd, he fled. As he was fleeing, they pelted him with bows and staves.

kapotiyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular of kapotī, the female of kapota. In the verse it refers to the speaker's mate.
kapotiyā.example_1: 128. ‘‘ Ahaṃ pure giddhigato kapotiyā, asmiṃ padesasmimubho ramāma;
kapotiyā.translation_1: 128. “Once, consumed by desire for my mate, we both sported about in this place;

sosayuṃ.meaning_2: caused to dry up; dried up
sosayuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] 3rd person plural aorist of the causative soseti (from √sus 'dry'). The text has sosayuṃ, a variant spelling for sosayuṃ/sosesuṃ; PEU analyses it as susa + ṇaya + uṃ.
sosayuṃ.example_1: Uṇho ca vāto tikhiṇā ca rasmiyo, te sosayuṃ tassa karīsamaggaṃ.
sosayuṃ.translation_1: The hot wind and the sharp sun's rays dried up its passage for excrement.”

temayī.meaning_2: causes to be moistened; wets; dampens
temayī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular in the text (so temayī). Causative double causative of √tim via temeti. Commentary form; compare PEU temeti.
temayī.example_1: Mahā ca megho sahasā pavassi, so temayī tassa karīsamaggaṃ.
temayī.translation_1: Then a great rain cloud suddenly poured down; it dampened its passage for excrement.”

nikkhamisaṃ.meaning_2: will go out; will leave; will depart; will exit
nikkhamisaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Future first person singular in -issaṃ (cf. PEU nikkhamissaṃ 'let me go'). The text form is nikkhamisaṃ with single s; sandhi of nikkhamissaṃ. Coordinate with the present nikkhamati.
nikkhamisaṃ.example_1: 136. ‘‘ Tato ahaṃ nikkhamisaṃ bhadante, cando yathā rāhumukhā pamutto;
nikkhamisaṃ.translation_1: 136. “Then I exited, Venerable Sir, like the moon released from the mouth of Rāhu;

kipillikāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Neuter plural form kipillikāni in the text (or masc plural -āni by analogy). Crushed on the ant-heap in the verse.
kipillikāni.example_1: 137. ‘‘ Vammīkathūpasmiṃ kipillikāni, nippothayanto tuvaṃ pure carāsi;
kipillikāni.translation_1: 137. “In the past, O bear, you used to move about crushing ants on the ant-heap;

paripothayiṃsu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd plural in the text; root-form poth later to pothayati. Alternatively connected to √puṭh.
paripothayiṃsu.example_1: Tato janā nikkhamitvāna gāmā, kodaṇḍakena paripothayiṃsu maṃ.
paripothayiṃsu.translation_1: Then the people came out of the village and beat me with bows.”

nikkhamisanti.meaning_2: will go out; will leave; will depart
nikkhamisanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Future 3rd plural of nikkhamati, formed with -issa-. The root √kam with prefix ni becomes kham before the ending, giving nikkhamati; the future base is nikkhamissa-, hence nikkhamisanti. The active sense and plural ending fit the prose Jātaka context.

atihīḷayānoti.meaning_2: very contemptible, he is; extremely despicable, he says
atihīḷayānoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of atihīḷayāna and the quotative iti. Analysis doubtful: PEU splits ati + hiḷa + ṇaya + āna; possibly atihīḷana + iti.

upavasitabbo.meaning_2: should be observed; should be practised; is to be kept (of a religious observance)
upavasitabbo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Potential participle used impersonally with uposatho as subject: "the Uposatha is to be observed". The -tabba suffix here has passive/obligation force.
upavasitabbo.example_1: Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā ‘‘ evaṃ upāsakā, uposatho nāmesa porāṇakapaṇḍitānaṃ vaṃso, upavasitabbo uposathavāso ’’ ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi –
upavasitabbo.translation_1: The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma discourse, said, "Thus, lay followers, the Uposatha is the custom of wise men of old, and the Uposatha observance should be practiced," and then he identified the Jātaka—

sineruubbāhanakavāto.meaning_2: wind capable of uprooting Mount Sineru; hurricane able to lift Mount Sineru
sineruubbāhanakavāto.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of Sineru (the mountain) + ubbāhanaka (uprooting, lifting) + vāta (wind). Nominative singular in the text. Alternative form sineruuppāṭanakavāta is given in PEU.
sineruubbāhanakavāto.example_1: Tañhi bhikkhuṃ satthā ‘‘ saccaṃ kira tvaṃ ukkaṇṭhitosī ’’ ti pucchitvā ‘‘ saccaṃ, bhante ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ bhikkhu ayaṃ nandīrāgo tādisaṃ kiṃ nāma nālolessati, na hi sineruubbāhanakavāto sāmante purāṇapaṇṇassa lajjati, pubbe satta vassasatāni antokilesasamudācāraṃ vāretvā viharante visuddhasattepesa ālolesiyevā ’’ ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.
sineruubbāhanakavāto.translation_1: Having asked that bhikkhu, "Is it true, as I am told, that you are backsliding?" and having heard the reply, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Teacher said, "Bhikkhu, why would this delight-passion not disturb someone like you? A hurricane capable of uprooting Mount Sineru is not ashamed before a withered leaf nearby. In the past, this passion has indeed disturbed even pure beings who had lived for seven hundred years having restrained the arising of defilements within themselves," and then he brought forth the story of the past.

bajjhituṃ.meaning_2: to be caught; to be trapped; to be bound
bajjhituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of the passive bajjhati (from bandh with assimilation). The PEU glosses it via badha but √bandh fits the sense of being caught in a snare.
bajjhituṃ.example_1: Sattamena pana raññā pesito sattamo luddo ‘‘ ajja ajjevā ’’ ti satta saṃvaccharāni bajjhituṃ asakkonto cintesi ‘‘ kiṃ nu kho imassa morarājassa pāde pāsassa asañcaraṇakāraṇan ’’ ti?
bajjhituṃ.translation_1: But the seventh hunter, sent by the seventh king, thinking, "Today, today," for seven years, being unable to catch him, wondered, "What, I wonder, is the reason this peacock king’s feet do not touch the snare?"

asañcaraṇakapāso.meaning_2: snare that had not stirred; trap that had not caught anything
asañcaraṇakapāso.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of asañcaraṇa (not moving; not caught) and kapāso (snare; trap), written as one word; nominative singular in the text. Takes the -o ending to agree with the subject.
asañcaraṇakapāso.example_1: Satta vassasatāni asañcaraṇakapāso taṅkhaṇaññeva sañcaritvā pādaṃ bandhi.
asañcaraṇakapāso.translation_1: The snare that had not caught him for seven hundred years moved at that very moment and bound his foot.

mantidattatthero.meaning_2: name of a monk, Elder Mantidatta
mantidattatthero.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name compound, nominative singular in the text. Two monks are named in the sentence: Dhanuggahatissatthera and Mantidattatthera.
mantidattatthero.example_1: Tesu dve mahallakattherā vihārapaccante paṇṇasālāyaṃ vasanti, eko dhanuggahatissatthero nāma, eko mantidattatthero nāma.
mantidattatthero.translation_1: Among them, two elderly monks lived in a leaf hut at the edge of the monastery; one was named Dhanuggahatissa, the other Mantidatta.

mantidattattherāti.meaning_2: thus the Elder Mantidatta; the Elder Mantidatta (they said)
mantidattattherāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Split is mantidattatthera + iti, the quotation ending -ti joined by sandhi; mantidattatthera itself is a name compound. mantidatta is a proper name, thera means elder (masc).

lālako.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Used as a noun for a fool in the text (nominative singular predicative). PEU suggests derivation from lāla + ṇvu, meaning stupid; the root is uncertain, so root fields are left empty.
lālako.example_1: ‘‘ Bhante, lālako vatāyaṃ kosalarājā cāṭimattabhojanameva bhuñjituṃ jānātī ’’ ti.
lālako.translation_1: ‘Venerable, this King of Kosala is a fool; he knows nothing but how to eat a bowlful of food.’

mantidattatthera.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of a monk. Used in direct address (vocative) in the text.
mantidattatthera.example_1: ‘‘ Bhante, mantidattatthera yuddhaṃ nāma sakaṭabyūhacakkabyūhapadumabyūhavasena tividhaṃ.
mantidattatthera.translation_1: ‘Venerable Mantidatta, battle strategy is threefold: Waggon-formation, Wheel-formation, and Lotus-formation.

sarīravidhūnanādīni.meaning_2: bodily shaking and so on; shaking of the body and similar actions
sarīravidhūnanādīni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative plural in the text; part of a compound describing bodily movements. Appears as sarīravidhūnanādīni (from sarīravidhūnanādi).
sarīravidhūnanādīni.example_1: Tattha byaggheti byagghasadise hutvā sarīravidhūnanādīni katvā ṭhite vase na kurute, attano vase vattāpetuṃ na sakkotīti attho.
sarīravidhūnanādīni.translation_1: In that context, byagghe means: those who have become like tigers, having performed bodily gestures and so on and being established (in that state), he does not put them under his power; the meaning is that he is unable to force them into his own power.

nitāḷeti.meaning_2: strikes down; knocks down; hurls to the ground
nitāḷeti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative of ni + √taḷ (taḷa tāḷane, 'hitting'); the commentary gloss explains the hawk felling its prey. Present 3rd singular in the text.
nitāḷeti.example_1: Tañca seno nitāḷeti, veyyagghiyeva sā gatī ’’ ti.
nitāḷeti.translation_1: The hawk strikes that one; such is the way of the tiger.”

nitāḷetīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form is nitāḷeti + iti (quotation), so the closure -ti is left out of the headword. Probably a causative of ni + √taḷ (to strike). The PEU gives ni + taḷa + ṇe, but ṇe is unlikely here; a *e causative fits the form better. The meaning is uncertain; check the commentary context.

tuṇḍotāraṇamattaṃ.meaning_2: just enough to dip the beak; merely a beak's dip
tuṇḍotāraṇamattaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text, the first tigers got only a beak's dip of meat. Accusative singular of a compound adjective.
tuṇḍotāraṇamattaṃ.example_1: Paṭhamāgatā ekavārameva tuṇḍotāraṇamattaṃ labhiṃsu, pacchā āgatā alabhitvā ‘‘ byagghamaṃsaṃ nāma kīdisan ’’ ti vadiṃsu.
tuṇḍotāraṇamattaṃ.translation_1: Those who came first got a single bite each, and those who came later asked, “What is tiger meat like?”

appodavaṇṇe.meaning_2: of the colour of waterless rice-gruel; pale like thick porridge without water
appodavaṇṇe.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes kummāsa (thick porridge) in the Jātaka verse; the commentary glosses appodakapāyāsasadise. Locative singular in the text.
appodavaṇṇe.translation_1: Thick porridge, ginger, lentil soup and many other things.
appodavaṇṇe.translation_2: ‘Thick porridge’ means porridge similar to dense gruel without water.

paṭiyāni.meaning_2: fine blanket; woollen rug; embroidered coverlet
paṭiyāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Listed with rajataṃ and kuttiyo as a luxurious textile; part of a stock list of beddings. In the text it is nominative plural. Compare paṭikā and Sanskrit pratyāna; some analyses take it as paṭa + yāna or a variant of paṭiyā.
paṭiyāni.translation_1: Silver and gold, and rugs and fine blankets.

uddiyāni.meaning_2: Uddiya blankets; blankets of the Uddiya kind
uddiyāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the verse uddiyāni ca kambalā is separated and glossed as uddiyāni nāma kambalā. Possibly the adjective uddiya (of Uddiya, a country) with nt plural nominative kambalāni, where final -a + ā- sandhi gives uddiyāni; the meaning field gives the sense as used in the text.
uddiyāni.example_1: 192. ‘‘ Kāsikāni ca vatthāni, uddiyāni ca kambalā;
uddiyāni.translation_1: 192. “And Benares cloth, and blankets of the Uddiya kind.
uddiyāni.example_2: Uddiyāni ca kambalāti uddiyāni nāma kambalā atthi.
uddiyāni.translation_2: ‘Uddiya blankets’ means there are blankets called Uddiya.

nāridā.meaning_2: giving women (to); yielding women (branches of a wish-fulfilling tree)
nāridā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the Jātaka story of the wish-fulfilling tree, describing branches that give women. Feminine form used as a noun for a branch, in the nominative singular; uttarā in the same verse is the matching form.
nāridā.example_1: Nāridā pacchimā sākhā, sabbakāme ca uttarā;
nāridā.translation_1: The western branch gave ladies, the northern gave all that one could desire;

chāyayāti.grammar: fem, instr sg, sandhi with iti
chāyayāti.meaning_2: with shade; by shade; by shadow
chāyayāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of chāyāya (instrumental of chāyā) + iti; chāyāya < chāyā. Given as chāyayāti, possibly chāyā + iti with contraction, or a variant spelling of chāyāya + iti. See chāyā.

paṭiyānicāti.meaning_2: O lady of the return journey; O lady on the return journey
paṭiyānicāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Uncertain analysis: looks like paṭiyānī with -cāti (-ca + iti), a feminine vocative, but no context is available to confirm.

cāhametamicchāmi.meaning_2: and I do not desire this; and this I do not want
cāhametamicchāmi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi resolving to ca + ahaṃ + etaṃ + icchāmi; negative particle na precedes it in the text. Aligned with na cāhametamicchāmi, verse 213.
cāhametamicchāmi.translation_1: 213. “I do not desire this, which comes from the gift of another;

uparopanakaviruhanaṭṭhānāni.meaning_2: places for planting and growing; places where they are planted and grow
uparopanakaviruhanaṭṭhānāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative plural in the text, referring to the places in the park where the fields were planted and grew.
uparopanakaviruhanaṭṭhānāni.example_1: Tānīdha khettānīti imasmiṃ uyyāne tāneva etāni uparopanakaviruhanaṭṭhānāni.
uparopanakaviruhanaṭṭhānāni.translation_1: These are the fields (tānīdha khettāni) means: 'In this park are these very same places where they were planted and grew.'

aṇḍacchedā.meaning_2: castrator; gelder; one who cuts off the testicles
aṇḍacchedā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative plural in the verse (aṇḍacchedā). The commentary glosses it with the synonym aṇḍacchedaka and explains aṇḍa as the testicles of oxen; from √chid (cut).
aṇḍacchedā.translation_1: Many people question them; they are gelded and marked men.
aṇḍacchedā.example_2: Aṇḍacchedā nilañchakāti bhatiṃ gahetvā balibaddānaṃ aṇḍacchedakā ceva tisūlādiaṅkakaraṇena lañchakā ca, lakkhaṇakārakāti attho.
aṇḍacchedā.translation_2: Aṇḍacchedā nilañchakā means having accepted a fee, they are those who castrate oxen and act as branders by using trident-marks and the like; in other words, they are brand-makers.

kuṭāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Written kuṭāni in the verse, but the prose gloss kūṭapāsādīni and the sense 'traps' point to kūṭa. Nominative/accusative plural neuter here; the commentary itself glosses it with kūṭa- in a compound. Doubtful reading: could also be taken as kuṭa, 'hut', but the gloss rules that out.
kuṭāni.example_1: 259. ‘‘ Araññe kuṭikaṃ katvā, kuṭāni kārayanti te;
kuṭāni.translation_1: “Having built huts in the wilderness, they set traps,
kuṭāni.translation_2: Kuṭāni kārayanti te means they set traps and snares.

āgodhā.meaning_2: as far as the lizards; (up to) monitor lizards; reptiles
āgodhā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the gloss āgo dhā macchakacchapaṃ is glossed as āgodhato pāṇayo, i.e. 'creatures from the iguana onwards'. The word is used adverbially in the text; some take it as an ablative from āgodhā. Printed here as a neuter compound.
āgodhā.translation_1: They kill hares and cats, lizards, fish, and tortoises.
āgodhā.example_2: Āgodhā macchakacchapanti thalajesu tāva āgodhato mahante ca khuddake ca pāṇayo bādhenti mārenti, jalajesu macchakacchape.
āgodhā.translation_2: Āgodhā macchakacchapan means among the land-dwelling creatures, first they torture and kill large and small living things from the iguana onwards, and among water-dwelling ones, fish and turtles.

ṭhapitavatikhāṇukā.meaning_2: stump of a fence that has been set up; standing fence-post
ṭhapitavatikhāṇukā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is nominative singular, in a simile for someone standing immovable. The compound is ṭhapita + vati + khāṇuka literally 'a stump of a fixed fence'.
ṭhapitavatikhāṇukā.example_1: Khāṇughātasamāti malīnasarīratāya jhāmakhette khāṇughātakehi bhūmiṃ khaṇitvā jhāmakhāṇukauddharaṇakamanussehi samānā,‘‘ aggahetvā na gamissāmā ’’ ti niccalabhāvena ṭhitattā nikhaṇitvā ṭhapitavatikhāṇukā viyātipi attho.
ṭhapitavatikhāṇukā.translation_1: Khāṇughātasamā means because their bodies are filthy, they are like the people who dig the earth in burnt fields to extract burnt stumps; the meaning is that they stand firm with the thought, 'I will not go until I have received it,' like a stump firmly fixed in the ground.

vipaṇentīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Form is vipaṇenti with the quotative -ti attached; 3rd plural present. The commentary explains it as they sell.

āvāhanti.meaning_2: brings in (a bridegroom); takes in marriage; marries into the family
āvāhanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the sentence it is glossed as āvāha, marrying a man into the family for one's own sons, as opposed to vivāhanti (giving daughters away). Third person plural present.
āvāhanti.example_1: Te evaṃ paresaṃ dadamānā vivāhanti nāma, attano puttānaṃ atthāya gaṇhamānā āvāhanti nāma.
āvāhanti.translation_1: Giving them away to others in this way is called vivāha (marrying off), taking them for their own sons is called āvāha (marrying in).

nilañchakāti.meaning_2: having a mark; marked; characterized; distinguished
nilañchakāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form nilañchakāti is nilañchakā + iti; here the adjective agrees with a plural subject. The PEU splits it as ni + lañcha + ṇvu.

aṇḍacchedakā.meaning_2: castrator of oxen; one who cuts the testicles
aṇḍacchedakā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Plural nominative in the text, in apposition to the ox-castrators; also glossed in the commentary as a maker of marks (lakkhaṇakāraka).
aṇḍacchedakā.example_1: Aṇḍacchedā nilañchakāti bhatiṃ gahetvā balibaddānaṃ aṇḍacchedakā ceva tisūlādiaṅkakaraṇena lañchakā ca, lakkhaṇakārakāti attho.
aṇḍacchedakā.translation_1: Aṇḍacchedā nilañchakā means having accepted a fee, they are those who castrate oxen and act as branders by using trident-marks and the like; in other words, they are brand-makers.

āmantanīyoti.meaning_2: to be consulted; worthy of addressing; fit to be spoken to
āmantanīyoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text the quotation particle -ti is attached (āmantanīyoti); the entry is for the main word. Probably an -anīya (ptp) formation from āmanteti; PEU splits it as ā + manta + manīya.

tālakandāni.meaning_2: palm tuber; edible shoot or root of the toddy palm
tālakandāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text tālakandāni is nominative/accusative plural, paired with ālūni (water-lily roots).
tālakandāni.translation_1: 'Digging for tubers' means digging for water-lily roots and palm tubers.

bilālikandatakkalakandāni.meaning_2: the roots and tubers called bilālika?; various roots and tubers
bilālikandatakkalakandāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Appears only in the gloss explaining bilālitakkalāni in the Jātaka commentary; the exact division and meaning of the parts are uncertain. A plural form.
bilālikandatakkalakandāni.translation_1: 'Various tubers' means various other types of roots and tubers.

saṅghāretvā.meaning_2: having gathered together; having collected; having swept together
saṅghāretvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of the causative saṅghāreti (saṃ + √har, 'to cause to carry together'). In the text it describes winnowing the grain together. Some editions read saṅgharitvā; the -etvā form points to a causative stem. From the Jātaka prose gloss on saṅghāriyaṃ.
saṅghāretvā.example_1: Saṅghāriyaṃ pasāriyanti ete sāmākanīvāre dhunanto saṅghāretvā puna sukkhāpite pasāretvā suppena papphoṭetvā koṭṭetvā taṇḍule ādāya pacitvā bhuñjāmīti vadati.
saṅghāretvā.translation_1: 'Spreading them out and drying them' means, he says, 'Winnowing those grains, spreading them out to dry, and when they are dried again, spreading them out, shaking them with a winnowing basket, pounding them, taking the rice, cooking it, and eating it.'

tambakipillakehi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental plural in the text (tambakipillakehi), meaning 'with red ants'. The compound is also cited as tambakipillaka 'red ant' in the PEU. The verb used is khādāpessāmi 'I will have (him) eaten', with the ants as instruments.
tambakipillakehi.example_1: So kuddho gantvā theraṃ akkositvā paribhāsitvā ‘‘ handāhaṃ, taṃ samaṇaṃ tambakipillakehi khādāpessāmī ’’ ti kodhavasena therassa sarīre tambakipillakapuṭaṃ bhindāpesi.
tambakipillakehi.translation_1: He grew angry, approached the Elder, abused and reviled him, and in his rage, he had a basket of red ants broken over the Elder’s body.

tambakipillakapuṭaṃ.meaning_2: nest of red ants; red-ant nest
tambakipillakapuṭaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text, object of bhindāpesi. The related entry gives tambakipillakapuṭaka as a neuter variant.
tambakipillakapuṭaṃ.example_1: So kuddho gantvā theraṃ akkositvā paribhāsitvā ‘‘ handāhaṃ, taṃ samaṇaṃ tambakipillakehi khādāpessāmī ’’ ti kodhavasena therassa sarīre tambakipillakapuṭaṃ bhindāpesi.
tambakipillakapuṭaṃ.translation_1: He grew angry, approached the Elder, abused and reviled him, and in his rage, he had a basket of red ants broken over the Elder’s body.

upajotiyo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A proper name. Nominative singular in the verses and the prose gloss.
upajotiyo.example_1: 8. ‘‘ Kvettha gatā upajotiyo ca, upajjhāyo atha vā gaṇḍakucchi;
upajotiyo.translation_1: 8. ‘Where have those gatekeepers, Upajotiya, Upajjhaya, and Gandhakucchi gone?’
upajotiyo.example_2: Tattha kvettha gatāti imesu tīsu dvāresu ṭhapitā upajotiyo ca upajjhāyo ca gaṇḍakucchi cāti tayo dovārikā kuhiṃ gatāti attho.
upajotiyo.translation_2: Therein, kvettha gatā means: ‘Where have those three gatekeepers—Upajotiya, Upajjhaya, and Gandhakucchi, who were stationed at the three gates—gone?’

mahakkasāvesu.meaning_2: with great defilements; full of impurity
mahakkasāvesu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative plural in the text, agreeing with the addressees. Compound of mahant + kasāva; the stem becomes mahak- before the consonant.
mahakkasāvesu.translation_1: You give gifts to those of great defilements, to the immoral and unrestrained.’

khaḷu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] An exclamation in the caṇḍāla dialect, repeated as "khaḷu khaḷū". Indeclinable; sometimes written as khaḷū.
khaḷu.example_1: So kampamāno satiṃ anupaṭṭhāpetvā cittapaṇḍitaṃ oloketvā caṇḍālabhāsāya eva ‘‘ khaḷu khaḷū ’’ ti āha.
khaḷu.translation_1: Trembling and forgetting his mindfulness, he looked at the wise Citta and said in the outcast dialect, “Hot, hot!”

khaḷūti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Unclear sandhi: probably khaḷu + iti, from khaḷopi (khala + api), meaning basket or rice pot. The text form is doubtful.

paṭisaṃyamissaṃ.meaning_2: will restrain oneself; will exercise self-control
paṭisaṃyamissaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Future 1st singular of paṭisaṃyamati (attānameva paṭisaṃyamissaṃ = I will restrain myself). The root √yam 1 with the meaning 'control' is used here.
paṭisaṃyamissaṃ.example_1: Attānameva paṭisaṃyamissaṃ, na patthaye putta pasuṃ dhanaṃ vā.
paṭisaṃyamissaṃ.translation_1: I shall exercise self-restraint alone; I do not desire sons, cattle, or wealth.
paṭisaṃyamissaṃ.example_2: Tattha na ciraṃ sīlaṃ rakkhitvā tassa phalena tvaṃ khattiyakule nibbatto, ahaṃ brāhmaṇakule, evāhaṃ duccaritassa ca phalaṃ suciṇṇassa ca mahāvipākaṃ disvā attānameva sīlasaṃyamena paṭisaṃyamissaṃ, puttaṃ vā pasuṃ vā dhanaṃ vā na patthemi.
paṭisaṃyamissaṃ.translation_2: Because I protected my virtue for a short time there, you were reborn in a Khattiya family by the fruit of that, and I in a Brahmin family. Thus, having seen the fruit of misconduct and the great consequence of good conduct, I shall restrain myself through moral discipline; I do not desire sons, beasts, or wealth.

khiṭṭādasakādīsu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative plural in the text (khiṭṭādasakādīsu = 'in the play-decade and the following ones'). Part of a series of ten-year decades of life in the Jātaka prose; manuscript spelling varies between khiḍḍā- and khiṭṭā-.
khiṭṭādasakādīsu.example_1: Yepi sakalaṃ vassasataṃ jīvanti, tesampi mandadasake pavattā rūpārūpadhammā vicchinditvā ātape khittanaḷo viya tattheva sussanti antaradhāyanti, taṃ odhiṃ atikkamitvā khiḍḍādasakaṃ na pāpuṇanti, tathā khiṭṭādasakādīsu pavattā vaṇṇadasakādīni.
khiṭṭādasakādīsu.translation_1: Even for those who live a full hundred years, the mental and physical states occurring in the decade of ignorance break off and disappear right there, like a reed thrown into the heat; they do not reach the decade of play, having surpassed that limit, and so too for the states occurring in the decade of play, the decade of beauty, and so on.

byasanno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text nominative singular. The commentary glosses visanno anupaviṭṭho, i.e. 'sunk, entered into'.
byasanno.example_1: 45. ‘‘ Nāgo yathā paṅkamajjhe byasanno, passaṃ thalaṃ nābhisambhoti gantuṃ;
byasanno.translation_1: 45. 'Just as an elephant deep sunken in the mire, seeing the shore, is not able to go forth;
byasanno.example_2: Evampahaṃ kāmapaṅke byasanno, na bhikkhuno maggamanubbajāmi.
byasanno.translation_2: So too am I, sunken in the mud of sensual pleasures, unable to follow the bhikkhu's path.'

visanno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text visanno is nominative singular; the commentary glosses it with anupaviṭṭho and osanno. It is a by-form of byasanna (vyasanna); both mean sunk into, submerged.
visanno.example_1: Tattha byasannoti visanno anupaviṭṭho ayameva vā pāṭho.
visanno.translation_1: Regarding byasanno (sunken): Fallen into, entered into; this is the reading.
visanno.example_2: ‘‘ Visanno ’’ tipi pāṭho, tasmiṃ vante osannoti attho.
visanno.translation_2: There is also the reading “Visanno”, meaning ‘one who is submerged in that vomit’.

manasī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Occurs in the phrase manasī karoti, 'bears in mind'. Locative singular of manas in form, but functioning as an indeclinable.
manasī.example_1: Ajjāpi me taṃ manasīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ kodhanaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi.
manasī.translation_1: Ajjāpi me taṃ manasīti: The Teacher told this story while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain irritable monk.
manasī.example_2: Imameva gāthaṃ manasī karohi, bhāsesi cenaṃ parisāya majjhe.
manasī.translation_2: Bear this very verse in mind and recite it in the midst of the assembly:

vajantyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine instrumental singular of the present participle, qualifying the mother: 'while she walked along'.
vajantyā.translation_1: “Sleeping in the open, the person who was nursed with milk while his mother walked along,

māgatosi.meaning_2: you have not come; you did not come
māgatosi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of na + āgatosi (āgacchati 'come' + -si 'you'), na contracted to mā before the vowel. Query where the teacher instructed the mendicant to come. Alternatively mā + āgatosi (prohibitive), but the sentence reads as a question: 'by whom were you sent to come here?'
māgatosi.example_1: 53. ‘‘ Kenānusiṭṭho idha māgatosi, vanibbaka cakkhupathāni yācituṃ;
māgatosi.translation_1: 53. “By whom were you instructed, mendicant, to come here to ask for the path of the eyes;

cakkhupathāni.meaning_2: range of vision; sphere of the eye; path of the eye
cakkhupathāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Commentary verse; plural accusative cakkhupathāni. Likely 'the range of vision' offered to the mendicant. Perhaps a text corruption.
cakkhupathāni.example_1: 53. ‘‘ Kenānusiṭṭho idha māgatosi, vanibbaka cakkhupathāni yācituṃ;
cakkhupathāni.translation_1: 53. “By whom were you instructed, mendicant, to come here to ask for the path of the eyes;
cakkhupathāni.example_2: Tenānusiṭṭho idha māgatosmi, vanibbako cakkhupathāni yācituṃ.
cakkhupathāni.translation_2: Instructed by him, I have come here, a mendicant, to ask for the path of the eyes.”

māgatosmi.meaning_2: I have come; I am arrived
māgatosmi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of āgato (past participle of āgacchati) and asmi (present of √as). The text reads māgatosmi; mā is likely a separate particle or sandhi element (mā + āgatosmi).
māgatosmi.example_1: Tenānusiṭṭho idha māgatosmi, vanibbako cakkhupathāni yācituṃ.
māgatosmi.translation_1: Instructed by him, I have come here, a mendicant, to ask for the path of the eyes.”

tadate.meaning_2: that for you; that (is) for you
tadate.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the verse yadicchase tvaṃ tadate samijjhatu; the commentary glosses yaṃ tvaṃ mama santikā icchasi, taṃ te samijjhatu, supporting taṃ + te. Printed tadate for tada te; the PEU entry tadattha looks like a different (Ta+attha) word.
tadate.example_1: Sa cakkhumā gaccha janassa pekkhato, yadicchase tvaṃ tadate samijjhatū ’’ ti.
tadate.translation_1: Go as one with vision in the view of the people, may that which you desire be accomplished for you.”
tadate.example_2: Yadicchase tvaṃ tadate samijjhatūti yaṃ tvaṃ mama santikā icchasi, taṃ te samijjhatūti.
tadate.translation_2: Yadicchase tvaṃ tadate samijjhatū means whatever you wish from me, may that be accomplished for you.

sīviko.meaning_2: Sīvaka; man of the Sivi people; name of a doctor
sīviko.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a doctor in the Jātaka stories. Nominative singular in the text. PEU gives both masculine and feminine forms; here masculine.
sīviko.example_1: Atha naṃ sīviko āha ‘‘ cakkhudānaṃ nāma bhāriyaṃ, upadhārehi, devā ’’ ti.
sīviko.translation_1: Then Sīvaka said to him, “The giving of eyes is a heavy thing, consider it, lord.”
sīviko.translation_2: 67. “Spurred on by the King of Sivi, Sīvaka, the one who does the bidding,

vacanaṃkaro.meaning_2: doing the bidding; obedient (to); carrying out the words (of)
vacanaṃkaro.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Vocative singular in the verse, addressed to Sīvaka.
vacanaṃkaro.translation_1: 67. “Spurred on by the King of Sivi, Sīvaka, the one who does the bidding,

uparūḷhesu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative plural in the text (uparūḷhesu cakkhusu): when his eyes had healed. The PEU treats it as a healing wound; literally 'grown over, healed up'.
uparūḷhesu.translation_1: 68. “Then, when a few days had passed and his eyes had healed,

nīdha.meaning_2: here; in this place; in this world
nīdha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi for na idha? Alternatively idha with reinforcing na? In the verses it means 'here'. Appears in verse as nīdha.
nīdha.example_1: 79. ‘‘ Ko nīdha vittaṃ na dadeyya yācito, api visiṭṭhaṃ supiyampi attano;
nīdha.translation_1: “Who, being asked, would not give wealth here, even that which is distinguished, even that which is most dear to oneself?
nīdha.example_2: Vassekimaṃ jīvitaṃ bhūmipāla, ko nīdha kantāya vinā vaseyya.
nīdha.translation_2: This life is but a single year, O protector of the land; who would live here without one’s desired?

konīdhāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of ko and idha; the word appears in the text as konīdhāti, with the ti (or iti) quotation marker joined on. No sentences were supplied, so the analysis rests on the form alone.

sīvikavejjo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a physician in a Jātaka story. Nominative singular in the text; the commentary identifies him with Ānanda.
sīvikavejjo.example_1: ‘‘ tadā sīvikavejjo ānando ahosi, sakko anuruddho ahosi, sesaparisā buddhaparisā, sivirājā pana ahameva ahosin ’’ ti.
sīvikavejjo.translation_1: “At that time the physician Sīvaka was Ānanda, Sakka was Anuruddha, the rest of the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly, but King Sivi was I myself.”

mākaṅkhi.meaning_2: do not doubt; do not hesitate; do not wait
mākaṅkhi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Prohibitive aorist with mā; the form mākaṅkhi is mā + kaṅkhi, 2nd singular aorist of kaṅkhati. The commentary prose repeats this sentence with 2nd person singular imperative; same meaning. Sometimes written mā kaṅkhi.
mākaṅkhi.example_1: Gaccha tuvampi mākaṅkhi, jīvissanti tayā sahā ’’ ti.
mākaṅkhi.translation_1: Go thou with them, and linger not, for they shall live with thee.”
mākaṅkhi.example_2: Gaccha tuvampi mākaṅkhi, jīvissanti tayā saha.
mākaṅkhi.translation_2: Go thou with them, and linger not, for they shall live with thee.”

kaḍḍhayati.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative form used as a gloss for avakassati; 3rd singular present. The simplex kaḍḍhati means 'pulls, drags'.
kaḍḍhayati.translation_1: Avakassatī (has drawn me) means it pulls; or it is pulled by sorrow.

kaḍḍhīyati.meaning_2: is pulled; is dragged; is drawn
kaḍḍhīyati.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Passive of kaḍḍhati, formed irregularly with -īya-. Third person singular, used in the explanation of avakassati: 'or it is pulled by sorrow (sokena)'.
kaḍḍhīyati.translation_1: Avakassatī (has drawn me) means it pulls; or it is pulled by sorrow.

upanivatti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text gives only upanivatti, which does not fit the present tense; the sentence's gloss upanivatti probably stands for upanivattati in an unusual or corrupt form, possibly influenced by the abstract noun in maraṇāyūpanivattathā, aorist sense 'she returned'. The PEU splits upa+ni+vatthu(vatu)+ī, but the construction is upa + ni + √vatt.
upanivatti.translation_1: Regarding maraṇāyūpanivattathā (she returned to die), she returned for the sake of dying.

kāromīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] kāromīti = karomi + iti, with sandhi ā for aṃ? Actually kāromi is 1st person singular 'I do'; the -ti is the quotative iti. For a dictionary headword this is given as 3rd singular karoti.

abhihāritunti.meaning_2: to bring here; to fetch this
abhihāritunti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi resolution of abhihārituṃ + iti, the -ti being the quotation particle; the underlying form is the infinitive abhihārituṃ of abhiharati (abhi + harati). The commentarial gloss takes it as 'to bring this'.

uggaṇhāpito.meaning_2: causes to learn; has taught; instructs; causes to take up
uggaṇhāpito.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Past participle uggaṇhāpito in the text, used passively: 'was taught; was instructed'. Spelling with ṇh after the prefix u.
uggaṇhāpito.example_1: Mātāpissa bhātaraṃ upasaṅkamitvā ‘‘ kiṃ te, bhātika, bhāgineyyo migamāyaṃ uggaṇhāpito ’’ ti pucchi.
uggaṇhāpito.translation_1: His mother approached her brother and asked, “Brother, has my son been taught the deer’s ruses?”
uggaṇhāpito.example_2: ‘‘ Nanu ahaṃ tumhehi asātamanto nāma na uggaṇhāpito ’’ ti?
uggaṇhāpito.translation_2: “Did you not fail to teach me the Asātamanta?”

pāmadoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Only the taddhita-style analysis pāmada (pa + mada, 'forgetful') with -ti is given in PEU; it looks like a present 3rd singular in the text, but the form is doubtful.

pupphakotveva.meaning_2: like a flower-tip; just as a flower-tip
pupphakotveva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of puppha + koṭi + eva (iva becoming -va) in the phrase pupphakotveva, no sentence provided in the source. Alternatively analysed as puppha + koṭiyā + iva; final member eva is emphatic.

pothiyamānesu.meaning_2: is beaten; is thrashed; is struck; is flogged
pothiyamānesu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Only the passive present participle pothiyamāna appears in the text, locative plural pothiyamānesu (agreeing with vanagumbesu). The base form is pothiyati; the more usual spelling is pothayati (√puth + *aya).
pothiyamānesu.example_1: Purisehi migānaṃ uṭṭhāpanatthāya vanagumbesu pothiyamānesu eko eṇimigo uṭṭhāya gamanamaggaṃ olokento rañño ṭhitaṭṭhānasseva vivittataṃ disvā tadabhimukho pakkhanditvā palāyi.
pothiyamānesu.translation_1: As the people beat the bushes to start the deer, one antelope arose, looked for a way to escape, and seeing the vacancy in the spot where the king stood, he broke through towards that side and fled.

lohituṇhīso.meaning_2: having a red turban; wearing a red headband
lohituṇhīso.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi compound describing a person (the king in the verse). Nominative singular lohituṇhīso in the text; glossed in the commentary as rattena uṇhīsapaṭṭena samannāgato.
lohituṇhīso.translation_1: He shines with a red turban, shining like the sun by day.
lohituṇhīso.translation_2: “Red turban” means he is endowed with a red turban-band.

lohituṇhīsoti.meaning_2: with a red turban; wearing a crimson headdress
lohituṇhīsoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form lohituṇhīsoti is lohituṇhīsa + iti. The word describes a king wearing a red uṇhīsa (turban or headdress).

tomarāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Neuter plural tomarāni in the verse. The PEU entry suggests a derivation from √tud with the suffix -ara and a comment on the diphthong, but the form is best treated as a masc a-stem noun meaning 'spear; javelin'.
tomarāni.translation_1: “Take up the bows, the javelins, and the spears;

isisīlācārena.meaning_2: sage's conduct and morality; ascetic virtue and practice
isisīlācārena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular in the text, paired with isidhammena. The compound is isi + sīla + ācāra; sīlācāra may be treated as a dvanda of sīla and ācāra.
isisīlācārena.example_1: Tena dhammena no vināti mahārāja, taṃ sattigumbaṃ corā coradhammena corakiriyāya vinesuṃ, maṃ isayo isidhammena isisīlācārena, tasmā sopi tena coradhammena no vinā hoti, ahampi isidhammena no vinā homīti.
isisīlācārena.translation_1: “Because of that Dhamma, we are not the same” (tena dhammena no vinā) means: O Great King, the robbers influenced that Sattigumba with their robber-Dhamma and robber-actions, while the sages influenced me with the sage-Dhamma and sage-conduct; therefore, he is not the same because of that robber-Dhamma, and I am not the same because of the sage-Dhamma.

visīlaṃ.meaning_2: immoral; devoid of virtue; without ethical conduct
visīlaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of vi (privative prefix) + sīla; accusative singular in the verse. Contrasts with sīlavanta in the same sentence.
visīlaṃ.example_1: Sīlavantaṃ visīlaṃ vā, vasaṃ tasseva gacchati.
visīlaṃ.translation_1: Virtuous or devoid of virtue, he falls under the power of that very person.

nopaseveyya.meaning_2: should follow; should associate with; should resort to
nopaseveyya.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Negated optative: na + upasevati, joined by sandhi to nopaseveyya. 3rd singular.
nopaseveyya.translation_1: The wise one should not follow the bad, he should follow the good;

sāḷūrasaṅghañca.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of sāḷūrasaṅghaṃ (accusative singular) + ca; the -ṃ becomes -ñ before c. Object of nisedhayitvā. The compound is sāḷūra + saṅgha.
sāḷūrasaṅghañca.example_1: 187. ‘‘ Sāḷūrasaṅghañca nisedhayitvā, dhanuṃ kalāpañca so nikkhipitvā;
sāḷūrasaṅghañca.translation_1: 187. “Having signaled to the pack of dogs, and having laid down his bow and quiver,

nisedhayitvā.meaning_2: having forbidden; having prevented; having stopped; having warded off
nisedhayitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of nisedheti (√sidh 1, caus), used in verse to mean having restrained or ordered back the dogs. The commentary glosses with nivārayitvā.
nisedhayitvā.example_1: 187. ‘‘ Sāḷūrasaṅghañca nisedhayitvā, dhanuṃ kalāpañca so nikkhipitvā;
nisedhayitvā.translation_1: 187. “Having signaled to the pack of dogs, and having laid down his bow and quiver,

sāḷūrasaṅghanti.meaning_2: pack of dogs; group of hounds
sāḷūrasaṅghanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form adds the quotation/sandhi ending -ti (sāḷūrasaṅghanti); entry is for the main word.

sattaliyothikañca.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The sandhi resolves as sattaliya + yothika + ca, where the final vowel of sattaliya combines with the initial vowel of yothika. The whole form is joined to the enclitic ca. The words refer to kinds of flowers: sattali ('sattali flowers') and yothika ('jasmine').
sattaliyothikañca.translation_1: 196. “I was gathering aṅkolaka, and atimuttaka, and sattali flowers and jasmine,

oceyya.meaning_2: having plucked; having picked; having gathered
oceyya.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -ya (cf. ocināti, oceti) used twice in these verses with pupphāni. The PEU split ava + ci + tvā gives the sense; the ending here is -ya, not -tvā.
oceyya.example_1: 198. ‘‘ Ahañca sālassa supupphitassa, oceyya pupphāni karomi mālaṃ;
oceyya.translation_1: 198. “And I, having plucked flowers from the well-blooming sāla tree, made a garland,
oceyya.example_2: 199. ‘‘ Ahañca sālassa supupphitassa, oceyya pupphāni karomi bhāraṃ;
oceyya.translation_2: 199. “And I, having plucked flowers from the well-blooming sāla tree, made a load,

āliṅgiyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text the absolutive has the emphatic/poetic ending -yā (āliṅgiyā), equivalent to āliṅgiya. The PEU entry instead treats āliṅgiya as a potential participle 'should be embraced', but the sentence is a finite clause 'we two embraced', so the absolutive reading is preferable: 'having embraced one another'.
āliṅgiyā.example_1: Āliṅgiyā aññamaññaṃ mayaṃ ubho, sakimpi rodāma sakiṃ hasāma.
āliṅgiyā.translation_1: We two embraced one another; sometimes we wept, sometimes we laughed.

tīhūnakaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text accusative singular in tīhūnakaṃ satta satāni (697 = 700 - 3).
tīhūnakaṃ.example_1: 204. ‘‘ Tīhūnakaṃ satta satāni ludda, yamidha mayaṃ vippavasimha pubbe;
tīhūnakaṃ.translation_1: 204. “Six hundred and ninety-seven years, huntsman, since we were parted previously,

yamimanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Unresolved sandhi; no sentences supplied. Analysis doubtful; perhaps a misreading or compound form.

aṅkolakādīni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative/accusative plural form in the text; aṅkolaka refers to the Alangium hexapetalum flower, with ādi meaning 'and so on'.
aṅkolakādīni.example_1: Ahañcāti ahaṃ panetassa paratīraṃ gatabhāvaṃ ajānantī supupphitāni aṅkolakādīni pupphāni ocināmi.
aṅkolakādīni.translation_1: Ahañcā means ‘But I, not knowing he had reached the other shore, gathered well-blooming flowers like aṅkolaka’.

sattaliyothikañcāti.meaning_2: and a measure called sattaliya; 'sattaliya (is) an othika' — and so it is said
sattaliyothikañcāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Difficult word, not found in the standard dictionaries; probably sattaliya + othikaṃ + ca + iti, an explanatory gloss ('sattaliya means othika') with quotative -ti. Doubtful analysis.

suvaṇṇayothikañca.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of suvaṇṇa (golden) and yothika (jasmine). Accusative singular in the text, joined with ca (suvaṇṇayothikañca).
suvaṇṇayothikañca.example_1: Tattha sattaliyothikañcāti kundālapupphañca suvaṇṇayothikañca ocinantī pana ‘‘ piyo ca me mālabhārī bhavissati, ahañca naṃ mālinī hutvā ajjhupessan ’’ ti iminā kāraṇena ocināmi.
suvaṇṇayothikañca.translation_1: Therein, sattaliyothikañcā means ‘I gathered jasmine and golden jasmine, thinking, “My beloved will be wearing a garland, and I, having become garlanded, shall approach him”’.

oceyyāti.meaning_2: having plucked; having picked; having gathered
oceyyāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] This is a variant of the absolutive, written here as oceyya because -tvā has become -yya; often printed as a quote with -ti, so the entry follows the main word. The PEU gives ava + ci + tvā, but the initial o- may belong to the root. Uncertain which root it comes from: √ci 1 (gather) fits the meaning of 'pluck', but the PEU separates the prefix ava.

kāḷāgaḷuñca.meaning_2: black aloes; black aloeswood; black eaglewood
kāḷāgaḷuñca.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text with sandhi -ñca (= kāḷāgaḷu + ca), glossed as kāḷa-agaru/candana. Same entry as kāḷāgaru.
kāḷāgaḷuñca.translation_1: Agaḷuṃ candanañcā means ‘black aloes and red sandalwood’.

tīhūnakanti.meaning_2: with three deficient; seventy-seven; less three than eighty
tīhūnakanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Probably a sandhi or compound of tīhi ūna and asīti (asīti + kanti?), meaning 77. Analysis uncertain.

nīdhāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form nīdhāti shows the prefix ni lengthened before the root; compare nidahati. Present 3rd singular.

bhallātiyarājā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name. Nominative singular in the text ('ahameva ahosin'). Compound containing rāja; final -ā is the nominative ending.
bhallātiyarājā.example_1: ‘‘ tadā kinnaro kosalarājā ahosi, kinnarī mallikā devī, bhallātiyarājā ahameva ahosin ’’ ti.
bhallātiyarājā.translation_1: “At that time the kinnara was the King of Kosala, the kinnarī was Queen Mallikā, and I myself was King Bhallātiya.”

pāricaratappamatto.meaning_2: unremitting in attending; diligent in serving
pāricaratappamatto.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Poetic compound in a verse; pāricarataṃ is the present participle of paricarati (attending), appamatta (not negligent).
pāricaratappamatto.example_1: 218. ‘‘ Sāyañca pāto udakaṃ sajāti, aggiṃ sadā pāricaratappamatto;
pāricaratappamatto.translation_1: “Morning and evening he draws water, he tends the fire always, unremittingly;

upadhārāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to be investigated; having had examined
upadhārāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Formed from upadhārāpeti, the causative of upadhāreti; āpetvā is the absolutive of the causative. Instrument for the investigation is not stated.
upadhārāpetvā.translation_1: Having investigated the vegetable business, he made it evident.

dunnikkayo.meaning_2: hard to remove; difficult to pull out; hard to uproot
dunnikkayo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the verse it describes a bamboo thicket (veḷu) that is hard to clear. The commentary glosses it as dunnikkaḍḍhiya, "hard to pull out". Nominative singular in -o.
dunnikkayo.example_1: 222. ‘‘ Daḷhasmi mūle visaṭe virūḷhe, dunnikkayo veḷu pasākhajāto;
dunnikkayo.translation_1: “The root is firm, wide-spread, and grown; the bamboo thicket is hard to remove;

dunnikkayoti.meaning_2: hard to drag out; difficult to remove
dunnikkayoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The -ti is the quotative particle; the entry is for the main word. The PEU gloss is obscure; du- is the negative prefix and nikkaya is related to kaḍḍhati 'to drag'.

kinnūdha.meaning_2: what here?; what now?; what indeed?
