kinnūdha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Variant of kinnu idha, used in direct address. In the commentary it introduces a question about the king's possessions; the text glosses it loosely.
kinnūdha.example_1: 224. ‘‘ Kinnūdha deva tavamatthi bhogā, pubbevahaṃ devaloke ramissaṃ;
kinnūdha.translation_1: “What possessions do you have here, O King? Previously I used to delight in the realm of devas;
kinnūdha.example_2: Kinnūdha devāti deva, ye tava bhogā, tesu kiṃ nāma bhuñjitabbaṃ atthi.
kinnūdha.translation_2: Kinnūdha devāti means: ‘O King, what is there to be enjoyed among the possessions that you have?’

vebhaṅgo.meaning_2: faulty administration (of medicine); wrong application; mishandling; ruin (of)
vebhaṅgo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is nominative singular, glossed by vipatti; the commentary explains it as the faulty administering of medicine. A prefix compound with vi-; some might analyse it as vebhaṅga from √bhañj, but the commentary treats it as a compound.
vebhaṅgo.translation_1: Like the faulty administration of medicine, its result is bad.
vebhaṅgo.example_2: Vipāko hoti pāpakoti tassa hi yathā nāma bhesajjassa vebhaṅgo vipatti, evamevaṃ vipāko hoti pāpako.
vebhaṅgo.translation_2: Vipāko hoti pāpakoti means just as the faulty administration of medicine is a ruin, in that same way the result is bad.

anavatthapetvā.meaning_2: without settling (on); without establishing; without fixing
anavatthapetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Glossed in the text by atuletvā and atīretvā. Negative absolutive: na + avatthapetvā; shown in the text's lemma as anavatthāya cintitaṃ.
anavatthapetvā.translation_1: Anavatthāya cintitanti means thought out without settling upon it, without weighing, without concluding.

uyojentī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle uyojentī (feminine) in the text, agreeing with sā; written with u- for classical uyyojeti. Root √yuj with prefix u-, causative.
uyojentī.translation_1: Urging him to go forth, she spoke a verse —

ekadoṇikanāvapamāṇaṃ.meaning_2: of the size of a single-hulled boat; as big as a one-trough canoe
ekadoṇikanāvapamāṇaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi compound used in the nominative singular neuter agreeing with sarīraṃ. Refers to the Bodhisatta's body in the Saṅkhapāla Jātaka.
ekadoṇikanāvapamāṇaṃ.example_1: Imasmiṃ pana jātake bodhisattassa sarīraṃ naṅgalasīsapamāṇaṃ ahosi, bhūridattajātake (jā.2.22.784 ādayo) ūruppamāṇaṃ, saṅkhapālajātake (jā.2.17.143 ādayo) ekadoṇikanāvapamāṇaṃ.
ekadoṇikanāvapamāṇaṃ.translation_1: In this Jātaka, the Bodhisatta's body was the size of a ploughshare, in the Bhūridatta Jātaka (Ja.2.22.784ff) the size of a thigh, and in the Saṅkhapāla Jātaka (Ja.2.17.143ff) the size of a trough-canoe.

abhimatthiyamāno.meaning_2: being crushed; being squeezed; being pressed upon
abhimatthiyamāno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Passive present participle, nominative singular masculine agreeing with matthako. The PEU entry connects it to abhimanthiyamāna; the reading with -tth- may reflect assimilation of -nth-.
abhimatthiyamāno.example_1: Dibbamantasutakālato paṭṭhāya mahāsattassa kaṇṇesu ayasalākapavesanakālo viya jāto, matthako sikharena abhimatthiyamāno viya jāto.
abhimatthiyamāno.translation_1: From the moment the magic charm was heard, it felt to the Great Being as if iron rods were being inserted into his ears, and his head felt as if it were being crushed by a sword point.

nippīḷi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular in the text; variant of nippīḷesi; the verb is not in the given root list, so the root key and signs are uncertain.
nippīḷi.example_1: Atha naṃ so naṅguṭṭhe gahetvā kaḍḍhitvā dīghaso nipajjāpetvā ajapadena daṇḍena uppīḷento dubbalaṃ katvā sīsaṃ daḷhaṃ gahetvā nippīḷi, mahāsattassa mukhaṃ vivari.
nippīḷi.translation_1: Then, seizing him by the tail, he dragged him, stretched him out at length, and squeezed him with a goat's-foot staff, making him weak; then he seized his head tightly and crushed him, causing the Great Being to open his mouth wide.

opitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of opeti; in the text it takes the object kheḷaṃ (spit) with the locative mukhe (into the mouth).
opitvā.example_1: Athassa mukhe kheḷaṃ opitvā osadhamantaṃ katvā dante bhindi, mukhaṃ lohitassa pūri.
opitvā.translation_1: Then he spat into his mouth, cast a spell with the herb, and broke his teeth; the mouth filled with blood.

cuṇṇayamāno.meaning_2: crushing to powder; grinding to powder; pulverising
cuṇṇayamāno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text has cuṇṇayamāno, nominative singular masculine of the present participle of a causative verb 'to crush to powder'; it qualifies the snake charmer. The PEU split cuṇṇa + ṇaya + māna is not followed here.
cuṇṇayamāno.example_1: Sopi ‘‘ nāgarājānaṃ dubbalaṃ karissāmī ’’ ti naṅguṭṭhato paṭṭhāyassa aṭṭhīni cuṇṇayamāno viya sakalasarīraṃ madditvā paṭṭakaveṭhanaṃ nāma veṭhesi, tantamajjitaṃ nāma majji, naṅguṭṭhaṃ gahetvā dussapothimaṃ nāma pothesi.
cuṇṇayamāno.translation_1: The man, thinking, “I will weaken the royal snake,” squeezed his body from tail to head as if crushing his bones to powder; then he performed what is called the cloth-wrap, the rope-rubbing, and the cotton blow, catching him by the tail.

sampūri.meaning_2: became full; was completed; came to an end
sampūri.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular in the text (māso sampūri: a month had passed). The PEU suggests present sampūrati; the form could also be read as an aorist ending in -i with passive sense.
sampūri.translation_1: A month had passed since he was caught.

maññāmī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present 1st singular in the text, used as a quotation lemma (maññāmīti). The gloss sallakkhemi ('I perceive') shows the meaning 'I think, I consider'. PEU gives the root as mana + ya + mi.
maññāmī.example_1: Evaṃ yaṃ yaṃ so hatthī kātuṃ na samattho, taṃ taṃ sabbaṃ rañño ārocetvā tassa asamatthabhāve attanā sallakkhitakāraṇaṃ ārocento ‘‘ maññāmī ’’tiādimāha.
maññāmī.translation_1: Having reported to the king everything that the elephant is unable to do, and wishing to report the cause he himself observed for that inability, he said the beginning of “maññāmi”.
maññāmī.example_2: Ṭhito thullāni gajjatīti ‘‘ so yasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhito thullāni pharusavacanāni vadati, tattheva te kulasantakaṃ dhanaṃ, evaṃ ahaṃ taṃ maññāmī ’’ ti bodhisatto kumārassa dhanaggahaṇūpāyaṃ ācikkhi.
maññāmī.translation_2: “Stands and loudly bawls”: “In the very place where that slave Nanda stands and speaks harsh, abusive words, your family wealth is there. This is how I think of it.” Having said this, the Bodhisatta taught the young gentleman the method for taking the wealth.

yamuggatejo.meaning_2: of mighty power; possessing great strength
yamuggatejo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Vocative singular yamuggateja in the verse; a bahubbīhi compound describing the nāga. yama- here intensifies, 'of outstanding power'. Print edition may read Yamuggatejo.
yamuggatejo.example_1: 243. ‘‘ Yamuggatejo uragoti cāhu, nāgoti naṃ āhu janā janinda;
yamuggatejo.translation_1: “They call him a snake, one of mighty power, a nāga, O King of men;

dubbissasametamāhu.meaning_2: hard to trust; this they said
dubbissasametamāhu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of du + vissasa + amata + āhu; in the verse it means "(that) is hard to trust, they said". Alternatively analysed as du + vissāsa + amata + āhu.
dubbissasametamāhu.example_1: 254. ‘‘ Addhā hi dubbissasametamāhu, yaṃ mānuso vissase amānusamhi;
dubbissasametamāhu.translation_1: “Superhuman beings may hardly win belief, they say, when a human places trust in a non-human.

dubbissasanti.meaning_2: is difficult to trust; is hard to get to know
dubbissasanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] 3rd plural future in form but treated here as present; possibly a future dubbissasissanti. The du- prefix assimilates before b.

tvevahaṃ.meaning_2: but not I; yet I do not
tvevahaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of tu (but) + eva (indeed) + ahaṃ (I). In both sentences it forms part of na tvevahaṃ ... bhaṇeyyaṃ, 'yet I would not say a lie'.
tvevahaṃ.example_1: Sabbā ca najjo paṭisotaṃ vajeyyuṃ, na tvevahaṃ rāja musā bhaṇeyyaṃ.
tvevahaṃ.translation_1: and all the rivers flow upstream, yet, O King, I could not lie.”
tvevahaṃ.example_2: Siluccayo meru samūlamuppate, na tvevahaṃ rāja musā bhaṇeyyan ’’ ti.
tvevahaṃ.translation_2: uproot Mount Meru from its base, yet, O King, I could not lie.”

anukampasī.meaning_2: shows compassion (to); has pity (for); sympathises (with); cares (for)
anukampasī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] 2nd singular present in the text (anukampasī = anukampasi), addressing the king. The root √kamp 1 means 'to shake, tremble'; with anu it takes the sense 'to tremble with sympathy for'.
anukampasī.example_1: 261. ‘‘ Anukampasī nāgakulaṃ janinda, mātā yathā suppiyaṃ ekaputtaṃ;
anukampasī.translation_1: “You show compassion to the Nāga clan, O King, just as a mother does to her only beloved son;

āṭāsakuntābhirudā.meaning_2: resounding with āṭā birds; echoing with the calls of āṭā birds
āṭāsakuntābhirudā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it qualifies rivers and lotus ponds (nominative plural -ā for -a stem). The commentary explains āṭāsakuntā as āṭāsaṅkhātehi sakuṇehi; kunta is probably a variant for kuna or kuṇa, so the compound may be āṭāsa + kuṇa + abhiruda. The compound is treated here as one word; abhiruda is from abhi + √rud.
āṭāsakuntābhirudā.example_1: 271. ‘‘ Najjo ca temā puthulomamacchā, āṭāsakuntābhirudā sutitthā;
āṭāsakuntābhirudā.translation_1: 271. ‘Rivers and lotus ponds filled with various fish, resounding with birds, and having beautiful landings,
āṭāsakuntābhirudā.translation_2: Āṭāsakuntābhirudā means resounding with birds known as āṭā.

āṭāsakuntābhirudāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Uncertain segmentation of a corrupt-looking form; possibly āṭā + sakuntā + abhirudāti or āṭāsakuntā + abhirudā + iti. No sentences supplied to confirm. Draft only.

āṭāsaṅkhātehi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental plural in the text, agreeing with sakuṇehi; the commentary explains āṭā as a kind of bird.
āṭāsaṅkhātehi.translation_1: Āṭāsakuntābhirudā means resounding with birds known as āṭā.

nīrajā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine forms are used here agreeing with bhūmi: nīrajā (nominative singular feminine), while nikkaddamā is a separate adjective. Sometimes confused with nīrāga (lust-free).
nīrajā.example_1: Antepure bhūmiyaṃ santharantu, nikkaddamā hehiti nīrajā ca.
nīrajā.translation_1: Let them spread them on the ground in the royal compound; it will be free of dust and mud.

nirajā.meaning_2: free of dust; dustless; free from impurity
nirajā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it agrees with bhūmi (nominative singular feminine, nirajā). Describes the ground of the royal compound as free from mud and dust.
nirajā.example_1: Nikkaddamāti evaṃ te antepure bhūmi nikkaddamā ca nirajā ca bhavissati.
nirajā.translation_1: Nikkaddamā means: In this way, the ground in your royal compound will be free of mud and free of dust.

svāssūti.meaning_2: so indeed his (own); and that indeed was his
svāssūti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi joined to the quotation marker iti, so probably su + assu + iti (so assu iti) rather than svā + assūti. Segmentation doubtful; no sentence given to confirm.

māgacchi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] mā + agacchi, aorist of gacchati (went) negated by the prohibitive mā. Some editions may read māgacchī with i as mā + agacchī.
māgacchi.translation_1: 303. A seer came there, over the ocean high,

virājayi.meaning_2: abandoned; freed oneself from; purified away
virājayi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular of the causative virājayati (vi + √raj + *aya). The PEU analysis 'Vi+ranja+ṇaya+ī' is doubtful; the object is kāmarāgaṃ. Another possible reading is that the form serves as an aorist of virājeti.
virājayi.translation_1: 314. Then, having gone forth, he abandoned sensual desire;
virājayi.example_2: Pabbajitvānāti taṃ itthiṃ manussāvāsaṃ netvā nivattitvā araññe isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā kāmarāgaṃ virājayi, virājetvā brahmalokūpago ahosīti.
virājayi.translation_2: 'Having gone forth' means having taken that woman back to human dwellings, he returned, went forth into the sage's going forth in the wilderness, and abandoned sensual desire, and having abandoned it, became one who entered the Brahma world.

brāhmalokūpago.meaning_2: gone to the Brahma world; reborn in the Brahma world
brāhmalokūpago.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text (brāhmalokūpago). Compound with upaga from upa + √gam; final -a of brāhmaloka elided before u-.
brāhmalokūpago.translation_1: Having abandoned sensual desire, he entered the Brahma world.”

vikandiṃsūti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text vikandiṃsu is aorist 3rd plural with -ti joined (vikandiṃsu + iti). The headword here is the present 3rd singular; the -ti is the quotative particle, not part of the word.

vissami.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Third person singular present in the text, with the vowel shortened to -i in the sandhi before 'thokaṃ' passage. Absolutive 'vissamitvā' also common in Jātaka prose.
vissami.translation_1: Finding no one, he rested a little.

tañcātiādimāha.meaning_2: that and (so on) — he said starting with 'tañ ca'; he said this and the rest
tañcātiādimāha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] A stock commentary phrase introducing a quotation: taṃ (that) + ca + āti ('so on') + ādim ('beginning') + āha ('he said'). Sandhi resolves as taṃ→tañ before c; sometimes analysed as taṃ + ca + ādi + āha with -m-āha joining. No sentences were supplied.

athetthātiādimāha.meaning_2: hereupon he said this and what follows; then he spoke starting with 'attha ettha'
athetthātiādimāha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of atha ettha iti ādim āha; quotation-mark -ti is enclosed, so the entry is kept as it stands for the sandhi. Possibly atha ettha iti ādim āha. ādim is accusative of ādi (beginning) used adverbially: 'starting with'.

māgacchīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of mā + āgacchati (prohibitive mā + present tense). Occurs as māgacchīti = mā āgacchati + iti. Probably a variant reading; the usual form is mā āgacchīti.

ajjekarattimattakameva.meaning_2: just this one night; only this single night remains
ajjekarattimattakameva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Looks like a sandhi of ajja + ekarattimattakaṃ + eva, with the final -ṃ of ekarattimattakaṃ elided before eva. Possible alternative analysis: ekarattimattakameva is itself a sandhi of ekarattimattakaṃ + eva, and ajja- is a separate word. The sense is 'only a single night (remains) from today'. The whole expression is unusual and may be a sandhi of several words; if treated as a single compound-like adverb, it could be pos ind, but here it is analysed as sandhi.
ajjekarattimattakameva.example_1: Chaṭṭhe pana divase sākhāya gahetvā ‘‘ rukkhadevate ajjekarattimattakameva sesaṃ, sace me rañño puttaṃ na desi, sve taṃ niṭṭhāpessāmī ’’ ti āha.
ajjekarattimattakameva.translation_1: But on the sixth day, grasping the branch, he said, “O tree-deva, only one night remains; if you do not grant a son to my king, I will finish you off tomorrow!”

ulloḷo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes the countryside (janapado) being in chaos if the princes renounce. Sometimes explained as ud + loḷa (agitation). The PEU entry gives 'commotion; noise'. Alternative analysis: ud + lul + a.
ulloḷo.example_1: Hatthipālassa soḷasavassakāle kāyasampattiṃ disvā rājā ca purohito ca ‘‘ kumārā mahallakā jātā, chattussāpanasamayo, tesaṃ kiṃ nu kho kātabban ’’ ti mantetvā ‘‘ ete abhisittakālato paṭṭhāya atissarā bhavissanti, tato tato pabbajitā āgamissanti, te disvā pabbajissanti, etesaṃ pabbajitakāle janapado ulloḷo bhavissati, vīmaṃsissāma tāva ne, pacchā abhisiñcissāmā ’’ ti cintetvā ubhopi isivesaṃ gahetvā bhikkhaṃ carantā hatthipālassa kumārassa nivesanadvāraṃ agamaṃsu.
ulloḷo.translation_1: When Hatthipāla was sixteen years old, seeing his bodily perfection, the king and the chaplain consulted together: “The young princes have become adults; it is the time for the umbrella ceremony, but what should be done with them? From the time they are anointed, they will become very masterful; renouncers will come, they will see them and also renounce the world; once they have done this, the countryside will be in chaos. We will test them for a while, and later we will perform the anointing.” Having thought thus, both of them took on the guise of ascetics and went, begging for alms, to the door of the house where the young prince Hatthipāla lived.

isivesaṃ.meaning_2: appearance of an ascetic; guise of a sage
isivesaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text. In the Jātaka commentary, the king and chaplain (and later the princess) take on the guise of ascetics.
isivesaṃ.example_1: Hatthipālassa soḷasavassakāle kāyasampattiṃ disvā rājā ca purohito ca ‘‘ kumārā mahallakā jātā, chattussāpanasamayo, tesaṃ kiṃ nu kho kātabban ’’ ti mantetvā ‘‘ ete abhisittakālato paṭṭhāya atissarā bhavissanti, tato tato pabbajitā āgamissanti, te disvā pabbajissanti, etesaṃ pabbajitakāle janapado ulloḷo bhavissati, vīmaṃsissāma tāva ne, pacchā abhisiñcissāmā ’’ ti cintetvā ubhopi isivesaṃ gahetvā bhikkhaṃ carantā hatthipālassa kumārassa nivesanadvāraṃ agamaṃsu.
isivesaṃ.translation_1: When Hatthipāla was sixteen years old, seeing his bodily perfection, the king and the chaplain consulted together: “The young princes have become adults; it is the time for the umbrella ceremony, but what should be done with them? From the time they are anointed, they will become very masterful; renouncers will come, they will see them and also renounce the world; once they have done this, the countryside will be in chaos. We will test them for a while, and later we will perform the anointing.” Having thought thus, both of them took on the guise of ascetics and went, begging for alms, to the door of the house where the young prince Hatthipāla lived.
isivesaṃ.translation_2: “Then why have you taken on the guise of sages?”

mokkhito.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] From mokkhati, the causative of √muc. In the text it is used in the sense of 'released (from)'; the commentary treats it as equivalent to mokkha. Past participle, nominative singular.
mokkhito.example_1: 346. ‘‘ Ayaṃ pure luddamakāsi kammaṃ, svāyaṃ gahīto na hi mokkhito me;
mokkhito.translation_1: 346. “In the past I performed a cruel action, this result of that has been seized by me, and I am not released;
mokkhito.example_2: Na hi mokkhito meti saṃsāravaṭṭe sati na hi mokkho ito akusalaphalato mama atthi.
mokkhito.translation_2: Na hi mokkhito me: With the cycle of samsara, there is no release for me from this fruition of unwholesome deeds.

orundhiyā.grammar: pr, caus of orundhati; or abs of orundhati
orundhiyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text orundhiyā is a gerund/absolutive meaning 'having restrained' or 'by restraining', from the causative stem orundh- (ava + rudh). The commentary glosses it with orundhitvā. The form may also be analysed as a causative absolutve orundhiyā; the headword is given as the present 3rd singular orundhati for convenience.
orundhiyā.example_1: Orundhiyā naṃ parirakkhissāmi, māyaṃ puna luddamakāsi kamman ’’ ti.
orundhiyā.translation_1: Restraining this, I will protect myself, so that I do not perform such cruel action again.”
orundhiyā.example_2: Orundhiyā naṃ parirakkhissāmīti idāni naṃ kāyavacīmanodvārāni pidahanto orundhitvā parirakkhissāmi.
orundhiyā.translation_2: Orundhiyā naṃ parirakkhissāmi: Now I will protect myself by blocking these gates of body, speech, and mind.

orundhitvā.meaning_2: having blocked; having closed off; having obstructed
orundhitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -itvā of orundhati (o + √rudh); alternative form of orundhiya. Used in the text of closing the doors of body, speech and mind.
orundhitvā.example_1: Orundhiyā naṃ parirakkhissāmīti idāni naṃ kāyavacīmanodvārāni pidahanto orundhitvā parirakkhissāmi.
orundhitvā.translation_1: Orundhiyā naṃ parirakkhissāmi: Now I will protect myself by blocking these gates of body, speech, and mind.

ketakapupphanettaṃ.meaning_2: with eyes like a ketaka flower
ketakapupphanettaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular modifying kumāriṃ; a poetic description of the maiden's eyes.
ketakapupphanettaṃ.example_1: 349. ‘‘ Passāmi vohaṃ daharaṃ kumāriṃ, mattūpamaṃ ketakapupphanettaṃ;
ketakapupphanettaṃ.translation_1: 349. “I see a young maiden, like one intoxicated, with eyes like the ketaka flower;

ketakapupphanettanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi compound. In the text it is ketakapupphanettanti = ketakapupphanetta + iti, nominative singular. Appears in the Ketakapuppha Jātaka.

ketakapupphapattaṃ.meaning_2: petal of a ketaka flower; leaf of the screw-pine flower
ketakapupphapattaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text, in a gloss explaining ketakapupphanetta ('eyes like ketaka petals').
ketakapupphapattaṃ.translation_1: Ketakapupphanettaṃ means having eyes as broad and long as the petal of a ketaka flower.

uttārayi.meaning_2: causes to cross over; brings across; lifts out (of); saves (from)
uttārayi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular uttārayi in the text; the gloss Udatārīti explains the aorist as uttārayi, 'brought across', i.e. out of the mud of sensual pleasures.
uttārayi.translation_1: Udatārīti means you lifted me up out of the mud of sensual pleasures.

uddhaṭāsītipi.meaning_2: removed; taken out; pulled up; lifted
uddhaṭāsītipi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Here the form is uddhaṭā, nominative singular of uddhaṭa, with the ends of the words -asīti and -api joined by sandhi.

katasudhāparikammo.meaning_2: plastered; whitewashed; with the plastering done
katasudhāparikammo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes the walkway (caṅkama). The compound is kata + sudhā + parikamma, literally "done plaster-work"; the PEU entry agrees. Nominative singular in the text.
katasudhāparikammo.example_1: Ekekissā paṇṇasālāya dvāre ekeko caṅkamo rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānaparicchinno katasudhāparikammo ālambanaphalako, tesu tesu ṭhānesu nānāvaṇṇasurabhikusumasañchannā pupphagacchā, ekekassa caṅkamassa koṭiyaṃ ekeko udakabharito kūpo, tassa santike ekeko phalarukkho, so ekova sabbaphalāni phalati.
katasudhāparikammo.translation_1: At the door of each leaf-hut was a walkway, partitioned for night and day, neatly whitewashed, with a bench for resting; in those various places were flowering shrubs covered with fragrant flowers of many colors; at the end of each walkway was a well full of water, and near it a fruit-tree, which bore all kinds of fruits.

pathavicālakadhammaguttatthero.meaning_2: Elder Dhammagutta, who shook the earth; the earth-shaking Elder Dhammagutta
pathavicālakadhammaguttatthero.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text. An epithet of the Elder Dhammagutta. pathavī is sandhied to pathavi before the compound member cālaka.
pathavicālakadhammaguttatthero.example_1: Imasmiṃ tambapaṇṇidīpe pathavicālakadhammaguttatthero, kaṭakandhakāravāsī phussadevatthero, uparimaṇḍalavāsī mahāsaṅgharakkhitatthero, malayamahādevatthero, abhayagirivāsī mahādevatthero, gāmantapabbhāravāsī mahāsivatthero, kāḷavallimaṇḍapavāsī mahānāgatthero kuddālasamāgame mūgapakkhasamāgame cūḷasutasomasamāgame ayogharapaṇḍitasamāgame hatthipālasamāgame ca sabbapacchā nikkhantapurisā ahesuṃ.
pathavicālakadhammaguttatthero.translation_1: In this island of Ceylon, those who went forth were the earth-shaking Elder Dhammagutta, the Elder Phussadeva, a resident of Kaṭakandhakāra, the Elder Mahāsaṁgharakkhita, a resident of Uparimaṇḍala, the Elder Malimahādeva, the Elder Mahādeva, a resident of Abhayagiri, the Elder Mahāsīva, a resident of Gāmantapabbhāra, the Elder Mahānāga, a resident of Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa; and in the company of Kuddāla, the company of Mūgapakkha, the company of Cūlasutasoma, the company of the wise Ayoghara, and the company of Hatthipāla were the last of those who went forth.

muruṃ.meaning_2: munching; crunching; with a munching sound
muruṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Reduplicated onomatopoeic adverb describing the sound of chewing (muruṃ muruṃ karontī). Not the noun mura (asura) or muraja (drum).
muruṃ.example_1: Itarāpi dārakaṃ mūlakandaṃ viya muruṃ muruṃ karontī khāditvā deviyā hatthavikārādīhi bheravaṃ pakāsetvā tajjetvā pakkāmi.
muruṃ.translation_1: The other one, chewing the child as if it were a radish or a bulb with a munching sound, devoured him; then, having displayed a terrifying appearance with her limbs and so forth before the queen, she threatened her and departed.

nijjhapanaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Glossed in the text by khamāpenti pasādenti, i.e. 'they appease or make serene, by means of offerings'. Also sometimes explained as 'patience; trusting'. Nominative/accusative singular neuter in the text.
nijjhapanaṃ.example_1: 375. ‘‘ Yakkhe pisāce athavāpi pete, kupitepi te nijjhapanaṃ karonti;
nijjhapanaṃ.translation_1: 375. “Ghosts, sprites, or the departed—even when angry, they can be appeased by acts of men;
nijjhapanaṃ.example_2: Na maccuno nijjhapanaṃ karonti, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.
nijjhapanaṃ.translation_2: But with death no appeasing can there be; so I’m resolved—a holy life for me.

saṃcuṇṇiyamāno.meaning_2: being crushed to powder; being ground down; being pulverized
saṃcuṇṇiyamāno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Passive present participle, nominative singular masculine agreeing with valāhako (cloud). Part of the simile likening the cloud crushed by the wind to the continuous disintegration of saṅkhārā.
saṃcuṇṇiyamāno.example_1: Yathā pana so valāhako vātavegena saṃcuṇṇiyamāno ‘‘ ahaṃ asukaṭṭhāne nāma uṭṭhito puna nivattitvā tattheva gantvā pakatibhāvena ṭhassāmī ’’ ti na labhati, yaṃ disaṃ gataṃ, taṃ gatameva, yaṃ antarahitaṃ, taṃ antarahitameva hoti, tathā sopi kalalādibhāvena gacchamāno gacchateva, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ koṭṭhāse saṅkhārā purimānaṃ purimānaṃ paccayā hutvā pacchato anivattitvā tattha tattheva bhijjanti, jarākāle saṅkhārā ‘‘ amhehi esa pubbe yuvā thāmasampanno kato, puna naṃ nivattitvā tattheva karissāmā ’’ ti na labhanti, tattha tattheva antaradhāyantīti dasseti.
saṃcuṇṇiyamāno.translation_1: But just as that cloud, being ground down by the force of the wind, does not have the ability to say, “Having risen in such a place, I shall return to that very place and remain in my natural state,” as whatever direction it has gone, it has gone, and what has disappeared has disappeared, so too, as one proceeds through the embryo state and so on, one just proceeds; in each stage, the volitional formations, having been conditions for the preceding ones, disintegrate right there without turning back afterwards; at the time of aging, the volitional formations do not have the ability to say, “We made this youth strong before, we shall return and do the same for him again,” but rather they disappear right there—this is what is shown.

jayituṃ.meaning_2: to conquer; to defeat; to overcome
jayituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -tuṃ from √ji. In the sentence it depends on ussahanti: 'are not able to conquer'. jayituṃ = jetuṃ.
jayituṃ.example_1: Na maccunoti tepi rājāno mahāsenassa maccuno senaṃ jayituṃ na ussahanti, na byādhijarāmaraṇāni maddituṃ sakkonti.
jayituṃ.translation_1: “Not from death” means even those kings are not able to conquer the army of the great death, nor are they able to trample upon aging, illness, and death.

upahanituṃ.meaning_2: to harm; to injure; to strike (at)
upahanituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive of upahanati (upa + √han). The text has upahanituṃ with the phonetic change a > i before the infinitive suffix -tuṃ; the same form also appears as upahanitvā. Commentarial gloss here: 'to harm (death) by breathing'.
upahanituṃ.example_1: Na maccunoti maccuṃ pana tepi assāsena upahanituṃ vā āvisituṃ vā na sakkonti.
upahanituṃ.translation_1: “Not from death” means they are not able to harm or enter into death with their breath.

āvisituṃ.meaning_2: to enter; to possess; to be present (in)
āvisituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -tuṃ. In the text it is coordinated with upahanituṃ ('to harm') and depends on na sakkonti ('they are not able').
āvisituṃ.example_1: Na maccunoti maccuṃ pana tepi assāsena upahanituṃ vā āvisituṃ vā na sakkonti.
āvisituṃ.translation_1: “Not from death” means they are not able to harm or enter into death with their breath.

aparādhaketi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is aparādhaketi = aparādhako + iti, so the -o has been elided before the quotation particle. The suffix -ka is added to aparādha, which comes from √rādh with the prefix apa.

daṇḍayituṃ.meaning_2: to punish; to beat; to inflict punishment (on)
daṇḍayituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -tuṃ from the denominative verb daṇḍayati. Here daṇḍayituṃ maccuṃ means 'to punish death'. The infinitive form is given as the headword per DPD convention.
daṇḍayituṃ.example_1: Na maccunoti tepi maccuṃ daṇḍayituṃ na sakkonti.
daṇḍayituṃ.translation_1: “Not from death” means even they are not able to punish death.

ayadāmaṃ.meaning_2: iron rope; iron chain; iron fetters
ayadāmaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text; the Bodhisatta cuts his iron fetters. The first element is aya (iron), with stem-form -a before dāma (rope).
ayadāmaṃ.example_1: Evaṃ mahāsatto catuvīsatiyā gāthāhi pitu dhammaṃ desetvā ‘‘ mahārāja, tumhākaṃ rajjaṃ tumhākameva hotu, na mayhaṃ iminā attho, tumhehi pana saddhiṃ kathentameva maṃ byādhijarāmaraṇāni upagacchanti, tiṭṭhatha, tumhe ’’ ti vatvā ayadāmaṃ chinditvā mattahatthī viya kañcanapañjaraṃ chinditvā sīhapotako viya kāme pahāya mātāpitaro vanditvā nikkhami.
ayadāmaṃ.translation_1: Thus, the Great Being, having given a discourse on the Dhamma to his father in twenty-four stanzas, said, “Great King, let your kingdom be yours, I have no need of it; but while I am speaking with you, disease, aging, and death are approaching me. Stay where you are,” and saying this, he cut his bonds and, like a mad elephant breaking a golden cage, he broke through his sensual desires, venerated his parents, and departed.

bhallā.meaning_2: name of a king; Bhalla; bear
bhallā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of one of the five sons of king Pañcāla in the Culla-haṃsa Jātaka (or Pañcāla Jātaka); here nominative plural bhallā in a list of names.
bhallā.translation_1: Haṃsa, Sattigumba, Bhalla, Somanassa, and Campeyyaka.

saṅgitā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the verse, used of the Jātakas as 'saṅgitā' (nominative plural); the text means 'fourteen Jātakas are compiled/collected'.
saṅgitā.translation_1: In the twenties, there are fourteen Jātakas compiled.

kūṭaḍḍaṃ.meaning_2: crooked judgment; false lawsuit; unjust decision
kūṭaḍḍaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of kūṭa (crooked; false) and aḍḍa (lawsuit; judgment). Accusative singular in the text, object of katvā and karitvā; refers to giving corrupt verdicts for bribes.
kūṭaḍḍaṃ.example_1: Atha naṃ divā lañjaṃ gahetvā kūṭaḍḍaṃ katvā upaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ rājā ‘‘ tumhe uposathikā ’’ ti amacce pucchanto ‘‘ tvampi ācariya uposathiko ’’ ti pucchi.
kūṭaḍḍaṃ.translation_1: Then, when he came to court after taking bribes and making crooked judgments during the day, the king asked him, “Are you observers of the Uposatha?”—inquired of his ministers, and then asked, “Teacher, are you too observing the Uposatha?”
kūṭaḍḍaṃ.example_2: Ahañhi tumhehi vinicchaye ṭhapito kūṭaḍḍaṃ karitvā lañjaṃ gahetvā parapiṭṭhimaṃsiko hutvā tassa divā katassa kammassa nissandena idaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavāmī ’’ ti vatvā gāthādvayamāha –
kūṭaḍḍaṃ.translation_2: For I, having been established by you at the judgment seat, having acted deceitfully, taking bribes, and becoming a backbiter, I experience this suffering by day as a result of that kamma I committed.” Having said this, he uttered two verses:

vikkhāletuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -tuṃ; in the text it depends on ārabhi, 'began to rinse'. The same verb is seen as vikkhāletvā and vikkhāletabba elsewhere.
vikkhāletuṃ.example_1: Punekadivasaṃ tasmiṃ vinicchaye nisinne aññatarā sīlavatī itthī aḍḍaṃ karontī gharaṃ gantuṃ alabhamānā ‘‘ uposathakammaṃ nātikkamissāmī ’’ ti upakaṭṭhe kāle mukhaṃ vikkhāletuṃ ārabhi.
vikkhāletuṃ.translation_1: Again one day, as he was sitting at the judgment seat, a certain virtuous woman was involved in a law-suit. Being unable to go home, she thought, “I will not transgress the Uposatha observance.” As the time for eating was near, she began to rinse her mouth.

kūṭaḍḍakaraṇanissandena.meaning_2: by the result of crooked litigation; through the consequence of fraudulent judging
kūṭaḍḍakaraṇanissandena.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular of kūṭaḍḍakaraṇanissanda, sandhi of kūṭaḍḍakaraṇa (nt) + nissanda (masc) in the instrumental. 'Crooked case/judgment' is kūṭa + aḍḍakaraṇa.
kūṭaḍḍakaraṇanissandena.example_1: Iti so uposathikāya itthiyā ambaphaladānassa nissandena tiyojanikaṃ ambavanaṃ paṭilabhati, lañjaṃ gahetvā kūṭaḍḍakaraṇanissandena pana piṭṭhimaṃsaṃ uppāṭetvā khādati, upaḍḍhūposathassa nissandena rattiṃ sampattiṃ anubhoti, soḷasasahassanāṭakitthīhi parivuto paricāresi.
kūṭaḍḍakaraṇanissandena.translation_1: Thus, by the result of giving a mango fruit to a woman observing the Uposatha, he acquired a three-league mango-tree grove. But by the result of taking bribes and making crooked judgments, he pulls out and eats his own back-flesh. By the result of observing half the Uposatha, he experiences prosperity at night, accompanied by sixteen thousand divine dancing girls, and enjoyed himself.

agyāyatanamāharinti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of agyāyatanaṃ āharati; with -ti quoted. Text form contains āharinti; possible sandhi with iti.

vikantetvātipi.meaning_2: having cut off; having sliced off
vikantetvātipi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form in the text is vikantetvā (absolutive of vikantati) with -iti appended; the sandhi ending is excluded from the headword, which is given as the present 3rd singular vikantati.

rūpapaṭṭapalimaṭṭhīvāti.meaning_2: like a rubbing on a painted picture; as if smudged on a picture
rūpapaṭṭapalimaṭṭhīvāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Likely rūpapaṭṭa-palimaṭṭha + iva + iti, a simile: 'like a smudge on a painted boards.' Cf. the stock phrase rūpapaṭṭa palimaṭṭha-iva. Uncertain; no sentence context supplied.

ambuni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text. The compound ambuja ("water-born") supports ambu = water.
ambuni.example_1: 15. ‘‘ Yaṃ kiñci ubhato tīre, phalaṃ patati ambuni;
ambuni.translation_1: 15. Whatever fruit falls into my waters from both banks,
ambuni.example_2: Sotassāti yaṃ ubhato tīre jātarukkhehi phalaṃ mama ambuni patati, sabbaṃ taṃ mama sotasseva vasānugaṃ hoti.
ambuni.translation_2: Of the stream (sotassā) means: whatever fruit falls into my waters from the trees growing on both banks, all of that becomes subject to my stream.

mabhisaṅgaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Probably ma ("me", sandhi of maṃ or me, or the negative particle) + abhisaṅga; accusative singular in the verse. Could also be analysed as sandhi or a mis-splitting.
mabhisaṅgaṃ.translation_1: do not delight in attachment, Sire; reject it.

āceyyamāno.meaning_2: being heaped up; accumulating; growing; flourishing
āceyyamāno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Text has āceyyamāno, a bhāva-variant of the passive present participle of caus. āciyati / ācikhati (gloss: āciyanto vaḍḍhanto). Nominative singular; vocative in the address to the king.
āceyyamāno.translation_1: O King, while you are young and flourishing, you desire death.
āceyyamāno.example_2: Āceyyamānoti maṃsalohitehi āciyanto vaḍḍhanto, taruṇova hutvāti attho.
āceyyamāno.translation_2: While flourishing (āceyyamāno) means: accumulating flesh and blood, growing, being young; this is the meaning.

āceyyamānoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text with the quotation particle -ti: āceyyamānāti. Passive present participle in the nominative singular.

cīyatī.meaning_2: accumulates; is collected; is heaped up; increases
cīyatī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Passive sense of √ci (gather); 3rd singular present. In the verse, pāpaṃ cīyati = evil accumulates.
cīyatī.example_1: Na cīyatī tassa narassa pāpaṃ, sace na ceteti vadhāya tassa.
cīyatī.translation_1: evil does not accumulate for that person if he does not intend killing for another.

isipūgasamaññāte.meaning_2: known well by the assembly of sages; approved by the sages; renowned by the assembly of sages
isipūgasamaññāte.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Text form is the vocative singular. The commentary glosses it as isigaṇena suṭṭhu aññāte isīnaṃ sammate, i.e. saṃ + ñāta rather than sam + aññāta. The PEU entry gives 'pūga' as the middle member, but the gloss uses 'gaṇa'; pūga can also mean assembly, multitude.
isipūgasamaññāte.translation_1: 20. O devī, renowned by the assembly of sages, when worldly things are known thus and exist,
isipūgasamaññāte.translation_2: Renowned by the assembly of sages (isipūgasamaññāte) means: thoroughly known by the assembly of sages, approved by the sages.

isipūgasamaññāteti.meaning_2: known as a multitude of sages; called the community of hermits, iti
isipūgasamaññāteti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of isipūgasamaññāta and the quotation particle iti; the -ti is iti, not a verb ending. The compound is isi + pūga + samaññāta.

pabodhare.meaning_2: awaken; arouse; make known; announce themselves
pabodhare.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In padapatha: pa + bodhare, but treated as a single verb; 3rd plural, glossed by pabodhenti ñāpenti. Alternative analysis: pabodhare could be 3rd singular āttaṁ pabodhati? No, it is plural kokilā. Not a sandhi of pa + bodhare, since bodhare is not a separate word; the form is pabodhati with -are ending.
pabodhare.translation_1: Resounding with the calls of flocks of swans, and here cuckoos announce themselves singing.
pabodhare.example_2: Kokilettha pabodhareti ettha ambavane kokilā vassantiyo attānaṃ pabodhenti ñāpenti.
pabodhare.translation_2: Here cuckoos announce themselves (kokilettha pabodhare) means: here in the mango-tree grove, cuckoos singing make themselves known, announce themselves.

nayantī.meaning_2: leads; guides; brings; conducts; interprets; explains
nayantī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is plural nayantī (3rd plural) glossed as nenti, and the causative sense 'leads; brings; interprets' fits all three sentences. Could also be analysed as present participle nayanta, but the gloss nenti points to a finite verb.
nayantī.translation_1: Nayantī means ‘they lead to their own will’.
nayantī.example_2: Attānanti taṃ āliṅgitvā ambavanaṃ nayantī attānañca te dadāmi tañca ambaṃ.
nayantī.translation_2: Myself (attānaṃ) means: embracing him and leading him to the mango-tree grove, ‘I give you myself and that mango.’

santisaṅkhātaṃ.meaning_2: reckoned as peace; designated as peace; called peace
santisaṅkhātaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular agreeing with sīlaṃ. Compounds of santi (peace) with saṅkhāta (reckoned, designated).
santisaṅkhātaṃ.translation_1: Peace and the Dhamma (santiñca dhammañcā) means: both virtue, which is reckoned as peace by the calming of immorality, and the Dhamma of good conduct.

pabodhareti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Text form pabodhareti looks corrupt; possibly a variant spelling of pabodheti (causative). Third person singular present.

vaṇṇayitvā.meaning_2: having described; having praised; having spoken in praise (of); having extolled
vaṇṇayitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -tvā of the causative vaṇṇayati (√vaṇṇ, 'praise'). Senses vary by context: 'having described' in the first sentence, 'having praised/spoken in praise of' in the second; PEU gives only 'to speak well of'.
vaṇṇayitvā.example_1: Vaṇṇayitvā ca pana tāpasaṃ tattha otāretvā ‘‘ imasmiṃ ambavane ambāni khādanto attano taṇhaṃ pūrehī ’’ ti vatvā pakkāmi.
vaṇṇayitvā.translation_1: And indeed, having praised it, she set down the ascetic there and, saying, “In this mango-tree grove, eating mangoes, satisfy your craving for yourself,” she went away.
vaṇṇayitvā.example_2: Evaṃ mahāsattena attano dāne vaṇṇite tamevatthaṃ parivattetvā ‘‘ mahārāja vessantara, sudinnaṃ nāma te dānan ’’ ti maddīpi tatheva dānaṃ vaṇṇayitvā anumodamānā nisīdi.
vaṇṇayitvā.translation_2: When the Great Being had described his gifts, and Maddī, repeating that matter, rejoicing in the gift, said, “Great King Vessantara, your gift is indeed well given,” she sat down.

aṅgadī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Possessive suffix -ī added to aṅgada (armlet). Describes a person ornamented with armbands; glossed in the commentary as dibbaṅgadasamannāgato. Nominative singular used adjectivally in the verse.
aṅgadī.translation_1: 28. ‘‘ Wearing garlands, a diadem, armlets, adorned with arm-bands, and anointed with sandalwood;
aṅgadī.translation_2: Adorned with arm-bands (aṅgadī) means endowed with divine armlets.

kāyūrīti.meaning_2: wearing an armlet; ornamented with armbands
kāyūrīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi adjective meaning 'one who has an armlet'. The text form kāyūrīti is kāyūrī + iti; the entry is for the main word. Analyse kāyūra as kāya + ūra, but the compound is lexicalised.

aṅgadīti.meaning_2: wearing armlets; wearing an arm bracelet
aṅgadīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The -ti is the quotative particle (iti), so the word itself is aṅgadī; the text has no sentence here, so the case in the text is unknown. Bahubbīhi from aṅgada (armlet) + -ī.

tiṭṭhasī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] 2nd person singular present of tiṭṭhati; the text's tiṭṭhasī is the same form with -ī sandhi before ti. Used in direct questions meaning 'why do you stand?'
tiṭṭhasī.translation_1: “Then why do you stand facing the sun?”
tiṭṭhasī.example_2: Netādisanti ‘‘ etādisaṃ brāhmaṇassa susīlino mukhaṃ na hoti, makkaṭo eso ’’ ti vatvā bodhisatto ekaṃ ummukaṃ gahetvā ‘‘ kiṃ ettha tiṭṭhasī ’’ ti khipitvā taṃ palāpesi.
tiṭṭhasī.translation_2: Netādisaṃ—having said, “A good, virtuous brahmin does not have such a face; this is a monkey,” the Bodhisatta took a firebrand and, crying, “Why are you standing here?” threw it at him and drove him away.

dārukaṭallakova.meaning_2: like a wooden puppet; as if a wooden doll
dārukaṭallakova.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of dārukaṭallakaṃ (nominative singular neuter) + iva, with the iva shortened to -va. In the text it modifies the subject so ('he dances like a wooden puppet'). The compound is dāru + kaṭallaka, 'wooden puppet/doll'.
dārukaṭallakova.example_1: So naccatī dārukaṭallakova, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.
dārukaṭallakova.translation_1: one dances like a wooden puppet; buy this jar full of that liquor!

kalahāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text kalahāni is nominative/accusative plural of the neuter noun kalaha. The verse lists quarrels alongside slander and other vices. Some analyses treat it as an adjective agreeing with the following items.
kalahāni.example_1: 44. ‘‘ Mānātimānā kalahāni pesuṇī, dubbaṇṇinī naggayinī palāyinī;
kalahāni.translation_1: 44. “It makes people conceited, causes quarrels and slander, ugliness, nakedness, and fleeing;

pesuṇī.meaning_2: slandering; backbiting; one who speaks divisive speech
pesuṇī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine form used as a noun in the text (nominative singular in a list of vices); the PEU treats it as an adjective meaning one who causes division between people.
pesuṇī.example_1: 44. ‘‘ Mānātimānā kalahāni pesuṇī, dubbaṇṇinī naggayinī palāyinī;
pesuṇī.translation_1: 44. “It makes people conceited, causes quarrels and slander, ugliness, nakedness, and fleeing;

dubbaṇṇinī.meaning_2: ugly woman; woman of bad complexion
dubbaṇṇinī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine form of dubbaṇṇī; nominative singular in the verse. Could also be read as an adjective agreeing with an implied feminine subject. The PEU entry dubbaṇṇiya is a related but different formation.
dubbaṇṇinī.example_1: 44. ‘‘ Mānātimānā kalahāni pesuṇī, dubbaṇṇinī naggayinī palāyinī;
dubbaṇṇinī.translation_1: 44. “It makes people conceited, causes quarrels and slander, ugliness, nakedness, and fleeing;

naggayinī.meaning_2: naked woman; (or) state of being naked
naggayinī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text reads naggayinī, probably a feminine adjective agreeing with the implied subject (a woman), or a noun 'nakedness'. The reading naggayinī may be a variant of naggī or naggā; the compound naggayinī is otherwise unattested.
naggayinī.example_1: 44. ‘‘ Mānātimānā kalahāni pesuṇī, dubbaṇṇinī naggayinī palāyinī;
naggayinī.translation_1: 44. “It makes people conceited, causes quarrels and slander, ugliness, nakedness, and fleeing;

niketo.meaning_2: home; dwelling; place of residence; haunt
niketo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the first sentence nominative singular in apposition to gatī; glossed in the commentary as nivāso.
niketo.example_1: Corāna dhuttāna gatī niketo, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.
niketo.translation_1: it is the destination and the home of thieves and scoundrels; buy this jar full of that liquor!

ucchedanī.meaning_2: destroying; wasting; bringing about the destruction (of); squandering
ucchedanī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it agrees with vittagataṃ (n.) as an adjective in the nominative singular; the PEU treats it as a noun meaning a squanderer of wealth. Possibly a feminine agent noun from ucchedana.
ucchedanī.example_1: Ucchedanī vittagataṃ kulānaṃ, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.
ucchedanī.translation_1: it brings about the destruction of families’ possessions; buy this jar full of that liquor!

dārukaṭallako.meaning_2: wooden automaton; wooden puppet; mechanical figure made of wood
dārukaṭallako.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is nominative singular and is followed by the emphatic -vā (vā); the gloss explains it as dārumayayantarūpaka. The second member, kaṭallaka, is rare; some editions read kaṭallaka as 'puppet, automaton'.

niketoti.meaning_2: home; dwelling; abode; place of residence
niketoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form in the text is niketoti = niketo + iti, so the headword is niketa. See also niketana.

andhakaveṇḍaputtāti.meaning_2: sons of Andhakaveṇḍa; the ten brothers of Pāsudeva
andhakaveṇḍaputtāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Plural in the text, with -ti (iti) attached; the entry is for the compound without it. A name for a group of ten brothers.

murumurāyantī.meaning_2: munching; crunching; making a crunching sound (while eating)
murumurāyantī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine present participle, nominative singular, agreeing with sā (the ogress). Onomatopoeic word; not from a listed root.
murumurāyantī.example_1: Sā tadā okāsaṃ labhitvā tassā passantiyāva taṃ allamaṃsapesivaṇṇaṃ kumārakaṃ gahetvā murumurāyantī khāditvā pakkāmi.
murumurāyantī.translation_1: She, at that time finding an opportunity, while the queen was watching, seized that child who looked like a piece of raw flesh, and champing it up, ate it and departed.

kovāsi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of ko (who?) + asi (you are). Part of the question kutosi kovāsi, 'from where have you come? who are you?'.
kovāsi.example_1: Kutosi kovāsi tadiṅgha brūhi, ācikkha jātiṃ vidito yathāsī ’’ ti.
kovāsi.translation_1: From where have you come? Who are you? Come now, speak! Tell me your birth and how you are known.”

vihiṃsayamāno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle, nominative singular masculine of the causative vihiṃsayati (= vihiṃsati). In the text it glosses sassamāno.
vihiṃsayamāno.translation_1: Thinking to harass (sassamāno) means intending to cause harm.

ghasitukāmo.meaning_2: wanting to eat; desirous of consuming
ghasitukāmo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of the infinitive ghasituṃ (from √ghas, eat) and kāma. Nominative singular in the text, agreeing with the subject.
ghasitukāmo.translation_1: Desirous of eating (jighaññan) means wanting to consume.

arinasattunti.meaning_2: the prince named Arinasattu; see Alīnasattu
arinasattunti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a prince, apparently a variant reading of Alīnasattu. The -ti at the end of the text form is the quotative particle, not part of the word.

abhyāse.meaning_2: presence; vicinity; nearness; close proximity; repeated practice; training
abhyāse.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the text, glossed by santike. Commentarial Sanskrit-like spelling of abbhāsa; also sometimes analysed as abhi + as + ṇa (repeated practice).
abhyāse.translation_1: Presence (ñatte) means near, in the vicinity—this is the meaning.

nārādhayī.meaning_2: did not please; did not satisfy; failed to please
nārādhayī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of na + ārādhayī (aorist 3rd singular of ārādheti, causative of √rādh). The sandhi form is kept as headword; the underlying verb is ārādheti. Verse context: 'nārādhayī taṃ' = 'did not please him'.
nārādhayī.example_1: 73. ‘‘ Kiṃ kamma krubbaṃ tava deva pāva, nārādhayī taṃ tadicchāmi sotuṃ;
nārādhayī.translation_1: 73. “What deed was I performing (krubbaṃ) at your feet, O Lord, that I did not please you? I wish to hear it;

udassaye.meaning_2: sets up; raises up; establishes; places (on)
udassaye.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] 2nd singular present in both sentences (udassaye = udassayasi, cf. PEU U+ā+sī+si). Commentary glosses it with ussāpesi and patiṭṭhāpesi.
udassaye.example_1: Yamajja rajjamhi udassaye tuvaṃ, rajjampi niccheyyaṃ, tayā vināhan ’’ ti.
udassaye.translation_1: That reason why you set me on the throne today; for I do not desire even the kingdom without you.”
udassaye.example_2: Yamajjāti yena anārādhakammena ajja maṃ rajjamhi tvaṃ udassaye ussāpesi patiṭṭhāpesi, taṃ me ācikkha, ahañhi tayā vinā rajjampi na icchāmīti attho.
udassaye.translation_2: That for which today (yamajja) means: “Tell me that unpleasing deed because of which you set me on, raised me up, and established me on the throne today; for I certainly do not desire even the kingdom without you”—this is the meaning.

tuviyaṃ.meaning_2: like you; similar to you; resembling you
tuviyaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text tuviyaṃ sarāmi: 'I remember (anything) of yours (like) this'. Possibly a sandhi of tava + iyaṃ (Sanskrit tvat + īdṛś?), or an emphatic form of tava. The PEU entry relates it to tumha + īya 'yours'; the sense in the verse fits 'like you; of yours'.
tuviyaṃ.example_1: 74. ‘‘ Na kammunā vā vacasāva tāta, aparādhitohaṃ tuviyaṃ sarāmi;
tuviyaṃ.translation_1: 74. “Dear son, I do not recall a single unkind act or word of yours;

tuviyanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The companion gives tuviya = tava + iya, 'yours'. In the text it is tuviyan-ti, with the quotative -ti; I take the headword as tuvīya, a pronominal adjective meaning 'yours'. If the -nt- belongs to the word itself (tuviyant-), the reading would be a present participle instead.

bhidā.meaning_2: having broken; having pierced; having split
bhidā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Commentary glosses it with bhitvā, an absolutive in -ā (cf. PEU bhidā < bhida + tvā). It is the reading of the verse and its gloss, not a feminine noun 'breaking'. Alternative analysis: fem abstract noun bhidā (breaking; piercing) from √bhid, which would fit the syntax less well.
bhidā.example_1: Kammāsapādo taṃ yadā pacitvā, pasayha khāde bhidā rukkhasūle ’’ ti.
bhidā.translation_1: When the ogre, having vanquished you, would roast and eat you on a spit of wood.”
bhidā.example_2: Bhidā rukkhasūleti tikhiṇarukkhasūle bhitvā pacitvā pasayha balakkārena khādeyyāti.
bhidā.translation_2: “On a spit of wood (bhidā rukkhasūle) means having pierced you on a sharp wooden spit, having cooked you, and having vanquished you, he would eat you by force.”

pañjalīkoti.meaning_2: with raised joined palms; with palms in añjali (and)
pañjalīkoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the adjective pañjalīka (with cupped hands raised in greeting) and the quotation particle iti, frequent at the end of a quoted exclamation. Occurs in Jātaka prose.

ānayitvā.meaning_2: having brought; having brought back; having fetched
ānayitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -itvā of āneti (causative of √nī with ā-). In the sentence it governs naṃ and is followed by adaṃsu.
ānayitvā.example_1: Atha naṃ mātupaṭṭhānakammassa phalena devatā sotthinā ānayitvā mātu adaṃsu.
ānayitvā.translation_1: Then, by the fruit of his deed of serving his mother, the devas brought him back safely and gave him to his mother.

paṭiāgaccha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Imperative 2nd singular in the text, with the ending -hi. The prefix paṭi- is written with i before the vowel ā.
paṭiāgaccha.example_1: Anuññātoti porisādena ‘‘ gacchā ’’ ti anuññāto devatānaṃ ānubhāvena sotthi paṭiāgaccha puttāti vadati.
paṭiāgaccha.translation_1: Given permission (anuññāto) means he says: “Dear son, return safely, having been allowed by the ogre with the words, ‘Go,’ and by the power of the devas.”

saṅkhātajātīmaraṇohamasmi.meaning_2: I am one who has understood birth and death; I am one by whom birth and death are understood
saṅkhātajātīmaraṇohamasmi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of saṅkhātajātīmaraṇa (adj, comp) + ahaṃ + asmi; first person singular in the text, first word of the verse.
saṅkhātajātīmaraṇohamasmi.example_1: Saṅkhātajātīmaraṇohamasmi, yatheva me idha tathā parattha.
saṅkhātajātīmaraṇohamasmi.translation_1: I am one who has understood birth and death; just as it is for me here, so it is in the next life.

saṅkhātajātīmaraṇohamasmīti.meaning_2: I am one for whom birth and death are reckoned; I am he whose birth and death are accounted; I am the one who has reckoned birth and death
saṅkhātajātīmaraṇohamasmīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of saṅkhāta + jātimaraṇa + ahaṃ asmi + iti, with jātimaraṇa in compound. The whole is a quoted clause; the quotation mark -ti is dropped only if the word were the main word, but here the whole string is a sandhi and kept as it stands.

santīpayitvā.meaning_2: having kindled; having set fire to; having persuaded; having appeased
santīpayitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive. The commentary glosses it as kindling (ādīpayitvā). Alternative analysis: saṃ + tīpa + √īr? or a denominative from tīpa? Doubtful.
santīpayitvā.example_1: Santīpayitvā paṭivedayittha, ādīpito dāni mahāyamaggī ’’ ti.
santīpayitvā.translation_1: having kindled it well, reported: ‘Now this great fire has been kindled.’ ”

pasayhakāri.meaning_2: acting by force; doing high-handedly; using violence
pasayhakāri.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Vocative singular in the verse. The same person is called pasayhakāri and the PEU gives pasayhakārī; sandhi form of pasayhakārī, adjective in -in agreeing with the addressee.
pasayhakāri.example_1: 91. ‘‘ Khādajja maṃ dāni pasayhakāri, kiṃ maṃ muhuṃ pekkhasi haṭṭhalomo;
pasayhakāri.translation_1: 91. “Eat me today, then, O you who act by force; why do you gaze at me repeatedly, horripilated?

bhañjāpetvā.meaning_2: having caused to break; having had (the wood) broken; having caused to destroy
bhañjāpetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative absolutive of bhañjati (√bhañj + causal *āpe + tvā); the form in the text is the absolutive of the causative verb bhañjāpeti, here 'having had the wood broken'.
bhañjāpetvā.example_1: Taṃ sutvā kumāro ‘‘ sace maṃ na khāditukāmosi, atha kasmā dārūni bhañjāpetvā aggiṃ kāresī ’’ ti vatvā ‘‘ palāyissati nu kho, noti tava pariggaṇhanatthāyā ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ tvaṃ idāni maṃ kathaṃ pariggaṇhissasi, yohaṃ tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbatto sakkassa devarañño attānaṃ pariggaṇhituṃ nādāsin ’’ ti vatvā āha –
bhañjāpetvā.translation_1: The prince, hearing that, having said: “If you do not wish to eat me, then why did you have the wood broken and the fire made?”—and when [the yakkha] said, “I wonder if he will flee or not; it was for the purpose of testing you,” [the prince said]: “How will you now test me, I who, reborn in the animal realm, did not allow Sakka, the king of gods, to test myself?”—having said this, he spoke—

kappile.meaning_2: Kapila (name of a country or region); Kapila's kingdom
kappile.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular in the verse (kappile). Probably the region named after the sage Kapila; PEU connects kappila with a Brahmin named Kapila.
kappile.example_1: Evaṃ tuvaṃ porisādā pamutto, viroca kappile mahānubhāva;
kappile.translation_1: So you, released from the man-eater, shine in the Kapila kingdom, O mighty one;

animmisāni.meaning_2: unblinking; not blinking; with unclosed eyes
animmisāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text animmisāni is nominative plural neuter, agreeing with akkhīni (eyes). The sandhi -ss- stands for na + nimmissa; some editions read animisāni.
animmisāni.example_1: Sopi taṃ nibbisevanaṃ katvā pañca sīlāni datvā ‘‘ yakkho nu kho esa, no ’’ ti pariggaṇhanto ‘‘ yakkhānaṃ akkhīni rattāni honti animmisāni ca, chāyā na paññāyati, acchambhitā honti.
animmisāni.translation_1: He, too, having made him well-behaved and having given him the five precepts, investigated him, thinking: “Is this a spirit or not?” and then considering: “The eyes of spirits are red and unblinking, their shadow is not to be found, and they are fearless.

omissakavanaṃ.meaning_2: mixed forest; thicket of mixed trees/flowers
omissakavanaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular in the text (subject of the clause). Compound with vana; omissaka means 'mixed, miscellaneous'.
omissakavanaṃ.example_1: Imesaṃ pana sattannaṃ vanānaṃ anantaraṃ sabbesampi tesaṃ kallahārādivanānaṃ vasena omissakavanaṃ yojanavitthatameva tāni parikkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ.
omissakavanaṃ.translation_1: Immediately after these seven thickets was a thicket of mixed flowers including all those white water-lilies and so on, also one league in breadth, which surrounded them all.

omissako.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes a dense forest of mixed trees (mahāvanasaṇḍo) in the Jātaka prose. Nominative singular in the text.
omissako.example_1: Tato khuddakarājamāsamahārājamāsamuggavanaṃ, tadanantaraṃ tipusaelālukalābukumbhaṇḍavallivanāni, tato pūgarukkhappamāṇaṃ ucchuvanaṃ, tato hatthidantappamāṇaphalaṃ kadalivanaṃ, tato sālavanaṃ, tadanantaraṃ cāṭippamāṇaphalaṃ panasavanaṃ, tato madhuraphalaṃ ciñcavanaṃ, tato ambavanaṃ, tato kapiṭṭhavanaṃ, tato omissako mahāvanasaṇḍo, tato veḷuvanaṃ, ayamassa tasmiṃ kāle sampatti.
omissako.translation_1: Beyond that was a grove of small and large kidney beans and mung beans, then a thicket of climbing vines like cucumber, pumpkin, and gourd, then a grove of sugar-cane the size of areca-nut trees, then a grove of plantains with fruit the size of elephant tusks, then a Sāla grove, then a grove of bread-fruit with fruit the size of water jars, then a grove of tamarinds with sweet fruit, then a mango-tree grove, then a grove of elephant-apple trees, then a dense forest of mixed trees, then a bamboo grove; such was his splendor at that time.

tambakipillikāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of tamba (red) and kipillika (ant). Plural nominative in the text (tambakipillikāni), perhaps better analysed as masc plural (tambakipillikā).
tambakipillikāni.example_1: Tadā cūḷasubhaddā paṭivātapasse ṭhitā, tassā sarīre sukkhadaṇḍakamissakāni purāṇapaṇṇāni ceva tambakipillikāni ca patiṃsu.
tambakipillikāni.translation_1: At that time, Cullasubhaddā was standing to windward; on her body fell dry twigs mixed with old leaves and red ants.
tambakipillikāni.example_2: Cūḷasubhaddā ‘‘ ayaṃ nāgarājā attano piyabhariyāya upari pupphareṇukiñjakkhapattāni pātesi, mama sarīre sukkhadaṇḍakamissāni purāṇapaṇṇāni ceva tambakipillikāni ca pātesi, hotu, kātabbaṃ jānissāmī ’’ ti mahāsatte veraṃ bandhi.
tambakipillikāni.translation_2: Cullasubhaddā thought, “This elephant king let fall pollen, filaments, and petals upon his dear wife, but on my body he dropped dry twigs mixed with old leaves and red ants. Very well, I shall know what to do!” And she harbored a grudge against the Great Being.

paṇḍūsi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Vocative form in address (varavaṇṇini follows it in the same vocative); variant of paṇḍūsī 'pale woman', cf. paṇḍū 'pale'. The final -i in the text may be a shortened vocative of paṇḍūsī.
paṇḍūsi.translation_1: 97. “Why do you grieve, O fair-limbed one? You are pale, O lady of beautiful complexion;

sonuttaro.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of the hunter who killed the elephant in the Jātaka story. Nominative singular in the text.
sonuttaro.translation_1: Hearing that, Sonuttara, terrified by the fear of death, spoke:
sonuttaro.example_2: Taṃ sutvā sonuttaro ‘‘ sādhu ayye, ahaṃ taṃ vāraṇaṃ māretvā tassa dante āharissāmī ’’ ti sampaṭicchi.
sonuttaro.translation_2: Hearing that, Sonuttara accepted, saying, “Very well, noble lady, I will kill that elephant and bring its tusks.”

mupeti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Rare poetic verb, perhaps a hyper-Pāḷi form of pavattati or an error for muṭṭheti/pavatteti; uncertain. Present 3rd singular in the verse.
mupeti.example_1: 111. ‘‘ Katthacchatī kattha mupeti ṭhānaṃ, vīthissa kā nhānagatassa hoti;
mupeti.translation_1: 111. “Where does he dwell, and to what place does he go? What is the path for him when he goes to bathe?

mupetīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Form in -peti with the quotative -ti attached. Possibly a variant or scribal form of muñcati (√muc); the quoted verb may also be read as māpeti or mucchati. Uncertain.

ayasiṅghāṭakehi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental plural in the text, in a list of iron tools. Spelling of aya (iron) before si-. See also ayosiṅghāṭaka.
ayasiṅghāṭakehi.example_1: Athassa sā tuṭṭhā sahassaṃ datvā ‘‘ gehaṃ tāva gaccha, ito sattāhaccayena tattha gamissasī ’’ ti taṃ uyyojetvā kammāre pakkosāpetvā ‘‘ tātā amhākaṃ vāsipharasu-kuddāla-nikhādana-muṭṭhikaveḷugumbacchedana-sattha-tiṇalāyana-asilohadaṇḍakakacakhāṇuka- ayasiṅghāṭakehi attho, sabbaṃ sīghaṃ katvā āharathā ’’ ti āṇāpetvā cammakāre pakkosāpetvā ‘‘ tātā amhākaṃ kumbhabhāragāhitaṃ cammabhastaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, cammayottavarattahatthipādaupāhanacammachattehipi no attho, sabbaṃ sīghaṃ katvā āharathā ’’ ti āṇāpesi.
ayasiṅghāṭakehi.translation_1: Then she, highly pleased, gave him a thousand, saying, “First go home; you shall go there after seven days from now.” Having thus sent him away, she summoned blacksmiths and commanded them: “Dear ones, we need an axe, a spade, an auger, a hammer, a bamboo-cutting knife, a grass-cutter, an iron staff, a peg, and an iron three-pronged fork. Quickly make all of them and bring them to us.” She then summoned leather-workers and instructed them: “Dear ones, it is appropriate for us to make a leather sack capable of holding a hogshead’s weight. We also need leather ropes, straps, elephant-foot shoes, and leather parachutes. Quickly make all of them and bring them to us.”

sonuttaropi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name. In the text the form is sonuttaropi = sonuttara + pi (also), nominative singular. A compound of sona and uttara.
sonuttaropi.example_1: Sonuttaropi attano parivacchaṃ katvā sattame divase āgantvā deviṃ vanditvā aṭṭhāsi.
sonuttaropi.translation_1: Sonuttara also, having made his own preparations, came on the seventh day, venerated the queen, and stood.
sonuttaropi.example_2: Sonuttaropi appatteyeva sattame divase dante ādāya bārāṇasiṃ sampāpuṇi.
sonuttaropi.translation_2: Sonuttara, taking the tusks, arrived in Benares even before the seventh day.

tirivacchagahananti.meaning_2: thicket of tirivacchaka grass; dense growth of tirivacchaka reeds
tirivacchagahananti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Text reads tirivacchagahananti = tirivacchagahanaṃ iti; one of six thickets in the Jātaka prose passage. The first element tirivaccha is a kind of grass/reed, perhaps related to tirivaṭa or tiriṭa; the PEU analysis 'lotus forest' is uncertain.
tirivacchagahananti.example_1: Sopi rājānañca deviñca vanditvā rājanivesanā oruyha rathe ṭhatvā mahantena parivārena nagarā nikkhamitvā gāmanigamajanapadaparamparāya paccantaṃ patvā jānapade nivattetvā paccantavāsīhi saddhiṃ araññaṃ pavisitvā manussapathaṃ atikkamma paccantavāsinopi nivattetvā ekakova gacchanto tiṃsayojanaṃ patvā paṭhamaṃ dabbagahanaṃ kāsagahanaṃ tiṇagahanaṃ tulasigahanaṃ saragahanaṃ tirivacchagahananti cha gahanāni, kaṇṭakaveḷugumbagahanāni vettagahanaṃ omissakagahanaṃ naḷagahanaṃ saragahanasadisaṃ uragenapi dubbinivijjhaṃ ghanavanagahanaṃ rukkhagahanaṃ veḷugahanaṃ aparampi veḷugumbagahanaṃ kalalagahanaṃ udakagahanaṃ pabbatagahananti aṭṭhārasa gahanāni paṭipāṭiyā patvā dabbagahanādīni asitena lāyitvā tulasigahanādīni veḷugumbacchedanasatthena chinditvā rukkhe pharasunā koṭṭetvā atimahante rukkhe nikhādanena vijjhitvā maggaṃ karonto veḷuvane nisseṇiṃ katvā veḷugumbaṃ āruyha veḷuṃ chinditvā aparassa veḷugumbassa upari pātetvā veḷugumbamatthakena gantvā kalalagahane sukkharukkhapadaraṃ attharitvā tena gantvā aparaṃ attharitvā itaraṃ ukkhipitvā puna purato attharanto taṃ atikkamitvā udakagahane doṇiṃ katvā tāya udakagahanaṃ taritvā pabbatapāde ṭhatvā ayasiṅghāṭakaṃ yottena bandhitvā uddhaṃ khipitvā pabbate laggāpetvā yottenāruyha vajiraggena lohadaṇḍena pabbataṃ vijjhitvā khāṇukaṃ koṭṭetvā tattha ṭhatvā siṅghāṭakaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā puna upari laggāpetvā tattha ṭhito cammayottaṃ olambetvā taṃ ādāya otaritvā heṭṭhimakhāṇuke bandhitvā vāmahatthena yottaṃ gahetvā dakkhiṇahatthena muggaraṃ ādāya yottaṃ paharitvā khāṇukaṃ nīharitvā puna abhiruhati.
tirivacchagahananti.translation_1: He also, venerating the king and queen, descended from the royal palace. Mounting a chariot and remaining on it, with a large retinue, he set out from the city. Passing through a succession of villages, towns, and districts, he reached the borderland. There he turned back the people of the district. Proceeding with the border-dwellers, he entered the wilderness and passed beyond human habitation. Then he sent back the border-dwellers too and proceeded all alone. He covered thirty leagues, reaching, one after another, eighteen thickets: first, six thickets (namely, darbha grass thickets, kāsa grass thickets, long grass thickets, basil thickets, reed thickets, and tirivacchaka grass thickets); then thorny bamboo bush thickets; cane thickets; mixed thickets; reed thickets (impenetrable even to a snake, similar to saragahana); dense forest thickets; tree thickets; bamboo thickets; another bamboo bush thicket; mud thickets; water thickets; and mountain thickets. He cut the darbha grass thickets and so forth with a sickle. He cleared the basil thickets and so forth with a bamboo-cutting knife. He felled the trees with an axe, and for the extremely large trees, he first pierced them with an auger. Thus making his way, he made a stairway in the bamboo grove. Having climbed a bamboo bush, he cut a bamboo pole, caused it to fall over the next bamboo bush, and went along the top of the bamboo bushes. In the mud thicket, he spread dry wooden planks and walked on them; spreading another plank, he lifted the previous one and again spread it in front, thus crossing it. In the water thicket, he made a canoe and, using it, crossed the water thicket. Standing at the foot of the mountain, he tied an iron grappling-iron with a rope, threw it upward, and caused it to fasten onto the mountain. Climbing by the rope, he pierced the mountain with an iron staff tipped with adamant, drove a peg into the hole, and stood on it. Then, pulling out the grappling-iron, he again caused it to fasten high above. Standing there, he let down the leather rope, took hold of it, descended, and tied it to the lower peg. Then, holding the rope with his left hand and taking a hammer in his right, he struck the rope, pulled out the peg, and climbed again.

omissakagahanaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text, one of the eighteen thickets.

Passing through a succession of villages, towns, and districts, he reached the borderland. There he turned back the people of the district. olokayī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular, glossed in the text with olokesi. Verse and prose in the Jātaka commentary; also analyzable as ava + lok + *e.
olokayī.example_1: 115. ‘‘ Āruyha selaṃ bhavanaṃ kinnarānaṃ, olokayī pabbatapādamūlaṃ;
olokayī.translation_1: Having climbed the mountain peak, the abode of kinnaras, he looked at the base of the mountain;
olokayī.example_2: Olokayīti taṃ kinnarānaṃ bhavanabhūtaṃ pabbataṃ āruyha subhaddāya dinnasaññāvasena heṭṭhā olokesi.
olokayī.translation_2: Olokayī means that, having climbed that mountain, which was the abode of kinnaras, he looked down below by means of the signs given by Subhaddā.

saratūṇiñca.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of saratūṇiṃ (quiver, neuter accusative singular) with the enclitic ca. Part of the phrase saratūṇiñca mahādhanuñca 'quiver and great bow'; accusative object of ādāya. The niggahīta becomes ñ before c.
saratūṇiñca.example_1: Tattha soti, bhikkhave, so luddo tattheva sattabhūmikapāsādatale ṭhitāya tassā subhaddāya vacanaṃ uggahetvā saratūṇiñca mahādhanuñca ādāya pabbatagahanaṃ patvā ‘‘ kataro nu kho suvaṇṇapassapabbato nāmā ’’ ti satta mahāpabbate vituriyati, tasmiṃ kāle tuleti tīreti.
saratūṇiñca.translation_1: Regarding so, monks, that fowler, having learned the words of Queen Subhaddā, who stood on that very seven-storied palace, and taking his quiver and great bow, arrived at the mountain region, where he searched among the seven great mountains, wondering, “Which one is called Golden Cliff?” At that time, he weighed and investigated.

olokayīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Form olokayī is aorist 3rd singular; -īti is sandhi of olokayī + iti, the quotation marker left out of the headword.

samappayī.grammar: pr, caus of samappeti; aor of samappeti
samappayī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular in -ī, from the causative samappeti (saṃ + api + √i). The PEU suggests a split saṃ + apa + √nī or saṃ + api + √i; the sense 'shot through, pierced' fits the sentence. Alternatively an aorist of samappayati with the stem samappaya.
samappayī.translation_1: and when the elephant came to his side, the doer of evil deeds struck him with a mighty arrow.

samappayi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular in -i of the causative samappayati (saṃ + √ap). Here it means 'struck, pierced' with sallena. The PEU alternative analysis saṃ + api + i > samaṅgeti is also possible.
samappayi.example_1: Tāya saññāya so mahāsattassa āgantvā ṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā taṃ passāgataṃ puthunā sallena samappayi vijjhi.
samappayi.translation_1: By that sign, the hunter, knowing that the Great Being had come and was standing there, struck and pierced him, who had come to his side, with a great poisoned arrow.

pacchimakāyīdīhi.meaning_2: from the hindquarters and the like; from the rear parts and others
pacchimakāyīdīhi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it contrasts with kumbhādīhi: an arrow entering at the navel would, if from the east, have entered by the forehead and left by the hindquarters. Vocative-like absolutive context. Possibly pacchimakāyehi + ādīhi as an alternative analysis.
pacchimakāyīdīhi.example_1: Vadhissametanti ‘‘ bhikkhave, so chaddantavāraṇo disā pakkantesu nāgesu subhaddāya kareṇuyā passe ṭhatvā sandhāretvā samassāsayamānāya vedanaṃ adhivāsetvā kaṇḍassa āgataṭṭhānaṃ sallakkhento ‘ sace idaṃ puratthimadisādīhi āgataṃ abhavissa, kumbhādīhi pavisitvā pacchimakāyīdīhi nikkhamissa, idaṃ pana nābhiyā pavisitvā ākāsaṃ pakkhandi, tasmā pathaviyaṃ ṭhitena vissaṭṭhaṃ bhavissatī ’ ti upadhāretvā ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ upaparikkhitukāmo ‘‘ ko jānāti, kiṃ bhavissati, subhaddaṃ apanetuṃ vaṭṭatī ’’ ti cintetvā ‘‘ bhadde, aṭṭhasahassanāgā mama paccāmittaṃ pariyesantā disā pakkhandā, tvaṃ idha kiṃ karosī ’’ ti vatvā,‘‘ deva, ahaṃ tumhe sandhāretvā samassāsentī ṭhitā, khamatha me ’’ ti tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā catūsu ṭhānesu vanditvā tāya ākāsaṃ pakkhandāya nāgarājā bhūmiṃ pādanakhena pahari, padaraṃ uppatitvā gataṃ.
pacchimakāyīdīhi.translation_1: Vadhissametan means: Monks, when the eight thousand elephants had gone off in various directions, that Chaddanta elephant, standing by the side of the she-elephant Subhaddā, while she was comforting and reassuring him, endured the pain. Observing the place from which the arrow had come, he thought: “If this had come from the eastern direction and others, it would have entered from the forehead and others and exited from the hindquarters and others. But this, having entered from the navel, shot out into space. Therefore, it must have been shot by someone standing on the ground.” Having thus considered, and wanting to examine the spot where he stood, he thought, “Who knows what will happen? It is proper to send Subhaddā away.” And having said, “Good lady, the eight thousand elephants have run off in various directions searching for my enemy. What are you doing here?” And when she replied, “Lord, I am staying here, comforting and reassuring you; please forgive me,” she walked clockwise around him three times, venerated him in four places, and when she had flown off into space, the elephant king struck the ground with his toenail, and the plank, having sprung up, was gone.

āvīkaronto.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Masculine nominative singular agreeing with satthā in the text; present participle of āvīkaroti, literally 'making visible (āvī)'.
āvīkaronto.translation_1: Revealing that matter, the Teacher spoke:

sannicihe.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular sannicite in the text, qualifying dante. The reading may also be analysed as locative of the absolutive sanniciya, but the PP sannicita fits better.
sannicihe.example_1: Jānātīti bahūnaṃ vāraṇānaṃ idha sannicihe dante jānāti.
sannicihe.translation_1: Jānāti (jānāti) means she knows the tusks stored here by many elephants.

pirasāmikassa.meaning_2: beloved husband; dear husband; former husband
pirasāmikassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Genitive singular in the text. Perhaps pira + sāmika; pira may be a by-form of piya (dear), or an otherwise rare word for 'former'. See purimabhave 'in a former existence' earlier in the sentence.
pirasāmikassa.example_1: Sā mahāsattassa chabbaṇṇaraṃsivicittadante maṇitālavaṇṭena gahetvā ūrūsu ṭhapetvā purimabhave attano pirasāmikassa dante olokentī ‘‘ evarūpaṃ sobhaggappattaṃ vāraṇaṃ visapītena sallena jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā ime dante chinditvā sonuttaro āgato ’’ ti mahāsattaṃ anussarantī sokaṃ uppādetvā adhivāsetuṃ nāsakkhi.
pirasāmikassa.translation_1: She took the tusks of the Great Being, which were variegated with six-colored rays, with a jeweled fan, and having placed them on her lap, she gazed at the tusks of her dear lord from a former existence. Thinking, ‘Sonuttara has come, having caused the death of such a majestic elephant by a poison-tipped arrow and having cut off these tusks,’ and remembering the Great Being, she aroused such sorrow that she was unable to endure it.

aphāli.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular of phāleti with the negative prefix na (na + aphāli form); here of the heart breaking. Root √phal 1 is a guess; possibly √phal 2.
aphāli.example_1: Tattheva tassā hadayaṃ aphāli, teneva sā kālamakāsi bālā ’’ ti.
aphāli.translation_1: Right there her heart broke, and because of that, that foolish woman died.”

sonuttarassa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a hunter in the Jātaka stories. Genitive singular in the text (sonuttarassa).
sonuttarassa.example_1: ‘‘ bhikkhave, yaṃ ekaṃ daharaṃ yobbanappattaṃ kumāriṃ kāsāyavatthaṃ anagāriyaṃ upetaṃ pabbajitvā imasmiṃ sāsane carantiṃ addasātha passatha, sā tadā ‘ visapītena sallena nāgarājaṃ vijjhitvā vadhehī ’’’ ti sonuttarassa pesetā rājakaññā ahosi.
sonuttarassa.translation_1: ‘Monks, the young maiden, who has attained youth, who wears saffron robes, who has gone forth into homelessness, and who is practicing in this Dispensation—whom you saw and now see—she was the royal maiden who at that time sent Sonuttara, saying: “Pierce and kill the elephant king with a poison-tipped arrow!”’
sonuttarassa.example_2: Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – āvuso, ito anekavassakoṭimatthake saṃsaritampi pubbaṇhe kataṃ taṃ divasameva sāyanhe saranto viya attano caritavasena uccattā tāya rājadhītāya ca sonuttarassa ca caritavasena nīcattā uccānīcaṃ caritaṃ idaṃ purāṇaṃ rāgādīnaṃ darānaṃ vigatatāya vītaddaro, ñātidhanasokādīnaṃ abhāvena vītasoko, rāgasallādīnaṃ vigatattā visallo attanāva jānitvā buddho abhāsīti.
sonuttarassa.translation_2: This is what was said: ‘Friends, even though this ancient conduct, with its highs—due to his own excellent conduct—and lows—due to the conduct of that royal maiden and Sonuttara—was long-practiced for many crores of years from this point, the Buddha spoke this, having known it himself, like one remembering in the evening what was done in the morning on that very day, being free from burning distress due to the absence of distresses like passion, free from grief due to the absence of griefs like those concerning relatives and wealth, and free from the arrow of defilements due to the absence of arrows like passion.’

pappomūti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text as pappomūti = pappoti + iti; the -ti is elided before the quotation particle. Verb of the tanādi class per the PEU note.

anibbattitvā.meaning_2: without being reborn (in); not having arisen (in); without coming into being (in)
anibbattitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Negative absolutive of nibbattati used in the sense of 'without being reborn (in a realm)'. Used adverbially in the sentence: nirayādīsu anibbattitvā.
anibbattitvā.example_1: Yena pappomūti yena mayaṃ nirayādīsu anibbattitvā devesu ca manussesu ca yasaṃ issariyaṃ sobhaggaṃ pāpuṇeyyāma, taṃ no kāraṇaṃ kathehīti.
anibbattitvā.translation_1: By which we attain (yena pappomū) means by which we, without being reborn in hell and other similar realms, may obtain status, sovereignty, and splendor among gods and human beings—tell us that reason.

svādhippāgā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of su + adhippāgā; glossed by the commentary as sucirato adhippāgā, gatoti attho. Occurs in verse.
svādhippāgā.translation_1: 144. “Then Bhāradvāja went directly to Vidhura’s presence;
svādhippāgā.example_2: Tattha svādhippāgāti so bhāradvājagotto sucirato adhippāgā, gatoti attho.
svādhippāgā.translation_2: Therein, went directly (svādhippāgā) means that Sucirata of the Bhāradvāja clan went forth, meaning he went.

svādhippāgāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Uncertain word, no sentence supplied: possibly a sandhi, or a misreading. The analysis is a guess and needs checking against the text.
