upanīlā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Attributive, modifying pokkharaṇī in the text; part of the compound veḷuriyūpanīlā. upa here has an intensifying or approximative force.
upanīlā.example_1: Veḷuriyūpanīlāti veḷuriyena upanīlā, tasmiṃ nāgabhavane veḷuriyamayā pasannasalilā nīlobhāsā anekavaṇṇakamaluppalasañchannā pokkharaṇīti attho.
upanīlā.translation_1: Beryl-hued (veḷuriyūpanīlā) means dark blue due to beryl; it means that in that nāga realm there is a pond made of beryl, with clear water, green-hued, and covered with lotuses and water lilies of various colors.

āsanamabbhihāsi.meaning_2: went up to; approached; came to
āsanamabbhihāsi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text āsanam abbhihāsi: āsanaṃ + abbhihāsi, with the final vowel of āsana assimilated before the following vowel. 3rd singular aorist. The prefix abhi- with √har is sometimes given the sense 'approach'. The form is also sometimes resolved as aorist of abhihāti.
āsanamabbhihāsi.translation_1: laid out a beautiful, precious, jewel-adorned seat without being told.”

nisīdayī.meaning_2: seats (someone); causes to sit; makes sit down
nisīdayī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist or historical present form nisīdayī; causative of nisīdati, meaning 'seated (someone)'. In the text it is 3rd singular with an object, 'seated him'.
nisīdayī.example_1: 164. ‘‘ Tato maṃ urago hatthe gahetvā, nisīdayī pāmukhaāsanasmiṃ;
nisīdayī.translation_1: 164. “Then the nāga king, taking me by the hand, seated me on the principal seat;
nisīdayī.example_2: 1580. ‘‘ So puṇṇako kurūnaṃ kattuseṭṭhaṃ, nisīdayī pacchato āsanasmiṃ;
nisīdayī.translation_2: 1580. “That Puṇṇaka had the best of makers of the Kurus sit on a seat behind him;

pakkhālayī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative form of √khal 1 (to stumble, to wash)? The form pakkhālayī is an aorist 3rd singular or imperfect; the headword given here is the present 3rd singular. In the sentence it takes the object pādāni.
pakkhālayī.example_1: Pādāni pakkhālayī me janinda, bhariyāva bhattū patino piyassa.
pakkhālayī.translation_1: “O king, she washed my feet, just as a wife washes the feet of her dear husband.”

bhattū.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Genitive singular of bhattar (husband); the -ū is the normal genitive ending of ar-stems. Occurs in verse, patino is a gloss.
bhattū.example_1: Pādāni pakkhālayī me janinda, bhariyāva bhattū patino piyassa.
bhattū.translation_1: “O king, she washed my feet, just as a wife washes the feet of her dear husband.”

abbhihāsīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The -ti is a quotation or gloss marker; the entry is for abbhihāsi. The form shows the common doubling and aspiration of h after a prefix (abhi + hāsi), sro aorist 2nd singular. Alternatively it could be read as a gloss on abhihāsi of √hā 1 (abandoned), but the PEU points to abhiharati.

mātū.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Genitive singular mātū (cf. mātu) in the verse. The form is irregular because the genitive ending follows the contracted stem mātu-; the headword is the usual citation form mātar.
mātū.example_1: 189. ‘‘ Yathāpi mātū ca pitū agāre, putto piyo paṭivihito vaseyya;
mātū.translation_1: “Just as a dear son might dwell in the house of a mother and father, being cared for;

paṭivihito.meaning_2: cared for; looked after; attended to
paṭivihito.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Commentary glosses it as paṭijaggito (looked after). Nominative singular masculine agreeing with putto in the verse.
paṭivihito.example_1: 189. ‘‘ Yathāpi mātū ca pitū agāre, putto piyo paṭivihito vaseyya;
paṭivihito.translation_1: “Just as a dear son might dwell in the house of a mother and father, being cared for;

abhihantumpi.meaning_2: to destroy too; even to destroy; to strike down as well
abhihantumpi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of infinitive abhihantuṃ (abhi + hana + tuṃ) with enclitic pi; -ṃ + p- becomes -mp-. Same meaning as abhihantuṃ, with 'even' or 'too' added. The PEU's abhihantuṃ is an infinitive of abhihanati.
abhihantumpi.example_1: Tejo na sakkā mama tehi hantunti mama visatejo aññassa tejena abhihantumpi na sakkā.
abhihantumpi.translation_1: My power cannot be killed by them (tejo na sakkā mama tehi hantuṃ) means “My poison-power cannot be destroyed even by someone else’s power.”

addasinti.meaning_2: you saw; you caught sight of
addasinti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Authors' reading addasāsi + iti, aorist of dassati. Alternative form of addasāsi, second person singular aorist with ti.
addasinti.example_1: ‘‘ Addasāsin ’’ tipi pāṭho, ahaṃ ekāyane mahāmagge taṃ addasinti attho.
addasinti.translation_1: “You saw” (addasāsi) is also a reading, meaning “I saw you on the single main road.”

manulitto.meaning_2: anointed with ointment; smeared with oil
manulitto.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Glosses surosito in the text; nominative singular here. Probably mano (ointment) + litta, pp of limpati, though the first member is obscure.

paṭivihitoti.meaning_2: arranged; prepared; fixed up; put in order
paṭivihitoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text joined with iti: paṭivihito ti. The PEU entry lists it as ti (adj), from pati + vi + dhā; the -ita past participle of paṭiviharati (= paṭivihāra).

tavañcaḷāra.meaning_2: you and Āḷāra; you and Alāra
tavañcaḷāra.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of tavaṃ (accusative of tvaṃ, 'you') with the vocative proper name Āḷāra. The c represents tavaṃ + ca but no separate 'ca' sense is intended in the translation; the whole phrase addresses the Bodhisatta and Āḷāra.
tavañcaḷāra.example_1: Nāgañca sutvāna tavañcaḷāra, kāhāmi puññāni anappakānī ’’ ti.
tavañcaḷāra.translation_1: Having heard the Naga and you, Alāra, I shall perform many meritorious deeds.’”

vipalantiyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Form vipalantiyā is a feminine present participle (instrumental or locative singular) agreeing with mayi; reflects vipalapantī. The sentence is from the Jātaka commentary.
vipalantiyā.example_1: Yaṃ meti yena kāraṇena mayi nānappakārakaṃ vipalantiyā tvaṃ pabbajituṃ icchasi, tena kāraṇena tādisassa puttassa labhanaṃ mama dulladdhaṃ nāmāti.
vipalantiyā.translation_1: That (yaṃ me) means: “For which reason, while I am lamenting in various ways, you desire to go forth into monastic life, for that reason, the obtaining of such a son for me is called ill-gotten.”

tepitaṃ.meaning_2: Tipiṭaka; three baskets (of the Buddhist canon)
tepitaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Here ti- is the numeral 'three' (not the prefix), joined by sandhi to piṭaka; the text has te- before p. Mañjū tepitaṃ = Mañjūtipiṭakaṃ, 'Mañjū's Tipiṭaka'. Accusative singular.
tepitaṃ.example_1: Mañjū tepitaṃ apassantā, maññe dukkhaṃ nigacchantī ’’ ti.
tepitaṃ.translation_1: They are sweet, and not seeing you, I think they will incur suffering.”

assakīḷādīhi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text assakīḷādīhi is instrumental plural of an ādi compound meaning 'with horse sports and so on', i.e. the whole series beginning with horse play; the quotation gives assa + kīḷā + ādi.
assakīḷādīhi.example_1: Tassattho – yo ahaṃ pubbe catuājaññayuttaṃ sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ rathaṃ abhiruyha uyyānaṃ gacchāmi, mattakuñjare ca yodhemi, aññehi ca assakīḷādīhi kīḷāmi, svāhaṃ idāni sutasome pabbajite kathaṃ karissāmīti?
assakīḷādīhi.translation_1: Its meaning is: Previously, I who mounted a carriage drawn by four thoroughbreds and adorned with all ornaments, and went to the pleasure ground, and made intoxicated elephants fight, and played other horse-sports and so on—I indeed, now that Sutasoma has gone forth, how shall I act?”

paṭijānetvā.meaning_2: having promised; having acknowledged; having confessed; having agreed to; having granted
paṭijānetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In this context, paṭijānāti means to promise or agree to give; paṭijānetvā is 'having promised' (the bribe). Absolutive in -tvā, not inflected for case.
paṭijānetvā.example_1: Dhāti handimaṃ maṇikkhandhapiḷandhanaṃ, taveso hotu hatthe, puttaṃ apanehi, mā me antarāyaṃ karī ’’ ti sayaṃ puttaṃ hatthe gahetvā apanetuṃ asakkonto tassā lañjaṃ paṭijānetvā gāthamāha –
paṭijānetvā.translation_1: Foster-mother, here, this jeweled ornament is yours for your hand. Take away the child, do not make a hindrance for me.” Being unable himself to remove the child who was holding him by the hand, he promised her a bribe and uttered the verse:

menaṃ.meaning_2: with this; by this; through this
menaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the enclitic pronoun me (by/with me; for me) and enaṃ (this, it), instrumentative singular; the commentary glosses it as iminā. Some analyses take me as the instrumental of ahaṃ (by me) rather than a genuine enclitic.
menaṃ.example_1: Sutasome pabbajite, kiṃ nu menaṃ karissāmī ’’ ti.
menaṃ.translation_1: With Sutasoma having gone forth, what indeed shall I do with it?”
menaṃ.example_2: Tassattho – yaṃ nūna ahaṃ imaṃ lañjatthāya gahitaṃ pabhaṅkaraṃ suppabhāsaṃ maṇiṃ dadeyyaṃ, ko nu mayhaṃ sutasomanarinde pabbajite iminā attho, kiṃ nu menaṃ karissāmi , ahaṃ tasmiṃ pabbajite imaṃ labhissāmi, labhantīpi ca kiṃ nu kho etaṃ karissāmi, passatha me kammanti.
menaṃ.translation_2: Its meaning is: If indeed I would give away this radiant, well-shining jewel, grasped for the purpose of a bribe, what purpose is there for me with this if King Sutasoma has gone forth? What indeed shall I do with it? Even if I obtain this, with him having gone forth, what indeed shall I do with it? Look at my plight!”

ārabba.meaning_2: having begun; having undertaken; concerning; with reference to
ārabba.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it introduces the topic of the story ("concerning the temptation by his former wife"); often written ārabbha for ārabhitvā.
ārabba.example_1: Uddayhate janapadoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabba kathesi.
ārabba.translation_1: The Teacher, while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, gave this discourse beginning with ‘The land is scorched’ concerning the temptation of a bhikkhu by his former wife.

niḷinikā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of the king's daughter in the Jātaka prose; variant reading naḷinikā. Nominative singular in the text.
niḷinikā.example_1: ‘‘ Dhītā te, mahārāja, niḷinikā samatthā, taṃ pakkosāpetvā ‘ asukaṭṭhānaṃ nāma gantvā tāpasassa tapaṃ bhindāhī ’ ti pesehī ’’ ti.
niḷinikā.translation_1: “Your daughter, Great King, Niḷinikā, is capable. Having sent for her, send her (saying), ‘Go to such and such a place and break the ascetic’s austerity.’”

niḷinikāya.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name. Instrumental singular in the text (niḷinikāya).
niḷinikāya.example_1: Vanacarako sayaṃ assamaṃ agantvā tassa pana dassanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā niḷinikāya taṃ dassento dve gāthā abhāsi –
niḷinikāya.translation_1: The forester, not going to the hermitage himself, but standing at a place where it could be seen, showing it to Niḷinikā, declared two verses:

vidaṃsayantī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine nominative singular in -ī (vidaṃsayantī) agreeing with an implied female subject; the gloss vidaṃsayantīti dassentī confirms the meaning 'showing'. Causative present participle of vidaṃsayati, from vi + √dis with the -aya sign (daṃsa- by assimilation).
vidaṃsayantī.translation_1: Revealing her body parts, both hidden and exposed.

vidaṃsayantīti.meaning_2: makes visible; reveals; displays; makes clear
vidaṃsayantīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Text form vidaṃsayantīti = vidaṃsayantī + iti, present participle feminine nominative singular of the causative, qualifying a feminine subject; the -ti is a quotation marker.

tevaṃgataṃ.meaning_2: of such a kind; like that; such
tevaṃgataṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it modifies phalaṃ (nom sg nt). Explained by the commentary as evaṃgatikaṃ.
tevaṃgataṃ.example_1: 10. ‘‘ Ambho ko nāma so rukkho, yassa tevaṃgataṃ phalaṃ;
tevaṃgataṃ.translation_1: 10. “Sir, what kind of tree is that, whose fruit is of such a kind,
tevaṃgataṃ.example_2: Tattha yassa tevaṃgataṃ phalanti yassa tava rukkhassa evaṃgatikaṃ manoramaṃ phalaṃ.
tevaṃgataṃ.translation_2: In this context, whose fruit is of such a kind (yassa tevaṃgataṃ phalaṃ) means ‘whose, your tree's, delightful fruit is of such a kind.’

tevaṃgatanti.meaning_2: knowing the three Vedas; master of the three Vedas
tevaṃgatanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of tevijjaṃ (nominative/accusative singular) with ti, as in the text's tevaṃgatanti (= tevijjaṃ + iti? or tevijja + ti). The final -ṃ is assimilated before t. Alternative analysis as tevijjaṃ + āgataṃ is unlikely.

vañcayantī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle feminine nominative singular vañcayantī in the text, agreeing with sā; the reading vañcayantī is the caus. prp of vañcati meaning 'deceiving, tricking'.
vañcayantī.translation_1: Then she, deceiving him, uttered two verses:

paho.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Glossed by the commentary as pahu samattho. Nominative singular used predicatively with the infinitive vinetuṃ. The form paho shows a-stem inflection of the u-stem adjective.
paho.example_1: Paho bhavaṃ kaṇḍumimaṃ vinetuṃ, kurutaṃ bhavaṃ yācito brāhmaṇatthan ’’ ti.
paho.translation_1: The venerable person is able to heal this itching; I beg the venerable person to perform this service for a brahmin.”

āsādayinti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form āsādayinti is 3rd plural present of āsādeti (causative of āsīdati), with the ending -yinti. In the Jātaka prose it means 'they insult, abuse'. Note the variation āsādayanti.

potetvā.meaning_2: having caused to fall; having made fall; having knocked down
potetvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of the causative poteti (from √pat 1, 'fall'). In the text it explains panujjā: 'having made me fall'.
potetvā.translation_1: Panujjā means ‘then, having caused me to fall’.

paramasukhī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi compound of parama + sukhī (possessing supreme happiness). Nominative singular in both sentences, used as a predicate adjective with bhaveyya / bhaveyyaṃ.
paramasukhī.example_1: Karomi te kiñci kasāyayogaṃ, yathā bhavaṃ paramasukhī bhaveyyā ’’ ti.
paramasukhī.translation_1: I will make some medicinal decoction for you, so that the venerable person might become supremely happy.”
paramasukhī.example_2: Yaṃ te mudu tena vinehi kaṇḍuṃ, yathā ahaṃ paramasukhī bhaveyyan ’’ ti.
paramasukhī.translation_2: With your soft male organ, heal this itching, so that I may become supremely happy.”

etūti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] etu + iti, sandhi. eti is the present of √i (come, go); etu is its imperative 3rd singular. The -ti is the quotative iti, so the entry is for etu but lemma_1 given as etu.

cirāyituṃ.meaning_2: to delay; to tarry; to take a long time
cirāyituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive used with na sakkā ('cannot delay'). Also analysable as cira + √i with āya, i.e. 'to spend a long time'. Formed with -tuṃ from the denominative/causative cirāyati.
cirāyituṃ.example_1: Tattha rājīsayoti, samma, mayā na sakkā cirāyituṃ, aññe pana sādhusabhāvā rājisayo ca brāhmaṇisayo ca anumagge mama assamamaggapasse vasanti, ahaṃ tesaṃ ācikkhitvā gamissāmi, tvaṃ te puccheyyāsi, te taṃ mama santikaṃ nayissantīti.
cirāyituṃ.translation_1: Here, rājīsayo (royal sages) means, ‘Friend, I cannot delay. But other sages of good nature—both royal sages and brahmin sages—dwell along the path, near the path to my hermitage. I will go after telling them (to guide you). You should ask them, and they will lead you to my presence.’ This is the meaning.

tapanīpi.meaning_2: warming fire; fire for warming oneself
tapanīpi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine -ī stem, nominative singular used in the verse and glossed with tapanī ti. The appended -pi is the emphatic particle (tapanī pi), not part of the word.
tapanīpi.example_1: 26. ‘‘ Bhinnāni kaṭṭhāni huto ca aggi, tapanīpi te samitā brahmacārī;
tapanīpi.translation_1: “Your pieces of wood were cleft, and your fire kindled; your warming fire, celibate one, was prepared;
tapanīpi.example_2: Tapanīti visibbanaaggisaṅkhātā tapanīpi te samitāva sayameva saṃvidahitāva hoti.
tapanīpi.translation_2: Tapanī means, ‘your warming fire—which is called a fire for warming—was already prepared, arranged by yourself.’

nevātidīgho.meaning_2: not too tall; neither too long
nevātidīgho.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of na + atidīgho (na-eva > neva before a vowel). Describes the Bodhisatta's perfect proportions; nominative singular agreeing with bhoto.
nevātidīgho.translation_1: he was neither too tall nor too short, and his hair was extremely dark, like a black jewel.”

nabhyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text nabhyā is an instrumental or ablative singular ('below the navel'); the PEU entry nabha glosses 'sky', but nabhi/nabhī means navel. The form may rather belong to nabhī (navel), fem, or be a sandhi of nabhiyā. Related entry nabha.
nabhyā.example_1: 33. ‘‘ Akhīlakāni ca avaṇṭakāni, heṭṭhā nabhyā kaṭisamohitāni;
nabhyā.translation_1: “Without husks or stalks, placed at his waist below the navel;

saṃvāti.meaning_2: is fragrant; smells (of); gives off a scent
saṃvāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Third person singular present of saṃvāti. In the text it describes a hermitage that became fragrant, like a blue water-lily stirred by the wind.
saṃvāti.example_1: Nīluppalaṃ vātasameritaṃva, tatheva saṃvāti panassamo ayaṃ.
saṃvāti.translation_1: then this hermitage, just like a blue water-lily stirred by the wind, became fragrant.”
saṃvāti.example_2: Vātasameritaṃvāti yathā nāma nīluppalaṃ vātena samīritaṃ, tatheva ayaṃ imasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe assamo saṃvāti.
saṃvāti.translation_2: Vātasameritaṃva means, “Just as a blue water-lily stirred by the wind, so too this hermitage in this forest grove became fragrant.”

karavīkasussaraṃ.meaning_2: with a voice as sweet as the karavīka bird's; having a pleasant voice like the Indian cuckoo
karavīkasussaraṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The word is part of a longer compound in the text: rudaṃ ... karavīkasussaraṃ. Accusative singular here; may be analysed as an adjective or a bahubbīhi describing the voice.
karavīkasussaraṃ.example_1: Rudaṃ manuññaṃ karavīkasussaraṃ, hadayaṅgamaṃ rañjayateva me mano.
karavīkasussaraṃ.translation_1: His charming voice, a note like a most melodious karavīka bird, touches my heart; my mind is indeed delighted by it.

piḷayi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular with the ī shortened to i before the ending; the same form is listed in PEU under pīḷesi. In the text it describes the youth pressing against the woman with his hip.
piḷayi.example_1: Teneva maṃ uttariyāna māṇavo, vivaritaṃ ūruṃ jaghanena piḷayi.
piḷayi.translation_1: Because of that, the youth, having overcome me, pressed me with his hip using his opened thigh.

vicitravaṭṭaṅgulikāssa.meaning_2: having variegated round fingers; with beautifully rounded fingers marked with noble signs
vicitravaṭṭaṅgulikāssa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi compound describing hands; forms part of the longer compound vicitravaṭṭaṅgulikāssa (vicitravaṭṭaṅgulika + assa). In the text genitive singular.
vicitravaṭṭaṅgulikāssa.translation_1: His arms are gentle, with hairs resembling collyrium, and his hands are beautiful, endowed with round fingers variegated with noble marks, like coral sprouts.
vicitravaṭṭaṅgulikāssa.example_2: Vicitravaṭṭaṅgulikāssa sobhareti hatthāpissa varalakkhaṇavicitrāhi pavālaṅkurasadisāhi vaṭṭaṅgulīhi samannāgatā sobhanti.
vicitravaṭṭaṅgulikāssa.translation_2: Vicitravaṭṭaṅgulikāssa sobhare means that his hands too are beautiful, endowed with round fingers variegated with noble marks, like coral sprouts.

dijābhighuṭṭhaṃ.meaning_2: resounding with birds; filled with the calls of birds
dijābhighuṭṭhaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is the form dijābhighuṭṭhaṃ, agreeing with vanaṃ (neuter accusative singular) in the first verse and with an implicit neuter noun in the second. The second element is the past participle of abhighuṭṭha (√ghuṭṭ, not in the root list), meaning 'resounded'. Alternative split: dija + abhighuṭṭha.
dijābhighuṭṭhaṃ.example_1: 50. ‘‘ Vicitraphullañhi vanaṃ sutaṃ mayā, dijābhighuṭṭhaṃ dijasaṅghasevitaṃ;
dijābhighuṭṭhaṃ.translation_1: “Indeed, I have heard of a forest with variegated blooms, thronged with birds, frequented by flocks of birds;
dijābhighuṭṭhaṃ.translation_2: 1382. Resounding with flocks of peacocks and cranes, frequented by birds of various species;

tiriṭisaṅghā.meaning_2: swarm of dragonflies; swarm of cicadas
tiriṭisaṅghā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Spelling uncertain; tiriṭi (dragonfly, cicada) is also written tirīṭi. Locative singular in the text in a simile for the noise of ornaments in the rain. Sandhi alternative tiriṭisaṅghā could be nominative plural.
tiriṭisaṅghā.example_1: Tā piṃsareti tāni piḷandhanāni pāvusamhi pavuṭṭhe deve tiriṭisaṅghā viya viravanti.
tiriṭisaṅghā.translation_1: Tā piṃsare means that those adornments resound like swarms of dragonflies when the rain has fallen in the rainy season.

mikhalanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Uncertain; only the form mikhalanti is given. Analysis is doubtful: possibly a compound or a sandhi, or a mis-segmentation of the text. The final -ti has been taken as the quotative particle, giving an a-stem neuter; this should be checked against the Jātaka context.

piḷayīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form piḷayīti is an emphatic quotative variant (piḷayati + iti) of the causative piḷayati, with the final -a of the base lengthened before -iti. Covered by the PEU entry piḷayi (piḷa + ṇaya + ī).

kilāni.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Glossed in the text as kilāni, an alternative reading (ayameva vā pāṭho); nominative/accusative plural neuter. The edition writes khilāni, khila (callus) with -āni.
kilāni.translation_1: Khilāni means “calluses;” or this indeed is the reading.

asaṃgantu.meaning_2: not associating (with); not keeping company; not coming together (with)
asaṃgantu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Negative of saṃgantu (saṃ + √gam + tu). In the text it qualifies mitto (nominative singular) and is glossed as asamāgacchantassa purisassa.
asaṃgantu.translation_1: That very friend, for one not associating, decays through not living together.
asaṃgantu.example_2: Sveva mittoti so eva mitto asaṃgantu asamāgacchantassa purisassa tena asamāgamasaṅkhātena asaṃvāsena jīrati vinassati.
asaṃgantu.translation_2: Sveva mitto means “that very friend,” asaṃgantu means “for a person who does not associate,” and through not living together, which is called not associating, he jīrati (decays), meaning “is lost.”

tiriṭivaccho.meaning_2: Tiriṭivaccha; name of a rich man
tiriṭivaccho.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of the father of the woman in the story. Nominative singular in the text.
tiriṭivaccho.example_1: Athassā pitā tiriṭivaccho rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā ‘‘ deva, mama gehe itthiratanaṃ uppannaṃ, raññova anucchavikaṃ, lakkhaṇapāṭhake brāhmaṇe pesetvā taṃ vīmaṃsāpetvā yathāruci karohī ’’ ti āha.
tiriṭivaccho.translation_1: Then her father, Tirīṭavaccha, having approached the king, said, “Great King, a Woman-treasure has arisen in my house, suitable only for the king. Having sent Brahmins who read auspicious marks, have her tested and do as you please.”

sañjānitumpi.meaning_2: to recognise; to perceive; to know
sañjānitumpi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] With enclitic api: sañjānituṃ api, 'even to recognise'. Infinitive in -tuṃ.
sañjānitumpi.example_1: So taṃ ulloketvā kilesamadamatto satiṃ upaṭṭhāpetuṃ asakkonto ‘‘ abhipārakassetaṃ gehan ’’ ti sañjānitumpi nāsakkhi, atha sārathiṃ āmantetvā pucchanto dve gāthā abhāsi –
sañjānitumpi.translation_1: He, looking up at her, intoxicated by the intoxication of defilements, being unable to establish mindfulness, was unable to even recognize, ‘This is Ahipāraka’s house.’ Then, addressing his charioteer, desiring to ask, he spoke two verses.

petyā.meaning_2: from the father; on the father's side
petyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Rare/dialectal ablative of pitar, parallel to matyā; glossed pitito in the commentary. Often taken as pitiyā or pitu, but the metre and gloss support -yā.
petyā.example_1: 59. ‘‘ Ahañhi jānāmi janinda etaṃ, matyā ca petyā ca athopi assā;
petyā.translation_1: 59. “Indeed, O King, I know this [woman] from her mother and from her father; and also her [husband];
petyā.example_2: Tattha matyā ca petyā cāti mātito ca pitito cetaṃ jānāmi.
petyā.translation_2: In that [verse], matyā ca petyā ca means I know this [woman] from her mother and from her father.

avalokayantī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Causative of avalokati. The form in the text is the feminine present participle avalokayantī, nominative singular, agreeing with Ummādantī. Alternative reading: avalokayantī could be analysed as a present participle of a simple verb avaloketi.
avalokayantī.example_1: Tadā hi mayhaṃ avalokayantī, ummattakaṃ ummadantī akāsī ’’ ti.
avalokayantī.translation_1: For when Ummādantī looked at me, she indeed made me, the infatuated one, mad.”
avalokayantī.example_2: Avalokayantīti mayā avalokitā sayampi maṃ avalokayantī maṃ ummattakaṃ akāsīti attho.
avalokayantī.translation_2: Avalokayantī means when I looked, she herself, looking at me, made me mad—this is the meaning.

avalokitā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine nominative singular form agreeing with the implied 'I' (mayā ... avalokitā). Commentarial gloss of avalokayantī; the PEU treats avalokita as a past participle of avaloketi.
avalokitā.example_1: Avalokayantīti mayā avalokitā sayampi maṃ avalokayantī maṃ ummattakaṃ akāsīti attho.
avalokitā.translation_1: Avalokayantī means when I looked, she herself, looking at me, made me mad—this is the meaning.

aḷārapamhehi.meaning_2: with thick eyelashes; having dense, luxuriant eyelashes
aḷārapamhehi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes a woman's beautiful eyes. Instrumental plural in the text, agreeing with subhehi vaggubhi.
aḷārapamhehi.example_1: 63. ‘‘ Aḷārapamhehi subhehi vaggubhi, palobhayantī maṃ yadā udikkhati;
aḷārapamhehi.translation_1: 63. “When, with captivating and beautiful, charming eyes, enticing, she looks upon me;

tirīṭissa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Genitive singular tirīṭissa in the text. The PEU connects it to √tar with the kiṭi suffix; the form is irregular.
tirīṭissa.example_1: 66. ‘‘ Kadāssu maṃ kañcanajāluracchadā, dhītā tirīṭissa vilaggamajjhā;
tirīṭissa.translation_1: 66. “When indeed will Tirīṭi’s daughter, with a chest adorned with a golden net and a slender waist,

nāvabodhāmi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Negated by na, which is joined by sandhi as nā-. First person singular, present tense. The simplex is bodheti/avabodhati; avabodhāti is an irregular present form.
nāvabodhāmi.translation_1: from that moment on, I did not understand anything at all about my own mind.

ummādantyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name. In the text it is in the instrumental singular: 'having enjoyed Ummādantī' (ummādantyā).
ummādantyā.example_1: Ummādantyā ramitvāna, sivirājā tato siyan ’’ ti.
ummādantyā.translation_1: Having enjoyed Ummādantī, I would then be the King of Sivi.”

aḷārapamhehīti.meaning_2: split by flames; with flames as its mass; whose fire is split asunder
aḷārapamhehīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound of aḷāra (split) + pamha (flame?), to be checked. In the text it is aḷārapamhehīti = aḷārapamhehi + iti, instrumental plural with -iti, so the entry is made for the main word only.

saṃsandantī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present 3rd singular causative of saṃsandati used intransitively in the text; subject kimpurisī, object saraṃ. Alternatively 3rd plural of saṃsandati (√sand) but the singular subject supports the causative singular.
saṃsandantī.example_1: Pabbateti yathā himavantapabbate supupphitavane vīṇaṃ ādāya tantissarena attano saraṃ saṃsandantī kimpurisī kimpurisassa manaṃ harati, evaṃ harateva me manoti vippalapati.
saṃsandantī.translation_1: Pabbate means just as a kimpurisī on the Himālaya mountain, in a well-blossoming forest grove, taking a lute and harmonizing her own voice with the sound of the strings, captivates the mind of a kimpurisa, so too does she captivate my mind, thus he babbles.

mudubāhā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi compound used as an adjective; quoted in the commentary as a gloss of bāhāmudū. The PEU gives feminine gender, so also classifiable as fem.

ummadantyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Proper name of a woman in the Ummadantī Jātaka. Instrumental singular in the text (rañño mano ummadantyā niviṭṭho).
ummadantyā.example_1: Rañño mano ummadantyā niviṭṭho, dadāmi te taṃ paricārayassū ’’ ti.
ummadantyā.translation_1: ‘The king’s mind is attached to Ummadantī; I give her to you. Enjoy her as you please.’ ”

sāmikehī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental plural in the text (sāmikehī = sāmikehi). In this verse it means 'by the owners'. Sometimes written sāmika, sometimes sāmin.
sāmikehī.example_1: 80. ‘‘ Aññātakaṃ sāmikehī padinnaṃ, dhamme ṭhitā ye paṭicchanti dānaṃ;
sāmikehī.translation_1: “The gift that has been given by owners, being another’s property—those who are firm in the Dhamma, who receive such a gift;

yañcāpi.meaning_2: and whatever; and whichever; and also whatever
yañcāpi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of yaṃ + ca + api; api is an emphatic particle. Used in verse with the sense "and whatever ...". Sometimes analysed as yaṃ + ca + pi.
yañcāpi.example_1: 110. ‘‘ Assitthiyo ratanaṃ maṇikañca, yañcāpi me candimasūriyā abhipālayanti;
yañcāpi.translation_1: mares, treasure and gems, and whatever else my moon and sun watch over—
yañcāpi.example_2: 1439. ‘‘ Hatthī gavāssā maṇikuṇḍalā ca, yañcāpi mayhaṃ ratanaṃ pathabyā;
yañcāpi.translation_2: 1439. “Elephants, cows, horses, jewelled earrings, and also whatever treasure I have on earth;

cittavase.meaning_2: power of the mind; control of one's mind; will of the mind
cittavase.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is locative singular in the phrase cittavase na vatto, 'not under the control of his own mind'. Possibly also read as citta + vasa in the sense of 'subjection to the mind'. Not to be confused with cittavasī.
cittavase.example_1: So dhammamevānuvicintayanto, tasmā sake cittavase na vatto.
cittavase.translation_1: Contemplating only Dhamma, therefore, I am not subject to my own will.”

paṭidehi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Imperative 2nd singular of paṭidadāti, with the ending -hi. In the text it means 'give her back to me'. Sometimes analysed as paṭi + dehi.
paṭidehi.example_1: Sajāhīti manorathaṃ pana pūretvā sace te na ruccati, atha naṃ sajāhi mayhameva paṭidehi.
paṭidehi.translation_1: Sajāhī means: “But having fulfilled your longing, if you do not like her, then send her back; give her back only to me.”

vāḷukaghaṭaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text, in the phrase vāḷukaghaṭaṃ gale bandhitvā (having tied a sand-pot around the neck). The punisment imagery of tying a heavy pot to the neck to drown someone. vāḷuka is a variant spelling of vāluka (sand).
vāḷukaghaṭaṃ.example_1: Na tena so jīvatīti, samma abhipāraka, yo ‘‘ issaromhī ’’ ti pāpaṃ karoti, katvā ca kiṃ maṃ devamanussā vakkhantīti na uttasati na ottappati, so tena kammena na ca dīghakālaṃ jīvati, khippameva marati, devatāpi pana ‘‘ kiṃ imassa pāparañño rajjena, varamassa vāḷukaghaṭaṃ gale bandhitvā maraṇan ’’ ti lāmakena cakkhunā olokenti.
vāḷukaghaṭaṃ.translation_1: Na tena so jīvatī means: “Friend Ahipāraka, the one who does evil, thinking, ‘I am the lord,’ and having done so, is not scared or concerned, thinking, ‘what will devas and humans say about me?’—that person does not live long by that kamma, but dies quickly. Furthermore, even devas look upon this evil king with contempt, thinking, ‘what good is kingship for this evil king? It would be better for him to die with a sand-pot tied around his neck.’”

tyassāti.meaning_2: to her that; that (is) for her
tyassāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Probably tassā + iti, with doubling of the initial vowel (tyassā ti). No sentences were supplied, so the analysis is uncertain.

vātasamagatiassepi.meaning_2: even for a horse as swift as the wind
vātasamagatiassepi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of vātasamagati (wind-speed) + assa (horse, dat./gen. sg.) + pi (even). Locative/dative singular in the text; part of the gloss on assitthiyo.
vātasamagatiassepi.translation_1: Assitthiyo means: “women possessing supreme beauty, even those (quick) as horses equal to the wind.”

ekāparādhopissa.meaning_2: not even a single offence of his; not even one fault of his
ekāparādhopissa.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of ekāparādho (nominative singular of ekāparādha, 'a single offence') + api (even) + assa (genitive singular of idaṃ, 'of this one; of him'). In the text ekāparādhopissa … na diṭṭhapubbo: 'not even a single offence of his was seen before'.
ekāparādhopissa.example_1: ‘‘ Natthi devi, apica kho bodhiparibbājako kira amhākaṃ paccatthiko jātoti tassa sve ghātanatthāya pañca amacce āṇāpesiṃ, te pana naṃ māretvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ katvā vaccakūpe pakkhipissanti, so pana amhākaṃ dvādasa saṃvaccharāni bahuṃ dhammaṃ desesi, ekāparādhopissa mayā paccakkhato na diṭṭhapubbo, parapattiyena hutvā tassa mayā vadho āṇatto, tena kāraṇena socāmī ’’ ti.
ekāparādhopissa.translation_1: "There is not, Queen. But indeed, Bodhi the wandering ascetic, they say, has become our enemy. For the purpose of killing him tomorrow, I ordered five ministers. But they, having killed him, having made him into pieces, will throw him into the privy. But he taught us much Dhamma for twelve years. Not even a single offense of his was seen by me directly before. Having acted at the instigation of others, his slaying has been ordered by me. For that reason, I sorrow."

vidaṃsayaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle, masculine nominative singular, modifying a dog that bares its teeth. From the causative vidaṃsayati; the simplex stem daṃsa- stands for dis- with the -ṃ- of the present stem. The PEU entry vidaṃsayanta confirms the analysis.
vidaṃsayaṃ.translation_1: “But today that one barks defiantly, showing his white fangs,

upadānaṃvanodakaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of upadānaṃ (neuter nominative/accusative 'well') and vanodakaṃ ('waterless'). A variant of udapānaṃ read as upadānaṃ in this verse; the simile is of a well without water, i.e. a faithless person.
upadānaṃvanodakaṃ.translation_1: “One should not associate with a faithless person, just like a waterless well.

rahadaṃvudakatthiko.meaning_2: seeking water in a pool; one who wants water from a pool
rahadaṃvudakatthiko.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of rahadaṃ (accusative of rahada, 'pool') and udakatthiko ('seeking water'; udaka + atthika). The sandhi v- is the resolution of the final -aṃ before a vowel, as in the idiom rahadaṃ vudakatthiko. The whole phrase is a simile in the Jātaka commentary verse.
rahadaṃvudakatthiko.translation_1: One should cultivate a serene person, just as one desiring water seeks a pool.

bhajjayeti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text has bhajjayeti, a metrically lengthened form of bhajjaye, the 3rd singular optative of bhajjati; the PEU reading bhajjaye + ti is doubtful.

accābhikkhaṇasaṃsaggāti.meaning_2: too frequent association; meeting very often
accābhikkhaṇasaṃsaggāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text this is likely accābhikkhaṇaṃ + saṃsaggā + iti (or accābhikkhaṇa + saṃsaggā ti); the whole phrase means 'from too frequent association'. An alternative split is accābhikkhaṇa + saṃsaggā + iti, accābhikkhaṇa being an adverb ('very often').

mittiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text (mittiṃ bhindi, mittiṃ jirayetha). Formed from mitta; the PEU derivation from √mid is doubtful. Sometimes mitti is treated as an abstract noun in -i; some editions read metti.
mittiṃ.example_1: Akāleti ayuttappattakāle parassa piyabhaṇḍaṃ yācanāya mittā jīranti nāma, tvampi aticiraṃ nivāsena mayi mittiṃ bhindi.
mittiṃ.translation_1: The meaning of akāle is: “friends indeed decay by asking for another's beloved thing at an inappropriate time. You too, by dwelling too long, have broken the friendship with me.”
mittiṃ.example_2: Taṃ hissa dīpañca parāyaṇañca, na tena mittiṃ jirayetha pañño ’’ ti.
mittiṃ.translation_2: Indeed, that (person) is his island and refuge; a wise person should not destroy friendship with that (teacher).”,

saṃgatyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular in the text, glossed by the commentary as saṃgatiyā, i.e. association with the six classes of beings. The word is also found as saṃgatiyā with the same meaning.
saṃgatyā.translation_1: 139. “If the declaration is that by connection to classes of beings and by nature, (all phenomena) proceed;
saṃgatyā.example_2: Saṃgatyāti saṃgatiyā channaṃ abhijātīnaṃ taṃ taṃ abhijātiṃ upagamanena.
saṃgatyā.translation_2: By connection (saṃgatyā) means by the connection (or adherence) to the six classes of beings, by going to each of those classes of beings.

saṃgatyāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text saṃgatyā is instrumental singular, with -ti attached; the entry is for the main word saṃgati (saṃgatiyā → saṃgatyā).

āsandhipañcamā.meaning_2: four men (and the bier as the fifth) who carry a corpse
āsandhipañcamā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is part of the compound āsandhipañcamā; the simplex is not common elsewhere. See āsandhipañcama.
āsandhipañcamā.example_1: Iminā tassa ‘‘ cātumahābhūtiko ayaṃ puriso yadā kālaṃ karoti, tadā pathavī pathavīkāyaṃ anupeti anupagacchati, āpo … tejo … vāyo vāyokāyaṃ anupeti anupagacchati, ākāsaṃ indriyāni saṅkamanti, āsandhipañcamā purisā mataṃ ādāya gacchanti, yāva āḷāhanā padāni paññāyanti, kāpotakāni aṭṭhīni bhavanti, bhasmantā āhutiyo, dattupaññattaṃ yadidaṃ dānaṃ, tesaṃ tucchā musā vilāpo, ye keci atthikavādaṃ vadanti, bāle ca paṇḍite ca kāyassa bhedā ucchijjanti vinassanti, na honti paraṃ maraṇā ’’ ti imaṃ diṭṭhiṃ patiṭṭhāpesi.
āsandhipañcamā.translation_1: By this, that (minister) established this view: “When this person, consisting of the four great elements, dies, then the earth (element) progresses and proceeds to the earth-body, the water (element)… the fire (element)… the wind (element) progresses and proceeds to the air-body; the faculties migrate to space; four men (and the bier as the fifth) carry away the corpse until the cremation ground. The parts become evident, the bones become bleached; offerings end in ashes. That which is called a gift is taught by fools; their babbling is vain and false. Whatever people affirm a positive teaching—both the foolish and the astute—they are annihilated and destroyed from the breaking up of the body; they do not exist after death.”

ucchedī.meaning_2: holding the doctrine of annihilation; annihilationist
ucchedī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular masculine of the ī-stem adjective ucchedin, used as a noun for one who holds the annihilationist view. In the text it agrees with nara in a list of wrong-view holders.
ucchedī.example_1: Pubbekatī ca ucchedī, yo ca khattavido naro.
ucchedī.translation_1: one who believes in past action, and the annihilationist, and a person who advocates the Kshatriya doctrine.

idānī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text has idānī, metrical lengthening of the final vowel. Usually written idāni. Some works analyse it as idaṃ + dāni. A common idiom is kahaṃ ... idāni, meaning 'where is ... now?'.
idānī.example_1: ‘‘ bhante, lakuṇḍakabhaddiyatthero kira nāmeko tumhākaṃ sāvako madhuradhammakathiko atthi, kahaṃ so idānī ’’ ti.
idānī.translation_1: “Venerable sir, we understand you have a disciple who is a honeyed preacher named the Venerable Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya. Where is he now?”
idānī.example_2: So ‘‘ mama bhātike hatthipālakumāre sante kathaṃ paṭhamataraṃ mayhameva setacchattaṃ pāpuṇātī ’’ ti pucchitvā ‘‘ tāta, bhātā, te ‘ na mayhaṃ rajjenattho, pabbajissāmī ’ ti vatvā nikkhanto ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ kahaṃ paneso idānī ’’ ti vatvā ‘‘ gaṅgātīre nisinno ’’ ti vutte ‘‘ tāta, mama bhātarā chaḍḍitakheḷena kammaṃ natthi, bālā hi parittakapaññā sattā etaṃ kilesaṃ jahituṃ na sakkonti, ahaṃ pana jahissāmī ’’ ti rañño ca pitu ca dhammaṃ desento dve gāthā abhāsi –
idānī.translation_2: He asked, “When my brother Prince Hatthipāla exists, how is it that the white sunshade belongs to me first?” When told, “Dear one, your brother has gone forth, saying, ‘I have no need for kingship, I will renounce the world,’” he asked, “Where is he now?” and upon being told, “He is sitting on the bank of the Ganges,” he said, “Dear ones, there is no need for that which my brother has spewed out of his mouth; fools, beings of little wisdom, cannot abandon this defilement, but I will abandon it.” Then, teaching the Dhamma to the king and his father, he declared two verses—

katanissameti.meaning_2: one who has practiced the matter and passed for that matter
katanissameti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Possibly katanissamaṃ + iti with sandhi -aṃ > -e before i-. Katanissama is a bahubbīhi (kata + nissama). Only the PEU entry is available; no sentence to confirm.

caretiādimāha.meaning_2: said 'he walks' and so on; said 'one should behave' and the rest
caretiādimāha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of careti (3rd singular of carati, 'behaves; walks') and ādimāha ('said beginning with'). Quotation formula in the Jātaka commentary. The segmentation is uncertain: possibly care + ti + ādimāha; readings may vary in the manuscripts.

pañcacūḷākaraṇagaddūlabandhanagomayāsiñc.meaning_2: five topknots, leather straps, and sprinkling with cow-dung water (forms of humiliation)
pañcacūḷākaraṇagaddūlabandhanagomayāsiñc.construction: pañca + cūḷā + karaṇa + gaddūla + bandhana + gomaya + āsiñcana
pañcacūḷākaraṇagaddūlabandhanagomayāsiñc.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental plural of a long bahubbīhi compound, describing the five kinds of humiliation done to the ministers. Recorded as a single word in the text.
pañcacūḷākaraṇagaddūlabandhanagomayāsiñc.example_1: Rājā ‘‘ sādhu, bhante ’’ ti sampaṭicchitvā te sabbasaṃharaṇe katvā pañcacūḷākaraṇagaddūlabandhanagomayāsiñcanehi avamānetvā raṭṭhā pabbājesi.
pañcacūḷākaraṇagaddūlabandhanagomayāsiñc.translation_1: The king, having accepted (the advice), saying, “Very well, venerable sir,” stripped them of all possessions and positions, and having disgraced them with the five kinds of humiliation—making five topknots, binding them with leather straps, and drenching them with cow dung water—banished them from the kingdom.

saniḷīnikamavhayano.meaning_2: called together with Niḷīnikā; whose name is joined with Niḷīnikā (name of a previous life of the Bodhisatta)
saniḷīnikamavhayano.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of saha + niḷīnikā + avhayana; niḷīnikāya is contracted and saha becomes sa-. Nominative singular in the text, subject of the sentence. The PEU treat it as an adjective (ti); here taken as a masc noun naming the person.
saniḷīnikamavhayano.translation_1: The first is the one called Saniḷīnika; the second, moreover, is the excellent one with Ummadantī;

abhirūhi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular in the text; the prefix abhi- takes the form abhirūhi. The past participle abhirūḷha is related.
abhirūhi.example_1: So nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pāsādaṃ abhirūhi.
abhirūhi.translation_1: He, having circumambulated the city, ascended to the palace.

luñcantī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine nominative singular luñcantī used adverbially with viya ('as if plucking'). The gloss uppāṭenti confirms the sense 'pull out, pluck'. Sometimes analysed as a present participle of a denominator luñcati.
luñcantī.example_1: Athassa mukhato luñcantī viya gahetvā ekā nāṭakītthī taṃ gāyi.
luñcantī.translation_1: Then, as if plucking it from his mouth, a certain dancer woman took that (verse) and sang it.
luñcantī.translation_2: Therein, luñcanti means they pluck them out.

punnappunaṃ.meaning_2: again and again; over and over again; repeatedly
punnappunaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of puna and punaṃ (the second element assimilated to puna). Used adverbially in the text to mean 'again and again'.
punnappunaṃ.example_1: ‘‘ Jānāmi, bhante, amhākaṃ pana rañño idameva piyaṃ, tena naṃ punnappunaṃ gāyāmī ’’ ti.
punnappunaṃ.translation_1: “I know others, venerable sir, but this very (song) is dear to our king, therefore I sing it again and again.”

korunagaragāmavāsī.meaning_2: living in Korunagaramagāma; resident of Korunagaragāma village
korunagaragāmavāsī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi compound acting as a noun; nominative singular in the text, used in a simile of a young man from Korunagaragāma.
korunagaragāmavāsī.example_1: Ekacco hi kulehi saṃsaṭṭho viharati sahasokī sahanandī, ekacco mātāpitūsupi alaggamānaso vicarati korunagaragāmavāsī daharo viya, evarūpassa puthujjanassapi bhadrameva.
korunagaragāmavāsī.translation_1: Indeed, someone dwells associated with families, sorrowing and rejoicing together. Someone else, even with parents, wanders with a non-clinging mind, like a young bhikkhu from Korunaga City. For such a kind of worldling bhikkhu, it is truly a blessing.

atthasandassanī.meaning_2: revealing the purpose; explaining the meaning; showing the benefit
atthasandassanī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Describes a simile (upamā) in the text. Commentarial gloss: atthappakāsikā. Feminine form; declined like medhāvī.
atthasandassanī.example_1: 33. ‘‘ Esā te upamā rāja, atthasandassanī katā;
atthasandassanī.translation_1: This simile, which reveals the purpose, has been presented to you, O King.
atthasandassanī.translation_2: Regarding reveals the purpose (atthasandassanī): revealing the purpose.

asakkento.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle of the negative verb na sakkoti. Used with the infinitive uttarituṃ. Masculine nominative singular in the text, agreeing with mahāvāraṇo.
asakkento.example_1: Eko kira mahāvāraṇo gaṅgātīre caranto gaṅgāyaṃ patitvā uttarituṃ asakkento tattheva mato gaṅgāya vuyhi, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.
asakkento.translation_1: Indeed, a great elephant, wandering on the bank of the Ganges, fell into the Ganges and, being unable to get out, died right there and was swept away by the Ganges. This was said with reference to that [elephant].

udapatvāti.meaning_2: having flown up; having risen up; having flown away
udapatvāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Formed with -tvā from the present stem udappati / uppati; the text's pada is joined with -ti, which is not part of the word.

matthikoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Unrecognised form; no sentences supplied. Possibly textual corruption or a sandhi of matthiko + ti. Needs checking against the manuscript.

paṭipajjasu.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] 2nd singular imperative of paṭipajjati, the -ssu ending with the final -a assimilated to -u (paṭipajja + ssu > paṭipajjasu). In the text addressed to the prince: 'take possession'.
paṭipajjasu.example_1: Te putta paṭipajjasu, rajjaṃ niyyādayāmi te.
paṭipajjasu.translation_1: My dear child, take possession of those; I hand over the kingdom to you.

cāpadhāribhīti.meaning_2: by the bow-bearer, it is said; thus by the archer
cāpadhāribhīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of cāpadhāribhi (instrumental plural of cāpadhārī, 'bow-bearer; archer') with the quotative iti. Alternative analysis: cāpadhāribhi + īti. Compound of cāpa + dhārī, so no root fields.

siyyuntipi.meaning_2: they might be; they could be; and (they might be)
siyyuntipi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Not found in the supplied sentence; siyuṃ is optative 3rd plural of √as (honti → siyuṃ), ti is quotative 'iti', pi is emphatic 'also; even'. Alternative segmentation: siyuṃ + iti + pi. Check context.

imantiādimāha.meaning_2: here (iti) begins; this (is the beginning); so it is said
imantiādimāha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi joining imaṃ, iti and ādi-āha; the whole phrase means 'so he said, beginning with this'.

kambusaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Glossed as suvaṇṇaṃ (gold) in the Jātaka commentary; probably a rare or regional word. Accusative singular in the text (kambusaṃ vuccati).
kambusaṃ.example_1: Tattha kambusahatthāyoti kambusaṃ vuccati suvaṇṇaṃ, suvaṇṇābharaṇabhūsitahatthāyoti attho.
kambusaṃ.translation_1: Tattha kambusahatthāyo means that kambusa is called gold, thus the meaning is, “whose hands are adorned with golden ornaments.”

tatotiādimāha.meaning_2: said (starting with) "tato ti ādi"; began with "then"; spoke thus beginning with "tato"
tatotiādimāha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of a quoted phrase joined to āha: tato ti ādi + āha, "he said 'tato ti ādi' (i.e. 'then...', etc.)". Common commentarial idiom introducing a quotation. āha is the perfect/irregular aorist of √brū/vac, 'he said'.

koṭṭiyamāno.meaning_2: being pounded; being beaten; being hammered
koṭṭiyamāno.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Passive present participle; the text describes the hellish torment of being struck by iron stakes. Alternative analysis as a passive of koṭṭeti (√kuṭ 2).
koṭṭiyamāno.example_1: So hi devadattaṃ nissāya tassa vacanena pitaraṃ ghātāpetvā devadattassa saṅghabhedāvasāne bhinnaparisassa roge uppanne ‘‘ tathāgataṃ khamāpessāmī ’’ ti mañcasivikāya sāvatthiṃ gacchantassa jetavanadvāre pathaviṃ paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ sutvā ‘‘ devadatto sammāsambuddhassa paṭipakkho hutvā pathaviṃ pavisitvā avīciparāyaṇo jāto, mayāpi taṃ nissāya pitā dhammiko dhammarājā ghātito, ahampi nu kho pathaviṃ pavisissāmī ’’ ti bhīto rajjasiriyā cittassādaṃ na labhi,‘‘ thokaṃ niddāyissāmī ’’ ti niddaṃ upagatamattova navayojanabahalāyaṃ ayamahāpathaviyaṃ pātetvā ayasūlehi koṭṭiyamāno viya sunakhehi luñjitvā khajjamāno viya bheravaravena viravanto uṭṭhāti.
koṭṭiyamāno.translation_1: Indeed, he, relying on Devadatta and on his word, had his father killed. When sickness arose in Devadatta, whose assembly was divided after he caused a schism in the Saṅgha, and as he was travelling to Sāvatthī by palanquin, intending to ask the Tathāgata for forgiveness, he heard that Devadatta had entered the earth at the Jetavana gate. He thought, “Devadatta, having become an opponent of the Fully Self-Awakened Buddha, entered the earth and is destined for the Avīci hell. I too, relying on him, had my father, a righteous king who ruled in righteousness, killed. Will I too enter the earth?” Thus terrified, he found no mental pleasure in royal splendour. As soon as he fell into sleep, intending to “sleep a little,” he was thrown into a great iron earth nine yojanas thick, and it was as if he was being pierced by iron stakes and being devoured by dogs, torn to pieces; crying out with a terrifying roar, he rose up.

paṭiveditvā.meaning_2: having made known; having declared; having informed
paṭiveditvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text it is used of declaring oneself a lay follower (upāsakattaṃ paṭiveditvā).
paṭiveditvā.example_1: Tato ‘‘ ko nu kho me imaṃ bhayaṃ vinodetuṃ sakkhissatī ’’ ti cintetvā ‘‘ ṭhapetvā dasabalaṃ añño natthī ’’ ti ñatvā ‘‘ ahaṃ tathāgatassa mahāparādho, ko nu kho maṃ netvā dassessatī ’’ ti cintento ‘‘ na añño koci aññatra jīvakā ’’ ti sallakkhetvā tassa gahetvā gamanūpāyaṃ karonto ‘‘ ramaṇīyā vata, bho, dosinā rattī ’’ ti udānaṃ udānetvā ‘‘ kaṃ nu khvajja samaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā payirupāseyyāmī ’’ ti vatvā pūraṇasāvakādīhi pūraṇādīnaṃ guṇe kathite tesaṃ vacanaṃ anādiyitvā jīvakaṃ paṭipucchitvā tena tathāgatassa guṇaṃ kathetvā ‘‘ taṃ devo bhagavantaṃ payirupāsatū ’’ ti vutto hatthiyānāni kappāpetvā jīvakambavanaṃ gantvā tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā tathāgatena katapaṭisanthāro sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ pucchitvā tathāgatassa madhuraṃ sāmaññaphaladhammadesanaṃ (dī. ni.1.150 ādayo) sutvā suttapariyosāne upāsakattaṃ paṭiveditvā tathāgataṃ khamāpetvā pakkāmi.
paṭiveditvā.translation_1: Then, having thought, “Who, I wonder, will be able to dispel this fear of mine?”, and having known, “There is no one else apart from the Ten-Powered One”, and thinking, “I have greatly offended the Tathāgata; who, I wonder, will lead me and show me?”, he recognized, “No one else but Jīvaka can lead me.” So, attempting to devise a way to go with Jīvaka, he uttered the inspired utterance, “Truly, friends, it is a delightful moonlit night!”, and said, “Whom, I wonder, should I attend upon today, a recluse or a brahmin?” When Purāṇa’s disciples and others spoke of the virtues of Purāṇa and others, he did not heed their words. He questioned Jīvaka in return, and when Jīvaka spoke of the Tathāgata’s virtues, he was told, “Your Majesty should attend upon the Blessed One.” Having caused elephant carriages to be prepared, he went to Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. Having approached the Tathāgata, venerated him, and exchanged greetings with the Tathāgata, he asked about the visible fruit of recluseship. After hearing the Tathāgata’s sweet discourse on the fruit of recluseship, at the end of the discourse, he declared his status as a lay follower, sought forgiveness from the Tathāgata, and departed.

patāpano.meaning_2: Patāpana (name of a hell); burning; scorching
patāpano.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Name of one of the great hells, paired with Tāpana (sentence 1); the commentary explains it as 'burning exceedingly' (sentence 2). In the text it is nominative singular.
patāpano.translation_1: And then another, Mahāvīci, and Tāpana and Patāpana.
patāpano.translation_2: Patāpana (patāpano) hell is so called because it burns (tāpeti) exceedingly.

tāpayitvā.meaning_2: having tormented; having afflicted; having scorched; having burned
tāpayitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive of the causative tāpeti (√tap + *e). The PEU splits it as tapa + ṇaya + tvā; the causal base is tāpayi-. Used in the verse in the sense of tormenting the populace, matching tāpane paccati in the next line.
tāpayitvā.translation_1: having afflicted the people of the country, after death he is tormented in Tāpana hell.

vikkhambhato.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Adverbial ablative-like form of vikkhambha; here parallel with āvaṭṭato ('in circumference'), describing the extent of the hell. PEU's analysis is uncertain.
vikkhambhato.example_1: Svāyaṃ saha bhittīhi vikkhambhato aṭṭhārasādhikatiyojanasato, āvaṭṭato pana catupaṇṇāsādhikanavayojanasato, saha ussadehi dasa yojanasahassāni.
vikkhambhato.translation_1: Together with its walls, it is three hundred and eighteen leagues in width; in circumference, however, it is nine hundred and fifty-four leagues; including the Ussada hells, it is ten thousand leagues.

iccetetiādimāha.grammar: sandhi, ind + ind + ind + ind + ind + pr
iccetetiādimāha.meaning_2: thus, so; iti; and so on, etc.; thus, so; this, these; the beginning, the start; and so on; said; he said
iccetetiādimāha.construction: iti + ce + iti + ādi + imā + āha
iccetetiādimāha.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Compound sandhi of a stock phrase of the commentaries meaning 'he said (starting with) iti ce and so on, etc.'; the analysis is uncertain and the word does not occur in the sentences.

ceccoti.meaning_2: having incited; having stimulated; having urged
ceccoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Form is cecca + iti (quotation); the absolutive of the causative of √cit. The PEU entry suggests 'stimulate (with effort)', but this is uncertain.

tuttaṭṭītoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of the quoted word tuttaṭṭī with iti. No sentence context available, so the analysis is tentative.

cuṇavicuṇṇaṃ.meaning_2: crushed to fine powder; ground into dust
cuṇavicuṇṇaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Possibly a sandhi or compound of cuṇṇa + vicuṇṇa ("powder" + "powdered to bits"), used adverbially with karonti. The reading cuṇavicuṇṇaṃ may be a variant of cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ.
cuṇavicuṇṇaṃ.example_1: Nittacanti lohakumbhiyaṃ bahūni vasasahassāni pakkaṃ nīharitvā tigāvutamassa sarīraṃ nittacaṃ katvā jalitāya lohapathaviyaṃ pātetvā tiṇhehi ayasūlehi koṭṭetvā cuṇavicuṇṇaṃ karonti.
cuṇavicuṇṇaṃ.translation_1: Skinless (nittacan) means that after he has been cooked for many thousands of years in the iron cauldron and taken out, they make the body of that hell-being, which is three leagues in size, skinless; they then throw him onto the blazing iron ground and strike him with sharp iron stakes, grinding him into fine powder.

ayabalisaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The PEU splits as aya + balisa(ḷisa). Accusative singular in the text, object of khipitvā.
ayabalisaṃ.example_1: Athassa dīghe ciratāpite jalamāne phāle ādāya mukhaṃ vikkhambhetvā vivaritvā rajjubaddhaṃ ayabalisaṃ khipitvā jivhaṃ nīharitvā tasmiṃ vivaṭe mukhe taṃ ayoguḷaṃ sampavisanti pakkhipanti.
ayabalisaṃ.translation_1: Then, taking long, long-heated, glowing ploughshares, they pry his mouth open, throw in an iron hook fastened to a rope, pull out his tongue, and when his mouth is thus opened, they thrust and put in that iron ball.

ekadoṇikanāvappamāṇasarīrā.meaning_2: whose body is the size of a single-dugout canoe
ekadoṇikanāvappamāṇasarīrā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi compound describing the huge fish in the Jātaka; nominative plural in the text, agreeing with the subject.
ekadoṇikanāvappamāṇasarīrā.translation_1: Of excessive body (atikāyā) means whose bodies are the size of a single dugout canoe.

ayasūcimukhā.meaning_2: having a mouth of iron needles; with an iron-needle mouth; with a needle-sharp beak
ayasūcimukhā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Glossed in the text by aya + sūci + mukha. Nominative plural of the bahubbīhi compound ayomukha, describing worms in hell. The form here ends in -ā, so it can be read as nominative plural or as a sandhi variant of ayasūcimukhaṃ.
ayasūcimukhā.translation_1: Iron-mouthed (ayomukhā) means whose mouths are iron needles.

saṃgiddhāti.meaning_2: full of desire; greedy (for); eager (for); confused
saṃgiddhāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Form ends in -āti, probably a quotation or iti-joined form of saṃgiddhā (nominative plural or ablative?). The PEU gives two analyses: from √gidh (desire) and as saṃ + laddha. If the root analysis holds, the entry is a past participle.

koṭṭiyamānā.meaning_2: being struck; being beaten; being pounded
koṭṭiyamānā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Present participle passive of koṭṭeti (causative of √kuṭ 2), used in the locative absolute or as an adjective. Nominative plural masculine in the text.
koṭṭiyamānā.example_1: Ete vajantīti te paradārikā sattā nānāvidhehi āvudhehi koṭṭiyamānā ete simbaliniraye abhiruhanti.
koṭṭiyamānā.translation_1: These go (ete vajantī) means those adulterous beings, being struck with various weapons, ascend these hells of silk-cotton trees.

nanandaranti.meaning_2: they do not delight (in); is not glad (about)
nanandaranti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of na + nandaranti (3rd plural present of nandati). No sentences were supplied, so the analysis rests on the form alone.

ayasaṅkunā.meaning_2: iron spike; iron stake; iron hook
ayasaṅkunā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular in the text (ayasaṅkunā). Used of the instruments of torture in hell. Sometimes written ayo- instead of aya-.
ayasaṅkunā.example_1: Vaṅkenāti tassā sāmikavattādīnaṃ aparipūrikāya sāmikādayo akkositvā paribhāsitvā niraye nibbattāya lohapathaviyaṃ nipajjāpetvā ayasaṅkunā mukhaṃ vivaritvā balisena jivhaggaṃ nibbahanti, rajjubandhanena sabandhanaṃ kaḍḍhanti.
ayasaṅkunā.translation_1: By a hook (vaṅkenā) (refers to the torment where), due to her non-fulfillment of duties towards her husband and so on, and for having reviled and admonished her husband and others, and for being reborn in hell, (the wardens) lay her down on the iron ground, open her mouth with an iron spike, pull out the tip of her tongue with a hook, and drag the tongue, bound by rope-constriction.

virūpavā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Contracted nominative singular virūpavā (vant > vā). Opposite of rūpavā; the related entry virūpavesa takes virūpa as a prefix.
virūpavā.example_1: Tesu pana eko paññavā bhavissati virūpavā, eko rūpavā na paññavā.
virūpavā.translation_1: But among them, one will be wise but ugly, and the other will be handsome but not wise.

dhātigaṇaparivutā.meaning_2: surrounded by a group of wet-nurses; attended by a company of nurses
dhātigaṇaparivutā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahuvrīhi compound; feminine subject Pabhāvatī, so the form is nominative singular feminine. The second member parivuta is a past participle of parivāreti, but the whole word is treated as a compound adjective.
dhātigaṇaparivutā.example_1: Pabhāvatī sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā dhātigaṇaparivutā āgantvā sassuṃ vandi.
dhātigaṇaparivutā.translation_1: Pabhāvatī, adorned with all ornaments and surrounded by a group of nurses, came and venerated her mother-in-law.

vicinitukāmā.meaning_2: desiring to pluck; wanting to pick
vicinitukāmā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Likely a sandhi/compound of the infinitive vicinituṃ (from √ci 1, with vi-) and kāma; the infinitive is missing its final -ṃ. Feminine nominative singular in the text, agreeing with sā.
vicinitukāmā.example_1: Sā pañcavidhapadumasañchannaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ disvā nhāyitukāmā paricārikāhi saddhiṃ pokkharaṇiṃ otaritvā kīḷantī taṃ padumaṃ disvā vicinitukāmā hatthaṃ pasāresi.
vicinitukāmā.translation_1: She, seeing the pond covered with five kinds of lotuses, desiring to bathe, descended into the pond with her attendants. While playing, she saw that lotus and, desiring to pluck it, stretched out her hand.

āhaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Here āhaṃ is 1st singular, not 3rd; context 'ajjeva gamissāmī ti āhaṃ' shows it is the queen speaking: 'I said'. Alternative analysis as āha (3rd sg) is ruled out by the 1st-person -ṃ; compare āhaṃ = āha + aṃ, a perfect/parokkha form of √brū. The root list allows only 'brūti pr' for its pattern-like form, though this is a perfect (perf) headword in DPD.
āhaṃ.example_1: Sā saññaṃ paṭilabhitvā ‘‘ kusarājā kira maṃ hatthe gaṇhi, imināvāhaṃ hatthisālāya hatthichakaṇapiṇḍena, assasālāya assachakaṇapiṇḍena pahaṭā, ayameva maṃ hatthissa pacchimāsane nisīditvā uppaṇḍesi, kiṃ me evarūpena dummukhena patinā, imaṃ jahitvā ahaṃ jīvantī aññaṃ patiṃ labhissāmī ’’ ti cintetvā attanā saddhiṃ āgate amacce pakkosāpetvā ‘‘ mama yānavāhanaṃ sajjaṃ karotha, ajjeva gamissāmī ’’ ti āhaṃ.
āhaṃ.translation_1: She, upon obtaining consciousness, thought, “King Kusa, they say, seized my hand! This very one struck me in the elephant stable with a lump of elephant dung, and in the horse stable with a lump of horse dung. This very one, sitting in the back seat of the elephant, mocked me. What good is such an ugly-faced husband to me? If I live, having abandoned him, I shall obtain another husband!” Having thought this, she had the ministers who had come with her summoned, and said, “Make my vehicles and conveyances ready; today I shall go!”

suvaṇṇakaroṭiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text. karoṭi is a vessel or bowl; suvaṇṇa- 'golden'. PEU glosses it as 'golden box or casket', but the context is filling it with food.
suvaṇṇakaroṭiṃ.example_1: Sā tassa kathaṃ sutvā ‘‘ tena hi, tāta, appamatto bhaveyyāsi, mātugāmo nāma aparisuddhahadayo ’’ ti vatvā nānaggarasabhojanassa suvaṇṇakaroṭiṃ pūretvā ‘‘ idaṃ antarāmagge bhuñjeyyāsī ’’ ti vatvā uyyojesi.
suvaṇṇakaroṭiṃ.translation_1: She, having heard his words, said, “Then, dear child, you should be diligent, for women, indeed, have impure hearts.” And having filled a golden bowl with all kinds of excellent savory food, she said, “You should eat this on the way,” and dismissed him.

bhattakaroṭiyā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental singular bhattakaroṭiyā in the text. PEU splits as tatta + karoṭi; bhatta (rice; food) is more likely here.
bhattakaroṭiyā.example_1: So taṃ ādāya mātaraṃ vanditvā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā ‘‘ jīvanto puna tumhe passissāmī ’’ ti vatvā sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā pañcāvudhaṃ sannayhitvā bhattakaroṭiyā saddhiṃ kahāpaṇasahassaṃ pasibbake katvā kokanudañca vīṇaṃ ādāya nagarā nikkhamitvā maggaṃ paṭipajjitvā mahabbalo mahāthāmo yāva majjhanhikā paṇṇāsa yojanāni gantvā bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā sesadivasabhāgena puna paṇṇāsa yojanāni gantvā ekāheneva yojanasatikaṃ maggaṃ khepetvā sāyanhasamaye nhatvā sāgalanagaraṃ pāvisi.
bhattakaroṭiyā.translation_1: He, taking that, venerated his mother and circumambulated her three times, saying, “If I live, I will see you again.” He then entered the royal closet, girded on the five weapons, and putting a thousand kahāpaṇas into a bag together with the food bowl, took the Kokanuda lute and departed from the city. Proceeding on his way, being of great strength and great power, he traveled fifty leagues until midday. Having eaten his meal, he again traveled fifty leagues in the remaining part of the day, thus completing a hundred-league journey in a single day. In the evening, having bathed, he entered Sāgala City.
bhattakaroṭiyā.example_2: So tuṭṭho tassā saddhiṃ bhattakaroṭiyā kahāpaṇasahassaṃ adāsi.
bhattakaroṭiyā.translation_2: He, pleased, gave her a thousand kahāpaṇas along with the food bowl.

umhayamānā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The form is a present participle used in the feminine nominative singular; the ending -amānā is declined to agree with the feminine subject. The commentary glosses it with hasamānā, confirming the sense.
umhayamānā.translation_1: 11. “When the princess looks at me, smiling—
umhayamānā.translation_2: ‘Smiling’ means: displaying a cheerful demeanor, smiling.

nāḷāriko.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Nominative singular agreeing with the speaker in the verse: 'I was the cook then'. The reading nāḷāriko may be nāḷandāyako in some editions; a cook, a kitchen servant.
nāḷāriko.example_1: Nāḷāriko tadā homi, rājā homi tadā kuso ’’ ti.
nāḷāriko.translation_1: then I am not a cook; then I am King Kusa.”

umhayamānāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form is umhayamānāti = umhayamānā + iti, sandhi with the quotation particle; quoted form of the feminine nominative singular. The root is uncertain; the PEU suggests umhi.

umhāyeyya.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Optative 3rd singular in the text (umhāyeyya), from the causative stem umhāya. The prefix u- is unusual; also written as umhayati.
umhāyeyya.translation_1: if Pabhāvatī, with arms like an elephant’s trunk, would smile faintly at me.”

upasamphuseti.meaning_2: touches; makes contact (with); comes into contact (with)
upasamphuseti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text has the optative upasamphuseyya (3rd singular), formed from this present stem; causative upasamphuseti is also possible depending on context.

umhāyeyyāti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Optative 2nd singular with -ti quotation ending (umhāyeyyāti = umhāyeyya + iti); the main word is umhāyeyya, optative of the causative umhāyati. Uncertain reconstruction; possibly connected with √ud (be wet).

kaṇḍuyitvā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Absolutive in -itvā of a denominative/causative verb from kaṇḍu (itch); the text has thokaṃ kaṇḍuyitvā 'having scratched a little'. Possibly a by-form of kaṇḍūvati; PEU analysis as causative is uncertain.
kaṇḍuyitvā.example_1: Sā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā ‘‘ gacchatha tumhe, deva, katipāhaccayena naṃ tumhākaṃ vase karissāmi, passatha me parakkaman ’’ ti vatvā taṃ karaṇīyaṃ tīretvā pabhāvatiyā santikaṃ gantvā tassā vasanagabbhaṃ sodhentī viya paharaṇayoggaṃ leḍḍukhaṇḍampi asesetvā antamaso pādukāpi nīharitvā sakalagabbhaṃ sammajjitvā gabbhadvāre ummāraṃ antaraṃ katvā uccāsanaṃ paññapetvā pabhāvatiyā ekaṃ nīcapīṭhakaṃ attharitvā ‘‘ ehi, amma, sīse te ūkā vicinissāmī ’’ ti taṃ tattha pīṭhake nisīdāpetvā attano ūruantare tassā sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā thokaṃ kaṇḍuyitvā ‘‘ aho imissā sīse bahū ūkā ’’ ti sakasīsato ūkā gahetvā tassā hatthe ṭhapetvā ‘‘ passa kittakā te sīse ūkā ’’ ti piyakathaṃ kathetvā mahāsattassa guṇaṃ kathentī gāthamāha –
kaṇḍuyitvā.translation_1: Hearing his words, she said, “Go, my lord. After a few days, I will bring her under your power. See my prowess!” Having said this, she completed that task and went to Pabhāvatī’s presence. As if cleaning her living chamber, she removed even a clod of earth fit for striking, not leaving any remainder, and even removed her shoes. Having swept the entire chamber, she arranged a high seat in the chamber doorway, making a division at the threshold. She spread out a low stool for Pabhāvatī and said, “Come, mother, I will search for lice on your head.” Having made her sit on that stool and placed Pabhāvatī’s head on her own lap, she scratched it a little and then, saying, “Oh! There are many lice on her head!” she took some lice from her own head, placed them in Pabhāvatī’s hand, and said, “See how many lice are on your head!” Having spoken these endearing words, she, explaining the Great Being’s virtues, uttered the verse—

āviñcanarajjuṃ.meaning_2: pulling rope; rope used for drawing (a cart)
āviñcanarajjuṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular in the text; the rope held by the hunchback (khujjā). āviñcana is probably a pulling/drawing implement from √viñc? not in the root list.
āviñcanarajjuṃ.example_1: Atha khujjā āviñcanarajjuṃ gahetvā ṭhitāva ‘‘ nippaññe dubbinīte tava rūpaṃ kiṃ karissati, kiṃ mayaṃ tava rūpaṃ khāditvā yāpessāmā ’’ ti vatvā terasahi gāthāhi bodhisattassa guṇaṃ pakāsentī khujjāgajjitaṃ nāma gajji –
āviñcanarajjuṃ.translation_1: Then the hunchback, holding the pulling-rope, stood there and said, “You witless, ill-behaved girl, what use will your beauty be? Will we subsist by eating your beauty?” Having said this, she, proclaiming the Bodhisatta’s virtues in thirteen verses, roared what is called the ‘Hunchback’s Roar’—

pamini.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 2nd singular of a compound verb (pamāṇaṃ + gaṇhāti); the text glosses it with pamāṇaṃ gaṇhi. The form is also used for the 3rd singular.
pamini.example_1: Tattha mā naṃ rūpena pāmesi , ārohena , pabhāvatīti are pabhāvati, mā tvaṃ etaṃ kusanarindaṃ attano rūpena ārohapariṇāhena pamini, evaṃ pamāṇaṃ gaṇhi.
pamini.translation_1: Regarding the verses “Do not compare him by his appearance, Pabhāvatī, by his stature”: “Hey Pabhāvatī, you should not measure this King Kusa by his appearance or by his stature and girth. Do not make such a judgment.”

suvaṇṇakhacitakoseyyanivasanā.meaning_2: wearing silk garments adorned with gold
suvaṇṇakhacitakoseyyanivasanā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Explains koseyyavāsinī in the text; feminine form -nivasanā agreeing with the subject.
suvaṇṇakhacitakoseyyanivasanā.translation_1: Clothed in silk (koseyyavāsinī) means wearing silk clothing adorned with gold.

kakkūpanisevitaṃ.meaning_2: smeared with cosmetic powder; anointed with make-up powder
kakkūpanisevitaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Accusative singular agreeing with mukhaṃ. The first member is probably kakka (cosmetic powder), possibly with sandhi of final -a to -ū before upa-. The PEU splits it as kakka + upanisevita; the commentary glosses it as made-up powder.
kakkūpanisevitaṃ.translation_1: 37. “Surely, this face of mine, constantly anointed with perfumed powders, looked at in a mirror fixed on an ivory handle;

mātūva.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of mātu (genitive/dative of mātar, 'mother') + iva ('like'). The simile is mātūva putto, 'like a mother's son'. The final -u is shortened before iva.
mātūva.example_1: Thanesu me lambissati siṅgālo, mātūva putto taruṇo tanūjo.
mātūva.translation_1: —a jackal will surely suckle at my breasts, just as a mother’s own young son would.

khattiyehī.meaning_2: noble; warrior; member of the ruling caste
khattiyehī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Instrumental plural in the text: 'by the nobles'. Used here in the sense of rulers or warriors who abandon a body in the forest.
khattiyehī.example_1: Chinnaṃ vane khattiyehī avatthaṃ, siṅgālasaṅghā parikaḍḍhissanti.
khattiyehī.translation_1: —cut and abandoned in the forest by the nobles, packs of jackals will surely drag it away.

kakkūpanisevitantila.meaning_2: sesame anointed with the five kakka powders; sesame perfumed with the kakka-powder mixture
kakkūpanisevitantila.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Bahubbīhi compound, the word commented on in the Jātaka prose; the gloss explains kakkūpanisevita as smeared with five powders (mustard, salt, clay, sesame, turmeric). Text kakkūpanisevitantila; the comment resolves it as kakkūpanisevitaṃ.
kakkūpanisevitantila.example_1: Tattha kakkūpanisevitantila kakkūpanisevitanti sāsapakakkaloṇakakkamattikakakkatilakakkahaliddikakkamukhacuṇṇakehi imehi pañcahi kakkehi upanisevitaṃ.
kakkūpanisevitantila.translation_1: Therein, constantly anointed with perfumed powders (kakkūpanisevitaṃ) means constantly anointed with these five face powders: mustard powder, salt powder, clay powder, sesame powder, and turmeric powder.

kakkūpanisevitanti.meaning_2: smeared with cosmetic powder; using make-up powder
kakkūpanisevitanti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The text form kakkūpanisevitanti is the compound plus the quotative particle ti, which is not part of the entry. Possible alternative split kakka + upanisevita; the PEU gives kakku.

upanisevitaṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Paṭhamā-ekavacanaṃ (nominative singular) kakkūpanisevitantila padassa vivaraṇe āgataṃ, taṃ 'kakkehi upanisevitaṃ' evaṃ dissati. Kammavācī (passive) past participle (bhūtakālika kammavatthuka).
upanisevitaṃ.example_1: Tattha kakkūpanisevitantila kakkūpanisevitanti sāsapakakkaloṇakakkamattikakakkatilakakkahaliddikakkamukhacuṇṇakehi imehi pañcahi kakkehi upanisevitaṃ.
upanisevitaṃ.translation_1: Therein, constantly anointed with perfumed powders (kakkūpanisevitaṃ) means constantly anointed with these five face powders: mustard powder, salt powder, clay powder, sesame powder, and turmeric powder.

mayiṃ.meaning_2: in me; towards me; on me; in me (as an object of attachment)
mayiṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Locative singular of the first person pronoun (amhaṃ) often printed as mayiṃ. In the sentence mayiṃ paṭibaddhacittā means 'with minds bound to me'.
mayiṃ.example_1: Sace maṃsāni hariṃsūti amma sace te khattiyā mayiṃ paṭibaddhacittā mama maṃsāni hareyyuṃ, atha tumhe aṭṭhīni yācitvā anupathe dahāthanaṃ , jaṅghamaggamahāmaggānaṃ antare daheyyāthāti vadati.
mayiṃ.translation_1: ‘If (they) carry off (my) flesh’ (sace maṃsāni hariṃsu) means: Mother, if those nobles, with minds bound to me, were to carry off my flesh, then you, having asked for the bones, should cremate them. ‘Cremate it alongside the path’ (anupathe dahāthanaṃ) means you should cremate it between the footpaths and the main roads, she says.

udaṭṭhāsi.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Aorist 3rd singular of uṭṭhāti, with ud- assimilated to uṭ-. The PEU splits it as ud + ṭhā + ī; the text has the aorist udaṭṭhāsi and the subject is 'her mother'.
udaṭṭhāsi.translation_1: 45. “Her mother arose, a Khattiya lady like a goddess;

udaṭṭhāsīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The quote (it) is to be removed; the word is uṭṭhāsi, the aorist 3rd singular of uṭṭhāti, used here in the sense of udaṭṭhāsi (rose up from a sitting posture).

uparodati.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Appears in a verse (Ja comm); the exact sense is uncertain, possibly 'cries' or 'sings'. Present 3rd singular.
uparodati.example_1: 51. ‘‘ Asso ca sisati dvāre, kumāro uparodati;
uparodati.translation_1: 51. “And a horse neighs at the door, a young man performs;

sisatīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] -ti is the quotation marker joined to the verb; the reading sisatīti = sisati + iti. The PEU entry gives two senses, laughs and afflicts, with an uncertain derivation.

uparodatīti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] The word in the text is uparodati with the quotation particle -ti attached; the entry is for the verb alone. PEU glosses it as 'cries; plays and sings'.

paṭippharantī.meaning_2: resounding; echoing back; striking against; opposing
paṭippharantī.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Feminine present participle in the text, nominative singular agreeing with a feminine subject. The simplex √phar means 'suffuse, pervade'; with paṭi- the sense is 'to resound back, echo'. The commentary glosses it with paṭippharantī viya, 'as if echoing/resounding'.
paṭippharantī.example_1: Kokilābhinikūjiteti kusarājakule sāyaṃ pāto pavattanaccagītavāditūpahāraṃ paṭippharantī viya kokilehi abhinikūjite.
paṭippharantī.translation_1: Resounding with the cuckoo’s call (Kokilābhinikūjite) means resounding with cuckoos, as if it contrasts with the constant offerings of dancing, singing, and instrumental music, morning and evening, in Kusa’s royal family.

soḷārapaññāṇo.meaning_2: of great wisdom; possessing abundant knowledge
soḷārapaññāṇo.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Variant of uḷārapaññāṇa (soḷāra = saha + uḷāra); the commentary glosses it uḷārapañño. Nominative singular in the text, used of Kusa.
soḷārapaññāṇo.example_1: Kuso soḷārapaññāṇo, yo no dukkhā pamocaye ’’ ti.
soḷārapaññāṇo.translation_1: Kusa, of great wisdom, who would free us from suffering?”
soḷārapaññāṇo.translation_2: In this regard, of great wisdom (soḷārapaññāṇo) means of expansive wisdom.

soḷārapaññāṇoti.meaning_2: possessing abundant wisdom, it is said; "one of vast knowledge", it is said
soḷārapaññāṇoti.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Sandhi of soḷārapaññāṇo (nominative singular of the adjective soḷārapaññāṇa, itself saha + uḷāra + paññāṇa) with the quotative ti. Glossed in the commentary as uḷārapañño. The PEU treats it as a single adjective.

asambhitā.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In the text nominative singular feminine modifying an implied 'she'. The PEU entry asambhinna (na + sambhinna) is a different word with a different meaning; asambhitā is from na + sambhita, negating sambhita 'frightened, alarmed'.
asambhitā.example_1: Athassā mātā ‘‘ ayaṃ asambhitā kathaṃ katheti, addhā evametan ’’ ti saddahitvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā tamatthaṃ ārocesi.
asambhitā.translation_1: Then her mother, having believed, “This one speaks fearlessly; it is surely so,” having gone to the king’s presence, reported that matter.

vikuddho.meaning_2: not angry; free from anger; devoid of wrath
vikuddho.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] In these sentences vikuddho is glossed as nikkopo, so the vi- here is privative ('not angry'), not intensive. Nominative singular masculine in the text.
vikuddho.example_1: Vikuddho tyasmi kalyāṇi, mā tvaṃ bhāyi pabhāvati.
vikuddho.translation_1: Lovely lady Pabhāvatī, I am not angry with you; do not fear.
vikuddho.translation_2: Vikuddho tyasmī means, “I am not angry, free from wrath, towards you.”

nayituṃ.meaning_2: to bring; to lead; to take
nayituṃ.comment: [deepseek: deepseek-v4-flash] Infinitive in -ituṃ of neti (caus of √nī). The commentary glosses it with netuṃ. Used with taṃ (Pabhāvatī) as object: 'to bring her'.
nayituṃ.example_1: Bahuṃ maddakulaṃ hantvā, nayituṃ taṃ pabhāvatī ’’ ti.
